title: Pumpkin is good year-round, not just the fall
content:
Pumpkin is good year-round, not just the fall

 October 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 4A | Section: News 
 
 1077
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Signs of fall are everywhere. and the great pumpkin seems to be leading the way in decorating, drink flavors and recipes. Today I have some new and old pumpkin recipes for you to try. And yes, my pumpkins are displayed outside accompanied by several fall mums and a fall flag on the pole.Now let's get in the kitchen. The recipe will decide if I use canned pumpkin or a fresh cleaned and chopped pumpkin. I usually use canned pumpkin and keep different size cans in the food pantry for year round baking.Pumpkins are not a seasonal food as in the past. Remember "back in the day" when pumpkin was a Halloween and Thanksgiving food item and mincemeat, and cranberries were all seasonal foods?Most people still do traditional food items for certain holidays, but most of the world now eats what they want when they want.The name pumpkin comes from the Greek word "pepo". meaning "large melon."Pumpkins are a fruit (they contain seeds), but when it comes to cooking, they are often referred to as vegetables. The largest pumpkin ever grown was recorded in 2021 and weighed in at 2,72.9 pounds, over 1.5 billion pounds of pumpkin are produced every year. Give this family favorite a try.PUMPKIN PANCAKESWhisk 1/4 cup pumpkin puree with 1 egg until smooth. Add in 1 cup milk, 1 cup flour, 1 tablespoon sugar, 2 teaspoons baking powder, 1 teaspoon cinnamon, 1/2 teaspoon pumpkin pie spice and a pinch of nutmeg. Whisk all ingredients together until real smooth. Using a large spoon drop batter onto a hot greased griddle or fry pan and cook on both sides until done. serve hot with butter and syrup.BROWN SUGAR PUMPKIN SPICE PUMPKIN SEEDS2 cups raw pumpkin seeds (from 1 large pumpkin), 1/4 cup dark brown sugar, 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted, 2 teaspoons pumpkin pie spice, pinch of kosher salt. Preheat the oven to 300 degrees F.Place the pumpkin seeds in a colander and rinse away all the pulp and stringy stuff.Spread the seeds out on a rimmed baking sheet and roast until dried out, 30 to 45 minutes.Toss the pumpkin seeds with the sugar, butter, pumpkin pie spice and salt in a medium bowl until evenly coated. Return the seeds to the baking sheet, spread them out and roast until dry, about 35 minutes. Let cool, then break up into pieces before serving.BARBECUE PUMPKIN SEEDS1 pumpkin, Olive oil for tossing, Kosher salt, Brown sugar, Chipotle chile powder, ground cumin. Preheat the oven to 300¢ª F.Using a spoon, scrape the pulp and seeds out of your pumpkin into a bowl. Separate the seeds from the stringy pump, rinse the seeds in a colander under cold water, then shake dry. Don't blot with paper towels; the seeds will stick. Spread the seeds in a single layer on an oiled baking sheet and roast for 30 minutes to dry them out. Toss the seeds with olive oil, salt, brown sugar, chile powder and cumin. Return to the oven and bake until crisp and golden, about 20 more minutes.BAKED PUMPKIN DOUGHNUTS2 cups all-purpose flour, 2 teaspoons pumpkin pie spice, 2 teaspoons baking powder, 1 teaspoon kosher salt, one 15-ounce can pumpkin puree, 1 1/2 cups sugar, 1/3 cup vegetable oil, 4 tablespoons (1/2 stick) unsalted butter, melted, 1 teaspoon vanilla extract, 3 large eggs.TOPPING: 3/4 cup sugar, 2 teaspoons ground cinnamon, 3 tablespoons unsalted butter melted. For the doughnuts: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Whisk the flour, pumpkin pie spice, baking powder and salt together in a medium bowl. Beat the pumpkin puree, sugar, vegetable oil, butter, vanilla and eggs and together in another large bowl until smooth. Add the flour mixture to the pumpkin mixture and beat until just combined. Fill three 6-cup nonstick doughnut pans with the batter so that each mold is almost full. Smooth the tops with a moistened finger.Bake the doughnuts until a wooden pick inserted into the center comes out clean, about 15 minutes. Invert the doughnuts onto a cooling rack. For the topping: Stir the sugar and cinnamon together in a shallow bowl. Working one at a time, brush the doughnuts all over with butter, then dip them in the cinnamon sugar to coat. Serve warm or at room temperature.PUMPKIN PIE PARFAITS13 gingersnaps, chocolate wafers or graham crackers, 1 tablespoon unsalted butter, melted, 3/4 cup plus 1 tablespoon confectioners' sugar, 1/2 cup canned pure pumpkin, 2 1/2 teaspoons bourbon, pinch of freshly grated nutmeg, 1/2 cup white chocolate chips, 2 cups cold heavy cream.Put seven cookies in a resealable plastic bag and crush into crumbs with a heavy pan. Brush the bottoms and about 1 inch up the sides of six parfait glasses with the butter. Add a spoonful of crumbs to each and roll them around the insides of the glasses; pour out the excess crumbs and reserve for topping. Refrigerate the prepared glasses.Put 3/4 cup confectioners' sugar, the pumpkin, 1 1/2 teaspoons bourbon and the nutmeg in a food processor. Pulse until smooth, about 1 minute. Put the white chocolate chips in a microwave-safe bowl and microwave at 50% power until melted, about 1 minute, stirring halfway. Add to the pumpkin mixture and process until combined.Transfer to a large bowl. Beat 1/12 cups cream in a bowl with a mixer until soft peaks form; fold into the pumpkin mixture until smooth. Divide among the prepared glasses and refrigerate until ready to serve.Beat the remaining 1/2 cup cream with a mixer until foamy. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon confectioners' sugar and 1 teaspoon bourbon and beat until soft peaks form. Top the parfaits with the whipped cream, reserved cookie crumbs and the remaining six cookies.This next recipe is one of my daughter in law Shannon, and has become one our families favorites, plus it is healthy.PUMPKIN SPICE PROTEIN MUFFINS WITH BUTTERSCOTCH CHIPS1 cup old fashioned rolled oats, 1 cup pumpkin puree, 1 cup Greek yogurt, 2 large eggs, 1/2 packed cup vanilla flavored protein powder, 1 tablespoon pumpkin pie spice, 1 teaspoon cinnamon, 1 teaspoon baking powder, 1/2 teaspoon baking soda, pinch of sea salt, 1/2 cup butterscotch chips. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F.Add the oats to a blender or food processor and process until a flour forms (15-20 seconds). Add the pumpkin, Greek yogurt, eggs, protein powder, pumpkin pie spice, cinnamon, baking powder, baking soda and salt and blend again until well combined.Stir in the butterscotch chips. Pour into 12 greased muffin liners. Bake for 25-30 minutes or until a toothpick comes out clean. 25 minutes will be a little moist while 30 minutes won't be as moist. Enjoy.

title: Adkins Arboretum fills with fairies for festival
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Adkins Arboretum fills with fairies for festival

 October 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY - Toadstools, unicorns and pixies all passed by the fairy king and queen, who sat in thrones and held scepters.Adkins Arboretum had its annual Fairyfest in a light rain on Oct. 7. The soft rain dampened no one's spirits as live music filled the pavillion and crafts were made in the main building. Drawing inspiration from pre-Christian Great Britain and the Celts, the woods were alive with magic fairy houses.In past years Adkins has been overrun with fairy fans, so now they put a cap on how many can attend. Even with that they had over 500 people attend. There were food trucks including Scottish Highland Creamery. The musical talent included Ampersand and Allegra Choir, who gave some rich harmonic a cappella singing.There was even belly dancing put on by the Sammati Dance Troupe.Little children with unicorn hats got to ride horses with their grandparents and parents closely monitoring the journey. A lot of the festival is geared toward little girls. They are perfectly suited for this kind of magic.Jenny Houghton is the assistant director at Adkins, but today goes by "Queen Fairy." She has monarch butterfly wings to match her braided red hair.She said, "Fairfest was my brain child. I came up with it about eight years ago, and it has become our most well attended event.We are sold out today at over 400. Our first year we had over 700 but realized we didn't have enough parking." She focused on Adkins' mission and how it fits well with the event."It is just a fun day getting kids outside in nature and helping them realize how magical it is. We had a lot of 4 to 6 year olds, but that said we are seeing older kids. We have a lot of teen volunteers who enjoy it as much as the kids. It is with our mission, which is to create exceptional experiences outside," Houghton said.There is a bridge that serves as an entrance to Adkins. All along the walkway there were ornate floral structures built by sponsor Chesapeake Blooms.One aspect of the event is a collection of fairy houses that are placed along a woodland path.This year six people were recognized for their building efforts. They are: Cristina Swaine, Dawn Folmer, Sheri Lynch, Clara Terry, Connie Schroth and Nancy Bennington.Charlotte Reyes, 6, of Cambridge was getting face painting. title: Forging a Path - 20 years after the publication of 'Purple Hibiscus,' a generation of African writers have followed in Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's footsteps
author: Simon Lewis; College Of Charleston The Conversation
content:
Forging a Path - 20 years after the publication of 'Purple Hibiscus,' a generation of African writers have followed in Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's footsteps

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Simon Lewis; College Of Charleston The Conversation | Page: 6A | Section: News 
 
 1269
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Twenty years ago, in October 2003, 26-year-old Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie burst onto the North American publishing scene with her debut novel," Purple Hibiscus." Since then, Adichie's literary fame has only grown: She's published two more novels and a collection of short stories, while two of herTED talks have garnered tens of millions of views. In September 2023, she published her first children's book - a joyful celebration of mother-daughter love - under the nom de plume Nwa GraceJames.But the October 2003 publication of "Purple Hibiscus" didn't just signal the start of a single author's brilliant career. It also forged a path for a whole new generation of African novelists who had come to America as immigrants or students and who have been mining that experience in their writing.The struggles to get published by prior generations of African authors are almost legendary.Thirty years apart, Chinua Achebe and Tsitsi Dangarembga have both described how close their manuscripts of "Things Fall Apart" (1958) and "Nervous Conditions" (1988) came to being lost. Achebe's only copy of the manuscript was a handwritten draft. He sent it to a typing agency in London that nearly dismissed it as a joke. Dangarembga's manuscript sat unread in the basement of a British publishing house for years. Only when the writer stopped by the offices during a work trip to London did the editors agree to read it.Through attending American MFA programs, however, Adichie and her contemporaries were able to tap into the networks of agents and found their work snapped up by American publishers.Writers born in Africa who studied at American universities - Teju Cole, Yaa Gyasi, Uzodinma Iweala, NoViolet Bulawayo and Akwaeke Emezi, to name just a few - have followed in Adichie's footsteps."Purple Hibiscus" has been to these writers what Gabriel García Márquez's "One Hundred Years of Solitude" (1967) was to aspiring Latin American writers during the Latin American literary boom of the 1960s and 1970s, and what Salman Rushdie's "Midnight's Children" (1981) was to the proliferation of Indian writers in English from the 1980s on.While it would be reassuring to think that the current surge of African novelists represents a wider American interest in all things African, the success of these novels may also have to do with the fact that so many are actually set in the U.S.The recurrent theme of immigration to the U.S. gives many of these works direct - and instructive - relevance to U.S. readers. As Black outsiders in the U.S., African immigrants have a particularly acute insight into the way race and racism affect daily life in this country.One of the common features of these novels is the way in which they explore the tension of racial solidarity and mutual misunderstanding between African immigrants and Black Americans.When I first started teaching African literature, I often had difficulty finding books in print. Now my problem is deciding who to leave out of my syllabus. Here is a very brief list of some of the books that I would consider must-reads.1. Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, "Americanah" (2013) As its title suggests, Adichie's fourth novel, "Americanah," is arguably the definitive novel of contemporary African immigration to America.It tells the story of Ifemelu, a young Nigerian woman overstaying her student visa, and how she negotiates the new Black identity forced on her by the blunt instrument of American race-construction.In a brilliant metafictional move, Adichie has Ifemelu achieve internet fame by writing a blog dedicated to non-American Blacks: "Dear Non-American Black," Ifemelu writes, "when you make the choice to come to America, you become black. Stop arguing. Stop saying I'm Jamaican or I'm Ghanaian.America doesn't care. So what if you weren't 'black' in your country?You're in America now." Ifemelu's experience of racism is simultaneously hurtful and baffling to her. On the one hand, her illegal status makes her both psychologically and physically vulnerable. But at times American racism is almost comical; Ifemelu doesn't understand why an innocent reference to eating watermelon might be misconstrued, for instance, and she is totally bewildered by a shop assistant's attempt to avoid distinguishing between two shoppers by reference to their skin color.2. Yaa Gyasi, "Homegoing" (2016)Ghanaian-born Yaa Gyasi's debut novel takes the form of a series of skillfully interwoven stories set on either side of the Atlantic.Beginning with two half sisters, Effia and Esi, in the Gold Coast in the middle of the 18th century, the stories trace the two sets of the sisters' descendants through six subsequent generations in West Africa and the U.S. In the final two stories we meet the young teenager Marjorie, who, as the Americanborn daughter of Ghanaian parents, struggles to come to terms with her identity as one of Ifemelu's "Non-American Blacks." She finds herself ostracized by her Black classmates for "acting white" but is unable to enjoy a normal relationship with a white classmate. One of the only Black teachers at her high school tells her, "You're here now, and here black is black is black." 3. NoViolet Bulawayo, "We Need New Names" (2013)When "We Need New Names" appeared, Nigerian novelist Helon Habila accused NoViolet Bulawayo of peddling "poverty-porn" by pandering to American stereotypes of Africa.However, for Bulawayo's teenage protagonist Darling, it's American culture that is dangerously dysfunctional - and personally discombobulating. Darling finds American high school ridiculously easy, is horrified by the laxness of American parenting and is generally unimpressed by the urban blight she sees around her in the city she calls Destroyed, Michigan.Late in the novel, her mentally ill countryman Tshaka Zulu is shot to death by police when off his meds and ranting in his home language.You might think that such a violent, tragic event would be a major plot driver. Sadly, it seems to exemplify just one more random peril - little different from being hit by a car or struck down by cancer - that many Africans coming to America have to endure.4. Uzodinma Iweala, "Speak No Evil" (2018) Even wealth and class status offer no protection from such perils.In Uzodinma Iweala's "Speak No Evil," the main character, Niru, is the high-achieving son of high-achieving Nigerian parents in supposedly cosmopolitan Washington, D.C. The first three-quarters of the book appear to be exploring Niru's dilemma: how to come out as gay to his conservative parents.It turns out that Niru's gayness - an invisible characteristic, after all - is not the problem; his Blackness is. When he gets in a row outside a bar with his best friend, Meredith - an equally well-off, well-connected, high-flying white female classmate - someone calls the cops. In the space of a paragraph the inevitable has happened: Shots are fired. "You're safe," someone says to Meredith."He can't hurt you." By extraordinary coincidence, Adichie grew up in the very house that Chinua Achebe had lived in on the campus of the University of Nigeria in Nsukka.She, and the other writers of her generation, grew up in the house of fiction that Achebe and his generation established. The writers of that older generation were concerned with the material and cultural despoliation of colonialism. In Achebe's words, their task was to let their African readers know "where the rain began to beat" them.Today's African writers demand readers' attention by letting them know that for African and African-descended people in the U.S., although the winds may have shifted, the storm is far from over.Simon Lewis has been teaching African and Third World Literature at the College of Charleston since 1996.  ST. MICHAELS - There was an absence of horses, ferrets and turtles, and there was no presence of even one freaked out cat in a box. Dogs ruled on Sunday October 8, when over 50 were blessed at Christ Church.They strained at their leashes, sniffed around and got in line with their owners to see Rector Steve Mosher, who dressed in a white robe for outside ceremony.A reading from Genesis made God's creative powers known.Mosher read, "Let the waters bring forth swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the dome of the sky God blessed them and said 'Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas and let birds multiply on Earth.'" One at a time Mosher crouched down, touched each animal and gave a blessing.The crowd hung around after the last animal was blessed, enjoying perfect fall weather and their new four-legged friends.

Author takes to the seas with 'The Pirate Series'

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 7A | Section: News

 Maryland author Elizabeth Gagné recently self-published her second book "Evangeline Shores Forever" in July through Amazon Kindle.The book is her second book, and first in The Pirate Series after "Shores of Forever Search for Blackbeard's Treasure" was rewritten and changed to "Evangeline Shores of Forever." The 60-year-old Gagné, who writes under the pen name Bitsey Gagné, graduated from Charles County Community College (now College of Southern Maryland) in 1982 from the licenses practical nurse and registered nurse programs in 1984.Gagné retired in May after a 40-plus year career as a retired nurse in Charles and St. Mary's counties, the last 33 years as a dialysis nurse.Gagné's third book, "Angie's Soulmate," which was released in book and eBook form Sept.21, is available along with the other books at www.amazon.com.How long have you been writing, and how did you get started?I started writing back in 2016 while I was recuperating after having surgery for breast cancer, but I had an idea for this book long before that.What inspires you to write?I visit the Outer Banks in North Carolina several times a year. I love the story about the mystery about what happened to the lost colonists of Roanoke Island. Hence, this is where the idea for my story transpired and blossomed, somehow into the novel that it is now.Do you consider writing to be a career?I consider it my career now after retiring from nursing.What kind of writing process do you use?I used Microsoft word/One Drive initially after I wrote out my document for my first two books but am now just using my laptop.Who are some of your favorite authors and why?Nora Roberts, Diana Gabaldon, Deborah Harkness are three of the authors that I like to read. I enjoy reading and writing romance, paranormal suspense novels.What are you working on now?"Angie's Soulmate" is the sequel to my first book. It's a romance, suspense and paranormal novel about a young country singer who moves to Ocracoke Island and is visited by her ancestor's spirit, Evangeline.Evangeline leaves her with the clues to the whereabouts of Blackbeard's treasure and guides her to her soulmate.And to add a twist, have they stumbled upon what happened to the Lost Colonists of Roanoke Island?Please include a brief description of your book "Evangeline Shores Forever." Angie Harriott, an upcoming country singer/songwriter grew up in a small town called Ripley, Maryland. She spent her summers vacationing on Ocracoke Island listening to tales about Lost Loves and Blackbeard's treasure. After a difficult breakup with her boyfriend and sudden death of her father, she follows her dreams and moves to Ocracoke Island.Angie has always called the island the Shores of Forever, because of its rich and mystical history. She becomes entwined in a mystery and a romance as her new life begins. Evangeline, Angie's long ago ancestor's spirit, roams the shores looking for her lost love. She leaves Angie and her friends clues to the whereabouts of Blackbeard's treasure map and guides Angie to her true love. Angie wonders if there is such a thing as soulmates that can pass from one lifetime to another.

title: Lessons from the heartland - What live theater can learn from Branson, Missouri
author: Joanna Dee Das; Washington University In St. Louis The Conversation
content:
Lessons from the heartland - What live theater can learn from Branson, Missouri

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Joanna Dee Das; Washington University In St. Louis The Conversation | Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 1393
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In summer 2023, the publication American Theatre declared unequivocally that live theater was "in crisis" - particularly regional, nonprofit theaters. Writing for The New York Times, Isaac Butler preferred the phrase "on the verge of collapse." The numbers are stark. Not only have dozens of theaters across the country closed their doors since the COVID-19 pandemic hit in March 2020, but those that are still open have also contracted their seasons massively, producing 40% fewer shows than in 2019.What can regional, nonprofit theaters do to survive?One place to look for ideas is the tourist town of Branson, Missouri.Scholars and theater critics have ignored this mecca of live entertainment that attracts millions of people a year, largely because of its reputation for cheesy performances and political conservatism.I'm a theater and dance historian at Washington University, a liberal arts institution in a city. My politics differ from that of most Branson residents. But that's precisely why I am in the process of writing a book about the town's entertainment industry. In an age of polarization, could I challenge myself to approach the place with an open mind? I expected to feel discomfort; I did not expect to feel envy. In Branson, people really seemed to believe in theater's power.And nowhere more so than at Sight & Sound, a for-profit Christian theater. On a Wednesday afternoon in May 2023, I joined 2,000 other patrons to watch their performance of "Queen Esther," a musical retelling of the biblical story of Hadassah.In "Queen Esther," Hadassah adopts the name Esther and conceals her Jewish identity in order to marry the Persian emperor Xerxes.She faces challenges in the royal court and doubts herself. Eventually, she learns to trust in God that she was "made for such a time as this" and bravely saves the Jewish people from annihilation.The Old Testament story is not as well known as those of Noah or Moses, nor does the musical feature any celebrity performers. Yet approximately eight times a week, 40 weeks a year, Broadway-sized crowds watch "Queen Esther" in a town of 12,000 people in the Ozark Mountains.Embracing the spectacle Sight & Sound's formula is seemingly simple: "spectacle meets story." In one scene of "Queen Esther," over a dozen women in bejeweled gowns twirl with lengthy scarves, turning the stage into a hypnotic, swirling sea of color. In another scene, 45 cast members sing from windows and doorways across a 300-foot-wide set that wraps around three sides to immerse the audience in live surround sound. At several points in the show, Xerxes and his men gallop up the aisles on real horses. Members of the royal court also ride a mechanical, fullsized elephant across the stage.Nonprofit theater has long resisted the siren call of spectacle.For artists who have adopted the theories of cultural critics Theodor Adorno and Max Horkheimer, outlandish, flashy performances reflect cynical pandering to the sensory pleasures of the masses to make money.But spectacle creates an experience that only live performance can offer: a visual, auditory and even - in the case of the horses in "Queen Esther" - olfactory. The effect transports an audience to another world, drawing people off their couches with the promise that they, too, can become part of an experience to remember.While some theater owners are beginning to recognize the value of spectacle, there's another lesson from Sight & Sound: the value of offering hope that seemingly insurmountable obstacles can be overcome.What do audiences really want?In the wake of the commingled disasters of recent years - the COVID-19 pandemic, George Floyd's murder, climate change and an insurrection at the nation's capitol - university dance and theater departments, as well as nonprofit theaters, have changed their mission statements to include social justice as an explicit aim of their programs. They promise productions that confront racism, homophobia and authoritarianism head-on.Musicologist Jake Johnson has written about today's dominant impulse toward "theater to make the present dystopia even more real." But theatergoers have not necessarily responded positively. Since 2020, some audiences and critics have complained that theater is tilting too far toward preachy messages.And when staring out at empty seats, practitioners cannot help but question their faith in theater's power to effect social change.Sight & Sound's success suggests that the problem is less with the message of social justice and more with the approach."Queen Esther" is an ancient story of antisemitism, after all.But as Sight & Sound Chief Creative Officer Josh Enck explained in a 2022 podcast, the shows seek "not just to inform or educate" but "to inspire" - particularly since "inspiration is at the core of who God is." The animatronic elephant lumbering across the stage with a jeweled headdress is not a distraction from the serious business of salvation, but rather a way of unlocking an audience member's sense of awe and wonder.People flock to Branson Sight & Sound is also earnest, a feature that fell out of favor with high-art theater at the dawn of the 21st century, when the sense that everything was fake led to productions that dripped with irony and cynicism.Today's compounding sociopolitical crises have shaken the theater world out of complacency. But in the fierce urgency to confront the world's myriad problems, earnestness is still seen as simplistic, naïve or even duplicitous.Sight & Sound expanded to Branson in 2008 because its earnest approach fit with the town's long-standing entertainment industry, which began back in 1907 with the publication of Harold Bell Wright's wildly popular novel "The Shepherd of the Hills." Tourists flocked to see the real-life inspirations for the characters, and local residents often obliged by performing versions of themselves. In 1959, the Mabe family began performing the Baldknobbers Hillbilly Jamboree to provide nighttime entertainment to tourists who had come to boat and fish during the day.The following year, an outdoor drama based on Wright's novel opened, as did a theme park called Silver Dollar City that recreated an 1880s Ozark village.Over time, dozens of theaters were built, featuring variety shows that combined country, gospel, Broadway tunes, comedy, magic tricks, dance numbers, acrobatics and even animal acts. Musicals that fit Branson's brand of familyfriendly, Christian entertainment also popped up along its strip. Many shows featured singers such as Andy Williams, whose greatest hits had been released decades earlier.Some of Branson's performers didn't qualify as stars at all. "The Shoji Tabuchi Show," arguably the most popular in town during the 1990s, was headlined by a fiddler who had never produced an original hit song or been featured on the radio.Branson performers - whether acrobats or singers or comedians - shared something in common: earnest messages of appreciation for their audiences, whom they greeted in person during intermissions and after shows.Ignoring the sneers In 1991, the Ozark Mountain tourist destination burst onto the national scene when it was featured on "60 Minutes." Reporters from the coasts flocked to the Ozarks in disbelief after the segment aired.Wasn't America supposed to be obsessed with youth and celebrity, not aging or unknown singers? And wasn't earnestness merely hucksterism in disguise to dupe audiences into parting with their hard-earned money?The coastal critics scrambled to come up with the wittiest insults. One called Branson a "cultural penal colony." Another preferred the term "Town of the Living Dead." Even "The Simpsons" couldn't resist piling on.The show went on, undeterred: In 2021, a record-breaking 10 million people came to visit.While not every show has survived the COVID-19 pandemic, clearly some performers are doing something right.Comedians like Stephen Colbert have continued to mock Branson, but live theater is in too much of a crisis to dismiss the town's approach.The town demonstrates that theater can return to the mission of imagining new, better worlds onstage and inviting audiences to join in that mission with them. It can be the stuff of spiritual transcendence - even if it grabs your attention by galloping down the aisle on a horse.Joanna Dee Das is an Assistant Professor in the Performing Arts Department at Washington University in St. Louis.This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article here: https://theconversation.com/what-livetheatercan-learn-from-bransonmissouri-213534. title: Contemporary art galleries to open in Easton
author: Contributed
content:
Contemporary art galleries to open in Easton

 October 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 441
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Two new galleries have joined forces as contemporary art galleries at 5 N. Harrison Street in Easton.Spiralis Gallery, owned by Gail Patterson, features Contemporary Afro-Caribbean art, and The Zebra Gallery, owned by Susan Schauer John, an award-winning local fiber artist.The Spiralis Gallery launched its opening with some of its artwork being featured at the show "Things Fall Together" held at Out of the Fire Restaurant in Easton this past summer.John's fabric art was recently featured at the Smithsonian Craft Show in Washington, DC, and at the Oxford Fine Arts Fair."When I met Susan there was an instant connection. I think we both were searching for a way to bring a fresh perspective to the already wonderful art scene here in Easton," said Patterson "We believe collectors are inspired and informed by having a variety of art to experience, and the sophisticated collector enjoys the challenge of watching emerging artists unfold." "We hope to bring fresh, contemporary art that showcases the talents of remarkable contemporary artists from the area and around the world," John added."We will highlight Afro-Caribbean artists as well as fiber artists, and modern art that are catalysts for experiences and new perspectives." Both Patterson and John say their galleries will be actively involved in community-building with charitable organizations that fit within their mission.The space will have a new show every 10 weeks.A physician and art lover, Patterson launched her original gallery at Art Basel Miami and the Outsider Art Fair in 2012 and 2013. For 10 more years, her demanding medical career forced her to put her art gallery dreams on hold - until now."Afro-Caribbean art has always resonated with me, with its vibrant colors, exquisite patterns, and strong spiritual imagery," she said. "I am drawn inexorably to outsider artists, whose creations come directly from their souls." John has been an artist all her life, gaining inspiration and recognition in many art forms, including woodturning, portraiture and fiber arts.Her work has been exhibited and sold in galleries from Washington, D.C., to San Francisco and she has work in the permanent collection of the White House.Her work features animals, specifically species of birds native to the Chesapeake Bay region.Through fabric collage and creative stitching, she combines abstract and realism."Art is how I see the world, and what I see continues to evolve.This medium puts everything together," said John.The Gallery will be open for the first show, "Woman, Phenomenally," on Oct. 28, with a reception from 4:30 to 7 p.m. and an artist talk at 5 p.m. featuring Ernesto Beckford, a collage artist.A ribbon cutting and official opening will be held on First Friday, Nov. 3, from 4:30 to 7 p.m.

title: Have your wedding on a dime
author: Mary Hunt
content:
Have your wedding on a dime

 October 16, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mary Hunt | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 312
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I get a lot of mail on the subject of weddings - stories of joy and tales of woe, great ideas and even an occasional blooper. In nearly 32 years, I cannot recall a single time I've heard from a bride or groom who wished they'd spent more money on their wedding. The best wedding mail comes from brides who are so happy with their frugal choices they want to share their ideas with others.Our first guest list included everyone we knew.As the list grew (and grew), we realized that would be a really bad idea. Without intending to do so, we got very close to inviting people who would then feel obligated to attend a wedding for people they didn't really know that well. We decided to whittle that list, seeing our wedding as a more intimate event rather than a big everyone-we-know blowout.From where we started, we cut the list by 75%. That was the best decision ever.Our wedding was manageable, affordable and exactly what we wanted - an intimate celebration of joy. - Debbie When I worked in a bridal shop in Florida, we bought all our jewelry, gloves, veils and most headpieces wholesale from Accessory Wholesale in New Orleans. The company's website is open to the public (awnol.com/). For my own wedding, I bought all my bridesmaid's jewelry sets, bracelets, headpieces, gloves and jewelry - all for about $100, including shipping.That site rocks. And I swear this is the same stuff we bought, displayed in our lighted cases on black velvet, and sold for five to eight times the wholesale price.Because this is a wholesale company, there is a minimum order requirement of $75. - Kelly Don't be afraid of asking to borrow. If you know of someone who recently had a wedding, inquire about borrowing some of their stuff.Mary Hunt is the founder of EverydayCheapskate.com, a frugal living blog, and the author of the book "Debt-Proof Living."  "En plein air," a French term that means "in the open air," refers to the practice of painting entire finished artworks outdoors.Where an observer may see only a glimpse of a landscape, an artist sees light and atmosphere, shape and color, subject and form, all combining in a blaze of inspiration that compels the artist to capture it in paint.On Sat., Nov. 4, Adkins Arboretum will host the second annual Plein Air Adkins, a plein air paint-out, exhibit and sale, on the Arboretum grounds.The public is invited to explore the forest, meadows and wetland and observe as artists paint their original works.Artists will begin painting at 10 a.m. At 12:30 p.m., they will bring their completed works to the Visitor's Center for exhibition and judging.The juror is Alison Berry, a painter who exhibits in Maryland and Virginia and has participated and placed in numerous plein air events.Prizes will be awarded for first, second and third places and for honorable mentions. An Artist's Choice Award will also be given.Beltway Bistro, Blue Monkey Street Tacos and Ten Eyck Brewery will have food and drink for sale beginning at 11 a.m., and Fine Times will provide music during the exhibition and sale.All works created during Plein Air Adkins will be for sale during the exhibition.The event is open to any artist who wishes to participate. The artist registration fee is $20, and artists may register in advance or on the day of the event at adkinsarboretum.org. Observers are admitted free of charge.The event will take place in light rain or shine. In the event of heavy rain, it will be rescheduled for Sunday, Nov. 5. For more information, visit adkinsarboretum.org or call 410-634-2847, ext. 100.Plein Air Adkins is sponsored in part by the Caroline County Council of Art, Choptank Electric Cooperative and Unity Landscape Design|Build.

title: Historical Society remembers Walsh, recalls accomplishments
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Historical Society remembers Walsh, recalls accomplishments

 October 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: A1 | Section: News 
 
 508
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - It was an evening of celebrating achievements as well as remembering once again a Caroline County stalwart who contributed much and, with his recent passing, left a huge void.At its annual meeting Oct. 3, the Caroline County Historical Society remembered the achievements and generosity of James Owen Knotts "J.O.K." Walsh, who succumbed to COVID July 13.About 50 members of the society gathered for evening cocktails and hors d'oeuvres at Caroline Country Club.Acting President Charles Andrew welcomed new members and acknowledged local officials, museum docents, leaders of sister historical societies in Preston, Federalsburg and Ridgely, as well as Friends of Linchester Mill.Members renewed the tenure of two directors and elected two more. New on the board are Randolph Moore and Walter Palmer, and staying on are Carolyn Spicher and Jo Ann Staples.With deep ancestral roots in the county, Walsh was elected president of the society in 1987. His mission was to preserve the history, stories and, if possible, structures within the county. Under his leadership, 47 structures were restored, with many serving as tourist destination sites.Treasurer Carolyn Spicher credited Walsh with the solid financial footing of $1.3 million in the treasury.Two donors presented paintings to the society.Caroline native Clarence B. Mollock of Preston brought his 1988 painting of the Mill Dam at Linchester, where he used to swim and fish.Candi Minner of Denton presented a painting of the old Caroline High School by Bill Greenly, a longtime member of the society.Society member Kathy Mackel, Walsh's longtime partner, presented the annual report in a slide show depicting the society's current work projects, including the renovation of the historic Denton Fire House as a heritage center.Diana Lapsley shared memories of Walsh in a tribute that concluded with a suggestion that the center be renamed the JOK Walsh Heritage Center.Calling it "an important legacy," Lapsley said this last project Walsh worked on "is to be an information research center, a meeting place, a further opportunity to illustrate all of the county's rich heritage, and also a place to help visitors and locals to explore, learn about and enjoy all the other Caroline County historical projects." Becoming emotional as she commemorated her friend's legacy, Lapsley said, "I personally thank JOK for his friendship and enthusiasm, tenacity, bravery and generosity, as I know well that, even when busy and under pressure, he would take time to visit, entertain and look after his friends." "My hope is that we will all continue to get the work done that he started," she said. Quoting her granddaughter when she learned of Walsh's passing, Lapsley said, "Who is going to tell the story of Caroline County now?"

title: Oyster Fest Takes Center Stage This Weekend
author: Ted Black; tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Oyster Fest Takes Center Stage This Weekend

 October 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black; tblack@somdnews.com | Page: 8 | Section: News 
 
 762
 Words 

 Read News Document

 While crabs garner the headlines throughout the summer, the 57th annual U.S. Oyster Festival will take place this weekend at the St. Mary's County Fairgrounds on Saturday and Sunday, featuring the National Oyster Cook-Off and the U.S. National Oyster Shucking Competition taking center stage.While the cook-off is a one-day affair, the U.S. National Oyster Shucking Competition will transpire over both days and the winner will earn a berth in the International Oyster Festival in Galway, Ireland, next summer. In fact, last year's winner in Leonardtown, Dan Challet, recently finished ninth in the world title event in Ireland."The national oyster shucking championship brings people from all over the country to compete," said Tari Moore, chairperson for the 2023 U.S. Oyster Festival Committee. "Not only does the winner get a chase prize, they get to compete in the International Championship next September. Best of all, after the competition the contestants give the shucked oysters to anyone nearby interested in eating them."On Saturday, the 44th annual National Oyster Cook-off will highlight the festivities as contestants will be competing for cash prizes in three divisions - Hors d'ouevres, Soups & Stews and Main Dishes. Grand prize for first place is $300, second place will take home $200 and third place will garner $150, although the winners will attain immeasurable bragging rights for the entire year."This festival was started to highlight the importance of the oyster harvest to the entire region and there are so many events surrounding it now that it is really a festive, two-day event," Moore said. "Our oyster cook-off is amazing and we have three of the best judges anywhere judging the event. There are so many great recipes that people prepare and there is such a wide range of them that it really is hard to comprehend."Last year local residents more than held their own in the competitions as Deborah Reynolds ofWaldorf took first place the main dish category, while Ellynne Brice Davis of Leonardtown finished third in that category. Reynolds also took home first place in the Soups & Stews category. Ronna Farley of Montgomery County took first place in the best hors d'oeuvres division and grand prize in the U.S. Oyster Cook-Off competition.Those who attend the oyster cook-Offwill also have ample means of entertainment on each day. On Saturday around the fairgrounds guests can see Professor Horn-Punch &Judy in the show ring, the Chesapeake Mermaid in the auditorium for five different one-hour shows beginning at noon and kids can participate in inflatable rides throughout the day.Each of the two days will also feature plenty of musical entertainment as well. On Saturday, the Blair Ritch Project will perform from 10 to 11 a.m., followed by the Bootleggers from 11:30 .a.m to 12:30 p.m, One Trick Pony from 1 to 2 p.m., Wiskers from 2:30 to 3:30 p.m. and capped by Monkey Business from 4 to 5 p.m. Sunday will feature Bushmill Band from 11 a.m. to noon, Great Expectations from 12:20 to 1:30 p.m., Fast Eddy and the Boyz from 2 to 3 p.m. then ending with Fire from 3:30 to 4:30 p.m.IF YOU GOThe 57th annual U.S. Oyster Festival will take place this Saturday, Oct. 21, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Sunday, Oct. 22, from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. at the St. Mary's County Fairgrounds in Leonardtown. There will also be oyster shucking contests and various acts performing around the fairgrounds each day as well as musical acts in the pavilion on both days.Entry at the gate is $15 each day, although a two-day ticket is available for $20, while kids 10 and under are free. On Saturday, the fairgrounds will also host the 44th annual National Oyster Cook-Off, which includes cash prizes in three different divisions.For more information or to buy tickets in advance, go to www.usoysterfest.com.

Harrison Street in Easton.Spiralis Gallery - which is owned by Gail Patterson and features contemporary Afro-Caribbean art - is partnering with The Zebra Gallery, which is owned by Susan Schauer John, an award-winning local fiber artist.The Spiralis Gallery launched its opening with some of its artwork being featured at Out of the Fire Restaurant in Easton in the summer with the show, "Things Fall Together."Susan John's fabric art was recently featured at the Smithsonian Craft Show in Washington, and at the Oxford Fine Arts Fair in Oxford, Maryland."When I met Susan there was an instant connection. We believe collectors are inspired and informed by having a variety of art to experience, and the sophisticated collector enjoys the challenge of watching emerging artists unfold," said Patterson."I think of a gallery as not just a place to sell art but a physical space where we engage in relevant conversations, build community, and celebrate creativity."John agrees."We hope to bring fresh, contemporary art that showcases the talents of remarkable contemporary artists from the area and around the world. We will highlight Afro-Caribbean artists as well as fiber artists, and modern art that are catalysts for experiences and new perspectives," she said.The collaboration will include social justice components and work with local charitable organizations.The gallery space will have a new show every 10 weeks to keep the content fresh for collectors, the owners said."Afro-Caribbean art has always resonated with me, with its vibrant colors, exquisite patterns, and strong spiritual imagery. And I am drawn inexorably to outsider artists, whose creations come directly from their souls," Patterson said.Patterson previously operated the Art Basel Miami gallery and the Outsider Art Fair. John's work has been featured in galleries in San Francisco and Washington D.C. and has works featured in the permanent art collection of the White House."Art is how I see the world, and what I see continues to evolve. This medium puts everything together," saidThe gallery will be open for the first show, "Woman, Phenomenally," on Oct. 28, with a reception from 4:30 p.m. to 7 p.m. and an artist talk at 5 p.m. featuring Ernesto Beckford, a collage artist. A ribbon cutting and official opening will be held on First Friday, Nov. 3. from 4:30 p.m. to 7 p.m.For more: https://spiral-isgallery.com/and https://www.thezebragallery.

title: Photo talk to explore junction of science and art
author: Contributed
content:
Photo talk to explore junction of science and art

 October 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 9 | Section: News 
 
 278
 Words 

 Read News Document

 If it's the aim of the fine arts to give insight or inspiration, then the scientific image is worthy of consideration as an artistic medium, argues Norm Baker, a professor of pathology and art as applied to medicine at Johns Hopkins University.Baker will be speaking at the Tidewater Camera Club's Nov. 6 meeting, to be held at Unitarian Universalist Church in Easton from 7 to 9 p.m., on the subject, delving into the history of photography as a scientific discipline.Ironically, photography was invented by a scientist and not an artist.It was the scientists who realized the importance of this new and novel process to document and to elucidate their scientific activities. The idea of having objects draw themselves on a plate without the aid of an artist's hand is a concept that is foreign now, but that's exactly how one of the early inventors, William Henry Fox Talbot, described his Calotype process.Baker will make his case on the subject at the meeting, which is free and open to the public. This talk will examine how the context in which a photograph is viewed can have an effect on how the image is interpreted.Baker's photographs are in the permanent collections of more than forty museums, including The Smithsonian, The George Eastman Museum, The American Museum of Natural History, The Nelson-Atkins Museum and The Science Museum in London.He has published 9 books and numerous scientific articles and book chapters.His current traveling exhibition "Hidden Beauty: Exploring The Aesthetics of Medical Science" shows the beauty of medicine and the human body and will be going on a museum tour in 2014-2023. His latest book "Perambulations" was published in 2022 by Man & Lion Press.

title: Making pumpkin puree
author: Mary Hunt
content:
Making pumpkin puree

 October 23, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mary Hunt | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 327
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Hello, fall baking! I can't think of a better way to do that than with fresh, homemade pumpkin puree - the star of the show in so many fall recipes.HOMEMADE PUMPKIN PUREE RECIPEIngredients:2 whole small pumpkins Directions:With a sharp knife, cut off the tops of the pumpkins, right below the stem, and throw that top part into the garbage.Next, cut the pumpkins in half. Scrape the seeds and stringy insides using a big spoon or even an ice cream scoop. Place the seeds in a bowl to roast later (yum!), and toss the pulp and strings into the garbage. Repeat until all the pumpkin halves are cleaned out.Cut each of the halves into a couple of wedges.Lay a piece of parchment paper on a large sheet pan (cookie sheet). Spread out the pumpkin wedges on the pan, skin up or skin down - it doesn't matter. Place the pan in the oven and set to 350 F. Roast for about 45 minutes, or until the pumpkin pieces are fork-tender (very soft). Remove from the oven.Allow the pumpkin pieces to cool sufficiently so that you can handle them safely. Pull or scrape the skin from the pumpkin meat using a knife. Toss the skins into the garbage.Place a few chunks of roasted, skinned pumpkin into a food processor. Pulse small batches of pumpkin until totally smooth. (Add a tablespoon of water if it seems too dry to get it smooth. Too watery? Strain it through a fine mesh strainer to get rid of some of it.) As you complete a batch, pour it into a bowl, then continue until all the pumpkin has been pureed.A blender will work, too, but you may need to add a bit ofwater to produce a smooth puree. No food processor or blender? No worries. You can mash it up with a potato masher, or force it through a potato ricer or even a food mill.Mary Hunt is thefounder ofEverydayCheapskate.com, afrugal living blog, and the author of the book "Debt-Proof Living. title: From Overseas to Arm Sleeves - How Elkton's Massimiano marries art, community and service
author: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com
content:
From Overseas to Arm Sleeves - How Elkton's Massimiano marries art, community and service

 October 24, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1862
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ELKTON - Being, simultaneously, a town commissioner, tattoo artist, band member and military veteran may not be common for many people, but for Rob Massimiano, it is his life."I am grateful to have been able to make a living through my art because I have been an artist since I could walk," Massimiano said. "But I really enjoy being a part of the community and helping my friends and neighbors - I always have." Massimiano, 64, moved from the outskirts of Philadelphia to Elkton at the age of 17 with his mother, younger brother and younger sister in 1976. The family of four settled into a home at Locust Point.Massimiano finished high school at Bohemia Manor and went on to join the Navy in 1979 at age 20.In the Navy, Massimiano served as a Seabee where he operated heavy machinery building infrastructure all over the world for the US military. Massimiano recalled that the most common structures he and his comrades built outside of combat were runways, since they kept getting bombed."In combat, we were digging foxholes for the guys," Massimiano said. "We were in combat like everyday but the bombs never stopped hitting the runways either." One of Massimiano's most memorable moments from his time in service occurred when he was in Beirut where he said he was tasked with constructing underground bases for marines in the desert.His battalion would dig a huge hole, then place shipping containers in the hole before covering the containers with a layer of dirt, sandbags, lumber and chain link fencing.According to Massimiano, the chain link fencing covering the base caused incoming mortar rounds to scatter upon impact rather, than explode downward onto the containers."The fencing worked well because like the runways, those bases were hit several times and the marines were safe," Massimiano said. "It was cool." Between deployments, Massimiano was stationed at his home base in Gulfport, Mississippi. While in Mississippi during his first year in the military, he bought a guitar from a local pawn shop along with a book that he said he used to teach himself how to play guitar.Almost all of Massimiano's free time - prior to, and during his time in the military - was spent drawing.The addition of playing the guitar forced him to divide his free time between playing guitar and creating art which he said he loved."Drawing has occupied much of my time because I have been doing it since I could hold a pencil," Massimiano said. "Picking up a guitar was great because drawing and music all come from the same side of the brain." In 1984, Massimiano, who was 25 at the time, completed his five years of service in the Navy, during which time he received several medals. He recalled that the two he is most proud of are a Combat Action Ribbon from his time spent in combat in Beirut and a Marine Corps Expeditionary Medal that he received for his support of the Marine Corps.Massimiano returned to Elkton in 1985 where he bought the house he still lives in today.For the next year, he worked a variety of construction and heavy machinery jobs while filling his free time with drawing and guitar. Then, in 1986, Massimiano began a tattooing apprenticeship and discovered a new passion."I would frame houses all day and do my apprenticeship all night," Massimiano said. "It was like that for about a year." Massimiano noted that tattooing is the hardest art medium he has ever worked in, which is why he enjoys it so much."I have tried just about all art forms and if you ask any tattoo artist: tattooing is the hardest because you can not mess up," Massimiano said.Later that same year in 1986, Massimiano and his older brother opened a tattoo shop on East Main Street in downtown Elkton.The shop was one of three locations the brothers opened, the other two located over the border in Delaware.Massimiano ran all three locations on his own - changing the name to Tidewater Tattoos - after his brother moved down south.After 18 years at the small shop attached to the back of the Minihanes building in Elkton, and complications with keeping the Delaware locations staffed, Massimiano said he got the idea to consolidate Tidewater's operations to one shop directly across the street from the Elkton location."I was standing in the Elkton shop one day and I saw a for sale sign out front of the spot we currently own and I said, 'you know what, I'm going to close my Delaware shops and bring those artists here' and I've been operating here for 19 years since," Massimiano said.Massimiano runs the shop with his 28 year old son David, who Massimiano says "really keeps the flame under me." "He does great work," Massimiano said. "He is going to be better than me." As a professional tattoo artist, Massimiano is well known for his portraiture, wildlife and Polynesian tribal work. This has not only granted him the opportunity to travel the United States giving seminars on his technique, but he's also served on the board of directors for the National Tattoo Association as well as the board of directors for the Alliance of Professional Tattooists."I am always looking to help and counsel fellow tattoo artists and clients, and even legislation regarding the industry," Massimiano said. "It has been a pleasure of mine." After becoming a fixture in the Elkton community, Massimiano said he was approached by the Elkton Arts Council and asked to serve on the board of directors.Massimiano took the position and served on the board for about six years before moving to serve on the board for the Elkton Alliance.Massimiano said that serving on those boards were great experiences as they helped him better understand the town of Elkton and how he might be able to help move the town forward."There are people who sit back and live their lives and then there's the people who step forward who at least want to try to do the right thing and that's what I have wanted to do since I moved here," Massimiano said.Massimiano spent approximately seven years on the Elkton Alliance's board, balancing his board duties, tattoo shop operations and playing in his band, Plan B, before the passing of former Elkton Commissioner Mary Jo Jablonski in 2019.Jablonski and Massimiano were great friends, as they served on the Alliance board together prior to her becoming a commissioner, Massimiano recalled.Shortly after Jablonski passing, Massimiano paid tribute to his friend by drawing a portrait of her. Copies of the portrait were hung in the Elkton Administration Building and the Elkton Alliance offices.Since Jablonski had passed one year into her four year term as a commissioner, the Elkton Mayor and Commissioners held interviews to find a candidate to fill her position. Massimiano was one of 10 candidates.During the interview process, Massimiano remembers that Commissioner Earl Piner asked him: "if awarded the position as commissioner, what would you do to improve Elkton?" "Instead of trying to buffalo my way through the answer, I told them that I honestly didn't know what I could do because I didn't know what my powers or abilities would be as commissioner and what tools would be at my disposal," Massimiano said. "I said that once I figured it out, I would use every tool available to make Elkton a better place." Massimiano believes he was selected to finish Jabonski's term due to his ability to be honest and admit when he didn't know something."They appreciate my honesty and my ability to admit when I didn't know something, which I have always been that way," Massimiano said.Around the time that he became commissioner, Massimiano was still playing music, but Plan B had fallen apart due to the COVID-19 pandemic.With no band to play in but a passion for music still flourishing, Massimiano began solo performances in 2021. He said he was nervous for his first solo performance at the North East VFW so he brought his son David - who "shreds on the guitar" - and his friend who plays drums to turn the solo act into a band.While Massimiano, his drummer friend Box Turtle Bob and his son David were performing at the VFW, the former bass player from Massimiano's band Plan B walked in and saw the trio of musicians."He had his bass in his car so he grabbed it and got set up and just like that we became a four-piece band," Massimiano said. "We called ourselves The Nightcrawlers and now we are busier than Plan B ever was.The Nightcrawlers primarily play in and around Cecil County, but have gone as far as Newark, Del. and Harford County to perform classic rock.Now balancing his role as a town commissioner, a newly-formed band and Tidewater's ever-busy schedule, Massimiano chose to run for, and win, re-election as commissioner during Elkton's 2022 election - securing his current four year term.As commissioner, Massimiano said he is proud of the annual fishing rodeo he organizes and hosts each year, his part in bringing Southfields to fruition in Elkton and his ability to bring in a local flood control group to help Elkton alleviate flooding issues.Massimiano said he is happy with the direction Elkton is headed and would like to see more growth in the town, especially the arts."Being down here for so long, I have seen Elkton in many different stages," Massimiano said. "When I first came here, downtown Elkton was nice, lots of businesses, quiet, we all knew each other, and it was very nice and clean, and I think we are headed toward that again." Massimiano noted that Elkton is one of Maryland's designated art's districts and that he enjoys the abundance of creativity coming to the town. He aims to continue working with the Elkton Arts Council and the Elkton Alliance to further the town's artistic growth."I love the energy of downtown Elkton and being around other artists of all disciplines," Massimiano said. "We have a lot of artists here and I feel like I am just immersed in it and it is great and I would like to see that momentum continue and for more art to come in." He explained that Elkton's growth will only remain a positive thing in the town if the next generation of leaders are strong.Massimiano said that he hopes to implement a program where the town works with local high schools to get students involved with leadership in the town because "future leaders need to come from somewhere." Massimiano hopes to inspire Elkton town members to do the right thing when no one is looking because those are the acts that move a community forward."I painted the gazebo at the ballfields near Main Street, I pick up bottles when I see them on the sidewalk and I see other people doing the same things, and it is great," Massimiano said. "If there is something that needs to be done, we should do it regardless of if anyone sees us do it because that is the true measure of a good person."

title: CBMM launches new construction buyboat
author: Contributed
content:
CBMM launches new construction buyboat

 October 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 10 | Section: News

 Read News Document

 Bay Maritime Museum's Shipyard has completed its latest project with the launch of the 36-foot Chesapeake Bay buyboat Mr. Dickie.The Shipyard team began work on the new construction build last fall after finishing up its build ofMary-land Dove and worked over the past year under the direction of Shipyard Foreman Jeff Reed to bring the vessel to life.A contract build for owners Grigg and Cindy Mullen of Lexington, Va., Mr. Dickie will be on display later this month at the Sultana Downrigging Festival in Chestertown before returning to dock at CBMM."Grigg provided the opportunity for us to have our Shipyard team do a complete build from start to finish, creating a unique object in a way that realizes Grigg and our dream of a comprehensive construction that allows for public and Shipwright education," said Vice President of Shipyard Operations Christian Cabral. "It's been an incredible experience."The construction of the unique vessel in CBMM's Shipyard offered a glimpse into the past while highlighting the future for a historic style ofvessel vital to the story of the Chesapeake Bay.Buyboats are cross-planked workboats that were traditionally used for hauling oysters from skipjacks to market in season and anything else that needed transporting the rest of the year.Today, there are estimated to be fewer than 30 buyboats that continue to ply the Bay's waters.Mr. Dickie pays homage to the 60-foot buyboat Mundy Point, designed to bring the buyboat look to a scaled-down 36-foot version. It was constructed from heart pine, white oak, Atlantic cedar and western red cedar, and outfitted with a restored late-1930s Buda diesel engine.A retired engineering professor, Grigg Mullen maintained a hands-on role throughout the yearlong construction, working alongside CBMM's Shipyard crew whenever his schedule allowed.He and Cindy were on hand for a CBMM Member Night on Oct. 12 celebrating Mr. Dickie and the Oct. 20 launch for the new buyboat that is named in honor of the late Dickie Whaley, Mullen's neighbor growing up in Queen Anne's County."It's been a wonderful year building Mr. Dickie and working with the Shipyard folks," Mullen said. "Every time there was a decision to make, it was always - if we do it this way, it's going to be better. It's turned out wonderfully."With Mr. Dickie completed, CBMM's Shipyard will stay busy with a variety of projects heading into the winter months, including ongoing work on a pair of buyboats in its historic floating fleet.Winnie Estelle, CBMM's passenger-carrying 1920 buyboat, is amidst a refit that includes the removal, fabrication, and replacement of its structural timbers. 1938 buyboat Choptank is undergoing a final fit out, which involves building out the interior with cabins and heads for expedition-style overnight trips and outfitting it with modern safety equipment and a new rig.Findmore information about CBMM's Shipyard and itsprojects at cbmm.org/ship-yard.

title: Halloween tricks and treats
author: Mabel Savage; Country Cooking
content:
Halloween tricks and treats

 October 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mabel Savage; Country Cooking | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 1211
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Halloween Celebrations have changed through the years, but the fun ofthe young children getting dressed in their favorite attire has not.Attending the school parties and watching the children parade down the halls is priceless. Some towns still hold the annual Halloween parades through the downtown streets, complete with fire trucks, different businesses and clubs with displays, and candy being thrown to the children.The parade ends with Santa getting the early Christmas list from each child in exchange for that candy cane!Trick or treaters love getting lots of candy, which can be purchased at the big name stores by large bags. But for the school parties and other events, everyone loves homemade sweets and treats.My favorite treat to make was always sugar cookies, to which I added a mixture of red and yellow food coloring to reach a light orange color. Just before baking, I would place one candy pumpkin, candy corn or other Halloween candy symbol in the center of the cookie. Use your imagination, and have fun watching the children's faces light up!Today, I will include some of the recipes from years gone by, along with a few new ones.HALLOWEEN FUDGELine an 8 inch square pan with foil and spray with cooking spray. Open one bag - 12 ounce size-Nes-tle Toll House Halloween morsels and separate the orange pieces from the semi-sweet pieces. Starting with the semi-sweet morsels, measure how many were in the separated pile and add enough semi-sweet chips to make 1 1/2 cups total. You will get about 1 cup chips from the bag so you need to add more chips to make the 1 1/2 cups total. Add the semisweet chips to a saucepan with 1/2 cup sweetened condensed milk. Heat over low heat, stirring constantly until smooth. Remove from heat and stir in 1/2 teaspoon vanilla. Spread this in the foil lined pan with a spatula, spreading to fit the pan. Place this pan in the refrigerator for 10 minutes before starting the next step. Measure how many orange chips and add enough white chocolate chips to equal 1 1/2 cups. Add these chips to a pan with remaining 1/2 cup sweetened condensed milk. Heat over low heat until smooth, stirring constantly. Remove from the heat and add 1/2 teaspoon vanilla. Spread this carefully over the layer in the foil lined pan, spreading over the top to the edges. Immediately press at least 24 pieces ofcandy corn on the top. Chill to harden, remove and cut into slices and serve at room temperature.POPCORN BALLSPlace 7 quarts offresh popped popcorn in a large bowl and set aside. In a saucepan place 1 cup light corn syrup, 1/4 cup water and 1/4 teaspoon salt. Cook over medium heat until it forms a soft ball. Remove from heat and add 3 tablespoons butter, 1 teaspoon vanilla extract and orange food coloring, optional- stir until butter is melted. Immediately pour in popcorn and stir until evenly coated. Shape into 3 inch balls. Kids love these popcorn balls.RICE KRISPIES TREATSIn a large saucepan, melt 3 tablespoons butter over low heat. Add one package - 10 ounce size - marshmallows and stir until completely melted. Add 6 cups of Rice Krispies cereal and stir until well coated. Using a buttered spatula evenly press mixture into a 3 x 9 x 2 inch pan coated with cooking spray. Cool and cut into 2 inch squares. You can press a candy corn or other candy into the top of each square.HALLOWEEN SUGAR COOKIES1 and 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 3/4 cup unsweetened natural cocoa powder, plus more as needed for rolling and work surface, 1 teaspoon baking powder, 1/8 teaspoon salt, 3/4 cup unsalted butter, softened to room temperature, 1 cup granulated sugar, 1 large egg at room temperature, 1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract, Easy Cookie Icing, optional: gel food coloring for tinting icings. Whisk the flour, cocoa powder, baking powder, and salt together in a medium bowl. In a large bowl using a hand mixer or a stand mixer fitted with a paddle attachment, beat the butter and sugar together on high speed until completely smooth and creamy, about 2 minutes. Add the egg and vanilla and beat on high speed until combined, about 1 minute. Scrape down the sides and up the bottom ofthe bowl and beat again as needed to combine. Add the dry ingredients to the wet ingredients and mix on low until combined. Dough will be soft. Ifthe dough seems too soft and sticky for rolling, add 1 moreTablespoon offlour.Divide the dough into 2 equal parts. Dust 2 large pieces ofparch-ment paper or 2 silicone baking mats with cocoa powder (or flour). Place a dough halfon each. With a rolling pin lightly dusted with cocoa powder (or flour), roll the dough out to about 1/4-inch thickness. Use more cocoa powder/flour ifthe dough seems too sticky. The rolled-out dough can be any shape, as long as it is evenly 1/4-inch thick. Lightly dust one ofthe rolled-out doughs with cocoa powder or flour. Place a piece ofparchment on top. (This prevents sticking.) Place the 2nd rolled-out dough on top. Cover with plastic wrap or aluminum foil, then refrigerate for at least 1-2 hours and up to 2 days. Once chilled, preheat the oven to 350°F (177°C). Line 2-3 large baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone baking mats. Carefully remove the top dough piece from the refrigerator.Using cookie cutters, cut the dough into shapes. Re-roll the remaining dough, using more cocoa powder or flour to lightly dust your work surface and rolling pin, and continue cutting the dough until all is used. Work quickly so the dough doesn't become too warm or soft. If it does, stop what you're doing and place any unused dough back in the refrigerator for 10 minutes to stiffen up again. Repeat cutting into shapes with the 2nd half of the dough. Arrange shaped cookies on baking sheets 3 inches apart. Bake for 11-12 minutes or until edges are set. If your oven has hot spots, rotate the baking sheet halfway through bake time. Allow cookies to cool on the baking sheet for 5 minutes and then transfer to a wire rack to cool completely before decorating. Prepare the easy cookie icing. Divide the icing into separate bowls ifyou wish to tint it different colors using gel food coloring.Plain or decorated cookies stay soft for about 5 days when covered tightly at room temperature. For longer storage, cover and refrigerate for up to 10 days.GHOST S'MORES DIP1 bag ghost marshmallows,2 c. semi-sweet chocolate chips, 1/4 c. heavy cream, warmed, Graham crackers, for serving, Mini chocolate chips, for ghost eyes. Preheat the oven to 450°. In the bottom ofa 9" ovenproofskillet, baking dish, or pie dish, spread out chocolate chips and pour cream on top. Cover completely with a single layer ofghost marshmallows. Place mini chocolate chips over eyes and mouth. Bake until the chocolate has melted and the ghosts are golden, 8 to 10 minutes. Serve warm with graham crackers for dipping.REESE'S BATS1 bag of Reese's cups 1 package of Oreo cookies, 1 jar ofcreamy peanut butter, 1 bag ofcandy eyes. One ofthe easiest recipes and that is great to throw together for a snack or treat. Separate the Oreo cookies from the cream. Next, slice them in half. There may be some casualties as Oreos can be a bit crumbly, I suggest using a serrated paring knife. Next, attach them to your Reese's with a dab ofpeanut butter. Apply the same peanut butter method for the eyes and you've got your bats!

title: Replica Spanish armada ship on display at maritime museum
author: Contributed
content:
Replica Spanish armada ship on display at maritime museum

 October 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 9 | Section: News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The Nao Trinidad arrived in St. Michaels on Oct. 25, when it docked at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, where the replica historical boat will serve as a display of maritime heritage.The Nao Trinidad was the flagship of what was called Armada del Maluco (1519-1522), captained by Ferdinand Magellan.Five ships (naos) departed from Seville, but only two made it to the Spice Islands. Nao Trinidad was one of them.This beautiful replica weighs 150 tons, is 93 feet in length and has a 26-foot beam, three masts and a bowsprit. The height of the mainmast is more than 82 feet, with five sails and five decks, built with exquisite work in Iroko (an African hardwood) and pinewood.This ship has sailed to many different ports across the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic European Coast as a training vessel and floating museum.Naos have a unique and original design that made them the most advanced in naval engineering for their time, used first as cargo ships in Spain and then taking the lead as exploring vessels.The Nao Trinidad currently docked in Talbot County is a fullscale replica, faithful to the original's design and dimensions.More than a hundred artisans of the sea worked on its construction, including ship carpenters, rope masters and naval engineers.Visitors will be able to tour four decks to get a feel for how life was onboard during the ship's heyday and how it is to live today on an historical ship of these characteristics.They will be able to learn about the maneuvering and rigging of the boat and interact with the crew, who have the most amazing experiences from their long voyages.The boat will be available to visit at the maritime museum until Oct. 31 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.A ticket to enter the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum must be purchased to access the ship, except for museum members.IN addition to this ticket cost, the cost to board the ship is $12 for adults, $5 for children ages 6 to 17 and free for children 5 and under.

Cross St. as it is fully handicapped accessible.Once again, this year's exhibition dates opened with the Chestertown RiverArts Studio Tour Oct.28-29,10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the Sultana Education Foundation's Downrigging Festival.From the beginning, Castelli's annual show has been synonymous with the Downrigging. Now in its 23rd year, the festival is one ofthe largest annual tall ship gatherings in North America. The festival features a long weekend ofTall Ship sails, tours, incredible live bluegrass music, lectures, exhibits, family activities, regional food and more.For the last few years, the exhibition has included essays by Castelli for each newwork. In his own words he describes the day, activity or friendship that gives each painting its own story and meaning. Printed essays will be available at the gallery and on the MassoniArt website."Biscuit Beck taught me a lot about culling river oysters. Especially oysters that grew in fresher waters ofthe upper Bay and tributaries. He is the father and uncle to some ofthe other watermen in this col-lection."writes Castelli "I have known for many years that I standjust inside the outeredge ofthe watermen community. It allows them to have great fun at my expense, but it is and has always been good-natured."Visit massoniart.com for a listing of High Street and Cross Street galleries public hours. Private appointments may be arranged to suit your schedule.
