title: New mural brightens Preston
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
New mural brightens Preston

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1B | Section: News 
 
 622
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PRESTON - The rural farming scene painted at Mike's Liquors last week is large - at least 60 feet across - a scale fitting for the project, which town officials say is part of a larger effort to enhance downtown Preston."The town of Preston was interested in doing an art project. It is part of our Sustainable Community certification process, along with enhancing our parks and rec and everything downtown," said Amber Korell, the town manager. "We were able to secure a planning grant through the Maryland State Arts Council for $10,000 in collaboration with the Caroline County Arts Council." Korell said there were two designs submitted for this mural, along with four for a meditation wall, which will be completed at a later date.All the designs were put online, and the community voted for their favorite. At a commissioner's meeting, the artist's statements about their project were read aloud.111 votes were cast for Tindall's piece."This is exciting because it is the first Preston public art installation," the artist said. "I am super grateful to be able to do something like this.The community involvement has been extremely encouraging." Tindall used around five cans of paint and 10 spray paint cans to realize his folk art vision of a sunny day in Preston, including a red tractor, brilliant sun and rolling green farm land.Mike's Liquors was a cantaloupe orange before Tindall began his work, and there were lots of chips and imperfections in the surface of the wall.Tindall caulked and primed the surface to allow the art to stick to something. He even painted on a base primer before he could get creative.After painting for five days, he will apply polyurethane to weather seal it."I started sketching it in with spray paints and going in and fine tuning the details with a little artist's brush," he said on Monday. "I am 90% done.It is exciting to do larger works and be outside and engage with the people that stop by that are curious." People who drove by and saw the mural gave a supportive honk on their way by, Tindall said."I tried to pick subject material that was fitting for the area and that resonated with the community - something that was really going to brighten up the side of this building," he said."This is a prominent corner that receives so much traffic. It has turned almost into a folk art piece. What I am going to do this afternoon is go to the studio and cut out stencils. I am going to put up 'Preston' up in the sky. It will fit perfectly." Korrell and the town council have another art project in mind for a meditation wall and mural to be built in the James T. Wright Memorial Park.Jennifer Lenderking, with the winning design, went through the same voting process as Tindall."I want to get things done. I want to see that we are making progress," Korrell said. "We are really going to try to get what the community wants done. I am applying for a Maryland State Arts Council project grant. I have my project, I have my artist.I am going to apply for $30,000 to see if I get awarded for that."

title: Sultana Downrigging brings in the crowds
author: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com
content:
Sultana Downrigging brings in the crowds

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com | Page: 6A | Section: News 
 
 664
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Perfect weather, beautiful boats and tall ships, toe-tapping music, and a spectacular fireworks show made this year's Sultana Downrigging one of the best ever.The event, welcoming historical replicas of Colonial-era vessels and some of the most up-and-coming music bluegrass groups in the country, is the largest fundraiser for the Sultana Education Foundation located in Chestertown.Julia Knight, an event volunteer, was happy to see the crowds. "This is my third year volunteering, but we've been fans from the beginning," said Knight, "and it's so important what the foundation does here." Attendees young and old headed to the tall ships for tours and, for the lucky ticket holders, a ride on them.Sailing tickets were sold out before the event even happened.Crew members on the replica of the Kalmar Nickel, the tall ship of Delaware, provided information on the original vessel and its 1638 expedition that founded the colony of New Sweden, the first permanent European settlement in the Delaware Valley, now present-day Wilmington, Delaware.One of the present day 24-member crew gave instructions on how the boat was steered, as ship steering wheels were not invented yet at the time this ship was built. It took two people to steer, one man who was located in a lower deck with a whip staff in hand that rotated, and the mate up above who could see what was ahead and yell down directions below.Next up was the Maryland Dove, a replica from the Ark and Dove, one of two ships that first brought colonists to Maryland. Tale teller Michael Connor from the replica of the Dove told guests, "The Ark was a 400-ton capacity cargo ship hired by Cecil Calvert to transport about 140 colonists and their equipment and supplies to Maryland. The Dove was a much smaller 40-ton capacity cargo ship purchased by Cecil Calvert and investors so that the colonists would have their own ship to use once Ark had sailed for England." Attendees who appreciated restored classic boats were treated to a collection show put on by the Antique & Classic Boat Society, Chesapeake Bay chapter.Bob Wallace made his first 18' Gone Crab Skiff Krazy in 2016, proceeded to win seven competitions, and was named National Hard Crab Derby Champion. "Once I took it to the Crab Claw restaurant in St.Michaels," said Wallace. "The owner asked me to move it because all the customers wanted to come out and see it." Guy Beckley from Millington who brought his own boat to the pier said he came every year. "This is like Christmas for me," he said.Over in the Music Village tent, the crowds were enjoying some of the finest Bluegrass music in the region.The band Scraping Plates was first up and wowed the crowd with both old favorites and some of their new tunes. When asked how they got their unique name, guitarist and vocalist Andrew Jordan said the group began playing parties, and they never got time to eat. "We just went in the back kitchen and started scraping off what was left," he said.Miriam Satchell, owner of The Spicerie, and Chestertown Farmers Market vendor, said she was thankful for her hardworking staff. "The crowds are really enjoying it," she said."We're happy to be here." Oyster shucker order taker Sam Brahan said on Friday they shucked over 2,000 oysters. "Today will be more than that," she said on Saturday only an hour after opening.The Sultana Education Foundation provides hands-on educational opportunities that promote stewardship of the Chesapeake Bay's historic, cultural, and environmental resources. Over 200,000 students have taken courses so far, and the programming is always building.President and Founder Drew McMullen said this year's event was a big success, thanks to good weather, beautiful vessels, music diversity, the support of the community, and the large number of volunteers. "We are well into raising in the high, five-figures," he said. 
 
 Caption: LAURA TAYMAN
 
Tall ships line up in a row at the Sultana Downrigging Festival in Chestertown last weekend.

title: Sailing through history - Replica flagship from Magellan-Elcano expedition stops in St. Michaels
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Sailing through history - Replica flagship from Magellan-Elcano expedition stops in St. Michaels

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5A | Section: News 
 
 451
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The Nao Trinidad, a 93-footreplica of the flagship of the Magellan-Elcano expedition around the world, has docked in St. Michaels this week at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum.Through Sunday, museum visitors can step aboard the vessel and get a feel for what a world-wide adventure in the early 1500s looked like.The replica ship, which has sailed to ports across the Mediterranean Sea and Atlantic European coast, has four masts, five sails and four decks. It was built using pinewood and Iroko, African hardwood.The Nao Trinidad arrived in St. Michaels on Oct. 25 after trips to Oyster City and Delaware City.Nicolas Pastor, a crew member of the replica vessel, has been working on the ship for about four months. His favorite part of the ship is the crow's nest, located at top of the the ship's main mast.Pastor said crew members have to climb up there for maintenance and for when they want to put the sails out."We have to climb (up) there and pull the ropes out," he said.On a windy Tuesday morning, Reinhardt Sahmel, a member of the Tidewater Camera Club, snapped shots aboard the ship.He took photos of the rigging and ropes, equipment and the Spanish and American flags "waving in the strong breeze." Sahmel said he found out about the vessel's stop in St.Michaels from members in his camera club, who sent out an email saying it might make an interesting photo subject.A bit of a history buff, Sahmel said he has been reading about the conquest of the Incas and the Aztecs by the Spanish conquistadors.Nao Trinidad, he said, represents what the conquistadors used to travel around the world."This was an opportunity to actually walk around in one," he said.The Magellan-Elcano expedition led the first recorded sailing around the world, which took place between 1519 and 1522.There were five ships on the expedition. Only one of those ships, the Victoria, made the entire journey.The Trinidad made it all the way across the Atlantic Ocean, down South America's coast, through the Strait of Magellan and across the Pacific Ocean to the Moluccas.There, however, the ship sprang a leak in it's hull, stopping it from returning to Spain. The Trinidad was the second to last surviving ship of the expedition.

title: Christening time - CBMM debuting new welcome center, new boat built at shipyard

Christening time - CBMM debuting new welcome center, new boat built at shipyard

 November 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 761
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum will have a grand opening event on Saturday, Dec. 2, for its new Welcome Center.Ceremonies and events run from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the St Michaels museum.The waterfront museum's shipyard has also completed its latest project - a 36-foot Chesapeake Bay buyboat.The Welcome Center festivities will begin with a formal ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new building at 10:30 a.m. and continue with a festival-style celebration highlighting the theme of "Winter on the Chesapeake" that features authentic Chesapeake Bay experiences, including food demonstrations, hands-on activities, campus tours, and live music," The entertainment includes a performance by renowned smooth jazz saxophonist and St. Michaels native Anthony "Turk" Cannon, whose father Wilson "Turk" Cannon was an iconic waterman who is featured in the museum's "Oystering on the Chesapeake" exhibition.CBMM general admission is free for all guests that day. For more information checkout cbmm.org/WelcomeCenterGrandOpening."This is a truly exciting day in CBMM's history that has been many years in the making," President & CEO Kristen Greenaway said. "Our wonderful new Welcome Center is integral to CBMM's mission and takes the guest experience to the next level, and we look forward to sharing all that it has to offer with our friends and community partners at the Grand Opening.We're grateful to all who have played a part in making this building a reality and delighted to celebrate with everyone." The new Welcome Center totals 12,000 square feet with three exhibit spaces, a reception area and CBMM's Museum store."Guests will find a new orientation exhibition, 'Navigating the Chesapeake's Maritime Culture', constructed on a wall adjacent to the entrance that uses photos and artifacts to set up the themes found across campus," according to a press release from CBMM."'Water Lines: Chesapeake Watercraft Traditions' is an exhibition showcasing CBMM's small craft collection, some of which have been in storage and will be shared with guests for the first time." The upcoming "Stories from the Shoreline" exhibition will present an expansion of a the current "Waterfowling" exhibit including information on the ecology of the Chesapeake Bay The new Welcome Centers's Museum Store includes a historic photo of Crisfield's Horsey Brothers Department Store, and several exhibit vessels.Opening day events will feature.food, beer and cocktails and music from Anthony Cannon and his five-piece jazz ensemble."Performing at CBMM will truly be a full circle moment for me and my family," Cannon said. "St.Michaels is home and such a big part of who I am and the music that I play. It's an honor to be part of the Welcome Center's Grand Opening.We're going to have a lot of fun celebrating that day." CBMM shipyard also completed construction of its latest project - a 36-foot Chesapeake Bay buyboat called Mr. Dickie "The Shipyard team began work on the new construction build last fall after finishing up its build of Maryland Dove and worked over the past year under the direction of Shipyard Foreman Jeff Reed to bring the vessel to life. A contract build for owners Grigg and Cindy Mullen of Lexington, Virginia, Mr. Dickie will be on display later this month at the Sultana Downrigging Festival in Chestertown before returning to dock at CBMM," according to museum.Buyboats are crossplanked workboats that were traditionally used for hauling oysters from skipjacks to market in season and anything else that needed transporting the rest of the year. Today, there are estimated to be fewer than 30 buyboats that continue to ply the Bay's waters, according to CBMM."Grigg provided the opportunity for us to have our Shipyard team do a complete build from start to finish, creating a unique object in a way that realizes Grigg and our dream of a comprehensive construction that allows for public and Shipwright education," said CBMM Vice President of Shipyard Operations Christian Cabral. "It's been an incredible experience." According to an announcement from CBMM, "Mr. Dickie pays homage to the 60-foot buyboat Mundy Point, designed to bring the buyboat look to a scaled-down 36-foot version.It was constructed from heart pine, white oak, Atlantic cedar, and western red cedar, and outfitted with a restored late-1930s Buda diesel engine.The new boat was officially launched Oct. 20 and is named after the late Dickie Whaley, Mullen's neighbor growing up in Queen Anne's County."It's been a wonderful year building Mr. Dickie and working with the Shipyard folks," Mullen said. "Every time there was a decision to make, it was always-if we do it this way, it's going to be better. It's turned out wonderfully." For more about CBMM's Shipyard and its projects check out cbmm.org/shipyard.

title: Author Ananda Devi wins literature award
content:
Author Ananda Devi wins literature award

 November 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 8A | Section: News 
 
 366
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Author Ananda Devi has been named the 28th laureate of the renowned Neustadt International Prize for Literature.The award is from World Literature Today, the University of Oklahoma's award-winning magazine of international literature and culture, announced late Tuesday evening that Awarded in alternating years with the NSK Neustadt Prize for Children's and Young Adult Literature, the Neustadt Prize recognizes outstanding literary merit in literature worldwide.Born in Mauritius, Devi has become one of the major literary voices of the Francophone world with more than 25 books, including novels, collections of poetry, short stories, and essays.She has been translated into over a dozen languages and has received numerous literary prizes and decorations from Mauritius and also from France, with the title of Officier des Arts et des Lettres. In 2014, she received a major award from the Académie Française.The Guardian newspaper recommended her novel "Eve out of Her Ruins" on its list of the 100 best contemporary novels in translation by women writers.Award-winning writer and filmmaker Fabienne Kanor nominated Devi for the Neustadt Prize. Kanor has published seven novels and was awarded the French Ministry of Culture's Chevalier des Arts et des Lettres.Robert Con Davis-Undiano, World Literature Today's executive director, notes that "it is long overdue for Ananda Devi to receive an international honor of this magnitude. She is deserving, and I hope that this honor will be a springboard to more recognition for her amazing work." The Neustadt Prize is often referenced as the "American Nobel" for its reputation as a lead-up to the Swedish Academy's annual selection. Any living author writing from anywhere in the world is eligible for the Neustadt Prize. The jury is composed of international authors, and that fact helps shield the award from external pressure by booksellers, publishers, and others who may have interest in influencing the outcome.The Neustadt Prize is the first international literary award of its scope to originate in U.S. and is one of the very few international prizes for which poets, novelists and playwrights are equally eligible, according to a press release announcing Devi's award. Winners are awarded $50,000.

title: Former presidential yacht arrives in Cambridge - Franklin D. Roosevelt traveled on Sequoia to dedicate original Choptank River Bridge
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Former presidential yacht arrives in Cambridge - Franklin D. Roosevelt traveled on Sequoia to dedicate original Choptank River Bridge

 November 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 787
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - The 93-year-old Sequoia, a former presidential yacht, arrived in Cambridge from Belfast, Maine without incident on Monday.The 104-foot yacht has a storied past of presidential passengers.Beginning with former President Herbert Hoover, the ship served United States presidents for a total of 49 years. Although former President Jimmy Carter sold the ship in 1977, former President Ronald Reagan's administration used it for three years.The boat, a National Historic Landmark, was where former President John F. Kennedy's celebrated his last birthday. It was also the place where former President Harry Truman, former Canadian Prime Minister W.L. Mackenzie King and former British Prime Minister Clement Attlee got together to discuss the atomic bomb in 1945.And these are just a few of the many stories of presidents aboard the Sequoia.Covered in shrink wrap, the vessel came in by barge after a five-day journey from mid-coast Maine, where it had been stored for the last four years. Workers spent hours transporting the yacht from the barge to it's new home - outside the Richardson Maritime Center - where it will be renovated and put on display.Martin Hardy, chairman of the Richardson Maritime Center's board of directors, said he thinks the Sequoia will attract a lot of attention.He said it will benefit the museum's mission and give the museum the opportunity to establish its marine trades education.The yacht is expected to take at least five years to renovate.It is planned to stay in Cambridge for that time.Hardy said the museum has yet to work out a formal agreement with the yacht's owner Michael Cantor."There was a little bit of a rush to make this happen because the boat had to leave before the winter storms got too bad, but it had to stay there until hurricane season was over," Hardy said."So (there was) a very short period of time to do this. So we haven't even worked out an agreement." Hardy said the yacht's restoration will be a "complete, total rebuild." But he said significant cabinet work on the inside will remain."The desk where the president signed things and that kind of stuff," he said about what will be preserved.When work is complete, Hardy said Cantor will take the Sequoia up and down the coast for different organizations to view and use.In a news release from the museum, Cantor said the Sequoia's permanent home will be on the water."But Cambridge could be its home for repairs and refitting," Cantor added.This is not the Sequoia's first journey to Cambridge.Hardy said it traveled to Cambridge two times in its heyday. On one of those trips, former President Franklin D. Roosevelt traveled in on the Sequoia to dedicate the original Choptank River Bridge, which was funded by the New Deal, in 1935.The Sequoia also came by barge in 2019 for just a few days before traveling up to Maine.As the yacht was unloaded, spectators from Cambridge and neighboring towns came to watch.Peter Doolan, a Cambridge resident, said it was exciting to watch the ship's arrival Monday. Doolan called the yacht a piece of history that shouldn't be lost.Ken Guelta, who also came to see the ship's arrival, said he thought it was a waste of money. He said he didn't think it would be long until the ship looked like another old, forgotten boat, falling apart on land.According to the news release from the museum, Hardy said the Richardson Maritime Center has been planning to build a new building to house exhibits.They are now considering a building to house the Sequoia for its restoration.According to the news release, museum officials think the vessel will be beneficial for the Cambridge Harbor Project, which Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. is undertaking.The Cambridge Harbor project will include creating public spaces like a promenade and parks, a boutique hotel that has a restaurant and bar, and residential and mixed-use spaces. The museum is one of CWDI's partners.Executive Director Matt Leonard said CWDI has formed a partnership with the museum because of Richardson Maritime Center's mission aligns with its own, according to the news release."We are proud to be working with them on initiatives like the Sequoia project," Leonard said.

title: Chalk festival draws artists of all ages
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Chalk festival draws artists of all ages

 November 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 565
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - People of all ages and skills got to show off their chalk abilities during the second annual Chalk Arts Festival in Cambridge last weekend.The event, which began Oct. 28 and ended Oct. 29, gave attendees the chance to listen to music, eat, see chalk artists from around the country do their thing and, of course, put chalk to the pavement.The festival was held in and outside of the Dorchester County Office Building.California artist Lori Antoinette led chalk art workshops for all ages on both days of the festival.Cambridge City Council Commissioner Laurel Atkiss said it was nice to have an event where kids could immediately have fun and express themselves without having to stand in a line."I think an event like this where it's open and free to the families and it inspires kids to pick up something with their hands and be expressive, it's a really nice event," she said.Atkiss herself drew a fish on the pavement outside the County Office Building."I just followed my heart because the rockfish tournament was just over the hill yesterday and just went with the nautical, fishy theme," she said of her creation.Hoopers Island Chalk Artist Ed Krell originally had the idea for the festival before pitching it to the Dorchester Center for the Arts.In its second year, the DCA is still hosting the event, which celebrates chalk arts and raises awareness for mental health. Krell said he wanted the festival to raise awareness for mental health to honor his friend, who passed away.Throughout the event, mental health information was presented on the music stage.This year, the festival garnered more community support, from Dorchester County Tourism to Dorchester County Public Schools.Chalk artists visited DCPS middle and high schools the day before the festival started, to give workshops and teach students about chalk art.North Dorchester High School Art Teacher LaSara Kinser said her students loved getting to work with chalk."It's not a material that we've worked with yet this year," she said. "And so they were so stoked, very excited." Kinser said her students drew portraits using chalk during a workshop led by Krell.The portraits from DCPS students hung inside the County Office Building for the duration of the festival so attendees could look at them.One of those DCPS high school students, Zye Pinder, also attended and performed in the festival. Pinder and her friend Jade Bryant both performed with New Creation Marching Unit.Pinder and Bryant enjoyed the live music at the event. Bryant said she also loved the face paint.Chalk artist Randy Segura traveled from the suburbs of Denver, Colorado to attend the festival this year.For his first year at the festival, Segura said it was a fun time and the weather was nice."Not as big of a turnout as we imagined but for its second year, I think it's growing," he said. "And I think it'll just continue growing." After creating a 3D paintbrush, Segura began a portrait."I figured if I had time, I would do a portrait of my father-in-law who just passed away last Tuesday," he said.Atkiss said the weather made the event even better."I think the unseasonably lovely weather has been a real treat," she said, laughing.

During the station's very first fall membership drive, WHCP said it is proud to be among a select group of 17 NPR member stations that can offer the NPR+ podcast bundle of 16 podcasts as a thank-you gift to those joining or renewing their membership of at least $96 annually ($8 per month).Additionally, Premier Movie Theaters in Cambridge and Easton have partnered with WHCP, and the station is making two passes available to any current members (new, returning or sustaining at the $60 family membership level and above). "Individual annual memberships start at just $35, and you can become a sustaining monthly member for less than $7 a month, at whcp.org/donate." In addition to its regular programming, WHCP also operates a free public service with the Mid-Shore Reader, a round-the-clock radio reading service for those who cannot read the printed word on their own.Fresh daily readings of books, newspapers and magazines, including The Star Democrat, are read each week by local volunteers, as well as the monthly Attractions, Shore Monthly and Tidewater Times magazines."If you or someone you know suffers from vision loss, or who otherwise cannot see, hold, or comprehend the printed word, this service is available free of charge," said Starling. There are four ways to listen to WHCP Radio - on the air at 91.7 FM, via the WHCP app, online at whcp.org, or simply ask Alexa to "launch WHCP Radio."  LYNCH - Congratulations to local resident, veteran, singer, thespian and songwriter Earl French.A longtime resident of Lynch, he competed in the National Veterans Creative Arts Competition, VA Maryland Healthcare System, and won first prize for his original song: "The Wind." French, along with Ed Hall on saxophone, playing a jazzy desafinado, also won first place for instrumental/group jazz/R & B/soul.The competition was held at the Maryland State Fair on Sept. 9, where French competed against 15 other veteran talents.French acknowledged he's not sure what the next step is, but Kelsey Eisenhauer, the coordinator of the event, and a Music and Creative Arts therapist, told him they might know by December how it's going national.It's a song worthy of national acclaim.While strumming his guitar, he sings: "I'll ask the wind, won't you seek and find her. The wind. Kiss her to remind her." The lyrics were written in 1982 and came about by taking an emotional fragment from his life.French explained that a good writer friend was leaving for Japan.She showed him the brochure of who was going to be on the bill with her. French said, "Behind each personality of who was going to be playing, there was a star. That's where I came up with the line: 'On a star, she flew away.'" Love and loss is the theme of the song, and as much as it's well received everywhere, he's surprised how many people like it when they hear it.Several weeks back he was interviewed by 106.9 WCTR, and they played it over the airwaves.French displays his musical versatility in another original of his: "Lonestar." It's in the style of the gritty outlaw country songs; the kind Waylon Jennings or Merle Haggard sing.While French was attending Valley College in California in the '70s, he stayed with his professor for a time. One day, coming home from a hard day of landscaping, French wearily leaned against the door and the professor told him, he's got that Lonestar look in his eye.Lonestar was the kind of beer French drank, and from that quote, a song was created.French is unassuming and humble about his work, and was even surprised at winning first place at the fair.He shouldn't be, however. He's been a professional for many years, honing his craft, meeting other talented musicians and learning from them while working on several creative projects all around the country.He grew up near Memorial Stadium, watching the Baltimore Colts play, and learning the drums was his start into music. From there, he became the lead vocals for the Nomads, in 1960. He was only 16 years old playing rock n roll covers at the high school dances with a seven-piece band with horns. The Nomads played all over Baltimore, French said.His band life was put on hold when the Vietnam War kicked off.In 1965, as the United States rapidly increased its military forces in South Vietnam, French enlisted in the army as a medic. He was fortunate not be sent to the frontlines of the conflict. He was stationed in Nellingen Kaserne, an airfield east of Stuttgart, Germany, an engineering company, and ended up driving for supply.After he served two years, he came back and pursued music again. Following his aspirations, he landed in California, where a military friend encouraged him to stay there, use his GI Bill, and go to college.At Valley College, he studied theater, running the wild gambit of acting, music, entertainment and song writing.He's enjoyed it all, but lately, he's been more focused on song writing.French is strongly influenced by singer/songwriter, grammy winner, Kris Kristofferson, known for writing such moving, soulful songs like, "Help Me Make It Through the Night." "Take the ribbon from your hair.Shake it loose and let it fall" French, recalled meeting him in Long Beach, California, while working on lighting for his show. Before the show began, somebody motioned French over, asking if Kristofferson was there yet. French, seeing this was a great way to meet one of his idols, approached Kristofferson and told him about the guy asking for him.The next moment, he's escorting the famous singer/songwriter down a set of pitch black steps to find the man. Kristofferson then asked French to rustle up some booze for them.Having never been to Long Beach before that day, he searched far and wide, using his boss's van."I went back to the dressing room, to give Kristofferson the booze and stuff, but he said, no, sit down, have a drink with us," French said, laughing, recalling the off-beat personality of the songwriter.These connections happened to French his entire life. His skills, found their way to the silver screen, the theatre stage and the studios.He has 10 original songs in the play, "Helldorado," based on the gunfight at the O.K. Corral, mixed with humor.He played as a band member for E.F. Shotgun, in the movie, "Getting Over," a tuneful drama that features the rock group Love Machine, directed by Bernie Rollins.He's portrayed his favorite character, Dr. Einstein, in the play, "Arsenic and Lace," that played at the Garfield Center for the Arts.

title: Talbot Humane launches first annual holiday ornament
author: Contributed
content:
Talbot Humane launches first annual holiday ornament

 November 3, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 305
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Talbot Humane has introduced their inaugural holiday ornament.The idea was brought to Patty Quimby, Talbot Humane's executive director, and the TH Board, by the coordinating committee of the TH holiday "Pawsitively Fabulous Pet Boutique." The team presented the concept of establishing a shelter-animal-themed art contest across the community each year, with the winning selection becoming the annual ornament.In the late spring, TH launched the first contest and received a variety of fantastic submissions.While it was a tough decision, Quimby and the board ultimately selected Nicholas Casale's holiday pup design.Kristy Casale, Nicholas' mother, brought her very excited 9 year-old son into the front office of Talbot Humane just minutes before the contest was over.He had seen the contest and excitedly embraced the idea. He loves crafts, drawing and painting and has even landed a supporting role in an upcoming performance of "Elf." "We are thrilled to have a local child's vision of a Shelter Holiday Pup be the very first TH ornament to hang on Talbot County (and beyond) Holiday trees," said the shelter in a press release.The ornament will be sold at the Talbot Humane holiday "Pawsitvely Fabulous Pet Boutique," located directly next to Talbot Humane, from Nov. 2 to Dec. 23. The shop is open Thursday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and is filled to the brim with a wonderful assortment of items that will make great holiday gifts for all pet lovers."The Holidays are a very special time, and it is Talbot Humane's hope that the ornament(s) will become a celebrated family tradition within our community," said the shelter."Please come support our young local artist and Talbot Humane by purchasing your very own ornament.We look forward to sharing this special piece with you every year."

title: U.S. Postal Service unveils new 2024 stamps - Madonna and Child, Love, Flowers, Underground Railroad, Manatees highlight offers
content:
U.S. Postal Service unveils new 2024 stamps - Madonna and Child, Love, Flowers, Underground Railroad, Manatees highlight offers

 November 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 470
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The U.S. Postal Service has unveiled a batch of new stamps it will issue in 2024."As always, our stamp program features a broad array of subjects and designs. Stamps are miniature works of art and often tell a story that highlights our American culture, our people or an important point in our history," said Lisa Bobb-Semple, acting Stamp Services director for USPS in an announcement Oct. 23."Stamps also allow us to show what's important to us as we carefully select which stamp adorns our mail pieces. The 2024 stamps were designed to offer the American public a broad array of choices for those looking to collect stamps or send a special message," Bobb-Semple said.The Post Office said the released stamps are a partial list of the 2024 offerings and the designs are subject to potential changes. Summaries with the stamps are from the Postal Service along with information about their history and designers. 
 
 Caption: USPS The 2024 Love stamp features a stylized bird in flight bearing a message of love in its beak. Antonio Alcalá, an art director for USPS, designed this stamp with an original digital illustration by Katie Kirk.
 
USPS A new series of low denomination stamps will debut in 2024. Each stamp will showcase a different flower design. Ethel Kessler, an art director for USPS, designed the stamps.
 
USPS In 2024, a new Floral Geometry stamp, denominated at $1, will be available for purchase. The stamps lend an elegant and contemporary appearance to packages, large envelopes and other mailings. The stamps were designed and created by the firm Spaeth Hill. Antonio Alcalá served as art director for USPS.
 
USPS A new traditional Christmas stamp will be issued in 2024 featuring the Madonna and Child from the Workshop of Sassoferrato. Giovanni Battista Salvi da Sassoferrato (16091685), gained popularity for his modestly scaled depictions of the Madonna and Child. Greg Breeding designed the stamp, which will be sold in booklets of 20.
 
USPS New stamps in a booklet of 20 celebrate the winter season with lacy, symmetrical graphic forms inspired by snowflakes. Each stamp in the block of four includes a unique design in white against a background of a single color: navy blue, teal, tan or darkblue-green. Greg Breeding was the art director for the project. Bailey Sullivan designed and illustrated the stamps.
 
USPS The Save Manatees stamp will be issued to create awareness about the threats posed to this beloved marine mammal. Derry Noyes, an art director for USPS, designed the stamp and booklet cover using illustrator Nancy Stahl's original graphic design.
 
USPS
 
The Postal Service will issue its 10th stamp celebrating Kwanzaa in 2024. Observed from Dec. 26 to Jan. 1, the annual pan-African holiday brings together family, community and culture. The art was inspired by a live performance witnessed by the artist, Ekua Holmes, during a Kwanzaa event. Ethel Kessler, an art director for USPS, designed the stamp. 

 © Copyright © 2023 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Adkins Arboretum to display M(Other) Nature art exhibit
author: Contributed
content:
Adkins Arboretum to display M(Other) Nature art exhibit

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 8A | Section: News 
 
 549
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Nature is far from passive in the artwork of Caitlin Gill and Bridgette Guerzon Mills.In their joint show, M(Other) Nature, on view in the Adkins Arboretum Visitor's Center through Dec. 23, dreams, nightmares and reality intertwine.There will be a reception to meet the artists and learn more about their work on Sat., Nov. 11, from 2 to 4 p.m.The two Baltimore based artists had never met, but when they got together at Mills' studio to plan the show, they found they have a lot in common."We're drawn to similar materials," Mills said. "I found it interesting that we both use found natural materials in our work." "A big inspiration for us is materiality, texture and nature," Gill agreed. "We both seem particularly drawn to found objects, lace, insects and nests, and there's a lot of exploration with textiles." Both artists have always felt a strong connection with nature, particularly its feminine creative power."The title of their show, M(Other) Nature, refers to our culture's contradictory feelings about nature - that while we celebrate its beauty and creativity, we feel separate from it, as if we are something other than nature, and so have no qualms about exploiting its resources," said a press release about the event.Both Gill and Mills explore the life-giving aspects of nature, underscoring their mutual interest in its feminine qualities by using materials associated with women-cloth, lace, doilies and thread.Gill said, "Mother Nature as a metaphor is contingent on the feminine ability to create life. I think the need for knowledge as a mode of control and dominance is something nature has endured, similarly to women, so for me, this is an exercise in reclamation and liberation." Visitors may remember Mills's site-specific sculptures in the Arboretum's forest from several of the Outdoor Sculpture Invitational shows. A Master Naturalist, for last summer's show, she created a large book with nuts, seedpods, bark and moss stitched onto its cloth pages that explored trees' role in the health of the forest.Continuing this exploration, her materials for this show include similar found materials as well as cloth, lace, photo transfers of trees, birds and insects, paint, encaustic and actual hand-stitching so that her artworks bridge the real and the imagined. These are gentle works, lovingly made and carrying a sense of mystery and melancholy.Like Mills, Gill explores the contrast between vulnerability and the power of the life force but with an often disquieting focus on the physical experience of exploitation. A pale grub, part painted and part collaged, curls up alone and exposed on the loose-knit fibers of a sheet of handmade paper, while a beautiful golden-red fox, also a fusion of paint and collage, seems at first glance to be running until you read its title, "Fox, road kill." "The history of animal rights follows a nearly parallel trajectory to women's rights," Gill said."All my work is directly or indirectly about the feminine experience and its relationship to nature and western culture." This show is part of Adkins Arboretum's ongoing exhibition series of work on natural themes by regional artists. It is on view at the Arboretum Visitor's Center, located at 12610 Eveland Road near Tuckahoe State Park in Ridgely.Contact the Arboretum at 410-634-2847, ext. 100, or info@adkinsarboretum.org for gallery hours.

title: REMEMBERING A PATRIOT - DAR dedicates a bronze marker at the grave of Caroline Revolutionary War hero
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
REMEMBERING A PATRIOT - DAR dedicates a bronze marker at the grave of Caroline Revolutionary War hero

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 890
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GILPIN POINT - Descendants and dignitaries gathered Sunday, Nov. 5, to commemorate the valor and patriotism of a local Revolutionary War hero.Members of the General Perry Benson Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution honored the memory of Col.William Richardson by placing a bronze marker on his grave at 1 p.m. on the unseasonably warm and calm day.Richardson's descendants gathered to unveil the marker and place a wreath on his grave. About 100 people attended and participated in the ceremony at Gilpin Point Park near Harmony, on a tiny parcel of his former plantation.Born in 1735 in Talbot County, Richardson was colonel of the Fifth Regiment of the Maryland Line and the Eastern Shore Battalion of the Flying Camp. He fought at the Battle of Harlem Heights. He died in 1825 at Gilpin Point.Colonel Richardson Middle and High schools in Federalsburg are named for him.Colonel Richardson High School alumnus and band director Thomas Cheezum led the school's marching band in a selection of patriotic songs and armed forces hymns."I love it," Cheezum said. "I mean, this is something that I live for because I'm a part time historian, and I am a big believer in truth, justice and the American way." Chapter Regent Jerry Seiler served as mistress of ceremonies and introduced as the first speaker Elizabeth Deering, state vice regent of the Maryland State Society, Daughters of the American Revolution."We are one of the largest women's organizations in the world, with over 3,000 chapters in all 50 states, Washington D.C. and overseas," Deering said. "The placement of markers is a tangible way to honor and connect with Revolutionary War ancestors and to also raise public awareness of their service." "Today we honor a revolutionary war patriot, Col. William Richardson, who served our nation as a Continental Army officer, and later in life as a politician," Deering said. "He helped to decide whether Maryland should ratify the proposed Constitution of the United States." Also participating in the ceremony were other leaders of the Maryland State Societies of the Daughters and Sons of the American Revolution.Speakers included State Sen. Johnny Mautz (R - 37) and Caroline County Commissioner Frank Bartz.On behalf of the Commission, Bartz said the marker is a "symbol of our collective gratitude and a pledge to uphold the memory of those who laid the foundation for our nation" as well as "a lasting reminder of the courage, sacrifice and unwavering spirit that shaped the history of our great nation." Mautz presented a citation on behalf of the Maryland General Assembly."The most significant aspect of today is to have our students and our youth and our next generation here to understand how we got to where we are," he said."Thank you for allowing me to relive fond memories and create new memories today," Richardson descendant Kristen Dukes said. "By mere chance, my family and I have fallen into this honored lineage of a true patriot.We owe much to his great achievements, such as the establishment of Caroline County, his leadership at the Battle of Harlem Heights and his direct involvement in electing George Washington as the first President of the United States." Another descendant, Petty Utermohle, told the crowd her mother "loved to say that he was known as the 'Fighting Quaker.'" "He was a Quaker until he was removed or, as she put it, kicked out of the meeting house because he was a soldier, and they were peaceful people," she said. "Thankfully, he made that decision." Seiler credited Caroline County Parks and Recreation employees for sprucing up the area around the grave, which had become overgrown.Following the marker dedication by Elizabeth Hinson and Suzanne O'Donnell, the descendants gathered at the end of the grave to unveil the marker and lay a wreath.A 3-volley musket salute was followed by a CRHS band member playing Taps.The Rev. Daniel Gedman, pastor of St. Luke's Global Methodist Church in Denton, who prayed the invocation, also concluded the ceremony with a benediction.

title: 'Bringing life to a variety of women's experiences' - Denton's famed author Sophie Kerr celebrated with events Nov. 4
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
'Bringing life to a variety of women's experiences' - Denton's famed author Sophie Kerr celebrated with events Nov. 4

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 659
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Interest in the talent and work of Denton native and prolific author Sophie Kerr attracted dozens of new fans and existing aficionados to two events Saturday, Nov. 4, just down the river from her beloved hometown.Kerr, who grew up in the Sophie Kerr House in Denton in the late 19th century and became a popular author in the early 20th century, was celebrated with both matinee and evening "literary visits" at the old Caroline Country Club on Pealiquor Road.Headlining the celebration of her work and colorful personality was Washington College alumna Brooke Schultz, who researched Kerr's life and created a presentation that included photographs, pages of handwritten story drafts, letters and newspaper articles.Schultz, a reporter for the Associated Press and a former reporter of APG Chesapeake's Newark Post, did extensive research on Kerr, who wrote 23 novels, over 500 short stories, several plays and articles during her career as managing editor of The Woman's Home Companion, a leading periodical during the first half of the 20th century.The event was organized by Caroline County Council for Arts and the Caroline County Public Library.The 3-hour program included a local readers theatre group sharing dialogue from about a dozen excerpts, cocktails and a luncheon catered by the Chesapeake Culinary Arts Center, displays of novels and magazines featuring her stories, several raffles, and a performance by Wayne Martin and members the North Caroline High School Band.Master of ceremonies was CCCA board member and local playwright Keith Shaffer."It is so much fun to put this together and get a chance to read a lot of stuff by Sophie Kerr that I had not had a chance to read otherwise," he said."I love 'The Blue Envelope' and a couple of the other books she wrote. They're a whole lot of fun," Shaffer said. "I think she got a bad rap from the critics after she passed." "The Blue Envelope" was also the first Kerr novel Schultz read.She told the audience the New York Times called Kerr's works "light amusing fiction" and the Kirkus Reviews deemed it "easy, flimsy feminine fare." However, because of her half-million dollar endowment, and being something of a "myth on the Washington College campus," Schultz was drawn to research Kerr.Born in 1880, Kerr earned degrees from Hood College and the University of Vermont, and pursued a journalism career. She later wrote fiction for the leading magazines of the day, often with biting humor and critiques of the mores of her day.Many of Kerr's settings were based on the Eastern Shore, including a thinly disguised Denton, as well as Long Island and New York City.Schultz quoted Kerr's own words about her writing style. "She says, 'I have no propaganda spirit; the story's the thing. Time and time have indignant readers berated me for beliefs expressed in the speeches of my characters - beliefs which were at wide variance of my own, but perfectly in keeping with the character who expressed them.'" "She was taking controversial figures that people were seeing and she was humanizing them through entertaining fiction," Schultz said."So while she can contend that she had no propaganda spirit, she was ultimately bringing to life a variety of women's experiences to huge blocks of readers." Kerr's bequest to Washington College in 1965 established the Sophie Kerr Prize, the nation's largest undergraduate writing prize, awarded to a graduating senior who shows promise in literary endeavors. Kerr is buried alongside her parents in Denton Cemetery."One of the things that amazed me from the get-go is how many people - natives to this area - drive by the Sophie Kerr House day after day after day and have no idea all the stuff she did," Shaffer said.

title: Delicious Thanksgiving sides
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
Delicious Thanksgiving sides

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: 4A | Section: News 
 
 1230
 Words 

 Read News Document

 That big juicy turkey that just came out of the oven and is waiting to be carved does not get all the attention!Side dishes share the spotlight at many Thanksgiving dinners. Everyone loves side dishes and looks forward to piling them on their plates!The first dish that comes to my memory is when I go back to the country Thanksgiving dinner my mom would prepare. Mom always had her menu planned ahead of time, and the morning before Thanksgiving, she would get a basket and sharp knife and walk to the field on the farm where the fresh collard greens were growing.Mom loved cooking big dinners for family members, who came from afar to share the bounty of food that was mostly homegrown.She would cut the greens and mash them down in the basket until it was full.Returning to the house, we would chop the stems off, place them in a tub, pour cold water over them and sprinkle with some coarse salt. to bring any bugs to the top.After at least three to four times, we changed the water and shook the greens to ensure they were pest-free.In the house already on the stove was her largest pot, filled 1/4 of the way with boiling water and with either a ham hock or fat meat cooking for flavor.In came the clean greens that were gently dropped into the hot water. The lid was placed on loosely, and the rolling boil continued until the greens were tender. with us checking to see if more water was needed every so often.We'd sprinkle some table salt or coarse salt on top, and, during the last few minutes of cooking, sprinkle a very light amount of baking soda (yellow box) over top greens that will cause greens to steam up and fall back down.Recently, my daughter in law, Shannon, visited a local farm in Pittsville called Ard Brac Acres.While there, she picked up some bags of collard greens already cleaned as well as some ham hocks.Shannon put a "modern" touch on this dish, and let me tell you, they were amazing!Look up Ard Brac Acres on social media, as we will definitely be visiting them again soon for more country style dishes. Also, today, Nov. 8, is Shannon's birthday, so I'd like to wish her a very happy birthday!SHANNON's HAM HOCKS AND TURNIP GREENSUse a bag of collard greens purchased from the store. or two bags according to your crock pot size. Place one large or medium ham hock in a crock pot. season with 2 tablespoons minced garlic, 2 tablespoons apple cider vinegar, and 2 tablespoons sugar. Fill the crock pot to the top with chopped greens and pour a 32-ounce container of chicken broth or broth of your choice over greens. sprinkle top with salt and pepper to taste.Cover pot with lid and cook for 7 to 10 hours. Shannon (my daughter-in-law) cooked this and shared it with me. it is delicious and so much easier to make. try it and you will agree.GREEN BEANS WITH BACONThis is tasty, quick and easy. In a large skillet, cook four diced bacon strips with 1/2 cup chopped onion until the bacon is crisp. Meanwhile place 8 cups of fresh green beans, trimmed, in a large saucepan and cover with water. Bring to a boil and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, or until crisp-tender.Drain well and add the bacon mixture. Sprinkle top with salt and pepper and toss to coat. Serve immediately.This recipe is not the one grandmother or mom made, but it is great too.Give it a try.SWEET POTATON' MARSHMALLOWFor a Small casserole dish size. Mix together well with an electric mixer: 1 can sweet potatoes, 1 egg, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 1/4 teaspoons vanilla, 1/3 cup evaporated milk and 1/3 stick of margarine.Mix well and bake in a 350 degree oven for 30 to 40 minutes. Remove from the oven and top with one bag of large marshmallows and return to the oven just until the marshmallows turn golden brown. Remove from the oven and let set for a while before serving.CORNBREAD DRESSING WITH OYSTERS2 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more for greasing the dish, 1 diced yellow onion, 3 diced stalks celery, 5 minced cloves garlic, 8 cups crumbled cornbread, Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, 3 1/2 cups chicken stock, 6 large eggs, 1/2 cup chopped Italian parsley, 1 bunch fresh tarragon with leaves stripped and chopped, 2 cups shucked oysters with their juice. Heat the oven to 350 degrees. Butter a 9-by 13-inch baking dish.In a large skillet, melt the butter over medium heat.When the butter is foamy, add the onion and celery, and cook, stirring frequently, until softened, 6 to 8 minutes. Stir the garlic and cook until aromatic, about 1 minute.Stir in the crumbled cornbread and cook, stirring, until lightly browned, then remove from the heat. In a large bowl, beat the eggs until smooth. Whisk in the chicken stock, parsley and tarragon. Stir in the cornbread mixture and the oysters. Pour the dressing mixture into the prepared baking dish and bake until the dressing is set and golden brown, about 1 hour. (Alternatively, cover and refrigerate overnight before baking; see note.)Let rest for 5 minutes.GREEN BEAN CASSEROLEHeat oven to 350 degrees.In a large bowl, stir together 2 cans of green beans with 1 can of golden mushroom soup, half a can of water, and 1 cup grated cheddar cheese.Lightly mix and transfer to a 2 quart casserole dish. Sprinkle top with one can of fried onions. Cover with foil and bake for 30 minutes. Remove foil and bake for another 15 minutes until bubbly.ASPARAGUS CASSEROLEGoes great with baked ham. In a buttered casserole dish place a layer of asparagus and then a layer of crumbled cheese nips crackers.Wet with cream of mushroom soup mixed with water according to directions on the can. Finish the casserole with a few more crushed cheese nips. Bake in a 350 degree oven until asparagus is tender.OLD FASHIONED BREAD DRESSINGIn a skillet, cook 1 1/2 cups finely chopped onion in 1/3 cup butter with 1 1/2 cups chopped celery until tender.Add this mixture to 8 cups of dry small bread cubes which have been placed in a large pan. Sprinkle with 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, 1/8 teaspoon black pepper, 1/2 teaspoon poultry seasoning, 1/2 teaspoon sage, and combine well. Add 1/4 cup water and 1 beaten egg. Toss together with a fork. Stuff a thawed bird immediately and bake according to directions on the turkey label.ITALIAN GREEN BEAN CASSEROLE6 ounces Parmesan cheese, grated (about 1 1/2 cups), 1. cups Italian-style breadcrumbs, 4 garlic cloves, minced, 1 teaspoon kosher salt,. teaspoon black pepper, divided, 3 (28-oz.) cans Italian-style green beans, drained, 2 (9-oz.) pkg. frozen artichoke hearts, thawed, drained well and chopped,. cup extra-virgin olive oil, chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley.Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Combine Parmesan, breadcrumbs, garlic, salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper in a large bowl. Reserve 1/3 cup of the breadcrumb mixture then set aside. Add green beans, artichoke hearts, and olive oil to bowl with remaining breadcrumb mixture, and fold to combine well. Pour green bean mixture into a lightly greased 13-x 9-inch baking dish. Sprinkle reserved breadcrumb mixture evenly over the casserole.Cover with aluminum foil, and bake until heated through, about 30 minutes. Uncover and bake until lightly golden and bubbly, about 10 minutes. Sprinkle with remaining 1/4 teaspoon pepper, and if desired, chopped parsley.

title: Historic Preservation Alliance gets $150K for Handsell site
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Historic Preservation Alliance gets $150K for Handsell site

 November 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 554
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DORCHESTER COUNTY - The Nanticoke Historic Preservation Alliance was awarded $150,000 in 2023 Chesapeake Gateways Grant funding from the National Park Service to be used for a new center at the Handsell historic site north of Vienna."We were thrilled," NHPA Acting President Midge Ingersoll said. "For the Three Cultures Center, we need about $600,000.This really, to us, was going to be the kickoff." The Three Cultures Center will be built behind the preserved colonial "old brick house," known as Handsell. The house was once a part of Chicone Village, a Native American village."Three Cultures Center will basically provide everything at Handsell that we need to have a really nice, functioning heritage area site for heritage tourism visitors to Dorchester," Ingersoll said.The center will be about 2,500 square feet and will be built in the style of a 19th century barn.It will have public restrooms, an office for the NHPA and a large multipurpose space that can be used for programming and events.The Nanticoke Historic Preservation Alliance restored the historic plantation house known as Handsell. The Handsell house is built on the site of the Chicone Native American village.Ingersoll said that although the Handsell house has been restored and preserved in the last decade, it is small and without heating and plumbing."In order to really accommodate visitors and to have good programming and nice events, we need a building that will have public bathrooms, an office for us, a heated space and a large multipurpose space that can be used for programming, events, exhibits, all that kind of stuff," Ingersoll said.The center will help the NHPA continue to educate the public on the history of three cultures of people who have lived in the Nanticoke River region: Indigenous peoples, European settlers and African Americans."There are three cultures, and we try to tell the story of that contact period of about 100 years when these three very diverse cultures were living together on the same land," Ingersoll said.The NHPA was also awarded $47,500 for this building project from the Maryland Heritage Areas Authority, Ingersoll said.With both grants, the NHPA is about a third of the way to meeting its $600,000 goal.Ingersoll said they have applied for three additional grants that could result in an additional $100,000. She said they hope to get started on the project by the end of 2024 or, at the latest, early 2025.This project is one of 22 projects that NPS is helping to fund through Chesapeake Gateways Grants. According to a news release from NPS Chesapeake Gateways, the grant funding will "bring out familiar, untold, under-appreciated, or yet to be uncovered narratives and to promote resilient communities & landscapes through tourism, sustainability, conservation and local economies throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed." "Through these awards, our partners will affect meaningful change throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed," NPS Chesapeake Gateways Superintendent Wendy O'sullivan said in the news release."These projects are significant elements of our ongoing effort to refresh the National Park Service commitment to Chesapeake places, partners and communities."

content:

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 The Waterfowl Festival - one of the largest and most popular events in Talbot County and on the Eastern Shore - is back for its 52nd annual event.Here are some of the many events scheduled for the big local weekend celebrating ducks, geese, swans and other birds.· The festival kicks off Thursday (Nov. 9) with a Premier Night Party in downtown Easton. All six downtown Easton galleries will be open and the festival's featured artist Pati Stajcar will be at a meet and greet event for VIP guests.Featured poster artist Joe Seme and Stajcar, whose sculptor of crows 'Aesop's Fable' is an artistic centerpiece at the festival, will also be featured at events throughout the weekend· There will be a Salute to Veterans Ceremony on Friday, Nov. 10, starting at 9 a.m. at the VFW hall. That coincides with Veterans Day. The event includes performances by Saints Peter & Paul Choir & Easton Middle School Band (VFW).· The festival features live musical performances throughout the weekend at various local venues. A list of performers, times and locations can be found at https://waterfowlfestival.org/live-music/.· The Working Artists Forum will have its Annual Waterfowl Exhibit at the Church Church's Fellowship Hall in Easton. The WAF exhibit runs Thursday (Nov. 9) through Sunday (Nov. 12) featuring the works of 39 artists affiliated with the local art group. The artists' works will also be available for purchase.· Easton High School will host the 50th Annual Maryland Migratory Game Bird Stamp Design Contest for 2024-2025. The event is a partnership between the Waterfowl Festival and Maryland Department of Natural Resources. Entries will be on display starting Friday (Nov. 10). "People's Choice Voting will take place November 10-11, with judging being held on Saturday, November 11 at p.m.," according to announcement from the state agency.· There will be duck and other waterfowl decoy carvings, instructional events, lectures and exhibit throughout the weekend. That includes live carvings by Tim Kuka and Charles Jobes. The festival also features a photography exhibit and Plein Air Artists.· The festival also features popular field and retriever dog demonstrations, a raptor demonstration and kids and family events. The latter includes cornhole games, painting decoys, a soap carving class, kids' fishing derby and a live duck exhibit. The Chesapeake Mermaid conservation show will also have presentations throughout the weekend.There will also be plenty of food and beverage (including beer and wine) offerings. Waterfowl Festival is a cashless event with only debit and credit cards accepted.For more information and a detailed schedule checkout - waterfowlfestival.org Cover photos (Photo credits):Wikimedia Commons/Gzehn92; Wikimedia Commons/Wilfredor; Wikimedia Commons/Clément Bardot; Wikimedia Commons/Cephas

title: Smithsonian American Women's History Museum gathers stories
content:
Smithsonian American Women's History Museum gathers stories

 November 9, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A8 | Section: News 
 
 385
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Smithsonian American Women's History Museum has launched a new digital campaign on its website to gather stories from the public that will help shape the future of the museum.The campaign will ask contributors to share a story of a woman from their family, community or past who has inspired them to think differently. Submitted stories will feed into the museum's first digital exhibition to launch during Women's History Month in March 2024.Women have contributed to America's most defining moments-moments that shaped constitutional rights, yielded scientific breakthroughs and created the symbols of the nation. Yet a diversity of women's stories has not been widely told.The Smithsonian American Women's History Museum will expand the story of America through the often-untold accounts and accomplishments of women - individually and collectively-to better understand the past and inspire the future."We are excited to see what the stories that people share will uncover," Melanie Adams, interim director of the museum, said in a release. "This campaign is one of our first steps toward increasing the visibility of women in American history and recognizing the women who have shaped this country - in large and small ways. We look forward to sharing these stories with the world online and eventually in person, hopefully on the National Mall alongside other Smithsonian museums, which together create a rich and diverse picture of America's past, present and future." Approved by Congress in 2020, the museum is now seeking a physical location on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., to place women's history at the center of the American story. The storytelling campaign is one of several upcoming digital initiatives from the museum to engage with audiences and share inspiring content in the lead up to the opening of the physical building.About the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum The Smithsonian American Women's History Museum expands the story of America through the often-untold accounts and accomplishments of women - individually and collectively - to better understand our past and inspire our future. Through new scholarship, diverse viewpoints and innovative forms of exhibition, storytelling and participation, the museum inspires the next generation to create a more equitable world.The legislation creating the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum passed Dec. 27, 2020, and the museum is working with Congress to finalize a site for a building. Connect with the museum at womenshistory.si.edu.

title: Art is cornerstone of Waterfowl Festival
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Art is cornerstone of Waterfowl Festival

 November 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 7 | Section: News 
 
 1121
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - The Waterfowl Festival wasn't always an art mecca like it has become.Big time collectors come in droves to find sculptures, wood carvings, paintings and photographs of the natural world. For the very best, you can expect to pay north of $25,000.Or more.Some of the artists are here for the first time and others remember the good old days in '70s."It is an art festival, but it is also a fall festival. It is a celebration of fall on the Eastern Shore. It is that perfect time of year. The geese are flying. It is a homecoming for a lot of kids," said Charles Wrightson, president of the festival.And there is a new alignment of Guyette and Deeter having its massive art auction on Waterfowl Weekend, which will bring many more high roller collectors to the festival.Guyette and Deeter transformed the Country School fieldhouse into a bright white gallery space with millions of dollars worth of decoys, print art.The preview party on Friday night was packed. Some of the work was new and a lot of it was decades old.Other venues to look at and purchase art included the pavilion, the armory and Eastern Shore Land Conservancy, which was dedicated to wildlife photography.Chairman of the Art Committee is Martha Horner, who is in her 45 year at the festival."You should see my house it is full of art. Mostly from here.You can spend anywhere from $200 to there was a painting that sold for $35,000 last night.You can get a print if you can't get an original and they are pretty too," she said.She has been involved since the 1970s."The whole thing has grown in the 45 years. More restaurants, the Avalon, the Academy.And we as a festival are bigger too," she said. "We have like 1,000 volunteers, and they come back and back year after year." Al Barker is a oil painter from New Jersey who creates traditional landscapes."I was here at the inception in 1971," he said. "It was wild. Harry Walsh met me at the door at the mayor council building brought me upstairs.Took out a claw hammer and six penny nails and drove the nails in the wall, and we hung the paintings. Stuck 'em up.Maybe there were five or six artists. I come back. It's a fun weekend. They handle you like you are a movie star." The featured art sculptor was Pati Stajcar, whose bronze sculptor "Aesops Fable" depicts two ravens cunningly placing stones into a pitcher to make it seem like there is more water.The work evokes the dark power of crows and delights in their intelligence.The featured poster artist was Joe Seme from Wilmington, North Carolina. He delights in tromp l'oeil, which means to fool the eye. He loves to see people try to peel something off his paintings when there is nothing there to peel.He is self trained and loved to do mechanical engineering drawing.The poster painting is called "Eastern Shore." People were lined up to get him to sign a poster and roll it up in a tube.And like Northern Dutch painters before, every little item inside the frame of the cabinet in Seme's painting means something.His hero painters are William Harnett, Andrew Wyeth and Winslow Homer. In his poster painting you can find narrative object like a James Michener book, a duck decoy and vintage oyster cans. He is telling the story of a region and paints on illustration board.He said, "I have got to focus on the Eastern Shore. So what is the first thing? A decoy, an oyster can, waterman, books.I have all these books like Tom Horton. John Barth is my favorite writer. The hardest part is the titles. I made the decoy. I used to hunt." "Everything I do is personal," said Seme.There is one artist unlike any of the others. Her sewing-stitched animal portraits contain multitudes. Even within a kingfisher, there is a tropical fish. Whimsy and technique and adamantine focus create these.Implied within the color and pattern is that we are all connected-the flowers, birds and sky. If you are not looking closely, you won't get it. Her name is Susan Schauer, and she charges between $2,500 and $10,000 for these pieces that combine whimsy and conservation."I call myself a thread painter. But I have been told by some people in the art world that I need to come up with a name for what I do, since it isn't something that has been done before. Each piece takes between three and four months to create. I never undo. There are no mistakes. Generally the mistakes, I kind of accept them." Music is part of her process, and she can tell the difference between a night of work with rock and roll versus a night with classical music."I swear I can see a slightly different stitch," said Schauer.This mode of work has broken her out of the box. Even within her own creativity as a painter and a sketch maker, this new media is satisfying."I have finally broken out of 100% realism, and now I added abstraction in a new way.Abstraction has challenged me for 63 years, and I finally feel like I have gotten past that, but still in comfort zone of realism.It is a nice combination," said Schauer.She said she, like naturalist and artist John Audabon, has a true love of realism and getting the anatomy accurate.Sahm Doherty-Sefton, chairwoman of photography exhibit at Eastern Shore Land Conservancy, said "there are two huge galleries with beautiful work. The photographers are so knowledgeable about each and every situation for their images. You have got everything here from waterbirds, waterfowl, bears, foxes you name it, they have photographed it." Moving in to the galleries, there are several photographers.They have shot in Antarctica to Yellowstone to creeks down the street. There are eagles, bears and killer whales.Wildlife photographer Sharon Denny said "art is important because it is an outlet for everyone to turn to. When everything else in the world is so serious and difficult, it gives you the opportunity to go beyond reality and into a more expansive world of imagination.This has helped me." 
 
 Caption: TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Susan Schauer is a thread painter. Using a simple sewing machine, she renders anatomically correct animals, but with an abstract edge. If you look closer, there are lots of other animals within the plumage. It takes her four months to create one of these.
 
TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Sharon Denny is a Delaware wildlife photographer. She said art gives you an opportunity to go beyond reality to a more expansive world of imagination.
 
TOM MCCALL STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Here is the poster art original by Joe Seme. He carved the decoy below. He told passersby that if they bought the decoy for $15,000, that he would give them the painting.
