title: Filmmaker talks metaphors, process and cinematography
author: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com
content:
Filmmaker talks metaphors, process and cinematography

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com | Page: D3 | Section: News 
 
 1171
 Words 

 Read News Document

 For most of his life, Maryland filmmaker Samuel White has been focused on captivating audiences through the thought-provoking narratives and community-building aspects of his films, a drive that recently brought him recognition at the 2023 Cecil County Independent Film Festival."Through creating art, my hope is to get people wanting to talk about the art," said White. "Even if they disagree, I want people to communicate, talk about ideas and get to know each other and I think that's the reason I make films."White, 33, of Elkton, developed an interest in filmmaking after he saw the 1960 film 'Psycho' when he was 11 years old. White recalls seeing certain shots within the film the artistic intention of which peaked his interest.From that point forward, White took his enjoyment for writing stories and began to think of them as films until he began playing with his grandfather's camcorder to bring his ideas to life. Now, White says filmmaking is his favorite form of storytelling."I can not picture a time in my life where I didn't think cinematically," said White. "I don't know if I showed any talent as a filmmaker when I was a kid but at that time, I learned that the camera is an important storytelling tool."In high school, White was homeschooled under an umbrella program that granted him the opportunity to meet fellow students who were also interested in filmmaking. Based on their shared love of film, White and his friends created the "Cinematography Club," where they would get together and practice different filmmaking techniques.From 2004 to 2008, when White was in high school, video production technology was rapidly evolving with the introduction of HD video and video cameras. After White's senior year of high school, Digital Single Lens Reflection (DSLR) cameras took over the market."With the DSLRs, it was like a 'oh my god, we could actually do this,' moment for me with filmmaking because of how video friendly and available DSLRs became," said White.DSLR cameras often have interchangeable lenses, shoot on compact flash or SD cards and are capable of both still photography and shooting high quality video. To learn more about video technology, White attended Cecil College where he majored in Video Production."When I was at Cecil College, I didn't have an interest in the actual degree, I wanted to get as much hand on tech experience as I could and I did," said White. "It was fantastic because they gave me the tools and opportunities to work and learn with the technology and techniques."White said that his favorite course at Cecil College was called 'Gorilla Filmmaking,' where he had the opportunity to to work with top of the line filmmaking equipment while receiving guidance and criticism on his work from professional photographer and videographer Floyd Dean.During that class, White created his first short film that documented a female character suffering from an unknown problem that was slowly destroying her body. The horror film utilized only music - no dialogue - which White says was intentional, as it left much of the film up for interpretation."For me, the girl running around with her face falling off asking for help and being ignored was kind of like personal feelings I have had throughout my life relating to personal things," said White. "I enjoy films that are abstract that invite you to feel and interpret what you want."White graduated from Cecil College in 2012 and has gone on to build himself a filmmaking portfolio of 14 independent films; six of which he wrote and directed on his own.His most recent film, 'Safewords,' follows a soon-to-be bride and her adventure into an alternative lifestyle.The film won Best Full Length Feature and Best Scriptwriting.Safewords took three weekends for White and his crew of three to create, which he said took about 10 years off of his life expectancy due to stress."I didn't give myself enough time and it was a massive learning experience because of the amount of stuff I didn't know about while making an hour and a half long feature film," said White. "I am proud of the film and I am glad it turned out the way it did."White often holds his new films up against his 2020 film 'The Day Bingo Died,' as he said it is his favorite film that he has made to date.The film follows a brother and a sister who return to their childhood home to euthanize their family dog. Both siblings grieve the loss and decide to go to a bar after burying the dog. The siblings later end up intoxicated and arguing over who loved the dog more, which White said is the "weirdest mix between two adults acting like spoiled drunk children."Odd mix aside, White considers 'The Day Bingo Died' to be his favorite film because it presents viewers with an uncomfortable, yet relatable, view of grief and family."It plays on the power behind words and the expression of grief and how the differences between the two speak to human nature," said White."I love putting people in that uncomfortable space where they don't know if they should laugh or not because the uncomfortable feelings come from situations being relatable."Much of White's inspiration comes from directors Alfred Hitchcock, Lars Von Trier and David Zucker, as well as his personal competitive streak to build and improve film ideas using metaphor.White explained that he often views everything in his life as a scene in a movie, which helps him grow as a filmmaker because it allows him to connect metaphors to true meaning."When something emotional or interesting happens to me, I ask what it would look like visually and how would that fit into a story," said White. "If it's a fear of commitment, my metaphor would be a wedding ring stuck on a finger that irritates the skin - stuff like that."White's consistent hunt for metaphors to add into his films is what he says is the base of traditional filmmaking and is what makes his films art. But to keep the sense of traditional filmmaking alive, White said film festivals are essential as art on the big scene is slowly fading into the background."If you want to be a filmmaker, from now throughout the future, there will be less chances to get your film on an actual big screen, which is why I go to local film festivals - to keep the traditional art form of filmmaking alive because of streaming," said White.Looking to the future, White is working to grow his production company, Outsider Film Company, to a point where it can help independent filmmakers produce their work. The film company currently offers a variety of professional video services and can be found on Instagram or Facebook."I will be making art for the rest of my life," said White. "If you're considering making movies, Cecil County is a great place and you're in a great time period. Get out and give it a try."

 From Jan. 4 tho Feb. 25, the Main Street Gallery in Cambridge will be showing the works of their member artists in a special show called "Serendipity." The dictionary defines serendipity as an unplanned fortunate discovery, and the artists at the city's only artist owned-and-operated cooperative are promising just that."You don't know what you might find at our 'Serendipity' show," said Director Linda Starling."You may discover a beautiful painting at a significant discount or a unique piece of knitwear perfect for a cold winter day.Happy surprises await visitors to this show." Hours for "Serendipity" are Thursdays through Sundays from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.Two Second Saturday events are planned for the show. author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com

Bigger and brighter - Lights shine through fog at Cambridge Christmas parade

 CAMBRIDGE - Shrouded in fog, lights twinkled, blinked and glowed at the 74th annual Cambridge Dorchester County Christmas Parade Saturday evening.Although there was no snow for the "Snowflakes on Parade" theme this year, mild weather and a hazy atmosphere made for perfect parade watching conditions.Linda Bramble, who attended the parade with her nine-year-old granddaughter, Emily, said it was a good night for the parade."The wind's not blowing," she said, adding that the fog was a neat addition to the parade.Parade Co-chairman Bruce McWilliams thanked mother nature for stopping rain from pouring down Saturday evening."The fog made for some really nice pictures," he said.There were 105 floats registered in the parade this year, a few of which McWilliams said he knew didn't show.From bright red firetrucks to trucks decked out in wreaths and colorful lights to trailer beds covered in fake snow, residents and visitors watching the parade had a lot to keep them captivated. Floats embarked from Long Wharf Park, traveling down High, Poplar and Race streets before ending on Washington Street.A variety of performances, from marching bands to dance groups were interspersed throughout the parade.Ruby Kreiser, 10, said her favorite part, along with all the lights, was seeing the Eastern Shore Dance Academy, who danced to "The Nutcracker" at different spots along the parade route.Kreiser, who also attends the Eastern Shore Dance Academy said she was able to say hello to her friends dancing in the parade.The Dance Academy took home the judge's choice award in the parade.The National Judges Association out of Pennsylvania judged both the marching bands and floats at the parade. The 10 division winners included Dorchester Emergency Medical Services for best noncommercial adult float, Girl Scout Troop 131 for the best noncommercial youth float, Dorchester Dumpin' for the best commercial float and New Creation Marching Unit for the best marching unit on foot.When it came to marching bands, Snow Hill High School won the best band overall category.For best high school band, North Dorchester High School placed first, Mardela Middle and High School placed second and Crisfield High School placed third.For best middle school band, Salisbury Middle School placed first and North Dorchester Middle School placed second.Since the parade, McWilliams said they have received a lot of "super positive comments." "Everybody has said what a great time, what a great parade," he said.McWilliams said they are "extremely thankful" to the community for their donations as well as the participants for showing up."It was definitely a labor of love for the community," he said.And plans for next year's parade are already underway."Yesterday," McWilliams said laughing during an interview Monday about when plans had begun.For the next year's 75th parade, diamonds will be a major focus."Because it's the 75th annual," McWilliams said."We've got a lot of plans to make the 75th really shine."

title: An Old Wye Mill Christmas
author: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com
content:
An Old Wye Mill Christmas

 December 8, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com | Page: 8 | Section: News 
 
 493
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS - Christmas shoppers are offered the opportunity to step back in time and travel to the Old Wye Mill just in time to purchase unique gifts in a piece of history.The Old Wye Mill has been grinding grain on Maryland's Eastern Shore for well over 300 years. It supplied flour to a growing nation-and to George Washington's troops during the War for Independence.And it continues to run even today.Prominent colonial owners of the Mill included Richard Bennett III, Edward Lloyd III and IV (owners of Wye House) and Colonel William Hemsley.During the American Revolution, Hemsley was charged with procuring food for the Continental Army, shipping hundreds of barrels of flour across the Chesapeake Bay from Wye Mill and many others like it on Maryland's Eastern Shore. Historians dubbed the Eastern Shore the "Breadbasket of the Revolution." While the historic mill is open to the public during the warmer months, these Christmas Shoppe opportunities allow the mill to open its doors during the colder months. The last one will be held on Saturday, Dec. 16."We have a variety of items available for purchase perfect for the holiday season," said Ken Groves, vice president of the Mill's operations.In additional to multiple flour options made directly by the mill (wheat, einkorn, rye, barley, cornmeal, grits) the offerings also include Amish jams, baked goods (with flour from the mill), lovely needlepoint items, Christmas tree ornaments, glass knick-knacks, and pottery made by a local artist.Proceeds will go to the Friends of Wye Mill, a volunteer-run nonprofit that preserves and operates the Mill with funding from local and state grants, visitor contributions, and retail sales of stone-ground grain products.Volunteer Mary Alice Casey is the one who solicits and arranges the gifts for shoppers. "I'm the one that likes to organize," Casey said.She is also well-versed in the mill's history and came up with the outline of a children's story that is now being used in a published children's book by Talbot County author Timothy Young.The premise is based on a mouse in the mill that travels back in time through being stuck on the revolving wheel.The organization will welcome Young in a book-signing at the mill on May 4, 2024."We are working to include the book in the fourth grade curriculum in the county schools," said Champ McCulloch, another mill volunteer. "It contains so much history about the local area." To purchase grain products when the Mill is closed, please call 410-827-3850.

title: Dickens Festival summons the Christmas spirit in Chestertown
author: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Dickens Festival summons the Christmas spirit in Chestertown

 December 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 825
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - It was kismet this year's Dickens of a Christmas festival resembled foggy London.Kicking off the annual event, there were 145 runners for the 5k Run Like the Dickens this year; record-breaking participation numbers, said race organizer, Renee Bench.Around 8 a.m., Saturday, participants donned elves costumes, reindeer sweaters, striped stockings, even tutus and dashed through the starting point.The course took them through Wilmer park, around the cemetery, where they were greeted by the Ghost of Christmas Future, onto High Street. Jimi Kinstle, portraying Charles Dickens, encouraged racers at the finish.The quickest time for the men's race was from Theo Penders at 19 minutes and 24 seconds. The quickest time in the women's belonged to Zuleyka Martinez at 21 minutes and 31 seconds.As farmer's market vendors opened up so did the Dickens Welcome Center at 211 High Street.People were greeted at the entrance by Paul Heckles dressed in the fashion of a Victorian gentleman.Patrons could purchase a women's bonnet, have a silhouette of their likeness cut out, make a Christmas star decoration or buy a natural fragrance.Outside, the music kicked off at 10:30 a.m. with the O'McPub Band.Joe Basso and Ryan Allen McKinney took requests from the crowd, singing pub tunes and Celtic-infused pop melodies.After an hour, Kinstle returned, still as Dickens. He read "The Christmas Carol," a classic, which drew people to the ornate furniture placed about for those gathered to sip hot drinks.Kids were thrilled that Santa Clause was at his temporary Chestertown residence near Fountain Park.On Park Row, Kent County 4-H brought horses, goats, rabbits, cows and bunnies for their petting zoo.For those working up an appetite strolling about High Street, vendors like Happy Chicken Bakery and Chester River Spicerie, whose top seller was traditional cider and Masala Chai, were on hand to satisfy their cravings. Oysters were a huge demand as every year.Happy Chicken owner said this year they offered drinks, desserts and meals.Ham Pie, sold out quickly, he said.In the neighboring tent where alcohol was served, the mulled wine was a big hit with the crowd.The refreshments warmed everybody, making them full of good cheer to enjoy the multifaceted performances.After the stand-up comedy by Robert Mac, The American Rogues were greeted with loud cheers. An international Celtic band, the group is known for its multi-instrumental sound including reels, hornpipes, ballads, originals, covers, soundtracks, patriotic and military music and Irish foot-stompers.The six band members showed how versatile they were. Whether it was performing a dancing, upbeat Irish jig, a Guns N' Roses rock n roll cover with bagpipes or doing crowdwork, they had the audience drawn in.Good food, good music, and rousing entertainment was had by many.There were educational opportunities during the festival as well.At the Raymond Arts Center people met Assistant Professor of Literature, Katie Charles, lecturing on "The Making of A Christmas Carol," by Michael Norris.Nina Fleegle, executive director of Mainstreet Chestertown and organizer of the event, said this year was a better turnout than last. The rain stayed away and she was glad to see people coming out in the London-like conditions.She added this year was a little different because they left room for the various performers by choosing not to have as many vendors.This allowed patrons to take in performances like the carolers from River Voices, enjoy music from the Baltimore City Pipe Band and take in a riveting street performance on the steps of the Chesapeake Bank and Trust.There was ample space to see all that capped off by The American Rogues, who were urged by the crowd to keep playing into the night.Chestertown Police Chief Ron Dixon reported there were no issues during the festival. "Everyone was respectful and polite, on the festival grounds and throughout the whole town itself," he said.Pleased with this year's results and thanking the planning committee, volunteers and public, planning for the 2024 Dickens starts almost immediately, Fleegle said.Chestertown Mayor David Foster offered his commendations to Fleegle as well. "Thank you for soldiering through with the rain delay on Friday, and what I saw on Saturday was wonderful," he said.

title: Sweets And Treats For Everyone - Food
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
Sweets And Treats For Everyone - Food

 December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: 16 | Section: News 
 
 1452
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Everyone loves homemade sweets, but especially at Christmas.From the young cook to the young mother to the grandmother to the older great-grandmother to the retiree and the men in the kitchen - we love baking cookies, making candy and frosting loaf cakes to give as Christmas gifts.
These treats are so appreciated by the teacher, the mail carrier, the delivery person, your co-workers, your elderly neighbor, those who are unable to perform baking chores due to disabilities, anyone working right up until Christmas Eve. Everyone loves baked goods no matter who they may be. So many of us just love watching the faces of the recipients also.
The first step and the most important is to have a list of the cookies, candies and cakes you want to make. The second step is to make a list of the ingredients you will need and the third is to get the correct amount of supplies.
Storage containers for the finished products are important. I save cookie tins throughout the year and purchase other types of paper or cardboard containers whenever they are on sale.
Finally, choose the day or two where you can bake all day undisturbed. Carry out pizza that evening for the family. Maybe you want to reserve a day or afternoon for the children or grandchildren to help.
MISS MARY'S CHOCOLATE FUDGE Mix together one bag of semi-sweet chocolate chips, one small can of sweetened condensed milk and 1 tsp vanilla. Microwave for one minute and stir this mixture and pour into a 8 x 8 inch pan. Refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Remove and cut into squares.
ROCKY ROAD CANDY Melt 1/4 cup butter or margarine and 4 cups miniature marshmallows together in a double boiler.
Stir in 6 cups of Rice Krispies.
Press in a buttered pan.
Chill and cut into desired size. You can press some candy into the squares before chilling - preferably soft candies.
HERSHEY'S THUMBPRINTS Cream 1 cup softened butter and mix in 1/2 cup sugar, 1 tsp almond extract, 1/2 tsp salt and 2 cups flour.
Chill overnight. Roll into balls and place on a lightly greased cookie sheet about 2 inches apart. Push your thumb into cookie balls.
Add a small amount of raspberry preserves into the center of each ball - use about 1/4 to 1/2 tsp. Bake at 400 degrees for 10 to 12 minutes or until brown on the bottom. Chill before serving. You can use any favorite preserves.
CHOCOLATE CHIP COOKIES Blend 2 cups of Crisco with 2 cups white sugar.
Add 4 beaten eggs with 4 tsps vanilla; mix well. Add one cup brown sugar, 8 cups flour, 2 tsps salt, 2 tsps baking soda and blend well. Stir in 2 cups of chocolate chips.
Drop a few tsps on a cookie sheet. Bake at 350 degrees until lightly browned.
OATMEAL COOKIES Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Beat together 3/4 cup shortening, 1 cup firmly packed brown sugar, 1/2 cup granulated sugar, 1 egg, 1 tsp vanilla until creamy. Add 3 cups uncooked oats, 1 cup flour, 1 tsp salt, and 1/2 tsp baking soda. Mix well and drop by rounded tsp onto greased cookie sheets. Bake at 350 degrees for 12 - 15 minutes.
You may add chopped nuts, raisins, chocolate chips, and coconut. Makes 5 dozen.
M & M COOKIES Cream together 1 cup shortening, 1 cup packed brown sugar, 1/2 cup white sugar, 2 beaten eggs, and 2 tsps vanilla. Gradually add 2 1/4 cups flour, 1 tsp baking soda, and 1 tsp salt. Mix well and add 1 1/2 cups M & M's and mix. Drop by tspfuls on ungreased cookie sheets. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes at 375 degrees.
Kids love these cookies and like to help make them.
1950'S HOLIDAY PUNCH 1/4 cup sugar, 1 small jar (8 ounces) maraschino cherries,3 cups grapefruit juice, 1 large bottle club soda, 1 large bottle hi-spot lemon soda, 1 large bottle ginger ale, Citrus fruit slices.Combine first three ingredients; pour over ice into a large punch bowl.
Then add ice-cold hi-spot, club soda and ginger ale just before serving. Liquor if desired; stir gently. Makes about 30 punch cup servings.
TRIPLE TREAT HOLIDAY BARS 1 cup sliced natural almonds, finely chopped, 1 cup packed brown sugar,1 cup butter, softened, 1 egg,1 tsp vanilla (or 1/2 tsp vanilla extract and 1/2 tsp almond extract), 1/4 tsp salt, 2 cups all-purpose flour, 3 cups confectioners' sugar, 1/4 cup margarine softened, 1 tsp vanilla, 1 tbsps milk, 1/2 cup diced red candied cherries, 2 squares (2 ounces) unsweetened chocolate, melted and cooled, Whole almonds, for decorating.
Preheat your oven to 300°F. Set aside ¼ cup of the chopped almonds; add the remaining ¾ cup to a large mixing bowl with the brown sugar, butter, egg, vanilla and salt. Use a mixer to cream together until fluffy, then gradually mix in the flour on low speed. Press the cookie dough evenly into the bottom of a 9×13-inch baking pan. Bake for 20-25 minutes until the cookie base is light brown. (It will still be soft.) Remove to a wire rack and allow to cool completely.
Using a mixer, beat the softened butter, confectioners' sugar, vanilla and about 2 tbsps of milk together until fluffy, adding another spoonful or two of milk if the frosting is too thick to be spreadable. Spread the frosting over the crust, then lightly score the frosting into thirds. Sprinkle ¼ cup of finely chopped almonds over one section; in the center section, spread melted chocolate over the frosting.
Decorate the last third with candied cherries, pressing down lightly to make them stick. Chill for about 15 minutes, then cut into individual bars before the chocolate has fully set.
CANDY CANE SNOWBALLS 2 cups butter, softened,1 cup confectioners' sugar, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 3-1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup chopped pecans, 8 ounces white candy coating (melted), 1/3 to 1/2 cup crushed peppermint candies.
Cream butter and confectioners' sugar until light and fluffy, 5-7 minutes.
Beat in vanilla. Gradually beat in flour. Stir in pecans.
Refrigerate, covered, until firm enough to shape, 3-4 hours. Preheat the oven to 350°. Shape dough into 1-in. balls. Place 2 in. apart on ungreased baking sheets.
Bake until lightly browned, about 15 minutes. Remove from pans to wire racks; cool completely. Dip tops of cookies into candy coating, allowing excess to drip off; dip into crushed candies.
Let stand until set.
HOMEMADE PEPPERMINT PATTIES ½ cup sweetened condensed milk, 1½ tsp peppermint extract, 3 cups powdered sugar, 8 ounces dark chocolate chopped, 2 tsp oil. In a medium size bowl mix the sweetened condensed milk, peppermint extract, and powdered sugar together until thick dough forms. Sprinkle some powdered sugar on a flat clean work surface and place the peppermint dough on the sugar.
Using a rolling pin, roll out the dough to about 1/4 inch thickness. Using a medicine cup or other round object, cut out 1 inch circles from the dough. Place onto a wax paper covered baking sheet.
Place the peppermint patties into the fridge to allow to cool for about 30 minutes.
Place the chocolate in a heat safe bowl. Add the oil. Heat the chocolate in the microwave in 15 second intervals until the chocolate is fully melted. Stir until smooth. Using a fork, dip the peppermint patties into the melted chocolate and place back on the wax paper covered baking sheet. Once all patties have been coated, place the tray back in the fridge and allow the chocolate to set for another 30 minutes. Store the peppermint patties in the fridge until ready to be served!
NO COOK CHRISTMAS CANDY 1 box Betty Crocker Home Style Fluffy White Frosting Mix 7.2 oz. box, 1/3 cup light corn syrup, 1/2 cup boiling water, 1 lb. confectioners' sugar, 1 tsp vanilla extract or seeds from 1/2 vanilla bean, Assorted holiday sprinkles.
Cover two or more large baking sheets with parchment paper or waxed paper.
In the bowl of a standing mixer fitted with the whip attachment, combine the frosting mix (dry mix), the corn syrup, and the boiling water. Beat on high speed until stiff peaks form, about 5 minutes. With the mixer still running on medium, slowly add in confectioners' sugar a little at a time; mix until just combined. Don't over mix or you'll deflate the batter. Add the vanilla and mix briefly. The finished mixture should be billowy and light, and a little bit stretchy like classic divinity. Drop candy mixture by the heaping tsp onto the prepared pans. Immediately cover with sprinkles, if desired. Let candies stand, uncovered, until dry to the touch, about 6-8 hours. When the outside of the candies feel firm, turn over. Dry 6 more hours, or overnight. Store candies in an airtight container.

title: Federalsburg Parade Is Frosty Fun
author: Tom Mccall; Tmccall@Chespub.Com
content:
Federalsburg Parade Is Frosty Fun

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; Tmccall@Chespub.Com | Page: B5 | Section: News 
 
 303

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG - On Dec. 11, all the pageantry of the small town of Federalsburg came out.Pint sized beauty queens, manmade soapy snow and bright red fire engines rolled through the town. There was a judges' stand with the town's bicentennial "200" lit up in bright white beneath their stage.
The ballerinas and marching bands delighted the crowds as little kids gathered candy in the dark streets. If there was a Grinch, there was also a Santa.
All the fire apparatus were polished up from Hurlock to Preston to Denton. Federalsburgs' own volunteer fire crews lead the procession.
Several car clubs revved their lights and showed off their customizations.
One car club rolled by the judges' stand in complete silence, other than laughter from within a cockpit.
This inclusive event brought out the wonder in everybody from toddlers to grandmothers. It was cold. There were seated families wrapped in blankets. But people stayed to watch the whole procession on North Main Street.
There were so many Tootsie Rolls thrown that they languished in the street.
The closer you got to the Town Hall building, the more packed the crowd was. Some families brought sacks to gather the candy strewn from the fire engines. They all smiled when the dancing crew stopped in front of the judges and gave it their sassy best.

content:
Holidays - 'Above And Beyond'

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Local garden clubs honor Easton Airport with 80th Anniversary inspired Christmas treesResponding to Maryland's First Lady Dawn Moore's request for a holiday representation of Talbot County at the State Capitol Rotunda in Annapolis, the Talbot County Garden Club and the Oxford Garden Club joined forces once again.
After delivering a Waterfowl Festival themed tree to Annapolis in 2022, the garden clubs teamed for a new 2023 tree celebrating the 80th anniversary of Easton Airport.
"Featuring ornaments made of balsa wood, recycled aviation maps, and delicate punched airplane snowflakes, the flight-themed ornaments adorned a splendid holiday tree delivered to the Rotunda on November 29," according to a news release.
Managers at the Easton airport liked the tree so much they request a similar Christmas tree for the terminal building at the Eastern Shore airfield.
"The Annapolis tree features a handmade tree skirt that mimics the view of Talbot County farm fields and Chesapeake Bay watershed, as seen from the skies above.
The Easton Airport 80th Anniversary artwork, featured in posters and banners around Easton, MD, is also displayed in miniature on the festive trees. A hand-crafted model of Easton Airport's Air Traffic Control Tower, contributed by Dave Putman of the Easton Composite Squadron - Civil Air Patrol, sits atop both trees," release continued.
"We are extremely fortunate to have both of these volunteer-led garden clubs doing good work in Talbot County," Easton Airport Manager Micah Risher said.
"They have gone above and beyond to celebrate the holidays while honoring our 80th anniversary."
The Easton Airport recently marked the beginning of the Airfield Modernization Program with a groundbreaking ceremony in October.
"Over the next 6 to 8 years, roughly 80% of the airfield will be reconstructed, and will include the demolition of the Talbot County Business Center, and the shift of the existing Runway 4/22 1,900 feet southwest of its current position," airport officials.
The local garden advocates are also spreading Christmas and holiday cheer throughout the local area.
"The Talbot County Garden Club also gathered recently to decorate greens to enliven the holidays for the local community.
With help from Easton Utilities, the greens have been installed at the Talbot County Court House, Shore United Bank, and Easton Utilities' headquarters. Additional greens were provided to the Talbot County Free Libraries in Easton and St.
Michaels, the Easton Volunteer Fire Department, the Talbot County Visitor's Center/Easton Economic Development Office, and a number of downtown Easton businesses. In addition, club members fashioned 100 tabletop arrangements to brighten the holidays for local Meals on Wheels clients and will provide holiday arrangements to Talbot Hospice and the Talbot Interfaith Shelter," according to the release on the efforts.

Christmas Cheer - Maryland Stories: Cabaret Carolers Warm Up The Winter With Song

 During a busy month of performances for their talented, youthful group, the Children's Theater of Southern Maryland Cabaret Carolers will continue their merry delivery of glad tidings throughout the area this weekend by hosting a pair of concerts at two Calvert County establishments.Comprised of nearly two dozen elementary and middle school students primarily from Calvert County with several from St. Mary's County added to the mix, the Children's Theater of Southern Maryland Cabaret Carolers will perform on Saturday from 1 to 4 p.m. at Mrs.
Moo's in Prince Frederick then again on Sunday at the Bulrushes Cafe from 9 a.m. to noon.
"The carolers will perform three sets of six to eight songs at each location over those two days," said Southern Maryland Children's Theater public relations and social media manager Lara Reisman, who is slated to be the group's president for two years beginning next month. "Most of the group is from Calvert County, but we have a few from St.
Mary's County. They're a very talented, dedicated vocal group and they love to perform at area venues during the holidays."
In fact, the group's two performances this Saturday at Mrs. Moo's holiday open house and again the following morning at Bulrushes Cafe will put the finishing touches on a very busy month for the carolers.
Last Saturday, Dec. 9, the Cabaret Carolers performed for three hours at the Holidays Tree Lighting in Prince Frederick and several days earlier they performed at Asbury Solomons retirement community.
"The kids love to perform any time of year, but especially around the holidays," said Reisman, who has been associated with the group since its inception in 2001. "They enjoy rehearsing together and they can't wait to perform.
They usually do three sets of six to eight songs beginning at the top of each hour."
While most residents do not associate ice cream with the winter months and upcoming Christmas and New Year's Day holidays, Mrs. Moo's is going to sweeten the pot for the local group by unveiling an ice cream sundae named in their honor on Saturday.
Reisman admits that it is a fitting tribute to a youthful group that provides holiday cheer each winter.
Aly Cross, who has directed the group in "Newsies, Jr.," "A Christmas Story," "Beauty and the Beast" and "Once On This Island Jr." and will be directing "High School Musical" in the spring, also teaches all of the acting classes each semester.
In the spring, the acting classes will be held at the College of Southern Maryland's Prince Frederick campus.
"This group is very, very unique," Cross said.
"We have a great group of kids. There's no pressure on these kids to memorize things. It's a great chance for them all to sing Christmas carols together.
They're learning a little bit of choreography to go along with the songs.
When they performed at the Asbury Solomons they were overwhelmed by the response from the audience."

author: Debra Messick; Special To The Dorchester Star
content:
Hurlock Extends Warm Holiday Welcome

 December 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Debra Messick; Special To The Dorchester Star | Page: 8 | Section: News

 Words 

 Read News Document

 HURLOCK - For its first daytime Christmas parade in several years, the town of Hurlock got to celebrate the season under bright sunny skies, enjoying almost balmy temperatures.Despite the decidedly un-December-like weather, on the traditionally frosty month's second Saturday, Dec. 9, young and old alike turned out to line Main Street, eagerly awaiting the scheduled 12 o'clock noon start to the annual event, which this year featured the theme, "May the joy of the season be felt worldwide."
As the procession's dignitaries, marching bands, fire trucks, vintage vehicles, and festive floats found their places in line, parade emcee DJ Buddy Bloom III, situated across from Mom and Pop's Family Restaurant, kept spirits bright with tunes, updating the crowd as 'kickoff' time drew close.
According to parade director John Stitchberry, Jr., 74 participants in 94 individual units were featured in all. As Bloom introduced each, enthusiastic onlookers clapped and cheered, some sporting holiday themed t-shirts under light jackets, many accentuated with an array of Santa hat styles.
Youngsters eagerly clutched buckets and bags, ready to gather up the precious pre-holiday haul of snack sized Milky Ways, Skittles, and other sugar-laden delights, plus perennial favorites, oldfashioned red and white peppermint morsels, generously tossed their way from each slow moving vehicle and parade helpers on foot.
The town, most often noted for its venerable, historic train station (and popular special run each October), showed an equal reverence for the vintage cars, tractors, and other vehicles appearing throughout the parade, lending a nostalgic 'oldtimey' charm fondly invoking Christmases past.
Numerous area organizations, businesses, and churches, and pageant winners got into the holiday spirit as well, traveling atop work trucks and attached flatbeds creatively transformed into visions of miniature winter wonderlands, some complete with 'magically' conjured blowing snowfall.
As the hour-long event wrapped up, Santa and Mrs. Claus made their pivotal appearance, signaling the parade's end, but just the start of the official Christmas season.

title: Gunston celebrates 'art for everyone'
author: Laura Tayman; ltayman@aol.com
content:
Gunston celebrates 'art for everyone'

 December 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; ltayman@aol.com | Page: 4 | Section: News

 Read News Document

 The extraordinary talents of Gunston School students were on full display for family and friends at the school's mid-year Night of the Arts event.Head of School at Gunston, John Lewis, said the arts are so important that students are required to take art credits every year.
"You see where arts are being cut from schools across the nation," Lewis said. "The arts are not only good for the soul, but they promote collaboration of creativity and communication."
Photographs, woodworking pieces, pottery, drawings, and paintings filled the art room and hallways throughout Everdell Hall. Students in AP Art class offered multiple pieces of their work based on a certain theme.
Junior Isla McCollum chose to create works focusing on changes in life while Emma Sharp chose pieces that contrasted both really colorful subjects along with the starkness of black and white.
"My theme focused on what the world would look like if humans disappeared," student Elena Fraser said. "I included objects that we use every day as well as animals."
All three students said they would like to include art in whatever higher learning they choose to pursue. Marie Thomas, the school's director of External Relations, said they have had numerous students accepted into art schools across the country over the years.
Over on the performing arts side, music was provided by the Gunston Chorale and members of the school's Contemporary Ensemble. Members of the ensemble had collaborated with the Songwriting class to create an original song titled "Different Kind of High."
The school's theater students, the Gunston Players, performed scenes from a collection of Edgar Allen Poe stories, including "The Murders in the Rue Morgue," "The Fall of the House of Usher," The Cask of Amontillado," and the "Tell-Tale Heart."
Poets from the school had recorded themselves reading their own works. Guests were provided copies of the student-produced literary magazine, Debris, a print publication that celebrates the school's student writers and visual artists. The magazine features original artwork, photography, and poetry, and even musical performances (via QR codes).
Several impressive works of environmental art created by Chesapeake Watershed Semester students were on display including an eight foot papier-mâché sturgeon and a sea glass sculpture.
New this year was the "tech art" section which included demonstrations of different types of robotics.

title: Massey Air Museum curator, director retires
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Massey Air Museum curator, director retires

 December 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 484
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALENA - Don Hooker, Massey Air Museum curator and director, is leaving his position and relocating to South Carolina."Don will be massively missed for all that he has done for the Massey Air Museum," said museum volunteer Bill Dougherty who attended Hooker's achievements with a museum goodbye dinner at the airport this month.
Hooker was born in October 1934, on the Isle of Wight, UK, making him barely 6-years-old during the Battle of Britain in 1940. He remembers seeing the swirling high altitude contrails of air battles between the RAF and the Luftwaffe during World War II.
He emigrated to the United States in the early '60s after having worked for Saunders Roe and national service in the Royal Air Force. He came to Massey after retiring from Boeing Vertol as a project engineer on the CH-46 Sea Knight helicopter.
The Massey Air Museum at the Massey Aerodrome is a grass airfield on the Eastern Shore of Maryland that was transformed from corn fields into a working public use airport with a 3,000 feet grass runway that opened in 2001.
The museum was officially opened in 2002 as a non-profit organization dedicated to the education and the preservation of grassroots aviation in this country.
Hooker first started volunteering at Massey in 2007 after moving to Galena. He gravitated to preparation of the earliest artifact displays for the nascent museum.
"With hands-on expertise, he personally helped restore the donated aircraft, engines, etc., to fine display condition with the assistance of other volunteers here at Massey," Dougherty said. "Don took the DC-3 under his wing for restoration and, just as importantly, to maintain it."
"The large DC-3 made for a great experience to climb aboard a larger plane from days gone by," a tourist once wrote about meeting Hooker. "It was awesome to get in the cockpit and experience how pilots used to fly. The other planes on site showed the kids how planes of all sizes worked, including a great 100th anniversary replica of the Wright brothers plane that was restored on the premises."
"My tenure at the museum was wonderful,"
Hooker said. "Our members are all kindred spirits, and our work was such a rewarding experience for me."
Hooker was the driving force behind Massey's popular summer program for high school students titled "Introduction to Aviation Engineering."
"I believe the we need to start sharing our passion for flying with the younger generation," Hooker said.
When asked about his move, Hooker said there were a couple of reasons.
"We have a young grandson in South Carolina we would like to spend time with," Hooker said. "And we really want to downsize our housing situation."
"It's often said that no one is irreplaceable," Dougherty said, "but I fear that is not the case with our good friend and mentor, Don Hooker."

title: Local artists give longtime nativity new life
author: Doug Bishop; dbishop@chespub.com
content:
Local artists give longtime nativity new life

 December 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Doug Bishop; dbishop@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTER - Every year since 1952, the Kent Island Volunteer Fire Department has posted a traditional nativity scene outside the fire house. It began 71 years ago, when the fire department membership voted to have the late James Ball, a member of the fire department and local school art teacher, build and paint the original project. Ball was a former art teacher at the old Stevensville High School, which was located on the site where Stevensville Middle School stands today.The original fire building was constructed in 1947. Not married at the time, Ball resided at the firehouse which was within walking distance of the high school. If a fire alarm was sounded, Ball started all the emer-gency vehicles and opened the bay doors for the volunteers to arrive and have the equipment ready to roll immediately.
In those days, all communications with the fire department was done by rotary phones. There were no cell phones or digital devices to communicate with volunteer firefighters back then. Ball provided a great service living at the firehouse.
This year, members of the Kent Island Creators Club discovered the original nativity was in need of refurbishment and restoring. Though repainted numerous times over the past 71 years, it needed some tender loving care this time. The club mem-bers - Lee Ayers (who orchestrated this project), along with Robin Craig, Candice Whiting, Pam Kline, Kyle Conway, Mari Ann Donnelly and Darlene Winegartner - performed extraordinary detailed work on each of the nativity figures.
The scene depicts the baby Jesus, Joseph and Mary, the three wise men, shepherds, a donkey, a camel and four lambs.
Shortly after Ball completed the original nativity, his health began to fail. As the hospital bills mounted, Ball was unable to pay. The fire department membership voted to cover his hospital costs. Ball died in late 1954. Minutes from the membership meeting show the fire department voted to pay for a Christmas wreath to be placed on Ball's gravesite in December 1954.
Fire department President Jody Schulz said, "We're thankful we still have the nativity. It's a valued part of our fire department history. We've tried to take care of it over the years. We're also very thankful for these very talented local artists who volunteered their skills and talents to preserve it for us."
The nativity is lighted outside the main doors of the firehouse. It can be seen from Route 18 as you drive past the firehouse each night. If you want a more up-close look at the nativity figures, you can drive into the parking lot. Visitors are cautioned not to park in front of the firehouse bay doors. 
 
 Caption: DOUG BISHOP

 Note the detailed work of the images, of Joseph and Mary holding the baby Jesus above the manger filled with straw. The refurbishment was undertaken by members of the local Kent island Creators Club for the Kent Island Volunteer Fire Department.

From left, local Kent Island Creators Club artist Robin Craig, joins firefighters Mills Yslas and Patrick Reilly. Craig was just one of six other artists who this year repainted the nativity scene figures.

 The three "Wise men" with fresh paint on them. originally constructed in 1952, it has weathered the years and is stored within the firehouse during the other 11 months of the year.

title: Sculptor bends metal and wood - Local artist draws influence from past experience and the nature of the Chesapeake
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Sculptor bends metal and wood - Local artist draws influence from past experience and the nature of the Chesapeake

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 890
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROYAL OAK - Sculptor Cole Meyerhoff's workshop is full of clamps, power saws and TIG welders. He can cut and bend metal and wood into shapes that please him. He takes pleasure in the color and underlying texture in a board of walnut.He likes a clean solder. He is an avid Log Canoe racer.
Meyerhoff studied art at St. Marys College and has had several interesting and engaging internships from Maine to North Carolina to further his growth and vision.
One even included a stint as a shipwright.
But now he does his work at Darmand Creek Designs, which he relishes. He wears heavily worn Carhartts and a welding helmet.
Meyerhoff got his start when his dad borrowed a welder from a friend. His first weld was in a tractor fender.
"I never saw myself working for someone else. I have always been making or modifying things. I owe a large part of that to my dad," he said. "There is a theme of modification and adjustment. Once you start welding anything could be anything. You can put whatever you want together. It is a ton of fun." "It is like a hot glue gun.
You can go to town," he said.
Meyerhoff makes representational birds and rockfish and anchors. There is a giant metal crab claw at the Trippe Gallery in Easton, a gallery he has worked with for six years.
The art he makes draws heavy influence from his past experiences.
Meyerhoff took a gap year before college. He started that year at the vaunted Haystack Mountain School on Deer Isle, Maine.
"I mapped a year of programs that didn't overlap so it made an apprenticeship.
There were half a dozen studios in session with about 10 people in each one. The ceramics, writing workshops, textiles - they even have a glass hot shop. That was the fun place to hang out at the end of the day because they would just keep working," he said.
"Watching those guys was a lot of fun." After Maine, he went to Penland School of Craft in North Carolina.
"That place was incredible.
A lot of super talented people there. The instructors, the people taking classes all the fellowship artists that were there - that was very eye opening for me," he said.
Like a sailor Meyerhoff stopped in various creative ports before starting his own shop. Mastering craft is the north star that allows him express his vision. And he has a lot of fun doing it.
For the last three months of his gap year, he went to the Island School in the Bahamas for an internship.
This was an ocean based inquiry into native ecosystems.
You can see this appreciation of salty critters in some of his designs.
When he finally got to college he found that there were not many people in the art department doing metal work, which gave him free rein to create.
"My adviser said you have the studio, you have got the budget, nobody else is doing it. Go to town," Meyerhoff said. "That definitely shaped the style of work that I have gotten into now." He points to a 5-foot metal fish on the wall.
"That was the first representational piece that I had done. I have always liked more abstract work that is focused on the monumental, like Mark Di Suvero and Alexander Liberman," he said. "They make these giant metal things. I went to Storm King in upstate New York. It is a sculpture park.
You could spend a couple of days there. The park is huge. To go there and see that stuff in person for the first was spiritual after spending so much time reading about these guys." All this finds its way to what he is doing now, starting with the art trail organized by Mary Lou McAllister in St. Michaels.
"I wanted to do it, but I wanted something that theoretically could be marketable and sell, so I did a heron. It really got me to look more closely at birds.
To really hammer out the details of a heron, there is just so many cool little things. You have to look really hard," he said.
"I have done maybe six or seven birds. A couple of geese, one osprey on a nest.
They have all been in the gallery space with Nanny (The Trippe Art Gallery)," he said.
While his heart is in sculpture, Meyerhoff has a practical side too. He is doing marine fabrication building T-tops for boats.
He has a couple of bending machines to shape the metal for center console boats. One time he fixed a Log Canoe's broken rudder between races.
"I really like making things that you have an interaction with. You can tell when something doesn't feel right, like if you sit on a stool that is a little too small. I learned from making pottery that subtle little things can affect your experience with it," Meyerhoff said.
He is looking to a future of more marine fabrication and creative takes on furniture.
For now, Meyerhoff just likes making things.

 Cole Meyerhoff has many tools for his creative impulses. From massive crab claws to metal fabrication for nautical applications, he can make it.

title: An Italian seafood Christmas feast
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
An Italian seafood Christmas feast

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 1407
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Recently I attended a luncheon that featured mainly Italian dishes, and I was very impressed with both the number of dishes featured and that you could tell they were a labor of love. Especially my favorite - spaghetti and meatballs!My memory went back to my late Italian friend who served Italian Christmas dinners each year in honor of her Italian ancestry. So, I decided to do an Italian dinner this year in memory of my late friend.
In future columns I will feature others. One of the traditions my old friend's family always celebrated was The Feast of Seven Fishes or, Festa dei Sette Pesci.
A southern Italian tradition known as the "Vigilia di Natale" commemorates the wait for the midnight birth of the baby Jesus. Italian-American families around Christmas time gather together to celebrate Christmas with a huge dinner made up of seven different fish and seafood dishes coming in all different types of forms.
Italian-American immigrants - homesick for the land they left behind - combined classic Italian dishes with seafood. The sea was a representation of the connection between their home country and the new one.
The number seven stems from the biblical importance of the number and its lucky connotation. While many of these symbols are taken from Catholicism and Italian tradition, the Feast of the Seven Fishes is virtually unheard of in Italy and instead is considered an Italian-American tradition.
Baked Clams, Baccala, Mussels, Calamari and Lobster are some of the dishes you'll see being served. Here on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, we have oysters, rock fish and so many other forms of seafood native to our bays and Atlantic coast.
For a holiday so widely celebrated, the traditions surrounding Christmas are as unique as the ornaments that decorate your tree.
From decor, songs, stories and gifts, Christmas looks a little bit different in every home across the world, but the "reason for the season" never changes.
Whether you're having any of the below recipes or baking a chicken or turkey or prime rib with potatoes, the time you are spending with family and friends is the most important.
CLAMS WITH LINGUINE
Kosher salt, 12 oz linguine, 4 tbsp unsalted butter, 4 cloves garlic finely chopped, 2 tbsp chopped fresh parsley, pinch of crushed red pepper flakes, 2 dozen littleneck clams (scrubbed), 1/2 cups dry white wine, juice of 1 lemon plus wedges for serving, freshly ground black pepper.
In a large pot of boiling salted water, cook pasta, stirring occasionally, until al dente according to package directions. Drain, reserving 3/4 cup pasta cooking liquid. Meanwhile, in another large pot over medium heat, melt butter.
Add garlic, parsley and red pepper and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add clams and wine. Cover pot with a tight-fitting lid and cook until clam shells open, 7 to 10 minutes. (Discard any unopened clams.) Add lemon juice, linguine and 1/4 cup pasta water, tossing frequently and adding more pasta water if needed, until glossy and warmed through, about 2 minutes; season with salt and black pepper. Divide pasta among bowls. Serve with lemon wedges alongside.
BACON WRAPPED SCALLOPS
1 lb. dry sea scallops (about 14), Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 8 oz bacon (about 7 strips, not thick-cut), 2 tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 clove garlic (smashed), 1 tbsp. fresh thyme leaves, lemon wedges for serving.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Line a rimmed baking sheet with foil. Pat scallops dry with paper towels; season with 1/2 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Cut bacon slices in half crosswise so you get 3-to 4-inch long strips. Wrap bacon around scallops and secure with a toothpick. Arrange scallops on a prepared sheet. In a small skillet over medium heat, melt butter. Add garlic and thyme leaves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute. Spoon butter and thyme over scallops, leaving garlic in the pan. Roast scallops until bacon is crisp and scallops are cooked through, 15 to 20 minutes. Remove toothpicks.
Transfer scallops to a platter and serve warm with lemon wedges alongside.
MUSSELS WITH TOMATO AND GARLIC
2 tbsp. butter, 1 onion chopped, 3 cloves garlic minced, 1 15-oz. can diced tomatoes, 1/2 cup dry white wine, 2 tbsp. freshly chopped parsley, kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 2 lb. mussels (scrubbed and debearded).
In a pot over medium-low heat, melt butter. Add onion and cook until fragrant and soft, 5 minutes, then add garlic and cook until fragrant, 1 minute more. Add diced tomatoes, wine and parsley and stir until combined. Season with salt and pepper. Add mussels and simmer until all shells are open. Discard any shells that aren't open.
Garnish with more parsley and serve with a hard bread such as sour dough.
OYSTERS ROCKEFELLER
2 cloves garlic, 1 cup tightly packed fresh spinach, 1/2 cup roughly chopped green onions, 1/2 cup roughly chopped parsley, leaves and stems, 2 tsp. lemon juice, 1/2 cup (1 stick) butter softened, 3/4 cup Panko bread crumbs, 1/4 cup freshly grated Parmesan, 1 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 1 lb. coarse salt, 24 fresh oysters (shucked, shells reserved), lemon wedges for serving. Position rack in top third of oven and preheat to 450 degrees. Add garlic, spinach, green onions, parsley, lemon juice, butter and Pernod to a food processor and pulse until finely chopped. In a medium bowl combine, panko, Parmesan and oil. Sprinkle coarse salt over a large baking sheet to a depth of 1/2".
Arrange oysters in half shells in salt. Divide spinach mixture among oysters and sprinkle with Parmesan mixture. Bake until the spinach mixture is bubbling and the Panko is deeply golden, about 8 minutes. Serve with lemon wedges alongside.
GARLIC LEMON MAHI MAHI
3 tbsp. unsalted butter divided, 2 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil divided, 4 (4-oz.) mahi mahi fillets, kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 1 lb. asparagus trimmed, 3 cloves garlic finely chopped, 1/4 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 2 lemons (1 sliced, 1 zested and juiced), 1 tbsp. chopped fresh parsley plus more for serving. In a large skillet over medium heat, heat 1 tablespoon butter and 1 tablespoon oil until butter is melted. Add mahi mahi; season with salt and black pepper. Cook, turning occasionally, until golden on both sides, 4 to 5 minutes per side. Transfer to a plate. In the same skillet over medium-high heat, heat the remaining 1 tablespoon oil. Add asparagus and cook, tossing occasionally, until tender, 2 to 4 minutes; season with salt and black pepper. Transfer to a plate with fish. SteIn same skillet over medium heat, melt remaining 2 tablespoons butter. Add garlic and red pepper flakes and cook, stirring occasionally, until fragrant, about 1 minute, then stir in lemon slices, zest, and juice, and parsley.
Remove from heat. Return mahi mahi and asparagus to the skillet and spoon sauce over. Top with parsley before serving.
BAKED COD
4 cod filets (about 1" thick), Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 4 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 1 cup cherry tomatoes, 1 lemon, 2 garlic cloves (smashed but not peeled), 2 sprigs thyme, 2 tbsp. freshly chopped parsley. Preheat the oven to 400 degrees and pat cod filets with a paper towel until dry. Season all over with salt and pepper. Combine olive oil, cherry tomatoes, lemon slices, garlic, and thyme in a 9 by 13 inch baking dish.
Toss to coat and spread into an even layer. Nestle cod pieces into a baking dish.
Bake until fish is opaque and flakes easily with a fork, 15 to 20 minutes, depending on thickness of filets. Serve garnished with parsley, more lemon juice, and pan sauce.
GARLIC PARMESAN FLOUNDER
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 fillets flounder, Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 1/2 cup freshly grated parmesan, 1/4 cup bread crumbs, 4 cloves garlic (minced), juice and zest of 1 lemon, fresh chopped parsley for garnish. Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Drizzle 2 tablespoons of oil on a large baking sheet. Season flounder with salt and pepper.
On a large plate, combine parmesan, bread crumbs, garlic and lemon zest. Season with salt and pepper.
Dredge fish in bread crumb mixture, pressing to coat.
Place fish on a prepared baking sheet and drizzle with remaining 2 tablespoons of oil and lemon juice. Bake until golden and fish flakes easily with a fork, 20 minutes. Squeeze a bit more lemon on top and garnish with chopped parsley.
I wish each and every one of you a safe, warm and blessed holiday with family and friends. 
 
 Caption: METRO CREATIVE SERVICES

 Oysters Rockefeller come together in under half an hour and make a great addition to a holiday spread.

25th Denton parade draws hundreds - Lighting of the green, Christkindlmarkt also appeal to young and old

 DENTON - Hundreds of people lined Denton's Market Street for the town's 25th Holiday Parade 6 p.m. Thursday, Dec. 7.The mild evening was filled with the sights and sounds of an old-fashioned small-town parade.
Fire trucks blared sirens, horns and flashing lights; floats generated bubbles and confetti; some marchers threw candy and waved flags; and marching bands strutted and played holiday music.
On the grandstand was master of ceremonies Keith Shaffer and three judges: Caroline County Teacher of the Year Rob Honer, His Hope Ministries Director Stefanie Johnson and CASA of Caroline Director Amy Horne.
Trophy winners were Schaefer Farms and Greenhouses, first place float; Pure Country 4-H Club, second place float; Denton Volunteer Fire Company, best fire equipment; Lockerman Middle School, best marching band; Grace Upon Grace Dance Studio, best dance troupe; Maryland Rough Riders, best equestrian unit; Bill and Gail Towers' 1931 John Deere tractor, favorite automobile; Caroline-Dorchester County 4-H Fair Queen Skylar Blunt, favorite royalty; and Chesapeake Culinary Center, best use of lights.
The parade began at the Health and Public Services Building on South Seventh Street, and made its way down Market Street, past the Caroline County Courthouse, where the Rotary Club of Denton hosted the lighting of the historic green, along with the Caroline County Garden Club and Caroline County Recreation and Parks.
Rotary Club President Angel Perez welcomed the crowd, and members of the North Caroline High School chorus sang holiday songs and led the singing of "Silent Night." Shoppers lingered along Market Street and popped in and out of stores as they made their way along the shopping district.
For the first time, the outdoor Christkindlmarkt, sponsored by Downtown Denton Main Street Inc. was held in conjunction with the parade. Starting at 5 p.m. and ending at 8:30 p.m., the outdoor holiday market on the green at Third and Market streets featured a large lighted Christmas tree, craft vendors, food trucks, and Santa and Mrs. Claus.
Patti Wood of Patti's Petals welcomed the combined events. "The more the merrier," she said. "It helps to bring foot traffic in, and that's what we want."

 OXFORD - Less than two weeks remain to apply for the 40th prestigious Oxford Fine Arts 2024 show.The application is online with only three images required for submission.
Oxford Fine Arts has grown to welcome up to 50 top artists from the Mid-Atlantic region.
The new juror is Barrie Barnett, and the event chair is Karen Walbridge.
The images are sent to the juror anonymously, which always creates wonderful surprises as the juror curates the show based on a wide variety of high-quality mediums.
"Oxford Community Center is excited to create a dynamic experience for both the artist and the art enthusiast," the community center said in a press release. "The Fine Arts Committee is actively soliciting new Awards this year too! The 40th anniversary invites extra promotional activity and a broader reach, inviting even more regional artists to apply." The juried selection is shared with the accepted artists and announced to the public mid-February once the participants are confirmed. March through May, extensive promotions ensue and set the stage for a successful exhibition.
The show will be on display May 17 to 19.
The application Deadline is Dec. 31.
A $30 application fee is required for the online submission. Artists attend the opening preview gala on Friday, May 17, as meet-and-greet with passionate collectors. The following Saturday and Sunday, the gallery is open for sales 10 to 5 p.m.
Each day will offer opportunities to see artists' demos and enjoy the show.
Tickets to the gala include a free pass for the rest of the weekend so art lovers can return often.
For more information and to submit work for the 2024 show, visit oxfordcc.org or call 410-226-5904.
To learn more about Barnett, visit her website, barriebarnett.com.
The show has supported the Oxford Community Center since the 1980s with 30% of sales used to help fund OCC's mission to provide the region with a year-round schedule of free or reduced educational, cultural and recreational programs and events. title: Story swap to showcase the stories of the Mid-Shore's watermen
author: CONTRIBUTED
content:
Story swap to showcase the stories of the Mid-Shore's watermen

 December 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 682
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The son of a Kent Island waterman, Brent Lewis, has been around men and women who make their living on the Chesapeake Bay his entire life.Lewis said his mother early on shut down any thought that he might follow that path, but over the years, the local author and historian's appreciation for the demanding work and the characters who keep the industry alive has only increased.
It's why Lewis is so passionate about offering watermen a platform to share their stories.
"Living here for so long, I just had this idea that a lot of the people in our community don't really understand the watermen's life or what they do," said Lewis, who will host a Watermen's Story Swap on Thursday, Jan. 11 at 5:30 p.m. in the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum's Van Lennep Auditorium.
Lewis has emceed a handful of similar events over the past decade, and he's realized the power of gathering watermen together to explain their shared experience through enlightening, funny and often profound tales.
At CBMM, Lewis will lead a panel that features both working and retired watermen hailing from around the Eastern Shore.
The suggested ticket price is $8 per participant, with both in-person and virtual options available at cbmm.org/WatermenStorySwap.
The event is funded through CBMM's Regional Folklife Center under the Maryland Traditions program of the Maryland State Arts Council.
Lewis has found certain themes - mentors, bad weather, and unexpected Bay adventures, to name a few - to be universal, but ultimately, it's the panelists' unique memories collected over years on the water and the free-flowing format that make these conversations equal parts entertaining and unpredictable.
"You never know where we're going to end up," Lewis said. "We don't have to stick to the topics as long as everyone's involved and having fun. It kind of runs the gamut between really hearty belly laughs to more emotional storytelling." The author of four books with a fifth underway, Lewis has long helmed an oral history project with the Kent Island Heritage Society, and at the first story swap in 2016, held before a standing-room crowd in Grasonville, he brought together eight watermen who he'd interviewed for that project.
There have been other iterations, including a couple at Chesapeake College's Chesapeake Storytelling Festival, but it's been more than five years since the last one.
Lewis found a partner in CBMM through its Folklife Center to launch the latest Watermen's Story Swap, this time with the focus expanding beyond Queen Anne's County.
He and videographer Josh Willis are recording an ongoing series of oral histories as part of the partnership.
The Jan. 11 Speaker Event, bringing together watermen from the mid and lower Eastern Shore, will be documented among that group.
Lewis said working with CBMM's Director of Curatorial Affairs & Exhibitions Jen Dolde and Vice President of Education & Interpretation Jill Ferris has breathed new life into the project by backing his belief in the importance of capturing these stories - both the ordinary and extraordinary.
"Working with CBMM, their enthusiasm for getting these stories down before they're gone has helped keep my enthusiasm up," Lewis said. "I can tell by talking to Jen and Jill that this is something that they feel is positive and beneficial to the community. If we don't take the opportunity to document these watermen's stories, once they're gone, they're gone." As much as anything, Lewis is excited to reach a new audience with this Story Swap. He's worked hard to assemble a panel that will represent different voices within the industry and bring together watermen from across the Chesapeake.
With the group spanning geography and generations all together on Jan. 11, Lewis will start the conversation and see where it goes.
"It's a lot of fun," Lewis said. "If it goes right - and knock on wood I've never had one go badly - it's very entertaining, it's very informative, and I don't think the audience members forget it very quickly." 
 
 Caption: COURTESY OF KAREN SADLER

 CBMM will host a Watermen's Story Swap on Jan. 11 in the Van Lennep Auditorium, bringing together local watermen for a lively evening of tales about life working the Bay.

title: Massey Air Museum curator, director retires
author: LAURA TAYMAN
content:
Massey Air Museum curator, director retires

 December 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LAURA TAYMAN | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 488
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALENA - Don Hooker, Massey Air Museum curator and director, is leaving his position and relocating to South Carolina."Don will be massively missed for all that he has done for the Massey Air Museum," said museum volunteer Bill Dougherty who attended Hooker's achievements with a museum goodbye dinner at the airport this month.
Hooker was born in October 1934, on the Isle of Wight, UK, making him barely 6-years-old during the Battle of Britain in 1940. He remembers seeing the swirling high altitude contrails of air battles between the RAF and the Luftwaffe during World War II.
He emigrated to the United States in the early '60s after having worked for Saunders Roe and national service in the Royal Air Force. He came to Massey after retiring from Boeing Vertol as a project engineer on the CH-46 Sea Knight helicopter.
The Massey Air Museum at the Massey Aerodrome is a grass airfield on the Eastern Shore of Maryland that was transformed from corn fields into a working public use airport with a 3,000 feet grass runway that opened in 2001.
The museum was officially opened in 2002 as a non-profit organization dedicated to the education and the preservation of grassroots aviation in this country.
Hooker first started volunteering at Massey in 2007 after moving to Galena. He gravitated to preparation of the earliest artifact displays for the nascent museum.
"With hands-on expertise, he personally helped restore the donated aircraft, engines, etc., to fine display condition with the assistance of other volunteers here at Massey," Dougherty said.
"Don took the DC-3 under his wing for restoration and, just as importantly, to maintain it." "The large DC-3 made for a great experience to climb aboard a larger plane from days gone by," a tourist once wrote about meeting Hooker. "It was awesome to get in the cockpit and experience how pilots used to fly. The other planes on site showed the kids how planes of all sizes worked, including a great 100th anniversary replica of the Wright brothers plane that was restored on the premises." "My tenure at the museum was wonderful," Hooker said.
"Our members are all kindred spirits, and our work was such a rewarding experience for me." Hooker was the driving force behind Massey's popular summer program for high school students titled "Introduction to Aviation Engineering." "I believe the we need to start sharing our passion for flying with the younger generation," Hooker said.
When asked about his move, Hooker said there were a couple of reasons.
"We have a young grandson in South Carolina we would like to spend time with," Hooker said.
"And we really want to downsize our housing situation." "It's often said that no one is irreplaceable," Dougherty said, "but I fear that is not the case with our good friend and mentor, Don Hooker."

 OXFORD - Tred Avon Players unveiled an exciting lineup for the coming year as it enters its 43rd season of providing live theater to the Eastern Shore.The shows will be performed in partnership with the Oxford Community Center at 200 Oxford Road.
Flex Passes and individual ticket sales are available for all four shows at www.tredavonplayers.org.
'YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO REMAIN DEAD'
By Pat Cook Directed by Rob Sanchez Feb. 15-25, 2024 In this hilarious audience-participation murder mystery, narrator Harnell Chesterton takes the audience to visit a small community theater group staging a play set in the Deep South. The play's characters are all in an uproar because Fat Daddy, the patriarch of the family, is about to change his will. Is Fat Daddy the target of the killer? Is his wife, Sweet Mamma, looking to do him in? Or is it his son Earl, daughter-in-law Savannah or daughter Hyacinth?
Maybe it's the hired hand Clete! But - is it really Fat Daddy who is dead? Just wait until local police sleuth Officer Bainbridge begins his investigation!
'THE BOYS FROM SYRACUSE'
By George Abbott Music & Lyrics by Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart Directed by Liz Clarke April 18-28, 2024 The Boys from Syracuse is a spirited adaptation of Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors. Antipholus of Syracuse and his servant Dromio embark on a quest to find Antipholus' lost twin in the city of Ephesus, leading to a series of comical misadventures.
Against the backdrop of war between Ephesus and Syracuse, the travelers navigate chaos, encountering mistaken identities and humorous situations.
As Antipholus of Ephesus becomes entangled in debts and love interests, the narrative unfolds in a whirlwind of hilarity. Set in the 1930s, the musical features a fast-paced, funny script by George Abbott and a swinging score with timeless tunes like "Falling in Love With Love," "This Can't Be Love," and "Sing for Your Supper." "The Boys from Syracuse" is a delightful and tuneful tribute to Shakespeare's enduring comedic masterpiece.
'THE HALLELUJAH GIRLS'
By Jessie Jones, Nicholas Hope, Jamie Wooten Directed by Sammie Mooney Aug. 15-25, 2024 Hilarity ensues in the small town of Eden Falls, Georgia, as a group of spirited women decide to transform their lives at SPADEE-DAH!, an abandoned church-turned-day-spa.
Meeting every Friday, the friends, led by the high-spirited Sugar Lee, confront the realities of time and loss after the passing of a dear friend.
Each woman faces unique challenges - from romantic disillusionment and family troubles to stagnant marriages.
As they strive to pursue their dreams and embrace change, the women navigate comic twists involving unexpected ex-boyfriends, unlikely marriage proposals, and a determined rival threatening their beloved spa. Amidst the laughter and joy, this rollicking Southern comedy captures the women's journey overcoming obstacles, forging new paths and celebrating the bonds of friendship.
'BLITHE SPIRIT'
By Noel Coward Directed by Susan Patterson Oct. 24 to Nov. 3, 2024 Blithe Spirit unfolds in the home of writer Charles Condomine and his wife, Ruth.
Charles invites the eccentric medium Madame Arcati for a seance to gather inspiration for his book. Unexpectedly, the seance brings back Charles' first wife, Elvira, causing mischief that only he can witness.
Elvira accidentally causes Ruth's demise, resulting in Charles being haunted by both wives. The trio seeks Madame Arcati's help to send the spirits back, blending farce, emotion, and wit in this intensely funny and character-driven play.
