title: Stepping into the past - Museum explores Tubman's life through murals
author: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Stepping into the past - Museum explores Tubman's life through murals

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; mtrovato@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 941
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - In the back of the Harriet Tubman Museum and Educational Center on Race Street, one wall acts as a window into Tubman's life.Inside the museum, on one side of the wall, Tubman is painted as a young girl, about 13-years-old, at the Bucktown General Store.
"This was a pivotal time in her life," Linda Harris, the museum's director of events and docent, said. "It was considered her first act of defiance." Outside the museum, on the other side of the wall, Tubman is an adult, holding out her hand.
"(She's) coming back, rescuing family and those that wanted freedom," artist of both murals, Michael Rosato said.
Harriet Tubman, an abolitionist and social activist who was born into and escaped from slavery in Dorchester County in the 19th century, became well-known for her work on the Underground Railroad, a network of routes and safe houses that helped enslaved people escape to their freedom.
Inside the museum, the mural of a young Tubman and the Bucktown Store covers the entire wall - and the other three walls in the room.
With canvas and paint, Rosato has transformed the back room of the museum into the Bucktown Store, a significant place in Tubman's history.
The story goes that Tubman was asked to go to the Bucktown Store to get something for the master.
"And she didn't want to do it," Bill Jarmon, president of the Harriet Tubman Organization, said.
"Part of it had to do with the fact that she wasn't presentable." It had to do with her hair, Jarmon said. So she covered her hair with a cloth made from flaxseed.
When Tubman got to the store, she heard a noise at the backdoor and saw a young boy struggling to get away from his master. When the boy escapes and runs toward the door, Tubman is told to stop him. But she doesn't. She steps out of the way to let him go through. "Her first act of defiance," as Harris said.
As the boy escaped, Jarmon said, a two-pound weight was thrown at him.
However, the weight hit Tubman in the forehead instead, knocking her unconscious.
Harris considers Tubman's head wrap to be a very important piece of this story.
"She wraps her head in this linen made of flaxseed, which in fact - what I'm reading and what I believe now - cushions the blow from that two-pound weight being hurled at her," Harris said.
"Imagine if she had fixed her hair that day. She'd be dead." Sitting in the back room of the museum Wednesday, Dec. 20, Jarmon and Harris pointed to different parts of the room as they told the story. When they officially open this part of the museum - which they hope to do in January - visitors will feel even more immersed in the story.
They plan to put in wood floors and counters to resemble the store. And as they tell the story of Tubman's first act of defiance, Harris said she and her husband will play code songs, songs enslaved people used to share messages.
Eventually, Harris hopes to offer virtual reality goggles to visitors when they enter the room.
"We're going to make this thing come alive," she said.
The idea to do this all started when Harris learned that she would no longer be able to take visitors on tours inside the original Bucktown Store.
Harris said that considering how pivotal the store was in Tubman's life, she couldn't have people visit and not learn the story.
"So I said, 'Well, let's put it in the museum,'" Harris said.
To begin the project, Rosato, who lives in Church Creek and has been an artist for 33 years, went to the store and took photos of the walls.
"Every square inch of the walls and what was on the shelves," he said.
After that, he took the photos back to his studio on Race Street and put paint to canvas.
"(I) just started to recreate the store as close as possible and in a somewhat realistic fashion so when you're in that space you feel as though you can take things off the shelves," he said.
After completing each wall on the canvas, he would bring the canvases to the museum and glue them to the walls so that it looked as if he had painted directly on walls of the museum. To make it look as realistic as possible, Rosato had to consider light, shadow and perspective.
"When you create a painting that you want to look real and dimensional, you have to understand perspective and find the right vanishing point," he said.
"So when you're standing right in the middle of that room, every wall you look at, all the lines converge to a certain point. And that's what gives it a sense of depth." The project, which Rosato worked on in the fall, took between one and two months to complete.
He said that once it is open to visitors, he hopes they will get a sense of the rich history of Tubman's experience in Dorchester County.
"The possibility of being able to stand there and reflect back like, 'I'm in the store where she is.
This is what happened,'" he said. "And then going outside and seeing (adult) Harriet Tubman. This is the outcome."

title: 'It takes the whole community' - Academy Art Museum director reflects on Easton experience before leaving for New York
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
'It takes the whole community' - Academy Art Museum director reflects on Easton experience before leaving for New York

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: Community 
 
 932
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Academy Art Museum Director Sarah Jesse is moving on to the University of Rochester in March after a three-year stint in Talbot County.Although this institute is orders of magnitude bigger, she will continue her focus on community engagement with the arts.
Feb. 23 is her last day before she moves on to be director of the Memorial Art Gallery. She said she has enjoyed living and working in Easton. There is a search committee for the next candidate.
"I love this place. I love the people. I love the staff and the people who support this place. I love how important this place is to the area and how beloved it is," Jesse said. "That has made this job feel very rewarding. This has been a total professional highlight for me coming here. I have learned so much, and it has been excellent training for my next step. It has been so fun. I will miss it a lot." She feels she is leaving the Academy in excellent hands, and it is in excellent shape. Looking forward, her next post is in a larger city and connected to a university.
"It is a bigger institution.
The operating budget is $9 million, and the operating budget of this (The Academy) is $1.6 million.
So with that comes more resources, more bandwidth, more opportunity to do more ambitious projects.
It is bigger. It is a very large museum," Jesse said.
She worked at the museum at her undergraduate alma matter Oberlin College in Ohio, and the experience touched her.
She was first generation to go to college.
The Oberlin museum gave prized artworks, like those by Robert Rauschenberg, to students to live with in their dorm rooms. She wants to give that kind of radical outreach to the students at the University of Rochester.
"I have worked in museums for over 20 years.
Ultimately it comes from my working class background and growing up in a rural part of Michigan.
My parents worked in the automotive industry, and my parents did a lot to expose us outside of our rural isolated world. We did not have much access to art and culture," Jesse said.
But something from the arts hit her deeply, and she was hooked.
"When I did have a seminal experience at the Detroit Institute of Arts, it spurred this desire to want to have art in my life," she said.
She wanted to work at art institutes that reflected her passion for sharing art with all kinds of people.
"That has always been the motivation for working in the museum field.
Not just to serve the traditional audience, but to serve the nontraditional museum goer," she said.
"I would have considered myself nontraditional.
Seeing how museums have completely transformed my life makes me want to give other people the opportunity to have a relationship to art and to museums." This desire to break down barriers has been a guiding core principle in each of her museum jobs in the last 20 years. She worked with the Academy Art Museum board to get rid of the entrance fee.
They agreed. She called this a home run.
Elitism is a stigma that all museums bear, she said.
"We have more than made up the loss in revenue from the donation box next to the front desk.
And people say to me, 'I feel compelled to support this institution.' My mentor told me, 'Be compelling and the money will come.'" This follows through in her belief of what an art institution could be.
"My unapologetic path is to take this thing designed for the public good and make it for the public good. It has been a total collective effort and total partnership for donors, members, staff.
Everyone is on the same page and that makes it so easy," she said.
She wants to tout the current civil rights photography exhibit that came from the collection at the High Museum in Atlanta.
"The show uses contemporary artists who are using their work to talk about race in the United States. The title of the exhibition is 'A Fire That No Water Could Put Out.' It is taken from Martin Luther King's last speech before he was assassinated," she said. "It is a fitting title for the show because that fire still burns today in terms of we have made progress on civil rights, but there is obviously so much more this country needs to go to overcome the legacy of slavery." "It is an easy case to make for the value of art having this exhibition.
This work helped spur the civil rights movement and it not only documented it, it helped shape it," she said.
Like a librarian, Jesse's role as director is to have art speak to people.
"If you spend the time, if it is good artwork, it will reveal itself to you, it's meaning. It does require discipline and the ability to read images. I love doing in gallery programming where we are in front of a work of art or talking about a work of art with a group of people. Art of itself doesn't always speak to people. Having a facilitator and hearing people's observations can help you find meaning in it," Jesse said.
Speaking of her fondness of the Academy, could also mark her direction forward.
"I want to thank the community. Anything we have accomplished here has been because of collective effort. It takes the whole community of people to make this place live up to its public spirited mission," she said.

title: Black-eyed peas, traditions and superstitions
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
Black-eyed peas, traditions and superstitions

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 1415
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The cooks in my neck of the woods always cooked black-eyed peas for New Year's Day. This carried on for generations and still to this day remains a tradition.Mom bought that bag of peas ahead of time to make sure she had them before they sold out. Then she sat a piece of seasoning meat aside in the smoke house.
The most popular tradition on New Year's Day was to eat the black-eyed peas for good luck all year.
Well, the second biggest tradition of all was that no women were to enter the house on New Year's Day, as that was "bad luck." That did not work for me, as I tried to get out of helping mom cook or do dishes because I lived there and was not entering.
Well years later that changed somewhat to "women who accompanied the men to your house had to let the men enter first.
And I used to say "well let him do the dishes." Mom would cook a large pot of black-eyed peas with her seasoning meat and some potatoes. Then out came the big baking pans filled with homemade biscuits.
Sitting next to the biscuits was a jar of homemade jelly from last summer's canning and a dish with fresh churned butter.
No one asked for dessert, but everyone asked for more peas and biscuits.
From all over the world you find superstitions for New Years Eve and New Year's Day. Here are just a few I have heard over the years.
According to popular folklore or superstition, if these foods are eaten on New Year's Day, they guarantee good luck throughout the year: ¡ Peas or beans are said to symbolize coins or wealth. Choose traditional black-eyed peas, lentils, or beans to make a dish seasoned with pork, ham or sausage.
¡ Greens resemble money, specifically folding money. Make dishes using boiled cabbage or sauerkraut, collard greens, kale, chard, mustard greens, turnip greens or other green, leafy vegetables to ensure good fortune for the coming year.
¡ Pork is considered a sign of prosperity in some cultures because pigs root forward. Many southern New Year's Day dishes contain pork or ham, but feel free to serve a pork roast or baked ham as an entree.
¡ Cornbread might symbolize gold, and besides, it is essential with blackeyed peas and greens.
¡ In other cultures, fish, grapes, and ring-shaped cakes or doughnuts, or cakes with special treats inside symbolize luck.
Some believe that lobster could cause bad luck in the coming year because it moves in a backward direction and could mean setbacks in the year ahead. For the same reason, some believe chicken dishes should be avoided on New Year's Day. Chickens scratch backward, plus they are winged, so your luck could fly away.
Now for some blackeyed pea dishes and dishes people around the United States eat on New Year's Eve or New Year's Day.
BLACK-EYED PEAS
Begin by purchasing a bag of the dried blackeyed peas and soaking them in cold water, covering them. In a large soup pot, place the seasoning meat and cover with water, bring to a boil, let simmer.
After the beans have swollen and doubled in size, rinse in cold water and add to the seasoning meat, add more salt if needed and black pepper. When a rolling boil begins, turn flame back to achieve a steady boil, cover with a lid that is slightly ajar to avoid boiling over. As the beans cook, you can add in the last 45 to 50 minutes some whole corn, dumplings or some peeled white potatoes. Before adding the corn or other additions, check the seasonings.
Serve with your warm breads and enjoy this filling meal any time of the year.
TEXAS CAVAIR
2 14-oz. cans blackeyed peas (drained), 1 15.5-oz. can white hominy (drained), 2 medium tomatoes (chopped), 2 green tomatoes (chopped), 1 medium green bell pepper (chopped), 2 jalapeño peppers (chopped), 1/2 cup onion, (chopped), 1/2 cup fresh cilantro (chopped), 2 garlic cloves (minced), 1 8-oz. bottle Italian dressing, tortilla chips for serving. Stir together the first nine ingredients in a large bowl. Add the dressing to the black-eyed pea mixture, stirring until combined. Cover and chill for 2 hours. Drain. Serve with the tortilla chips.
HOPPIN JOHN WITH BRAISED OXTAIL
1.5 pounds oxtails, 1.5 tbsps salt (divided), 2 tsps black pepper (divided), 6 cups chicken stock, 2 cups dried black-eyed peas (soaked overnight), 2 cups diced yellow onions (from 2 medium onions), 2 cups diced carrots (from 5 medium carrots), 2 cups diced celery (from 4 stalks), 1/4 cup chopped jalapeño chiles (from 2 chiles), 4 garlic cloves (thinly sliced), 5 thyme sprigs, 3 fresh bay leaves. RICE:4 cups water, 1 teaspoon kosher salt, 1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper, 1 cup uncooked jasmine rice, 1/4 cup unsalted butter (cubed), 1/4 cup apple cider vinegar, 1/2 cup chopped scallions.
Prepare the peas: Heat a Dutch oven over high and add canola oil. Sprinkle oxtails evenly with ½ tablespoon of the salt and 1 teaspoon of the black pepper, and place in the Dutch oven. Cook until browned on all sides, about 4 minutes per side. Remove oxtails from the Dutch oven. Pour off drippings, leaving browned bits in the Dutch oven, and add stock. Bring stock to a boil over high, using a wooden spoon to scrape browned bits from the bottom of the Dutch oven. Return oxtails to Dutch oven; reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer until tender, 1½ to 2 hours. Using a slotted spoon, transfer oxtails to a plate, and let cool slightly.
Add peas, onions, carrots, celery, jalapeño, garlic, thyme sprigs, and bay leaves to stock mixture; reduce heat to low, and cook, partially covered, until peas are soft, about 1 hour. Stir in remaining 1 tablespoon salt and 1 teaspoon black pepper.
While peas cook, pick oxtail meat from bones, and set aside. While the peas finish cooking, preheat the oven to 300°F. Bring water, salt, and cayenne pepper to a boil in a medium saucepan over medium-high.
Reduce heat to medium; add rice and stir. Simmer gently, uncovered, stirring occasionally, until rice is al dente, about 15 minutes.
Drain rice in a fine wiremesh strainer, and rinse under cold water. Spread rice out on a rimmed baking sheet. Dry rice in a preheated oven for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Scatter butter evenly over rice, and continue to dry, stirring every few minutes, until all excess moisture has evaporated, and grains are dry and separate, about 5 more minutes. Add oxtail meat and cider vinegar to peas. Using a slotted spoon, transfer peas to a large serving bowl. Add rice, and carefully toss together. (Pour enough oxtail gravy over the top to moisten the peas without making the dish too soupy, about 1 cup.) Garnish with scallions.
INSTANT POT BLACKEYED PEA SOUP
1 tbsp olive oil, 1 cup chopped yellow onion, 1 cup chopped carrots, 1/2 cup chopped celery, 2 large garlic cloves, (minced), 1/4 tsp crushed red pepper, 6 cups chicken broth (such as Swanson's),3 thyme sprigs, 2 cups roughly chopped and stemmed collard greens, 1 14.5-oz. can fire-roasted diced tomatoes (drained), 1 (3/4-lb.) smoked ham hock, 1 lb. dried black-eyed peas (soaked overnight), 2 tbsps red wine vinegar, 1.5 tsps salt, 1 tsp black pepper.
Select the saute setting on Instant Pot or a pressure cooker. Times, instructions, and settings may vary according to cooker brand or model. Select high temperature setting and allow to preheat 2 to 3 minutes.
Add olive oil to the cooker, and heat until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add onion, carrots, and celery; cook, stirring often, until vegetables are softened, 2 to 3 minutes. Stir in garlic and crushed red pepper and cook for 30 seconds. Stir in chicken stock, thyme, collards, tomatoes, ham hock, and black-eyed peas. Press cancel. Cover cooker with lid, and lock in place. Turn the steam release handle to the sealing position.
Select manual/pressure cook setting. Select high pressure for 10 minutes.
(It will take 10 to 15 minutes for the cooker to come up to pressure before cooking begins.) Let the pressure release naturally for 15 minutes. Carefully turn the steam release handle to the venting position and let steam fully escape the float valve. This will take about 2 to 3 minutes. Remove lid from cooker. Remove ham hock from cooker; pull meat off bone, and chop to equal about 1/3 cup. Discard bone. Stir chopped ham, vinegar, salt, and pepper into soup.
Happy new year to all my readers! Here's to a happy and healthy 2024!

title: Digging through Maryland's past - Historic St. Mary's City fort gives glimpse of Colonial life
author: Michael Reid; mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Digging through Maryland's past - Historic St. Mary's City fort gives glimpse of Colonial life

 January 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid; mreid@somdnews.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 838
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It lay buried in the earth for more than 300 years.And though it was discovered five years ago, work continues to this day on the 17th-century St.
Mary's Fort in Historic St.
Mary's City.
The fort, which was built by colonists upon their arrival from England in 1634, existed until 1642 in what is now St. Mary's County.
"We have a pretty decent snapshot of where the lines of the fort are. We have suspicions of where some of the major buildings are," Historic St.
Mary's City Acting Executive Director Travis Parno said. "But we have research questions to the moon and back." "I think it's important to get to know the history of how the first colony started, but we also have a much longer period of occupation out here by the Native Americans," Jessica Edwards, site director, said. "We want to tell everybody's story that was out here." Parno said archaeologists have recovered projectile points dating back 10,000 years, in addition to Colonial-era ceramics, cannonballs, religious artifacts and glass beads that were used for trade.
Recently, the firing mechanism of a 17th-century musket was pulled from the ground.
"The Colonial period was a punctuation mark; it's not the start of a sentence," Parno said. "We have archaeological evidence dating back 9,000 to 11,000 years, so the colonists moving through the area is the tail end of it." Arguably the most important find to date was in 2019 when crew chief Stephanie Stevens discovered a Spanish-made Caravaca cross while sifting dirt.
"I saw the cross sitting there [in the dirt], and I freaked out," Stevens said.
"I started smacking Jess [Edwards'] arm. I could tell it was a significant find." "We were able to determine, and I swear I cannot make this up," Parno said of the find during COVID-19, "that these were given out because they believed they would ward off the effects of pandemics." When the approximately 150 colonists arrived in the area, the location made an impression on Father Andrew White, who wrote it had "as good ground as I suppose is in all Europe," and the Potomac was "the sweetest and greatest river I have ever seen, so that the Thames is but a little finger to it." The colonists likely lived in longhouses built by the Yaocomaco while the fort was being built.
The colonists endured malaria and dysentery, and went through what they called "seasoning," which was if they survived their first year their life expectancy would shoot up. Still, life expectancy was merely 24 for males and 27 for women.
"It's a pretty grim time," Parno said, "which is why we have about 400 burials near the church." Later, the colonists started growing tobacco, which Parno said was "the gold rush of the 17th century," and added it was so lucrative legislation was enacted requiring colonies to have a certain acreage of corn or wheat for every acre of tobacco because "they didn't want people to starve themselves." Parno said relations with the Indigenous people were good, "but that doesn't mean everything was all sunshine and rainbows." That was put to the test a few years later when colonist John Elkin shot and killed a Yaocomaco leader.
In 1642, the Susquehanna killed two colonists near what is now Naval Air Station Patuxent River.
That year is the last time the fort is referenced in official documents.
"Why did the fort disappear?" Parno asked. "That's the big question in my mind." The fort was originally thought to be on the St.
Mary's River, but former longtime chief archaeologist Tim Riordan thought it would be near Mattapany Road - colonists referred to it as the Mattaponi Path - which had a freshwater spring and was used by the Indigenous to reach the river.
"It's about surveillance, it's about control, maintaining a real good eye on what's going on," Parno said.
Riordan referenced a May 30, 1634, letter from Leonard Calvert, which said, "
We have seated ourselues, wthin one halfe mile of the riuer, wthin a pallizado of one hundred and twentie yarde square we haue mounted one peece of ordnance in parts most convenient; a fortification (we thinke) sufficient to defend against any such weake enemies as we haue reason to expect here" "It's the lack of data that we have," Parno said on why excavating the fort is vital. "It's like any sort of scientific frontier where you're dealing with an area that is understudied, under-appreciated and understood. When people think history, the 17th century often gets overlooked, [but it was] the laboratory where all of our social, religious, racial ideas [merged]." For more information or

title: Bishop pays surprise visit to St. Elizabeth's
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com

Bishop pays surprise visit to St. Elizabeth's

 DENTON - The Most Reverend William W. Koenig paid a surprise visit to St. Elizabeth of Hungary Roman Catholic Church the first Sunday of Advent, Dec. 3.It was the bishop's first visit to the church in Denton, which is part of the Caroline County parish that includes St. Benedict Church in Ridgely.
Koenig is bishop of the Catholic Diocese of Wilmington, comprising Delaware and Maryland's Eastern Shore.
Koenig preached the homily and celebrated Holy Communion with the Rev. Christopher Coffiey and Deacon Bill Nickum of Denton. He reminded the congregation who filled the sanctuary that Advent is a time of "longing for a savior."
He shared the story of Saint John Paul II, who visited his native Poland shortly after he was elected pope in 1979.
As Pope John Paul II "offered Mass in Warsaw, there were 300,000 people who attended that Mass, and there were millions who were watching on TV in Poland, as well as the other Eastern European countries," Koenig said.
"He spoke about the faith of the Polish people and their desire for freedom," Koenig said. As the pope preached, a threeword chant arose from the crowd, first quietly, then increasingly louder.
The chant "wasn't 'Communists, go home,' it was, 'We want God, we want God," Koenig said. "They knew that they needed a savior."
"They knew that that Savior was the one who was going to free them from the tyranny of Communist atheism, that the Savior had come to set us free," he said.
"As we begin the season of Advent, may we open our hearts up by first acknowledging and growing in the awareness of our need for a Savior, a Savior who wants us as much as we want him."
The Rev. Christopher Coffiey, pastor of St. Benedict-St. Elizabeth parish thanked the bishop for visiting, recalling that he had mentioned to Koenig a few months earlier that he had not yet visited St.
Elizabeth's, and Koenig answered, "Well, one day I might shock you, and I might come."
"So I think the bishop really fulfilled the Gospel today, which says, 'Ye not know the day nor the hour,'" Coffiey quipped as the congregation laughed.

 EASTON - "Auld Lang Syne," played on the bagpipes by Randy Welch, cascaded down Harrison Street once the giant Maryland crab had descended and the large 2024 sign had lit up.At First Night Talbot, the crab drop signaled the beginning of the new year, as it has for nearly two decades.
This was the first time newlyweds Sheldon and Jodi Neal had witnessed the crab drop. The Caroline County locals decided this was how they wanted the to spend their "last official night of winter break."
"We both work for the school system," Jodi Neal said. "So we're like, what do we do?" Going into 2024, along with getting to celebrate their first anniversary, the Neals are excited to become grandparents. Their grandchild is due in April.
Sheldon Neal said his resolution is to put in more time at the gym.
"Because I've been slacking on that this year," he said. "Eating all her good cooking, you know. It's catching up to me."
Wyatt Burnett and Tory Lydy, who just moved to the area from Arkansas, weren't exactly sure of their 2024 resolutions as they waited for the clock to strike 12.
"Resolutions are hard," Lydy said, adding that her resolution will probably be to travel more.
Although First Night Talbot offers different entertainment and events leading up to the midnight crab drop - including a 9 p.m. crab drop for those who can't make it to midnight - Burnett and Lydy only came out to see the drop.
"We took a nap before we came down here," Burnett said. "Otherwise we would be dead."
Starting at 6 p.m., children could do crafts and play games in the Waterfowl Building, and people could watch performances at Easton Town Hall and the Avalon Theatre.
Karen and Jim Knauss said they enjoyed listening to the Julie Parsons Project play at the Avalon.
"It was nice to see people my age up there performing," Jim Knauss said, laughing.
"And their voices sound really, really good, I thought."
A little after 10:30, The Knausses weren't sure if they would make it to see the crab drop.
"We had dinner at Scossa, so we, on purpose, got two espressos to try and stay awake," Jim Knauss said.
First Night Talbot's was free of charge for its 30th year, giving everyone the opportunity to enjoy the variety of performances and experiences.
"I think it's incredible that the town has offered this freely, which allows families to come in," Karen Knauss said. "It's really nice."

title: Tracking Native American cultural heritage - Washington College's Dr. Julie Markin awarded $40k grant for new archaeological work on Upper Choptank
content:
Tracking Native American cultural heritage - Washington College's Dr. Julie Markin awarded $40k grant for new archaeological work on Upper Choptank

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 610
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Dr. Julie Markin, associate professor of anthropology and archaeology and director of archaeology at Washington College, was recently awarded a $40,000 grant through the Maryland Historical Trust to study the indigenous cultural heritage of Maryland's Upper Eastern Shore and its inhabitants' social landscapes prior to contact with European settlers and explorers.The grant will provide for an archaeological survey and excavation of the watershed, conducted by the Washington College Archaeology Lab, as well as paid internships for students, public programming and presentations, and open lab opportunities which will be open to volunteers from the public at large.
Markin's project unites archaeological data with geographic information, environmental reconstruction and historical accounts, with the goal of developing a more robust database from which to ask questions about the nature and complexity of civilizations on the Chesapeake Bay's Eastern Shore, an area that has historically received less study and attention than its counterpart chiefdoms across the Bay.
"The research proposed by Dr. Markin will help fill a critical gap in our knowledge about pre-contact indigenous history on Maryland's Eastern Shore," said Maryland Historical Trust Chief Archaeologist Dr. Matthew McKnight, who noted that most of the archaeological work in the state requires consideration of cultural resources and archaeological sites in project planning.
"In areas like the Upper Choptank watershed that have seen less development, our understanding of prehistory is much more limited than places where more publicly funded construction is taking place. We are happy to have assistance from Washington College in documenting the important resources of the region for the Maryland Inventory of Historic Properties," said McKnight.
Markin views archaeology as a means by which we can ask, and attempt to answer, when and why inequalities arise.
She notes that even though the Eastern Shore received limited attention from early English settlers, mid-17th-century accounts describe Eastern Shore groups living in chiefdoms headed by hereditary leaders receiving tribute from subordinate groups. Traditional markers of complex chiefdoms - structures with status indicators and maize agriculture - are absent however, suggesting that Eastern Shore complexity has a different flavor.
"In terms of historical records, we don't know much of what the social and economic landscape looked like before John Smith made his way to the Chesapeake and modern-day Maryland," noted Markin. "Extensive archaeological investigation can help construct a better social geography of the Late Woodland/Contact period in the Upper Choptank." In addition to the excavations and fieldwork, Markin has plans to develop public programming that will engage students and community volunteers in open lab sessions throughout the 2024-2025 academic year.
Volunteers from the community will also be invited to participate in archaeological investigations conducted over the next two summers and fieldwork conducted throughout the academic year.
The grant will also allow for the development of public presentations and talks to community organizations about the project and its findings as well as an exhibit at the Caroline County Historical Society building in Denton, which would bring together project interns, the Caroline County Historical Society, and Washington College students minoring in museum, field, and community education.
"The research grant to Professor Markin is not only a testament to her stature as a scholar but also to the innovativeness of her approach to addressing important knowledge gaps," said Washington College Provost and Dean Kiho Kim.
Those wishing to follow along with the research and find out how to participate as a volunteer are encouraged to follow the Washington College Department of Anthropology webpage and Instagram account at@wacanthropology for blogs, short videos and updates from the field.

title: Art on a Plate - The Unstoppable Trend of Charcuterie Boards in Modern Culinary Culture
author: Beth Neels; Wealth Of Geeks
content:
Art on a Plate - The Unstoppable Trend of Charcuterie Boards in Modern Culinary Culture

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Beth Neels; Wealth Of Geeks | Page: 6A | Section: News 
 
 1141
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Charcuterie boards are everywhere you look.According to Simplot Foods, 52% of Americans know about charcuterie. Of those who have tried it, 76% love the concept.
These boards are on social media feeds and in magazines or books. More restaurants offer a charcuterie board as a shareable appetizer or main entree. Entire tables decked out with tons of meats, cheeses, bread, fruits, nuts, and spreads.
Why?
Charcuterie boards are gorgeous. Even simple boards can be" works of art," according to Lauren Moss of WNDU News. They're colorful, and no two are ever the same.
According to the Institute of Culinary Education, the term "charcuterie" comes from the French chair cuit.
The literal translation of this word is "cooked flesh." It refers to the preservation of meat and came about before the days of refrigeration.
Today, charcuterie has taken on a whole new meaning.
These boards have become intricate, often stunning, displays of a chef's individuality.
Why is Charcuterie So Appealing?
Charcuterie boards are perfect for holiday entertaining occasions, but are also all the rage at baby and wedding showers, birthdays, and backyard get-togethers with friends. You could even bring one to the beach with a suitable storage container.
Charcuterie platters are easy to put together. They're a stress-free option, as opposed to more traditional meals. The more random they are, the better.
Charcuterie boards scale to any party size. Some are perfect for large crowds, like this seafood charcuterie board, but they're also excellent for an intimate date night with your partner.
These boards require zero culinary skills. If you can slice a piece of cheese, you can make a charcuterie board. Get the kids involved, too. They love to help place all the goodies. Plus, cleanup is easy. You only have to wash a few serving vessels.
Charcuterie boards are great for entertaining since they encourage people to gather, socialize, try new foods, or choose their favorite pairings.
Have a Theme in Mind Charcuterie boards - or grazing platters - should have a theme. A theme will give you a direction for your planning, buying, and building.
Keep in mind that virtually anything goes.
Use the seasons to your advantage. For instance, incorporate turkey, mini pumpkins, or apples as great options for an autumn board. Use foil-wrapped candies, cookies, cranberries, oranges, or chocolate salami for Christmas.
A Valentine's Day board would be great with raspberries or chocolate-covered strawberries. Make it in the shape of a heart to show that special someone you care.
Hosting a baby shower?
The board could incorporate pink or blue foods, along with cute baby favors. Birthday boards should include the favorite foods of the person you're celebrating.
Edible flowers add a unique touch to a board, such as one themed for spring. Seasonal fruits, like strawberries, are also welcome on these boards.
A game day board could include football-shaped cookies decorated with the teams' colors.
Make It Yourself Businesses that focus just on charcuterie boards are cropping up everywhere, taking advantage of the popularity of charcuterie boards and grazing platters. You can even purchase pre-made boards at your local grocery store or online. These tend to be pricey, however, and usually don't have nearly as many ingredients as the homemade versions.
General Rules for Planning a Board The Huffington Post recommends using at least three types of each type of food for a charcuterie board.
Incorporate different types of cheeses, including soft, hard, and semi-soft cheeses.
For more visual appeal, use several different colors of fruit, like berries, apples, and grapes.
Try new things on every platter, whether a new cheese, starfruit, kiwi, persimmon, or a different type of meat.
Use small bowls or ramekins for dips, jams, pickles, and olives. Be sure to provide serving tools like spoons, forks, tongs, and cheese knives. Affordable utensil kits are available online and at home stores.
Decide which board or boards to use to display the charcuterie. A giant board isn't necessary. Several smaller boards are just as effective.
Plan on serving 2-3 ounces of meats and cheeses for an appetizer portion.
For fruit and vegetables, buy smaller quantities. You will only use one or two apples, even for a large crowd.
If you incorporate plants, make sure they're all edible.
Everything on a charcuterie board should be edible unless it is obviously purely decorative, such as a "Happy Birthday" sign.
Don't Break the Bank A charcuterie "board" doesn't necessarily have to be made of wood. Use whatever you have on hand. Serving boards can be marble, china, or even plastic. Buy them at garage or rummage sales, flea markets, or wherever you can find lovely display pieces at a discount.
Don't over-buy. It's easy to get carried away and spend hundreds of dollars on a charcuterie board, but that's not necessary. Check your pantry or refrigerator before shopping, and use what you have on hand.
Your refrigerator's jams, pickles, or olives are perfect for a board. So are the nuts and crackers stored in the pantry. Also, buy at discount stores instead of high-end stores to lower your costs.
The Assembly Process Start with larger items, since they will be focal points, and space them out on the board. The cheeses are an excellent place to start.
Take hard cheese out of the refrigerator about 30 minutes before service for better flavor. Hard cheeses that aren't quite at room temperature are easier to cut, according to Food & Wine.
The next step is placing the bowls with mustards, jams, jellies, olives, and pickles. Bowls are also good for fruit like blueberries to keep them in one place.
For a stunning board, arrange meats artistically.
Meat roses are all the rage, but there are other artistic ways to place them. They should be easy for guests to pick up, so don't just place them flat on the board. Fold the meats into ribbons or rolls or make small clumps, so picking them up with a small fork is easy. Prepare these ahead of time, wrap them in plastic, and place them in the refrigerator until needed.
Fill in spaces with other fruit cut into single-serve portions. Dried fruits work well here, too. Finally, add nuts and smaller items, but save room on the board for bread and crackers. If there are still some empty holes on the board, strategically place small sprigs of fresh herbs or greens, like arugula or baby kale.
The Final Slice Charcuterie boards are not just trendy. They're a testament to the joy of sharing and the art of presentation.
They're more than just a collection of meats and cheeses.
They're a canvas for creativity and a centerpiece for conversation with friends and family. Best of all, there's no wrong way to make a charcuterie.
So gather up your favorite ingredients and let a charcuterie board make your next gathering a memorable one.

title: Old Christmas - History, traditions and celebrations of Jan. 6 holiday
content:
Old Christmas - History, traditions and celebrations of Jan. 6 holiday

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 479
 Words 

 Read News Document

 You might have thought Christmas was over. You might also associate Jan. 6 with the political events of 2021.But Jan. 6 is actually the end of traditional 12 Days of Christmas celebrations.
The 12 days marks the birth of Jesus (Dec. 25) through the Coming of the Magi (the Three Wise Men).
Some customs count the 12 days from sundown Dec. 25 until the morning of Jan. 6.
Early Christians celebrated Christmas on Jan. 6 until the Roman Empire moved the holiday to Dec. 25 in the 336 A.D. during the reign of Emperor Constantine. The late December date took the place of pagan holidays celebrating Roman gods and the Winter Solstice.
Still, Jan 6. continued to be celebrated as Christmas by Britons and other Europeans in the Julian calendar.
The changeover to the Gregorian calendar in 1582 moved Christmas to Dec. 25 and closer to the Winter Solstice.
It was adopted by the British and Irish in 1752 which helped bring the calendar change to the American colonies.
Other European countries, including Russia and its Eastern European neighbors, did not switch over until the early 20th Century. Orthodox Christians still celebrate Christmas on Jan. 7.
Still, Jan. 6 holds a place in Christmas celebrations for Armenians, the Irish as well as folks in Appalachia and some Christian believers such as the Amish and Mennonites.
Armenians - who are among the earliest in the Christian faith - still celebrate Christmas on Jan. 6.
In Ireland, the Jan. 6 celebrations have included women getting together for their own holiday festivities and the men of their households handling the cooking, cleaning and other chores for a day.
In Appalachia, Old Christmas still has a place for some with traditions such as getting together with family and friends, putting candles in windows and holiday food such as versions of fruitcakes (including apple stack cake), mincemeat pies and Christmas hams and serenading friends and neighbors.
There are also Appalachian superstitions that animals can speak at midnight on Old Christmas Day Jan. 6.
That superstition is on top Appalachians' holiday traditions such as eating ham hocks, black-eyed peas and greens on New Year's Day for good luck.
The Amish and Mennonites also celebrate Old Christmas with cakes, pies and other holiday foods as well as religious services.

title: 160-year-old Indigenous dog pelt studied in Smithsonian’s collection
author: Staff Writer
content:
160-year-old Indigenous dog pelt studied in Smithsonian’s collection

 January 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 1079
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Researchers from the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History led a new analysis that sheds light on the ancestry and genetics of woolly dogs, a now extinct breed of dog that was a fixture of Indigenous Coast Salish communities in the Pacific Northwest for millennia.Anthropologist Logan Kistler and evolutionary molecular biologist Audrey Lin analyzed genetic clues preserved in the pelt of "Mutton," the only known woolly dog fleece in the world, to pinpoint the genes responsible for their highly sought-after woolly fur.
The study's findings, published Dec. 14, 2023, in the journal Science, include interviews contributed by several Coast Salish co-authors, including Elders, Knowledge Keepers and Master Weavers, who provided crucial context about the role woolly dogs played in Coast Salish society.
"Coast Salish traditional perspective was the entire context for understanding the study's findings," said Kistler, the museum's curator of archaeobotany and archaeogenomics.
Coast Salish tribal nations in Washington state and British Columbia bred and cared for woolly dogs for thousands of years. Prized for their thick undercoats, the dogs were sheared like sheep and often kept in pens or on islands to carefully manage their breeding and to care for the canines' health and vitality. Coast Salish weavers used the dogs' wool to craft blankets and other woven items that served a variety of ceremonial and spiritual purposes. Woolly dogs themselves possessed spiritual significance and were often treated as beloved family members. As emblems for many Coast Salish communities, woolly dogs adorned woven baskets and other art forms.
By the mid-19th century, this once thriving dog wool-weaving tradition was in decline. In the late 1850s, naturalist and ethnographer George Gibbs cared for a woolly dog named Mutton. When Mutton died in 1859, Gibbs sent his pelt to the nascent Smithsonian Institution, where the fleece has resided ever since. However, few were aware of the pelt's existence until it was rediscovered in the early 2000s.
Lin first learned about Mutton when she was a Peter Buck postdoctoral fellow at the museum in 2021.
"When I saw Mutton in person for the first time, I was just overcome with excitement," said Lin, who is now a postdoctoral researcher at the American Museum of Natural History. "I had heard from some other people that he was a bit scraggly, but I thought he was gorgeous."
She was surprised to find out that virtually no work had been done on the genetics of woolly dogs, which disappeared around the turn of the 20th century. She teamed up with Kistler and they reached out to several Coast Salish communities to gauge their interest in working together on a potential research project on woolly dogs.
Many in the Coast Salish communities were eager to share their knowledge.
"We were very excited to participate in a study that embraces the most sophisticated Western science with the most established Traditional Knowledge," said Michael Pavel, an Elder from the Skokomish/Twana Coast Salish community in Washington, who remembers hearing about woolly dogs early in his childhood. "It was incredibly rewarding to contribute to this effort to embrace and celebrate our understanding of the woolly dog."
To complement the perspectives they received from Pavel and other Coast Salish people from British Columbia and Washington state (the text from their interviews is available in the study's supplementary materials), Lin, Kistler and their colleagues began analyzing Mutton's genetic code. They sequenced the woolly dog genome and compared it with the genomes of ancient and modern breeds of dogs to determine what set woolly dogs apart. They also identified certain chemical signatures called isotopes in Mutton's pelt to determine the dog's diet and teamed up with noted natural history illustrator Karen Carr to create a life-like reconstruction of what Mutton looked like in the 1850s. Carr's work is the first in-depth reconstruction of a Coast Salish woolly dog in nearly three decades.
Based on the genetic data, the team estimated that woolly dogs diverged from other breeds up to 5,000 years ago — a date that lines up with archaeological remains from the region. They also discovered that Mutton was genetically similar to pre-colonial dogs from Newfoundland and British Columbia. The researchers estimate that nearly 85% of Mutton's ancestry can be linked to pre-colonial dogs. This ancient ancestry is surprising because Mutton lived decades after the introduction of European dog breeds. This makes it likely that Coast Salish communities continued to maintain woolly dogs' unique genetic makeup until right before the dogs were wiped out.
In total, the team analyzed more than 11,000 different genes in Mutton's genome to determine what gave woolly dogs their fluffy fleece and wool fibers that could be spun together to create yarn. They identified 28 genes that have links to hair growth and follicle regeneration. These included a gene that causes a woolly hair phenotype in humans, and another linked to curly hair in other dogs. Similar genes were even activated in the genomes of woolly mammoths.
However, Mutton's genetics could tell the researchers little about what caused the dogs to decline. Traditionally, scholars have speculated that the arrival of machine-made blankets to the region in the early 19th century made woolly dogs expendable. But insights from Pavel and other traditional experts revealed that it was improbable that such a central part of Coast Salish society could be replaced.
Instead, woolly dogs were likely doomed by numerous factors impacting the Coast Salish tribal nations after European settlers arrived. Due to disease and colonial policies of cultural genocide, displacement and forced assimilation, it likely became increasingly difficult or forbidden for Coast Salish communities to maintain their woolly dogs.
"It was thousands of years of very careful maintenance lost within a couple of generations," Lin said.
But despite their disappearance, the memory of woolly dogs is still embedded into Coast Salish society. And Pavel thinks their understanding of woolly dogs is only getting clearer thanks to the new research effort.
"All of our communities held a certain aspect of knowledge about the woolly dog," Pavel said. "But when woven together, as a result of participating in this study, we now have a much more complete understanding."
About the National Museum of Natural History
The National Museum of Natural History is connecting people everywhere with Earth's unfolding story. It is one of the most visited natural history museums in the world. Opened in 1910, the museum is dedicated to maintaining and preserving the world's most extensive collection of natural history specimens and human artifacts. The museum is open daily, except Dec. 25, from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Admission is free. For more information, visit https://naturalhistory.si.edu/.

National Portrait Gallery reveals Oprah Winfrey portrait

 Oprah Winfrey's portrait is now on display at the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery. Chicago-based artist Shawn Michael Warren painted Winfrey in a purple taffeta dress amidst a lush garden at her California home. The full-length portrait with the frame, approximately 6 feet, 10 inches by 5 feet, 8 inches, is commissioned for the museum's permanent collection.As a global media leader, philanthropist, producer, actor, author and entrepreneur, Winfrey has made significant contributions to American popular culture, which earned her a place in the National Portrait Gallery.
The painting was revealed in a ceremony the morning of Dec. 13 in the museum's Robert and Arlene Kogod Courtyard. Speakers included Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch, National Portrait Gallery Director Kim Sajet, Winfrey and Warren. More luminaries from television, publishing, business, arts, culture and Hollywood were in attendance at the portrait reveal.
"Through her rise to fame as host and producer of The Oprah Winfrey Show, Oprah demonstrated an unparalleled ability to connect with people and inspire them to become the best versions of themselves," Sajet said. "Her vision and spirit deserve recognition in the nation's Portrait Gallery, and we are delighted to celebrate her with this commissioned portrait by Shawn Michael Warren, who has reflected her warmth and compassion in this painting."
The commission for this new painting in oil on canvas was led by Rhea L. Combs, the museum's director of curatorial affairs.
"Artist Shawn Michael Warren's remarkable attention to detail and keen knowledge of color theory are fully represented in this vivid, large-scale portrait of Oprah Winfrey," Combs said. "Warren's approach to portraiture includes in-depth study and research, as well as shooting numerous photographs and making various sketches during his sittings. It is apparent that the level of care and keen observation that are a part of his artistic practice are on beautiful display here. As someone who grew up in Chicago watching and admiring Oprah on television, in this painting Warren has been able to deftly capture the wonderful spirit and engaging energy of Oprah Winfrey."

title: Civil Rights Photographs come to Academy Art Museum
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Civil Rights Photographs come to Academy Art Museum

 January 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Arts 
 
 579
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — There is a new photography exhibit about the Civil Rights era hanging at the Academy Art Museum, and to walk through it is to see decades unfold.It is called "A Fire That No Water Could Put Out" and comes from the High Museum of Art in Atlanta. It will be in Easton until March 10.
According to Sarah Jesse, the executive director of the Academy Art Museum, the show was hung chronologically on purpose.
"It makes it like a visual depiction of a history book that stirs your emotions more than just reading a book," she said. "It starts in the late 1950s — so pre Civil Rights movement — to the sanitation worker strikes where Martin Luther King was called in to help resolve the issue. That was his last public speech before he was assassinated. Then it is post Martin Luther King's funeral and what happened in the aftermath all the way to contemporary artists' responses."
These mostly black-and-white images were curated to thread the needle from the freedom riders on their buses to present day protests for Freddy Gray and the Black Lives Matter movement.
The visual iconography of protest used by the photographers was filled with newly integrated schools, white people taunting Black customers at lunch counters and firehoses trying to dissuade crowds from gaining ground.
Gordon Parks, who started as a photojournalist and moved on to direct movies including "Shaft," captured one of the few color images in the show. It depicts a Black family confronted with two seperate water fountains, one marked for use only by white people. It is called "At Segregated Drinking Fountain, Mobile, Alabama" and was taken in 1956.
One of the show's iconic images is "Daddy, I Want To Be Free Too," captured by Ernest Withers in 1961. This silver gelatin print shows a dad pushing his stroller with his daughter past a car of white police officers. Atop the stroller is the message "Daddy, I want to be free too" on a placard.
There are other photographic luminaries like Roy DeCarva, Bruce Davidson, and Danny Lyon, who all have striking images, featured in the exhibit. But when the exhibit leaves the past, it confronts the viewer with a continuation of the Civil Rights movement and Black Americans' struggle for equality into the current time.
One current artist, Dawoud Bey, came up with a time traveling portrait device. He takes a photo of a 10-year-old girl and another of a 70-year-old woman and makes a diptych.
In 60 years, how much has this time traveler seen? How much potential exists in the younger person living under oppression? What if there was no oppression and people could just grow gracefully old?
Jesse had a historically-grounded interpretation of the Bey diptychs that interpret four school girls killed in a Birmingham church for a modern viewer.
"The child is the age that the children, the four girls, were when they were murdered. And the adult is how old they would have been 55 years later," she said. "Loss of innocence and loss of life, loss of potential."
In the introduction to the show it said, "Following his death in Memphis, Dr. King's enormous funeral procession through Atlanta took over the city's streets with thousands of heartbroken Americans who gathered to celebrate his life and legacy. While his assassination is often described as the closing bookend on the Civil Rights movement, activism across the intervening years has proven that the movement for racial equality and justice in the United States is ongoing."

title: Holiday gallery sale features local artists
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Holiday gallery sale features local artists

 January 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Arts 
 
 800
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — A new show is in the works following the astounding success of the November-December annual Holiday Show at the Chestertown RiverArts Gallery. This season, there were plenty of traditional paintings and art pieces but also intricate jewelry, festive holiday crafts and woodworking.Styles ranged from folk, traditional, abstract and whimsical. Patrons could browse or purchase a one-of-a-kind piece over the holidays.
The top sellers this year, RiverArts Board member Carol Droge said, were items like Moravian stars, created by Kris Kelley, the Arts Education Coordinator.
One of Kelley's favorite pieces to make, the stars are made with Tiffany-style stained glass. Each one, Kelley said, takes about an hour to create.
And they made beautiful Christmas decorations.
The stars were placed beside the homemade wreaths, another seasonal best seller.
Like the stars, the design for them is straightforward but elegant. The crafter, Amos Rudderow said they sell as well as anything he's ever done.
Finding everything he needs in his yard, it takes him about 20 minutes to make. The side pieces are hard wood; the uprights are birch branches. The rest is decorative placing using skill Rudderow has honed over the years.
They were a success with the public, selling 22.
Rudderow's wreath-making is closely related to his membership with the All Seasons Garden Club in Chestertown. Since he's retired he's been working with the club on projects, offering scholarships to the science students at the high school since 2013. The club is always looking for new members, meeting on the second Monday of each month during the periods Sept.-Dec. and Feb.-June at the Sacred Heart Roman Catholic Church.
For those who enjoy blending their art with their fashion, Ronn Akins' custom jewelry was on display.
Akins works with semi precious metals, silver and gold filled. The whole process requires finding the items, organizing them on a bead board, fusing glass, cutting and then placing the items in a kiln. His work yielded alluring results, selling 17 of them. A piece of his jewelry takes at least three hours to create. "It's a lot of dedication involved," he said, "but I enjoy it."
For traditional art lovers there was plenty to see and purchase as well. There were impressive flower paintings from Amanda King. She enjoys making floral pieces between her job as a nail technician at "P Nails." Her style is mixed media, using traditional paints as well as pressed flowers.
Her piece, "Olivia," was inspired by the daughter of the owner of the "China House." With all of her art, she thinks about a person she likes when she creates. Relatively new to the Chestertown art scene, she was welcomed by RiverArts with open arms in May. Two pieces she submitted for December, one a painting of poinsettias, and another of pressed black sunflowers were both sold.
King thanked the people who encouraged her to move forward with her art, recalling how nervous she was when she first submitted her works to RiverArts. "They automatically called me an artist," King said. "They were all so welcoming and friendly to me."
She offered encouragement to anyone who wants to pursue art. "I think everybody, if they have a positive attitude, can do this. Don't let shut doors be an obstacle."
Patrons at the gallery could go from King's tapestry of organization and colors to the surreal beauty of an abstract painting by Sheila Exum. Born in Chestertown, Exum's been involved in art since she was a child and has been painting for eight years now. Although many of her pieces are sold, including the latest one in Chestertown entitled, "Misty Copeland," a famous ballerina, she also sees art as a chance to give back to the community. King recently donated art to a ballet company in Wilmington and some sports pieces at a silent auction.
Of all the arts, she enjoys painting the most, and hopes to make it a career one day.
She's taking strides because on Feb. 9, her artwork will be displayed courtesy of the Good Aesthetic Gallery presenting the "TIDAL WAVE" group exhibition at the Rehoboth Art League.
King said her pieces are getting bigger and she is currently working on another painting of a ballerina, acknowledging she appreciates the grace in the postures.
The talent all these artists demonstrated this year was commended by those running the gallery.
Droge said, "Everyone has been extremely helpful and it's been a wonderful turnout."
Right now, the gallery walls are bare while they prepare for the next show on March 1, a new idea featuring clay works.
Executive Director, Chris Sade announced the show will be called "Grounded." The instructor for the Studio, Manager Kris Neiman, will head it up and will feature the works of local clay artists.
Participants will hear from these potters and a little about the process as well, adding a workshop element.
"The community will be amazed at what they can do," Sade said.

title: CBMM unveils new 12,000 square foot Welcome Center
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
CBMM unveils new 12,000 square foot Welcome Center

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Gigantic photographic prints and artifacts, like old duck hunting boats called sink boxes and a log canoe, hang on the walls.There is a scintillating fresnel lens that used to focus light in a lighthouse. It is four feet tall, glass and filled with rainbows.
The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum has built a 12,000 square-foot welcome center that reorients the whole 12 acre campus. Its has clean lines. It is all about function with this museum that is totally flexible in changing up its exhibits.
Now the starting point of where the museum experience begins is clear, and it directs you straight to the opening exhibit — "Navigating the Chesapeake's Maritime Culture" — which is rich with imagery of the region's shipbuilding history.
There are three exhibit spaces and a gift shop in the museum's new space, as well as a wooden ramp to make it fully ADA accessible.
After raising $10 million dollars, CBMM broke ground on the project in 2022. The grand opening was last month.
There is a second exhibit in the new space called "Water Lines: Chesapeake Watercraft Traditions."
This focuses on small crafts, which are suspended in an art-gallery-like setting. What once were covered in salt and barnacles are now hung in the air, ready for inspection by museum-goers.
Jen Dolde, director of curatorial affairs and exhibitions, thinks of the new building as a grounding and a beginning for people to understand CBMM's whole campus.
"They will have the framework to understand what makes this region unique. There are some core concepts we are trying to get across, like the Chesapeake as a highway, the Chesapeake as a community where tradition and innovation intersect," she said.
Jim Koerner, exhibition designer and manager, says he works hand in hand with Dolde.
"It is a collaborative process. We bounce things back and forth, like what objects we want to put in and what stories we want to tell, and then come up with the best ways to present that information," he said. "We look at the whole campus as one story that we want to tell in different chapters."
Koerner likes how the way an object is hung can make it abstract, and thus more curious.
"We have the actual object and then a model diorama next to it that shows how it was used," he said.
Dolde followed him, "It elevates objects of use, everyday objects, tools, and makes them like art."
Every boat is hanging on cantilever racks on the wall.
"We want to elevate them, elevate the artistic aspect, the craft aspect and the functional aspects and the story aspect," Koerner said.
Boats are more than wood and screws.
"We really wanted to take that fundamental appreciation for the craft of shipbuilding and boat building, which is core to what we do, but also bring in the people that used them," Dolde said.
"This building is open storage on steroids. As the months go on, and even from year to year, we have the space and the ability to integrate more and more objects. This will help us tell the story in much richer ways. Flexibility keeps things fresh," she said.

title: Casting call: 'The Boys From Syracuse'

 OXFORD — Tred Avon Players will be hosting auditions for its upcoming musical production of "The Boys From Syracuse," which will be performed April 18 to 28 at the Oxford Community Center.AUDITION DATES
Auditions will be held at the Oxford Community Center, 200 Oxford Road, on:
Tuesday, Jan. 30 from 6 to 8:30 p.m.
Wednesday, Jan. 31 from 6 to 8:30 p.m.
Saturday, Feb. 3 from 1 to 3:30 p.m.
PLAY SUMMARY
Filled with two sets of twins, mistaken identity, and women chased and chaste, "The Boys From Syracuse" was the first musical ever adapted from Shakespeare.
Identical twins Antipholus of Syracuse and Antipholus of Ephesus were separated as children in a shipwreck. Both have menservants, also twins, both named Dromio.
When the Syracuse set arrive in Ephesus, mishaps and mischief ensue as they are mistaken for their brothers by merchants, wives and mistresses. Perplexed partners, disgruntled courtesans and outraged policemen are left in the duo's wake before this show's tangled web is unraveled.
Based on Shakespeare's "The Comedy of Errors," "The Boys From Syracuse" is often considered the finest of all Rodgers and Hart. With big band, late 1930s swing numbers, familiar songs include "Falling in Love with Love," "Sing for Your Supper," and "This Can't Be Love."
CASTING NOTES

CITIZENS OF EPHESUS Male and Female, age 18-70s of all vocal ranges. Spoken roles include Merchant of Ephesus, Merchant of Syracuse, Sorcerer, Tailor, Apprentice, Fatima, Emilia, Maids and Courtesans.
Liz Clarke will direct "The Boys From Syracuse," with Sam Stenecker as music director and Cavin Moore as choreographer. They ask that you come prepared to:
Sing a song of your choosing with two copies (preferred), not to exceed 48 bars of music. Ideally, you will choose music that is in keeping with the character and vocal range of your preferred role.
Learn and dance a short movement sequence.
Read selected scenes from "The Boys From Syracuse" script that will be provided during the audition.
PRODUCTION CREW
"The Boys From Syracuse" will also need a production crew — sets, lights, sound, and stage crew. If you are interested, come to any audition to find out more information, or send an email to auditions@tredavonplayers.org.

 CAMBRIDGE — Bigger and better than before, the Ice and Oyster Festival is coming back to downtown Cambridge for its third year this Saturday.Expected inclement weather prompted festival organizers to cancel Friday night's portion of the event. But on Saturday, Jan. 13, from noon to 8 p.m., the festival will give residents and visitors the chance to check out and take pictures of intricate ice sculptures, eat oysters from different vendors and listen to live music.

Dorchester Chamber of Commerce President Bill Christopher said there will be nearly 50 ice sculptures at the festival this year.

Although some of the sculptures are pre-carved, others are carved in place. Christopher said Ice Lab has been working on the pre-carved sculptures since early December.
"Ice Lab does an awesome job, in terms of what they do, in terms of building these sculptures," he said. "I absolutely encourage people to come out and watch them and see what they do."
For the "oyster" part of the festival, more than five oyster vendors will be at the event. Those who aren't big oyster fans are encouraged to try out downtown Cambridge's local restaurants, Christopher said.
There will be two different stages with live music playing throughout the festival.

title: 'Ingenuity Mars Helicopter' prototype joins the National Air and Space Museum collection
author: Staff Writer
content:
'Ingenuity Mars Helicopter' prototype joins the National Air and Space Museum collection

 January 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 433
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum has accepted into its collection an aerial prototype of the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter. The prototype has been donated to the museum by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.In April 2021, Ingenuity became the first aircraft to fly in the atmosphere of another planet when it made its first flight on Mars. The prototype NASA has donated to the museum was used in tests at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in a simulated Mars environment and was the first Ingenuity prototype to demonstrate that flight on Mars was possible. The results of those tests gave NASA the confidence to commit to sending Ingenuity there.
"None of Ingenuity's accomplishments would have been possible without years of development and testing, requiring prototypes and engineering and flight models to learn and better understand design challenges and work through solutions," said Matt Shindell, curator of planetary exploration at the National Air and Space Museum. "We are excited to bring this crucial piece of this story into our collection."
In May 2016, the prototype Mars helicopter achieved the first powered, controlled free flight in simulated Mars atmospheric conditions. The test took place inside JPL's Space Simulator, a 25-foot-wide vacuum chamber that had been evacuated and backfilled with a thin carbon dioxide atmosphere similar to that found on Mars.
The full-scale prototype's dimensions are very similar to those of Ingenuity. However, because it is a prototype, its components differ slightly from its flown counterpart.
The prototype does not have a solar panel or battery because it was connected to an external power source, and its computer and avionics were also kept off-board. Keeping these components external to the prototype reduced its mass and helped to correct for the difference in gravity between Earth and Mars during tests.
The Ingenuity Mars Helicopter prototype joins a robust collection of Mars exploration-related artifacts, including the Mars Pathfinder prototype, the Sojourner rover back-up Marie Curie, the Mars Exploration Rover Surface System Test-Bed and a model of the Curiosity rover.
The Ingenuity prototype will go into storage for the immediate future and will eventually be displayed at one of the museum's two locations.
The National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C., is located at Sixth Street and Independence Avenue S.W. and is open every day except Dec. 25 from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.
Admission is free but timed-entry passes are required to visit. The Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center is located in Chantilly, Virginia, near Washington Dulles International Airport and is open every day except Dec. 25 from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Admission is free and timed-entry passes are not required, and parking is $15.
