title: Locals born on Feb. 29 share how their Leap Day birthdays shape their worldview
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Locals born on Feb. 29 share how their Leap Day birthdays shape their worldview

 February 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 855
 Words 

 Read News Document

 People who are born on leap day look at the world a little differently.They only get a birthday every four years. Some of their parents were strict about only celebrating every four years and others made every year special.
But regardless of their celebratory traditions, for those who are born on Feb. 29, birthday milestones always look a little different than normal.
"My mother said when I turned 4, of course, they had a big celebration. At 4 you kind of have a sense of what it means. It is a special day. By the time I was five, my birthday year, there was no (Feb.) 29. It was rather traumatic for me," said Frank Narr of Cambridge.
Only getting birthdays in four-year terms has shifted his view on life slightly, he said.
"As I got older as a leap year celebrant, I tend to chronicle my life in four-year segments — 4, 8, 12, 16 and so on. As I look back, each segment is unique, and I can point to at least one significant event in my life," Narr said.
His parents tried to make up for the deficit of birthdays.
"My mom made a big deal on leap years. I always wanted a pair of Chuck Taylor Converse sneakers. For my 12th birthday, I can remember that. It was big deal. I went from Sears sneakers to the Chuck Taylor Converse sneakers. When I got to 16 now you are in High School. How do you celebrate your birthday, especially in the off years? As I have gotten older and think about the off years and I say to myself between 11:59 on Feb. 28 and midnight — my day is that minute," Narr said.
He said he is 15 leap years old this year.
"When I turned 13 all my daughters were older than me. That was the joke," Narr said.
"When I got older and got my first car in Maryland, I chose to get personalized license plates. I put 'Feb 29' on them. I worked in D.C., and I would drive around the beltway. I got honks left and right. I had fun. It attracted a lot of attention on the day," said Narr.
Being a leap day celebrant has put him in an existential mind frame.
"You get to a point where you realize there are less of them than more of them. I try to really treasure the time and the moments because you realize it is another four years until you have one. I am just different, and I chalk that up to being a leap year guy," he said.
As the Earth makes its rotation around the Sun, it takes 1/4 of a day longer to make the journey than the 365 day calendar lasts. So, a whole day, leap day, is added to the calendar nearly every four years.
People born on the leap day are pretty rare. Only about 5 million people worldwide have a Feb. 29 birthday, about 0.06% of the world's population.
Amazingly, one of Narr's neighbors also had a leap day birthday.
"We move in to our new home, and our next door neighbor — the woman — was born on leap day as well."
"That truly is the first time I have ever met someone who was a leap year baby. She was 5, 6, 7 leap years older than me. I would make a point of going to see her, and we would just bask in the day. You kind of had that little twinkle in your eye. We get each other and we have lived this life of uniqueness," Narr said.
Another Leap Day celebrant is Will Freda, who teaches at The Gunston School.
"Yes, my parents were rather adamant about my birthday being only once every four years. Growing up, we would only celebrate on the actual day, not in the years in between. At first, it was difficult for me to understand why other kids got to celebrate every year, and ultimately the experience impacted me in two ways," Freda said.
"One: birthdays, as you might imagine, started to mean absolutely nothing to me. I distinctly remember that on my 12th (third) birthday, I had a bad day. From then on, I no longer believed that birthdays could really mean much, since four years of karma had not amounted to anything. Now, even though I have a real birthday, I do not do anything to celebrate," Freda said.
"Two: once birthdays stopped meaning something to me, other special days lost importance as well. As someone with a birthday once every four years, holidays like Christmas and New Year's Eve seem to happen rather frequently. Something like, 'Oh, it's Christmas again,'" Freda said.
But finding a silver lining, Freda said that his Leap Day birthday has helped him see the value of living in the moment.
"All of this might sound negative initially, but I think this experience has inspired a sort of mindfulness. I will admit that I no longer look forward to anything, but the benefit of that is that my focus can remain more squarely in the moment. In a sense, if none of the days are special, then every day is," he said.

title: Art and basketball: Shelton Hawkins brings his art to downtown Easton
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Art and basketball: Shelton Hawkins brings his art to downtown Easton

 March 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 845
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — For Shelton Hawkins, a month-long art show at The Zebra and Spiralis Galleries in downtown Easton is about more than his accomplishments as an artist.Yes, the show will give Hawkins the chance to show off photos of the many basketball courts around the world that he has painted in collaboration with other artists.
And yes, "At the Buzzer!" — a show that marries art and basketball, and opens Friday at 5 p.m. — will be Hawkins' first real-deal art show since becoming a full-time artist a couple of years ago.
But, in the bigger scheme of things, Hawkins sees this show as a step toward Black people feeling more comfortable downtown.
"For me, it's kind of tough being in downtown Easton," he said. "There's not a lot of Black people. I still don't feel comfortable just walking around downtown Easton."
Hawkins said he wants to make sure that Black people feel part of the downtown community.
"The more opportunities I get to keep showing up and show the positivity that we do in the community, the more comfortable I think people of color will start to be," he said.
Hawkins also hopes his show will inspire the next generation of artists on the Eastern Shore.
"If I can do it, anybody can do it," he said. "Like, I want to see somebody else in 10 years doing something similar where I can be like, 'Man, I can't believe they're painting indoor basketball courts for the NBA, or they're designing courts for the high school, or whatever the case may be."
Susan Schauer John, director and curator of the Zebra Gallery, said she wants to bring "fresh, emerging" artists to the gallery.
"Shelton is just the beginning," she said.
"At the Buzzer!" will feature Hawkins' photography, paintings and drone work, which captures the bright, multi-colored basketball courts that he has painted across the globe. The show brings March Madness into the gallery.
From a painting of the University of Michigan's Fab Five to a photo of a woman holding a paint bucket on a basketball court in Queens, New York — reminiscent of photographer Gordon Parks' 1942 piece, "American Gothic" — Hawkins has a story behind each piece of art in the show.
A LIFE OF ART AND BASKETBALL
Before becoming a full-time artist, Hawkins spent years as a basketball coach. He went from coaching high school basketball at Saints Peter and Paul High School to assistant coaching college basketball at Chesapeake College and at the University of Maryland Eastern Shore.
Both art and basketball have always been important in his life. As a child, Hawkins remembers sitting at the table, drawing with his dad.
"Those were my favorite memories with him," he said.
Although born in Easton, his mother's career in the United States Army meant that Hawkins' family moved around.
"When we were moving to Germany, we had a layover in Paris," he said. "My dad took me to Paris to go see artwork. So early on, I was engaged with travel and art."
PLAYING IN COLOR
After his cousin passed away at the basketball court at Idlewild Park in Easton, Hawkins spent a decade trying to get the court refurbished.
"I wrote a letter to the town," he said. "They couldn't understand the concept of why you would want to do anything to this basketball court."
After years of writing the town, in 2019, with the help of now Mayor Megan Cook, Hawkins got the go-ahead from the town to breath life back into and paint the courts at Idlewild Park and Moton Park.
"The very next court we did was LeBron James' court," he said. "My life took off after that."
Hawkins has painted courts all over the world, from Easton to Tokyo. The project is called "Play in Color."
This effort is not a solo one. Generally, when he goes to a new place for a project, Hawkins said he tries to work with a local artist.
"So it doesn't look like we're coming in there to a person's community and telling them what should go on the basketball court," he said.
One of his favorite collaborations was with artist James Little in Memphis, who recently did a collab with Kith and New Balance.
Collaboration is key in Hawkins' eyes. And his collaborators aren't all well-known artists. One of his regular collaborators is his five-year-old daughter, Parker Dash.
"Every project that I have ever done, my daughter has been a part of."
From the black border on one of his paintings to a basketball that the two of them painted together — Parker Dash's work will also be on display at Hawkins' show.
For Hawkins, whose father passed away nearly three decades ago, this is a way to do with his daughter what his dad did with him.
"I feel like in 20 years, she's going to remember all the moments of us being at the table, how many times she's been in a gallery just kind of running around," he said.
Hawkins' show is open for the month of March at The Zebra and Spiralis Galleries, located at 5 N. Harrison Street. The first-time event for the show will kick off on March 1 from 5 to 10 p.m.

title: National Portrait Gallery celebrates Women’s History Month
author: Staff Writer
content:
National Portrait Gallery celebrates Women’s History Month

 March 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 516
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery will celebrate Women's History Month with a free, all-ages festival and in-person and online programs and exhibitions.March kicks off with the annual Women's History Month Festival in the museum's Kogod Courtyard on Saturday, March 9, from 11:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. Visitors of all ages can enjoy story times, performances, art activities, scavenger hunts and more.
There will also be workshops with The Washington Ballet; a Ruth Bader Ginsburg portrait workshop with Debbie Levy, author of I Dissent: Ruth Bader Ginsburg Makes Her Mark; and zine-making with artist and activist Jennifer White-Johnson.
In conjunction with the Women's History Month Festival, the Portrait Gallery will host a conversation with Opal Lee, the "grandmother of Juneteenth," and her portraitist Sedrick Huckaby. Lee is the retired teacher, counselor and activist who led the push to make Juneteenth a federal holiday.
Huckaby, an Outwin Boochever Portrait Competition finalist, was featured in the museum's recent "Kinship" exhibition. His life-sized oil painting of Lee is now on view in "Recent Acquisitions." This free conversation will take place March 9 at 3:30 p.m. in the McEvoy Auditorium after the Women's History Month Festival has concluded.
The Portrait Gallery will also host a Women's History Month Trivia Night with New Columbia Pub Quiz March 26, from 5 to 6:45 p.m. in the Kogod Courtyard. At this happy hour event, participants can test their knowledge of the incredible women in the Portrait Gallery's collection.
The free collections-themed trivia can be played individually or in teams of up to six people, and prizes are awarded at the end of the evening. The Courtyard Café will be open during the event, with snacks and beverages available for purchase.
In the galleries, this year's "Recent Acquisitions" showcases women's achievements and will remain on view through Oct. 27. Each of the 21 portraits either represents a remarkable woman or was created by a woman artist. Sitters include artist Ruth Asawa, singer Beyoncé Knowles-Carter, astronomer Vera Rubin, photographer Ming Smith and entrepreneur and philanthropist Madame C.J. Walker.
The museum's recently commissioned portraits of Earth and planetary science professor Walter Alvarez by Carmen Lomas Garza (2019) and Rabbi Sally Priesand by Joan Roth (2022) are also on view for the first time. The newly commissioned portrait of Oprah Winfrey by Shawn Michael Warren (2023) hangs alongside this exhibition.
For those who cannot make it to the museum, the Portrait Gallery's Google Arts & Culture page, which has received more than 2.7 million views, includes 12 digital exhibitions on the history of women in the United States. New exhibitions including "Do a Good Turn Daily" and "Shaping History, Envisioning the Future: Public Art by Women" will debut this March.
National Portrait Gallery
The Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery tells the multifaceted story of the United States through the individuals who have shaped American culture. Spanning the visual arts, performing arts and new media, the Portrait Gallery portrays poets and presidents, visionaries and villains, actors, and activists whose lives tell the nation's story.
The National Portrait Gallery is located at Eighth and G streets N.W., Washington, D.C. For more information, call 202-633-1000 or connect with the museum at npg.si.edu.

title: Locals collect historical items in an attempt to preserve Cordova's story
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Locals collect historical items in an attempt to preserve Cordova's story

 March 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 698
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CORDOVA — Teresa and Dale Dawson, the owners of Tuckahoe Seafood, are collectors and storytellers.They document the history of Cordova along with steaming and selling crabs. Their collection of ephemera marking the ups and downs of life in an Eastern Shore town makes up the Cordova Community Historical Society, nestled in Tuckahoe Seafood.
"Cordova was big around 1900," Dale Dawson said. "It was bustling because of the railroad. It was originally called Thimbletown. They had the largest packing cannery in Talbot County for tomatoes, beans and corn. It was the Talbot Packing Company. Farming in general changed from truck farming, which was produce, to grain farming. It all switched and the canneries went down hill."
"Our main focus is collecting memorabilia and information just so it doesn't get lost. Cordova has been long overdue to have a historical society," said Teresa Dawson.
This team enjoys going down historical rabbit holes together.
"One of my favorite stories is about Doc James. His name was James Fair," Teresa said.
Getting excited, Dale started to finish her sentences.
"Doc James lived in a little shanty, and he was really old. He was born in 1876 because he got a certificate from the President for being born during the cenntenial," he said. "... People used to come from Philadelphia and New Jersey. They would line up to meet with this guy as a healer."
There was another alarming story from Cordova.
"Cordova had a bank, and it was robbed around 1930 or 1932," Teresa said. "They blew the safe with nitro and got like $1,500. It was looted again. They people came back another year. They blew the safe door, and the owner heard it. They ran away, but didn't get any cash."
These citizen historians do it mostly for fun.
"If we don't do this, it is going to be lost," Teresa said.
Of all the items in their store, Teresa said her favorite is a pastel painting of the Baptist church by Jenny Willis, who died in 1952.
"We were thrilled to get it. She was a suffragette and a local correspondent for Cordova for The Star Democrat. She was a renaissance woman. A writer, a painter, a gardener. Really interesting," she said.
Dale's favorite item is a wooden box that was used to hold baking soda called "Parrot Monkey."
"It has the original address. It came in on a steamboat from Coveys Landing. They would come to the ramp and transfer cargo. So that is my favorite. We have tried to find more information on the steam boat business. The railroad put that out of business and trucking put the railroad out of business," he said.
The seafood business and museum is housed in a building built by Dale's father in 1946. It was a mechanic's garage.
Tuckahoe Seafood has been selling crabs since 1987 and collecting historical pieces almost as long.
They have gotten so many donations that they are running out of room in the seafood store. Every available surface has some historical object.
"We need a permanent home, because this is not ideal. It needs to be stored in a climate controlled (environment). It needs to have some more care put into it," Teresa said.
The Dawsons have helped to create a the Cordova Historical Society. They started having meetings once a month. They have had fund raisers and sold calendars and stickers.
"We have a president, a vice president, a secretary and a treasurer. It is very loose. We would like this just to be fun. We love meeting and talking about history. Show and tell at the end of the meeting," Teresa said. "Our main focus was trying to get Ingram's gas station restored and buy it. That is what we were fundraising for. But he is not selling it to us."
"We thought that would be a perfect location for a little museum," Dale said.
The historical society host events like Cordova Day, which will take place on March 9 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Cordova firehouse.
"We are going to have other people in the community, not just ours, who have exhibits and memorabilia on Cordova. We will have quilters and Rhonda's Round Biscuits, who does the beaten biscuits. It is going to be a day to celebrate Cordova," Teresa said.

title: Questions without answers at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Questions without answers at the library

 March 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Business 
 
 1053
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In the summer of 1968, when I was 16, I got to go on a bicycling tour of Europe with six other boys and our high school Latin teacher.We visited most of Western Europe that year, with side trips by boat to Morocco and Greece, but we based our travels out of the ancient Bavarian city of Augsburg. Our teacher had relatives there, and friends, who put us up whenever we visited.
I had worked hard the previous summer to earn enough money to help pay for the trip, and I couldn't have been more excited about getting to go. Up to that point, mine had been a fairly parochial childhood — all my friends were white, we all spoke with a slight Southern accent, our parents were all preparing to vote for Richard Nixon in the next election and we all supported our country's war in Vietnam (this was the year of the Tet offensive).
Looking forward to the trip, I was fascinated by the idea of "foreignness," that the countries I would visit would — each in its own way — be different from anything I had ever encountered before. In this, I was not disappointed.
The first time we bicycled into Augsburg, at the end of a long hot ride, our Latin teacher's aunt met us at her door with ice-cold pitchers of a pink liquid that I assumed was lemonade. But I was wrong — she had, she told us, prepared the drink fresh for us from rhubarb she'd harvested that morning from her garden. I will never forget how refreshing and exotic that "rhubarbade" tasted on my tongue.
One of the other families we visited in Augsburg had a son our age and a daughter a year or two younger. Our teacher had told us beforehand that the father had served as a waist gunner in the Luftwaffe during World War II. Needless to say, this made us all curious about him. We were of the generation whose fathers, almost without exception, had also fought in that war, against the Axis.
If I was expecting jackboots and a house run with ironclad National Socialist discipline, I was in for a surprise. The house was like many middle-class residences I knew back home in Kentucky, and the family that lived there couldn't have been more relaxed and welcoming.
Indeed, the daughter turned out to be a stunning blonde whom, over the course of that summer, I courted as best I could.
We had a number of interesting experiences on that trip.
1968 was Europe's summer of rebellion. We were in Paris when the Bastille Eve riots broke out and Charles de Gaulle's gendarmerie attacked anything on the Left Bank that looked like a student. A member of our group ended up in a French emergency room.
In Franco's Spain and the Junta's Greece we saw what life was like under a repressive military dictatorship. And in Morocco we were approached by little boys trying to sell us "some really good stuff."
But most unsettling for a kid who'd grown up in a family that flew the American flag every Fourth of July was the young Europeans I met that summer on trains and in youth hostels who questioned me about America's involvement in Vietnam.
Up until that point in my life it had always been my country right or wrong (though the idea that America could ever actually be wrong would never have crossed my mind). But now, suddenly, I was meeting a new class of peers who not only didn't think America incapable of error, they believed she was in fact currently embarked upon one of the gravest mistakes any country could ever make.
The night before we returned home, I can remember lying in my bunk in a youth hostel worrying over what I had experienced that summer.
I thought I was in love with a girl whose father — a nice man I knew and liked — had fought for Adolf Hitler. For the first time in my life I had personally experienced the fact that good nations, full of good people, could not only get it wrong, they could get it disastrously wrong. And, perhaps unsurprisingly, I was no longer so certain my own country couldn't screw up too.
That night of doubt took place over half a century ago and, in a sense, it is with me still.
I was outraged by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, but I am still haunted by a photograph taken on one of the battle's first days of a dead Russian soldier lying face-up in the street, his body covered with a light blanket of snow. That young man had no idea what he was getting into when his commander ordered him to march south, and now his life was over before it had truly begun.
How do you reconcile the sympathy you feel for such an innocent with the horror of what he had been sent to Ukraine to do?
All of which is my long way of explaining why I checked out Burkhard Bilger's new book, "Fatherland," and lost myself in all that its author encountered as he researched the life of his grandfather — his mother's sweet and loving "Papa" — the elementary school teacher adored by his students, the district administrator sent by the Third Reich to oversee the occupied Alsatian town of Bartenheim, the man who did everything in his power to save the people under his jurisdiction from labor camps and worse, the man who was a card-carrying member of the Nazi party, the man suspected of murder, the man who, after the German surrender, was tried for war crimes and escaped the gallows by a hair's breadth.
If you too sometimes find yourself occupying neither the right nor the left but an uneasy middle ground, if the answers to life's questions appear neither black nor white but gray, if you wonder if there is any way to resolve such quandaries, to reconcile the irreconcilable, then I heartily recommend Bilger's book.
It won't answer all your questions, but it may give you cause to hold fast to them as the world swirls around you with belligerent assurances that this way of thinking, or that way of thinking, is right, and anyone who thinks otherwise is irredeemably wicked.
You can find "Fatherland" in the Talbot County Free Library's biography section under BIO GÖNNER.

title: ‘Day of Dance’ proves beautiful gift to the community
author: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat
content:
‘Day of Dance’ proves beautiful gift to the community

 March 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 630
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — As the piano played, young dancers filled the stage exploring master classes of ballet, modern dance, hip hop and choreography. A "Day of Dance" is one of the many gifts that Carole Cascio left to the community.On Saturday, Feb. 24, dancers, ages 12 and up, filled the Decker Theatre in the Gibson Center at Washington College in Chestertown for a free community event hosted by the Carole Cascio Fund for Mind and Movement Dance Connections.
Upon arrival, registered dancers signed in and received a bag full of healthy drinks and snacks. All dancers were invited to participate in four master classes taught by special guest artists Kristi Schaffner (ballet) with piano accompanist Joann Moorer, Renee Gerardo (modern dance), Adrienne Kraus Latanishen (hip hop), and Melinda Bloomquist (composition/choreography).
This was the fourth "Day of Dance" sponsored by the fund. Both Chesapeake College and Washington College have offered their theaters to host these events.
Each "Day of Dance" showcases different artists and a variety of dance styles with a mission of the Fund, "to introduce students of all ages and levels to connecting mind, movement and dance, and to support developing artistry in young people through choreography and dance."
Locally, Cascio was known as a beautiful artist for both watercolor and pottery, but many did not know about her former dancing career.
Peter Pucci, a former dance student of Cascio, said, "It was because of Carole that I became a professional dancer, a choreographer, a movement director, an artistic director, a professor of dance and composition, a dance filmmaker, a producer, a mentor to young dancers and finally the executive director of the Carole Cascio Fund at Carole's request."
In addition to dance and creating art, Cascio also taught Pilates at the Kent Island Senior Center in Stevensville and at Chesapeake College for many years. With a heart for creating and a love for the arts, Cascio was an inspiration to countless people.
"Carole and I had many conversations over the last five years of her life about how to bring dance into her community, to elementary schools, middle schools, high schools and to Chesapeake College," Pucci said. "They were fun, lively conversations with all kinds of ideas being tossed about. Little did I know then that she was preparing me for the job of directing her foundation. It is truly a full circle endeavor for me and, in the great tradition of modern dancers, of giving back to the community just as she did to hundreds of dancers over her career."
To honor Cascio's dreams of bringing dance into the schools, Pucci is actively working with Queen Anne's County Public Schools to encourage and enhance the dance programs at the middle and high schools. To date, the Cascio Fund has planned, sponsored and held many dance classes, including a combined hip hop master class with Queen Anne's County High School dancers and with students from Centreville Middle School.
The Fund also brought a four-century-old dance style and India Dance Teachers Deepti Mukund Navile, Gowrie Velayudhapillai and Tulsi Rughoonundun to teach dance workshops at Kent Island and Queen Anne's County high schools.
On Friday, March 8, there will be a free performance courtesy of the Carole Cascio Fund by the New York Dance Project from New York City at the YMCA in Centerville from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m. Seating opens at 5 p.m. For more information, visit newyorkdanceproject.org/programs/the-company.
Pucci shared this performance will be "very serendipitous" as Cascio donated the funds to create the new pickleball courts at the YMCA where the dancers will be performing. Before this event, there will also be a free ballet masterclass at QACHS for all dancers 12 and up. Pre-registration is required. See the website for more information.
For more information or to support the Carole Cascio Fund for Mind Movement Dance Connections, visit carolecasciofund.org.

title: Maryland stories; Art students leave their mark at library
author: Sarah Meador somdnewsintern@chespub.com
content:
Maryland stories; Art students leave their mark at library

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Sarah Meador somdnewsintern@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 394
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Several high school student artists are bringing new life to the walls of Windy Hill Elementary School's library in Southern Maryland.The Northern High School National Art Honors Society members, some of them returning to their old stomping grounds, have been covering the elementary school library walls in hand-painted murals over the past year.
Christopher Angus, librarian at Windy Hill, reached out to all four public high schools in Calvert County, asking if any had art students who would be interested in filling in the library's empty walls.
Northern's National Art Honors Society stepped up to volunteer — and left four new murals on the walls last year.
"It's definitely transformed our library," Angus said. "The work they've done is absolutely incredible. They put in countless hours of their own time."
In January, club members returned at Angus' request to paint two new murals at the school in Owings.
Northern NAHS President Emma Nguyen has returned to her old elementary school multiple afternoons each week to work on the new murals with other NAHS members.
"Since I went to this school, I remember that I really loved murals," said Nguyen. "It inspired me when I was a kid, so I kind of want to bring that back to the school with the library murals here."
Windy Hill Elementary art teacher Margaret Pike painted the library's first few murals, allowing her former students to follow in her footsteps.
"It's cool to hear from the teachers, staff and students how much they like them," Caroline Hyder, Northern NAHS vice president, said.
Hyder and Angus each recalled students excitedly recognizing their favorite characters on the walls in the early stages of pencil sketches.
"It's really cool for them to see what's possible," Angus said, noting that the murals painted by high school students serve as an inspiration to the elementary schoolers, especially those with a love for art. "It just makes it that much more worth it."
Angus is hopeful that the murals painted by the group of Northern students will inspire other high schools in the county to collaborate with middle and elementary schools to share similar experiences.
Though these murals scheduled to be completed in mid-April will leave the library walls almost completely covered, that doesn't mean Northern's art students are done at Windy Hill Elementary. When teachers walk through the library, Angus said, they ask when the art honor society is going to paint their classrooms.

title: Veteran Chesapeake Bay photographer shares the secrets of his craft with local camera club
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Veteran Chesapeake Bay photographer shares the secrets of his craft with local camera club

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: Local News 
 
 818
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Veteran Chesapeake Bay photographer David Harp goes out when all the other photographers stay in.He goes on oyster boats, skipjacks and kayaks when its snowing. If it is deeply unpleasant out, he gears up and goes out with the locals. In the summer, he gets up early for great light and is often done shooting swans by 7:30 a.m.
On Monday he spoke and showed his work to a crowd from the Tidewater Camera Club at the Unitarian Universalist Church. There were about 30 people in attendance plus several Zoom members. The lecture was titled "Observations of a Watery World."
Harp will critique club member's photographs and gave them an assignment to "shoot wind." He chuckled at the Zen-like instruction to see something that is invisible. He insisted there were no rules.
"We are all about getting photographers the information they need to progress. So we have speakers and assignments, and Dave Harp will give critiques of the submitted work. He is always a crowd pleaser. He is local. We love it," Tidewater Camera Club President Jack Upchurch said.
In his introduction of Harp, Upchurch said, "His inspiration comes from exploring literal and figurative edges, shorelines, communities, habitats and traditional work life where culture and nature connect."
Harp's work is to document the Bay. The critters, the locals and the ever-moving landscape all come into play.
He studies weather systems, tide charts and animal behavior, all to predict a ripe photographic opportunity.
Harp is a former Baltimore Sun Magazine photographer who has created five books with naturalist and writer Tom Horton. Never one to stop learning, the duo have moved in to super high detailed 4K video filmmaking with the help of filmmaker Sandy Cannon Brown.
"We have this synergy that is 44 years together. We finish each other's sentences. He does the words. I do the pictures. Our mantra has always been, 'The whole is greater than the sum of its parts,'" Harp said.
The three of them worked on a film called "A Passion for Oysters." They also made a film about the larger waters that feed the Chesapeake, "Water's Way: Thinking Like a Watershed."
"When I met Tom Horton in 1981 at the Baltimore Sun, we started doing stories about the Chesapeake Bay," Harp said. "I pretty much decided that is really what I wanted to do. I took a vow of poverty to do work on the Bay instead of commercial work."
He said they have done eight documentary films about the Chesapeake.
This is not a casual endeavor and after decades of doing this work, he knows where good photographs might happen. Smith Island, Tangier Island and the sea-consumed Holland Island have all provided story-driven photographs.
One of his most used tools is the kayak.
"Most of the time I am not in the middle of the Bay. I am in a marsh gut. I am in a stream. I don't even go out in the main stem of the Choptank River," he said.
"... I love being in the kayak. I love being on the water. You are very quiet. You can paddle up to stuff. You can go up these creeks. That is where the life is. Where land and water meet, that is the whole point of the Chesapeake Bay. We have 10 or 12,000 miles of shoreline," he said.
He is just as interested in the men and women who make their living on the bay. Gill netters, oyster tongers and crab pickers all have prominent roles in his work. He gets embedded. Stays for the whole day and finds rapport with his subjects. If a captain says, "It is going to be cold. We start at 4 a.m. We don't get back until 4 p.m. and bring your own food," then he commits to enter their world entirely.
The lessons he's learned through the work, Harp said, have inspired him to work with local photographers.
"Basically photographers take chaos and make order out of it. We take a big scene and key in one person or one thing and that is what makes a great photograph," Harp said. "The great photographer Elliot Erwitt said, 'Photography is about observation. It is about finding something interesting in an ordinary place. It has little to do with what we see, but how we see it.'"
He distilled his teaching into four words — look, see, observe discern. He put these works in stark black and white on the screen for those in attendance Monday.
"The other thing that is really important to me, is creating opportunity. I go over weather forecast, tide tables, through behavioral research on animals. It is not just chance. It is actively pre-visualizing what you want in a photograph, and if something comes out of the blue, you are ready for it."
How does he sum up over 50 years of focused effort, tens of thousands of images and moments have been witnessed with his lens?
"I go where the life is," he said.
The crowd applauded.

title: Celebrating 250 years of Caroline County
author: STAFF REPORT
content:
Celebrating 250 years of Caroline County

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: STAFF REPORT | Section: Events 
 
 251
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It has been 250 years since Caroline County was created, formed from inland sections of Dorchester and Queen Anne's counties.It was named for Lady Caroline Eden, sister of the sixth Lord of Baltimore and then Lord Proprietor and wife of the royal governor.
The weekend of March, 15, the Caroline County community will commemorate the past 250 years and the changes that have taken place since the county's founding.
Festivities will kick off with a VIP celebration event hosted by the Caroline County Historical Society on Friday, March 15, from 5 to 8 p.m. at the Museum of Rural Life.
Guest speaker Julie Markin, director of archaeology at Washington College, will present on a recent dig at Barwick's Landing, the presumed location of a tavern operated by James Barwick until 1783.
Refreshments will be offered, and tokens will be given, redeemable at participating downtown Denton businesses.
Tickets are $50 and are available online at donorbox.org/250th-anniversary-vip-event-tickets.
Continuing the celebration March 16, Market Street between Second and Fifth Streets in Denton will be closed to traffic to accommodate pedestrians for a St. Patrick's Day themed event.
The Chamber of Commerce will host a scavenger hunt with cash prizes. Registration will be open at 8 North Second Street during the event.
The event will feature a petting zoo, trike races, a cornhole tournament, cooking demonstrations, street bowling and potato spoon races.
There will be a DJ and performances from the North Caroline and Colonel Richardson High School jazz bands, To the Point Dance Studio and the Arts Center Drums and Dance Circle.

National Cherry Blossom Festival returns to Washington D.C.

 March 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 The Smithsonian American Art Museum is collaborating for the 11th year in a row with the National Cherry Blossom Festival for a series of in-person and virtual cherry blossom-themed public programs. The museum's cherry blossom family activities and celebrations are part of its hands-on program series, designed to spark learning, creativity and appreciation for the arts.The museum's popular Cherry Blossom Celebration for children and families will be presented in person Saturday, March 23, from 11:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. Weather permitting, the event will begin on the museum's F Street plaza with a Japanese taiko performance by the drumming group Nen Daiko.
Other performances in the museum's courtyard include double-dutch jump rope and other jump roping displays with Kangaroo Kids, and an all-vinyl music set of Japanese soul, funk, boogie, pop and disco by Les The DJ.
More information is available on the museum's website at https://americanart.si.edu.
Attendees can create their own cherry blossom-themed crafts and a spring-themed scavenger hunt will be available so visitors can explore the American Art Museum's galleries. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase at the Courtyard Café. This program is free, but registration is encouraged.
A cherry blossom-themed in-person workshop, part of the museum's series "Beyond the Studio," is scheduled for Sunday, March 24, at 1 p.m. Nicolas Shi, the official artist of the National Cherry Blossom Festival, will lead participants through an activity inspired by Washington's beloved cherry blossoms. This program costs $15 and requires advance registration by March 10 at 7 p.m.
The Art & Me Preservation Family Workshop, a virtual hands-on, artmaking workshop designed for children ages 3 to 8 and their caretakers, will take place Saturday, April 6, at 11 a.m. Families will discover how delicate sakura have been depicted in landscapes, figure paintings and prints for centuries, and how Smithsonian conservators preserve these beautiful yet fragile artworks. Then participants will create their own cherry blossom-inspired creations. This program is cohosted by the museum and the Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art. This program is free, but registration is required.
A temporary video projection, co-presented by the National Cherry Blossom Festival and the museum, will illuminate the museum's facade from Wednesday, March 20, to Saturday, March 23, 8–9 p.m. Cherry blossom-themed artworks from Washington artists Robin Bell, Matthew Curry, Jonathan Monaghan and Shi will be projected onto the northwest corner of the building (Ninth and G streets N.W.). Each night, Bell will create a new video tableau, building new visuals upon the previous nights' work and mixing them live. Support for this event is provided by the DowntownDC BID and Park West Gallery.
Additional family activities are available on the Smithsonian American Art Museum's Family Zone webpage, including seasonal crafts, coloring pages inspired by artworks from the museum's permanent collection, videos and more.
About the Smithsonian American Art Museum
The Smithsonian American Art Museum is the flagship museum in the United States for American art and craft. It is home to one of the most significant and inclusive collections of American art in the world. The museum's main building, located at Eighth and G streets N.W., is open daily from 11:30 a.m. to 7 p.m. The museum's Renwick Gallery, a branch museum dedicated to contemporary craft, is located on Pennsylvania Avenue at 17th Street N.W. and is closed temporarily.
Check online for current hours and admission information. Admission is free. Follow the museum on Facebook, Instagram and YouTube. For more,, call 202-633-1000 or 202-633-7970 or visit americanart.si.edu.
About the National Cherry Blossom Festival
The National Cherry Blossom Festival is one of the world's great celebrations of spring. The 2024 festival runs from March 20 to April 14 and includes four weeks of events featuring diverse and creative programming promoting traditional and contemporary arts and culture, natural beauty and community spirit.
The public can add the 2024 festival dates and signature event dates to their calendar and visit NationalCherryBlossomFestival.org or call 877-44-BLOOM for more information.

title: Castelli shares salty tales at museum
author: TOM MCCALL
content:
Castelli shares salty tales at museum

 March 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TOM MCCALL | Section: News 
 
 576
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Over 100 people gathered on March 5 at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum to hear about Marc Castelli's year on the water.The Kent County watercolorist, who works from photographs of boats and watermen, had many salty tales to tell as he showed his slideshow. The show, which Castelli has presented at the museum almost annually for more than a decade, is a visual diary of his year embedded with watermen.
"We have been doing this since 2012," said Pete Lesher, chief historian at the Maritime Museum. "This is clearly something that a lot of people look forward to.
Lesher called it "Castelli's year-in-review out with the watermen."
Castelli goes further than just bearing witness. He is collecting material for his artwork.
"Every day he goes out with the watermen in all weather conditions, in various locations, in various fisheries," Lesher said. "He creates a certain empathy with the culture of the watermen by educating us on their world."
Castelli gets his information from those who work on the water. He gets on board their workboats with a camera to collect images for his paintings. He knows the Chesapeake by river, and he knows the different ways fish are harvested.
Castelli showed a picture of an invasive blue catfish. Watermen use hooks on long lines to catch them.
"They can get up to 60 pounds," Castelli said. "They eat almost anything that swims in the water — 70% of the biomass of the James River are blue cats."
He said the Bay needs more than one processing plant for blue catfish.
This processor, Nick Hargrove, sells his product to the Maryland Food Bank and government institutions, such as correctional facilities and schools.
Castelli argues that based on what he has observed, this is not enough to address the volume of blue catfish infiltrating the Chesapeake's ecosystem. During the event Tuesday, he argued for a change in the law to allow for grinding up blue catfish for uses like cat food and fertilizer.
Castelli shared his thoughts on oyster populations, dolphin habitat and other issues he observed alongside the Chesapeake's watermen.
He brings an eye trained by art history to see abstract patterns in the water, on a perch's shiny scales and in a basket full of writhing crabs. With this trained eye, Castelli said, he has the ability to show the extent of waterman culture and to bring attention to their issues.
"If you look for and read in the print media and on TV, you will get the idea that this culture is done," Castelli said. "It is not. That it is moving on."
He noted that the majority of the men working the water are in their 50s up to 70s and 80s.
"It is very hard to get young people to work that hard," Castelli said.
Castelli works as hard as the watermen.
His Nikon was so filled with aquatic detritus after his year on the water that the camera company refused to clean out his camera.
"I take very detailed pictures with a lot of attention to textures and the shades of the colors," Castelli said. "I hate painting crabs, and I hate painting flannel as much as I hate painting nets.
He said he is fascinated by light and water. He shoots thousands of pictures of water.
All this emphasis on shapes repeating and light reflecting is weighted in his paintings by a passionate defense of the watermen themselves.
"When you are out there you are in a totally different world without any political biases going on," Castelli said.

title: Irish-inspired meals for St. Patrick's Day
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Irish-inspired meals for St. Patrick's Day

 March 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1235
 Words 

 Read News Document

 This year, as always, St. Patrick's Day is celebrated on March 17, which happens to fall on a Sunday.Celebrations, including parades and parties, are not limited to those of Irish descent. All who enjoy the Irish foods, drinks, fun-filled parties and dancing are welcome to join in.
This day is an observance of the death of Saint Patrick, the Patron Saint of Ireland. What originally began as a public feast day in the 17th century has turned into a variety of celebrations.
My mother's family was of Irish descent — the McCabe and Hudson clans. I have seen my mother do an Irish jig as she danced as she talked about her Irish bloodline. Enjoy today's recipes come with an Irish touch, and many of these we enjoyed growing up.
With the small line of Irish descendants in my family, I knew very little about Ireland — until 1970. I had just begun a career in different aspects of the newspaper world. I started in the composition of the Delmarva News in Selbyville, Delaware. There I learned many different areas of the newspaper make-up department and as they say — "the ink got in my blood."
A few weeks after my training began, a new kid on the block came to work in this department, a kid I will never forget. Muriel was fresh from Ireland. She had married a U.S. Soldier and become a citizen.
This job was to be a wonderful opportunity for all of us. Our lunch times were spent showing our Muriel around the small town, the hamburger joint we gathered at each day, the Five and Dime store we used and much more. Of course we were late going back to work.
CORNED BEEF AND CABBAGE
Place one medium onion, cleaned and quartered, in a 5-quart slow cooker. Combine 3 cups water, 3 minced cloves of garlic, 1 bay leaf, 2 tbsps sugar, 2 tbsps vinegar, and the contents of the spice packet that comes with the beef brisket. Mix well and set aside. In the slow cooker, place 4 medium peeled and quartered potatoes over top of the onions. Pour the spice mixture over potatoes and place one corned beef brisket, about 2 to 3 pounds, on top. The final layer will be 1 small head of cabbage, cut into wedges. Cover and cook on low for 8 to 9 hours, or until the meat and vegetables are tender. Remove the bay leaf before serving.
TRADITIONAL IRISH BREAKFAST
One 13-ounce can English-style baked beans (such as Heinz beans with tomato sauce), 2 tbsps Irish butter (plus more softened for serving), 1 1/2 cups quartered white button mushrooms, salt and freshly ground black pepper, 1 large ripe plum tomato (cut crosswise into 4 slices), 2 slices Irish bacon (back bacon), Canadian bacon or American-style bacon (about 3 ounces), 2 white pudding sausages (about 4 ounces pricked with a fork in several places), 2 black pudding/blood sausage patties (about 2 ounces), 4 slices whole grain or black bread, 4 large eggs, bitter orange marmalade for serving, brewed Irish breakfast tea for serving.
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Line a large baking sheet with foil or parchment paper. Heat the baked beans in a small, covered saucepan, stirring occasionally, over low heat. Meanwhile, heat a large nonstick skillet over medium-high heat and then add 1 tbsp of the butter. When it melts, add the mushrooms, season with salt and pepper and brown on one side for 1 to 2 minutes. Toss the mushrooms and push them to one side of the skillet. Add the tomatoes to the other side, season with salt and pepper and cook, turning once, until browned on the edges and slightly softened, about 1 minute per side. At the same time, continue to cook the mushrooms, tossing occasionally, until browned and tender, 2 to 3 minutes more. Transfer the mushrooms and tomatoes to the prepared baking sheet, keeping the components separate, and place in the oven to keep warm.
Add the remaining butter to the same skillet and melt over medium heat. Add the bacon, white pudding and black pudding and fry, turning occasionally, until browned, about 4 minutes. Transfer to the baking sheet with the mushrooms and tomatoes, leaving the fat in the skillet. Put the bread on the other side of the baking sheet and place in the oven. Let the bread toast, flipping once, while you fry the eggs. Heat the fat in the skillet over medium heat. Crack the eggs into the skillet, season with salt and pepper and fry, flipping once, about 3 minutes total for over-easy eggs with slightly runny yolks. Remove the baking sheet from the oven and divide each of the components between two plates. Serve more butter and the marmalade on the side for the toast and hot tea as your beverage.
IRISH SODA BREAD
4 cups all-purpose flour (plus extra for currants), 4 tbsps sugar, 1 tsp baking soda, 1 1/2 tsps kosher salt, 4 tbsps (1/2 stick) cold unsalted butter (cut into 1/2-inch dice), 1 3/4 cups cold buttermilk (shaken), 1 extra-large egg (lightly beaten), 1 tsp grated orange zest, 1 cup dried currants.
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Line a sheet pan with parchment paper. Combine the flour, sugar, baking soda and salt in the bowl of an electric mixer fitted with the paddle attachment. Add the butter and mix on low speed until the butter is mixed into the flour. With a fork, lightly beat the buttermilk, egg and orange zest together in a measuring cup. With the mixer on low speed, slowly add the buttermilk mixture to the flour mixture. Combine the currants with 1 tbsp of flour and mix into the dough. It will be very wet. Dump the dough onto a well-floured board and knead it a few times into a round loaf. Place the loaf on the prepared sheet pan and lightly cut an X into the top of the bread with a serrated knife. Bake for 45 to 55 minutes, or until a cake tester comes out clean. When you tap the loaf, it will have a hollow sound. Cool on a baking rack. Serve warm or at room temperature.
CREAMY POTATO SOUP
This is one of my go-to soups and a family favorite. It is creamy, hearty, comforting soup. While the toppings are optional, I recommend using them for the loaded baked potato style.
Combine 6 cups peeled diced russet potatoes, 1 1/2 cups chopped yellow onion, 1 1/4 cups peeled and diced carrots, 1 cup diced celery and two 14.5-ounce cartons of chicken broth in a large stockpot. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Cover pot and bring to a boil over medium heat and continue to cook about 15 to 20 minutes longer until potatoes are very soft when pierced with a fork. Meanwhile, in a medium saucepan, melt 1/3 cup butter over medium heat adding 1/3 cup all-purpose flour and only cook 1 additional minute while whisking constantly and start slowly adding 2 1/2 cups milk. Cook until mixture lightly bubbles and begins to thicken. When the potatoes are tender, add the thickened mixture to the stockpot with the potato mixture, stirring gently. Remove from heat and ladle into bowls for serving. Have some toppings available for those who want them. Use crumbled bacon, chopped cooked ham, shredded cheddar cheese, chopped green onions or chives. Enjoy this tasty Irish potato soup.
Happy St. Patrick's Day to you and your family.

title: Candle Light Cove 'Peep Show' tradition continues to evolve
author: Staff Writer
content:
Candle Light Cove 'Peep Show' tradition continues to evolve

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Events 
 
 380
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — In March 2018, Candle Light Cove introduced to its residents a somewhat quirky and fun contest that used the holiday-themed marshmallow treats known as Peeps to create artistic entries.Six years later, the "Peep Show" has become an anticipated tradition that now is part of the senior living community's Spring Festival.
"This is our fifth 'Peep Show.' It continues to grow and get better each year," said Grace Lyons, Candle Light Cove's community relations director. "We've added the Spring Festival component, and this allows folks from the community to come to Candle Light Cove and view the Peep Show displays in person. Attendees can also vote for their favorite three displays."
Candle Light Cove's Spring Festival will be held from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on March 16 at the senior living community, located at 106 West Earle Avenue in Easton.
"Peep Show" entries may be dropped off at Candle Light Cove between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. during the week leading up to the festival, with a deadline of March 15 for final entries. Contest first-, second- and third-place winners will be announced after the "Peeples Choice Awards" voting concludes at 2 p.m. on March 16.
The $5 contest entry fee and other proceeds of the Spring Festival/Peep Show will benefit the Alzheimer's Association and the Parkinson's Foundation. The Spring Festival will include local vendor booths, food trucks and an appearance by the Easter Bunny.
"The 'Peep Show' displays use the delicious marshmallow treats to create a sculpture, mosaic, diorama or any other type of visual art," Lyons said. "The displays are colorful, with a mix of the blue, pink and yellow Peeps used to create artwork."
The 2023 "Peep Show" first-place display by Home Instead was modeled after the Netflix TV supernatural comedy series "Wednesday."
Candle Light Cove's inaugural "Peep Show" in 2018 was included in what then was known as "Beak Week." Even back then, the creative juices flowed in displays such as "Mary Peepkins," a tribute to Disney character Mary Poppins, and "Fly Peeps Fly," a nod to the Super Bowl champion Philadelphia Eagles' "Fly Eagles Fly" slogan.
The COVID-19 pandemic led to the cancellation of one scheduled "Peep Show," but the contest has rebounded impressively, event organizers said.
"The creative entries keep on coming," Lyons said. "The 'Peep Show' continues to grow."

title: MuSE creates dynamic space for Eastern Shore community
author: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Kent County News
content:
MuSE creates dynamic space for Eastern Shore community

 March 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Kent County News | Section: Business 
 
 343
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — "Every artist needs a muse," says Valerie Imbruce, director of Washington College's Center for Environment and Society.Behind that statement is a year of "tremendous energy and ambition" poured into Washington College's MuSE Museum at 210 S. Cross Street in Chestertown.
MuSE, a "Museum of Student Engagement," opened with a private reception March 5.
The community resource that goes beyond Washington College and is available to the public will be open select hours Fridays and Saturdays and by appointment.
The museum will host a number of rotating exhibits highlighting Washington College teaching, experiential learning and research with opportunities for sharing, learning and dialogue in a community space.
"We are trying new things," Imbruce said, "We have three main goals: experiential learning for our students 'learning through doing,' research environmental issues that are important to society for people, and community engagement because we can't really foster more environmental awareness without broad public understanding. And anything we do in a community we have to work together."
Imbruce is keen on building relationships people to people. "This is the perfect place to have a venue where you can bring in different constituencies and make it a collaborative space," she said, "and open what the college is doing to other people, the public, or other community partners."
For Imbruce this means having a space for exhibitions, where they can have events to host shared dialogues and give a space to show student work, most of which is place-based on the Chestertown-area and the Eastern Shore region.
"We see this (museum) as a shared resource for the community," she said.
The first exhibit "Teaching & Transformation: Semester in the Chesapeake Classroom" is on display for viewers of all ages until August 2024.
MuSE is open on First Fridays from 4:30 to 7 p.m., on Saturdays from 9 to 11 a.m. during the Chestertown Farmers Market, and by appointment. There is no fee. This space is also available upon request for group showings.
For those interested in submitting an exhibition proposal idea, there is a request form for proposals. For more information, email Laura Chamberlin at lchamberlin2@washcoll.edu.

 DENTON —The bloody fingerprint on the program of Fond Farewell says a lot. There is a contested will at stake that is worth millions, but with every passing moment, there are more people claiming the dough.This launches the hijinks for "Fond Farewell," a murder mystery dinner theater that played to a packed house at the Caroline Country Club on Friday and Saturday nights. According to Debby Bennett, chair of the murder mystery committee, "people kept calling asking to purchase tickets after our deadline. We sadly had to say no to them."
There was a bombshell vamp and a scheming personal assistant, and there was a cowgirl cop trying to figure it all out.
And the audience was laughing while trying to figure out who is the rightful heir to Ben Fullman's fortune. This is all complicated when a surprise guest shows up on death's door with a knife sticking out of his bloodied gut. It was all in good fun, and the crowd was fully invested in the broad humor.
It was an audience participation show. Black "funeral" bands were given out to audience members at the door, and those who wore them opted to be included as part of the play. The actors were in character before the play started and even stayed in character during the dinner that followed their performance.
Kendall Teague, a planning committee member for the event, called the fundraiser "an exceptional success."
"The unexpected plot twists, hilarious dialogue and high-level audience participation brought on roars of laughter that filled the room all evening," Teague said. "In fact, several attendees shared with us that they hadn't laughed that hard in a very long time."
This was a successful fundraiser for the Caroline County Arts Council, which was a co-presenter with the Caroline County Public Library. There were several sponsors, including Simpkins Roofing and Siding, Foam Works, Big Bass USA, the Foundry, Shore United Bank, Hillside Coffee Roasters and On Your Mark.
All the actors volunteered their time, as did Director Keith L. Shaffer.
"I thought both nights were fabulous. It was so fun," Bennett said. "The food was great. The Culinary Center always does such a terrific job."

title: National Museum of Asian Art presents 'Do Ho Suh: Public Figures'
author: Staff Writer
content:
National Museum of Asian Art presents 'Do Ho Suh: Public Figures'

 March 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Arts 
 
 1042
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art presents "Do Ho Suh: Public Figures," a sculpture by contemporary Korean artist Do Ho Suh commissioned to celebrate the museum's 100th anniversary. The monumental plinth will be unveiled April 27 and installed on the museum's Freer Plaza for five years, facing the National Mall in Washington, D.C.First presented as part of Public Art Fund's 1998 exhibition "Beyond the Monument" (Brooklyn, New York), "Public Figures" challenges the notion of heroic individualism and the stability of national narratives. For the work, Suh created a plinth for a monument; however, its imposing form is not a base to support a heroic figure or to mark a particular historic event, but rather a massive weight held aloft by many small, individualized figures caught in mid-stride.
Prominently placed in the center of the United States capital where it will be visible to some of the 25 million visitors to the National Mall each year, the commission dovetails with the global movement to rethink the role of the monument.
The unveiling of "Public Figures" marks the culmination of the National Museum of Asian Art's centennial celebrations. In 2023, the museum honored its 100th anniversary with a yearlong series of events and programs that deepened public understanding of Asian art and cultures and their intersections with America.
Ushering in the museum's second century, this will be the first new sculpture to be displayed in front of the building in over three decades.
"Suh's monument will prompt visitors to ask questions — about individual and collective identity, whom we memorialize and why," said Chase F. Robinson, the museum's director. "'Public Figures' is an embodiment of our museum's commitment for our next 100 years: to serve as a resource for learning, reflection and collaboration. It also reflects our deepening engagement with the art and culture of Korea, which we have championed since we first opened our doors in 1923."
Drawn from his shifting experience of the idea of "home," his work explores how objects make tangible the power of place and memory. Internationally recognized for his large-scale installations, Suh was among the earliest contemporary artists whose work was featured at the museum.
His site-specific work "Staircase-IV" was exhibited in 2004 as part of the museum's "Perspectives," a series of exhibitions focusing on the work of leading contemporary artists from Asia and the Asian Diaspora.
"Suh's interpretation of the idea of a 'monument' resonates in the center of Washington, D.C., where so much of the city is dedicated to commemorating figures and events from all over the world," said Carol Huh, associate curator of contemporary Asian art at the National Museum of Asian Art.
Korean art initiatives
Presented with support from the Korea Foundation, "Public Figures" is part of a larger initiative to raise the profile of Korean art and culture in the National Museum of Asian Art's galleries, programs and public spaces. In 2023, the museum opened "Park Chan-kyong: Gathering" (through Oct. 13), the first solo museum exhibition dedicated to the Seoul-based artist in the United States. Since its founding as the Freer Gallery of Art, the museum was one of the first in the U.S. to display Korean art. Today, it cares for close to 800 Korean objects; the entire Korean collection can be viewed online.
Thanks to a matching gift from the Korea Foundation, the museum recently established an endowment to support a curator of Korean art and culture to grow the Korea program and collection; the selection announcement is forthcoming. The curator will also contribute to the design of a new annual celebration of Korean art and culture that will coincide with the mid-autumn festival of Chuseok and expand the museum's engagement with the Korean and Korean American community.
With the growing prominence of Korean culture across the globe, the museum has increasingly shared its historical art collections alongside Korean popular culture in programming featuring film, food, music and performance.
About the artist
Suh (b. 1962, Seoul, South Korea; lives and works in London) works across various media, creating drawings, film and sculptural works that confront questions of home, displacement, memory, individuality and collectivity. Suh is best known for his fabric sculptures that reconstruct to scale his past and present homes and studios in Korea, Rhode Island, Berlin, London and New York. Through form, architecture and materials, Suh reflects on the metaphorical and psychological dimensions of public and private spaces.
Suh earned bachelor's and master's degrees in painting from Seoul National University before moving to the United States, where he would receive a Bachelor of Fine Arts in painting from Rhode Island School of Design in 1994 and a Master of Fine Arts in sculpture from Yale University in 1997. Solo exhibitions of his work have recently been organized at National Galleries of Scotland, Edinburgh (2024); Museum of Contemporary Art Australia, Sydney (2022); Buk-Seoul Museum of Art, Seoul (2021); Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Los Angeles (2019); Victoria & Albert Museum, London (2019); and The Brooklyn Museum, Brooklyn (2018), to name a few.
About the National Museum of Asian Art
The Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art is committed to preserving, exhibiting, researching and interpreting art in ways that deepen our collective understanding of Asia and the world. Home to more than 46,000 objects, the museum stewards one of North America's largest and most comprehensive collections of Asian art, with works dating from antiquity to the present from China, Japan, Korea, South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Islamic world. Its rich holdings bring the arts of Asia into direct dialogue with an important collection of 19th- and early 20th-century American works, providing an essential platform for creative collaboration and cultural exchange between the United States, Asia and the Middle East.
Beginning with a 1906 gift that paved the way for the museum's opening in 1923, the National Museum of Asian Art is a leading resource for visitors, students and scholars in the United States and internationally. Its galleries, laboratories, archives and library are located on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., and are part of the world's largest museum complex, which typically reports more than 27 million visits each year. The museum is free and open to the public 364 days a year (closed Dec. 25), making its exhibitions, programs, learning opportunities and digital initiatives accessible to global audiences.
For more information about the museum, visit www.asia.si.edu.

title: St. Michaels art vendors seek to host event at Muskrat Park
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels art vendors seek to host event at Muskrat Park

 March 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 557
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Wednesday evening, the St. Michaels commissioners meeting featured a lively discussion between local art vendors and members of the St. Michaels Business Association about allowing vendors to use Muskrat Park to sell their art.Trish Payne and Mark Montoya are part of Talbot County's local art community. Together with other art vendors, they run the Makers Market, a local event that allows vendors to sell their art on weekends.
"It's been my experience that there are an awful lot of people locally who are extremely talented in the arts," Payne told the council. "And they were looking for a place where they could share their art."
For the past two years, the Makers Market has been hosted by the St. Michaels Inn, but Payne is requesting permission to host it at Muskrat Park, which is located off the town's harbor. This would allow vendors to be near foot traffic, Payne said, since hosting at the St. Michaels Inn does not provide enough traction for the artists to share their work.
Payne requested the use of the park every other Saturday or every second Saturday starting in April and continuing until September. There will be between 15 to 20 vendors, and Payne has begun taking a waitlist for other vendors who would like to participate.
The commissioners approved the event. Commissioner Joyce Harrod said it seemed like a nice idea for the town.
Members and leaders of the St. Michaels Business Association, including Casey Burgess, vice president of the association, were in the crowd. Burgess was a vocal opponent of the Makers Market's request.
"My concern is that other businesses may have real problems with it. Not because of what you guys are doing but because of the fact that we have such high costs for our business properties and things like that. It will take away from the businesses," she said.
Jennifer Smith, president of the business association, said she could see negative responses from the business community. Smith suggested they look elsewhere for their event and said the parking lot on Boundary Lane might be a more suitable location.
The parking lot is about half a mile from the center of the town.
"Our whole purpose for a move is to go where we can pick up foot traffic. Where people do not have to get in a car to go there," Montoya said. "And you know, if we can pick up pedestrians, it will stimulate traction. People will shop all around it to stimulate business because more people are coming to town."
Payne said she couldn't imagine the vendors negatively affecting local businesses because they are selling oil paintings, handmade jewelry and crochet animals.
Brooke Kenrow, a resident of St. Michaels, showed her support for the Makers Market. She said she is a big fan of art festivals and craft fairs and believes it will benefit the town.
"I'd like to say that I personally, as an attendee, have always shopped locally, once I've taken the time to be there, get there, spend that time and spend the afternoon there," Kenrow said. "And I think it would be a nice addition to our town during the summertime."
The commission ultimately approved a trial run of the Makers Market at Muskrat Park for the second Saturdays in April and May to assess impacts, with the option to move it to Boundary Lane if problems arise.

title: Visiting artists welcomed by Kent Cultural Alliance
author: Staff Writer
content:
Visiting artists welcomed by Kent Cultural Alliance

 March 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Arts 
 
 578
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Kent Cultural Alliance announces its first class of visiting artists for the SFW Residency for spring 2024.This inaugural residency session features three talented artists and educators from Alvin, Texas; Baltimore, Maryland; and Luray, Virginia. These artists will work under a collective theme of "land" as they explore agriculture, soil, family farms and more with local partners for the session — Kent County 4-H, Kent County High School Future Farmers of America, and Harborview Farms.
This social practice residency has its foundation in community engagement and seeks to create broader participation around issues important to the people who call this county home.
THE ARTISTS
Canadian-American Austen Camille is an artist, writer, builder and naturalist whose studio practice is built on her early years moving schools and cities and working to note the particularities of a place. Residing in Alivn, Texas, Camille seeks reciprocal relationships between the built and natural environment in her work. Camille's interdisciplinary practice incorporates painting, sculpture, installation, writing, research, performance, new technologies and localized materials. She seeks to forge connections between the arts and other disciplines through it. She received her BA in studio art at Reed College and her MFA in painting at Temple University.
Alyssa Dennis is an interdisciplinary artist, earth activist, educator and clinical herbalist from Baltimore, Maryland. Her art practice centers on conventional forms of building and the convenience that keeps us compartmentalized within a dangerously abstract relationship with nature and our own bodies. The imagery she creates explores the impact of manufactured landscapes on our internal and external ecosystems, shaping our existence with non-human life and, ultimately, ourselves. Dennis's work combines drawing, sculptural installation and the social/environmental practice of herbalism. In her multidisciplinary practice, she questions who the players are and what are the means for reclaiming non-human kinships as a necessary form of embodiment for the reversal of cultural and climate upheaval.
With a focus on printmaking, sculpture, storytelling and community, Dennis McNett is a multifaceted maker. Hailing from Luray, Virginia, he is known for his larger-than-life woodcut print-covered puppets and masks that are used to lead narrative ceremonies and public processions. McNett has had more than 30 visiting artist and lecturer appointments across the U.S. and abroad. He holds a BFA from Old Dominion University and an MFA from Pratt Institute, where he taught from 2004-2013. His works have been featured internationally at the Victoria and Albert Museum, the MOHS exhibit, the Museum of Print History and more.
The Kent Cultural Alliance offers several opportunities for the community to engage with resident artists. Some of those opportunities include the following dates. All events at the alliance's Raimond Cultural Center, 101 Spring Ave., Chestertown.
