title: Biography of 18th century poet Phillis Wheatley is winner of George Washington Prize
author: Staff Writer
content:
Biography of 18th century poet Phillis Wheatley is winner of George Washington Prize

 September 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 199
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The author of a new biography of Phillis Wheatley, one of the country's first major poets, has received a $50,000 history award.David Waldstreicher's "The Odyssey of Phillis Wheatley: A Poet's Journey Through American Slavery and Independence" is this year's winner of the George Washington Prize, which honors works arising from the Revolutionary War era. Wheatley was the first American Black woman to publish a book and was among the most famous writers of her time, her many admirers including Washington.
The Washington prize is jointly presented by Washington College, the Gilder Lehman Institute of American History and by the maintainers of Washington's home in Mount Vernon, Virginia.
"Phillis Wheatley was admired by George Washington, and she led an extraordinary American life. Despite enslavement to a Boston merchant family, she rose to become an unforgettable poet. Her exquisite verse was fearless in questioning issues such as slavery and discontent with British rule," Doug Bradburn, president and CEO of Mount Vernon, said in a statement. "David Waldstreicher's compelling biography offers a long overdue account of Wheatley's life and works, expanding our understanding of America's complex history."
The prize was created in 2005, with previous winners including Ron Chernow, Annette Gordon-Reed and Rick Atkinson.

title: Denia Mejia: Creating art from Honduras to Easton
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Denia Mejia: Creating art from Honduras to Easton

 September 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — From the streets of Honduras to the walls of the Eastern Shore, art for Denia Mejia, an international artist based in Easton, has not only been a universal language but a pathway for support, advocacy, culture and love.Mejia has devoted her life to making complex and colorful murals, portraits and hand-painted dresses.
Native to Honduras, Mejia's passion for art began as a child and was encouraged by her father. As one of five children, she knew her future in art would be a difficult one, but her father saw her talent, and together would sell her paintings on the streets of Honduras to pay for her attendance at the La Escuela Nacional de Bellas Artes.
As she got older, she began to face health issues and would have epileptic seizures. Through art, she was able to express her thoughts and feelings toward her health. She also learned to use her art to advocate for people facing difficulties.
According to Mejia, becoming an artist is a privilege she can never live without.
"I make my art with love because it means so much to me," Mejia said. "That love inspires me to keep going and to keep creating."
During and after university, Mejia used art to advocate against injustices happening around her. Whether it was drawing attention to local elections or spreading awareness of the lack of quality drinking water, she looked to inspire change through her works.
Through the years, Mejia continued her art and had a family who inspired her. But her life was disruptive when she learned of her daughter's heart condition. And though she loved her native country, she had to leave to provide the best healthcare for her child.
"My motivation to come to this country was because of my daughter's heart illness," Mejia said. "She required a heart surgery, and that is why I made my way to Maryland. Thank God I was able to make it here and that she received the proper care."
Mejia said her daughter has improved vastly since her surgery, and she is proud to provide for her through her art.
Estela Vianey Ramirez, a Hispanic outreach coordinator for Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, said Mejia's art has made an impact on the Hispanic communities in the area.
According to Ramirez, Mejia's art is powerful, and she is impressed by the emotion and work that goes into every piece created.
"I think she puts so much into every painting she does," Ramirez said. "It's her safe space. It is a way that she can communicate. She was an activist in Honduras, so that's a way that she can communicate to the world how an artist feels or what's going through their mind. She motivates other generations to pursue that kind of career."
Victoria Gomez Lozano, deputy director of Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, said Mejia is paving the way for immigrant artists in the area.
"Denia is a very talented artist and we would love to see her art appreciated locally as a local immigrant artist who belongs to this community," Gomez Lozano said. "Someone to be proud of for her talent."
Mejia looks forward to continuing her work and to finding different avenues to impact her community. Updates on her work can be found on her Facebook page, Pinturas Artisticas Mejia.
"I love what I do, what I make, what I learned to do," Mejia said. "I do it with dedication and with motivation."

title: Fall showcase at Studio B Art Gallery
author: Staff Writer
content:
Fall showcase at Studio B Art Gallery

 October 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 139
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Studio B Art Gallery in Easton is hosting a special exhibit featuring artwork created during the gallery's Plein Air Workshop last month with Master Jove Wang.The exhibition will include new paintings by WangThe workshop focused on plein air techniques, composition, and capturing the local landscape's natural beauty.
"This exhibition is a unique opportunity to experience the incredible talent of both Jove as artist and teacher," said Betty Huang,owner of Studio B Art Gallery. "We cannot wait to unveil the artistry he will bring to the studio for the fall showcase."
Studio B Art Gallery is located at 7 B Goldsborough Street in historic downtown Easton, Maryland. The gallery represents nationally and internationally known painters Lani Browning, Hiu Lai Chong, Bernard Dellario, Ken DeWaard, Betty Huang, Qiang Huang, Charles Newman, Daniel Robbins, Master Jove Wang, and sculptor Rick Casali.
For more: www.studiobartgallery.com

title: Pretty In Pink shows art and awareness
author: Tom McCall
content:
Pretty In Pink shows art and awareness

 October 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Arts 
 
 366
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Friday, The Waterfowl Building was full of pink art to be sold to raise money for The Clark Comprehensive Breast Center in Easton. Pretty in Pink, an awareness drive, and it is highlighting breast cancer awareness month, showcased over 60 framed pieces by Working Artists Forum artists.There were rows of paintings hung with bright lights. Many of the artists were breast cancer survivors. All of the artists wanted to give back.
There were pink tables set up with University of Maryland Shore Regional Health Clark Comprehensive Breast Center pamphlets. Half of this effort was to educate about breast cancer prevention for men and women. When men get breast cancer, it is usually worse because they don't check until it is too late.
Stacey Sass, chairwoman of Pretty in Pink, said, "The Clark Comprehensive Breast Center in Easton is doing amazing things for patients, men and women, who can't always afford everything. They do an incredible job with timely diagnosis."
She is a 27-year breast cancer survivor. She said that one in eight women will have a diagnosis in their lifetime.
"This is the first time Working Artist Forum has done a charity event. We are a group of about 120 artists who have been juried into this group. Everyone really stepped up. We had 48 members contribute work," Sass said.
A lot of the educational outreach was aimed at getting people to be checked early.
"Breast cancer is not something you should be a afraid of. There is help here. You can go to the Clark Center regardless of their status of insurance, of immigration, income and get diagnosed and learn about treatment options," Mary Ford said.
On her committee, Ford did all of the group's graphics and social media.
Mary Ellen Lynott said, "The younger generation tends to think, 'That is my mom's generation,' but the statistics is it is really hitting us younger."
Lori Yates was there with her work on display.
"That is the tricky part. Getting these women in for screenings," Yates said. "It is really miraculous where we are with breast cancer. There is so much that can be done. It can be caught like before it is really even cancer."
She recommended getting checked once a year.

title: 'Sailing to Freedom' exhibit opens at Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
'Sailing to Freedom' exhibit opens at Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum

 October 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 523
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum's new exhibit shows changing perspectives of the Chesapeake Bay's relationship with the Underground Railroad by centering stories of freedom seekers."Sailing to Freedom: The Maritime Dimensions of the Underground Railroad" explores the lesser-known maritime aspects of the Underground Railroad and highlights stories of African Americans' journeys to freedom along Atlantic Coast water routes, including the Chesapeake Bay.
The exhibit features art, narrative accounts of freedom seekers, interactive exhibits, boat diagrams and historical maps detailing the routes taken by those seeking to escape from slavery.
Jen Dolde, director of curatorial affairs and exhibitions, said inspiration was taken from University of Massachusetts professor Tim Walker, Dartmouth and a scholarly book with several chapters of essays exploring aspects of freedom seekers along the Atlantic coast and in the Chesapeake region.
"People have this preconceived notion that it's primarily land-based routes, and that's not true at all, especially in coastal regions, places like the Chesapeake, where waterways were always our form of transportation," Dolde said.
According to Jill Ferris, vice president of Education and Interpretation for the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, the leadership team has been intentional on adopting language to center the lived experiences of the freedom seekers.
Ferris said historically people who were self-emancipating themselves were considered to be runaways and were painted with language to depict them as fugitives. Ferris describes the laws freedom seekers were running from as "abusive, restrictive and dehumanizing."
"If you shift from a mindset that somebody is a fugitive, that they're running away, that they're working outside of the law, and you put them at the center," Ferris said. "You give them agency and power. They were freedom seekers, they were active in their own efforts to claim and stake out their own freedom when society was trying to take it from them."
Dolde said freedom seekers would seek passage on whaling vessels or learn of safe communities through watermen. Some even went as far as shipping themselves to freedom, such as in the case of Henry Box Brown, who mailed himself in a wooden crate to abolitionists in Philadelphia.
In the exhibit, under a cartoon of Brown, there is a wooden crate created by local middle school students. The students, participants in the museums' summer program, researched primary sources, visited different museums and gathered research of the size of the crate before making the replica.
In conjunction with opening this exhibit, the museum will host speakers at the end of October and in December, as well as pilot a new student and adult group guided program called Seeking Freedom, which will focus on primary sources and first-person perspectives to uncover stories of freedom seekers.
But what stands out to Ferris is the opportunity "Sailing to Freedom" provides people seeking information and curious about freedom seekers' stories.
"Whenever we're talking about a topic that can be really emotionally challenging to take in," Ferris said. "… everybody needs to come in their own space and in their own time. And I think one of the things that I'm most proud of with this (exhibit) is providing a number of different opportunities for people to engage in the way that they are most comfortable engaging."

title: 'Exploring the Surface' features art by Evie Baskin
author: Staff Writer
content:
'Exploring the Surface' features art by Evie Baskin

 October 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Arts 
 
 399
 Words 

 Read News Document

 At the First Friday event on Oct. 4, Evie Baskin was the featured artist with The Artists' Gallery in her newest show, "Exploring the Surface." The theme for this show was originally inspired by a workshop Baskin took earlier this year in Alexandria, Virginia which involved painting with oil on copper. The use of copper as a substrate for an oil painting originally began in the Medieval times as Flemish masters favored, copper for its smooth surface which allowed for fine detail and increased durability. Included in Baskin's show in October will be paintings using various surfaces and mediums, ranging from oil on copper, canvas and birchwood panels, pastel on sanded boards and paper, to drawing in silverpoint over coated paper.Over the years, Baskin's work has continued to evolve and change. Her use of various substrates in this show exemplifies her desire to explore texture and light while incorporating the use of mediums she has continued to use over the years that include oil, pastel and silverpoint. The subject matter for "Exploring the Surface" includes portraits, both human and animal, along with landscapes on the Eastern Shore and beyond.
As a native Floridian, Baskin graduated from Florida State University in Tallahassee in 1976 with a degree in Visual Art. After raising her family in Key West, she moved to Alexandria, Virginia where she managed a law firm in Washington, D.C. while taking classes at The Torpedo Factory in her spare time. In 2007, she and her husband, Jonathan, moved to Chestertown where she began to work with pastel for the first time under the leadership of Mary Pritchard and Claudia Post. In 2015, Baskin became a partner with The Artists' Gallery and remains a juried member of the Working Artists' Forum in Easton, Chestertown Riverarts, the Portrait Society of America and the Maryland Society of Portrait Painters in Annapolis.
The public is invited to visit The Artists' Gallery on First Friday, Oct. 4, for an opening reception from 5-7:30 p.m., with light refreshments and to meet the artist. Baskin's creative work will be featured in the gallery throughout the month of October. The Artists' Gallery is located at 239 High Street in Chestertown and is open Tuesday through Saturday from 10-5 and Sundays from 12:30-4:30 p.m. For more information on The Artists' Gallery, please visit www.theartistsgalleryctown.com or call the gallery at 410-778-2425. title: Museum preserves history with digital scanner
author: Tom McCall
content:
Museum preserves history with digital scanner

 October 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 524
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — White gloves and intense focus are needed to run the new Danish scanner at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum.Some of the museum's oldest artifacts from the 1780s are run through the contactless machine. No liquids of any kind are allowed in the Norman and Ellen Plummer Center for Museum Collections to protect the invaluable documents.
In July, the museum got a world-class large-format scanner. It can make super high resolution images of mostly flat objects. It will be used to digitize not only the museum's vast holdings of nautical information, but to support other organizations with their databases.
This includes materials that are challenging to handle and reproduce, including ship/sail plans, charts/maps, posters, artworks, framed items behind glass, rolled items and some three-dimensional artifacts.
Museum staff will work alongside volunteers to safely scan the materials, upload reference images to its online catalog of over 85,000 records and make them available to worldwide audiences.
As part of the project, the museum will provide free scanning services for other heritage tourism partners on special days, improving the availability and quality of graphic resources for exhibitions, publications and other historical projects.
The scanner is the HD Apeiron/42, made by Contex, designed in Denmark and first introduced in Europe. The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum is one of the first sites to use this technology in the U.S.
It has five cameras inside of it and is much bigger than a standard 11-by-17-inch flatbed scanner.
There is a husband and wife team that is cataloging ships plans. AJ Daverede is a retired naval architect, and Heidi is an engineer. He spent 23 years as an archivist at the National Archives. There are tens of thousands of documents to be scanned in the museum's collection, and they are volunteers.
"It is going to be great to get all this stuff online and give people access to it," Heidi said, "to have good quality scans."
Currently they are cataloguing Trumpy yachts that were built between 1910 and 1972. There are ship plans for these stately and sleek yachts.
Some of the drawings are torn or are in bad shape. So the advantage of digitizing is it minimizes handling.
Assistant curator Gabriella Cantelmo said that they look at digitization as a preservation method.
"If they get torn or crumble into dust, which is a possibility, we have them," Cantelmo said.
"It is really important because part of our mission is access to Chesapeake-based culture and history. By digitizing these ship plans and making them available online or at request of researchers, we are furthering that access," Cantelmo said.
She scanned a watercolor of "Wye Island Maryland" by Matthias Bordley, 1781. It showed a long-gone windmill on the island. The resolution is so high, you can look at a tiny portion of the art, and it is clear.
The museum was able to get this machine through a Maryland Heritage Area Authority grant.
"They want to know how we are serving the community. Not only with our collection, which serves the community, but also with this outreach. It is part of our stewardship responsibility and we take it very seriously," said Jen Dolde, director of curatorial affairs and exhibitions.
You can see this work at collections.cbmm.org.

title: Mid-Atlantic Small Craft Festival: A living museum in St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Mid-Atlantic Small Craft Festival: A living museum in St. Michaels

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 574
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — This last weekend the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum was filled with the energetic buzz of dozens of families camping outside with unique watercraft for the 41st annual Mid-Atlantic Small Craft Festival.Sailors and builders from around the region showed off their small craft boats, including sailing, skiffs, rowing shells, kayaks, canoes, paddle boats, prams and one-of-a-kind boats.
Vera England, a longtime attendee, said the event began in 1983, back when the maritime museum had fewer buildings and the well-loved dock was just a beach. She said there were probably 10 to 15 people who attended that first year, and by the second year it had grown significantly.
"It was a living museum. That was our goal," England said. "Small boats were possibly dying out. … We wanted people to get on the water. We wanted children to know what boats were like. The museum was very, very supportive of keeping the tradition of small boats and small boat buildings."
England describes the event as "multigenerational" in its family-friendly approach and encouragement of young children's involvement. According to England, there is no better example of the multigenerational work of the small craft festival than the Blackwell family.
Adam Blackwell began attending the small craft festival when he was in second grade. It soon became a part of his family's tradition. Blackwell said as a child he learned to sail and row with other children (one of whom would later become his wife).
After taking a break from attending due to school, Blackwell came back, met his wife again, got married and has now decided to continue the tradition by bringing his own children to the small craft festival every year.
"It's kind of funny because they're playing with some of the children of the kids that I played with growing up. It's fantastic watching the kids. They're happy. They're running around. They're outside on boats. It's beautiful."
According to England, this festival has created a community of boat lovers. But to keep the community going, people need to invest in events like the small craft festival through not only individual engagement, but also empowering young people to learn traditions, build their own crafts and sail through the Chesapeake Bay.
"Appreciate the water. Appreciate the traditions. Appreciate the fact that these traditions are ephemeral," England said. "If there isn't a place to keep them alive, they will fade and you won't move. And that's very important. That's part of what we try to do, is keep traditions alive, keep the idea of working with your hands to build the small boat."
Blackwell said it is amazing to see the confidence his children have developed through sailing. They're interest began as a shared love learned by their parents and has become something all of their own. They have preferred crafts, have been on the water independently and know when to ask for help. His children's passion reminds him of the pull sailing had on him.
Blackwell said that on his wedding day, his father-in-law read aloud an old log book from the small craft festival when Blackwell and his wife were young. In it were descriptions of his wife and his sister playing outside and enjoying nature.
"(My father-in-law) then goes, 'and the Blackwell boy was out on the water the entire time,'" Blackwell said with a laugh. "And that was my entry in the log book as a child. 'The Blackwell boy was out on the water the entire time. We didn't see him.'"

title: German artist brings powerful pieces to downtown Easton
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
German artist brings powerful pieces to downtown Easton

 October 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Through visually stunning paintings of zebras made from recycled cans collected in crisis zones to brightly colored paint portraits, Erdman Hummel is able to tell stories about the complexities of war and how to continue moving with hope.The Zebra Gallery hosted Hummel, a German artist and international journalist, last Friday evening. Hummel's paintings will be on display at the gallery through October.
According to Hummel, his path toward being an artist was a challenging one. Hummel, who was born under comunitst rule in East Germany when the Berlin Wall was still up, learned early on the importance of art.
Hummel said in the political context of Berlin, government approval was needed before any artist could practice their craft. At the age of 20, after a few of his artist friends were denied by the government, Hummel secretly opened his own gallery, which was forbidden at the time. Eventually, Hummel had an encounter with the Secret Service in East Germany, and it led to his imprisonment.
While in prison, Hummel read about zebras. To his surprise, zebras, over millennia, have never been domesticated. Hummel said he found inspiration from the animal and used it as a mantra during his time in prison.
"I decided these zebras are a symbol for me," Hummel said.
After spending over a year in prison, Hummel's release was negotiated by the West German government. After the Berlin Wall came down, Hummel decided to devote his life to sharing information and began his career in broadcast journalism. Over the years, Hummel has reported on war zones and crisis areas in Africa, Asia, Afghanistan, Iraq and Gaza.
And now Hummel has come back to art, focusing on the animal that kept his spirit going while he was in prison. His pieces are portraits of brightly colored zebras.
Gail Patterson, owner of the Spiralis Gallery, a separate gallery that occupies the same space as the Zebra Gallery in downtown Easton, said she has a strong appreciation for the uniqueness of the gallery's art, particularly with Hummel's work.
"This is just so unique compared to the waterfowl art and even open air art," Patterson said. "I mean, just everything about it is different for our town… I love (Hummel's) colors and the way there's some camouflaging."
Susan Fay Schauer, owner of the Zebra Gallery, said she was excited to include Hummel in her gallery.
"(Hummel) only paints zebras, and many of them he makes out of aluminum cans that he collects around the world," Schauer said. "He's a German war correspondent, so he collects unusual cans from war zones."
Hummel said he is excited to share his art with the Eastern Shore. According to his biography, the zebras changed the way he viewed his own liberty and the complexities of life.
"Zebras are a symbol of freedom for me," Hummel said. "I translate this freedom into joy of color. As a painter, their stripes give me an opportunity to put complementary colors against one another. Zebras are very individual. No animal is like another. Each has a unique stripe drawing."
This report has been updated from an earlier version to correct the name and title of the Spiralis Gallery's owner.

title: Fairyfest brings hundreds to Adkins Arboretum
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Fairyfest brings hundreds to Adkins Arboretum

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 419
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — Families entered through an enchanted bridge into a world of wings, fairy houses and pirate hooks on Saturday afternoon at Adkins Arboretum's Fairyfest.The annual festival joined hundreds of young children and families together on a sunny Saturday, with many dressed up in costumes and exploring activities such as potion making and pirate ship sword fighting.
Abby Lorenz, Adkins Arboretum's director of public engagement, said the best part about the event is seeing first-time festivalgoers explore a new world at Adkins, a 400-acre native garden nestled within Tuckahoe State Park.
She emphasized the event brings children who didn't have a ton of open space or exposure to gardens to a unique outdoor setting.
"That's really important to me," Lorenz said. "Getting to see kids that didn't have that be able to experience that and dress up and be with their families and all those things. That's really the big magic for me."
Saturday's four-hour event included outdoor games, food vendors and indoor craft activities. There were performances by the Allegra! Women's Chorus from Easton and the Mid Shore Dance Academy. Dancers also performed throughout the day at the "magical maypole," wrapping it up with a finale before the end of the afternoon.
Attendees walked through nature trails to view more than 20 portable fairy houses before voting for their favorites. The fairy houses were made out of natural materials such as pine cones, flowers and pumpkins.
The festival used to accommodate close to 1,000 attendees before organizers set a registration limit due to parking on site. This year's registration was limited to 400.
Lorenz said the event was put on by 25 volunteers and nine full-time staff members. It was her first major event for Adkins Arboretum, after beginning in the public engagement position just last month.
"I (saw) a lot of different gardens across the country," Lorenz said. "And I fell in love with Adkins. That really helps bring the community that raised me into the community that I love.
"When I walk into these woods, it's like the woods that I found when I was a child behind my grandparents house that inspired me to really like figure out who I was and gave me the space to think and create," Lorenz said. "But it's like times a thousand. And it's free and open to the public. And I get to share that."
Lorenz pointed to Plein Air Adkins as the arboretum's next signature event on Nov. 2, where the public can watch artists paint in the outdoors and later purchase those pieces of art.

title: Recipes for Oktoberfest celebrations
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Recipes for Oktoberfest celebrations

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1103
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Oktoberfest was first held in Munich, Germany in 1810 to celebrate the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese of Sansony-Hildburghausse. The original date was Oct. 12, and it lasted for several days.Oktoberfest eventually developed to begin in the middle of September and carry on until the middle of October. The celebration exploded with costumes, all kinds of foods and beverages, dancing, music and parades.
This continual celebration that lasted for weeks was held outside of town in a large spacious meadow. Since 1950, the festival has only started after the official gun salute and the mayor shouting "O' zapft is," which means "it's tapped," and offering the first mug to the Minister-President of the State of Bavaria.
Let us explore some of that delicious food that was piled on several lines of endless tables. One of the most popular traditional recipes is schnitzel.
Schnitzel are thin cutlets and can be made with just about any kind of meat. You can have veal schnitzel most affectionately known as "Wiener schnitzel," pork schnitzel, chicken schnitzel and turkey schnitzel, among many others. The meat is pounded thin with a meat tenderizer, then breaded and fried.
For our next one, a longtime favorite of my family, German Chocolate Cake. German chocolate is not really from Germany. German chocolate is a sweet chocolate invented by a man named Sam German in 1852 for Baker's Chocolate. The moniker stuck, and we still call it German chocolate to this day. If you can't find German chocolate, either milk chocolate or semisweet chocolate will do instead.
WIENER SCHNITZEL4 (5-oz) veal cutlets (or chicken or pork cutlets if you like), 1/4 cup all-purpose flour, 1/2 tsp kosher salt, 2 large eggs (well beaten), 1/2 cup bread crumbs, Oil or lard for frying.
Place veal cutlets between sheets of plastic wrap and use a heavy, flat-surfaced pan, rolling pin or meat mallet to pound the meat evenly to 1/4-inch thickness. To bread the schnitzels, set up 3 shallow dishes: Mix 1/4 cup all-purpose flour and 1/2 tsp kosher salt in the first dish, 2 large beaten eggs in the second dish, and 1/2 cup breadcrumbs in the third dish. In a large skillet, heat at least 1/4-inch of oil to 350 degrees. This takes about 8 minutes, and the oil will just start to shimmer and smoke a bit. Working one at a time, dredge cutlets first in flour until the surface is completely dry. Dip in egg to coat, allow the excess to drip off for a few seconds. Roll quickly in the breadcrumbs until coated. Do not press the breadcrumbs into the meat, as this will moisten them and not make for a crispy coating.
The crust should not adhere completely but form a loose shell around the schnitzel. Immediately place the meat in the pan with the hot oil. Do not crowd the pan. Cook the schnitzel in batches, if necessary. Fry the schnitzel for 2 to 3 minutes on one side, until golden brown. Make sure the breaded meat "swims" in fat. Contrary to instinct, the breading will take on less oil than if the meat is sticking to the pan. Also, the breadcrumb topping has a chance to puff up a little, and your cleanup is easier. You may want to swish them around a little with your fork to make sure they are not sticking to the pan. Turn them over once and fry an additional 2 to 3 minutes or until both sides are golden brown and the meat registers an internal temperature of 145 degrees. Remove from pan and allow the oil to drain off.
PORK CHOPS AND SAURKRAUTThis next recipe is best made in a Dutch oven. 1.5–2 lb boneless pork chops about 1/2 inch thick, 2 tbsps olive oil, 4-6 medium russet potatoes, 1 apple, 18 ounces sauerkraut (undrained), 1 tsp caraway seeds, 1 onion.
Peel and dice the potatoes, apple and onion, Set them aside. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. While the oven preheats, pat the pork chops dry with a paper towel and season very lightly with salt and pepper. Heat a large Dutch oven on the stovetop over medium-high heat. Add the oil. Once the oil is shimmering (about 1 minute), add the pork chops. Brown on each side for about 3 minutes per side. They should easily release once they're ready to be flipped. Set the pork chops aside and add the sauerkraut to the hot dutch oven. With a wooden spoon, gently scrape the bottom to deglaze it. Add the onion, potatoes and apples and then lay the pork chops on top. Sprinkle the caraway seeds. Cover and bake in the oven for one hour. Remove the dutch oven, allow to cool slightly and serve.
GERMAN CHOCOLATE CAKE4 ounces German sweet chocolate (chopped), 1/2 cup water, 1 cup butter (softened), 2 cups sugar, 4 large eggs (separated, room temperature), 1 tsp vanilla extract, 2 1/2 cups cake flour, 1 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 cup buttermilk. FROSTING: 1 1/2 cups sugar, 1 1/2 cups evaporated milk, 3/4 cup butter, 5 large egg yolks (room temperature, beaten), 2 cups sweetened shredded coconut, 1 1/2 cups chopped pecans, 1 1/2 tsps vanilla extract. ICING:2 ounces semisweet chocolate, 1 tsp shortening.
Line three greased 9-inch round baking pans with waxed paper. Grease waxed paper and set aside. In a small saucepan, melt chocolate with water over low heat; cool. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a large bowl, cream butter and sugar until light and fluffy, 5-7 minutes. Beat in egg yolks, one at a time, beating well after each addition. Blend in melted chocolate and vanilla. Combine flour, baking soda and salt; add to the creamed mixture alternately with buttermilk, beating well after each addition. In a small bowl and with clean beaters, beat the 4 egg whites until stiff peaks form. Fold a fourth of the egg whites into the creamed mixture, fold in remaining whites.
Pour batter into prepared pans. Bake 24-28 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean. Cool for 10 minutes before removing from pans to wire racks to cool completely. For the icing, in a small saucepan, heat sugar, milk, butter and egg yolks over medium-low heat until mixture is thickened and golden brown, stirring constantly. Remove from heat. Stir in coconut, pecans and vanilla. Cool until thick enough to spread. Spread a third of the frosting over each cake layer and stack the layers. In a microwave, melt chocolate and shortening; stir until smooth. Drizzle over cake. This is not a cake that requires refrigeration, since the flavors will be best at room temperature.

title: Taste of Cambridge brings delectable treats to downtown Cambridge
author: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com
content:
Taste of Cambridge brings delectable treats to downtown Cambridge

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JIM JOHNSON jjohnson@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 297
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The weather was perfect Saturday, drawing a large crowd to the 16th Taste of Cambridge event."We were extremely thrilled with the turnout," said Christina Wingate-Spence, Cambridge Main Street executive director. More than 300 Taste of Cambridge tickets were sold and the overall crowd in downtown Cambridge was upwards of 800, Wingate-Spence said.
The event — the second hosted after a hiatus during the COVID-19 pandemic — featured 11 cook-off contest competing for best crab soup, best crab cake, best Eastern Shore fare and best desserts.
Winners were:
Crab soup: Blue Ruin bar and restaurant.Crab cake: Blue Ruin bar and restaurant.Eastern Shore fare: Vintage 414 wine bar.Dessert: Blackwater Bakery and Eats.
Ticket holders voted for the people's choice award, which went to Blue Ruin's crab cake.
The judges for the four awards were: Laurie Forster, an author and national expert on all things wine; Tami Weber, WBOC morning show host; and Gena Levy, owner of Bay Country Bakery in Cambridge.
In addition to the cook-off contestants there was a Kid Zone, featuring a face painter and bounce houses. A giant crab balloon archway created by Cabin Fever Play Centre was the backdrop for many selfies.
Two stages featured a variety of entertainment. On the main stage at the intersection of Race and Gay streets, the Soul Crackers, an 11-piece ensemble from the Washington, D.C., area, made a repeat performance. They were followed by the Radio Pilots, a rock cover band, which received an enthusiastic welcome from the crowd.
On the second stage, located at the intersection of Muir and Race streets, a variety of students performed; along with Inland Fusion featuring Nancy and Jody; and Jayme D., a solo artist.
The event drew people from across the Eastern Shore and Washington, D.C. Wingate-Spence said the downtown shops had a large influx of customers throughout the day.

 Nnedi Okorafor is an award-winning author who has garnered international acclaim for her work on Marvel's "Black Panther" comic book series, but her writing career unexpectedly took off following a life-altering event while in college.Okorafor, who writes African-based science fiction and fantasy novels for children and adults, stopped by Leonardtown High School Oct. 11 to talk about her career. St. Mary's College of Maryland Community Affairs Liaison Kelsey Bush served as moderator.
Building on the work of Stan Lee and Ta-Nehisi Coates — whose "Black Panther" comics were adapted into a blockbuster movie in 2018 — Okorafor authored several issues of "Black Panther — Long Live the King," a continuation of the series and earned Hugo nominee for best novella.
In addition, she authored "Wakanda Forever," which was adapted into a global hit movie, as well as its spin-off, "Shuri."
"I had a problem with Wakanda in general because the concept of it just didn't make any sense to me," she said. But during her early years, the two things that she loved more than anything was track and field, tennis and bugs.
"I loved sports and then bugs," Okorafor said, adding her mom was a Nigerian Olympic javelin thrower while her dad was a nationally known hurdler. "I thought I was going to be an entomologist. I didn't grow up wanting to write at all."
She later excelled at tennis — she said she had a 114 mph serve and she and her sister were "like Venus and Serena before Venus and Serena" — but at the age of 13 was diagnosed with scoliosis.
After playing singles her freshman year at the University of Champagne in Illinois, she was told the disease had compressed her spine and needed surgery. Following the operation, she was paralyzed from the waist down.
"You take an athlete that could do all that and you paralyze them?" she said. "That was my identity."
She sought solace in an Isaac Asimov book and eventually regained feeling in her lower body.
"It was in that moment of pure darkness descending on me that my mind just turned to storytelling," she said. "And as soon as I started doing it, it was like a light switched on and that light pushed all that darkness that was descending on me and went away."
She later took a creative writing class on the advice of a friend, whom she had a crush on, and "it opened up my world."
Okorafor — who moved with her parents to America in 1969 — said the hardest novel she's written was "Death of an Author," which is scheduled to be released in January, though she declined to say why.
She said a close second was "Who Fears Death," which she said she started writing on the night of her father's wake.
"I was very, very close to my father and it's literally autobiographical," she said. "The pain I was going through I just poured it all into that novel and still is the darkest novel I've written."
Marvel contacted her and asked her to write "Spiderman," though she declined.
"It was too much," she said. "I'm not jumping in the deep end when I don't know how to swim. Plus I just can't relate to that [story]. I like to start small. A lot of people would have jumped at that, but for me I like to build my way there and be comfortable and feel natural."
She said working with Marvel was quite stressful.
"The thing about Marvel is that once you agree and say, 'Yeah, I'll do that,' you have days to come up with a summary, which is scary because you have these beloved characters and if you come up with something wrong you'll hear about it in many ways," she said of the three-issue series she authored.
Among Okorafor's other works are the "Binti" trilogy, the "Akata Witch" books — both of which are optioned for the screen — and her latest, "She Who Knows."
To watch the whole interview, go to www.youtube.com/watch?v=MKv-8LS9RC0.

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Life 
 
 395
 Words

 OXFORD — The Oxford Business Association is hosting the 14th annual Picket Fence Auction. Eleven artists have painted their four slats of fence in nature themes. There is everything from birdhouses to dogs to frogs.You can bid live, by the website or by proxy. Online bids had to be in by Oct. 14. The live auction is at the Oxford Community Center on Saturday at 5 p.m. Brian Wells is the auctioneer.
"It is a lot of fun. They are usually packed with people trying to get the numbers up. It is quick. Five to six," said Liza Ledford, president of the Oxford Business Association.
The 28-inch high fences will be auctioned to support a wide array of good causes. Some people plant their art picket fence in their homes. Others place them outside for all to enjoy.
There is a treasure hunt map that showed where the fences were placed around town.
"When you come across the ferry, there are maps and little rack cards. People take them and try to find all 10 fences. It gives the tourist with ice cream in hand a way to explore the town. The location changes every year," Ledford said.
She said the picket fences usually go for between $350 and $3,000 each.
"We tried to retire it around 12 years ago, but it is back by popular demand. The town loves these fences, which have become iconic in the town branding," Ledford said.
Here are the artists and their causes.
Josepha Price's "The Songbird" auctions to benefit For All Seasons.Donna Clarke's "Blanketed in Chesapeake Vibes" will benefit Project Linus.Annie Mathews' "Heron Sunset Silhouette" will help The John Wesley Museum."Turtle Time" by Maggii Sarfaty will benefit Shore Rivers.Jacqui Gosselin's "Oyster Love" will support Sts. Peter and Paul.Diane Evans' "The Artist's Work at Sunset" will support Water's Methodist Church."Transformation" by Sue Stockman will benefit Talbot Interfaith Shelter."Dark and Froggy Night" by Mary Ford will support Oxford Community Center."Sallies Peeps" picket fence painted by Sally Fronk will help CASA.Allan Mielke's fence is "Who Let The Dogs Out." It will benefit Talbot Humane Society.
The 11th artist is John Tochko. His work will support the Oxford Museum.
"We feel proud to produce the picket fence auction because it benefits 10 other charities. The artists are donating all their time and energy," Ledford said.

Community parade celebrates Dan Tabler’s 100th birthday

 CENTREVILLE — A parade of emergency vehicles, American Legion Riders and community members lauded a life well lived during a 100th birthday celebration for local community legacy Dan Tabler Oct. 13.Orchestrated by the Goodwill Fire Company, in which Tabler has been a member for over 75 years, the parade took off from the firehouse and made its way to the Tabler residence on Elm Street for a celebration of the century alongside friends, family and the Centreville community.
Commending Tabler's outstanding contributions to the community and the American Legion,
Jason Miller, American Legion vice commander of the Detachment of Maryland and Jeff Davis American Legion Post 18 member, presented certificates of recognition.
Centreville's Jeff Davis American Legion was chartered in 1935 with Tabler one of its charter members, Miller said.
According to Miller's research, at 90 years of membership, Tabler stands as one of the longest serving Sons of the American Legion members in the country.
Tabler is former editor, writer and longtime columnist for the Record-Observer.
Tabler was grateful for the recognition from the community and credited his success and dedication to the local community as, "love what you do."
Surrounded by friends, family and an appreciative community, Tabler presented one of his trademark lines when asked about how he feels, "I've never felt better in my life."

St. Michaels announces gingerbread contest, ornament

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 421

 Read News Document

 Bakers and pastry chefs of all ages and talent levels are encouraged to get their gingerbread house games on with the return of the Christmas in St. Michaels Gingerbread House competition this December and a purse totaling $2,000 in prizes up for grabs.The competition is an important component of the fundraising the all-volunteer organization achieves with the annual event, with the creations highlighted and on display at the Gingerbread "House" Preview Cocktail Party at the Woman's Club of St. Michaels on Thursday, Dec. 12, beginning at 5 p.m.
"We are encouraging participants to donate their creations for our silent auction, to be held the evening of the cocktail party," says this year's Gingerbread House Competition Co-Chair Michele Lowe. "All auction proceeds support the beneficiaries of Christmas in St. Michaels."
Entrants can pick their category for participation, which includes master chefs and caterers, adults, young adults, children, children with adults, kit-made houses, and non-profit organizations. Participation is free, with pre-registration needed at christmasinstmichaels.org/events.
The 2024 Christmas in St. Michaels Collectors Ornament has also been announced and is the 21st in the series. This year's ornament depicts the Chesapeake deadrise workboat with its crew and a friendly canine companion. The image was provided by St. Michaels artist Sherry Smith.
The boxed ornament is available for purchase at select local retail shops and the weekend-long Christmas in St. Michaels Marketplace and Sweet Shoppe. Online purchases can be made at www.christmasinstmichaels.org/ornament.
The deadrise workboat has been a staple among Chesapeake watermen for decades. "Deadrise" refers to the almost flat, V-shaped hull that provides a shallow draft to accommodate the waters in creeks and rivers of the Eastern Shore. Boats range from 25-45 feet in length and are powered by large, inboard four- or six-cylinder engines, usually diesel-fueled.
Workboats typically sport women's names on the transom or bow, paying tribute to wives and daughters. Others, such as the one in this ornament, refer to the town, river or creek the boat calls home port.
"It is typical to see dozens of these deadrise workboats plying the waters of the Eastern Shore in the wee hours of the morning as they seek the day's catch, returning to the pier in the early afternoon to get their catch to market," says Christmas in St. Michaels Chair Pat Martin. "We're honored to add this limited-edition ornament to our collection to pay tribute to watermen and their boats in the St. Michaels area and the Chesapeake Bay region at large."
Event details, online ticket and ornament purchases, and more about Christmas in St. Michaels are at christmasinstmichaels.org.

title: Telling stories in 'all caps' — Fresca Frankie creates art from bottle caps
author: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Kent County News
content:
Telling stories in 'all caps' — Fresca Frankie creates art from bottle caps

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Kent County News | Section: News 
 
 1144
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Saturday after Saturday small groups come and gather outside the booth of Fresca Frankie at the Chestertown Farmers' Market because, especially on a sunny day, her colorful and subtly shiny wares catch the light in just the right way that it attracts the eye and draws the marketgoer in for a closer look."Oh, they're bottle caps!" one curious patron said. "That's so cool!"
And that is usually followed up by a lot of "oohs" and "aahs" as they get the opportunity to see what's inside each small circumference of metal— a metal that was saved from the scrap bin at one time or another and now enjoys a second life as a sweet little canvas of Frankie's making. When you consider that the size of that canvas is approximately just one-inch, you become keenly aware that there must be something truly special going on in each one.
Lisa "Frankie" Ford, a Centreville resident, has been gracing the maker's row of the Chestertown Farmers' Market with those eye-catching bottle cap designs for more than a decade now, after spending most of her professional career in health care as an occupational therapist. In that role, she leaned heavily into the part of her personality that enjoys communicating with and helping others, and she said she relished the aspects of the work that enabled her to help patients heal through crafting, which became a vital part of their physical and emotional recovery.
"When I first started there was a lot more emphasis on utilizing crafts as a form of therapy," she said.
She recalled a stroke patient in particular, who really struggled with her fine motor skills.
"The craft was basket weaving," she noted. "And she had a lot of trouble getting the weave [to lay] right, or the material would break off in her hand."
As frustrating as the process was, she said, the patient persevered, eventually completing the project and placing the misshapen vessel on her mantel at home. The patient told Ford her kids would later ask why it was on the mantel when it was less than perfect, and the patient replied, "Because that's my recovery. It represents my recovery. It's the story of it."
Those stories and moments still resonate with Ford. However, there would be less and less of them as the health care industry began to change over the years. There came a point, Ford said, when she realized that she would need to change, as well. With the support and encouragement of her husband, Ford left health care to pursue crafting in various forms.
"My husband told me that he never saw me smile more than when I was at the farmers market," she said, and so her full-throttle adventure into full-time crafting began.
Around that time, she said, someone happened to gift a book of bottle cap art to her.
"I would be the first to tell you that I did not invent this idea," she said. She did, however, improve upon it and lend her own imagination to the task. Working with the caps would prove frustrating at first, she explained, as the glues suggested for the practice did not stand up to real-time wear.
"They were non-toxic and water-soluble; which I thought was a good thing."
And then she said she remembered a little piece of advice that her father had relayed to her often when she was growing up.
"'There's nothing that a good two-part epoxy can't fix.'"
Taking her dad's wisdom to heart she perfected her process of application and the concepts for bottle cap charms came fast and furiously. Each reimagined bottle cap artwork is designed to either be worn on a chain as a necklace or attached to a loop so it can be used as a key chain.
To help her mom present her designs in their best light, Ford said her daughter, Abigail, who was modeling at the time, suggested having the charms professionally styled for a photoshoot.
It is clear when visiting Ford's booth that her daughter had a great idea as this imagery and all the other enhancements that Ford adds to create a unique shopping experience is working. Trays of charms are labeled to convey varying areas of interest and styles, areas like sports, celestial, Maryland-centric, and hobbies. Marketgoers tend to linger and browse longer because there is so much to see; from details that are pinhead-sized to the overall aspect of the experience of shopping there and chatting with Ford, which she said is what she loves most about what she does.
And all that chatter results in a nice return customer base for Ford. In fact, if you're already wearing a Fresca Frankie when you visit the booth, her customer loyalty program kicks in automatically, offering a great discount on any pair from her up-cycled earring line.
In addition to her bottle cap charms, Ford displays her unique earring designs that she creates from recycled vintage jewelry. This aspect of her business has proven to be popular as legions of vintage jewelry lovers who wish to purge their troves, regularly contribute to the cause, so there is no shortage of resource material. And everyone wins because Ford provides discounts off of future purchases to those who donate their costume jewelry.
Rounding out her fashionable offerings are the bright and pretty displays of necklaces and bracelets she makes from soda can beads that she rolls herself by hand. She has a "secret-sauce" process for creating this line of lightweight and stackable accessories, which she admits discovering as a happy accident while trying to solve a design challenge.
Frustrated while trying to make a bracelet from a colorful strip of metal from an Arizona iced tea can, her subconscious fidgety fingers rolled the metal into a cylindrical bead, and eureka, the soda-can bead necklace was born. And you can literally see thousands of these shiny elements in containers catching that sun around her booth, where Ford continues to answer her customers' questions.
"Where do you get your ideas from?"
"Do people save their bottle caps for you?" The quick answer to that one is —"yes!"
And Ford is super grateful to those who do reach out and provide her with resources that would normally just get tossed.
Another customer comes by to take a closer look at a specific design and says, "How clever!" — and then asks about how the charm can be worn. Ford explains about the option to wear it as a necklace and tags her comment with something she explained she often tells a potential customer.
"Get used to people getting a little bit closer to you than they normally would when you're wearing it."
Fresca Frankie's booth will be open at the Chestertown Farmers' Market through the end of the year, and then returning for the spring market. You can check her out at her online Etsy shop and on Facebook. Those interested in donating vintage costume jewelry, can contact her via email at frescafrankie@yahoo.com

title: Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra opens Ensemble Series
author: JOHN MALIN Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra opens Ensemble Series

 October 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JOHN MALIN Special to the Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 252
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A synergistic fusion of the arts occurred on Sunday, Oct. 20, as the Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra launched it's 2024/2025 season Ensemble Series with a woodwind quintet concert at the Academy Art Museum in Easton.The highly accomplished musicians were all members of the orchestra and included Rachael Yokers on flute, Noelle Drews on oboe, Cheryl Hill on clarinet, Karl Shea on bassoon and Beth Lunt on French horn.
The program featured several lesser-known composers, ranging chronologically from the early 19th to the 21st century.
Starting with a very lively and bright piece, "Passacaille" by Adrien Barthe, the program moved through the soft, melodic and haunting "Eyes" by Roma Cafolia to the five joyeus and playful movements of "Quintette en Ut" by Claude Arrieu (actually Louise -Marie Simon), who used a male name so her compositions would beat the gender barriers of the early 1900s.
The concert included five more composers from Japan, France and the United States, and the audience was challenged to identify the five dance rhythms in the "Five Easy Dances" by Denes Agay. These dances were played with a boldness and presence that had plenty of feet tapping.
It was a really delightful and uplifting concert set in the lovely venue of the Academy Arts Museum. The blending of the five instruments was very pleasing, and for me the combination of bassoon and French horn playing counterpoint bass melodies and rhythms was great. The musical skills on show were what we have come to expect from one of our local gems, the MSO.

title: Celebrating Hispanic art and artists with poster contest
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Celebrating Hispanic art and artists with poster contest

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 456
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — From iconic Hispanic icons like Frida Khalo, to colorfully rich portraits of Guatemala landscapes, to a tree with all the Hispanic flags hanging from its branches, the Academy Art Museum was filled with a variety of portraits.In celebration of Hispanic cultural heritage, the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center hosted a poster competition and invited community members to rejoice in the submissions.
Every year, the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center asks the Hispanic community to participate in choosing a theme for the annual celebration. Victoria Gomez Lozano, deputy director for Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, said the theme for this year is "Ser Hispano, es Ser Valiente," which translates to "Being Hispanic is Being Brave."
The top three posters win prizes, and the first place poster will be used as the official poster for the 2025 Hispanic Heritage Month in Easton.
Roxana Tapia, judge of the competition, said the first, second and third place winners this year came from various ages and ethnicities. But they all had the common goal of celebrating Hispanic heritage.
"You don't even have to be a Latina in order to participate," Tapia said. "What I liked about this year is that we have people from all ethnicities. So if for any kids, I invite them to come over and participate, it's always fun. (Artists) should be proud of their work."
The winners of this year's competition were Piper Hambleton and Ellis Williams for their collaborative work. Their poster portrayed a large tree with flags from every Latin American and Hispanic country attached to its branches.
Alberto Gamez, a judge and ChesMRC board member, called the colorful art piece "The Tree of the Nations."
"I love that it was like a tree of life, but each branch had a different nation, and they covered a lot of them. So I love that it included everybody," Gamez said.
Gamez said he enjoyed all the art submitted this year and the various stories attached to the works, including third place winner Ahias Murillo, whose portrait "I Paint My Own Reality" showed Frida Khalo with an array of Latin American flags behind her. According to Gamez, the piece spoke on the identity and growth of Latinos.
The second place winner Majo Arrivillaga, whose portrait of two faceless individuals was meant to depict the different faces migrants have while traveling to the United States, also included a colorful landscape of Guatemala.
Arrivillaga said she loves drawing because it allows her to show people the beauty within the Latino community and encourages Latino artists of all ages to take the leap and share their work with their community.
"Being Hispanic, for me, is being a person who works, studies and centers their family," Arrivillaga said. "We are multifaceted and we can do it all. That's what makes us brave."

title: NYC dancers bring color, talent, fun to Stevensville
author: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat
content:
NYC dancers bring color, talent, fun to Stevensville

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 276
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Grace, beauty and talent enchanted 150 guests at the Cascia Vineyard in Stevensville on Oct. 6.As evening began along the Chesapeake Bay, guests filled lawn chairs and blankets as they sipped wine, relaxed in the sunshine and were mesmerized by the acclaimed Ballet Hispanico Pa'lante Dancers.
The stage displayed dancers in a plethora of colorful, intricate costumes. The many costume changes and variety of dances held the attention of the audience of all ages. With admiration and excitement, the audience was then invited on stage to try salsa dancing to culminate the performance.
Just hours before the performance, young dancers (ages 14 and above) also enjoyed a complimentary ballet masterclass at Kent Island High School taught by ballerina Nicole Duffy from the Hispanico Pa'lante Dancers. These young dancers were invited to audition for the Ballet Hispanico Summer Intensive at the class as well.
Peter Pucci, executive director of the Carole Cascio Fund for Mind Movement Dance Connections, yet again brought another quality performance and an amazing opportunity to Maryland's Eastern Shore. These beautiful and inspiring performances would not be possible without the Carole Cascio Fund. Each performance is a gift that brings a piece of New York City's talent directly to the community.
Inspired by late dancer and instructor Cascio's memory and love for dance, it is the mission of her fund to "introduce students of all ages and levels to connecting mind, movement and dance, and to support developing artistry in young people through choreography and dance."
In addition to the beauty these events bring, local teamwork and collaboration were also beautifully displayed. Pucci offered his thanks to the many amazing helpers for making these events possible.

title: Dr. Dodson House decked out for Halloween with "Alice in Wonderland" theme
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dr. Dodson House decked out for Halloween with "Alice in Wonderland" theme

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 448
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — With the help of artists from her gallery, Susan Oberreither spent about three months getting the Doctor Dodson House ready for Halloween.Oberreither, who purchased the historic house at 200 Cherry St. in St. Michaels in 2021, has been decorating the house for Halloween the last few years.
"It's just a fun way to bring the community together and encourage others to decorate as well and celebrate Halloween," she said.
Oberreither's decorations go beyond hanging skeletons and stretching cobwebs over bushes. Last year the theme was "Day of the Dead Regatta." This year, it's "Alice in Merry-Go-Land."
The house's upper-floor porch boasts a display of carousel pieces from the 1940s that light up at night. In between the carousel pieces are the King and Queen of Hearts.
"And the queen is holding up a head, like 'Off with her head,'" Oberreither said.
On the first-floor porch, there are "Alice in Wonderland" characters dressed up for Halloween, Oberreither said.
"So it's like the 'Alice in Wonderland' characters are having a masquerade ball on a carousel. That was the idea," she said, laughing.
Oberreither said she is most proud of the dollhouse she built. It is a replica of the Doctor Dodson House with Alice crashing through it. Oberreither, who started to build the dollhouse in August, said she went to "great lengths" to get the details of the house right.
The Doctor Dodson House — a two-story, brick, federal-style home — is the house that Frederick Douglass reconciled with his former slave master Thomas Auld in.
Oberreither said that when she bought the house, it reminded her of the homes in Lambertville, New Jersey, a place she used to visit that goes big with decorations every Halloween.
"And so I thought I just wanted to do something like that to bring joy to all of the people walking by," she said
Oberreither said that where the house is located gets a lot of foot traffic. She said she took a drone photo on a Monday afternoon and there were about 30 people outside the house looking at the decorations and taking photos.
"(There's) been really good, overwhelming support from the residents," she said about the community response to the display. "And then the tourists love it as well."
Charlotte Johnston, who has a home in Annapolis and likes to visit St. Michaels, said Oberreither puts in a lot of effort when it comes to Halloween decorations.
"She just really goes all out," Johnston said.
Oberreither said it takes help from her friends who are artists at her gallery, Studio 2 Saint Michaels, to get parts of the display assembled.
"So it was my brain child," she said. "But I definitely had a lot of creative talent behind me by accessing those artists."

title: Years in the making: John Wesley Church in Oxford completes renovation
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Years in the making: John Wesley Church in Oxford completes renovation

 October 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 621
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — When he moved to Washington, D.C., Wayman Pinder often traveled back to his Eastern Shore hometown down the unassuming Oxford Road.On the way, he saw a dilapidated building that he almost couldn't recognize. It was the John Wesley Methodist Episcopal Church, no longer used for services and worsening in condition by the year.
"I had to ride by this church where I used to be the organist, where I went all my life," Pinder said.
Following the church's closure in the mid-1970s, its exterior deteriorated, with roof problems, an unkempt cemetery and outhouse, and a lack of what once was a thriving group of community residents to look after the church. Pinder, now back in Oxford, felt it was ready to fall down at any moment.
"And to see it look like that, it hurt," Pinder said.
Pinder and his sister, Virginia Gibson, are just two of the many community members who have poured endless hours into renovating and rededicating the John Wesley Church. Earlier this month, the church celebrated a formal ribbon-cutting for its renovation — which has been an ongoing effort since 2003.
Renovations have included extensive roof repairs, a new wheelchair-accessible ramp, chimney and siding replacements and significant archaeological work on the cemetery that surrounds the building.
In the 2000s, the church was lifted to repair the foundation. Gibson notes that archaeological surveying found buried bodies beneath the church, which are now memorialized with gravestones in an expanded cemetery.
Upon walking in today, the church is welcoming and clean, with names of restoration donors and volunteers on the pews and window panes. It doesn't host services anymore, but it has hosted weddings and funerals.
"The inside of that church is just wonderful compared to what (it was)," Pinder said.
The restoration process wasn't always smooth sailing. Former John Wesley Preservation Society Vice President James Hollis founded the restoration efforts in 2003, Gibson said.
"We were spinning wheels for about five or six years," she said. Gibson attributed much of the credit to former Oxford Commissioner Kathleen Radcliffe, the preservation society's former president.
"She really mended (it) together," Gibson said. "She really was the person."
Through weekly and monthly meetings, board members rallied community support, hosted fundraisers and gathered the needed permits to fix up the semi-abandoned piece of history.
The preservation society gained official nonprofit status in 2014. Restoration took off thereafter, with major repairs performed by local contractors both outside and inside of the church.
Adjacent to the church is the Nellie Brooks Leatherberry Cook Shop, which Gibson said acts as the society's meeting room. An original stove used in the building still remains today. Nellie Leatherberry, born in Oxford in 1908, provided meals to churchgoers.
"People would actually sit in here and eat the best food ever made," Pinder said.
The cook shop became Talbot County's first African American Museum site in 2015. The church next to it has just as much history. Originally bought in 1838 as Oxford Neck Church, documents show it was a mixed congregation, with 31 white members and 26 Black members.
In 1875, the church was rebuilt to the single-room white building it has been since, becoming a part of the Oxford community and the Eastern Shore Black community until its closure in the 20th century.
Though the church hasn't hosted weekly services for decades, it has remained a cornerstone of the Oxford community. It's been home to quilt shows and community gatherings, and even served as a water stop for local cycling races.
Many board members and community volunteers have memories associated with the church, Pinder and Gibson both said. Whether they were members or their parents or grandparents were, many Oxford residents seem to resonate with the small but chronicled building off of Oxford Road.
"For us, it's personal history, too," Pinder said. "We experienced it."

title: Thousands of oyster lovers sip, slurp, savor at annual Oysterfest
author: Tom McCall
content:
Thousands of oyster lovers sip, slurp, savor at annual Oysterfest

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 544
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Smoked, fried or raw — local oysters were served to over 3,000 bivalve lovers attending the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum's OysterFest Saturday.There was an oyster stew competition and an oyster slurping eating competition. Two live bands, Swamp Donkey and JCT 33, lit up either end of the museum's campus.
"We have people coming in to sample six different local restaurants that have provided oyster stews. Each with their own recipe. They get to vote a, b, c, d, e, f, and we will reveal the winner after all the ballots have been cast," said Pete Lesher, the chief historian at CBMM.
The oyster stew competition had three winners. Third place went to Gourmet by the Bay, second place to The Oaks Waterfront Inn and first place to Bistro St. Michaels. It was a double blind system where even the neutral ladlers serving the voters didn't know who made their soup.
Glistening silver raw oysters on the half shell were enjoyed as pristine white historic nautical craft gleamed on the docks.
The oysters came freshly caught by the Talbot Watermen Association and freshly farmed from the Choptank Oyster Company. Slow Descent Oysters provided smoked oysters with butter, garlic and hot sauce or with smoked gouda, onion and maple bacon.
For the adults, there were craft beers, cocktails and oyster shooters with bloody Mary mix and vodka. There were workers checking IDs as customers queued up.
There was even an oyster slurping contest. Contestants slurped six oysters fast to become "Slurp King or Queen."
Although the food offerings were the primary draw for the event, vendors offered everything from belts with the Maryland state flag on them to maritime crafts.
Eve Johnson pulled in a vintage Bluebird bus and put out her Wild Raven Boutique clothes on the boardwalk.
"This is a boho vintage hippie mixture. Usually it is what I am wearing that people want, like these palooza pants. This might be a our fourth time at this event. Great food, great people, great music, great shopping and beautiful views," Johnson said.
Younger visitors had a whole children's section with wooden model sailboat building and a little pool to launch them in. Cheerful volunteers made it all come together.
A big draw for the crowd was the American Chesapeake Club Retriever demonstrations. Handsome Chesapeake Bay retrievers showed off their retrieving abilities as an announcer educated on the finer points of the breed and its talents. The fit, golden-brown dogs charged across a decoy-strewn lawn to get to the plastic target and bring it back. The audience cheered and the dogs' tails wagged.
There were several presentations, including one by author Eric Cheezum, who gave a cultural history lecture on Chessie. The sea monster is said to have first been sighted in 1978.
There was also an lecture about oyster reef building with discarded hockey sticks called Rink2Reef.
Logan Clark, event and group services lead for CBMM said, "Incorporating both sides of the campus is a challenge and making sure there is entertainment on both sides. There is music, vendors and oysters on both sides. This year we have a big slate of programs happening in the VLA (Van Lennep Auditorreum), including a cooking demo."
No matter what drew the crowds to the museum, this year's turnout was impressive. Parking overflowed down Talbot Street to Perry Cabin.

title: A Caroline County witch finds peace, community
author: Tom McCall
content:
A Caroline County witch finds peace, community

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 470
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GREENSBORO — Witch James, a Caroline County witch, has a philosophy that informs their practices."Everything is push or pull," Witch James said. "By pushing and pulling, you complete the circuit. It is energy for me."
"People ask me all the time, 'Are you a good witch or a bad witch?' I don't believe in good and bad," they said. "I am electric."
Its a philosophy James, who lives outside of Greensboro, shares with a community of witches who call the Eastern Shore home. They have gatherings of up to 20 people of lots of different faith traditions. Christians, Muslims, Wiccans and atheists have all been a part of this circle, James said.
Coming from West Virginia, James was searching for community when he got to Caroline County. Struggling to find people with whom they aligned, James thought, "If you don't have community, build it." They started a Facebook group.
"I started taking full moon classes. I started advertising that I did readings and cleansings. I posted on Denton Happenings that there are over 400 energy workers, witches, shamans, whatever you call us."
This time of year, James' found community is preparing for celebrations of Samhain, an ancient holiday. James said it is the most sacred time of year for them personally.
"The Catholic Church created Halloween off of Samhain," James said. "... Witch's holidays do not go by the Gregorian calendar. They go by the lunar calendar. This year it falls on Nov. 1.
"The new moon is the weakest point in the veil between the living and the dead throughout the whole year. That is what Samhain is," he said.
These practices are not always well received by people outside the witch community, James said.
"In Caroline County, most people don't feel safe to be out. I had six death threats last year," they said.
James knows of six covens in Caroline County and is part of four of them. "They are all closed groups. Mine is an open group because there needs to be an open group," they said.
But Witch James said the witches' non-violent belief system is accessible to people who are not part of the witch community. They are open to sharing.
"Sometimes I have people out here to do readings for them. I do tarot readings. I do pendulum readings. I do aura readings," James said. "Some people can see or feel the electromagnetic fields of other people. We are all electro-bio machines, and that is what an aura is."
James' family has deep tradition of healing as well.
"My family have been herbalists and healers for generations — the last 14 that I could find through my mother's side. My mother talks to the dead. My grandmother talked to the dead. My great grandmother talked to the dead," they said.
Asked what is great about the witch's path, James said, "The biggest take away is finding peace."
