title: A Talbot County actress invited Sonia Sotomayor to her show. Sotomayor came
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
A Talbot County actress invited Sonia Sotomayor to her show. Sotomayor came

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GLEN ECHO — In 1974, Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor, then a Princeton student, wrote a letter of complaint to her university to call attention to the low Latino student numbers, the absence of Latino administrators and faculty members, and the lack of any courses dealing with Latino culture.That letter pushed the increase in Latino enrollment in Princeton University and was a critical moment in Sotomayor's life. This event is featured in the musical "She Persisted," a show centered on history's most famous women and how modern girls can take inspiration from their stories.
The musical is showing at Adventure Theatre in Glen Echo, Maryland. Victoria Gomez, a Talbot County resident, plays Sotomayor in the show.
Inspired by her character, Gomez decided to take a lesson from Sotomayor and wrote a letter to the justice.
"I admire your work and perseverance you have that led you to becoming the first Latina on the Supreme Court," Gomez wrote in her letter. "You are a role model for many people but especially for aspiring Latinas who dream big, like myself."
In the letter, Gomez shared her story of coming to the United States with her mother as a child. She wrote how honored she was to play Sotomayor in the musical.
Because of that letter, Sotomayor and her family sat in the front row of the Adventure Theatre Sunday.
Gomez said she is honored to be casted in this empowering musical. For Gomez, her passion for the theater began when she was a student at St. Michaels Elementary School when her class went on a field trip to see a musical.
For Gomez, the theater has opened a new world to explore and grow in. She has learned to advocate for herself and has developed a strong sense of her identity.
While on stage, Gomez jumped and sang with immense enthusiasm as she played a curious young Sotomayor in the Bronx with dreams of being a detective. Then later, as she played a college-aged Sotomayor, she comprised the emotional uncertainty of a young woman who sought to make change for her community.
Gomez said while studying for this role, she learned Sotomayor's strong connection to the women in her family. Like Sotomayor, Gomez was encouraged by her mother and grandmother, who taught her to be "proudly Latina" and to help those in her community.
"(Sotomayor's) mom was always someone who helped everyone in the community, which is something that I immediately related to in terms of my mom," Gomez said. "...She's already helping everyone, but even outside of that, she is such a wonderful role model for me to have. And I just really connected with (Sotomayor) in the way that she saw her mom as such an impactful role model."
"She Persisted," based on the children's book by Chelsea Clinton, follows the journey of Naomi, a fourth-grade girl struggling with perfectionism.
Play director Mary Hall Surface, said her hope for the play was to celebrate not only the historical figures and their stories but to really highlight the central character and her struggles.
"I think that is a pervasive feeling of young women and young boys as well, and not to mention grown women, all of us really, as we struggle to sort of measure ourselves against other people and find our own strengths and power and purpose," Hall Surface said.
After the final song of the play, Gomez's mother and Sotomayor, rose to their feet and gave her a standing ovation.

title: Megalodon teeth exhibit comes to Maryland museum
author: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Megalodon teeth exhibit comes to Maryland museum

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 637
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Calvert Marine Museum this month unveiled a new exhibit featuring a never-before-seen set of teeth from an extinct megatooth shark known as megalodon.The 53 teeth from one individual shark believed to be over 50 feet in length were collected over a period of six years from one location along Calvert Cliffs, according to a release from the Calvert Marine Museum.
The new exhibit, titled "Out of the Vault," opened Nov. 1 in the museum's Mezzanine Gallery and features rare and scientifically significant fossils that reveal a unique glimpse into the prehistoric past of the Chesapeake Bay region.
The extinct shark megalodon (aka Otudus megalodon) continues to be a source of endless popular and scientific fascination. This insatiable interest certainly comes from the large size of its serrated teeth and macro-predatory habits.
Megalodon was one of the largest predators ever, thought to have obtained a body length of up to 65 feet.
Doubtless, megalodon dominated the marine ecosystem for nearly 20 million years prior to extinction about 3.6 million years ago. Remarkably, though, what is mostly known about megalodon has come from studying its many fossilized teeth and few vertibrae.
Many tens of thousands of megalodon teeth have been found around the world, the vast majority having been preserved and found in isolation. However, but exceedingly rare, an individual megalodon died and many of its teeth were preserved together in association. Worldwide, there are fewer than a dozen associated partial detentions of megalodon known.
The marine museum in Solomons recently announced a newly associated set of megaloon teeth found along Calvert Cliffs on the Chesapeake Bay. This set includes 53 teeth from a wide range of tooth positions in the giant shark's mouth, from large front teeth measuring 5½ inches long to remarkably small black teeth only just over ½ inch in length.
This is the first associated set of teeth of megalodon to have ever been found along the fossil-famous Calvert Cliffs.
The megalodon teeth were found by both professional and avocational paleontologists including John R. Nance, who initially discovered the stash of teeth, Victor J. Perez, Robert "Bob" Hazen and Margee Hazen, Stephen Groff, Brian Bartron, William "Bill" Counterman, Marcus Jones, Daryl Serafin and Steven Victor. Matt Blomgren and Cindy Eckerd allowed the museum to cast their finds, while many other individuals helped scour that beach over several years.
Several other collectors have found teeth from this shark, and those remain in private collections.
"During the winter of 2015-2016, we heard a rumor of someone who found a bucket of megalodon teeth from this same location, and probably from the same shark. He has become affectionately known as 'Bucket Guy,'" according to the marine museum, which is hoping to contact the person.
Note that the teeth on display were not found at Calvert Cliffs State Park and trespassing through private communities to get to the cliffs is not permitted. Digging in the cliffs is dangerous and is prohibited on all state and federal lands.
On private land, permission must be granted from the owner(s) before digging. If you see a skull, bone or unusual fossil in the cliffs you can report it to the Calvert Marine Museum paleontology department at 410-326-2042. The museum cannot confiscate fossil finds like megalodon teeth.
if you goThe Calvert Marine Museum is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Admission if $11 for adults, $9 for seniors, veterans, AAA and AARP members; $6 for children ages 5-12; children under 5 and museum members are admitted free.
Highlights of the new exhibit "Out of the Vault" include: fossilized shrimp burrows, teeth from an ancestor of the modern great white shark, skull remains of extinct dolphins, parts of a giant leatherback turtle shell, miocene elephant teeth, fossils of miocene hermit crabs and the associated set of teeth from the megalodon.
For more information about the museum, upcoming events, or membership, visit www.calvertmarinemuseum.com or call 410-326-2042.

title: History and mystery: Haunted High Street tour shares Cambridge folklore
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
History and mystery: Haunted High Street tour shares Cambridge folklore

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 546
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Walking past the grand, historic High Street homes on a sunny day, ghosts might not be top of mind.But after the sun has set, Chesapeake Ghost Tours brings history lovers and thrill seekers alike on a journey down the haunted street, telling stories of local history and strange happenings.
Mindie Burgoyne, founder of Chesapeake Ghost Tours, considers Cambridge's High Street the most haunted street in Maryland. She said those that come on the tour will be "entertained by the mystery and informed by the history."
The tour — which was primarily developed using the folklore collections at Salisbury University's Edward H. Nabb Research Center, books, newspaper articles and personal interviews — begins right outside the Dorchester County Circuit Courthouse. Guides take tourgoers down High Street toward the Choptank River before looping around and coming back up the street. The tour ends at the graveyard attached to Christ Episcopal Church.
On Friday, Burgoyne led a small group around the street, stopping in front of homes to tell stories about mischievous ghosts, cat ladies and even murder.
Burgoyne believes that in areas like High Street that have had a "high injection of emotion," it creates a hole in the "veil between the dimensions." She said that over the years, people would hear things while walking in the area of High and Spring streets.
Past the courthouse and toward the water, Burgoyne told the story of an old murder that took place in the foyer of what is now the Cambridge House Bed and Breakfast at 112 High St. Burgoyne said two men had an altercation in the foyer of the house that involved an umbrella and a fireplace poker. She said the incident ended with a gunshot.
The previous owners of the bed and breakfast would find umbrellas and fireplace pokers missing, Burgoyne said. When she interviewed them, they told her the story connected the dots for them.
"Well no wonder our pokers and umbrellas are missing," the previous owners told her.
The bed and breakfast is one of many properties on High Street that Burgoyne can share history and stories about. Her favorite stories are about the Josiah Bayly House at 207 High St. Built in the 1700s in Annapolis and moved to Cambridge by barge, the Bayly House is known as the oldest house in Cambridge.
Burgoyne said one woman she interviewed who lived there said she always had a sense that they weren't alone in the house.
The tour ends under fragrant yew trees in the graveyard of the Episcopal church. On Friday, as tourgoers pointed their phone flashlights at old gravestones, Burgoyne told a few last stories and shined a light on one grave stone practically enveloped by a yew tree, poking out just enough to be noticeable.
Shasta Ingram, who lives in Howard County, said she didn't have one particular story on the tour that was her favorite.
"I just liked looking at the houses and hearing the history," she said. "Because, you know, there's so much history."
Those interested in taking the tour on High Street, or doing another ghost tour through Chesapeake Ghost Tours, can book online at chesapeakeghosts.com. Walking tours are available most weekends from March through October and parts of November. In December through February, the company often has bus tours in areas not covered on the walking tours.

title: The animal in our midst at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
The animal in our midst at the library

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Columns 
 
 744
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Recently, I read an article about a poultry processing plant on Virginia's Eastern Shore that employed underage immigrants to work overnight shifts servicing machines that rapidly decapitated, declawed and disemboweled chickens.Not surprisingly, all the spinning blades and belts occasionally maimed one of the youngsters, who, because they were miles from home and parents in a strange country whose language they did not understand, had to suffer in silence or risk losing their sole source of income.
The essay reminded me of Upton Sinclair's "The Jungle," which described how, in the early 20th century, Eastern European immigrants were similarly harnessed to Chicago's newly-industrialized slaughterhouses.
Thinking about what Charles Dickens did for people incarcerated in debtors' prisons and John Steinbeck did for seasonal agricultural workers, I wondered why there wasn't a modern equivalent to Sinclair out there who could write a book like "The Jungle" to awaken us to the conditions under which some people in the United State must live and labor even today.
But, then again, maybe it's me. Has television's nightly catastrophe parade so inured me to human suffering that I can't see the forest for the trees? Are such works being written and I've just failed to recognize what their authors are trying to accomplish?
Julia Phillips' new novel "Bear" tells the story of two sisters, Elena and Sam. For years now the women have been caring for their mother, who is slowly dying from an unnamed chronic illness. The family lives on the remote island of San Juan, off the coast of Washington State, in a poorly-insulated, dilapidated house that is on the verge of collapsing under the weight of its years.
Elena is employed as a waitress in the local country club, while Sam works long shifts behind a concession stand in the ferry that moves wealthy tourists to and from the island. During the pandemic, the ferry ceased operations, and their mother's medical bills sunk the sisters deep in debt.
Written in the third-person, "Bear" is told from Sam's point of view. She hates her work, hates the contempt with which the wealthy tourists treat her, hates her bondage to a life with few pleasures other than the love she feels for her sister and mother.
But Sam has a dream. When eventually, inevitably, their mother passes away, Sam and her sister will be free to sell their home (and the valuable real estate it sits upon), which means they'll be able to move to a warmer clime and begin living the sort of life she imagines the tourists she waits upon live.
Then one night, as she is taking a break out on the ferry's upper deck, Sam sees something remarkable in the oily blackness of the water beneath her. It's a bear, swimming alongside the boat, making for the shore of their island.
As it happens, the bear takes up residence in the forest that surrounds the two sisters' home. Elena, who is the older of the two and has borne the brunt of bill-paying, housekeeping and caregiving — Elena who arrives home from work each day exhausted and stinking of griddle grease and fried onions — sees the bear as a sort of other-worldly figure, one that has brought into their threadbare existence a hint of magic and even enchantment.
While the hardship of Elena's life moves her to try to befriend the bear, the hardship of Sam's makes her see the beast as a threat to her dreams. What if her beloved sister strays too close to the thing, what if it kills her, if it takes from Sam the one person she loves besides the mother she knows she will soon lose?
The tension between these two divergent views and the wild animal that instigates that tension creates a narrative force at once both troubling and seductive. We want everything to work out for the sisters. We don't see how everything possibly can.
It is this dilemma that drives "Bear" and made me think that, in a subtle way, a way somehow appropriate for our time, Phillips has written a modern equivalent to Dickens' "Little Dorrit," Steinbeck's "Grapes of Wrath," and Sinclair's "The Jungle." For it is the crushing, inescapable reality of Sam and Elena's poverty that puts them at loggerheads, that drives them toward the bear — one armed only with love, the other with a gun.
You can find Phillips' "Bear" (as well as Dickens, Steinbeck, and Sinclair) at the place we visit to try to reconcile such irreconcilables: the Talbot County Free Library.

title: Lions Halloween parade celebrates over 50 years
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Lions Halloween parade celebrates over 50 years

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 259
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — In a tradition of more than 50 years, the Chestertown Lions Club held its Halloween Parade on Saturday along High Street.Performing this year was the Kent County High School marching band led by Jodi Bortz, the Sudlersville Middle School Marching Band led by Ronald Demby and the Delmarva United Marching Band led by Mark Mumford.
The parade began at 1 p.m., and in addition to the bands, the Chestertown Volunteer Fire Company came through, rumbling their engines and tossing candy.
Floats added to the fun, like the Pirate's Cove float and the Radcliffe Creek School float driven by a storm trooper from "Star Wars."
Grand Marshal was Roger Williams, a Lions member for 53 years, who received the Melvin Jones Award from the Lions International Foundation for dedicated Humanitarian Services. Williams served in many roles within the County over the years as well.
Following the parade, club members were available to judge contestants for the costume contest, emceed by Brian Moore of WCTR. The contestants also marched in the parade, from groups preschool, elementary, middle, high school/adults and, new this year, a category for pets.
There was an array of costumes, from super heroes, pirates, dinosaurs, princesses, video game and anime characters, providing a fun yet tough time for the judges to decide on the best of each group.
Winners received cash prizes and hearty applause from the impressive number of people in attendance lined up on both sides of the street.
The day went off as Lions member Dwight Wilmot expected, fun and worry-free.
"What a gorgeous day to be out," he said.

title: Dia de los Muertos celebration embraces traditions of growing Latino population
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Dia de los Muertos celebration embraces traditions of growing Latino population

 November 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 607
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Community members and organizations are finding ways to celebrate and immerse in the different cultural events and traditions brought to the Eastern Shore by the growing Latino population.Dia de los Muertos, a vibrant two-day holiday from Latin America, celebrates and honors departed loved ones. In collaboration with Samantha Martinez and the Talbot County Free Library, the Academy Art Museum hosted a celebration beginning Thursday and ending Saturday evening to embrace the holiday's traditions and bring them to a new audience.
Martinez said she was honoring her two grandmothers in the ofrenda displayed during an intimate event on Friday evening. Ofrendas are home altars created by the family members or loved ones of a person who has died. They are intended to welcome the deceased to the altar setting.
"To me, it is an extension of honoring their life," Martinez said. "So me being able to honor them and celebrate them and bring all their favorite things, is a way for my relationship to continue, even though it's not physical and tangible here on this earth."
It is part of the holiday to display favorite foods and items of the deceased on the ofrendas. Martinez said she brought her grandmother's favorite flowers, Carmex lip balm, nail polish, conchas (Mexican sweet bread) and a bible.
According to Martinez, Indigenous people of Latin America believed that upon death, the individual's soul did not die and continued to live in Mictlan, a place of rest. In time, this pre-Hispanic celebration merged with the Catholic celebration of All Souls Day and has evolved into the present Dia de los Muertos celebration.
On Friday night at the Academy Art Museum, people gathered around marigold flowers and shared traditional pan de muerto (bread of the dead) as they honored loved ones whose photos decorated the ofrendas.
Martinez and several others shared the stories and joys of their loved ones and took time to celebrate the lives they lived.
The night before, the Talbot County Free Library hosted a create-your-own mini altar to contribute to a larger community-wide altar located at the Academy Art Museum on Friday and Saturday.
The ofrendas will be available for the public to view on Saturday evening. Community members of the Eastern Shore are invited to celebrate the holiday and enjoy traditional music and dance performances.
Jennifer Chrzanowski, interim director of the Academy Art Museum, said the museum has been working on outreach to the Latino Community on the Shore through events like Dia de los Muertos as well as initiatives to have translated exhibitions for the Spanish speaking community.
This particular event was done through an initiative where the museum invites community members to create unique and interesting programs for better community building. Martinez collaborated and led the creation of the event as a way to extend community outreach.
"It's important that there are no barriers for people to come in and be a part of this community," Chrzanowski said. "So we just feel this is an extension of making this museum more inclusive, more welcoming for anybody."
Martinez said she would love to expand the event to a parade one day, with face painting, music and catrinas (paper mache female skeleton). Martinez encourages the community to join in celebration and learn more about Dia de los Muertos.
"To be open to see how other people celebrate and honor their ancestors, and to think outside of the box when we think about grief or when we think about death," Martinez said. "This is a way to make it more intimate and make it less scary for people and less finite, but to (also) celebrate in a way that honors our ancestors and the reason why we are here today."

title: 53rd Waterfowl Festival set to begin Thursday
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
53rd Waterfowl Festival set to begin Thursday

 November 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1641
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Thousands will pack the streets of downtown Easton this weekend for the 53rd annual Waterfowl Festival, the town's much-anticipated yearly tradition.On Thursday, it kicks off with opening ceremonies at the Tidewater Inn on Dover Street. Then on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, festivalgoers can enjoy all that Waterfowl has to offer.
Festival Director Deena Kilmon says, "there's something for everybody," whether it's hunting and outdoors enthusiasts, food lovers, history buffs, families or Eastern Shore natives.
"We try with the festival to tell the story of the Eastern Shore and to showcase how it is to live here, essentially," Kilmon said. "It's all about us."
Kilmon said this year's expected attendance may be "more than ever," noting that ticket sales for Thursday's opening ceremonies and premiere night are higher than in years past.
"We have had record VIP ticket sales," Kilmon said. "We're well into the 700-attendee mark at this point. So we know if that's any indication of the general admission, then yeah, it's going to be the biggest year ever."
A number of expanded offerings and additions make this year's festival unique, Kilmon said.
This year's festival will include an enhanced focus on children's activities. Kilmon said a new "Quackin' Trail" will help kids find activities to do all over the festival instead of just being concentrated in one area. Admission for kids 10 and under is free with a paid adult present.
The PNC Art Pavilion — located at 40 S. Harrison St. — will be "about double in size" compared to last year, Kilmon said. Featured at the pavilion will be the festival's featured artist, Texas-based Ronnie Wells, with sculptures and paintings.
"He is a revered artist. He's got sculptures in pretty much every major city in the United States," Kilmon said. "It's worth it just to come see some of these guys and see their beautiful art, even if you can't afford to buy it."
The Avalon Theatre will be home to the Duck Blind Bar, along with the festival's new brew, "In Flight." The Waterfowl-licensed beer will be available while it lasts, along with other seasonal beers and cocktails.
At Easton VFW Post 5118, the Chesapeake Bay Pavilion will host live music all three days, raptor demonstrations and expanded shopping opportunities.
Festivalgoers can expect to see new Waterfowl merchandise and an expanded bus line, according to Kilmon. She added that attendees are asked to park at Easton Elementary School, Easton Middle School, Easton High School or the Easton Elks Lodge.
In her first year as the festival director, Kilmon was emotional when asked about her favorite part of the Waterfowl Festival.
"For me, it is absolutely just seeing Easton shine," Kilmon said. "It's almost emotional. It is emotional, I guess. It's where Easton comes together and we just showcase the beautiful community that we are. We see our families, we see our friends, and we celebrate going into the fall and the winter season together, and it's just a wonderful experience."

title: Adkins Arboretum hosts plein air painters
author: Tom McCall
content:
Adkins Arboretum hosts plein air painters

 November 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Arts 
 
 417
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — The smell of linseed oil wafted into the forest as over 50 artists competed in Plein Air Adkins at the Adkins Arboretum on Saturday. There was food and drink, nature and art all combining to create a perfect fall day."We had almost 250 attendees and 55 artists," said Ginna Tiernan, executive director of Adkins Arboretum.
There was lots of food and drink.
"Ten Eyck provided mimosas and bloody Marys, and Craft Bakery and Night Kitchen provided great food and drinks including pastries and lunch items," Tiernan said. "Diane Mullaly got us started and is our advisor on this event, and she won first prize," she said.
Mullaly learned a lot about running a Plein Air quick contest from her time at the Plein Air Easton.
"I brought Ginna the idea about four years ago about creating an event like this. I created sort of a slower version of the quick draw. The painters started at 10 and ended at 12:30. A half hour longer than Plein Air Easton. Quite a few sold," Mullaly said.
For Mullaly the passion goes deeper than her creativity.
"I am deeply involved with the arboretum. I am a Maryland master naturalist and a trained docent there. I am there a lot and I just adore that place. I always feel so good when I am there. It is very healing and relaxing. Being able to paint there in that beautiful environment is such a treat," Mullaly said.
Beth Bathe was the judge and was generous with her time with all artists.
Bathe said, "Judging the works of over 50 artists this past Saturday at Adkins Aboretum was a true honor as each painting vividly showcased the rich colors and textures of the autumn season. Live music, wonderful food and drink and beautiful artwork all for sale made a great day for the artists and the community."
There were collectors who have also attended the Plein Air Easton event. They came to see and purchase more great art.
The winners were Mullaly, second place winner Abby Ober and third place winner Maryellyn Lynott.
There were honorable mentions too. These included Lori Yates, Lynn Lewis, Ronaldo Dorado, Stephen Walker and Sheryl Southwick.
There was a tie for Artist's Choice — Nancy Fine and Toni Wolf.
Event Sponsors included Caroline County Council for the Arts, Maryland State Arts Council, Enel and Unity Landscape Design/Build. Live music was provided by Fine Times.
Although the Arboretum got a 20% commission of any art that sold, the main benefit was attracting lots of people to spend time in nature.

title: Marigold Market: a community for upcoming artists on the Shore
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Marigold Market: a community for upcoming artists on the Shore

 November 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 364
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Marigold Market, a community vendor event, made its big debut Saturday at the Talbot County Historical Gardens. The event featured over 25 local artists, live music and family-friendly activities.The Marigold Market, named for its fall theme and coinciding with Dia de los Muertos, aimed to support emerging artists and create community.
Helen Fegan, a jewelry artist and co-organizer of the market, said the idea for the Marigold Market began in April when she reached out to her friend Natalie Calloway, a local artist, asking if she would be interested in putting the event together.
"We wanted it to be something that was a really open-space and people could feel comfortable, whether they have done this 100 times or whether they have never done one, and that was the case for a lot of our artists," Fegan said.
Fegan began making jewelry a couple of years ago and was in a place where she was ready to sell her jewelry at a market. When she began to look for a market to sell at, she noticed a few roadblocks for new vendors, including booth fees and a lack of confidence in selling their work.
Fegan and Calloway sought to change these roadblocks and provide an opportunity for new artists like themselves to encourage each other and find support on the Shore.
Calloway is a ceramic artist and is fairly new to the art community. When Fegan pitched the idea of creating their own market she was thrilled with the idea, and on Saturday morning she was stunned by the immediate community support but most of all happy with the growing confidence she saw with all the new artists selling their work.
"We wanted to start something that is for new, upcoming artists who haven't really been a part of much recently because they're still in the shadows and nervous," Calloway said. "So we wanted a welcoming community for them."
Fegan said she hopes to hold another market in the spring and plans to grow the event into a community for artists around the Shore.
"We're just so stunned and happy with the community support and the feedback," Fegan said. "It was really great to know that everyone loved it."

title: King Arthur comes to life at Chesapeake Culinary Center
author: Tom McCall
content:
King Arthur comes to life at Chesapeake Culinary Center

 November 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 374
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Legend and actors combined with swords, griffins and maidens at "the Legend of King Arthur and His Knights" literary evening on Saturday Nov. 2.Thespians in medieval garb stood behind 12 lecterns and read from historical texts like "Once And Future King." It was pure storytelling in a reader's theater format.
About 30 guests had the stories read to them and then dined on a period meal provided by the Chesapeake Culinary Center.
Caroline County Council of Arts and Caroline County Public Library presented the show.
The source materials were collected from hundreds of years of writing from people like John Steinbeck, Lord Alfred Tennyson and J.R.R. Tolkien.
Sir Thomas Malory is the principle purveyor of the the Arthurian story, and he wrote from a prison cel, director and writer Keith L. Shaffer said. The holy grail, the round table, Merlin and the sword in the stone have captivated people for centuries.
"It is really the legend of King Arthur from the beginning where he pulls the sword from the stone, to his marriage to Gwynevere, to the final battle and even after the final battle. It is readers theater, so it is all reading the script and gesturing and facial expressions," Shaffer said of Saturday's event.
The community outreach extended into the North Caroline High School art students, who painted banners that went for silent auction.
Debby Bennett is the chair of the literary committee.
"We started meeting in the summer. Keith is our director but he is also the script writer. Kendall (Teague) organized the silent auction. We will continue the silent auction for a couple of weeks at the Foundry. We have a lot of talent in this county," Bennett said.
She said this is the first time that they have not picked an author for their literary event. They chose a character that several people had written about.
"Keith has read a lot of authors about Arthur. It is a project of love. It has got the arts. It has got literature It is about books and reading, and community," Bennett said.
There were sponsors sitting in the audience.
"The arts is always something we want to support, because we believe it teaches people how to think and how to put themselves in someone else's shoes," sponsor Michelle Christopher said.

title: Mayor Megan Cook brings down duck gavel, officially opening 53rd Waterfowl Festival
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Mayor Megan Cook brings down duck gavel, officially opening 53rd Waterfowl Festival

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 324
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The 53rd annual Waterfowl Festival officially began Thursday evening at the Tidewater Inn, where Megan Cook, mayor of Easton, was welcomed onstage to officially open the festival with the banging of the duck gavel.This three-day festival welcomes thousands of waterfowl enthusiasts to Talbot County each year to appreciate local wildlife, art, heritage, food and community.
Throughout the Thursday evening ceremony, citations were given to organizers of the festival, longtime volunteers were honored for their service and a featured artist unveiled new work.
The ceremony began with opening remarks by Eric Milhollan, president of the executive board for the Waterfowl Festival. He welcomed all attendees, recognizing them for joining the festival and supporting conservation efforts.
In his speech, Milhollan shared his long history with the festival. Beginning with volunteering with his father and later becoming involved with his own family as an adult, Milhollan shared his pride for the countless families who have long-standing traditions of volunteering for the festival.
"I'm proud to have my oldest son cheering for the second year. He's joined by his two brothers and sister, all coming home from college to help for the weekend at the festival that's been part of my life and my family's life," Milhollan said. "I believe in the crowd and see that many who have similar stories in passing the tradition of the festival to their families. This is what allows us to celebrate 53 years."
Throughout the evening, several people were honored, including a memoriam for Kim Perry Whiteley and Hall of Fame presentations for Blenda Armistead, Ron Flohr and Butch Townsend. A waterfowl statue was unveiled by this year's Waterfowl Festival Featured Artist Ronnie Wells.
As Cook held the opening gavel in her hand, she looked to the leaders of the Waterfowl Festival, and they all smiled.
"Are we ready? All right, we're ready. Let's go," Cook said before banging the duck-shaped gavel against the podium and officially opening the Waterfowl Festival's 53rd year of celebration.

title: KCA donates to instruments to school music program
author: Staff Writer
content:
KCA donates to instruments to school music program

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The music department at Kent County High School received a donation last month for new instruments.John Schratwieser, executive director of Kent Cultural Alliance, announced a $10,000 donation to the music program at a Kent County Board of Education meeting Monday, Oct. 14.
The money will be used to purchase instruments including saxophones and a performance piano for the Tom McHugh Black Box Theater at Kent County High School. Remaining funds will be used for instrument maintenance and parts.
Schratwieser said he was "standing on the shoulders" of Leslie Prince Raimond and the late Tom McHugh who, through the Kent County Arts Council, began supporting the arts in Kent County Public Schools decades ago.
"We're happy to continue that tradition," Schratwieser told the Board of Education members. "We know that you do the best that you are able to do with the resources that you have. We are happy to build upon that."
Raimond was the longtime director of the Kent County Arts Council, which is now the Kent Cultural Alliance. McHugh founded the Mainstay music venue in Rock Hall after retiring from a teaching career that included Vassar College in New York.
The Kent Cultural Alliance has contributed $25,000 to the schools' music program over the last two years, including funding from the Robert F. Schumann Foundation, a family foundation named for the father of local musician and environmentalist Ford Schumann. Additional support came from the Shared Earth Foundation, led by Caroline Gabel.
The Kent Cultural Alliance has also donated about $10,000 to the school system's visual arts programs over the last five years as well, including funding for two new kilns, digital drawing devices, field trips and more.
"Know that Kent Cultural Alliance will always be there to advocate for the Kent County Public Schools," Schratwiser said. "Because we believe in the power of arts education."
Mary Boswell-McComas, superintendent of Kent County Public Schools, thanked the Kent Cultural Alliance for its continued support of the arts programs, saying she is deeply grateful.
She said that the county's small student enrollment creates budget challenges.
"It's a testament that as a community, we refuse to allow fine arts to be marginalized," McComas said. "And we could not continue to offer the programming and resources that we do without our partnerships."
Gina Jachimowicz, director of teaching and learning for Kent County Public Schools, agreed.
"Without the generous support of our community, we would not be privy to the amazing advantages that our students have seen and the generous donation that the Kent Cultural Alliance has provided," Jachimowicz said.
Discover more about Kent County Public Schools and its programs at www.kent.k12.md.us.

title: The story behind this year's Waterfowl Festival poster and artist
author: Tom McCall
content:
The story behind this year's Waterfowl Festival poster and artist

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Ronnie Wells has been coming to the Waterfowl Festival for 28 years. But this year is a little different — he has been chosen as the featured poster artist.When this Texan got the call for this monumental honor, he realized he had to make the art. He was asked to create a sculpture and a painting to be made into the 2024 poster. The two works are of canvasback ducks landing in water only to discover that there is a stiff-looking decoy they have come to.
"They asked me would you be willing to do the poster as well as the sculpture. I said I would be honored," Wells said.
Wells based the works on a Ward Brothers 1936 canvasback duck decoy. Wells thinks 1936 was decoy carvers' peak year of expertise and creativity.
"I have always admired the Ward Brothers and their contribution to the art of decoy carving. I recently collected a 1936 model Canvasback Drake, which I used in the sculpture and the poster. They were artists and didn't even know it," Wells said.
Wells calls the canvasback the king of ducks. He loves the distinct noise their shorter wings make when they fly.
Wells is a hunter, and he said there are canvasbacks that make it to Texas.
"I have never killed a canvasback. I actually knocked one down and never found it and it bugs me to this day," he said. "It is one of my favorite ducks to paint and sculpt. They are such a magnificent looking ducks. They have a wide body and a Roman nose as far as a beak. Thick neck, they call them bull necks."
His inspiration for the poster and the sculpture was clear to him.
"When they called, I first thought of ducks as kind of my forte, and then I thought canvasbacks. The third thing I thought about was the Ward Brothers," he said.
After he got the call from the festival to create the poster, he started making thumbnail sketches of ducks. He sent that pencil sketch in for approval. Ultimately he created the final image in oil.
Wells has had a long career in the arts. He got an art degree and made a living as a medical illustrator. At the hospital where he worked, young doctors kept buying the miniature bronzes that he brought in to the office and put on his desk.
Wells will have an exhibit set up in the clear-roofed tent across from the Waterfowl Building during the festival. While still getting ready, he and his wife Patricia are unloading the art to be displayed. She handles all the driving and cleaning the sculpture with a Swiffer.
"He sculpts while I drive the box truck," she said.
Wells made three big sculptures for the festival. One has already sold.
The official festival sculpture was taken to the Tidewater Inns Crystal Room for the unveiling Thursday night. He made copies, and each one sells for $35,000.
As a market, a cultural event and a community of friends, the festival, "is such a fun thing to do. I have two of my old duck hunting buddies that we hunted in East Texas for 30 years. They came just for this event. I was shocked when they said they are going to be there. They are staying at the Tidewater. That is an honor in itself,' said Wells.
"This is kind of my swan song," he said, "even though it is a canvasback."

title: 'Better sense of what's inside': Wildlife sculptors apply taxidermy experiences to art
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
'Better sense of what's inside': Wildlife sculptors apply taxidermy experiences to art

 November 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 487
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Standing near his cast bronze birds in the Waterfowl Festival's PNC Pavilion on Harrison Street, wildlife sculptor Paul Rhymer talked about a skill that has aided his trade: taxidermy."A lot of wildlife sculptors started out as taxidermists," he said, adding that it's a common enough practice that a whole article could be written on it.
Although Rhymer took up taxidermy as a kid because his father did it, painting and drawing were Rhymer's first true loves. In the '80s, while working as an entry-level illustrator at the Smithsonian, Rhymer discovered an opening there for an entry-level model maker and taxidermist.
"I had the experience as a taxidermist with my dad," he said. "And so that taxidermy experience, messing around the basement with my dad, led to this career."
Rhymer fell in love with his new career. In the late '90s, he traded in his paints for clay and took up sculpting. And after a 25 years, he retired from the Smithsonian, giving him more time to sculpt.
For Rhymer, understanding an animal and its anatomy is helpful when it comes to sculpting.
"When you skin an animal out because you're mounting it, then you really know the anatomy," he said.
And Rhymer isn't alone. Sculptor Don Rambadt, who creates mixed metal welded sculptures, said taxidermy experience can give "a better sense of what's inside."
"Because I was actually looking at how the bones are articulated," said Rambadt, who did bird taxidermy as a volunteer at the Milwaukee Public Museum for a few years.
Both Rhymer and Rambadt consider these outside experiences important in their art careers.
Rambadt, who grew up loving nature, animals and art, started his college career studying natural resource management. After getting kicked out of college and taking a few years to work, he went back to college on a general biology track. At that time, he took a few art classes and was introduced to welding as an art form.
"By the end of that semester I had changed my major, transferred schools and was showing in galleries by the time I graduated," he said. Rambadt's knowledge of science has helped inform his art.
He said his career combines his two loves: science and art.
For Rhymer, who is a Marylander, a lifetime of outdoor activities — from hunting to birdwatching to fishing — has contributed to his work.
"You can watch the mannerisms of how things move, and what they do and their behavior," he said.
Rhymer, who started showing his art at the Waterfowl Festival in 2004, appreciates the tradition of it all.
"It's the granddaddy of wildlife art festivals," he said. "Because it's the Waterfowl Festival and I started out as a duck hunter, I love those roots that it started out as a waterfowl show. ... And I love the hook of art and conservation."
Both Rhymer and Rambadt's art can be found in the PNC Pavilion during the festival. Their work can also be found on their websites, rhymerstudio.com and donrambadt.com.

title: Why are decoys so expensive? Artists, collectors share the value of carvings, community
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Why are decoys so expensive? Artists, collectors share the value of carvings, community

 November 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 653
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON – Decoys have long been used in hunting communities, but to the crowd at the Waterfowl Festival, the wood carvings serve more than just a utilitarian purpose.According to Cooper Rossner, a Talbot County decoy carver, the imitation birds and mammals can also be used as historic art pieces for nature lovers.
As a teenager in south New Jersey, Rossner was mesmerized by a carving demonstration in a natural sciences high school class. Rossner said right before his eyes, a carver turned a piece of wood into a Canada Goose.
This demonstration would be the first step into his lifelong passion for carving decoys. The carver at his school would soon become his mentor, and the following weekend he met an additional mentor during a Ducks Unlimited event.
"I was probably 15 years old, and here I am turning 30 in a week, and I'm still obsessed with it, still carving every chance I get," Rossner said. "... carving is my world, and is my mind, and is my heart and soul. It puts everything that I love together: working with my hands, artwork, the history of it, the wildlife, the hunting aspect — it wraps it all up."
The hours of labor and craft artists like Rossner put into the carvings mean sometimes decoys come with a hefty price tag.
Jon Deeter, co-owner of Guyette and Deeter, a decoy auction firm, said his firm surpassed $200 million in total sales during 2020. In his experience, decoys at his firm would minimally be sold at $300. The most his firm had sold a single decoy for was $480,000.
According to Deeter, pricing on decoys depends on a variety of factors. Vintage decoys made between 1850-1950 tend to be more valuable than contemporary decoys made after 1962. Additionally, the history and ownership of a decoy also impacts its value, similar to how provenance affects the value of fine art.
Rarity and originality also play a large role in the pricing of a decoy. The decoys made by renowned carvers like the Ward Brothers from Crisfield, Maryland can fetch prices in the six-figure range. Limited production, unique design or age can often command premium prices at auction, with the record being $1.144 million for a pair of decoys.
Deeter emphasized that decoy collecting is an expensive hobby, but many collectors are not purchasing the high budget decoys and are there for the simple pleasure and admiration of skilly crafted decoys and the history behind them.
Tyler Bryan, an Eastern Shore collector and hunter, said he has around 75 decoys and enjoys the story and history associated with the decoys he purchases.
Bryan said he came to collecting naturally, influenced by his upbringing on the Eastern Shore and his fascination with nature. But one of the main reasons he continues to collect is the close community of decoy collectors.
"The decoy collecting community is really a fantastic group of people," Bryan said. "It's tight-knit. Everyone knows each other. Most people know what everyone collects, and they're very helpful."
Bryan recommends decoy newcomers seek out a mentor because there are facets to collecting that will be much easier to someone if they have a trusted mentor to guide them along the way. According to Bryan, plenty of people within the decoy collecting community are happy to take on a mentee.
Rossner said decoy collecting often gets associated with much older people and can be seen as a "dying craft," but in his eyes, it deserves more recognition for the layers of complexity it holds and the community that has welcomed him.
Rossner said he encourages anyone interested to spend time with other carvers and collectors and learn more about the shared love this community has for decoys.
"There's lots of people still doing it, but not as many as there once were," Rossner said. "So you are living history when you're carving a decoy or you're doing an art form … you're doing something that's been handed down generation by generation."

title: States apart, Waterfowl artists build lasting friendships
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
States apart, Waterfowl artists build lasting friendships

 November 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 517
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Jim Green and his wife, Kara, traveled from Hermosa, South Dakota, a small town with less than 400 people, to Easton this weekend. He's been bringing his wildlife sculptures to the Waterfowl Festival for around a decade.The South Dakota couple was stationed inside of the Waterfowl's main building for the Art at the Armory display. Directly across sat Carol Heiman-Greene and her husband, all the way from Orange, California.
The two artists and their respective spouses aren't just acquaintances. They're friends, or better yet, family.
"I come back year after year, and these are like my families," Heiman-Greene said of the fellow artists she's come to know. Kara Green used that exact same word — family — to describe her and her husband's friendship with the Heiman-Greenes and others.
Carol Heiman-Greene, who's been an exhibitor at the Easton festival for about 20 years, says there's a "core" of artists who have been at Waterfowl and other festivals for a long time. She said when new artists come, it's a joy to welcome them into the family, too.
On Saturday, Heiman-Greene pointed out her painting of a California condor vulture, laughing since Jim Green had a sculpture of a California condor for sale.
Through the ups and downs of travel, sales and weather, Heiman-Greene said artists have "all sorts of tales (they) can share" with one another.
"You come to these (festivals), and you see your friends from last year and years previous," Jim Green said. "It's so nice to connect with people."
Green says he loves those friendships with fellow artists not just for the relationships, but also to expand his work in an environment rich with creative ideas.
"You have a tendency to think of the world as built on artists when you come to these, because you see so many of them," he continued. "And then you get home and you're in this desert of nobody else around you that does this. So it's really nice to have that creativity, that creative aspect of things to bounce ideas off of other people."
For the Green couple, it's not a competitive environment. Last year, Jim Green said someone stopped by to let him know they recreated his raven coat rack sculpture.
"I know there are other artists that would kind of take that the wrong way," he said. "But I was like, 'Yeah, where are the pictures? I love that.'"
Both Carol Heiman-Greene and Jim Green said the people, atmosphere and weather at Waterfowl combine to make the festival one of their favorites. While Green said his sales are typically solid at Waterfowl, even if they weren't, the three-day event is still his "favorite one of the year."
"I love coming here to see the atmosphere and everything there is about Maryland," Heiman-Greene said. "It's really fun. It has such a small-town atmosphere."
Despite living states and plane rides apart, the annual Waterfowl Festival tradition has helped bring the Greens and Heiman-Greenes together as artists and friends. It's a trend Jim Green hopes continues for years to come.
"Art sells art," Jim Green said. "If you can't have all boats rise, you shouldn't be in the boat."

title: Giving thanks for my mother and her recipes
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country cooking
content:
Giving thanks for my mother and her recipes

 November 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country cooking | Section: News 
 
 1452
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Today I am pulling a favorite cooking column of mine from a few years ago. Not only do I love it, but I had a request from one of Mom's great granddaughters who had heard about it and wanted to see a repeat. This column fits right in with your holiday dessert planning, so enjoy.GIVING THANKSToday I am starting my column by giving thanks for the 52 years I was blessed with having one of the most influential women in my life — my mother. Mom was born on July 4, 1911, and died on Nov. 18, 1997 after a brief illness.
Mom graduated at the age of 16 after completing 11 years of school, as required in those times. By the age of 21, she had married my father; bought a farm; built a house, barn and chicken house; and was raising hogs and cows along with growing truck crops for market.
Did I forget to mention my parents throughout the years had nine sons and two daughters?
What a wonderful family life we had — the most complaining I ever heard her say was, "How many more can we feed at the table, 'cause company is coming or get them fresh eggs from the hen house for breakfast or I will eat after everyone else has eaten.'"
Laura Hudson Hitchens was not a woman to back down from whatever life handed her — she made the most out of a little and asked for nothing in return from anyone. I can never fill her shoes, but I have never given up trying.
Mom loved to cook anything, and she never really had a favorite food to cook, but her desserts were loved by everyone as she made the best pie crust ever. And those biscuits came in a close second! Let's make some Thanksgiving desserts today.
FOOL PROOF PIE CRUST4 cups flour, 1 1/3 cup shortening, 2 tsp salt, 1 tbsp sugar, 1 egg, 1 tbsp vinegar, 1/2 cup water.
Mix flour with shortening, salt and sugar. Set aside. Beat together egg, vinegar and water. Begin sprinkling the dry and wet ingredients together. Turn ingredients together with a fork. Chill 15 minutes or longer in the refrigerator before working into pie crust. Remove from the refrigerator and break into portions. Work the dough on a floured surface until smooth and proceed to roll out into the appropriate size crust you need.
EASY PIE DOUGH1 cup shortening, 1/2 cup boiling water, 3 cups flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt.
Cream together shortening with boiling water. Beat well. Add flour, baking powder and salt. Mix lightly and roll out on a floured surface.
PUMPKIN PIE2 cups pumpkin, 5 tbsp flour, 1/2 cup white sugar, 3/4 cup brown sugar, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp nutmeg, 1/2 tsp pumpkin pie spices, 1/2 tsp cinnamon, 3 cups milk, egg whites.
Mix pumpkin, flour, sugars, salt and spices. Add milk. Beat egg whites and fold into the mixture last. Pour into an unbaked pie shell and bake in a preheated 450-degree oven for the first 15 minutes and then 350 degrees until toothpick inserted comes out clean — maybe 20 to 25 minutes.
SWEET POTATO PIE3 cups mashed sweet potatoes, 2 cups evaporated milk, 4 eggs, 2 1/4 cups sugar, 2 tsp lemon extract, 1 1/2 tsp vanilla, 1/4 tsp baking powder, 1 tbsp milk, 1 cup coconut (optional)
Combine sweet potatoes, evaporated milk, eggs and sugar. Beat at a high speed and then add lemon extract and vanilla. Then mix baking powder with 1 tablespoon milk and add to potato mixture. Add coconut, if desired. Mix well and put in two 9-inch baking pans (pie pans) and bake in a preheated 375-degree oven for one hour.
APPLE PIE4 cups peeled and diced apples, 1/4 cup lemon juice, 1/2 cup sugar, 1/4 cup flour, 1/4 tsp salt and 1/4 cup half and half.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Prepare pastry for one two crust 9-inch pie. Place one crust on the pie plate. Mix apples, lemon juice, sugar, flour, salt and half and half. Mix well and pour into the unbaked pie crust. Cover with the remaining crust and cut slits in it, seal and flute the edges. Bake until the crust is brown, and juice begins to bubble — 50 to 60 minutes. You can place small strips of foil around the edges of the crust, before baking, to keep edges from burning. Remove foil for the last 15 minutes of baking. You can also add 1/2 cup chopped walnuts.
OLD FASHIONED MINCE PIE28-oz jar prepared mincemeat, 1/12 cups diced apples.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Place one unbaked pie crust on a 9-inch pie plate. Mix mincemeat with apples. Pour this mixture into the pie crust. Cover the top with another unbaked pie crust. Flute edge and seal. Cut slits into top crust and bake for 40 to 45 minutes.
NO ROLL PIE CRUST3 cups flour, 2 tsp sugar, 1 tsp salt, 1 cup vegetable oil, 1/3 cup milk.
Mix ingredients gently to combine. Divide in half and place each half of dough in a regular 9-inch pie pan. Pat out gently Push pastry up the sides and form a nice edge with your thumb and finger. Prick pastry on the bottom to prevent bubbling of the pastry during baking. Bake in a preheated 350-degree oven with your favorite filling or bake empty — let cool and add your favorite filling.
NEVER FAIL CRUST5 cups flour, 2 tsp salt, 1 tsp baking powder, 2 cups shortening, 1 egg, water, 1/4 cup vinegar.
Combine flour, salt, baking powder and shortening until coarse crumbs. In a measuring cup beat egg lightly with a fork and add enough water to equal 3/4 cup. Add vinegar and slightly beat with a fork again. Pour the egg mixture into the flour mixture and stir just to make a ball. Roll out shells for your pies. I found that with this recipe if you place the shell in the pie pan and freeze slightly then the shell does not shrink during baking.
IMPOSSIBLE COCONUT PIE4 eggs, 2 cups sugar, 1/2 cup flour, 2 cups milk, 1 tsp vanilla, 1 can flaked coconut.
In a blender, mix together ingredients. Pour into two 9-inch pans, lightly greased. Bake at 350 degrees for 30 minutes or until set.
PECAN BARSFor crust: 1 cups unsalted butter at room temperature, 1/2 cups packed brown sugar, 1/2 tsp salt, 2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour.
For filling: 1/2 cup unsalted butter, cut into pieces; 1 cup packed dark brown sugar, 1/3 cups honey, 2 tbsp bourbon, 2 tbsp heavy cream, 1/2 tsp kosher salt, 1 tsp pure vanilla extract, 3 cups pecan halves chopped roughly.
Heat oven to 350 degrees. Lightly coat 9- by 13-in baking pan with cooking spray. Line with parchment, leaving an overhang on two long sides; spray parchment.
To make crust, using an electric mixer, beat butter, brown sugar and salt until light and fluffy. Reduce mixer speed and gradually mix in flour until small clumps form. Press into the bottom of the prepared pan. Using a fork, poke holes all over then bake until light golden brown, 20 to 25 min. Let cool while making filling.
For filling, in a small saucepan on low, combine butter, sugar, honey, bourbon, heavy cream and salt. Increase heat and bring to a boil; boil for 2 min. Remove from heat and stir in vanilla, then fold in pecans.
Pour mixture over baked crust, return to oven and bake until nuts are golden brown and edges are bubbling, 25 to 30 min. Let cool completely in the pan, then use overhangs to transfer to a cutting board and cut into pieces.
APPLE PEAR CRISP1/2 cup old-fashioned oats, 3 small Gala or Empire apples (peeled and chopped), 2 medium pears (peeled and chopped), 1 tbsp water, 2 tsp brown sugar, 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon, 1/2 tsp ground ginger, 1/2 cup dried cranberries, 1/3 cup chunky sweetened peanut butter, 3 tbsp whole wheat flour, 1/4 cup fat-free whipped cream.
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Spread the oats in a single layer on a jelly-roll pan. Toast them 5 to 8 minutes or until golden brown, stirring once halfway through. In a 4-quart saucepan, combine the apples, pears, water, sugar, cinnamon, and ginger. Cook on medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 10 to 12 minutes or until sugar dissolves and fruit softens. Remove from the heat and stir in the cranberries. Divide the mixture among 6 shallow 12- to 16-ounce baking dishes.
In a medium bowl, combine the oats, peanut butter, and flour. Rub the mixture between your fingers to form small clumps then sprinkle it over the fruit mixture in the baking dishes. Bake for 15 to 20 minutes or until browned and bubbling. To serve, top each crisp with 1 tablespoon of whipped cream.

title: Younger generations pitch in to continue Waterfowl tradition
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Younger generations pitch in to continue Waterfowl tradition

 November 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 662
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With more than 25,000 people attending this year's Waterfowl Festival, organizers needed all hands on deck to pull off the three-day event, including contributions of Easton's younger generations.Waterfowl Festival Executive Director Deena Kilmon said her largest takeaway from this year's festival was the involvement and participation of youth volunteers.
"That is like my number one success story, the engagement of the kids, helping the festival, learning about the artists, learning about what the festival does," Kilmon said. "That was an incredible part of the success for me, as well as the hundreds and hundreds of adult volunteers that help us every year. But just seeing all those kids was just joy."
Kilmon said more than 200 high school students volunteered during the festival. She added that the lead points of contact at the different venues included many younger volunteers this year.
Kilmon also noted that expanding the festival's offerings for families and younger adults were goals for this year.
Throughout the weekend, families could be found at every corner. The Bay Street area had a fishing derby for kids and a "beer wetlands" tent tailored for younger adults. The Phillip Wharf Environmental Center brought its Fishmobile to show off live animals and educate children on the creatures in the Chesapeake Bay.
Behind the Easton Elks Lodge, Sean Mann Outdoors, a Trappe sporting goods store, held duck and goose calling clinics for kids on Saturday and Sunday.
Instructors Sean Mann and Nick Michael taught children ages four through 14 the basics of calling, passing down the skills in hopes of cultivating a young generation of callers. After Saturday's calling clinic, Mann asked parents to let their children use the duck and goose calls they were given to take home.
"Parents, please encourage these youngsters to call," Mann said.
Across town at the Bay Street Ponds, EJ Milhollan, 22, served as chair of the beer wetlands area for the second consecutive year. He's the son of Eric Milhollan, president of Waterfowl's Board of Directors.
"I've always worked at Waterfowl, and it was an opportunity that was kind of thrown at me, and I said, 'Why not?'" EJ Milhollan said. "And they asked me to come back this year. It was a good time last year."
For the Milhollans, the festival has always been a family affair. While it was Eric Milhollan's first year as board president, he's been involved as a volunteer ever since he was a child. Now, his wife and four children — EJ and 20-year-old triplets — carry on that family Waterfowl tradition.
Eric Milhollan sees the festival's growth as not simply attracting a new group of people, but "attracting more groups with different likes."
"It's community, it's family, it's downtown," he said. "You just see everything changing. It's just a fun place to be."
"The backbone of the festival, for this weekend, is certainly art," he continued. "But it's certainly tickets as well. You see different age brackets that like different things. So if you've been over to sportsmans' (pavilion), that attracts a certain type of people. And whether it's music, whether it's beer, whether it's just hanging out and the food, there's something for everybody."
Kilmon noted that by putting an emphasis on outdoor activities like the fishing derby, beer wetlands and calling clinic, the younger generations learn of Waterfowl's conservation and preservation efforts.
"All those outdoor activities really worked well to get our kids outside, get our families outside, and (help) them understand why we do what we do," Kilmon said. "To preserve these wide-open spaces for these kids to have when they grow up. I think these kids that we attracted to us this fall, hopefully, will engage with us throughout the year."
Reflecting on how involved he and his family have become, Eric Milhollan said his four children are bringing their friends over to enjoy the festival and continue its momentum.
"Just passing that off to different generations is what keeps it going," Eric Milhollan said. "And you see a lot of that here. You see a lot of families."

title: Academy Art Museum gets new director
author: Tom McCall
content:
Academy Art Museum gets new director

 November 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Arts 
 
 511
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Charlotte Potter Kasic, the new director of the Academy Art Museum, has a lot of ideas. But her first weeks, she said, will be dedicated to completing a listening tour.Her latest post was the Barry Art Museum in Norfolk, Virginia, where she was executive director. Now she has a new challenge with helming the Academy.
"Every time I see a challenge, I lean in," Kasic said.
She was not entirely unfamiliar with the Academy Art Museum before applying for the job.
"When Eric Neil left the Academy in 2012 or 2013, he became the director of the Chrysler Museum of Art, and I was the director of the Chrysler Museum Glass Studio, which was like an annex," Kasic said.
She's been impressed with the museum's existing work and potential.
"When you break it down, there are classes. There are programs and exhibitions. There is collections. There is fundraising. There are galas. It is wild how much happens here with so little. I think this place is doing a great job of hitting a lot of audiences," she said.
Kasic is excited to work with the staff to continue these efforts.
Kasic has past in glass blowing, in which she said she learned about collaboration and teamwork. She created Cirque de Verre (circus of glass), which traveled around the United States to museums and art spaces that had glass blowing furnaces.
"Glass I love because you work in teams. It is hot. It is visceral. There is a lot of strong communication skills," Kasic said. "I like things to be immersive, multisensory and interdisciplinary. When you think of olfactory, that is how you access your deepest memories. Music can change your mood in a minute. Art can do that as well."
Kasic has a masters degree from Rhode Island School of Design and has done residencies at Penland, Oxbow, Pilchuck and in Australia.
After the Chrysler she moved to Vermont to start a family. She ended up being the director at the Yestermorrow Design Build School, which celebrates sustainable design and craft.
The siren song of Norfolk brought her and her family back to the Chesapeake, where she joined the team at the Barry Museum. She says it has become the glass art capital of the East Coast. There, Kasic helmed a 25,000 square foot expansion and closed out a $23 million campaign.
Now at the Academy Art Museum, she sees a collaborative community that brings Plein Air, The Craft Show and the Waterfowl Festival into the institution. She also has a clear-eyed approach to what the Academy can offer the community.
"I would like to see more of our permanent collection on view. We have so much that exists but people don't get to see," she said.
Even with these plans, she realizes that there is a lot of collaborating to be done.
"It is important to say how invested the board is in this place. I have seen more board involvement and more community investment than any other organization I have been in. People are so dedicated. It is really remarkable and it speaks to the strength of this place," she said.

title: Museum opens art-making studio
author: Staff Writer
content:
Museum opens art-making studio

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 476
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Hirshhorn Art School, a first-of-its-kind art education experience, opened inside the Smithsonian's Hirshhorn Museum on Oct. 30. Combining elements of a professional artist's studio, museum galleries and clubhouse, the new and flexible 1,700-square-foot hub will offer structured programming and open-studio sessions guided by museum educators and teaching artists four days a week for visitors of all ages."Hirshhorn Art School asks visitors to 'think like an artist,'" said Melissa Chiu, museum director. "When the Hirshhorn opened in 1974, museum education was in its infancy and largely grounded in observation. We've since found that experiential art learning is both highly effective and in demand."
Designed for varying ages, abilities and interests, Hirshhorn Art School programs will be organized into thematic, artist-focused semesters and will build on the work of Hirshhorn Kids and ARTLAB as well as public programs for adult audiences.
The first semester, "Boundary Breakers," will introduce the biographies, materials, techniques and philosophies of originals such as Anni Albers, Mark Bradford and Barbara Hepworth, whose artworks are on view. In its first year, Hirshhorn Art School expects to host more than 25,000 in-person visitors and 75,000 more virtually with livestreamed lessons and anytime resources.
Hirshhorn Art School offers programs Wednesdays–Saturdays:
Storytime Studio, Wednesdays, 10 a.m.–1 p.m.Children ages up to 8 years will connect an artwork on view with a children's book and engage in hands-on activities that develop self-expression and visual storytelling. Drop-ins welcome.
School Studio, FridaysGuided by museum educators and teaching artists, students in grades three through eight will explore the hows and whys of art-making, inspired by Hirshhorn collections and exhibitions. These weekly morning and afternoon sessions, lasting 60–120 minutes, must be reserved.
Open Studio, Saturdays, 10 a.m.–3 p.m.Guided by museum educators and teaching artists, visitors of all ages will be invited to respond to modern and contemporary art history, with a focus on Hirshhorn exhibitions. Drop-ins welcome.
Emerging Artists, Saturdays, 3–5:30 p.m.Teens ages 14–19 will collaboratively focus on the works of living artists. The debut season invites consideration of Bradford and his monumental work "Pickett's Charge" (2017). This program builds upon ARTLAB, the Hirshhorn platform for teens, which served an average of 4,000 student artists. Pre-registration is required.
As part of Hirshhorn Art School's outreach, art educators will continue to build upon the museum's library of almost 50 online projects and three free in-gallery activity guides. The Art School classroom has a built-in loop system to support visitors who use hearing aids, as well as a quiet area and tactiles.
Hirshhorn Art School is the public expression of Hirshhorn Education, a central pillar of the national museum of modern and contemporary art, whose mission amplifies the importance of the voices of artists on behalf of the Smithsonian Institution.
The Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden is the national museum of modern and contemporary art. Part of the Smithsonian, the Hirshhorn is located on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. For more information, visit hirshhorn.si.edu.

title: Benson's birds: AAM art exhibit explores vintage prints
author: Staff Writer
content:
Benson's birds: AAM art exhibit explores vintage prints

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 267
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A new exhibit at the Academy Art Museum in Easton highlights sporting, waterfowl and bird prints from American artist Frank W. Benson.The prints are from AAM's collection and the exhibit runs through Dec. 8.
The exhibit is entitled "Sporting: Frank Benson's Waterfowl Prints."
Here are some details about the artist and his prints from AAM:
"Born and raised on the North Shore of Massachusetts, American artist Frank W. Benson (1862–1951), grew up sailing, fishing, hunting, and birdwatching. These interests persisted throughout his life, and he ultimately became one of the fore- most American practitioners of the genre of printmaking known as the sporting print.
In the early 20th century, Benson established a reputation as a painter of portraits and landscapes inspired by French Impressionism. He joined a group of Boston and New York painters known as "The Ten" who organized carefully curated annual exhibitions of paintings between 1898 and 1918. He was also interested in printmaking, particularly etching. Beginning in 1914, he returned to his early fascination with birds, ultimately creating more than 300 images of the many species of waterfowl native to the beaches and marshes of New England.
Sporting prints by Benson first entered the Academy's collection in 1987 when Berlin Voorhees included two of the artist's waterfowl etchings with a larger gift of late 19th and early 20th century works on paper. The collection grew to encompass more than 30 works by Benson, largely due to the generosity of the late Robert K. Keller, who began donating prints from his collection to the Museum in 2001 and continued with these gifts until his death in 2009."
For more: https://academyartmuseum.org/sporting-frank-bensons-waterfowl-prints/

title: Waterfowl Festival soaring to new heights
author: Staff Writer
content:
Waterfowl Festival soaring to new heights

 November 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 579
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Congratulations to the many people who made this year's Waterfowl Festival a success.The annual celebration of wildlife, art, music and history brought between 25,000 and 30,000 people to Easton last weekend.
Congratulations, too, go to Deena Kilmon in her first year as executive director of the festival. She is definitely at the top of the list for a rookie of the year award.
If there was any fear of a drop-off with new leadership, Kilmon put those fears to rest and set a high bar for success in coming years.
"We know we broke every record we've ever broken," Kilmon said on Monday.
"We had the highest attendance ever," Kilmon said. "It's hard for us to gauge because not everyone buys a ticket. But we do know that every parking space was full and every bus had about 45 minutes to an hourlong wait, and we had to add three buses on Saturday to accommodate the people."
Kilmon got a helping hand from Mother Nature who blessed the weekend with lovely weather and temperatures approaching 80 degrees under sunny skies for several of the days.
The executive director said multiple vendors — many of whom are already asking about next year — sold out or had record days at the festival.
If you have a 2025 calendar already, mark the weekend of Nov. 14-16 for the 54th Waterfowl Festival. We have no doubt that Kilmon will improve upon the tremendous success of this year's festival.
The success of the Waterfowl Festival is a success for the town of Easton and Talbot County too.
Downtown Easton shops were packed all three days of the festival, and restaurants had waiting lists for tables.
Kilmon called the relationship between the festival and local businesses "incredibly important."
"We're symbiotic," she said. "So if they succeed, we succeed and vice versa."
The three-day festival has an economic impact of more than $3 million each year, Kilmon said. It benefits hotels, restaurants, retailers and even local nonprofits.
"It's typically one of the biggest fundraising events of the year because a lot of the food vendors and people involved in the festival, they are nonprofits," Kilmon said. "And they're allowed to keep their proceeds, so it's extremely important to a lot of people."
At a breakfast Friday morning, Talbot County Economic Development and Tourism Director Cassadra Vanhooser extolled the virtues of the business community that makes the "wonderful things" that happen in the county possible.
"It's that private investment along with the public investment that builds the community," she said. "And it's the festivals like the Waterfowl Festival — the granddaddy of them all — that weaves that fabric of the quality of life that we all love so much."
The festival may have just celebrated its 53rd anniversary, but it continues to grow and evolve.
Throughout the festival venues music filled the air and complemented the many duck and geese calls typical of the festival. Overall there were 38 musical acts on multiple stages.
"That made the festival have a different vibe this year, I think," Kilmon said, "just made it more of a friendly family party on every corner."
Feedback has been "incredibly positive," and Kilmon is excited to begin work on continuing Easton's Waterfowl tradition.
"Fifty-three years of our community coming together just gets better every year," Kilmon said. "And we're already working on next year, believe it or not."
It is good that Kilmon and her team are already working on the 2025 show. This year's show will be tough to top. We have no doubt they will rise to the challenge.
