title: Country Cooking: Memories of cranberry sauce
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Memories of cranberry sauce

 November 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1179
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We always had cranberries at Christmas and Thanksgiving dinners. Mom used the whole cranberries that you served with a spoon.One time on the Sunday after Thanksgiving Thursday, our parents, my three younger brothers and I were invited to a dinner in a nearby larger town. We were prompted on the way there (or threatened) to be on our best behavior or else — we never tested that "or else."
This strange looking dish came past with red slices of something on it that quivered when shook, and we all four said "no thanks" and passed it on. Oh, but no. Mom said "oh you all love that" and proceeded to plop a piece on our plate.
That is when the trouble started. We rolled it, we slapped it and finally mashed it, leaving the prettiest design ever.
On the way home, we were told that it was canned cranberry sauce. To this very day I have a can of cranberry sauce waiting to be opened, sliced and served on the holiday table. As I look across my kitchen this morning at my can of sauce, I think of Mom standing in her bib apron, smiling and saying, "what did you all think was on that plate?"
The reporter came out of me at an early age, so I said, "Jimmy said it was liver, Ollie said it was brains, Richard said it was jello and I said I would investigate."
GREEN BEANS WITH BACON4 diced bacon strips, 1/2 cup chopped onion, 8 cups fresh green beans (trimmed), water, salt and pepper.
This is tasty, quick and easy. In a large skillet, cook bacon strips with chopped onion until the bacon is crisp. Meanwhile place green beans in a large saucepan and cover with water. Bring to a boil and cook for 8 to 10 minutes or until crisp-tender. Drain well and add the bacon mixture. Sprinkle top with salt and pepper and toss to coat. Serve immediately. This recipe is not the one grandmother or mom made but is great too. Give it a try.
SWEET POTATO N' MARSHMALLOW1 can sweet potatoes, 1 egg, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 1/4 tsp vanilla, 1/3 cup evaporated milk, 1/3 stick margarine, large bag of marshmallows.
For a Small casserole dish size, mix together well with an electric mixer: sweet potatoes, egg, sugar, vanilla, evaporated milk and margarine. Bake in a 350-degree oven for 30 to 40 minutes. Remove from the oven, top with marshmallows and return to the oven just until the marshmallows turn golden brown. Remove from the oven and let set for a while before serving.
CORNBREAD DRESSING WITH OYSTERS2 tbsps unsalted butter (plus more for greasing the dish), 1 yellow onion (diced), 3 stalks celery (diced), 5 cloves garlic (minced), 8 cups crumbled cornbread, kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, 3 1/2 cups chicken stock, 6 large eggs, 1/2 cup chopped Italian parsley, 1 bunch fresh tarragon (leaves stripped and chopped), 2 cups shucked oysters with their juice.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees. Butter a 9-by-13-inch baking dish. In a large skillet, melt the butter over medium heat. When the butter is foamy, add the onion and celery, and cook, stirring frequently, until softened, 6 to 8 minutes. Stir the garlic and cook until aromatic, about 1 minute. Stir in the crumbled cornbread and cook, stirring, until lightly browned, then remove from the heat. In a large bowl, beat the eggs until smooth. Whisk in the chicken stock, parsley and tarragon. Stir in the cornbread mixture and the oysters. Pour the dressing mixture into the prepared baking dish and bake until the dressing is set and golden brown, about 1 hour. (Alternatively, cover and refrigerate overnight before baking.) Let rest for 5 minutes.
GREEN BEAN CASSEROLE2 cans green beans, 1 can golden mushroom soup, half a can of water, 1 cup grated cheddar cheese, one can fried onions.
Heat oven to 350 degrees. In a large bowl, stir together green beans with golden mushroom soup, water and cheese. Lightly mix and transfer to a two-quart casserole dish. Sprinkle top with fried onions. Cover with foil and bake for 30 minutes. Remove foil and bake for another 15 minutes until bubbly.
ASPARAGUS CASSEROLEThis goes great with baked ham. In a buttered casserole dish place a layer of asparagus and then a layer of crumbled cheese nips crackers. Wet with cream of mushroom soup mixed with water according to directions on the can. Finish the casserole with a few more crushed cheese nips. Bake in a 350-degree oven until asparagus is tender.
OLD FASHIONED BREAD DRESSING1 1/2 cups finely chopped onion, 1/3 cup butter, 1 1/2 cups chopped celery, 8 cups dry small bread cubes, 1 1/2 tsp salt, 1/8 tsp black pepper, 1/2 tsp poultry seasoning, 1/2 tsp sage, 1/4 cup water, 1 beaten egg.
In a skillet, cook chopped onion in butter with chopped celery until tender. Add this mixture to bread cubes, which have been placed in a large pan. Sprinkle with salt, black pepper, poultry seasoning and sage, and combine well. Add water and beaten egg. Toss together with a fork. Stuff a thawed bird immediately and bake according to directions on the turkey label.
ITALIAN GREEN BEAN CASSEROLE6 ounces parmesan cheese (grated), 1 1/4 cups Italian-style breadcrumbs, 4 garlic cloves (minced), 1 tsp kosher salt, 3/4 tsp black pepper (divided), 3 (28-oz.) cans Italian-style green beans (drained), 2 (9-oz.) packages frozen artichoke hearts (thawed, drained well and chopped), 2/3 cup extra virgin olive oil, fresh flat-leaf parsley (chopped).
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Combine parmesan, breadcrumbs, garlic, salt, and 1/2 tsp pepper in a large bowl. Reserve 1/3 cup of the breadcrumb mixture then set aside. Add green beans, artichoke hearts, and olive oil to bowl with remaining breadcrumb mixture, and fold to combine well. Pour green bean mixture into a lightly greased 13-by-9-inch baking dish. Sprinkle reserved breadcrumb mixture evenly over the casserole. Cover with aluminum foil, and bake until heated through, about 30 minutes. Uncover and bake until lightly golden and bubbly, about 10 minutes. Sprinkle with remaining 1/4 tsp pepper, and if desired, chopped parsley.
HONEY SPICE BREAD2/3 cup packed brown sugar, 1/3 cup 2% milk, 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1-1/2 tsps baking powder, 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon, 1/2 tsp ground nutmeg, 1/8 tsp ground cloves, 2 large eggs (room temperature), 1/2 cup honey, 1/3 cup canola oil. GLAZE: 1/3 cup confectioners' sugar, 2 tsps 2% milk.
Preheat the oven to 325 degrees. In a small saucepan, combine brown sugar and milk. Cook and stir over low heat until sugar is dissolved. Remove from heat. In a large bowl, whisk flour, baking powder, cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves. In another bowl, whisk eggs, honey, oil and brown sugar mixture until blended. Add to flour mixture; stir just until moistened. Transfer the batter to a greased 8-by-4-inch loaf pan. Bake for 50-60 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean (cover top loosely with foil if needed to prevent overbrowning). Cool in pan 10 minutes before removing to a wire rack to cool completely. In a small bowl, stir glaze ingredients until smooth, drizzle over bread.

title: Historic Sotterley screens, holds panel discussion on 'Grandma's Hands'
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Historic Sotterley screens, holds panel discussion on 'Grandma's Hands'

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 665
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Family recipes are passed down through the generations and the film "Grandma's Hands" focuses on six Southern Maryland individuals who cherish those recipes.Historic Sotterley held a screening and panel discussion with the stars of the film along with writer, executive producer, director and narrator Craig Sewell on Nov. 13 at the museum in Hollywood.
"This was a passion project for me," said Sewell. "Kitchens are magic places, whether they're commercial kitchens or home kitchens, because it's about where everything happens. It's where smiles happen and tears happen and stories happen and the aromas happen. Kitchens are places where people come together."
The 58-minute film was funded through a Maryland Heritage Areas Authority grant and filmed by the Southern Maryland National Heritage Area.
"Ask someone about their grandmother and chances are the story will quickly end up in the kitchen. And once there, the real story begins," Sewell said to open the film. "Lives change, but the food will always be with us. Food is powerful. It nourishes our bodies, it excites our tastes, it is infused and marinated in emotion and it provides us with a solid connection to our past. For generations our grandma's hands have made memories, continued traditions and blessed us with the knowledge of who we are."
The film stars six individuals who recreate their grandmother's recipes: Lexington Park's Teandre Thompson (bread pudding), Waldorf's Mary Louise Booth Webb (crackling bread), Newburg's Tiffany Barber (tomato sauce with meatballs), Benedict's Franklin A. Robinson (chili sauce), Greenbelt's LaWann Stribling (macaroni and cheese) and Lothian's Kayla Griffith (sweet potato pancakes).
Thompson said her grandmother Theresa Young would create "a masterpiece dessert using a few ingredients and her hands. She didn't use measuring cups and spoons; she did it just by sight. I'm not that daring yet."
The 98-year-old Webb, who cooked the dish in her grandmother's farm kitchen located near Zekiah Swamp, said it was made as a way to use everything of the pig.
Robinson, who lives at Serenity Farm, said his grandmother would make the sauce at the end of the tobacco harvest.
"For me these recipes are a way of keeping all of these people I've known alive," Robinson said. "Every time I open the cookbook, I remember my grandmother at her wood stove and my other grandmother who lived on another farm. It's remembering them and honoring them."
Barber, who lives on Grace Haven Farm, said her grandmother would take Wonder bread, slather it with the sauce and layer it with Parmesan cheese.
"My grandmother's recipes were the center of my childhood," Barber, who still uses her grandmother's cast iron skillet, said in the film, "and it's something I carry forward with my kids."
Barber said dinner at her two-table dining room — which is essential for eight children and five grandchildren — "became that place where you learned to express yourself, having conversations about what matters to you and those connections. Dinner matters, meals matter. It's the connection you build around that meal."
Griffith, who lives on the family farm, said her grandmother Lillian would make pancakes with chocolate chips, whipped cream, sprinkles, "the whole nine yards"
"She could not sit down for more than a minute or two," she added. "She would get up, make sure everyone had something on their plate. To most of us she would say, 'You don't have enough,' but [to my grandfather it would be] 'Earl, you're eating too much.'"
The film viewing earlier this month was the season finale of Historic Sotterley's Common Ground series.
"Throughout the peninsula that is Southern Maryland, people have gathered, cooked for centuries," Sewell says in the opening minutes of the film. "The recipes are messengers from whence we came. Food and recipes can divide a family, a region, even a culture."
Maryland Public Television will air a 27-minute version of the film — focusing on three of the cooks — at 7 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 23.
The hour-long version of the film will premiere on mpt.org, pbs.org and the PBS app starting on Sunday, Nov. 24.
Find out more about the film at destinationsouthernmaryland.com/discover/grandmas-hands.

title: Wolves arrive at Wilmer Park

Wolves arrive at Wilmer Park

 Wolves have arrived at Wilmer Park to art lovers and residents' anticipation. "The Wolves" created in 2000 by Sally Matthews is the 16th sculpture from the Peter and Hanna Woicke collection, and can be seen at Wilmer Park in front of Aunt Sarah's Playground.According to Elizabeth Healy of the Chestertown Public Arts Committee, they were installed in the afternoon of Nov. 13, overseen by Dave Hegland, acting chairman of the Committee, after being stored for minor stability repairs at the Woicke's property in St. Michaels.
Hegland pointed out, the sculpture was repaired and conserved by Howard Wellman of Wellman Conservation and his team, then were de-installed and palletized for transport by Howard Wellman and Ben Herr of Anthony's Flowers and Landscaping.
According to Hegland, the work was well worth it.
Back in early September, he told the Chestertown Council the wolves were one of the most highly anticipated of their pieces.
He later told the Kent News, "This has been our most anticipated sculpture and in the short time since its installation we have seen adults and children enjoy the thrill and mystery of these life size sculptures walking in the tree line at Wilmer Park."
There are five wolves, each weighing 350 lbs., rugged and lifelike from a distance; bronze snouts pointing towards the water, trekking through fallen leaves.
Up-close you see their craftsmanship and appeal.
And very shortly, the wolves will be joined by the next sculpture, Durbar. The sculpture weighs approximately 3500 lbs and is about 15 ft tall, to be installed in the South East corner in Bailey Park. The complex structure will be disassembled and reassembled by an art team.
Durbar will set on a concrete pad installed by the Chestertown Streets and Public Works Department, Hegland said.
The Peter and Hannah Woike Collection consists of 23 outdoor sculptures which are diverse in style, subject matter and origin. For more information about Chestertown Public Art go to chestertownpublicarts.com/.

title: Mid-Shore Community Band celebrates differences
author: Tom McCall
content:
Mid-Shore Community Band celebrates differences

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 476
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Copper timpani, sliding trombones, heraldic trumpets and a focused baton are just some of the instruments making up the 45-member Mid-Shore Community Band. Band Leader Matt Fullerton keeps all the moving pieces in order.The band brought its music to Thompson Park on Nov. 9 during the Waterfowl Festival, and band members commanded a range from flutes to thundering drums.
But the most significant diversity the band exhibits is not in its musical abilities, but in the ages of its members.
Members of the band range from high schoolers to those in their upper 70s. There are people from all different walks of life who come together to make music.
"We do this because we love music. If nothing else it is therapy. No, it is a lot of fun," Fullerton said.
Fullerton has been conducting since 1975 and has a masters in music. He taught the band at Easton Middle school for 30 years. He said he can play most of the instruments in the band.
Tracie Thomas, who plays clarinet, has been in the band since its founding in 2009.
"One of the best parts is getting to play with my old musical director from middle school, Matt Fullerton," she said. "Just being able to play is the best part. We generally have a season, and we will have a repertoire for the season that we select for each concert. Of course we already have Christmas music out. We have started rehearsing for that."
She said they have everything from jazzy Christmas to sleigh ride Christmas music.
"We really try hard to be a part of the community. Our band is here to serve other nonprofits like we are today. Every concert we have played is no charge and often raising money for another organization. Everybody here is volunteering their time," Thomas said.
There was also a vast expanse of musical choices on display at the Nov. 9 concert, including a theme from the Disney film Fantasia "Night On Bald Mountain," a medley of computer gaming songs, a march and a hoedown.
"It includes themes from Assassin 33, 'Bratja' from Full Metal Alchemist, 'Dragon Born' from Skyrims, 'Sadness and Sorrow' from Naruto and 'Baba Yetu' from Civilization 4," Fullerton said of the gaming medley.
He noted that Hollywood used to produce most music, but the successful gaming industry is paying composers to make the digital worlds come alive.
"The same backing that creates that, as they do for themes for movies. It is possible that more people hear these than some of the pieces more than some of the movie themes," Fullerton said.
Of course the band also played a crisp "Star Spangled Banner" and got the crowd on their feet.
They practice at the Easton High band room every Tuesday at 7 p.m. They always looking for new players, even if they haven't dusted off their tuba in 10 years. To learn more, visit mscb.org.

 The Allegra Women's Chorus, an integral part of the Allegro Academy, is rapidly becoming a choral force to reckon with on the Eastern Shore.Directed and conducted by Amy Morgan, on Nov. 17, the 13 female voices with piano and cello accompaniment produced a very musical and emotive program of 12 songs set upon a theme of nature, life relationships, experiences, sadness and joy within the community of mothers and daughters.

title: Thanksgiving made simple: Top tips for hosting small gatherings
author: Laura Sampson Food Drink Life
content:
Thanksgiving made simple: Top tips for hosting small gatherings

 November 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Sampson Food Drink Life | Section: Life 
 
 807
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As we move through life, there will be times when smaller gatherings of friends and family naturally happen. We can't change it, we can't pretend that it's anything different. But we can accept and embrace it.Maybe it won't always be this way. Or you may decide to change how you celebrate completely. Whatever happens with that is in the future. You can make changes in the future.
The only way to move forward this year with a smaller gathering is to embrace the good things about it, even if you don't want to. You might discover a few things about yourself or come up with new ways to enjoy family gatherings.
Celebrate with small gatherings
Cooking for fewer people allows you to change how you've always done things. If you're struggling with change or celebrating when you just don't feel it, that's okay.
Moving forward with a traditional dinner with fewer people can be a blessing. Fewer people means less money spent, which can be nice in the pocketbook. But other things are amazing, too.
Try new things
You can change up what you usually make. Instead of a 20-pound turkey, you can try a small prime rib, turkey breast or something else fancy, perhaps a beef Wellington or a roasted duck.
If you don't need a huge turkey, you can relax a little and sleep in it, or you can make a special breakfast that morning instead of making and stuffing a bird at 5 am. With no reason to be up so early, you can sleep in, make a leisurely breakfast and still get everything done in time.
Streamline the menu
Because you're making a dinner that doesn't include the world's biggest turkey, you're free to cut down on stuffing recipes, cranberry sauces and all that jazz. Even if you're making a turkey, you don't need that much food.
That means it's the perfect time to try something new, like corn pudding or fresh bread. Or the ultimate homemade pie with homemade pie crust. The sky is the limit here, so pick something and perfect it, then amaze your guests.
Make it a potluck
If you are having a smaller gathering, it's the perfect time to call for a potluck. You can make a main dish or two because you'll be doing less in other places. And everyone else can bring sides. Assign them to people so they know what to make and what will be on the menu.
You can serve a potluck buffet style if that's interesting to you. Then, the table is simple, clean and elegant.
If you're serving potluck style, you can keep your current table the size it is. That means no stuffing people into a small space or finding and dragging out more chairs and stools. Plus, no table prep means more time to relax or clean the house.
Speaking of tables
If you're making a smaller, cozy dinner for fewer people, it's the perfect time to do something new and different with your table this year. Add a tablecloth, beautiful candles, pumpkins, flowers or anything else your creative mind desires.
Pull out the fancy special dishes and the silver and make beautiful, small feasts. Just because it's smaller doesn't mean it isn't special or meaningful.
Less pie stress
When you have a house full of guests, you often feel like you have to whip up several pies or desserts. With fewer guests, you can make one and be done. Or go fancy and order from a bakery that will make you the dessert of your dreams.
Change it up
Try new things this year. Instead of having dinner at your regular time, try a new time. Or insist everyone bring their favorite game and host a game night with friends or family. Kick off the Christmas season by choosing a favorite movie and enjoying it together. There's no end to ways you can innovate the day with family or friends.
It's just smaller, not less important
Thanksgiving doesn't have to be a grand affair to be meaningful. Sometimes, embracing a smaller gathering allows us to focus on what truly matters: The people around the table, the flavors we love and the moments we share.
This year, rather than seeing a smaller gathering as something or somebody missing, try to view it as an opportunity to create a more intimate, relaxed celebration. A simplified menu, a cozy setting and a slower pace can make this Thanksgiving feel refreshingly different.
It's a chance to try something new, let go of old expectations and perhaps even start new traditions that feel just as special. Whatever the size of the gathering, the spirit of Thanksgiving lives on in the connections we make and the gratitude we feel.
Laura Sampson of Little House Big Alaska is on a mission to teach modern family-oriented home cooks how to make old-fashioned foods new again. She shares her passion for home cooking, backyard gardening and homesteading on her website and blog.

title: Thanksgiving leftovers: What to do with them
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Thanksgiving leftovers: What to do with them

 November 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: News 
 
 1137
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Thanksgiving dinner is over, and there are lots of leftovers to be eaten in the days to come. My family always said the first round was great, the second round was good and thereafter was "OK."Today I will share some recipes and ideas for moving those foods.
Line the countertop with plastic containers that have lids to package small individual meals. Place a small amount of each food in the containers to be reheated. Lunch is packed or a quick meal-on-the-run. Maybe a shut-in or elderly neighbor would appreciate a dish or two.
Freeze any food that could be eaten in a week or so. Those turkey leftovers are great frozen to be used in that pot of soup on a cold winter day, especially the carcass with a little meat on it.
TURKEY POT PIE2 tbsps butter, 1 onion (chopped), 2 stalks celery (chopped), 3 carrots (chopped), 4 tbsps flour, 4 cups chicken or turkey stock, 2 potatoes (peeled and diced), 2 cups shredded turkey, 2 tbsps chopped parsley, 1/2 cup frozen peas (thawed), 1 prepared pie crust, 1 egg (lightly beaten).
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Melt butter in a saucepan and cook chopped onion until tender. Stir in celery and carrots and cook for 2 minutes. Stir in flour and cook for 2 minutes. Add chicken stock and bring to a simmer. Add potatoes and simmer until tender. Stir in turkey, parsley and peas. Pour mixture into the casserole. Top with pie crust and brush with egg. Bake for 30 minutes until the crust is golden.
THANKSGIVING POTATO SKINS6 to 8 small to medium russet potatoes, 1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, Kosher salt, 1 1/2 cups leftover mashed potatoes, 1 1/2 cup leftover turkey (chopped or shredded), 1 1/2 cups leftover stuffing, 1 cup grated sharp white cheddar, 1/2 cup cranberry sauce.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Scrub potatoes well, then gently pierce with a fork five to six times. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Roast potatoes until tender and a knife can be inserted without resistance, 50 to 60 minutes. Let cool on a baking sheet. Cut each potato in half lengthwise. Using a spoon, carefully scoop out potato flesh, leaving a 1/4-inch border; reserve potato flesh for another use. Using a pastry brush, lightly brush inside and outside of potato skins with oil; season with salt. Reduce oven temperature to 400 degrees. Set a wire rack in a baking sheet. Arrange potato skins skin side down on rack and roast until just beginning to crisp, 25 to 30 minutes. Let cool slightly. Layer each potato skin with leftover potatoes, leftover turkey, and leftover stuffing, then top with cheese. Continue to roast until the cheese is melted and the filling is warmed through, about 15 minutes more. Arrange potatoes on a platter. Top with cranberry sauce.
DEEP FRIED GREEN BEANSToss 1 pound leftover cooked or raw green beans with 1 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper and 1 cup buttermilk. Soak for 15 minutes. Season 1 cup cornmeal with salt and cayenne. Dredge the green beans in the cornmeal, then deep-fry in 2 inches of 375-degree vegetable oil until golden brown, 2 to 3 minutes.
LEFTOVER TURKEY AND STUFFING REUBENS4 tbsps unsalted butter (room temperature), 8 slices rye bread, 4 tbsps Russian dressing, 8 slices Swiss cheese, 2 cups leftover stuffing (warmed slightly), 2 cups sauerkraut, 1 pound leftover thinly sliced turkey, salt and freshly ground black pepper.
Position a rack about four inches from the broiler heat source and preheat. Line a baking sheet with foil. Spread some butter on one side of each slice of bread. Place four pieces, buttered side down, on the prepared baking sheet. Spread some of the Russian dressing on the sides facing up. Top each with a slice of cheese and evenly crumble some of the stuffing over the cheese. Top each with some sauerkraut, turkey and then the remaining cheese on top. Put the open-faced sandwiches under the broiler and cook until the cheese melts, about 2 minutes. Remove the baking sheet from the broiler. Spread the rest of the dressing on the uncovered side of the four remaining bread slices, place on top melted cheese and push down, buttered side up to finish the sandwiches. Return to the broiler and toast sandwich, carefully turning once so both sides get nice and golden brown, about 2 minutes total, serve hot.
GRILLED TURKEY SANDWICH¾ cup mayonnaise, ¼ cup basil pesto, 4-6 slices crusty Italian bread or sourdough, 1/4 cup butter or margarine, 8 or so slices of your baked turkey, artichoke hearts, sliced tomatoes, whatever cheese you like (such as provolone cheese or sliced mozzarella).
In a small bowl, mix mayonnaise and pesto. Spread 1 side of each bread slice with butter. Turn bread slices butter sides down; spread other sides with 1 tbsp pesto mixture each. Top eight bread slices with turkey, artichokes, tomatoes and cheese. Top with remaining bread slices, butter sides up. In a sandwich grill or 12-inch skillet, cook sandwiches over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until bread is toasted, and cheese is melted.
THANKSGIVING LEFTOVER NACHOS1 cup sour cream, 1 tbsp minced chipotle chile in adobo (plus more sauce for serving), 10 cups tortilla chips, 2 cups shredded leftover turkey meat, 3 cups shredded cheddar cheese, 2 cups shredded Monterey Jack cheese, 2 cups thinly sliced leftover cooked Brussels sprouts, 1 1/2 cups leftover cubed roasted butternut squash, 1 cup packaged french-fried onions, 1 cup lightly packed cilantro leaves or parsley leaves, 1/2 cup sliced black olives, 1/4 cup chopped pickled jalapenos.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Stir the sour cream and chipotle chile together in a small bowl. Cover with plastic wraps and refrigerate. Scatter half the chips on a rimmed baking sheet. Top with one-third of the turkey, cheeses, Brussels sprouts, butternut squash and fried onions. Scatter the remaining chips on top followed by the remaining two-thirds of turkey, cheeses, Brussels sprouts and fried onions. Bake until the cheeses are melted and bubbly, about 5 to 7 minutes. Drizzle the nachos with chipotle sour cream and extra adobo sauce. Garnish with cilantro, black olives and jalapenos.
I'd like to wish everyone a safe, happy and healthy Thanksgiving.
Please take the time to check on your shut-in or elderly neighbors as they might not be as fortunate as others. There is nothing that puts a smile on someone's face like a nice big plate of food.
As you sit down together at the Thanksgiving dinner table, give thanks for all that we have — no matter how little or much, give thanks to those serving our country at home and abroad, give thanks for anyone working today so others can be home, and bless the hands who prepared your meal.
See you next week as we enter December and some amazing Christmas cookie recipes. God bless you all.

title: Art teacher Bridget Whited gets 2024 Fine Arts Award
author: Staff Writer
content:
Art teacher Bridget Whited gets 2024 Fine Arts Award

 November 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 241
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot County Retired School Personnel Association Fine Arts Committee Chair Elizabeth Wildasin awarded the organization's 2024 Fine Arts Award to Bridget Whited, the Saint Michaels Middle High School Visual Art Educator, during the group's autumn luncheon.Whited has taught there for the past 17 years. She believes that "art is for everyone" and emphasizes this when connecting programs and lessons with service learning and collaboration among students and the surrounding community.
Currently, she is the AP studio art educator and the National Art Honor Society sponsor. In 2014-2015, Whited was honored as the Talbot County Public Schools Teacher of the Year and was a state finalist. Most recently, she received the Maryland Art Education Association Advocate for Inclusivity Through Art Award, which highlighted her dedication to making visual art accessible to all.
Whited is a Talbot County resident, is married and has two young children.
"She is very deserving of the TCRSPA Fine Arts Award, and we look forward to seeing her for many more years teaching her students and encouraging their creativity," the organization said in a press release. "We are thrilled to present our 2024 Fine Arts Award to her."
TCRSPA celebrated its 60th birthday this year. The organization's primary purpose is informing school retirees and protecting their local and state benefits, providing special social events to socialize with former colleagues, and strengthening participation in community activities. It welcomes retired faculty, administrators and staff to inquire about membership.
For more information, contact jkohn@goeaston.net.

title: Ridgely sports new model train station
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Ridgely sports new model train station

 November 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 437
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — The Town of Ridgely has a new display of its historic railroad station.Bob Anderson, 86, built a model of the Ridgely Train Station, a part of the town's unique charm that dates back to the 19th century. Anderson's model mimics the train station's antique glass windows and green roofing that are still seen today on West Railroad Avenue.
Anderson said despite some cramps in his hands and wrist, he was able to finish the model in around six months. His daughter, Ridgely Clerk-Treasurer Stephanie Berkey, helped him complete the project.
"I've never built anything like it in my life," Anderson said. "We tried to make it as authentic as we possibly could."
On Nov. 4, Anderson's model station was presented to the Ridgely Town Commissioners and placed in the Ridgely Town Hall. It will eventually be taken to the Ridgely Train Station, Ridgely Historical Society President Cathy Schwab said.
"It was awesome. I was so happy and proud, mostly happy for him," Schwab said. As part of its mission, the historical society works to maintain and preserve the railroad station and its history.
Anderson, a longtime Eastern Shore resident who spent time in the Coast Guard, said building models has become a hobby for him in recent years. His next project will be constructing a model of the USS Enterprise that played a crucial role during World War II.
The train station took lots of patience and attention to detail, Anderson said, placing wood planks down one by one. Anderson said there are more than 1,000 wooden planks on the deck of the model station.
"Each one was done one at a time," Anderson said. "I like to make things right. … I don't rush. I do not rush."
The train station fit into the town's hope of becoming a booming city on the East Coast. But developers from the Maryland and Baltimore Land Association failed financially in the early 1900s, and the town never became the "dream city" many had envisioned.
It closed in 1976, but the building remained, housing businesses and the Ridgely Town Hall in the 1990s. Town historians view it as a centerpiece of the small town.
"It starts out and still is the heart of Ridgely," Schwab said. "If the train had not gone through the town and stated that we needed to have a station and a hotel, there would be no town."
Anderson called the station on West Railroad Avenue "a relic" and said he was happy to contribute to the town's preservation and recognition of the historic railroad. Schwab echoed the same.
"To preserve what we had is just a wonderful reminder of who we are," Schwab said.

title: Members’ Exhibition 2024 at Academy Art Museum
author: Staff Writer
content:
Members’ Exhibition 2024 at Academy Art Museum

 November 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 409
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Academy Art Museum in Easton has announced the winners of its annual Members' Exhibition.The exhibition is open now and runs through Dec. 29.
The museum's annual Members' Exhibition "invites artists to submit imaginative, traditional, and experimental works in any medium," according to an announcement. Many of the pieces in the exhibition are for sale and can be purchased.
This year's juror is Robyn Asleson, curator of prints and drawings at the Smithsonian Institution's National Portrait Gallery.
"Her exhibition projects at the Portrait Gallery include "Brilliant Exiles: American Women in Paris, 1900–1939" (2024), the team-curated "Kinship" (2022), and "Portraits of the World" (2016-20), a series of spotlight exhibitions featuring individual portraits on loan from international museums, placed in conversation with works from the Portrait Gallery collection. She was also venue curator for the exhibition "John Singer Sargent: Portraits in Charcoal" (2020)," According to AAM.
AAM is hosting the exhibition at the Waterfowl Building (40 S. Harrison Street)
in downtown Easton. Hours for the exhibition are Tuesday and Wednesday, 10 a.m. — 4 p.m., Thursday (Dec. 12 and 19) 10 a.m — 7 pm, Friday, 10 a.m. — 4 p.m., Saturday and Sunday, 12 p.m. — 4 p.m. Closed Mondays, and December 24 through 26.

title: Look backward, not forward
author: Staff Writer
content:
Look backward, not forward

 November 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 376
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I caught an article in a recent Star Democrat mentioning funds that were possibly going to be allocated for a new kids playground. (Full disclosure: Anything we can do to keep our young population pointed in the right direction I am all for.)But it got me thinking of how things have changed in the half century since I was one of those kids growing up in Easton.
For us, a playground was simply where we stopped and the action of the day began. A garden shed could become Command Central, our secret fort of the day. Almost any out-of-the-way spot could be commandeered as GI Joe's headquarters.
Talbot Town Hill was the go-to skateboard challenge – on homemade boards of course – and no helmets, naturally. Playing cards clothes pinned to our bikes sent a clackety warning to anyone who happened to see us – we meant business. No surprise, we built the bikes ourselves too.
Looking back, I give us credit for being resourceful. Hand lines, earthworms and Kool-Aid for fuel were the necessities for fishing trips to any bridge. (Aside: I remember checking the mailbox daily for three agonizing months waiting to get my free Kool-Aid pitcher).
We went through a Wild West stage, converting a couple of old wagons to "covered" wagons. Freedom had few boundaries. Our curfew was simply when it got dark or when we got hungry.
When I was 10, my family moved to Glebe Villa on Goldsborough Creek into an aptly named haunted house, and the good times went up a notch. The water became our streets and boats became our wheels. Waterskiing, the original boogie boards, bridge jumping and more fishing.
Mock orange fights with my new clan the "villa gorillas." Neighborhood football, many a campfire. Walking in the woods, my first pocketknife. Ahh, those were the days.
Friendships I have to this day were members of this then — "exclusive" club. Well I guess I am starting to look backward more than forward these days.
"You're turning into your dad," someone recently told me. What an honor, I said to myself. Thanks again, and lots of love to all of my friends and family.
P.S. Please reach out to this great community and lift someone's spirit, there are many ways, be yourself, it's free.
ROO WOOD
Easton

title: Country Cooking: Christmas cookie making fun
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Christmas cookie making fun

 December 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1335
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Stepping back in time reveals a lot of memories for me. Holiday baking was extra special, as my mother, my sister and I each liked to bake different desserts.Mom loved making pies, cakes, puddings and custards. My sister liked making candies of all kinds "and especially fudge."
I was the cookie maker. They would not have hit Betty Crocker's list, but my late brother-in-law, Sonny, loved them. He ate them perfectly baked, burned or mushy. He also said they were the best.
Brother Ollie said even the chickens wouldn't eat them when he threw them into the poultry yard.
I have improved through the years, and now each holiday I have a grandson, Colin, who joins me in the love of cookie baking. As a matter of fact, we do our first batch on Thanksgiving evening.
It is so much fun baking with the children, watching them be so excited to do this "on their own."
I am going to begin this cookie column today with my mom's favorite cookie.
GINGERSNAPS1 1/2 sticks unsalted butter, 1 1/4 cup granulated sugar, 1/4 cup lightly packed brown sugar, 1/3 cup molasses (not black), one egg, 1/2 tsp salt, 2 tsps baking soda, 1/2 tsp ground ginger, 1 tsp ground cinnamon, 1/4 tsp ground cloves, 2 1/4 cups all purpose flour.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Line baking sheets with parchment paper. In a large bowl using an electric mixer, beat butter, 3/4 cup granulated sugar, and brown sugar until light and fluffy, about two minutes. I use the paddles on the mixer for this. Add molasses and egg and beat again until well combined. Add in salt, baking soda, ginger, cinnamon, cloves and flour and beat until well combined. In a shallow dish add 1/2 cup granulated sugar. Scoop the dough into 1 1/2 tablespoons balls, roll into the sugar in the dish and place on the baking sheet, leaving plenty of room for cookies to spread. Bake for 15 minutes or until cookies have spread and the surface looks cracked. Let the cookies cool completely on the baking sheets before moving to wire racks. Store cookies in an airtight container. This recipe makes 28 cookies. I use Brer Rabbit or the Grandma's brand of molasses. Enjoy.
CHRISTMAS SWEET AND SALTY TOFFEE35 saltine crackers, 1 cup butter, 1 cup packed brown sugar, 1 3/4 cups semisweet chocolate chips, 1 bag red and green holiday M&Ms, 1 jar holiday sprinkles.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Line a baking sheet or jelly-roll pan with tin foil and coat with cooking spray. Line the baking sheet with Saltine crackers. Set aside. In a medium-sized saucepan, melt butter and brown sugar. Bring to a boil, stirring continuously, and let cook until bubbling, about 2 minutes. Pour mixture over crackers in an even layer and bake for 12 to 15 minutes. Top immediately with chocolate chips and let melt. Smooth chocolate out into an even layer, then top with red and green M&Ms and holiday sprinkles. Cut into squares, then cool until the chocolate has hardened.
CHOCOLATE CRINKLE COOKIES1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour, 3/4 cup unsweetened cocoa powder, 1 tsp kosher salt, 1 tsp baking powder, 3/4 tsp baking soda, 1/2 cup butter (melted), 3/4 cup granulated sugar, 1/2 cup packed brown sugar, 3 large eggs, powdered sugar for rolling.
In a large bowl, combine flour, cocoa powder, salt, baking powder and baking soda. In a medium bowl, whisk together melted butter, sugars and eggs until well combined. Pour into dry ingredients and mix until just combined. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and refrigerate for two hours. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees and line two large baking sheets with parchment. Place powdered sugar in a small bowl. Scoop about 2 tablespoons of dough and roll into a ball. If dough is too sticky, wet your hands slightly to help roll dough. Roll dough into powdered sugar, coating well and then place on a prepared baking sheet two inches apart. After rolling all the dough in powdered sugar, roll each piece again in powdered sugar. This will help get a more dramatic crinkle when the cookies bake. Bake cookies until cookies puff and crack, about 14 minutes. The edges will just be set, but the cracks will still look slightly underdone. Let cool on a baking sheet.
CANDY CANE SNOWBALLS2 cups butter (softened), 1 cup confectioners' sugar, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 3 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup chopped pecans, 8 ounces white candy coating (melted), 1/3 to 1/2 cup crushed peppermint candies.
Cream butter and confectioners' sugar until light and fluffy, 5-7 minutes. Beat in vanilla. Gradually beat in flour. Stir in pecans. Refrigerate, covered, until firm enough to shape, 3-4 hours. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Shape dough into one-inch balls. Place two inches apart on ungreased baking sheets. Bake until lightly browned, about 15 minutes. Remove from pans to wire racks; cool completely. Dip tops of cookies into candy coating, allowing excess to drip off; dip into crushed candies. Let stand until set.
OLD FASHIONED CHOCOLATE COOKIES1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 1/2 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt, 1/3 cup shortening, 1/3 cup butter (softened), 1/2 cup granulated sugar, 1/2 cup brown sugar, 1 egg (beaten), 1 tsp vanilla, 1 6-ounce package semi-sweet chocolate chips, 1/2 cup chopped nuts (optional).
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. In a medium bowl, sift together flour, salt and baking soda. Set aside, In a large bowl, cream together shortening, butter, sugars, egg and vanilla. Gradually combine half of the flour mixture into the wet mixture. Use a rubber spatula to incorporate the other half of the flour mixture if the dough gets too thick for the mixer. Stir in the chocolate chips. Roll the dough into tablespoon-sized balls. Place on a baking sheet lined with parchment paper, two inches apart. Bake for 7-10 minutes. Remove from the oven when cookies are slightly golden around the edges and soft on the tops. Leave cookies on the pan for 2-3 minutes to continue cooking outside of the oven. Let cool until firm to touch. Serve immediately or store leftovers in an air-tight container.
ITALIAN THUMBPRINT COOKIES2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup salted butter (firm but not cold), 2/3 cup granulated sugar, 1 1/2 tsp vanilla extract (could be substituted), 2 large eggs (yolks and whites divided), 1 cup unsalted pistachios (finely chopped), 1/2 cup strawberry preserves, 4 ounces white chocolate or semi-sweet chocolate (melted).
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In the bowl of an electric stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment and set on medium-high speed, whip together butter, granulated sugar and vanilla bean seeds until mixture is pale and fluffy, about 4 minutes. Blend in egg yolks (setting egg whites aside in a small bowl). With the mixer set on low speed, slowly pour in flour and mix until combined (mixture will seem dry at first but will start to come together). Form dough into a ball, cover with plastic wrap and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Whisk egg whites with 2 teaspoons water until frothy. Place chopped pistachios in a small bowl. Remove cookie dough from refrigerator and scoop dough up 1 tablespoon at a time and shape into balls. Drop each ball into egg white mixture and toss to evenly coat, then immediately transfer to bowl with chopped pistachios and roll to evenly coat sides and bottom with pistachios (I just left a circle on top uncoated for indenting). Transfer cookie dough balls to Silpat or parchment paper lined baking sheets (fitting 15 per sheet). Using your thumb, make an indentation in the center of each cookie and fill each indentation with a heaping 1/2 tsp of jam. Bake in a preheated oven 14-16 minutes. Allow to rest on a baking dish several minutes before transferring to a wire rack to cool. Cool cookies then fill a piping bag or small Ziploc bag with melted chocolate and cut a small tip off the corner and drizzle with melted chocolate. Store cookies in an airtight container.
See you next week for more Christmas recipes.

title: Festival of Trees brings holiday cheer, hope to Talbot County
author: KENIA ITZEP Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Festival of Trees brings holiday cheer, hope to Talbot County

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KENIA ITZEP Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 370
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Tidewater Inn's Gold Ballroom was once again transformed into a warm winter wonderland for the 39th annual Festival of Trees. Over 100 beautifully adorned trees, small and large, captured the spirit of the season while supporting a cause close to the community's heart — raising funds for Talbot Hospice."The festival has grown exponentially over the years," said Karla Wieland-Cherry, chairman of the Festival of Trees. Since its inception in 1986, the event has raised over $4.7 million, providing critical funding for Talbot Hospice's operating budget.
This year's festival featured 50 beautifully decorated trees sponsored by individuals and businesses, as well as 50 smaller trees, ranging in size from 12 to 36 inches, available for purchase. Each display reflects the creativity and care of the decorators, many of whom return year after year.
One such decorator, Andrea Tull Wilson, has been contributing her talents for 15 years and now includes her two sons in the tradition. This year, their tree's theme is "A Cup of Cocoa," capturing the warmth and comfort of the season.
The festivities began with a formal gala on Friday night, setting a celebratory tone for the weekend. On Saturday morning, attendees participated in a pet-friendly 5K Fun Run/Walk, while that evening brought the magical "Candles by the Candlelight" event. Spectators joined in singing carols by candlelight, sipping hot cocoa and enjoying seasonal treats.
The highlight of the event remains the Festival of Trees itself, with this year's theme, "Holiday Traditions," inspiring creativity and community spirit. Volunteers worked tirelessly to craft each tree's unique display, making the ballroom a true holiday showcase.
Throughout the festival, visitors enjoyed holiday-themed performances by local musicians and artists, while festive gifts were available for purchase. Families made cherished memories in the Garden Room, where children decorated ornaments and shared their Christmas wishes with Santa Claus.
Since its founding, Friends of Hospice has worked tirelessly year-round to support hospice patients and their families through the Festival of Trees, ensuring that the hospice "does not turn anyone away," regardless of their insurance or ability to pay, as Wieland-Cherry emphasized.
Proceeds from the event directly support hospice services, providing compassionate care for those facing life-limiting illnesses.
To learn more about the Festival of Trees and Talbot Hospice, visit festival-of-trees.org.

title: Explore Maryland: A Tuba Christmas returns
author: Staff Writer
content:
Explore Maryland: A Tuba Christmas returns

 December 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 527
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In what has become a growing tradition both locally and nationally, the Solomons will host the annual Tuba Christmas Saturday, Dec. 14, where onlookers will be treated to a free concert that features a set list of nearly a dozen Christmas favorites performed by tuba and euphonium players of all ages.Among the primary local events planned Dec. 14 at the Our Lady Star of the Sea in Solomons is a rehearsal slated from 11 a.m. to noon followed by an hour-long concert set to commence at 1 pm. In all, roughly a dozen songs will be performed by musicians whose expertise is either the tuba or euphonium and the event is free for audience members of all ages.
According to the set list provided by organizers of the Tuba Christmas, "Adeste Fidelis" will open the proceedings and then will be followed by "Deck The Halls," "God Rest Ye Merry Gentlemen," "The First Noel," "It Came Upon A Midnight Clear," "O Little Town of Bethlehem" and about a dozen other songs before the musicians can take a graceful bow for the audience.
Conceived exactly 50 years ago in 1974 by Harvey Phillips as a tribute to his teacher and mentor, William J. Bell, who was born on Christmas Day in 1902, the inaugural Tuba Christmas was conducted by Paul Lavalle in the heart of New York City on the famed Rockefeller Center Ice Rink on Dec. 22 half a century ago. Bell is considered a legend in the musical field and this even annually honors his legacy and numerous great artists, according to information provided by Tuba Christmas organizers.
Coincidentally, the first Tuba Christmas featured music arranged by American composer Alec Wilder, who passed away almost exactly six years later on Christmas Eve in 1980. Bell's legacy was honed by years of professional integrity, personal values and a camaraderie envied by thousands of other instrumentalists, regardless of their chosen instrument preference.
Like Bell, Wilder has a reputation that has long outlived him. Although he passed away nearly 45 years ago and one day before his music celebration reached an annual zenith, Wilder is still remembered for his work composing many solo and ensemble compositions for tuba and euphonium. He was also a loyal supporter of every effort to improve the literature and public image of various brass instruments.
Part of the celebration of the 51st Tuba Christmas celebrates Wilder's memory and genius and offers performers in this concert in particular to express their respect and gratitude to all composers who continue to embrace the inherent value of brass instruments through their compositions and allows them the chance to contribute to the solo and ensemble repertoire for tuba and euphonium.
If you go
Tuba Christmas in Solomons will take place Saturday, Dec. 14, beginning at 1 p.m. at the Our Lady Star Of The Sea, located at 225 Alexander Lane. Tuba and euphonium players of all ages are invited to attend, with the registration for players slated for 10:30 a.m. and a fee of $10 is required.
The hour-long concert, which features a set list of nearly a dozen Christmas favorites, is free to audience members. For more information, contact Brian Brown at 443-404-1098 or brownbl@comcast.net.

title: Rescue Fire Company Train Garden celebrates 90 years
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Rescue Fire Company Train Garden celebrates 90 years

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 309
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE —Rescue Fire Company Train Garden Chairman Gary Hickman's father was visiting the train garden on Gay Street the day of the Pearl Harbor attack in 1941."He was just here that day as a child," Hickman said.
Eighty-three years later, the RFC Train Garden — the longest continually running train garden in the country — is celebrating its 90th anniversary.
Hickman said this milestone is so important because "the gentlemen back in 1934 had the forethought to be able to put this together for the community and the children of the community."
Hickman remembers coming to the train garden as a kid. He said he loved trains as a child.
"I used to come here as many times as I could during the Christmas season when it was open," he said.
That love never drifted for Hickman, who plans to continue on with his role as chairman for as long as he can.
On a Monday evening, families slowly made their way in and out of the old City Hall on Gay Street, where the train garden is located. Quaid Windsor, 4, walked around the train garden with his parents as he snacked on popcorn. He said he liked the trains the most.
Hickman said support from the local business community makes it possible for the train garden to keep chugging along.
"When I was growing up as a kid, it was a hobby, and it was an affordable hobby," Hickman said. "And now things are so expensive. ... And all of these sponsors re-sponsor us every year and they give us money so we can continually change and add things and buy new engines and upgrade things as we go along."
Hickman said that with continued volunteer support from the fire company, he sees the train garden making it to the 100-year mark in another decade.
"As long as I'm around, we're going to continue," he said.

title: Celebrate Kwanzaa at the Anacostia Community Museum
author: Staff Writer
content:
Celebrate Kwanzaa at the Anacostia Community Museum

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 535
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Smithsonian's Anacostia Community Museum is celebrating the seven days of Kwanzaa with performances, storytelling, and craft and dance workshops. The museum has welcomed the local community to celebrate Kwanzaa for over 50 years, and it will debut archival images of past celebrations with a nightly display on the museum's façade from Dec. 19 to Jan. 2, 2025."The Smithsonian's Anacostia Community Museum has been celebrating Kwanzaa since the early 1970s," Melanie Adams, director of the museum, said. "Museums are spaces for personal reflection and shared connections, and we encourage the community to join us throughout each of the seven days, as we gather family, friends and neighbors to learn, reflect and share."
Activities connect to the theme of each day: Umoja (Unity), Kujichagulia (Self-Determination), Ujima (Collective Work and Responsibility), Ujamaa (Cooperative Economics), Nia (Purpose), Kuumba (Creativity) and Imani (Faith). Visitors of all ages can take part in the free festivities. Each event takes place from noon to 2 p.m. A full schedule is below:
Thursday, Dec. 26 — Kwanzaa Opening Ceremony, Umoja (Unity)
The weeklong celebration kicks off with this afternoon gathering, uniting families and communities. Storyteller and griot Mama Ayo leads the traditional candle-lighting ceremony, pours the libation honoring ancestors and shares the history of Kwanzaa. Taratibu Youth Association, a performing arts group for the youth of the African diaspora, will follow. Registration is requested.
Friday, Dec. 27 — Family Workshop, Kujichagulia (Self-Determination)
A family workshop led by Jessica "Culture Queen" Hebron, a Grammy-nominated teaching artist and children's musician, will encourage self-determination through affirmations, song, dance and hands-on activities. Registration is requested.
Saturday, Dec. 28 — Verbal Gymnastics Workshop, Ujima (Collective Work and Responsibility)
This live interactive storytelling workshop will honor those have inspired visitors' lives, prompting visitors to share stories of their personal heroes. The theater company Verbal Gymnastics will then play back these stories with actors and musicians. Registration is requested.
Sunday, Dec. 29 — Memory Box Craft Workshop, Ujamaa (Cooperative Economics)
Families will decorate and fill their own memory box in this arts and crafts workshop led by artist Tamara Thomas. Participants are encouraged to bring their own photos and trinkets. Thomas will also lead an Ujamaa vision project, discussing what is needed in local communities and the benefits of having a family or community business. Registration is recommended, but not required.
Monday, Dec. 30 — African Dance Workshop, Nia (Purpose)
African cultures imbue every dance with purpose, from rites of passage to communing with the spiritual world. Khepera Wellness, a community-oriented yoga studio, will celebrate Nia through this African Dance Workshop, guiding participants through intentional movements. Registration is recommended but not required.
Tuesday, Dec. 31 — Family Kwanzaa Bag Workshop, Kuumba (Creativity)
Local artist Rain will lead families in this arts and crafts workshop creating and decorating family Kwanzaa bags. The bags can be used in many ways, including carrying handmade Kwanzaa gifts or the fruits of the harvest. Registration recommended but not required.
Wednesday, Jan. 1, 2025 — Spiritual Dance Workshop, Imani (Faith)
A performance and workshop on miming and liturgical dance guided by Crazee Praize starts the new year. Landle and Antoinette Jones will then lead a discussion on what gifts and talents keep participants hopeful despite life's challenges. Registration recommended but not required.
For more information about the Anacostia museum, visit www.si.edu/newsdesk/anacostia-community-museum.

title: 'So many sources of inspiration if we just look”:New art gallery celebrates inspiration
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
'So many sources of inspiration if we just look”:New art gallery celebrates inspiration

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Showcasing a world of inspiration around us, Stevensville's newest gallery and art studio Abstract Truth held an official gallery opening Nov. 29.A retired architect, gallery artist Ray Moldenhauer, of Grasonville, focuses his attention on creating abstract paintings and sculptures with dimension, noting "art is a natural extension of architecture."
Outgrowing his previous space at My Little Studio, Moldenhauer remarked the new location is proving to be a blessing.
Leaning into layers in his art as well as in his gallery, Moldenhauer designed the space to take full advantage of the existing glass enclosed cubicles and provide natural light.
By staggering the paintings from one cubicle to another, the gallery visually takes on a special 3D experience from one space to another. Many of the paintings are mounted back to back on the glass to create an allusion of them floating in the space, according to Moldenhauer.
"At night, the extensive front glass wall of the building just glows and reflects the beautiful artwork within," he said.
"I love the idea of flowing paintings," he said.
Moldenhauer utilizes many different creative techniques for his work. From traditional brushes and sponges, to business cards to even finger painting, Moldenhauer isn't afraid to try something new with his inspiration. Moldenhauer also incorporates resin, cellophane, and even foam to create something completely new.
For Moldenhauer it is the inspiration behind each artwork that brings forth its beauty and meaning and makes it "more than just another landscape or sunset."
Moldenhauer's work typically starts with a Bible verse and lets his inspiration guide his hand, for instance, Moldenhauer sculptures based on the Pillars of Creation present an abstract look of the universe.
As an accomplished SCUBA diver, Moldenhauer also finds inspiration in the natural world of water, sunsets and sunrises.
Moldenhauer also takes inspiration from the surrounding Eastern Shore, has also incorporated his love of the Eastern Shore into his work.
His very first sculpture "Be Still" repurposed an old sailboat skeg and was selected for the Maryland Federation of Art's Off The Walls 2024 exhibition.
According to Moldenhauer Abstract Truths are works that, "in some way, reveal God," and each art piece has a corresponding Bible verse accompaniment for patrons to take to heart.
For artists just starting out, Moldenhauer encouraged finding inspiration around you in what you enjoy doing and where you enjoy being.
"There are so many sources of inspiration if we just look," he said.
Moldenhauer welcomes everyone to discover the work for themselves, noting the studio gallery isn't for the purpose of business or making money, "it's about sharing art," he said.
Moving forward, Moldenhauer looks to collaborate and connect with the surrounding art community and plans to eventually have rotating monthly artists featured and juried art exhibits.
Abstract Truths is located in the Stevensville Art and Entertainment District at 214 Island Plaza Court. and typically open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m.
Special showings are available by appointment at 410-490-6302.
Moldenhauer is an award winning abstract artist and Maryland Federation of Art juried exhibitor. He is also a Christian author and music writer with a Youtube channel and Instagram account.

title: Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfits continues next 2 Saturdays in Denton
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfits continues next 2 Saturdays in Denton

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 437
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Children gathered at the Wharves of Choptank Visitor & Heritage Center on Saturday for an afternoon full of crafts, wooden toys, painting and more as the holidays quickly approach.In an event put on by the Caroline County Council of Arts and The Foundry, its art gallery, children were welcomed to build their own toys, greet Santa and meet the Grinch. Two more Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfits Saturdays are scheduled: Dec. 14 and Dec. 21 from noon to 4 p.m.
Caroline County Council of Arts Executive Director George Karos said the event is a "fun way to celebrate the holidays."
"Everyone can make art and spend time with loved ones — especially a win-win as proceeds go towards supporting local youth programs and spreading holiday cheer," Karos said in an emailed statement.
Megan Krizovensky, program manager for Caroline County Council of Arts, said in an interview that last weekend's event was a success. It's the first time the art organization put on Santa's Workshop.
"It was pretty good," Krizovenksy said of Saturday's turnout. "I know the first week we expected to be a little slower. But we actually had at least 50 children there, and we were prepared for over 100. So we're hoping that (Dec. 14 and Dec. 21) can pick it up much bigger just for the kid's sake."
Last Saturday, the Chesapeake Culinary Center participated in the event and donated cookies and cocoa. Krizovenksy said Earth Tones Cafe will be donating food for this Saturday.
Additionally, students from Caroline County Public Schools are volunteering, gaining student service learning hours. The first-time event runs fully on donations, Krizovenksy added.
"The event is completely donation-based with all proceeds going to support local youth programs through the Caroline County Council of Arts," she said.
Krizovensky said local artist Steve Mead, formerly the board treasurer for the arts council, was integral in the event's formulation.
The hope is that Santa's Workshop can continue in the future, with some of this year's proceeds working to fund a second annual Santa's Workshop. Registration is free with a suggested donation of $15 per child.
"The goal is to create a magical experience for kids who otherwise might not have a great holiday," Krizovenksy said. "We want to make sure that it's free. Our mission is to enrich the community through the arts, and Caroline County itself is a unique place anyway with a lot of deep-rooted tradition. So we're trying to create authentic experiences that reflect and celebrate the spirit of that community."
To register for Dec. 14 or Dec. 21, sign up at carolinearts.org/events/santas-workshop-in-the-island-of-misfit-toys/ or visit The Foundry Art Gallery at 401 Market St. in Denton.

 December 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Christmas 
 
 412
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Dozens of gingerbread designers are competing for one of several cash prizes and for the admiration of the community this weekend.The St. Michaels' gingerbread competition is back in full swing after a nearly five-year hiatus. An array of intricately built gingerbread houses will be on show this weekend at the St. Micheals Woman's Club for the Gingerbread "House" Competition and Display.
Proceeds from the sale of these creations support the beneficiaries of Christmas in St. Michaels, including family service organizations, education and child development programs, and community enhancement organizations and programs.
Michele Lowe and Andrea Robinson, co-chairs of the Gingerbread Committee, both said they were fairly new to the area and heard of a St. Michaels gingerbread competition but had never witnessed it themselves.
Lowe said the memory of the competition was incredibly strong among the community and Lowe and Robinson felt a need to step up and bring back the beloved tradition.
"Everybody has been wanting this back since (2019)," Lowe said. "I guess we finally got coerced, and it's been a great success. We had a lot of the donations from the St Michael's Community Center, Critchlow Adkins (Children's Centers), who are also both beneficiaries."
Lowe mentioned that a young girl in the area, who last competed in 2019, had been eagerly awaiting and planning new designs for when the competition came back.
The gingerbread entries are divided into seven categories with cash prize awards. The categories cater to different skill levels and ages, including Master with a $500 prize and Adult with $300 first prize.
Additionally, there are categories for younger participants including young adults with a $100 prize, and children with and without an adult with a $100 prize for the respective categories.
Finally, there are categories for nonprofit organizations, Candy Backus Award (best depiction of the Eastern Shore) and a People's Choice Award.
Judges for the gingerbread competition include Commissioners of St. Michaels President Alfred Mercier, President and CEO of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum Kristen Greenaway and St. Michaels Police Chief Jeffrey Oswald.
Prizes will be awarded on Sunday at the Woman's Club of St. Michaels at 2 p.m.
Robinson said she is happy with the support they have received this year and encourages people to continue their support into the new year.
"Thank you for your support, and please make gingerbread at home next year," Robinson said. "In order for us to keep doing this we need everybody to be excited next year and participate and start planning their creation for next year."

title: Abstract Truths studio art gallery opens in Stevensville
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Abstract Truths studio art gallery opens in Stevensville

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 509
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Showcasing a world of inspiration around us, Stevensville's newest gallery and art studio Abstract Truth held an official gallery opening Nov. 29.A retired architect, gallery artist Ray Moldenhauer, of Grasonville, focuses his attention on creating abstract paintings and sculptures with dimension, noting "art is a natural extension of architecture."
Outgrowing his previous space at My Little Studio, Moldenhauer remarked the new location is proving to be a blessing.
Leaning into layers in his art as well as in his gallery, Moldenhauer designed the space to take full advantage of the existing glass enclosed cubicles and provide natural light.
By staggering the paintings from one cubicle to another, the gallery visually takes on a special 3D experience from one space to another. Many of the paintings are mounted back to back on the glass to create an allusion of them floating in the space, according to Moldenhauer.
"At night, the extensive front glass wall of the building just glows and reflects the beautiful artwork within," he said.
"I love the idea of flowing paintings," he said.
Moldenhauer utilizes many different creative techniques for his work. From traditional brushes and sponges, to business cards to even finger painting, Moldenhauer isn't afraid to try something new with his inspiration. Moldenhauer also incorporates resin, cellophane, and even foam to create something completely new.
For Moldenhauer it is the inspiration behind each artwork that brings forth its beauty and meaning and makes it "more than just another landscape or sunset."
Moldenhauer's work typically starts with a Bible verse and lets his inspiration guide his hand, for instance, Moldenhauer sculptures based on the Pillars of Creation present an abstract look of the universe.
As an accomplished SCUBA diver, Moldenhauer also finds inspiration in the natural world of water, sunsets and sunrises.
Moldenhauer also takes inspiration from the surrounding Eastern Shore, has also incorporated his love of the Eastern Shore into his work.
His very first sculpture "Be Still" repurposed an old sailboat skeg and was selected for the Maryland Federation of Art's Off The Walls 2024 exhibition.
According to Moldenhauer Abstract Truths are works that, "in some way, reveal God," and each art piece has a corresponding Bible verse accompaniment for patrons to take to heart.
For artists just starting out, Moldenhauer encouraged finding inspiration around you in what you enjoy doing and where you enjoy being.
"There are so many sources of inspiration if we just look," he said.
Moldenhauer welcomes everyone to discover the work for themselves, noting the studio gallery isn't for the purpose of business or making money, "it's about sharing art," he said.
Moving forward, Moldenhauer looks to collaborate and connect with the surrounding art community and plans to eventually have rotating monthly artists featured and juried art exhibits.
Abstract Truths is located in the Stevensville Art and Entertainment District at 214 Island Plaza Court. and typically open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m.
Special showings are available by appointment at 410-490-6302.
Moldenhauer is an award winning abstract artist and Maryland Federation of Art juried exhibitor. He is also a Christian author and music writer with a Youtube channel and Instagram account.

title: Garden Club 'decks the halls' in Centreville
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Garden Club 'decks the halls' in Centreville

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 430
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The festive scents of seasonal pine and holly filled American Legion Jeff Davis Post 18 as the Queen Anne's County Garden Club Members prepared the town with festive cheer Dec. 5.The long-standing annual decorating is traditionally the Thursday before the Centreville Christmas parade, according to club president Laura Blaylock.
"This is the highlight of the year," she said, and is a favorite among all members who, with a potluck breakfast and lunch, and many of whom in yuletide sweaters, spend all day together preparing.
Throughout the hall, stations were set up for wreaths, swag, garland, bows and putting the final touches on holiday magic to decorate Centreville in a glow of greenery.
Members designed over 100 floral arrangements to be hand delivered to hospice care and home bodies in need of Christmas cheer.
"It is our way of getting in the Christmas spirit and getting others in the Christmas spirit as well, " Blaylock said.
Member Jane Chambers, of Kent Island, has been a garden club member for about 50 years and said her favorite part is seeing the finished product displayed throughout the season "and it's a fun group that does good for the community," she said.
With help from local department staff, wreaths, garland, and long lines of blooming swag adorned historic aspects all through town, including the Queen Anne's County Library, Shore United Bank, the Tucker House, the Historic Courthouse, and Chesterfield Cemetery.
From wreath decoration design to floral arraignments, "It never ceases to amaze me the amount of creativity from everyone," Club Vice President Robin Lanham said.
On Arbor Day, the club celebrated its 90th anniversary with a tree planting honoring first responders at the Fallen Heroes Memorial at Route 18 Park in Centreville.
The club recently decorated crab pots to create a crab tree unique to Queen Anne's County and pay tribute to the watermen and preside over the Annapolis state house.
"It made quite a splash, people loved it," club treasurer Paula Kumar.
The object of the garden club is to stimulate the love of gardening, to aid in the protection of native plants and birds, to encourage civic planting and beautification, and to teach children to love and care for all growing things, according to Blaylock
Covering a wide spectrum of horticulture topics including guest speakers and field trips, the club is always seeking new members and anyone interested in not just gardening but local pollinators, native plants, floral design or seeking to enhance their green thumb.
Queen Anne's County Garden Club is part of the Federated Garden Clubs of Maryland Inc. District 1.
More information can be found by contacting Blaylock at laura.blaylock804@gmail.com.
