title: Country Cooking: treats to keep kids occupied
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: treats to keep kids occupied

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1240
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I am sure your major shopping is completed, menus planned, gifts wrapped and that final grocery list waiting to be completed.However, the children are out of school and the excitement is mounting. I have a few suggestions to help keep them busy.
Before that I have a recipe from the past I want to include. My mother loved making pies, and one of her favorites for the Christmas holidays was always mincemeat pie.
HOMEMADE MINCEMEAT PIEPie crust, 4 cups peeled chopped apples, 1 1/2 cups diced cooked beef, 1 1/2 cups raisins, 1 1/2 cups white sugar, 1 cup beef broth, 1 large orange (peeled, sectioned, seeds removed and cut into small bite size pieces), 1/2 cup molasses, 1/4 cup sweet pickle juice, 1/2 cup pineapple juice, 1 tsp ground cinnamon, 1 tsp ground nutmeg, 1/2 tsp ground cloves and 1/2 tsp salt.
This recipe will make two 9-inch pies. Prepare enough crust for bottom and a top crust for two 9-inch pie plates and sit aside. If you only want to make one, just store the extra mincemeat filling in the refrigerator for later use. In a large bowl combine apples, beef, raisins, sugar, beef broth, orange, molasses, pickle juice, pineapple juice, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves and salt. Mix well and let sit in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes before placing in pie shells. Preheat the oven at 375 degrees. Place pie shells full, place top crust on, cutting slits in crust. Bake for at least 30 mins. Serve warm. I must tell you that this recipe is somewhat modern, as the recipe from the '40s and '50s used hog meat and whiskey for flavor.
I must tell this story that we siblings still laugh about. When mom made her mincemeat, she would have our farm worker go to the liquor store and get her a half pint of whiskey, and she hid it until ready to use. That day when he gave Mom the whiskey, she placed it in the oven in a small pot. Forgetting this, the next morning she preheats the oven and before she can put the pan of biscuits in, the bottle of whiskey explodes. The stove had to be completely taken apart and the whiskey smell lingered for days. Mom was teased for many years about this.
I have some fun making yummy treats for the kids to help you make. Before we start that portion of the column let me suggest some fun projects for the kids to help past the time.
Purchase a packet of the white paper placemats (no design) and plenty of crayons. Have the kids design placemats for the dinner table, making plenty to use throughout the holiday. Make a contest, and upon completion each child gets a candy cane with everyone being the winner.Take some old Christmas cards/paper from last year, cut and paste the designs on large file cards, write a message and drop them off to shut-ins and nursing homes. Or do a special batch for those serving our country, the first responders in your area and anyone working this holiday.
CHRISTMAS CHEX MIX6 cups cereal, 3 cups of Rice Chex and 3 cups Corn Chex cereal (Store brand works just as well); 2 cups miniature marshmallows; 1 cup mini pretzel twists; 15 oz vanilla candy coating (about 9 cubes from 20-oz package); 3 tbsps holiday-colored sprinkles or nonpareils; 1/4 cup powdered sugar; 1 cup holiday-colored M&M'S.
Line a large rimmed cookie sheet with waxed paper. In a large bowl, mix cereal, marshmallows and pretzels. In a medium microwavable bowl, microwave candy coating uncovered on High 60 to 90 seconds, stirring after 1 minute, until almost melted. Stir until smooth. Pour onto cereal mixture; mix well. Spread on cookie sheet; sprinkle with holiday sprinkles, and cool completely, about 15 minutes. Break into bite-size pieces. In 2-gallon resealable food-storage plastic bag, add coated cereal pieces and powdered sugar. Seal bag; shake to coat. Remove from bag; discard any remaining powdered sugar. In large serving bowl, mix coated cereal mixture and M&M'S.
CRACKER SNACK-WHICHES48 round buttery crackers (such as Ritz), 8 Swiss cheese slices (cut into 1-inch squares, divided), 8 Black Forest deli ham slices (each cut into three equal strips about 1 1/2-in. wide), 1/4 cup red pepper jelly (such as Braswell's), 2 tbsps unsalted butter (melted), 1 tsp Dijon mustard, 1 tsp Worcestershire sauce, 1/2 tsp everything bagel seasoning, 1/4 tsp garlic powder, 6 cornichons (halved lengthwise and crosswise optional).
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Arrange 24 of the crackers, top sides down, on a large parchment paper-lined rimmed baking sheet; top each cracker with 1 piece of cheese and 1 strip of ham, folding ham strip into thirds and lightly pressing down. Layer each ham strip with 1/2 teaspoon pepper jelly and another piece of cheese. Top with remaining 24 crackers, top sides up, to form a sandwich. Stir together melted butter, Dijon mustard, Worcestershire sauce, everything bagel seasoning, and garlic powder until combined. Brush butter mixture evenly on top of cracker sandwiches. Bake in a preheated oven until the cheese has melted and the tops are golden brown, 10 to 12 minutes. Garnish each cracker sandwich with a piece of cornichon threaded onto a wooden pick, if desired. Serve immediately.
PIGS IN A BLANKET12 beef hot dogs, 1 large egg, 1 tbsp water, 1 (17.3-oz.) pkg frozen puff pastry sheets (thawed but cold), All-purpose flour, 2 tbsps Dijon mustard (plus more for serving), 1 tbsp everything-bagel seasoning.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper. Pat hot dogs dry using paper towels, and pierce each hot dog three times using a fork. Whisk together egg and water in a small bowl. Set aside. Roll out one puff pastry sheet on a lightly floured work surface into a 12-inch square. Cut pastry in half lengthwise; cut each half crosswise into three equal pieces. Repeat the procedure with the second puff pastry sheet. (You will have a total of 12 pieces.) Brush mustard crosswise down the center of each pastry piece; top each with one hot dog. Brush edges of pastry with egg mixture; roll up, and seal overlapping edges. Place seam side down on prepared baking sheets. Freeze until firm, about 30 minutes. Cut each log crosswise into four equal pieces, trimming ends as needed. Brush tops with remaining egg mixture, and sprinkle evenly with seasoning. Bake in a preheated oven, one baking sheet at a time, until golden brown, 20 to 25 minutes. (Keep the second baking sheet chilled until ready to bake.) Serve warm with additional mustard.
CHRISTMAS COAL1 (13 oz.) package oreos, 5 cups marshmallows, 4 tbsps (1/4 cup) unsalted butter.
Line a square baking dish with parchment paper and grease generously with non-stick spray. Also spray rubber spatula with non-stick spray. Place Oreo cookies in the food processor and pulse until finely ground. Place butter and marshmallows in a large, microwave-safe bowl and microwave for 1.5 minutes, stirring every 30 seconds with rubber spatula, until mixture is melted and smooth. Pour Oreo crumbs into marshmallow mixture and stir until everything is evenly incorporated, then press mixture (leaving the top uneven and shaggy) into a greased and lined baking dish. Let the mixture cool and set completely, then break into pieces and place in stockings or paper bag for "serving."
Note: pick up plenty of breakfast foods for next week's annual Christmas breakfast column and a bag of those black eyed peas for my annual New Year column.

title: Cambridge puts on first annual Mistletoe on Main event
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Cambridge puts on first annual Mistletoe on Main event

 December 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 339
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Main Street held its first ever Mistletoe on Main event Saturday, bringing families and friends to downtown for a festive time.The event included around 12 vendors spread across Poplar Street, pet photos with Santa, a breakfast with Santa, letters to Santa for children and a caricature artist.
There were also special Christmas cocktails offered at various downtown restaurants and bars near Poplar Street, which was shut down for the daylong event,
Christina Wingate-Spence, Cambridge Main Street's new executive director as of July, said she hopes Mistletoe on Main becomes an annual event that city residents grow accustomed to.
"Just to provide something for the families to be able to do (during) the holiday season," Wingate-Spence said. "I always say that Cambridge is beautiful any time of year, but during the holidays, there's just something special about it."
Many attendees brought their dogs for pictures with Mr. and Mrs. Claus. The photos raised proceeds for Baywater Animal Rescue and Dorchester County Dog Control, said Wingate-Spence.
Cambridge resident Scott Tull and his 3-year-old son, Jaxon, walked Poplar Street Saturday afternoon, with Jaxon enjoying the kids station and putting on a temporary crab tattoo.
Gary Schuler and his wife, Karen, braved the cold weather as one of the event's vendors. Gary, a machinist by trade, talked to customers interested in his pop-up tent decked out with his homemade metal art.
Karen Schuler said the metal crab ornaments — which run as large as four feet by four feet — are especially popular in Cambridge. She also paints keychains and other items for sale.
Other vendors sold homemade crafts, desserts and sweet treats, and jewelry.
Wingate-Spence said Mistletoe on Main was designed to support local businesses and give local residents another holiday event to enjoy. She sees opportunity to expand it next year and for years to come.
"More vendors," Wingate-Spence said of what may be added in 2025. "Certainly, we can expand upon breakfast with Santa. But I think just continuing to perhaps grow the vendors, grow the street activity, and just (get) more people to come out."

title: Star shines bright over Still Pond nativity scene
author: Staff Writer
content:
Star shines bright over Still Pond nativity scene

 December 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 363
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STILL POND — Just off Route 292, on a chilly Friday night, the star that church lay minister Justin Bitter created using welded scrap metal and an LED rope light, burned brightly in the trees. The Christmas hymns that were sung resonated with the 85 in attendance for the nativity scene beside the road.At the creche, maintained year-round by hardworking volunteers, local children dressed in robes and sandals. Telling the story of Jesus, Joseph, Mary, the wisemen, shepherds and animals, was Eddie Taylor, board member of Still Pond-Betterton Methodist Charge.
The reading of the gospel story followed by classic hymns with audience participation is a beloved tradition, now in the 10th year.
As night fell, seated atop bales of straw, attendees endured the cold sipping hot cocoa, enjoying Christmas cookies, and singing along as Taylor narrated the gospel scenes.
The story was told with Taylor's wit and affection, followed up by a hymn introducing the kid actors and actresses.
As Taylor read, "He is Christ the Lord. And, this is how you will know who he is….you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger," congregants sang the first verse of "Angels We Have Heard on High"; the angels of Still Pond were introduced, making their way to the manger.
During the production, Noel the donkey, Rosie and Annie the sheep, and Cookie Dough and Lollipop the goats were provided by Party Animals LLC., from Sudlersville, a company the church has relied on regularly during this event.
Owner of the company, Ashley Winterstein regretted she could not personally be there this year as this is her favorite holiday event. She was on a float with their 4-H club at Sudlersville's first annual Christmas Parade and Tree Lighting.
"Taylor is my favorite narrator," Winterstein added.
Pastor Greg Boege, replacing the late and greatly missed Pastor Bill Carroll, was pleased with how the event came together.
"Everybody did their part and we pulled it off," he said.
Boege said for those interested in a similar service, without the animals, in a more meditative, reflective atmosphere, they will hold their Christmas Eve service in Betterton at 5:30 p.m. followed by a service at the Still Pond location at 6:30 p.m.

title: Archaeologists work with Indigenous Peoples, DNR
author: A.J. Metcalf Maryland Department of Natural Resources
content:
Archaeologists work with Indigenous Peoples, DNR

 December 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: A.J. Metcalf Maryland Department of Natural Resources | Section: State News 
 
 880
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Indigenous sites in Maryland have been dated as early as 12,000 years ago by archaeologists. Many Indigenous people lived along the then Susquehanna River, using the resources provided by the land.As the Susquehanna's channel widened and the Chesapeake Bay began to form about 10,000 years ago, a majority of these settlements were inundated by water. The people who lived there moved, often following food resources such as oysters and fish.
"The Chesapeake Bay has long been a vital resource for people including Native Americans, especially as the Bay began to form," said Julia A. King, professor of Anthropology at St. Mary's College of Maryland. "It provides all sorts of seafood. The rising waters created marshlands that sort of acted as a refrigerator by providing animals and plant species that people could use. A lot of native settlements were located near riverine environments and marsh."
Thanks to state and federal grants, a growing relationship with today's Piscataway descendants, and a strong partnership with Maryland's Department of Natural Resources, King has been working with her students and colleague Travis Hanson, an archaeologist, to uncover the history of Indigenous peoples in Southern Maryland.
On a cloudy fall day earlier this year, Hanson joined park rangers and others at Chapel Point State Park to detail their ongoing work in the park as part of the Department of Natural Resources' annual Science Week. In pre-colonial times this area was home to the Potobacs, who were part of the Piscataway Chiefdom, which had emerged on the shores of the Potomac River around 1200 AD.
Hanson guided the small group through a narrow trail at Chapel Point State Park to an area next to a natural spring where paw paw trees were growing. The area was chosen for exploration due to the concentrations of oyster shell middens–basically dumping areas for discarded oyster shells, which indicate people had been gathering nearby and eating oysters. In 2023, Hanson, King and others dug several small test pits to search for artifacts and any structural remains.
Evidence indicates there was an extensive Indigenous settlement in the area that likely stretched to the other side of the Potomac.
"We found lots of projectile points, ceramics, and stone tools," said King. "We only scratched the surface and found hundreds of artifacts."
Through her work, King has developed a collaborative relationship with contemporary Piscataway descendants including Francis Gray, the tribal chairman of today's Piscataway Conoy Tribe, one of three state-recognized tribes in Maryland. Gray joined the group that had gathered at Chapel Point.
"We've come to understand that by having conversations with archaeologists and researchers we can help each other out," Gray said. He noted that through their collaborative work they've been able to confirm Native American community locations and find ways to protect those sites.
"It's important for researchers and others to understand that they're finding artifacts that belonged to a people who still exist," Gray said. "This whole river here was not one small concentrated community. Like the Nanticoke, Choptank, and Wicomico, these were all metropolises before colonization, people lived on both sides of the Potomac River."
King hopes that through further research the team can discover the location of the Jesuit mission where Father Andrew White operated. White led the first Catholic Mass in the English-speaking colonies after Maryland colonists first arrived in the new colony in 1634. His parish was set up around 1641 in Chapel Point, although the exact location is unknown. Finding the parish may help inform the history of how early colonists interacted with the Piscataway and other tribes in the area.
What is known–the arrival of the colonists caused feuds among the Piscataway, who had previously been attacked by colonists from Jamestown. Records uncovered from that time suggest that the Piscataway Tayac Kittamaquund–the tribe's chief–killed his brother to take power in an effort to normalize relations with the arriving colonists. Kittamaquund's older brother–Wannas–had mistrusted the English.
Despite some initial normalizing of relations, the English colonists expanded their reach and took over the land once foraged and farmed by the Piscataway and other Indigenous peoples during the next several decades.
Gray hopes that the history of the Piscataway can be more accurately told and preserved through respectful archaeology, signage in state parks and interpretive education about Indigenous Peoples throughout Maryland.
"This is just woods to most people, they don't see the history," Gray said, as he stood in the middle of the former dig site at Chapel Point State Park.
At the Department of Natural Resources, staff are working with Gray, King, and Hanson to better tell the story of the Piscataway. During the fall event, the department's Environmental Justice Officer Mariah Davis discussed opportunities with Gray and park staff to create interpretive programs, written in coordination with the tribal community, to educate visitors about the rich Indigenous heritage in Southern Maryland at the park.
Davis and Gray also discussed opportunities to collaborate with the Piscatoway Canoy Tribe to grow culturally important crops and plant species on park land.
Gray welcomed the idea and suggested that a red cedar be planted in a prominent position at Chapel Point.
The red cedar tree is a sacred plant for the Piscataway people. They consider the evergreen as full of life and believe its red center core represents the life-blood of all animals, including man.
"We don't want the footprint of our people to be erased," Gray said.

title: All I want for Christmas: a chimney ... and pony
author: JAMES L. SNYDER
content:
All I want for Christmas: a chimney ... and pony

 December 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JAMES L. SNYDER | Section: Columns 
 
 874
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The best holiday for me is Christmas. I enjoy everything about Christmas except paying for many gifts. But looking back, it's all been worth it. I can't think of anything I would ever change.It's the one time of the year that families get together who usually aren't together during the year because of work schedules and so forth.
I look forward to our great Christmas gatherings. There was a time in our family when the number of family members increased every year. I thought when we had children, that would be the end of it. But wouldn't you know all of our kids decided to have their own kids? And it's even come to the point where some of our grandkids are having their own kids.
Oh boy, when will this stop?
Actually, I hope it doesn't stop.
Everybody looks forward to the Christmas holiday and everything associated with it. It is very hard to have a bad Christmas, no matter what seems to happen.
After our Christmas holiday, I was sitting in my easy chair drinking coffee and reflecting on all the Christmases I had as a child. Those were fun times. I got to see relatives I haven't seen the rest of the year.
It was then I remembered something — the worst Christmas I ever had. I had forgotten about this, but all of a sudden, it came to mind.
When I was young, before I became a teenager, my parents would take me and my siblings downtown to meet Santa Claus. We would sit on his lap, take a candy cane from him, and tell him what we wanted for Christmas.
When we were done, he would say, "Ho, ho, ho," give us a Merry Christmas look, then send us back to our parents.
I vividly remember the first time I told him that I would love to have a pony for Christmas. He agreed to bring me a pony, and then he did his "ho, ho, ho" routine.
When I got up that Christmas, I noticed no pony under the Christmas tree. As I thought more about it, I realized that nothing was under the Christmas tree that I had asked Santa for. I couldn't understand it. My parents told me Santa would bring me the Christmas presents I asked for. Of course, I believed them.
Several Christmases passed, and the same thing happened or didn't happen. And I was just a little bit confused about this guy called Santa Claus. Why wasn't he good to his word?
I remember the year I turned 13. I was now a teenager, and so I had graduated to that smart level of being a teenager.
At school, we were having some kind of Christmas party, and they were talking about Santa Claus coming down the chimney to put presents under the Christmas tree and in the stockings hung by the fireplace. I didn't think too much of it at the time.
That Christmas Eve, as we were getting our Christmas tree all "holidayed" up, I felt that something was missing with our Christmas decorations. Then, it hit me rather strongly.
"Dad," I cried in alarm. He looked at me and said, "What's wrong son?"
I looked at him angrily and asked, "Dad, where is the chimney?"
With a curious look, he responded, "What are you talking about?"
"It's beginning to make sense," I seriously said to my father. "I now know what's wrong with our Christmas. I now know why I haven't got my pony."
My dad had no idea what I was talking about and asked me to explain.
"This week in school they were telling us all about Christmas and Santa Claus and Rudolph the red nose reindeer. One of the things they told us was that Santa Claus comes down the chimney to bring his gifts."
I paused for a moment and then continued, "So, that's why I've not got my pony for Christmas. Dad, where is our chimney?"
My dad was momentarily confused and had no idea how to respond to what I was saying.
"Well, son," my father said, "we don't have a chimney. We don't even have a fireplace so we don't need one."
"How then is Santa going to get me my Christmas presents under our Christmas tree I asked for while sitting on his lap?"
Thinking back over that now, I couldn't help but laugh. My father had a hard time explaining to me why we didn't need a chimney for Christmas time. Every year, just before Christmas, I ask, "Dad, will we have a chimney this year?"
After a while, he got tired of hearing me ask that question and refused to come up with any more excuses.
I was confused about Santa Claus and Christmas, not knowing what to believe. It took me some time to sort out the Christmas holiday.
As I reflected on this, I thought that many things in life need sorting out. We believe something and then find out it wasn't the truth.
Jesus addressed this in John 8:31-33, "Then said Jesus to those Jews which believed on him, If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free."
The truth about Jesus and His birth sets us free, and that truth can only be found in the Word of God.

title: Country Cooking: Breakfast on Christmas morning
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Breakfast on Christmas morning

 December 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1372
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Christmas morning has arrived finally, and the kids are having a grand time opening presents, running through the house and trying to play with the gifts all at one time. Mom is trying to keep the parts and pieces in one box while dad is trying to put Legos back in the right boxes.After a couple of hours everyone is getting hungry.
This is the time of morning when Christmas past and Christmas present comes into play. Christmas morning from my childhood is so much different from today. My mother was up Christmas morning early and had the bacon and scrapple cut and ready to fry. The biscuits were made and ready to bake.
As soon as the last gift was opened the gas stove was turned on, iron frying pans ready, oven heating up, table being set, homemade butter and jellies on the table and the big aluminum coffee pot starting to perk.
Oh my — I can still smell that Christmas morning breakfast cooking. There was not an empty chair at the table. The phone was ringing as the family called asking "is breakfast ready?"
Now times have changed, but it's just as much fun on Christmas morning with kids laughing, ripping open gifts, parents hooking up electronics, inserting gift cards in the correct gaming slots and getting air pods in the ears correctly.
Later the grandparents arrive for a breakfast brunch consisting of homemade waffles, microwave bacon and breakfast casserole dishes.
Yes, the world has changed as it does with every generation but the reason for the season is still the same, and families gather to celebrate, no matter how much is under the tree or how little.
Enjoy today's recipes to share with everyone and send some of your favorites to me at my email address so I can share with the readers (mmsavage21145@gmai.com).
PANCAKE CASSEROLECooking spray, pancakes, 6 large eggs, 1 1/2 cups heavy cream, 1 cup whole milk, 1/4 cup granulated sugar, 1 tsp vanilla bean paste, 1/4 tsp kosher salt, unsalted butter and maple syrup for serving.
Lightly coat a 13-by-9-inch baking dish with cooking spray. Arrange pancakes in a baking dish in three rows, overlapping slightly, starting at one long end. Whisk together eggs, cream, milk, sugar, vanilla and salt in a bowl. Slowly pour mixture over pancakes. Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or up to overnight. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Bake the casserole, covered, in a preheated oven for 25 minutes. Uncover and continue baking until the center is set, about 25 minutes. Let stand for 5 minutes. Dot with pats of butter; drizzle with syrup.
CHEESY SAUSAGE, EGG AND HASH BROWN CASSEROLE3 tbsps olive oil (divided), 8 ounces ground pork sausage, 1 sweet onion (diced), 1 poblano chile pepper (seeded and chopped), 1 red bell pepper (seeded and chopped), 1 ½ tsps kosher salt (divided), 2 cups refrigerated diced potatoes, ¾ tsp garlic powder, 4 ounces your favorite shredded cheese (about 1 cup), 5 large eggs, ¼ cup heavy whipping cream, 1 tbsp minced fresh chives.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees with an oven rack about 6 inches from heat. Heat one tbsp of the olive oil in a 10-inch cast-iron skillet over medium-high. Add sausage. Cook, breaking up sausage into pieces with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and just cooked through, about 4 minutes. Remove sausage to a medium bowl with a slotted spoon; set aside. Do not wipe the skillet clean. Add sweet onion, poblano chile, red bell pepper and ½ tsp of the salt to the skillet. Cook over medium-high, stirring occasionally, until onion is tender and peppers have charred in spots, about 8 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon to bowl with sausage. Wipe the skillet clean. Heat the remaining 2 tbsps of olive oil in a skillet over medium-high. Add diced potatoes to the skillet in an even layer. Cook, undisturbed, until browned on bottom, about 5 minutes. Add ½ tsp of the salt. Continue cooking, stirring occasionally, until golden brown and crispy on most sides, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat. Return sausage and pepper mixture to skillet and add garlic powder. Stir to combine. Stir in ½ cup of the cheese until just combined. Whisk together eggs, cream, and remaining ½ tsp salt in a medium bowl. Pour over mixture in skillet, and tilt pan to allow eggs to distribute. Top with remaining ½ cup each of the cheeses. Bake in a preheated oven until eggs have set and cheeses have melted, about 8 minutes. Increase oven temperature to broil, and broil until cheeses have turned golden brown, 2 to 3 minutes. Remove; let stand for 5 minutes. Sprinkle with chives. Slice and serve immediately.
BISCUITS AND GRAVY CASSEROLE1 lb ground pork sausage, 1/2 cup chopped yellow onion (from 1 small onion), 1/4 cup plus 1 tbsp unsalted butter, 1/3 cup (about 1 1/2 oz.) all-purpose flour, 3 cups whole milk, 6 oz pepper Jack cheese (shredded), 3/4 tsp kosher salt, 1/2 tsp black pepper, Cooking spray, 1 (25-oz.) pkg frozen Southern-style biscuits (such as Pillsbury Grands), 2 tbsps minced fresh chives.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Place sausage and onion in a large skillet over medium, and cook, stirring often, until sausage crumbles and is no longer pink and onion is translucent, 6 to 8 minutes. Transfer mixture to a plate lined with paper towels to drain. Wipe the skillet clean. Reduce heat to low, and add 1/4 cup of the butter to the skillet; cook, whisking often, until melted. Whisk in flour until smooth. Cook, whisking constantly, 1 minute. Gradually whisk in milk; increase heat to medium, and cook, whisking constantly, until thickened and bubbly, 5 to 6 minutes. Whisk in shredded cheese, and cook, whisking often, until cheese is melted and mixture is smooth, 30 to 40 seconds. Stir in sausage mixture, salt, and pepper.Transfer mixture to a lightly greased (with cooking spray) 13-by-9-inch baking dish. Arrange biscuits on top of sausage mixture. Bake in a preheated oven until biscuits are golden brown and gravy is bubbly, 30 to 35 minutes. Microwave remaining 1 tbsp butter in a small microwavable bowl on high until melted, about 20 seconds. Remove the casserole from the oven; brush biscuits with melted butter, and sprinkle with chives. Let stand for 10 minutes before serving.
SLOW COOKER CINNAMON ROLL CASSEROLECooking spray, 1/2 cup granulated sugar, 1/2 cup packed light brown sugar, 1 tsp ground cinnamon, 2 (16.3-oz.) cans refrigerated southern homestyle biscuits (separated and cut into fourths), 1/2 cup salted butter (melted), 2 tbsp salted butter (softened), 4 large eggs, 1/4 tsp kosher salt, 2/3 cup plus 2 to 3 tbsp half-and-half (divided), 2 tsp vanilla extract, 1/2 cup chopped toasted pecans, 1 (3-oz.) pkg. cream cheese (softened), 2 1/4 cups powdered sugar.
Line bottom and sides of a 6-quart slow cooker with aluminum foil; lightly coat foil with cooking spray. Stir together granulated sugar, brown sugar, and cinnamon in a small bowl. Toss together biscuit pieces and 1/2 cup melted butter in a large bowl until biscuits are coated. Working in batches, add biscuits to granulated sugar mixture, and toss to coat; transfer biscuits to prepared slow cooker. Sprinkle any remaining sugar mixture over biscuits in a slow cooker. Whisk together eggs, salt, 2/3 cup of the half-and-half, and 1 tsp of the vanilla in a bowl until well combined; pour over biscuits in a slow cooker. Sprinkle with pecans. Beat cream cheese and 2 tbsps softened butter with an electric mixer on medium speed until thoroughly combined, about 30 seconds. Add 1 cup of the powdered sugar and remaining 1 tsp vanilla; beat until smooth, about 1 minute. Gradually add remaining 1 1/4 cups powdered sugar to cream cheese mixture alternately with 2 tbsps of the half-and-half, beating on high speed until frosting is smooth, creamy, and a little loose, about 1 minute, adding remaining 1 tbsp half-and-half, 1 tsp at a time, if needed to reach desired consistency. Drizzle half of the frosting over the biscuit mixture in the slow cooker. (Cover remaining frosting and set aside until ready to serve.) Cover slow cooker; cook on LOW until center of casserole is set and biscuit bottoms are browned, 3 1/2 to 4 hours. Drizzle casserole with remaining frosting; serve warm.

 EASTON — Cars lined up on North Washington Street to view a large display of holiday lights and the Easton Church of God's Drive-Thru Live Nativity on a cold and rainy Friday evening.Those that pulled into the Easton Church of God and drove around were greeted by an array of Christmas lights, music, decorations and inflatable holiday characters. Gift bags and hot chocolate were handed out, and Santa greeted attendees.
Easton Church of God Family Pastor Josh Maxwell said the live nativity has been going on for a little more than a decade.

Maxwell said everyone has come to love the annual event that tells the story of Christmas, making it a tradition not just for the church, but for the entire community.

title: Black-eyed peas, traditions and superstitions
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Black-eyed peas, traditions and superstitions

 December 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1472
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The cooks in my neck of the woods always cooked black-eyed peas for New Year's Day. This carried on for generations and still to this day remains a tradition.Mom bought that bag of peas ahead of time to make sure she had them before they sold out. Then she sat a piece of seasoning meat aside in the smoke house.
The most popular tradition on New Year's Day was to eat the black-eyed peas for good luck all year.
Well, the second biggest tradition of all was that no women were to enter the house on New Year's Day, as that was "bad luck." That did not work for me, as I tried to get out of helping mom cook or do dishes because I lived there and was not entering.
Well years later that changed somewhat to "women who accompanied the men to your house had to let the men enter first. And I used to say "well let him do the dishes."
Mom would cook a large pot of black-eyed peas with her seasoning meat and some potatoes. Then out came the big baking pans filled with homemade biscuits.
Sitting next to the biscuits was a jar of homemade jelly from last summer's canning and a dish with fresh churned butter.
No one asked for dessert, but everyone asked for more peas and biscuits.
From all over the world you find superstitions for New Years Eve and New Year's Day. Here are just a few I have heard over the years.
According to popular folklore or superstition, if these foods are eaten on New Year's Day, they guarantee good luck throughout the year:
Peas or beans are said to symbolize coins or wealth. Choose traditional black-eyed peas, lentils, or beans to make a dish seasoned with pork, ham or sausage.
Greens resemble money, specifically folding money. Make dishes using boiled cabbage or sauerkraut, collard greens, kale, chard, mustard greens, turnip greens or other green, leafy vegetables to ensure good fortune for the coming year.
Pork is considered a sign of prosperity in some cultures because pigs root forward. Many southern New Year's Day dishes contain pork or ham, but feel free to serve a pork roast or baked ham as an entrée.
Cornbread might symbolize gold, and besides, it is essential with black-eyed peas and greens.
In other cultures, fish, grapes, and ring-shaped cakes or doughnuts, or cakes with special treats inside symbolize luck.
Some believe that lobster could cause bad luck in the coming year because it moves in a backward direction and could mean setbacks in the year ahead. For the same reason, some believe chicken dishes should be avoided on New Year's Day. Chickens scratch backward, plus they are winged, so your luck could fly away.
Now for some black-eyed pea dishes and dishes people around the United States eat on New Year's Eve or New Year's Day.
BLACK-EYED PEAS
Begin by purchasing a bag of the dried black-eyed peas and soaking them in cold water, covering them. In a large soup pot, place the seasoning meat and cover with water, bring to a boil, let simmer. After the beans have swollen and doubled in size, rinse in cold water and add to the seasoning meat, add more salt if needed and black pepper. When a rolling boil begins, turn flame back to achieve a steady boil, cover with a lid that is slightly ajar to avoid boiling over. As the beans cook, you can add in the last 45 to 50 minutes some whole corn, dumplings or some peeled white potatoes. Before adding the corn or other additions, check the seasonings. Serve with your warm breads and enjoy this filling meal any time of the year.
TEXAS CAVAIR
2 14-oz. cans black-eyed peas (drained), 1 15.5-oz. can white hominy (drained), 2 medium tomatoes (chopped), 2 green tomatoes (chopped), 1 medium green bell pepper (chopped), 2 jalapeño peppers (chopped), 1/2 cup onion, (chopped), 1/2 cup fresh cilantro (chopped), 2 garlic cloves (minced), 1 8-oz. bottle Italian dressing, tortilla chips for serving.
Stir together the first nine ingredients in a large bowl. Add the dressing to the black-eyed pea mixture, stirring until combined. Cover and chill for 2 hours. Drain. Serve with the tortilla chips.
HOPPIN JOHN WITH BRAISED OXTAIL
1.5 pounds oxtails,1.5 tbsps salt (divided), 2 tsps black pepper (divided), 6 cups chicken stock, 2 cups dried black-eyed peas (soaked overnight), 2 cups diced yellow onions (from 2 medium onions), 2 cups diced carrots (from 5 medium carrots), 2 cups diced celery (from 4 stalks), 1/4 cup chopped jalapeño chiles (from 2 chiles), 4 garlic cloves (thinly sliced), 5 thyme sprigs, 3 fresh bay leaves. RICE:4 cups water, 1 teaspoon kosher salt, 1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper, 1 cup uncooked jasmine rice, 1/4 cup unsalted butter (cubed), 1/4 cup apple cider vinegar, 1/2 cup chopped scallions.
Prepare the peas: Heat a Dutch oven over high and add canola oil. Sprinkle oxtails evenly with ½ tablespoon of the salt and 1 teaspoon of the black pepper, and place in the Dutch oven. Cook until browned on all sides, about 4 minutes per side. Remove oxtails from the Dutch oven. Pour off drippings, leaving browned bits in the Dutch oven, and add stock. Bring stock to a boil over high, using a wooden spoon to scrape browned bits from the bottom of the Dutch oven. Return oxtails to Dutch oven; reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer until tender, 1½ to 2 hours. Using a slotted spoon, transfer oxtails to a plate, and let cool slightly. Add peas, onions, carrots, celery, jalapeño, garlic, thyme sprigs, and bay leaves to stock mixture; reduce heat to low, and cook, partially covered, until peas are soft, about 1 hour. Stir in remaining 1 tablespoon salt and 1 teaspoon black pepper. While peas cook, pick oxtail meat from bones, and set aside. While the peas finish cooking, preheat the oven to 300 degrees. Bring water, salt, and cayenne pepper to a boil in a medium saucepan over medium-high. Reduce heat to medium; add rice and stir. Simmer gently, uncovered, stirring occasionally, until rice is al dente, about 15 minutes. Drain rice in a fine wire-mesh strainer, and rinse under cold water. Spread rice out on a rimmed baking sheet. Dry rice in a preheated oven for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Scatter butter evenly over rice, and continue to dry, stirring every few minutes, until all excess moisture has evaporated, and grains are dry and separate, about 5 more minutes. Add oxtail meat and cider vinegar to peas. Using a slotted spoon, transfer peas to a large serving bowl. Add rice, and carefully toss together. (Pour enough oxtail gravy over the top to moisten the peas without making the dish too soupy, about 1 cup.) Garnish with scallions.
CHILI ROASTED BLACK-EYED PEAS
2 cans black-eyed peas rinsed and drained, 3 tbsps olive oil, 1 1/2 tsps chili powder, 1 tsp pepper, 3/4 tsp ground cumin, 1/2 tsp salt.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Combine all ingredients in a medium bowl. Transfer mixture to a lightly greased 17-by-12-inch jelly roll pan. Bake for 45 to 50 minutes or until crispy and dry, stirring every 10 minutes. Let cool for 20 minutes.
INSTANT POT BLACK-EYED PEA SOUP
1 tbsp olive oil, 1 cup chopped yellow onion, 1 cup chopped carrots, 1/2 cup chopped celery, 2 large garlic cloves, (minced), 1/4 tsp crushed red pepper, 6 cups chicken broth (such as Swanson's),3 thyme sprigs, 2 cups roughly chopped and stemmed collard greens,1 14.5-oz. can fire-roasted diced tomatoes (drained), 1 (3/4-lb.) smoked ham hock, 1 lb. dried black-eyed peas (soaked overnight), 2 tbsps red wine vinegar, 1.5 tsps salt, 1 tsp black pepper.
Select the saute setting on Instant Pot or a pressure cooker. Times, instructions, and settings may vary according to cooker brand or model. Select high temperature setting and allow to preheat 2 to 3 minutes. Add olive oil to the cooker, and heat until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add onion, carrots, and celery; cook, stirring often, until vegetables are softened, 2 to 3 minutes. Stir in garlic and crushed red pepper and cook for 30 seconds. Stir in chicken stock, thyme, collards, tomatoes, ham hock, and black-eyed peas. Press cancel. Cover cooker with lid, and lock in place. Turn the steam release handle to the sealing position. Select manual/pressure cook setting. Select high pressure for 10 minutes. (It will take 10 to 15 minutes for the cooker to come up to pressure before cooking begins.) Let the pressure release naturally for 15 minutes. Carefully turn the steam release handle to the venting position and let steam fully escape the float valve. This will take about 2 to 3 minutes. Remove lid from cooker. Remove ham hock from cooker; pull meat off bone, and chop to equal about 1/3 cup. Discard bone. Stir chopped ham, vinegar, salt, and pepper into soup.
Happy New Year to all my readers. Here's to a happy and healthy 2025.

title: New podcast seeks to bring new perspectives, a sense of place to Underground Railroad
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
New podcast seeks to bring new perspectives, a sense of place to Underground Railroad

 December 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 527
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Rooted Wisdom Podcast is an extension of the film "Nature's Role in the Underground Railroad," but with a twist.The producers and host want to incorporate multiple different avenues of Underground Railroad history, expanding beyond the scope of the film to explore themes like criminal justice inequality, redlining and voter suppression, and to highlight local histories through guided experiences.
"The podcast itself goes into the legacy of the Underground Railroad and how it is still in the tapestry of our contemporary issues today that we feel," George Burroughs, one of the podcast's producers, said. "From teenage criminal justice, inequality, redlining, redistricting, voter suppression, and we also, in the podcast, wanted to be able to go to different locations. We wanted to take it a step further and let (podcast host) Tony (Anthony Cohen), as a historian, interpreter, interview other people and to really dive into these issues."
The podcast's first series was released in September, and it showed three different perspectives about the Underground Railroad.
"The first three episodes, Tony talks with a filmmaker, a nonprofit leader and a wildlife photographer," Lauren Giordano, a podcast producer, said. "So getting those perspectives on the history and how that shows up for them and their work, in their lives, I think was something that was kind of unique about that."
But the podcast is not completely divorced from the natural, geography-based perspective of the film it's based off of. The podcast has nature references as well.
The guests on the Rooted Wisdom podcast, along with the host, bring multiple perspectives on how nature played a part in the Underground Railroad from their professions or experiences.
Adkins Arboretum in Tuckahoe State Park hold a big focus the podcast, as they do in the film.
The producers and the host believe that locals can look around and find that there is so much history of the Underground Railroad in their community. Their way to learn this history, the producers said, is through Rooted Wisdom.
"My background is in the history of the Underground Railroad, and as a Marylander, starting 30 years ago, I came to realize how much of that history played out on the Eastern Shore," Cohen said. "Not only Tubman and Douglas, but many of the abolitionists of the 1830s and whatnot had Maryland roots, and so the history is really anchored there."
"So I was involved in the community, and of some of those efforts which led to the establishment of the Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway, the 123-mile route through Dorchester and Caroline counties that roughly follows her route."
Although the Rooted Wisdom podcast is Maryland-based, the plan is to expand. The producers and host believe that the podcast can give everyone a perspective from their own personal community with the history of the Underground Railroad.
"I think all of the podcasts that we've done and that we're envisioning or planning are really partly focused on a sense of place," Cohen said. "So I think as we travel around the state and eventually around the country doing this story, we'll be bringing, or bringing to light, a story that itself is often underground, and I think that'll be powerful for people."
To listen to the podcast, visit rootedwisdom.org/podcast.

title: Temple B'Nai Israel in Easton celebrates Hanukkah
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Temple B'Nai Israel in Easton celebrates Hanukkah

 January 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Saturday, Temple B'Nai Israel and community members gathered together for a community Hanukkah candle lighting. The celebration and observance is continuing through sundown on Thursday.Rabbi Fred Scherlinder Dobb, interim rabbi for the temple and Satell Center for Jewish Life on the Eastern Shore, emphasized Saturday's candle lighting as a tradition that strengthens Easton and the surrounding community.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook and Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher were two of the community members who attended, Dobb said.
"This is an opportunity to unite the members of Temple B'Nai Israel with the broader community," he said. "Year to year, different area clergypeople, and elected officials and others are able to join us."
Barbara Spector, president of the Temple B'Nai Israel's Board of Trustees, said there was singing, lighting of Hanukkah menorahs and games.
Hanukkah is considered a festival of lights and lasts eight days, in which Jewish people gather to light a candle in a menorah each day. It stems from the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in the second century B.C.
"This eight-day holiday falls around the new moon that is closest to the winter solstice," Dobb said. "So it comes at the time of greatest darkness, both daytime and nighttime. And in that darkness moment, we introduce light."
This year, Hanukkah began Dec. 25. Temple B'Nai Israel celebrates with latkes (fried potato pancakes), sufganiyah (jelly donuts) and a dreidel (a four-sided spinning top).
As the only full-service synagogue in Talbot and neighboring counties, Temple B'Nai Israel is a sacred place for many that practice Judaism. Since beginning his interim role in November, Dobb has come to appreciate the diversity of those that attend the temple's programs and services.
"I am consistently astounded by not only the depth of thought and positivity of the members of this temple community, but also of the region as a whole," Dobb said. "I have not met someone from Easton and Talbot County who I have not been impressed by in some way.
"Irrespective of faith, or political affiliation or race, folks are sharing a spirit of sorts. And the larger community is clearly stronger for that ethos."
Spector and Dobb admit that distance is a challenge for many, especially in the rural Eastern Shore compared to other parts of the region. Temple B'Nai Israel sees people often come from Centreville, Cambridge, Stevensville and Chestertown, among other areas.
Dobb welcomes the challenges that may come with accommodating a wide range of people and practices.
"People of all backgrounds and ideologies and levels of observance, as well as different comfort and knowledge with tradition and Hebrew, all come together for the same events and the same worship services," Dobb said. "So finding the range of sweet spots that will touch everyone in some way is both a challenge and an opportunity."
Dobb said the Hannukah celebration is about "hope and community."
The rabbi said the theme of Saturday was that "we are all in it together."
"That applies to the civic fabric of our region and the democracy of which we are a part," Dobb said. "It also applies to the natural world for which we are all responsible, and we have to work together to caretake one another, as well as to be good stewards of the land and the day. These things can only be done in unison, and blessingly, that spirit of unity in the broader community is strong and growing."

title: Delaware art exhibit showcases letterpress work
author: Post staff report
content:
Delaware art exhibit showcases letterpress work

 January 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Post staff report | Section: News 
 
 637
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The letterpress studio of Lead Graffiti was voted Newark's favorite artist of 2024 in a recent citizen poll by the Newark Post. That inspired the Newark Arts Alliance to dedicate its January exhibition to an overview of Lead Graffiti's work over the past two decades and its dedication to "printing slowly & patiently via letterpress in Newark, Delaware."The solo exhibition, "Lead Graffiti: An Exhibition of Letterpress and Book Arts" runs through Jan. 17 at the Newark Arts Alliance Gallery, located in the Shoppes at Louviers on Paper Mill Road. A public reception will be held on Jan. 10 from 6 to 8 p.m. The gallery is open to the public Tuesday through Saturday from noon to 4 p.m. daily and noon to 8 p.m. on Fridays.
Lead Graffiti was formed in 2008 by Ray Nichols and Jill Cypher as an experimental letterpress laboratory. The husband-and-wife team of artists/designers focused on public causes, a love of words and typography, passing historical and technical information forward, and a playful disregard for the usual design rules.
Located in a 2,200-square-foot space in Newark's Sandy Brae Industrial Park, Lead Graffiti is packed with cases of wood and metal type, printing presses of all kinds, a working hot-metal Intertype linecaster, and all the gear that Gutenberg would have known.
The studio's letterpress work is included in more than 75 significant collections of libraries and institutions, along with solo exhibitions at The British Library in London, the Hamilton Wood Type Museum in Two Rivers, Wisconsin, and the American Institute of Graphic Arts in Philadelphia. Lead Graffiti has been written up in Sports Illustrated Magazine and makes a grand entry in printer/author Chris Fritton's book The Itinerant Printer, where he wrote, "Lead Graffiti is the incorrigible, unpredictable, and uncompromising brainchild of Ray Nichols and Jill Cypher — a shop where the only rule is there are no design rules, and the thing you learn every day is that there's always more to learn."
Nichols and Cypher have given dozens of talks and tours to various organizations and student groups and conducted numerous in-house and online workshops related to letterpress and bookmaking. One of the studio's major projects was an endurance letterpress series of 115+ broadsides produced over five years (2011 — 2015), visually documenting the daily events of the Tour de France in handset type and ink on paper.
For three decades as a professor and director of the visual communications program at the University of Delaware, Nichols helped lead the program to an international reputation. He was also co-director with his teaching colleague Bill Deering of the program's summer study abroad to London.
Beginning in 2001, the trips were for students in advertising and graphic design to visit design studios, advertising agencies, filmmakers, and museums to provide experiences with design creativity, typography and historical perspectives. A pair of early visits to the letterpress studio of Alan Kitching and the St. Bride Printing Library unexpectedly provided Nichols and Cypher with two life-altering experiences. Their creative focus switched from blink-of-the-eye advertising design to the slow and patient world of letterpress printing and book arts for the next two decades.
In 2002, Nichols, Cypher and Deering founded Raven Press at the University of Delaware. Over the next four years, it became a new teaching tool. Cypher's interests in typography, colorful paste paper painting and exploring various forms of bookmaking also benefited Raven Press externally. Upon Nichols' retirement from teaching in 2006, the couple formed Lead Graffiti, collecting presses and cases of type to continue their creative work.
In 2006, their first major post-teaching project solidified their intellectual connection to Newark. As volunteers, Nichols and Cypher were tasked with designing, photographing and producing the 300-page hardback book "Histories of Newark: 1758 — 2008." The design is highlighted by their photography of a citizen's band of about 4,000 Newark residents that runs through the book.

title: Country Cooking: Eating like the King
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Eating like the King

 January 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Life 
 
 1157
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Unbelievable that my teenage idol, Elvis, turns 90 today. Millions of fans from all over the world come to Memphis to gather at Graceland to reflect on memories together.The younger generation want to hear about our stories from the early days of Elvis — his music, his singing and moving style, and our parents' thoughts on this "good looking guy" who ripped the music world apart.
I have met some great folks from across the ocean who are in their 30s, 40s and 50s who are so interested in Elvis' early career days and the reaction to his music from the older generation.
Graceland is just a small part of the must-see sights in Memphis. Sun Records studio is open for touring and is widely considered the birthplace of rock 'n' roll. Many famous singers have recorded there, such as Elvis, Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis and Conway Twitty, just to name a few.
Each time I go it's like my first time — amazing.
Not only is the tour of Graceland awesome, but downtown Beale Street is loaded with great food and sights to see. Whatever kind of food you like is available in and around Memphis. Southern-style eating is everywhere you turn.
HOMEMADE MEMPHIS STYLE BBQ SAUCE2 tbsps unsalted butter, 1 small onion (finely chopped), 2 cloves garlic (minced), 2 cups tomato sauce, 1/2 cup cider vinegar, 1/3 cup rice vinegar, 1/3 cup molasses, 3 tbsps Worcestershire sauce, 2 tbsps packed dark brown sugar, 2 tsps yellow mustard, 1 tsp Louisiana hot sauce, 1 tsp Kosher salt, 1 tsp freshly ground black pepper, 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper.
Melt butter in medium saucepan over medium heat. Add onion and cook until softened, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and cook until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Add tomato sauce, cider vinegar, rice vinegar, molasses, Worcestershire sauce, brown sugar, mustard, hot sauce, salt, black pepper and cayenne, and stir to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low and simmer until slightly thickened, about 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally. Transfer sauce to the jar of a blender and blend until smooth. Let cool to room temperature, transfer to a jar and store in the refrigerator for up to a month.
SMOKY GRILLED CHEESE2 slices sourdough bread, 1 cup freshly grated Monterey Jack cheese, Memphis BBQ sauce (for serving), 2 tbsp butter.
Prepare the grilled cheese by spreading butter on one side of each piece of bread. Lay one piece of bread butter side down on a skillet, top with cheese, and place the other piece of bread on top creating a sandwich. Turn the heat to medium-high and cook for 4-5 minutes on each side. Before removing the grilled cheese, you can top each side with shredded cheese and cook until the cheese is melted and crispy. Remove the grilled cheese from the skillet and serve hot with the Memphis BBQ sauce to dip in.
MEMPHIS STYLE CHICKEN NUGGETS1 lb boneless skinless chicken cubed, 1 egg, 1/3 cup bread crumbs, 1/4 cup shaved parmesan, Memphis BBQ sauce.
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Cut the chicken tenderloins into small nugget-like cubes. Whisk 1 egg in a small bowl. In a large zip lock bag, combine bread crumbs, and parmesan. Coat each piece of chicken in egg and then place in the bag with the breading. Once you have done this with each piece, close the bag and shake well. Each piece of chicken should be covered in breading. Place the breaded chicken on a sheet pan and place in the oven to bake for 30 minutes. Serve warm with Memphis BBQ sauce for dipping.
MEMPHIS DRY RUB RIBS1 slab pork loin spare ribs (also called baby back ribs), 5 tbsps light brown sugar, 4 tsps smoked paprika, 1½ tsps black pepper, 1 tsp granulated garlic or garlic powder, 4 tsps kosher salt, ½ tsp chili powder, ¼ tsp onion powder, ¼ tsp ground cumin, ¼ tsp dried oregano, ¼ tsp rubbed sage, ¼ tsp dried marjoram, ¼ tsp dried parsley, ¼ tsp white pepper, 1 cup white vinegar, 1 cup water.
Adjust the oven rack to the middle of the oven. Preheat the oven to 250 degrees. Stir together the sugar and all of the spices in a small bowl. Reserve ⅓ of the spice mixture in a separate bowl. Place the ribs on a large baking tray, meat side down. Slide a knife just barely under the edge of the membrane at one end of the ribs and then use that loosened edge to pull the membrane off the ribs. (I find it easiest to grab the edge of the membrane with a paper towel and pull it off that way). Pat the ribs dry with a paper towel. Apply the rub generously to the front and back of the ribs (leaving the reserved amount for later use). Place the ribs meat side up on a large foil-lined baking sheet and cook for about three hours, until the ribs are tender. Pour the vinegar and water into a shallow baking dish. Remove the cooked ribs from the oven and dip them into the vinegar water. Place the wet ribs onto a cutting board or a clean baking sheet and season immediately with a coating of the reserved dry rub. Cut the ribs apart between the bones.
GUS'S WORLD FAMOUS FRIED CHICKENThis next recipe is a 24-hour marinade of the chicken, a full day before you plan to cook it.
1 lb boneless skinless chicken breast cut into three pieces (or, your standard bone-in chicken pieces like Gus's does. I went with boneless chicken breasts for this recipe because they are a challenge), 1 cup corn starch, ¼ cup (4 tbsps) all purpose flour, 1 tbsp ground black pepper, 1 tbsp sweet paprika, 1 tbsp cayenne pepper, 1 tsp Kosher salt, 1 cup water (Note: 1 ½ cups is too much. On my first go, I actually ended up with 1 ¼ cup water and poured off a little water in the morning that had gathered on top of the marinade and that is how I came up with the 1 cup measurement).
Marinade for 24 hours In the refrigerator, keeping everything refrigerated to protect against bacterial growth. Remove the chicken from the marinade/batter and if everything goes well, the batter/slurry will cling to the pieces. You may need to agitate the batter/slurry to assure that it coats the chicken pieces. Fry at 325-350 degrees. Use a neutral vegetable or corn oil. I've become a big fan of sunflower oil as it has a high smoke point, but, yeah, vegetable, corn, peanut oils are fine if that is what you have. I do not recommend canola oil as it smells like frying fish and adds an unpleasant fish taste to fried foods.
There are so many places to visit in Memphis to eat. If you ever make it there, please check out Gus's Fried Chicken, Charlie Vergos' Rendezvous, Central BBQ, The King Jerry Lawler's BBQ, Rum Boogie Café and BB King's Blues Club.

title: Artists' exhibit honors Historic Sotterley
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Artists' exhibit honors Historic Sotterley

 January 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: State News 
 
 708
 Words 

 Read News Document

 An exhibit at the Leonardtown library is helping to tell the story of Historic Sotterley."Moments in Time" features the works of watercolor painter Pamela Callen, photographer Damien Wilkinson and multi-disciplinary Joi Lowe.
"I want people to know who Sotterley is, what it is and I just want them to get a glimpse of the history because I don't want that to be erased," said Lowe, who helped set up the exhibit. "I want people to see what it was, but it's also a beautiful site with many, many stories and we help tell those stories. It's important."
The exhibit — which is "acknowledging spiritual connections to the landscape of Historic Sotterley" — will be at the Leonardtown branch through the end of January when it will move to the Lexington Park library.
"It's very exciting," said Susie Glauner, who is the executive director of the St. Mary's County Arts Council, which is sponsoring the exhibit. "We are thrilled to be able to offer the gallery partnerships, both for the benefit of the artists as well as St. Mary's County residents and visitors so that more people can see the local talent we have here in the county."
Callen, who has three paintings in the exhibit — "Slave Dwelling," "Manor House" and "Fall in the Fields" — had a lengthy career as a foreign service member for the U.S. Agency for International Development and spent a number of years in developing countries.
As a result, she said, "The human condition means a lot to me. That's one of the appeals of Sotterley is that you have both sides of the coin there — the slave dwelling and the Manor House."
The Solomons resident said when she was painting "Manor House" a few years back an elderly couple appeared so she painted them in.
"But when I did that they became the main focal point and that really wasn't what I wanted," she said. "I wanted the sky and the house and the beauty so I painted them back out. When you have the brush in your hand you can change the world."
When she painted "Fall in the Fields" last year, she started thinking.
"We have a lot of [hay bales] in Southern Maryland, but at Sotterley it's so special because one of the things you think about when you look at this vast expanse of land and the water is the people who did that work, so you think about them," Callen said. "You think about who lived in the manor house and who kept them going doing all the work in the fields and living in that slave dwelling. You think about that when you're out there and there's nobody around except you and your paint."
Wilkinson took up photography as a hobby a few years back but started getting more invested in it last year.
He has three photographs in the exhibit: "Beautiful Yet Broken," "Reflections of the Past" and "Portals to Relics."
"I would just kind of point-shoot [my camera] and hope it would come out OK," said the 43-year-old Great Mills resident, who said he recently "just fell back in love with photography again. I was really excited to get out there [to Sotterley] and take pictures."
Lowe has four pieces in the show: "This Time, Stephen Marley," "Mariposa" and "Catalpa Piece with Paper," as well as a 10-foot piece made from marbles, gemstones, wood and pieces of a maple tree titled "Born Free."
She said one piece she did titled "Royal" included collecting honey locust seed pods from a tree in front of the Sotterley slave cabin.
"I spent so many days at that cabin collecting those seed pods," the 47-year-old California resident said, "and so many times I felt like I was having conversations. Who else was collecting these seed pods?"
Lowe also has a current show through the end of January at the Lexington Park Library and artist Jay Anderson has an exhibit hanging at the Port of Leonardtown Winery.
The "Moments in Time" exhibit is in the Maryland Room at the Leonardtown Public Library, located 23630 Hayden Farm Lane. The library is open 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Mondays to Thursdays and 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays.
For more information on the exhibit or to purchase pieces in it, email Joi Lowe at joi_lowe@yahoo.com.

title: Stephen Harvey is bringing jazz to St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Stephen Harvey is bringing jazz to St. Michaels

 January 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 718
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST MICHAELS — When Stephen Philip Harvey is playing the saxophone, the sounds that come from the horn of the golden instrument are lively, rhythmic and attention-grabbing.Harvey, a celebrated and well-decorated musician from the Eastern Shore, has a generational love for music.
Its a love he shares with those running the Windon Distilling Company in St. Michaels, who have invited the musician to be a part of unveiling their newest endeavor.
Having just finished its 11th year of production, the distillery is opening a new event space, Golden Hour, next to its staple tasting room. Harvey will be performing a sold-out show to mark its opening Friday night.
The distillery's founder Jaime Windon said in a press release, "this space is designed for showcasing the things we love the most: rum cocktails alongside brilliant and inspiring music, art and community. To be able to debut it while enjoying jazz along with our friends and neighbors in January is a dream."
Harvey was raised in a family passionate about music and would perform for their local church. Raised on gospel music, he soon expanded his repertoire into jazz and gained an appreciation for gathered sounds and instruments.
According to Harvey, it's not uncommon for someone in his family to break into song.
"My love for music is really a family love for music," Harvey said. "My whole family are singers and musicians… (there are times) we would be on a walk to meet up together in a space, and then someone would be like, 'oh, let's sing this hymn,' and then we break out into four part harmony. My wife was very startled by it the first time she was at a family event."
As Harvey grew up, his curiosity in music began to change away from gospel when his high school band director encouraged him to join the jazz band. From there, his relationship with music took several twists and turns.
When he got to college, his interest peaked in studying music education before choosing to focus on Western European art music, where he learned song styles of Italian, German and French musicians.
But it was American music through idioms of bebop, hard bop, vocal jazz and then big band jazz that made Harvey want to commit the rest of his life in exploring those sounds.
"It's this really interesting hobby/career where I feel like I can just do it forever and always discover new things, even looking back and going forward," Harvey said. "So discovering new things as I write and discovering new things as I listen to people who have performed and recorded in the idiom before me is so cool, especially since you come from this family that loves music so much."
Today, Harvey is a professional musician, composer and bandleader. He has released seven full albums throughout this career, with "Library Card" being his latest release.
Additionally, his compositions have been performed by an array of ensembles across the world including the National Youth Jazz Orchestra, ensembles at the Peabody Conservatory of Music and several universities across the nation.
Harvey sees his upcoming performance as part of an effort to expand jazz music's presence in the area, a mission the distillery's owners are also on board with.
Windon said she is a fan of jazz and was incredibly excited to host Harvey and his trio Sphinx as the first musical act at Windon's new event venue.
For Windon, Harvey has an electric presence.
"I have a great appreciation for jazz music of all kinds of styles, and so I liked that his music felt classic and familiar, but yet fresh," Windon said. "… There's a charisma, to me, that Stephen has that I think is also reminiscent of jazz musicians that I've always known and gravitated towards."
Harvey said he has performed in Easton and his concert will be his first time playing in St. Michaels. He shared that he's excited to establish himself on the Eastern Shore and share his love for jazz.
"My whole vibe since I've moved down here is seeing what a vacuum of jazz and Black American improvised music is on the Shore," Harvey said. "There's like none, and I would love to produce as many shows as possible, whether they are in conjunction with Lyon Rum and the Golden Hour or anywhere else. I'm just excited for any opportunity to play inside of this county."

title: Museum to host annual appraisal fair
author: Staff Writer
content:
Museum to host annual appraisal fair

 January 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 284
 Words 

 Read News Document

 St. Clement's Island Museum in St. Mary's County will host its annual Appraiser Fair from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Saturday, Jan. 25, at 38370 Point Breeze Road in Colton's Point.The fair allows individuals to meet with expert appraisers to determine the value of prized possessions and heirlooms and how to care for them.
Appraisers will be available to offer oral appraisals in fine arts, dolls, coins and currency. The fine arts category includes ceramics, pottery, glassware, artwork/paintings, music boxes and small furniture pieces.
Fine arts appraisers include Commonwealth Antiques and Appraisals Owner Henry Lane Hull, and Bill Curry, owner of Hammer's Antiques and Collectibles. William Parron of Bill Parron Coin Co., will be available to appraise coins and currency, while Linda Neeley of the Black-eyed Susan Doll Club of Southern Maryland will appraise dolls.
Individuals will be seen on a first-come, first-served basis and are encouraged to bring items that can be carried by hand. Items that do not fit the categories will not be accepted for appraisal.
Appraisals are not certified; however, a certified appraisal can be made at a later date. The public may experience long wait times for fine art appraisers.
Items in the fine arts category are limited to two items per person at a fee of $5 per item. Other category fees are $5 each. Cash, credit card, and check are accepted.
Friends of the St. Clement's Island and Piney Point Museums members get two free appraisals and may enter the event venue starting at 9:30 am.
The Washington Conservation Guild, a nonprofit organization of conservation professionals, will offer free preservation guidance for the items you bring to the Appraiser Fair.
For more information, call St. Clement's Island Museum at 301-769-2222 or go to Facebook.com/SCIMuseum.

title: Water's Edge Museum will celebrate upcoming anniversary celebration
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Water's Edge Museum will celebrate upcoming anniversary celebration

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 439
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Saturday, the Water's Edge Museum, Talbot County's first African American museum, is celebrating its four-year anniversary with music, art, food and a celebration of leaders on the Eastern Shore.In attendance will be Leroy Potter and his group at the Maryland Spirituals Initiative. They will perform for attendees and talk about the founding Black families and the legacy they left behind.
Kay Brown, a Queen Anne's native and co-director of the museum, said she is honored and proud to be working with such rich pieces of art and history.
According to Brown, from the walls to the staff, every bit of the museum is a part of the living history of the area, and through her time as co-director Brown has enjoyed watching the connection and joy people have visiting for the first time.
"It's just rewarding that we are on to something and people just like and when you come to the museum it's not like we're trying to kick (guests) out but they don't want to leave," Brown said. "They say they're so enamored of everything in the museum. Even our floors have history."
Over its four-year existence, the Water's Edge Museum has cultivated an abundance of programs and different galleries. Included in the galleries is the Environmental Justice as a Civil Right Galleries, where the museum presented photography, paintings, historic maps and high resolution cartography on how climate change is impacting underserved rural communities on the Chesapeake Bay.
In addition to celebrating the museum's four year anniversary, the team at Water's Edge will also honor Tish Moaney, who is described as the backbone of Oxford's Waters Church.
Moaney died this month, and in honor of her legacy the Water's Edge team will be playing some of her songs and a video.
Ja'lyn Hicks, curatorial and graphic designer for the museum, is a fourth generation native to the Eastern Shore. She said this museum empowered her to take pride in her community and embrace the stories of those around her.
More than anything, Hicks hopes the attendees of the event will find comfort in expressing and finding themselves especially during these unsure times.
"We are living in times that are hard and changing and there's a lot of uncertainty and there's also this fear that causes you to want to shrink into yourself and be like, 'I don't want to share my culture. I don't want to put myself out there. I don't know what's at risk by sharing my identity.' And so I'm hoping that by coming to our event, they feel that it's an environment where they can truly be themselves or even see themselves in some of the artwork," Hicks said.

title: Behind the scenes of a production about going behind the scenes
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Behind the scenes of a production about going behind the scenes

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 642
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — English playwright Michael Frayn's "Noises Off," opening Feb. 21 at the Garfield Center, is a play within a play. It features a troupe of American actors putting on a touring play called "Nothing On."In "Noises Off," the audience sees the dress rehearsal of "Nothing On" in Act I. In Act II, they witness the hilarious drama and tension between the actors backstage during the performance. Act III shows how things have comically deteriorated two months after opening night.
This meta storytelling offers an exaggerated glimpse of life backstage during theatrical productions. The play relies heavily on its set design.
Characters must time their responses perfectly, running through multiple doors in the proper English manor set. Like Kramer from "Seinfeld," but with a much larger cast of nine, they break windows, rush down steps, trip, slip, fall, scratch, drink and fight.
The set requires both an English manor setting and a backstage setting. It rotates between acts, with everything on rollers and interchangeable pieces from steps to platforms, all connected by pins and hinges.
"It is well-loved by professional and community theatre audiences, even though it requires a huge, two-story set that rotates between acts to show both the front and backstage areas of a touring play," according to a press release.
The interchangeable set requires meticulous planning and on-the-fly adjustments. Director and scenic designer Steven Arnold has extensive set design experience from his theater studies and his work on "The Play That Goes Wrong" in January 2022.
Like this story, that play featured a two-story set in an English manor. Arnold recalled that at one point, every item on the second story fell off the wall — from coat hooks to large chunks of the wall itself.
"The whole set was rigged," he said. In one scene, while actors stood on a platform, the floor was hinged to fall three times.
He said that while that was his craziest set, "Noises Off" might be the most complex to assemble.
The reason: doors are everywhere — upstairs, on the sides, in the attic, study, bathroom and bedrooms — with platforms and steps mirrored on both sides. Technicians are securing the set to the existing theater framework, and constructing railings and walls to ensure actor safety.
The set is tall enough that gallery viewers are level with actors on the second floor, Arnold noted.
His self-designed plans lie on a table beside the stage. Each floor plan was built to scale, with squares representing one foot, making construction easier for his contractor and workers.
Arnold praised his team: Butch Clark, contracted GCA technical director; Carmen Grasso, who has designed and built the "Noises Off" set for three previous productions; and Benji Price, theater assistant learning from both men.
Production stage manager Allison Jones is instrumental, Arnold said, along with construction help from Jeff Russell, Jim Landskroener and Jim Johnson.
The crew is working steadily on safety features so actors can begin rehearsing.
"The movement of this show is frantic and fast and can be dangerous unless what you have on this stage, with all its components, is solid, built well and safe to use," Arnold said.
Why tackle such an enormous project?
"It's a fun romp," Arnold said, grinning. He noted that audiences called "The Play That Goes Wrong" one of the funniest, most entertaining shows they'd seen.
The actors appreciate the elaborate set, which helps them stay in character, Grasso remarked.
It also helps the audience suspend disbelief and feel transported to a proper English manor.
"There are lots of places that ask their audience to use their full imagination. But when you can give your audience a big, grand set, they love it. It adds a different flavor to their experience," Arnold said.
"Noises Off" runs weekends from Feb. 21 through March 9. Shows are at 8 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays, and 2 p.m. Sundays. For tickets, visit garfieldcenter.org or call 410-810-2060 Wednesday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.
