title: Garlic to wasabi: Wild chocolate pairings give Valentine's a delicious twist
author: Robin Donovan Food Drink Life
content:
Garlic to wasabi: Wild chocolate pairings give Valentine's a delicious twist

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Robin Donovan Food Drink Life | Section: News 
 
 1158
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Chocolate-covered strawberries and hazelnut cream-filled truffles are classics, but why play it safe this Valentine's Day? There's a world of unconventional pairings that bring out chocolate's rich complexity in unexpected ways. Soy sauce, blue cheese or Kalamata olives may sound like strange partners for sweet chocolate, but that's the point — these daring pairings are bold and delicious, giving standard Valentine's Day offerings an exciting new twist.Why unusual chocolate pairings workThe magic behind these unconventional combinations lies in chocolate's unique chemical makeup. Cocoa contains both bitter compounds, like theobromine, and fats that mellow those sharp edges. When paired with salty, savory or even spicy flavors, chocolate's sweetness becomes more pronounced, and its richness shines through.
Scientists call this effect "taste contrast enhancement," where opposing flavors make each other more vibrant. According to a study in Flavour Journal, the interplay between sweet and savory flavors can enhance our taste experience. For instance, when you combine savory, meaty umami with sweetness, it creates a more complex and satisfying flavor profile.
Chocolate and cheese: A match worth melting forCheese boards and chocolate trays rarely mingle at the same table, but they should. Chocolate, especially dark chocolate with a hint of bitterness, pairs beautifully with creamy, tangy and even funky cheeses.
Take blue cheese, for instance. Its saltiness and pungent flavors contrast perfectly with the deep cocoa notes of dark chocolate. It's the same principle that makes salted caramel irresistible — sweetness tempered by salty and savory undertones.
For a milder approach, try rich brie with milk chocolate. These two creamy ingredients melt together into something unexpectedly lush. Add dried figs or almonds for texture, and you've got a dessert that could replace the standard cheese plate.
Chocolate and soy sauce: Sweet, salty and savorySoy sauce's salty umami highlights cocoa's natural sweetness without overpowering it. There's even a Japanese company that makes chocolate-flavored soy sauce, combining two fermented ingredients — cacao beans and soybeans — into one umami-rich seasoning.
A sprinkle of soy sauce over dark chocolate ice cream — or even just a square of good-quality dark chocolate — is transformative. The umami kicks in just as the chocolate dissolves, adding depth without excess salt. If you're feeling adventurous, a dash of soy sauce in a cup of hot chocolate lends a richer, more rounded flavor profile.
Chocolate and olive oil: A Mediterranean revelationOlive oil is celebrated as a base for salad dressings and marinades, but its potential in desserts is usually overlooked. Paired with dark chocolate, a fruity extra-virgin olive oil adds silky texture and subtle bitterness that enhance the chocolate's depth.
Drizzle olive oil over a slice of flourless chocolate cake, sprinkle with flaky sea salt, and you'll wonder why you haven't done it sooner. For an easy experiment, try dipping pieces of dark chocolate into a small dish of olive oil and topping with a pinch of salt. The combination is addictive.
Chocolate and chili: A kick of traditionWhile chili and chocolate might seem like a modern trend, the combination has ancient roots. The Aztecs and Mayans famously combined cacao with chili peppers to create a bitter, spicy drink known as "xocolatl." It's a powerhouse pairing, with chili enhancing chocolate's bitterness while adding a lingering heat that begs for another bite.
Spicy chili peppers pair best with dark chocolate that contains a high percentage of cocoa. A pinch of cayenne in a cup of hot chocolate is an easy way to test the waters, or you can try chili-dusted truffles for a fiery twist. Other spicy additions include ginger, pink peppercorns and cinnamon.
Chocolate and black garlic: The umami powerhouseBlack garlic might not be a pantry staple, but it deserves a spot on your experimental dessert list. It starts as fresh garlic — sharp and aromatic — and as it ages and ferments, develops a mellow, caramelized flavor.
"The sweet molasses and balsamic undertones in black garlic make it a great flavor addition to many desserts," according to Black Garlic North America, the continent's largest black garlic processor. It's sweet and sticky, similar to a raisin or date, making it a perfect complement to chocolate.
"One of the remarkable things about black garlic is just how many layers of flavor it has," says Katy Heath, founder of Balsajo, a black garlic producer in the United Kingdom. Try black garlic in chocolate ganache or as a secret addition to rich, fudgy brownies. It adds complexity without overwhelming the dish.
Chocolate and Kalamata olivesIf you're an olive lover, don't sleep on this combo. Dark chocolate has fruity notes that complement the saltiness of the olives, and the result is kind of mind-blowing.
"We all know how a pinch of sea salt can enhance dark chocolate, but just wait until you experience what black olives can do," says Food52 writer Cathleen Clarity, who uses Kalamata olives in her molten dark chocolate and black olive cake. "Their brininess and slightly bitter taste are the perfect complement to the molten dark chocolate."
Chocolate and matcha: An earthy fusionCombining chocolate with matcha, finely ground green tea powder, creates an intriguing flavor profile. The earthy bitterness of matcha complements the sweetness of chocolate, creating a delightful balance.
Matcha works especially well with white chocolate, known for its pronounced sweetness and creamy texture. Matcha's bitterness tempers the sweetness of white chocolate, while the chocolate's creaminess softens the tea's intensity, creating a smooth, complex and satisfying flavor profile.
Chocolate and wasabi: An unexpected heatPairing chocolate with wasabi, the Japanese horseradish commonly served with sushi, creates a surprising blend of sweet and spicy flavors. Wasabi's heat differs from that of chili peppers, hitting more in the nasal passages than on the tongue, and it dissipates more quickly. Wasabi cuts through the richness of the chocolate, exemplifying how contrasting flavors can both balance and accentuate each other.
White chocolate-coated wasabi peas capitalize on the addictive quality of the sweet-spicy, creamy-crunchy snack phenomenon. In Japan, you can even find wasabi and white chocolate KitKat bars made with wasabi from the Shizuoka prefecture, famous for its production of the spicy root.
To explore this combination at home, add a dollop of wasabi paste to chocolate ganache, hot fudge sauce or hot chocolate. Wasabi's heat sneaks up on you and can be quite potent, so start with a modest amount and adjust to taste.
The takeaway: Make bold moves this Valentine's DayWhen selecting a Valentine's gift this year, don't default to the same boring heart-shaped box of chocolates everyone goes for. Instead, surprise and delight your Valentine with unexpected chocolate pairings. If nothing else, these adventurous combinations are great conversation starters, and if they strike a chord with your sweetheart, they'll make the gesture — and you — unforgettable.
Robin Donovan is the author of more than 40 cookbooks and the founder and creator of All Ways Delicious, a food site loaded with easy recipes for the best dishes from around the world. Her writing and recipes have been featured in major media outlets including Huffington Post, MSN, Associated Press, Buzzfeed, Cooking Light, PopSugar, Chicago Sun-Times, Fitness, Parade, Mercury News and many others.

title: Julia Child's kitchen at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Julia Child's kitchen at the library

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 696
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Monday, March 3, at 6 p.m., in the Easton branch of the Talbot County Free Library, it will be my honor to interview Paula Johnson about her newest book, "Julia Child's Kitchen: The Design, Tools, Stories, and Legacy of an Iconic Space."Full disclosure: Johnson is a lifelong friend of mine. She is also a distinguished curator at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Among her many curatorial triumphs, it was Johnson and co-curator Rayna Green that brought Julia Child's kitchen to the museum in 2001. Almost a quarter of a century later, it remains one of that institution's most popular exhibits.
I was one of the lucky fellows who received a copy of Johnson's new book when it came out in October.
Initially, truth be told, I wasn't sure what I would think of a book about a kitchen, fool that I am. Anyone who knows Julia Child, read her books or watched her television shows, knows that a book about Julia Child's kitchen is a book about Julia Child.
It's been a long time since I've had so much fun reading a book.
And the word "fun" is apt. Again and again in the book, as people recall cooking with Child in her kitchen or a meal they shared there, the word they use to describe both their host and the place is "fun."
Which is not to say that serious labor did not take place in that kitchen.
The book makes it clear that Child and her husband Paul were both workhorses. In the early television shows, the sponsoring public television station, WGBH Boston, couldn't afford retakes or editing. Julia had to begin upon a complicated recipe, carry it through, instructing all along, and arrive at a finished product that she could take a bite out of in just 28 minutes flat. The cameras shut off at 28 minutes, and there was no going back.
To accomplish this feat of legerdemain, she and Paul would practice for hours at home before a show, choosing which elements of a recipe to demonstrate, deciding how to demonstrate those elements and carefully working out the language to use in explaining them.
The whole thing was choreographed from beginning to end and different stages of the cooking prepared in advance so that, "through the magic of TV," they could be displayed at the proper time as if just pulled from the oven.
Yet somehow, Julia always came across as relaxed and enjoying herself. And it wasn't a guise.
One of the things I found most endearing about "Julia Child's Kitchen" is the way sections on subjects such as the kitchen's organizing principles inevitably end up revealing the love Paul Child felt for his wife, the care he took in setting up that kitchen and showcasing her art. In letters to his brother, Paul sometimes referred to his wife as "Julie."
Julia called her kitchen "the soul of the house," and her nephew, Alex Prud'homme, called the table where meals were served in that kitchen "the center of the universe."
Unsurprisingly for that time and a family of their class, the Childs had a formal dining room, but Julia's preferred place to serve friends a meal was the kitchen. Julia's unpretentious attitude toward entertaining (and herself) is made clear in her explanation for the placement of that kitchen table, "I want the dining table in the middle of the room because, like a sheepdog, I need to be right there in the midst of everyone."
That statement is so characteristic of the woman we meet in Johnson's book. Julia Child never fails to charm, yet somehow she never seems to patronize or fawn.
The book itself is like a party at Julia's house. You meet fascinating people, hear terrific stories, experience a magical place, and, at the very least, get to imagine yourself enjoying extraordinary meals.
Speaking of stories, I can tell you from long experience that the author of "Julia Child's Kitchen" is a great storyteller in person as well as in her writing. And so I ask the pleasure of your company on March 3 at 6 p.m. for an evening in Julia Child's kitchen, courtesy of the Smithsonian's Paula Johnson. Trust me, you're in for a real treat.

author: Staff Writer

Cars, art and beyond: Academy Art Museum exhibit highlights Bugatti family's legacy

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 495
 Words 

 Read News Document

 "Bugatti: Reaching for Perfection", an exhibit highlighting the art, technology, race cars and automobiles of the Bugatti family, is currently open at the Academy Art Museum in Easton.AAM's Bugatti exhibit runs through April 13.
"This captivating exhibition showcases a rare collection of Bugatti automobiles, sculpture, and furniture, along with a trove of related ephemera that brings the Bugatti legacy to life. Highlights include five vintage Bugatti cars from the North Collection of Maryland's Eastern Shore, eight striking bronze sculptures from the Arsidi-Scuderi Collection of Switzerland, and iconic pieces of furniture designed by Carlo Bugatti, who pioneered a unique blend of artistic creativity and technical mastery. Visitors will also encounter rare photographs and advertisements, offering a deeper understanding of the Bugatti family's unparalleled influence on the worlds of art, design, and automotive innovation," according to an announcement from AAM.
"Ettore Bugatti, famous for his race cars and luxurious automobiles, and his son Jean, known for their forward-thinking designs, reshaped the world of automobiles into something that was both technically sophisticated and beautifully artistic. From grand prix race cars to the iconic Type 57 touring models and the miniature 'Baby' ugatti, the exhibition immerses visitors in the world of high-performance automobiles that symbolize the dynamic energy of the 20th century. This exhibition is not just about cars—it's a tribute to the intersection of art, engineering, and modernity that defined Bugatti's legacy," the AAM announcement continued.
AAM offers free admission and has a number of other events related to Bugatti exhibit and automobiles. Here is rundown from AAM.

title: Local artists win Poe awards
author: Staff Writer
content:
Local artists win Poe awards

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 214
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Local student artists from Kent Island High School captured all four finalist spots in the visual art category of the esteemed Saturday 'Visiter' Awards, presented by Poe Baltimore.The competition celebrates a new generation of artists inspired by Edgar Allan Poe's life and works, honoring creativity in media, art, performance, and writing.
The awards ceremony took place at Westminster Hall & Burying Ground in Baltimore — an iconic "Poe Place." The evening included a catacomb tour and a murder mystery event to commemorate what would have been Poe's 216th birthday.
Student finalists, are senior Brooke Register, junior Alexis Detamore, junior Grace Hartlove, and senior Mark Monroe, who claimed the top honor with a mixed media piece, "No Pain; I Am Done," inspired by Poe's tale "The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar."
KIHS Art Department Chair Andrea Schulte said, "Mark was awarded $1,879 and a commemorative plaque in recognition of this achievement."
The Saturday 'Visiter' Awards are named for the periodical that famously launched Edgar Allan Poe's literary career. Poe won the original award for his short story "MS Found in a Bottle" while living in Baltimore. Today, the awards recognize works that adapt Poe's life or writings and original works inspired by his legacy, continuing to celebrate his profound influence on the arts and literature worldwide.

title: 14-year-old on his way to becoming a minister
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
14-year-old on his way to becoming a minister

 February 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 786
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Javion Jones has been living his life through God since a very young age.When Javion was just 5 years old, his mother Taryn Bell can recall him setting up his toy cars, pencils, and decks of cards as his congregation to preach too.
"He would take number two pencils, and that was his church," Bell said. "He would sit there and preach to the pencil or if there were toy busses he used to have little toy cars, that was his church. Or he would play with just playing cards. I mean, I would have cards all spread out."
Now at just 14 years old Javion is further along in his career choice than most others his age. He works at Benny Smith Funeral Home as an assistant, and he is a minister in training at Union Baptist Church.
His potential for the craft was discovered years ago by many former Pastors of the church but Rev. Demetruis A. Price truly took Javion under his wings.
The Rev. Demetrius A. Price, pastor of Union Baptist Church, came to Easton from Washington, D.C., in May 2023.
Early in his time at the church, Price was going over the schedule for the installation service and wanted to have every age group accounted for. A member of the church suggested Javion to pray.
During the prayer, Price said he saw the anointing of God upon Javion's life.
"When he prayed, I felt and saw the anointing of God upon his life, and I knew right then and there that God had called him into the ministry," Price said.
PATH TO MINISTRYWhen Price arrived at Union Baptist Church, he asked God to allow him to be able to pour back into someone young who came into ministry young, just like him.
"I come to this church, and I see a country church, family church, different than across the bridge, and I'm like, 'why here?'" Price said. "And then when I met Javion, then I realized God had answered my prayer."
Price was called to ministry at 16, a couple years older than Javion. He knew what Javion would face and wanted to be there for him.
Javion's call to ministry was no surprise to anyone, but Javion didn't think it would come so soon.
"I was listening to two preachers one night," Javion said. "I was like, 'man, I want to be like them.' So the Lord had just spoke this to me. He was like, 'you're called. I'm walking to your calling.' Never to know that this calling would be so soon. I thought, like, I would be preaching at the age of like 20."
Bell was very happy that Price was here at the church when Javion got the call. She was not surprised that her son was called to ministry but she was happy that Price was here to mentor him.
"I think I always knew," Bell said. "I always knew he had it in him. So when Rev. Price and I talked, I felt so proud. I was happy that Rev. Price had came to me and told me his story and wanted to put Javion under his wing."
Javion's new position, minister in training, is difficult. He is in a rigorous year-long course in which he must learn the Bible and other essential lessons. When he is finished in April, he must do a trial sermon.
Also with his role, he is a regular minister in rotation at his church. He is in rotation with other ministers to get up on Sunday mornings and read scriptures and pray. He also will go to the hospital to visit sick or shut-in church members.
When Javion graduates the class, he will know everything that it takes to properly conduct himself as a minster.
Being a minister in training and a assistant at a funeral home is a lot of responsibility for a 14-year-old, but Price believes he can handle the sacrifices and the responsibility.
"That was the one thing that really amazed me with him, and again, I think it spoke to really his anointing," Price said. "Because when a person is anointed to do a work, with the anointing comes capacity to do it, and that's what I notice about him. The boy goes to school, he works with the funeral homes, and if he's not in this church, he's in somebody else's church."
The most challenging and most rewarding part for Javion is the responsibility of educating his peers. He says when he started ninth grade at Easton High School, everyone including students and teachers, called him "preacher" because of the way he carried himself.
The way Javion wants to engage his peers is to teach them the word of God.
"The word of God is how I can touch a generation," he said.

title: Academy Art Museum adds trustees
author: Staff Writer
content:
Academy Art Museum adds trustees

 February 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 582
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Academy Art Museum in Easton has elected four new trustees to serve on its board — Ron Flohr, Denise Grant, Victoria Gomez-Lozano and Holly Townsend."We are delighted to have this talented group of Trustees join our Board and are grateful for their commitment to furthering the Academy Art Museum's mission of making art available to everyone on the Eastern Shore," Board Chair Donna Alpi said.
Here are biographies of the four trustees provided by AAM in a press release.
Ron Flohr has more than 20 years of experience in financial services. As a Certified Financial Planner, his professional focus is to work with individuals and businesses to identify their financial goals and customize investment and wealth management strategies to achieve them. An active community member, Ron has served as president of the Easton Waterfowl Festival, a past board member of the Easton Rotary Club, the Mid Shore Early Learning Center, a past board member and president of the Talbot Country Club and a past board member and commodore of the Chesapeake Bay Yacht Club.
Denise Grant is an accomplished executive with over 30 years of experience developing strategies and implementing solutions in the corporate, public and social impact sectors around the world. She is the founder and CEO of Overlook Strategies and serves as a Senior Advisor to Heidrick & Struggles, the leadership and organizational consulting firm. She has worked with boards and CEOs of some of the world's most high-profile NGOs and social impact organizations on a wide range of matters. She has led broad organizational assessments and initiatives, counseled boards regarding governance and other matters, and conducted top leadership succession projects. Early in her career, Denise practiced law for nearly a decade, including as an attorney with Morgan, Lewis & Bockius LLP. Denise is a Presidentially appointed Trustee of the Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board which governs the nearly $500 million global Fulbright cultural and educational diplomacy program. She has served as a Trustee at Transylvania University and on numerous Boards of Directors including the Wolf Trap Foundation for the Performing Arts, the Bryce Harlow Foundation, the Avalon Foundation and the East Tennessee State University Development Corporation.
Victoria Gomez Lozano was born and raised in Chihuahua, Mexico and has lived in the United States for 16 years. She is a graduate of Tecnologico Espiritu Santo, Guayaquil, with a Banking and Finance degree. During her career in the fields of banking and industry, she realized her desire to serve the people in her community as a leader, mentor and interpreter. Now in her sixth year as a member of the Chesapeake Multicultural Center's administrative staff, she serves as their Hispanic Outreach Coordinator. Victoria has served on the board of Talbot County Public School's Education Foundation Board, Talbot Mentors, and the East-End Neighborhood Association. She is currently the Board Chair of the Department of Social Services.
Holly Townsend is the founder of the Townsend Group, a company that provided a variety of services designed to increase non-dues revenues for associations and foundations. These services included sales, custom research, video production, cross-platform media programs, creative services and financial services. As its President and CEO for 35 years, she set the company vision, made all strategic decisions, and oversaw all business operations. Her clients included scores of national blue-chip associations and foundations in a wide range of industries and professions including housing, education, healthcare, the arts, design, architecture and urban planning, engineering, criminal justice, and law. Holly previously served on the Board of Trustees of the Avalon Foundation.

title: 'Symmetrical Bodies' on display at St. Mary's College
author: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com
content:
'Symmetrical Bodies' on display at St. Mary's College

 February 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 491
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Longtime St. Mary's College of Maryland art professor Susan R. Johnson remembered the impact that her mother and Hollywood actresses had on her family growing up in Los Angeles, and through the first week of March guests and students will have the chance to get a glimpse of that impact on full display.Earlier this month on a Tuesday afternoon inside the genuinely cozy confines of the Boyden Art Gallery inside the Montgomery Hall on campus, Johnson spoke to a gathering of students and guests to discuss the recent unveiling of her new exhibit "Symmetrical Bodies."
The new show features super-lifelike images of women in various roles adorned on material typically relegated to banners and flags.
"Throughout the centuries there have been so many ways that women have been photographed and visualized in advertisements," said Johnson, who moved from New Jersey in 1993 to begin her teaching career at St. Mary's College. "A lot of them were featured in so many ways in magazines and on postcards and it's amazing to see how the images have changed over the centuries."
As Johnson noted in her presentation to the audience last Tuesday, her "Symmetrical Bodies" project draws inspiration from the ideal of body symmetry, an unattainable perfection and beauty that contrasts with the reality of human diversity. Her work will be displayed on the walls of the Boyden Art Gallery through March 7, offering onlookers to see and appreciate her concepts.
"My mother was a big influence on me in every aspect of my life," Johnson said. "We grew up in Los Angeles, so Hollywood was a big influence on my mom. You can see in the objects that I created, images of Judy Garland, Audrey Hepburn and Liz Taylor, and none of them really appear as though we remember them because each side of their face is different from the other."
In addition to the symmetrical images, the portraits are done on a cloth material that naturally blurs the images. While photos and drawings are basically crystal clear by design on post cards and magazines, Johnson's works on material designed for other purposes, purposely blurs the images of each of the females she has highlighted on works in the gallery.
"In actuality, the images of the women are larger than life," Johnson said. "There is symmetry, but their images are far from perfect and there is a blurred effect created by the material. But that is also done by design. It is meant to highlight the fact that there is no perfect body symmetry. We always look for perfection, but it is really not attainable."
If you go
The new art exhibit "Symmetrical Bodies" created by St. Mary's College of Maryland art professor Susan R. Johnson will be on display in the Boyden Art Gallery located inside the Montgomery Hall, which is on campus of St. Mary's College. For more information regarding the exhibit and operating hours, contact the school during business hours at 410-895-2000 or go to www.smcm.edu/boyden-gallery.

title: 'Subversive' exhibit pushes the boundaries of fiber and thread art'
author: Staff Writer
content:
'Subversive' exhibit pushes the boundaries of fiber and thread art'

 February 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 929
 Words 

 Read News Document

 "The Subversive Thread" — an exhibit and series of events at the Academy Art Museum — "showcases four artists who challenge the conventional boundaries of fiber and thread art."That is according to an announcement from the downtown Easton museum.
"The Submersive Thread" features fiber and threadworks by Han Cao, Jennifer McBrien, Michael-Birch Pierce, and Stacey Lee Webber. The exhibit runs through March 30
Here is rundown of the artists and their work, according to the AAM announcement.
Han Cao infuses found photos with modern narratives, using needlework to add texture and depth. Each piece invites viewers to engage intimately, bridging past and present through stitches that connect distant figures to contemporary observers. Cao's sense of humor adds another layer of depth to her work: through subtle nuances and playful elements, she examines conventional perceptions and invites viewers to approach her artwork with curiosity and joy.i
Jennifer McBrien's striking Warrior Women series features a dramatic departure from the typical confines of embroidery hoops, with vintage toile curtain panels cascading freely from their frames. McBrien's hybrid figures, merging avian and female forms, symbolize the fragility of endangered species, evolving alongside the deteriorating fabric. Complementing the series is the poignant installation Hanging Them Out to Dry, a visceral commentary on the plight of endangered birds. Hung on a clothesline, embroidered vintage napkins evoke a sense of vulnerability, emphasizing the urgent need for conservation efforts to safeguard threatened species from extinction.
Michael-Birch Pierce explores identity through embroidery, blending traditional techniques with contemporary themes. At the heart of Pierce's practice lies an intimate exploration of the self and the narratives chosen to weave around it. Through the medium of embroidery, Pierce delves into the layers of identity, often cloaking their creations in the superficial trappings of high fashion and costume. Their work challenges notions of authenticity, inviting viewers to peel back layers of artifice and notice the essence beneath.
Stacey Lee Webber's choice of American currency as a medium is particularly poignant. By stitching directly onto artifacts of commerce, she forges a tangible connection between past and present, laborer and leader. Ultimately, the act of embroidering through dollar bills becomes an act of defiance — a subversion of the traditional notions of value and representation, making symbols of capitalism available for introspection and critique.
The exhibition is organized in conjunction with the Museum's 27th Annual Craft Show in October. "represents a pioneering initiative for AAM as it embarks on a new path to integrate exhibitions of contemporary craft into its well-established 3-day event. The Museum seeks to enrich the visitor's experience by showcasing examples of modern craft alongside traditional work."
This exhibition was made possible through Westobou Gallery in Augusta, Georgia.
There are a number of other upcoming events at the Easton museum. according to AAM.
AAM Film Series: Unraveling Narratives
Now through March, 2025
(Film pass: $25 members, $35 non-members, per film $10 members,$15 non-members, includes beer and popcorn for members, $5 non-members) .
Dive into the themes of The Subversive Thread exhibition through Unraveling Narratives, a curated monthly film series that brings fiber art's cultural intersections to the screen. Join us for thought-provoking documentaries and narrative features, followed by facilitated discussions connecting the films' stories to the exhibition's exploration of fiber, craft, and culture. From powerful documentaries like Yarn to artist profiles like Outsider: The Life and Art of Judith Scott, this series invites audiences to experience fiber art in an entirely new dimension. Screenings are open to all, with refreshments provided for post-film discussions.
The Subversive Thread Art Cart: Stitching Stories
Every Thursday through March 27, 5-7 pm
Explore the art of embroidery and its connection to storytelling, line drawing, and mark-making. Throughout the exhibition's run, this mobile art-making station will be available to invite visitors to experiment with embroidery techniques. Inspired by the work of fiber artists featured in The Subversive Thread, this drop-in program offers examples of stitches and materials for creating your own textile art. Whether you're a seasoned stitcher or new to fiber arts, this hands-on experience brings a tactile dimension to the exhibition's themes of identity, craft, and creativity.
The Subversive Thread Art Cart: Stitching Stories with Jennifer McBrien
Thursday, February 13, 4:30 - 7 pm
Don't miss the chance to stitch with The Subversive Thread artist Jennifer McBrien at the Art Cart! Whether you're new to embroidery or an experienced stitcher, Jennifer will guide you through basic techniques or help you bring your own design to life. Additionally, please feel free to bring a piece of fabric and a concept to work on. Jennifer will be in the gallery from 4:30 pm until the "Threads of Disruption" lecture.
Threads of Disruption: A Contemporary Craft Conversation
Thursday, February 13, 6 pm
The exhibition's featured artists—Han Cao, Jennifer McBrien, Michael-Birch Pierce, and Stacey Lee Webber—share their unique approaches to fiber and thread art. This dynamic event begins with four mini-presentations from each artist, offering personal insights into their creative processes and the themes driving their work. Following these presentations, a lively discussion, led by the exhibition's curator, will explore the thematic connections of identity, subversion, and value that unite the artists' practices while highlighting the unique perspectives that set each artist apart. The evening concludes with an open Q&A session, offering an opportunity for meaningful dialogue with the artists.
Threads of Sound: Improvisational Music Inspired by The Subversive Thread
Friday, March 28, 5:30–7:30 pm
Experience the intersection of art and music with musicians Robert Hitz and Felicia Harrington in a dynamic, live musical experience directly responding to the textures, narratives, and themes of the exhibition. Guided by the exhibition's curator, this performance will explore the dialogue between visual and auditory art forms, weaving together an evening of creativity, inspiration, and discovery.

title: Dorchester County auctioneer earns state title after serious injury
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Dorchester County auctioneer earns state title after serious injury

 February 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 707
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Dave Yearsley has put in the hard work and overcome challenges to continue on with his love for auctioneering.From winning a competition with a 103 degree fever that was so bad he could barely see the bidders to becoming the 2025 Maryland Bid Calling Champion after experiencing a truck accident that resulted in a brain injury, Yearsley has persevered for his passion.
Since his first auction at the Ward World Championship in the early 1970s — when he was just a preteen — Yearsley, a Dorchester County resident, has auctioneered all over, from Texas to Missouri to the United Arab Emirates.
It all started with a daring decision.
Yearsley was 11 years old when he entered "the ugliest duck you ever saw" into a competition at the Ward World Championship, he said. His parents took him to the event in Salisbury, which also had an antique decoy auction. Sitting in the stands as Walton P. Taylor auctioned off antique decoys, Yearsley noticed Taylor's rhythm and told himself, "Wow, that's something I gotta learn to do."
"So I went home and I practiced all year long," Yearsley said, "and was terrible."
The next year, Yearsley was back at the championship with his parents and another "ugly duck" he had carved.
"So I'm 12," he recalled. "I got away from my mom and dad on purpose because I knew what I was going to do."
Yearsley ducked under a roped off area where the auctioneer, Taylor, was. With security guards watching, he went up to Taylor and shook his hand. "And I said, 'Mr. Taylor, my name's Dave Yearsley, and I want to sell decoys with you today.'"
After what felt to Yearsley like "the longest minute," Taylor said, "Young man, anybody that's got the guts to stand in front of me, you're damn right you're going to sell ducks with me today."
At this point, Yearsley's parents were searching for their son. Yearsley's mom was not happy when she found him onstage.
"She came racing up in front of the stage," Yearsley recalled. "'David, you get down here right now!' (she said)."
When Yearsley asked Taylor what he should do, Taylor replied, "It's time for you to learn not to listen to your parents."
From there, Taylor took Yearsley under his wing.
"He was my mentor," Yearsley said.
It took Yearsley two years to "get somewhat competent" at auctioneering, he said. To improve his speed, he practiced over instrumental bluegrass music.
"Instrumental bluegrass music has a definite beat," he said, adding that he got every instrumental bluegrass album he could to practice over.
In auction school, Yearsley learned tongue twisters, like "Betty Botter bought some butter," to improve his craft.
AGAINST THE ODDS
In September 2018, Yearsley got into a serious truck accident. His vehicle rolled over and he came out of it with a brain injury. It was possible he would not be able to walk or talk again. Eventually, both abilities came back to him, although his speech would slur.
"I didn't have good tongue control," he said.
Yearsley was told he would probably never be able to auction again. He said his doctor told him to keep trying because practicing might help bring back the skill.
"And that's what happened," Yearsley said.
In January, Yearsley was named Maryland's Bid Calling Champion by the Auctioneers Association of Maryland.
Lynne Zink, a past president of the association and the chair of the contest, said the annual competition brings auctioneers from across the state to vie for the title.
"Once someone has won the championship, then they don't get to compete again," she said. "So David will always be our 2025 champion."
Yearsley didn't think he would win it.
"I don't cry much — and I didn't let anybody see me do it — but I cried," he said about his response to winning the award. "I said, 'My god, how could I ever do this?'"
Yearsley wasn't the only one to shed a tear after he won. Zink, who is also an auctioneer and has known Yearsley for years, was happy to see Yearsley win the Maryland title.
"Whenever you see something like that, it's encouraging because he can be a role model for others," she said. "So when the doctors give you a prognosis and then you beat the odds, gosh, it makes everybody happy. Some of us were teared up."

title: Real or not, Chessie the sea monster is part of Maryland culture
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Real or not, Chessie the sea monster is part of Maryland culture

 February 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 607
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — In the late 1970s and early 1980s, the Chesapeake Bay gained a mystery.Multiple sitings of an unknown creature stirred concern and intrigue that a sea monster lurked in Maryland and Virginia's waters.
During a presentation at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum Thursday evening, historian Eric A. Cheezum talked about the "thoroughly modern monster," putting its discovery in context of the times.
Cheezum started off his presentation with a grainy video that fills the screen with blue. Despite the video's poor quality, many in the audience of the event thought they saw something moving in the video.
Taken of the Bay off Kent Island on Memorial Day in 1982, the grainy video launched Chessie "into the international firmament of cryptozoology," or the study of hidden animals, Cheezum said. Although it was not the first Chessie siting, it was a big moment in Maryland pop culture.
Chessie has been described as long, dark creature, smooth like a snake, that moves fast through the water in a motion that is different than other serpents.
Robert and Karen Frew, the couple who captured the video of who they believe was Chessie, were "relatively new transplants" to Kent Island, Cheezum said. They had a waterfront home, and, for them, the Bay was a place for recreation.
Cheezum considers the video camera the most notable part of the Frews' story. He said that having a camera on the Eastern Shore in 1982 was "at least as rare as a sea monster" due to the wealth necessary to afford it.
The video camera was a symbol of the change happening on the Eastern Shore.
After World War II, the areas surrounding the Chesapeake Bay developed very fast, Cheezum said. "And suddenly you have people in rural places who have never been in those places before," he said.
The shoreline also started to shift from a place of work to a place for recreation. Almost all the people who claimed to have seen Chessie were on the Bay for recreation, not watermen who had been working on the water for generations.
Cheezum said this falls into the theme of "natives versus outsiders," with the outsiders being tourists and suburbanites. He also noted that at the time of these sitings, movies like "Jaws" and "Piranha" were popular.
Amateur Chessie investigator Wayne Lawson said the reason watermen didn't see Chessie in the water was because they they weren't sitting there, scanning the water. They had work to do.
In 1993, a manatee was discovered in the Bay after it swam up the coast, Cheezum said. The manatee, which made this journey more than once, was named Chessie.
Cheezum said he thinks there's a strong likelihood the people who spotted Chessie were actually seeing manatees.
"I hate being that on the nose," he said. "Because I want to believe too."
But, even if the creature was a manatee, it has shaped Maryland culture. Cheezum mentioned the Chessie-shaped boats that people can take out in Baltimore's Inner Harbor. He talked about a children's book featuring Chessie that aimed to teach kids the importance of protecting the environment.
In the 1970s, Marylanders started to appreciate the Bay and its heritage more, Cheezum said.
"And Chessie somehow seems to kind of sum all that up," he said, "which is really weird because there's about a million other things that could sum up the Bay besides a sea monster."
After Cheezum's presentation, Joseph Kempf — who now believes Chessie was a manatee that people mistook for a sea monster — asked why watermen never saw Chessie if the creature had been a manatee the whole time.
Cheezum replied that people see what they want to see.
"The thing that is observed is shaped by the observer," he said.

title: Country Cooking: Inventive recipes from the 1940s
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Inventive recipes from the 1940s

 February 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1294
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Yes, it is that time of year again. And I do not mean Super Bowl, or Valentine's Day or tax time. It is a time that I let slip by quietly.I was born on Feb. 11, 194... My mother told me it was 3 degrees that February morning. I was born at home, so that meant the doctor traveled across town on snow- and ice-covered roads. My sister was 10 years old and at that time. I already had six older brothers, soon to be followed by three more brothers.
My sister's birthday was Feb. 15, and she did not want to share birthday parties. Some world and national news in the 1940s included the Italian partisans killed Mussolini, Hitler committing suicide after destroying major cities in Germany, World War II ending, Harry Truman taking the office of President after Roosevelt passed away.
Not only were things hard on our Bishopville farm, but the whole world was feeling the impact of World War 2. Creativity blossomed during the Great Depression and carried on into the 1940s.
The decade of the 1940s brought many things to our world: The microwave oven, ball point pens, Velcro, Tupperware and the frozen orange juice.
History has shown us again and again that financial hardship drives people to get a little more inventive in the kitchen.
Wartime rations necessitated substitutes and ingredient-stretching techniques. As a matter of fact, on the back of my birth certificate are stamps for sugar and flour. Thankfully, my parents never needed to use them.
After the war ended, food manufacturers explored methods that gave products a longer shelf life. During the latter half of the decade, more convenience products arrived on shelves as scientists delved into researching food preservation.
Like most 1940s recipes, meatloaf experienced a resurgence in popularity during the Great Depression. The use of bread or cracker crumbs helped stretch the ground beef as it was getting harder and harder to come by.
When the soldiers came back home from the Pacific they also brought home a love of SPAM. Philippines, Guam, Hawaii and Okinawa were places Spam was the most popular. Most of the time eggs were mixed with Spam because they were cheap and most everyone had chickens in the backyard.
"Victory Gardens" were another big thing in the 1940s. Many papers circulated various vegetable recipes. Soups and stews were cost-effective meals that could also stretch more precious ingredients such as meat and dairy.
No bake cookies that used things such as Corn flakes were served in just about all houses, even the White House.
One invention that has surely at one time or another been in just about everyone's hands — the corn dog — was created by German immigrants in Texas, who were sausage-makers finding resistance to the sausages they used to make. They have been credited with introducing the corn dog to the United States in the early 1920s, though the serving stick came later.
Carl and Neil Fletcher can claim that having introduced their "Corny Dogs" at the State Fair of Texas sometime in 1942. In 1946, on Muscle Beach in Santa Monica, California, Dave Barham opened the first Hot Dog on a Stick location.
So, as you see, the corn dog has a long disputed history, but boy are we glad to have it.
Here are some recipes from the 1940s this week to not only celebrate my birthday but to revisit a time where counting every penny and getting creative was a must.
HOMEMADE CORN DOGS1 cup yellow cornmeal, 1 cup all-purpose flour, ¼ cup white sugar, 4 tsps baking powder, ¼ tsp salt, ⅛ tsp black pepper, 1 cup milk, 1 egg, 1 quart vegetable oil for frying, 2 (16-oz) packages beef frankfurters, a pack of wooden skewers.
Combine cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, salt and pepper in a medium bowl; stir in milk and egg to make a batter. Heat oil in a deep fryer or large saucepan to 375 degrees, pat frankfurters dry and insert a skewer into each one, roll frankfurters in batter until well coated. Fry two or three corn dogs at a time in preheated oil until lightly browned, about 3 minutes. Drain on paper towels.
1940s BROWN SUGAR MEATLOAFCooking spray, ½ cup packed brown sugar, ½ cup ketchup, 1 ½ lbs lean ground beef, 2 large eggs, 1 small onion (chopped), ¾ cup milk, ¾ cup finely crushed saltine cracker crumbs, 1 ½ tsps salt, ¼ tsp ground black pepper, ¼ tsp ground ginger.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Lightly grease a 5-by-9-inch loaf pan. Press brown sugar into the bottom of the prepared loaf pan and spread ketchup over sugar. Mix all remaining ingredients thoroughly in a mixing bowl and shape into a loaf. Place on top of the ketchup and sugar crust. Bake in the preheated oven for 1 hour or until juices are clear.
SPAM AND EGGS2 large eggs (beaten), 1 container fully cooked luncheon meat, 2 oz Cheddar cheese (grated).
Cube the meat. Heat a nonstick skillet over medium heat. Pour eggs into the skillet, then scatter luncheon meat over top. Cook and stir until eggs are nearly set, 3 to 4 minutes. Sprinkle cheese over top and stir until cheese is melted, 1 to 2 minutes.
GARDEN FRESH TOMATO SOUP4 cups chopped fresh tomatoes, 2 cups chicken broth, 4 cloves garlic, 1 large slice of onion, 2 tbsps butter, 2 tbsps all-purpose flour, 2 tsps white sugar to taste, 1 tsp salt to taste.
Combine tomatoes, chicken broth, garlic cloves and a large slice of onion in a stockpot over medium heat. Bring to a boil, and gently simmer for about 20 minutes to blend flavors. Remove from heat and run the mixture through a food mill into a large bowl or pan, Melt butter over medium heat in the now empty stockpot. Stir in flour to make a roux by cooking, whisking constantly, until the mixture turns medium brown. Gradually whisk in a bit of the tomato mixture to prevent lumps from forming, then stir in the rest. Season with sugar and salt to taste.
NO BAKE COOKIES½ cup white sugar, ½ cup light corn syrup, 2 tbsps butter, ½ cup peanut butter, 3 cups of corn flakes cereal.
Bring sugar and corn syrup to a boil in a saucepan over medium heat. Stir in butter and peanut butter until thoroughly combined, then remove from the heat. Place cornflakes into a large bowl. Pour peanut butter mixture over top and mix until cornflakes are well coated. Drop 1-tablespoon scoops of the mixture onto a waxed-paper lined baking sheet. Flatten slightly if desired, then allow to cool for 30 minutes before serving.
STUFFED PEPPERS
1 cup cold water,½ cup uncooked long grain white rice,1 tablespoon vegetable oil,1 pound ground beef,6 medium green bell peppers,16 ounces tomato sauce, divided,1 tablespoon Worcestershire sauce,¼ teaspoon garlic powder,¼ teaspoon onion powder, salt and ground black pepper to taste,1 teaspoon Italian seasoning. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Bring water and rice to a boil in a covered saucepan. Reduce heat to low and simmer until rice is tender, about 20 minutes. Meanwhile, heat oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add ground beef and cook until evenly browned and crumbly, 7 to 9 minutes. Hollow out bell peppers by removing and discarding the tops, seeds, and membranes. Slice the bottoms of the peppers if necessary to make sure they stand up straight. Arrange peppers in a baking dish with the hollowed sides facing upward. Prepare filling by mixing cooked beef, cooked rice, 1/2 of the tomato sauce, Worcestershire sauce, garlic powder, onion powder, salt, and pepper. Spoon an equal amount of filling into each hollowed pepper. Mix remaining tomato sauce and Italian seasoning in a bowl, and pour over the stuffed peppers. Bake in the preheated oven, basting with sauce every 15 minutes, until peppers are tender, about 1 hour. 

 © Copyright © 2025 Star Democrat, Chesapeake Publishing Group (Adams Publishing/APGMedia). All rights reserved.

title: Chef of St. Michaels restaurant named James Beard semi-finalist
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Chef of St. Michaels restaurant named James Beard semi-finalist

 February 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 571
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After the cold temperatures of a January morning cut his hunting plans short, Ruse executive chef and partner Michael Correll went home to take a nap before work.When he woke up, text messages from the restaurant's partners were blowing up his phone. Then the general manager of The Wildset Hotel — which houses the restaurant in St. Michaels — called.
"So my first thought is something's wrong," Correll said.
When he picked up the phone, the general manager congratulated him. Correll had been named a semi-finalist of the James Beard Award for best chef in the Mid-Atlantic.
"I was just numb," Correll said about how he felt when he learned the news. He called his mom, who started crying.
"It's the biggest accomplishment an American chef can have," Correll said. "I mean, besides Michelin Guide, James Beard is like the biggest one."
Established in 1990, the James Beard Awards recognize leaders in the culinary arts and food media industries, according to the James Beard Foundation's website. He said the day after he received the news, the entire restaurant cheered for him during happy hour.
"I think the coolest thing about the whole process is just the outpouring of love from people," he said. "Like people I haven't talked to in a long time, people who I didn't even know knew me, people just reaching out."
Correll has been serving elevated fare, switching up menus by the season and scouring the area for the best seafood since Ruse opened on Talbot Street in 2021. From the start, the restaurant aimed to bring a Washington, D.C., caliber of dining to the heart of St. Michaels, focusing on sustainable seafood and local ingredients, Correll said.
For Correll, inspiration comes from trying different foods and keeping a finger on the pulse.
"The restaurant industry is constantly evolving and changing, so it's just being aware of what's going on," he said. "But also it's like, you have to put your own flair on it."
That inspiration doesn't just come from fine dining. Correll said inspiration can come from any good flavor combination. He said he was inspired to create a steak tartare dish after eating a carne asada taco with salsa roja.
When it comes to the quality of seafood, Correll sources from different places to ensure it's fresh.
"I do things the hard way," he said. "Which is like, I find a guy who sells the best of something, and I buy that from that person. ... Just because that's how you get the best product. You have to work for it."
Allie Balin, Ruse's food and beverage director, said Correll and the entire restaurant is all about supporting local watermen, farmers and small businesses. She said Correll is collaborative when it comes to developing the menu too.
"Anyone who's involved in any artistic pursuit, getting feedback on what you're creating can be challenging," she said. "And Mike takes it extremely well. His goal is just to create the best possible product."
As someone who played sports when he was younger, Correll sees the kitchen as a team sport of sorts. He said that a team mentality makes a kitchen successful.
"I think that's what makes us special is the team," he said. "Because, I'm not trying to brag, but food's always going to be good. But the team is what takes it to the next level."
Correll said he will find out in April if he made it to the final round of the James Beard Awards.

title: Frederick Douglass' Valentine's Day birthday honored by his family
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Frederick Douglass' Valentine's Day birthday honored by his family

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 686
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Frederick Douglass never knew his exact birthday.Like many born into slavery, the exact date was never recorded. Douglass knew it was sometime in February but not the exact day.
Douglass chose to celebrate on Valentine's Day because his mother called him her "little Valentine."
"Yes, he celebrated his birthday on Valentine's Day," Douglass' five-time great nephew Tarence Bailey Sr. said. "Feb. 14 through Feb. 20, you can say it's the most important week of Black History Month because that's the week of Frederick Douglass' birth and death."
Douglass has strong roots in Talbot County and throughout the Eastern Shore.
Born in Talbot County in 1818, Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey Douglass was enslaved for 20 years in Baltimore and on Talbot County farms. He fled north in 1838 and changed his name to Frederick Douglass. His brilliance, eloquence and courage, quickly brought him to the forefront of the abolitionist movement.
He was known for his skills as an orator, with many of his speeches remembered to this day.
"He spoke in Denton on Halloween 1883, and Douglas took the train from Wilmington to Denton," author and historian John Muller said. "Then when he was leaving and he spoke in front of the County Courthouse in Denton... there was so many people they didn't fit inside. The crowd had to go outside."
According to Muller, Douglass also spoke in Cambridge, St. Michaels, and many more Eastern Shore locales.
Douglass and his work are inspirational to many Americans, but it goes deeper than just inspiration for the Bailey-Groce Family Foundation, Bailey said.
The Bailey-Groce Family Foundation is run by multiple Douglass family members who grew up on the Eastern Shore. It is one of two family foundations operated by descendants of the Douglass bloodline.
"I think for my family here from Talbot County and from Eastern Shore as a whole, it's a whole lot different for us," Bailey said. "Being raised on the Shore and then having the relative like him, you look at it differently than the average person does."
Three years ago, the foundation started hosting a birthday celebration for Fredrick Douglas between Feb. 14 and 20, close to his birthday and the anniversary of his death. This year's celebration will be held on Feb. 22 due to a scheduling conflict.
The birthday celebration is held to help fundraise for an African American Cultural Center and an African American Historical Society, institutions the foundation plans to establish in Talbot County.
The event will begin at the historic Avalon Theatre at 3:45 p.m.
This year's event will feature a homecoming performance by Ayla Dennis, who was featured on American Idol.
"She's actually a Bailey family descendant," Bailey said. "So it's going to be a history making to have her singing at the Avalon, which was a formerly segregated theater down the street from where the slave auction once was, right there by the courthouse where Frederick Douglass spoke, having his relatives actually headlining for his birthday in a formerly segregated theater."
Other entertainment for Douglass' birthday celebration includes a county group from Atlanta, Georgia; a concert violinist from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; a featured poet from Brooklyn, New York; and many more.
After the performances, the foundation will host a VIP dinner at the Waterfowl Building in Easton. The foundation wants everyone to wear African-style clothing to honor Douglass' heritage.
"Frederick Douglass was a very classy dude. We like to keep his birthday the way he would want it," Bailey said. "He was John Q when it came to his clothes. Everything he wore was Brooks Brothers. So he was always dressed to the nines. So I know that at his birthday party, he would want everybody in there dressed as well as him."
The Foundation continues to host these types of events not just to raise funds, but to keep Douglass' legacy alive, Bailey said.
"Uncle Frederick is the main reason, the only reason that I that keeps me going, that keeps me pushing," Bailey Sr. said. "The goal is much bigger, Fredrick Douglass himself is the inspiration, because if it wasn't for him I don't know if we would have made it this far."
For more information about the celebration or to purchase tickets, visit avalonfoundation.org/events.

title: Chesapeake legacy honored at Frederick Douglass Day Celebration
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Chesapeake legacy honored at Frederick Douglass Day Celebration

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 355
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Leaders in maritime heritage, arts and social justice gathered at Washington College for the annual Frederick Douglass Day of Acknowledgement, celebrating African American contributions to the Chesapeake Bay region.The ceremony, co-hosted by Washington College and Bayside H.O.Y.A.S (Helping Our Youth Achieve Success) at the Decker Theatre on campus, opened with Maryland Public Television's Emmy-winning documentary "Water's Edge: Black Watermen of the Chesapeake".
Film Director Alexis Aggrey joined a panel discussion alongside Salisbury University Professor Emerita Clara Small, Minorities in Aquaculture CEO Imani Black, and fifth-generation fisherman Capt. Tyrone Meredith. Artist Marc Castelli and Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum Chief Historian Pete Lesher rounded out the panel examining the bay's role as an economic and cultural cornerstone for African Americans.
Composer Marlon Saunders performed selections from "ISAAC: A Musical Journey," commissioned by the Kent Cultural Alliance. The work chronicles Isaac Mason's escape from slavery in Chestertown and his emergence as a community leader.
This year's Frederick Douglass awards recognized Rev. James Jones, convener of Caucus of African American Leaders on the Eastern Shore; Vincent Leggett, author and founder of Blacks of the Chesapeake Foundation; and Saunders, founder of The Seamless Voice.
Social media influencer Tyshawn "YVNG SWAG" Johnson received the Bayside H.O.Y.A.S Shooting Star award. The 25-year-old entertainer, known for his role on Nick Cannon's Wild 'N Out and various brand partnerships, represents a modern parallel to Douglass's own mastery of public image.
Johnson's family, including two sisters and one brother, are all from the Chestertown area and attended schools here. Even before signing a record deal, (he signed with Atlantic Records as a high school senior) Johnson had an active Facebook and Instagram account with thousands of followers. A video of him dancing reached 1 million views on Instagram over the summer of 2016.
The honorees reflect Douglass's diverse legacy, from his early exposure to maritime life near Wye Mills to his later emergence as a prominent public figure who skillfully managed his public persona.
"This was the best event yet," said John Queen, H.O.Y.A.S. president. "The documentary and panel were greatly received. People absolutely loved the Marlon Saunders performance, and the award recipients are always top-tier community leaders and class acts."

title: New sculptures enhance Chestertown's public art collection
author: Staff Writer
content:
New sculptures enhance Chestertown's public art collection

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 255
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Four new sculptures from the Peter and Hanna Woicke Collection have arrived in town, with one already installed and three awaiting placement."Super Duty Yellow," created in 2013 by American artist Jeremy Thomas, now stands in Gateway Park at Route 20 and Flatland Road. Thomas crafted the abstract piece by welding metal sheets together and inflating them with forced air, creating forms that evoke everything from birthday balloons to fortune cookies.
The remaining three pieces are temporarily housed at Robert Ortiz Studios, 207 S. Cross St., where the public can view them weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to noon and 1:30 to 5:30 p.m., and Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
"Inchworm (for John Coltrane)," a 2000 work by Lee Kelly, features swirling Cor-Ten steel forms that echo the jazz legend's fluid playing style. The piece's steel wheels offer a subtle nod to Coltrane's nickname, "Trane."
Don Rambadt's "Woicke's Owl," commissioned by the collectors in 2000, continues the artist's minimalist approach to bird sculptures, similar to his local works "Sentinel" at the Cerino Center and "Strength of Community" at Cannon and Mill streets.
"Fully Empowered" by Maryland artist Ella Tulin was featured in the United Nations' "Progress of the World's Women" exhibit in 2000. The 1987 sculpture represents Tulin's significant contribution to the feminist art movement.
The Woicke Collection, now fully gifted to the town, comprises 23 pieces from American and international artists. The Public Arts Committee works with town officials to place the sculptures throughout Chestertown, with installation handled by local artisans Ben Herr, Mat Warrington and Rob Glebe.

title: 5th annual Fire & Ice Festival a success despite weather challenges
author: Konner Metz
content:
5th annual Fire & Ice Festival a success despite weather challenges

 February 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 629
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — With ice sculptures positioned at restaurants, stores and downtown landmarks, many Easton residents and visitors enjoyed the fifth annual Chesapeake Fire & Ice Festival last weekend.Friday brought clear skies for the event's opening night, while Saturday attendees endured rainy conditions. Despite the suboptimal weather Saturday, festival organizers say it was a success.
Holly DeKarske, executive director of the Easton Economic Development Corporation, said solid crowds made their way to the festival Saturday before the afternoon rain hit.
There were over 60 ice sculptures around town, including a firetruck and firefighter in front of Easton's Town Hall. Attendees watched the firetruck carving process happen Friday evening.
"We had more ice this year," DeKarske said. "And it was spread out from The Market at Dover Station down to Talbot Town (Shopping Center) all the way down to The Academy (Art Museum). So it was nice to get traffic walking and flowing all through town."
In the Waterfowl Festival building on South Harrison Street, children enjoyed crafts. Across the way, many gathered around fire pits for food, drinks and games. St. Michaels-based Lyon Rum served cocktails and Delmarva Craft offered local wines and beers.
DeKarske said the fire pavilion was a major addition to this year's festival, especially as people looked for cover from the rain.
"It worked out really well, and we'd like to do that again," DeKarske said. "People seemed to really enjoy that, and being able to have the music right there and have a beer garden. We had some snack food, but of course, we want you to go and eat at the restaurants."
With five years of Chesapeake Fire & Ice complete, DeKarske hopes it can grow in the future. She pointed out that she'd like to see not just more locals, but more out-of-town visitors in attendance.
"It's also great to have people from out of town who will spend the night in our hotels," DeKarske said. "And that brings in accommodations tax, which helps fund the county and our municipalities. It's great to bring those dollars in."
Adding a day onto the festival schedule is a possibility, she said.
"If we can find a way to maybe expand into Sunday a little bit to encourage sort of that two-night stay, it'd be great," DeKarske said. "And just help to sort of feed the tax base here, which would be nice."
Carlos Mir, known by his stage name of "Cascading Carlos," has performed at the festival since its inception. The skilled juggler and two-time Guinness World Record holder was at his usual spot last weekend, Thompson Park at the corner of Dover and Washington streets.
Mir performed for festivalgoers, including many families, spinning and juggling fire. Easton residents Sara Guest and Jude Spillman were the two of the first to watch Mir work his magic Friday evening.
Mir said the first annual Chesapeake Fire & Ice Festival was a hit. He recalled crowds of people filling up the grass around Thompson Park and standing on the brick walls.
"The way they kicked it off, it was the first year, everything seemed to be like, it was a novelty," Mir said. " … The success of that one, I came back the next year. And I did Friday night and Saturday."
The skilled performer has been back every year since. Mir said it's an "awesome event" put on by organizers and the Town of Easton.
As evening turned to night Friday, more attendees gathered at Thompson Park to get a close look at Mir's performance.
Mir said his favorite part about the event is interacting with the audience, especially children.
"You just look at everyone playing with analog," Mir said. "They're playing with toys, they're not on the digital end of it. And you just see it. I just love that aspect of the juggling and what I can offer to people."

author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:

 February 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Read News Document

 History was brought to life with a performance telling the story of Harriet Tubman, an Eastern Shore native and one of the most significant abolitionists of her era.The Friends of Maxwell Hall, a group dedicated to preserving and bringing to light the history of the hall, put on a performance Feb. 15 featuring Shemika Renee, a first-person historical performer,
Mike Callahan, a member of the Friends of Maxwell Hall, shared a little bit of the property's history with Southern Maryland News.
The historic property was built by George Maxwell, a Scottish immigrant, approximately 255 years ago. Maxwell was a merchant and sold goods to local people and had grown tobacco on his property.
The house, situated on the Star Spangled Banner Trail, was in despair by the 1980s with holes in the ceiling and was purchased and remodeled to become the landmark it is today.
While Maxwell enslaved people, the story told at the house was one of triumph.
Renee delivered a riveting telling of Tubman's life through her perspective.
Renee started her performance by detailing the early years of Tubman, including her life-changing traumatic head injury that caused severe headaches throughout her life and narcolepsy.
She detailed how Tubman actually became "Harriet Tubman" as it was not her given birth name. Tubman was born Araminta Ross and had the nickname "Minty."
When she was older, she took her mother's name — Harriet — and her husband's last name of "Tubman" and became Harriet Tubman.
"I wanted to be free," Renee said while in character. "I will never forget that first sunrise when I knew I had crossed the border. … It was like the sun was gleaming down through the leaves, and the gold was just shining on my hands."
Echoing Tubman's actions of constantly going back to help family, friends and others find freedom, Tubman said, "I feel that I could have saved so many more people if they had even known that they was in bondage."
The Friends of Maxwell Hall hosts an annual colonial fair the third weekend of October every year, spirit investigations and a variety of other events. To find out more, go to www.friendsofmh.com/events.

title: Trapping on the Eastern Shore (copy)
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Trapping on the Eastern Shore (copy)

 February 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1623
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Back in the late 1950s and early 1960s, my younger brother Ollie would trap and hunt whatever was in season.My dad was very happy when he came home with rabbits and squirrels. The only thing he could not get my dad to eat was the muskrat, better known as the marsh rabbit.
He sold the meat to local folks who loved it, and mom loved it because he sold them as fast as he trapped them.
My brother would save the hides and stretch them on a special piece of board designed to fit the hide. He had them drying out for a certain number of days and then would package them up and ship them to his buyer.
His buyer was the late Mr. Clark Harrison Sr. of Preston. After several shipments, Mr. Harrison would send my brother a check.
Years ago, I contacted Mr. Harrison and told him the story of my 14-year-old brother, who later retired from the United States Army and did three tours of duty in Vietnam. I will dedicate today's column to those two men — the late Clark Harrison Sr. and Ollie Lowe Hitchens Jr.
Along the Eastern Shore, trapping traditions have been passed down to sons, grandsons and nephews. Living here and working on the water or in the fields near huge ditch banks, it was only natural for these locals to trap muskrats.
They'd set their traps, then go to work farming or crabbing then check the traps for an extra bounty. The muskrat numbers were once estimated to be in the millions here on the Eastern Shore, but that number soon dwindled, as you can imagine with all the trapping.
Just the sight of these animals was enough for me with the fur on, let alone skinning and cooking them.
You guessed it — I've never tasted muskrat, but I've cooked it. The first one I ever cooked was right in my Preston Road kitchen under the guidance of my late husband, John Williamson Sr., who loved them.
JOHN R.'S FAVORITE MUSKRATTrap, clean and cut muskrat in half. Soak in a large pot of cold, salted water for several hours — changing water several times. Finally, after draining well, place the meat in a large pot, cover with water, bring to a boil, boiling for 5 minutes. Remove meat from the pot, rinse and clean out the pot well. Then spray the pot with a non-sticking spray, add the meat, half cover with water. Cook until meat falls apart. Add to taste: sage, red pepper, salt and bacon or sausage grease. Don't be afraid of adding any of these ingredients and just keep adding until you can taste all of them. Cook down as much as you want but do not let it cook dry. Serve with a favorite potato dish of your choice and a green vegetable.
MUSKRAT STEWClean, cut in pieces and soak three muskrats in cold water and salt. After at least two hours, drain water off and rinse meat well. In a large pot, place the meat and just enough water to cover them. Add 2 teaspoons ground sage, 1/2 teaspoon bacon grease, salt and pepper to taste. Let cook over medium heat for 4 to 5 hours. Start on high heat until it starts boiling, then reduce heat to simmering. Let cook until meat is falling off the bone. Serve over cooked rice.
FRIED MARSH RABBITClean, cut up and soak one or two marsh rabbits in salty water for several hours — changing water several times. Rinse well in several changes of water. Remove from water and pat dry. In a large bowl add flour, sage, salt and pepper. Dredge the pieces of meat in the flour mixture and place in a fry pan with cooking oil and add 2 or 3 strips of bacon. Brown on both sides, adding more sage if needed. When meat is browned on both sides, add some water to the pan, turn heat down and let simmer as the meat becomes tender and a gravy forms.
BISHOPVILLE BULLFROG LEGS2 lb or 14 sets fresh or frozen frog legs, 1/3 cups milk, 2/3 cups corn flour, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp red pepper, shortening, or cooking oil for deep frying, lemon halves, 1/2 tsp accent food enhancer, 1/2 tsp garlic powder.
In a medium bowl combine corn flour, salt, pepper, accent and garlic powder. Coat Frog legs with corn flour mixture, In a saucepan or deep fryer heat about 2 inches melted shortening or cooking oil to 375 degrees. Fry coated frog legs a few at a time in deep hot oil for 1 to 2 minutes or until done. Drain on paper towels.
HOPPING JOHN WITH VENISON2 full deer shanks, 1 tbsp oil, 1 tbsp your favorite All spice blend, 1 tsp salt, 4 cups beef stock, 3 garlic cloves (smashed), 1 celery stalk (chopped). Hoppin' John: ½ pound of dried black-eyed peas, 3 strips of bacon (chopped), ½ cup diced onion, ½ cup diced bell pepper, 1 clove garlic (minced), 1 celery stalk (diced), 3 cups of the reserved braising liquid, 2 tbsp your favorite All spice blend, 2 tsp salt, 1 cup of yellow rice (rinsed and drained), thinly sliced scallions for garnish. Bring a large pan to high heat on the stove. Rub the shanks with oil, All spice blend and salt. Once the pan is hot, sear each side of the shanks. Turn on the slow cooker and set it to low. Place the seared shanks inside and add the stock, garlic and celery. Allow the mixture to cook for 8 hours or until the meat falls off the bone. I cooked mine overnight. Once cooked, remove the meat from the slow cooker and set it aside. Strain and reserve the braising liquid for the next steps. For the Hoppin' John, place the black-eyed peas into a bowl and cover them with water. Allow them to sit while you complete the following steps. Bring the Dutch over to medium-high heat and stir in the chopped bacon. Brown the bacon and then remove bacon from the pan, leaving the grease behind. Stir in the onion, bell pepper, celery and garlic. Cook, frequently stirring, until the onion turns opaque.
Drain the remaining water from the black-eyed peas. Stir the peas into the pot. Add three cups of the braising liquid from the deer shanks, the All spice blend and salt. Bring the mixture to a boil, reduce the heat to low, cover, and allow to simmer for 45-60 minutes or until the peas begin to soften. You do not want them to completely cook. While waiting, shred the deer meat. When the peas are al dente, there should be about two cups of liquid remaining. Add more if needed. Stir in the rice and the shredded deer and bring the mixture back to a simmer. Cover and allow to cook for 20 minutes or until the rice is done. Serve with the sliced green onions atop, along with some biscuits.
RABBIT STEW3-4 pounds rabbit, 6 potatoes (quartered), 8 carrots (sliced), 1 medium onion (chopped), 1 tsp salt, 1/4 cup beef consommé, 3/4 cup beef broth, 3/4 tsp pepper, 1/4 tsp basil, 2 bay leaves, 1/4 tsp rosemary, 1/4 tsp thyme. Cut rabbit into pieces. Layer onion, potatoes and carrots in the bottom of a crock pot. Add spices to the pot. Add rabbit, salt, pepper, consommé and about 3/4 cup beef broth. Cover and cook on low for 8 hours. Thicken gravy as desired.
BRAISED RABBIT2 rabbits cut into serving pieces, 1/4 pound bacon, 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 medium onion (sliced into half-moons), 1 head garlic (cloves peeled but not chopped), white part of a fennel bulb (chopped roughly), a handful of dried mushrooms, 1/2 pound fresh mushrooms, 3 bay leaves, 1 tbsp dried oregano, 1 tsp fennel seeds, 3 cups good stock (chicken or vegetable), 5 spring onions, 1 cup finely chopped fennel fronds, 2 tbsp fresh chopped oregano, salt. Cook the dried mushrooms in 2 cups of hot water. Let them sit, covered, for at least 1 hour. Heat the olive oil in a Dutch oven and cook bacon until crispy. Remove the bacon and turn the heat up to medium-high. Salt the rabbit pieces and brown them well. Add the chopped onion, fennel bulb and the dried mushrooms and saute until they begin to brown. Add the fresh mushrooms and garlic and saute until they begin to brown. Add salt. Add the Armagnac and stir well to combine.
Turn the heat all the way up and add back the rabbit, the bacon, and add the bay leaves, fennel seeds and dried oregano and mix well. Pour in just enough stock just to cover the rabbit. Do not totally submerge it. Bring to a simmer, taste for salt (add more if need be), cover and set over low heat for an hour, or 45 minutes if you are using chicken or domestic rabbit. After an hour, test to see if the meat is tender. You want it to be practically falling off the bone. At this point you can pull the rabbit from the pot, remove from the bone and add back to the pot or keep it in the pot on bone. Add the green onions, garlic and fennel fronds and stir to combine. Simmer uncovered for 3 minutes or until you believe it is done. Be careful to not overcook.
There are a few opportunities coming up for you to enjoy a great muskrat dinner without having to stare down skinned muskrats. This year, the 76th annual National Outdoor Show will be held Feb. 21 and 22, located at the South Dorchester K-8 school at 3485 Golden Hill Rd. in Church Creek. The muskrat will be served on Saturday only at 1 p.m.

author: Staff Writer
