title: A New-Englander brings her poetry to the Eastern Shore
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
A New-Englander brings her poetry to the Eastern Shore

 April 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Columns 
 
 731
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Poetry is a funny thing. Really, it's a shape-shifter.I'm a little slow when it comes to poems. I can only read one at a time and can only do that when I have the time to really give the poem the attention it deserves — which sadly, even in retirement, seems to happen less and less often these days.
That "shape-shifter" remark is the result of Sue Ellen Thompson's poem "The Nest," published in her most recent book, "Sea Nettles" (811.54 Thom).
I read "The Nest" for the first time, I don't know, maybe a week or two ago. Sitting by the fire, a glass of bourbon on the table beside me, I made my way through its three simple verses and was pleased.
The first and third verses were spot on, but I sort of slid over the second. On the whole, I thought it a good poem, if perhaps not one of Sue Ellen's best. I am a big Sue Ellen Thompson fan. She is far and away one of my favorite poets.
But I also know myself well enough not to trust a first reading. Even mid-poem, my mind can wander and miss something important. Maybe it's the bourbon.
Anyway, last night I gave "The Nest" a second chance. And I thank the nine muses that I did.
The poem concerns something with which I am all too familiar these days: aging — a pair of older friends, husband and wife. He is just out of the hospital and visibly reduced by his illness. She is worried, attentive. That second verse I blew over in my first reading ends with a sentence describing the wife:
Her features still have their fine,
flared edge, but fear of losing him
has made their beauty more difficult
to admire, like the silver serving dish,
its surface battered by knives.
My brain's voice-over tends toward exclamation, and this line elicited an unqualified "Oh my God!"
I mean, where do poets come up with analogies like that? Who would ever think to compare the damage fear can effect upon a well-preserved beauty to a silver serving dish? But isn't it perfect? Think about the women you've known who have lived long enough and loved well enough to know what losing the love of their life will cost them. For that matter, think about the men.
A silver serving dish battered by knives. I'd give my left arm to come up with a simile like that, and I coasted right over it on my first reading, missed it entirely. Shape-shifters indeed.
Though I suspect Sue Ellen will always be a New Englander at heart (and there is, I believe, something austere and flinty about her writing that, to my Southern ear, smacks of the Northeast), she has now lived in Talbot County for almost 20 years.
Anyone who's ever swum in the Chesapeake will recognize in the title of her latest book the influence our region now holds upon her as well. What a gift it is to have a poet of her accomplishments living here. Her readings at the Avalon, her lectures at the Talbot County Free Library, the classes she teaches — she has enriched our lives.
Not too long ago, I shot Sue Ellen an email extolling Jane Hirshfield's poetry and thanking her for introducing me to that wonderful writer. Sue Ellen, ever generous, replied that Hirshfield is, in her opinion, an "essential poet." I love that phrase, that idea, that there are poets out there that are essential, necessary, like oxygen or water.
In her anthology, "The Autumn House Anthology of Contemporary American Poetry" (811.508 AUTU), Sue Ellen has introduced me to any number of "essential poets" — Doug Anderson, Hayden Carruth, Robert Hass, Maxine Kumin, Sharon Olds and Jane Kenyon come immediately to mind.
But there is of course another. The Eastern Shore holds many treasures, but surely one of them is Sue Ellen Thompson.
On Monday, April 14, at 6 p.m. in the Easton branch of the Talbot County Free Library, Sue Ellen will present a combination lecture/reading she's entitled "Writing About Family." If you know her poetry, I'm sure you have been struck, as I have been, by how candidly and unflinchingly Sue Ellen writes about those she loves.
I am very much looking forward to hearing how she manages to handle such volatile material without damaging the very relationships she seeks to honor.
Oh, and don't forget: April is National Poetry Month. See you in the 800s.

title: Easton teen's pursuit of music takes her to contests, college and American Idol
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Easton teen's pursuit of music takes her to contests, college and American Idol

 April 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 514
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At 12-years-old, Easton resident Ayla Dennis' singing hobby became an aspiration."My mom introduced me to music," Dennis said. "We always would sing and dance around the house, but as I got older and I'd say about 12, I just started singing and realized there was something here."
Quiana Handy, Dennis' mother, said Dennis was introverted when she was younger. One day Handy picked Dennis up from middle school and noticed Dennis singing in the back seat. Handy then continued to notice Dennis singing and eventually asked her, "Have you thought about singing?"
Handy heard about a voice competition in Cambridge, and she registered Dennis for it. Dennis was the only child in the competition. She won first place.
Dennis, now 18 and a freshman at Salisbury University, has sung at multiple different events and competitions since. She made it past auditions on American Idol.
After her first competition, Handy and Dennis began posting clips of her singing online, which gained traction locally and nationally. The posts led to American Idol reaching out.
"I got like a DM (direct message) on Instagram, and they're basically telling me how much they liked me as an artist," Dennis said. "I auditioned, and I was 16. I went through the first audition, and then we did the audition in California."
Dennis moved on to "Hollywood Week," the second round of auditions where final competitors are selected, where she was sent home. Her audition never aired.
But while her journey on American Idol was quick, she credits the experience for many lessons.
"It was a super quick American Idol journey, but it also taught me a lot," Dennis said. "It taught me how to not listen to other people and also being comfortable with feedback because you get a lot of feedback."
While attending Salisbury University, Dennis plans to hone in her singing and songwriting skills. Her goal is to be a singer and songwriter.
She has continued in singing competitions at Salisbury, and she recently competed in the National Association of Teachers of Singers competitions, where she won first place in regionals competing in commercial singing.
While Dennis has teachers and peers who help her, she credits her mother as her biggest motivator.
"Growing up with a single mother has been challenging," Dennis said. "My mother has shaped me into the young woman and artist that I am today."
"I am incredibly grateful for my mother because she has never tried to change me," she said. "Instead, she has always encouraged me to be my authentic self and has supported me in everything I wanted to pursue."
Handy credits Dennis for taking on a lot of responsibility and helping push her to continue being the mom she is today.
"I call Ayla my gem," Handy said. "She truly is perfect. It has been very challenging, Ayla has always been like the other parent in the household, helping with her her brother and her sister, and I just I'm forever grateful for her.
"There's no way I can ever thank her enough. She always says how I help and push her, but she doesn't know that she's done the same for me."

title: KCHS students perform with professional musicians
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
KCHS students perform with professional musicians

 April 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 556
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL— Kent's Got Talent was the annual event the night before, but at the Mainstay, on Sunday, Kent County High School students showed they have plenty of talent to spare.The group of talented musicians earned an impressive $1,900 for their free-to-the public fundraiser: Generations Band Together, sponsored by the High School Music Boosters program, a group of parents and alumni students who provide physical and financial support for all the music programs at Kent County High School.
"Generations Band Together," is a talented collaboration of professional musicians and five accomplished high school band students. They had practiced for two months on multiple styles of music, from the band Chicago to Herbie Hancock to Mozart.
The band members are Beckett Vivier, alto sax and drums; Phoebe Preston, clarinet; Teo O'Brien, tenor sax; Lynden Saunders, piano; and Bjorn Birkmire, trombone. Adult players include Philip Dutton, vocals; Dave Sharp, bass; Frank Gerber, drums; Nevin Dawson, strings; Mark Quigley, guitar; Sem Ortiz, vocals; and Dave James, volunteer band leader.
James said to a crowd buzzing with anticipation, he has three goals playing with the students.
To have fun playing music, to see the joy in them when they play and learn music, and to thank those who support the music.
With sentimentalities aside, they showed versatility that practicing once a week as a group can do for already talented musicians, performing 14 numbers that evening.
Herbie Hancock's "Cantaloupe Island" started things off with a steady, smooth beat to get the audience in the mood. Then Ortiz sung "From the Start," by Icelandic singer-songwriter Lauffey. She went right into "The Girl From Ipanema" by Stan Getz, convincing the crowd to sway.
In "Daydream by Design" by Gaby Moreno, Vivier portrayed his versatility leaving his sax behind for the drums in a jazz type piece with mellow percussions accompanied by somber, beautiful violins. Frank Sinatra fans enjoyed mouthing along to "Fly me to the Moon," as well as some other well-thought pieces.
After a 10-minute intermission, the audience was treated to a duet of strings and clarinet, four numbers of Mozart's 12 duets, performed by Dawson and Preston. The crowd clapped and tapped their feet to "C-jam Blues," in the style of Duke Ellington and Mile's Davis' "Freddy Freeloader."
The afternoon culminated with an amazing rendition of the rock and roll classic, Chicago's "25 or 6 to 4," driven by the drums, while leaving plenty of jam room for explosive solos featuring every musician — closing out with Gerber's own solo. The crowd gave them a standing ovation, a well-earned, well deserved response to the show.
This is their third performance and more are planned.
The money raised by the Boosters will go toward a litany of items including band uniforms, gloves, shoes, ribbons, transportation, meals, instrument accessories and anything and everything in between.
Money will go toward their annual bus trip, this time to Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, which cost $12,000 for the bus.
Kent County Commissioner Ron Fithian was in attendance and enjoyed the music. The commissioners were thanked during the proceedings for providing $1,000 during one of their regular meetings in March.
Other than musical fundraisers, the Boosters raise money by selling concessions in school events, conduct car washes, paint nights and hunt down community grants. Their annual concert, "Seasonal Sensations," is a holiday dinner and music event that draws a great number of support from the community as well.

title: Country Cooking: Guest cook shares memories and recipes of Dad
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Guest cook shares memories and recipes of Dad

 April 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1283
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Today's guest host is my son, John, who remembers my days in the kitchen cooking food that his father liked even though I may have not ever eaten.Most of the time, my son would taste them at least, even though I might not, and sometimes he loved them. Even though his dad died 31 years ago, the recipes are still occasionally cooked and never forgotten.
So, in memory of John R. Williamson, a Korean War veteran, let's get started.
FRIED GREEN TOMATOES
Each year, my dad looked forward to the tomatoes fresh from our garden. As soon as the green ones appeared, the fried green tomatoes that we all loved appeared on the table.
6 green tomatoes, 2/3 cup flour, salt, pepper, 1/2 cup milk, 4 tbsps butter.
Cut tomatoes into 1/2-inch slices after washing them well. In a bowl, mix together flour, salt and pepper to taste, and milk. Melt butter — or use oil — in a fry pan. Coat the tomato slices on both sides with the flour mixture and place in the heated oil. Fry on both sides until lightly browned. Drain on paper towels, keeping warm until served.
Use the remaining flour mixture to make a gravy in the fry pan drippings, stirring quickly to keep from burning — removing from heat when slightly thickened. At this point you can add sugar if you like. I like mine as is with a little spicy mayo.
SWEET POTATO PIE
My dad would eat cake or cookies, but he loved homemade pie of any type. Mom would always make pies "from scratch" for the family for this reason. One of his favorites was sweet potato pie.
THE CRUST: mix 4 cups flour, 1 1/2 cups shortening, 1 tablespoon white sugar and dash of salt, Set aside. Then mix 1 beaten egg with 1/2 cup cold water and 1 tbsp vinegar. Combine flour mixture with egg mixture and mix into dough. This will make 5 to 6 (9 inch) size crust. Store left-over dough, wrapped in saran wrap, in the refrigerator.
FILLING: Cream together 1 stick softened butter with 1/2 cup brown sugar and add 2 cups mashed sweet potatoes and 3 slightly beaten eggs. Mix well and add 1/3 cup corn syrup, 1 can evaporated milk, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp lemon extract, and 1 tsp vanilla. Mix well and pour into unbaked pie crust. Bake in preheated 425-degree oven for 10 minutes, reduce heat to 350 degrees and continue to bake for 45 to 50 minutes . Remove from the oven and sprinkle with nutmeg to taste.
SWEET POTATO BUSCUITS
While we are on the subject of Sweet Potatoes, Mom's sweet potato biscuit recipe was one of Dad's favorites and mine too.
2 1/2 cups biscuit mix, 1/3 cup soft butter, 1 cup mashed sweet potato, 1/2 cup milk.
Preheat oven to 450 degrees. Combine biscuit mix with butter, sweet potato and milk. Mix until soft dough forms. Pour dough onto a lightly floured surface, knead 3 to 4 times only. Break off balls of dough, shape into biscuits and place in an ungreased baking pan. Make about 18 biscuits, and bake for 10 to 12 minutes.
OYSTER STUFFING
Oyster stuffing was another one of Dad's favorites and was present at every holiday dinner.
1/2 cup chopped celery, 1/2 cup chopped onions, 1 bay leaf, 1/4 cup butter, 6 cups dry breadcrumbs, 1 tbsp dry parsley, 3 cups fresh shucked oysters, 2 beaten eggs, 1 tsp poultry seasoning, 1 tsp salt, dash black pepper.
In a medium saucepan cook celery, onions, bay leaf and butter, but do not brown. Discard the bay leaf and stir in breadcrumbs and parsley. Drain the juice from oysters, reserving the juice. Mix oysters in breadcrumbs along with eggs, poultry seasoning, salt and pepper. Mix lightly and add some of the reserved oyster juice, if necessary, for a moist dressing. Stuff the bird — turkey or oven stuffer hen — with this mixture or bake in a casserole dish. If stuffing a bird bake according to package directions or bake at 375 degrees for 30 to 35 minutes in a casserole dish.
OYSTER FRITTERS
For as long as I can remember, my dad loved oyster fritters. Whether from carnivals, church Sunday dinners or home made by my Mom, you'd find him with a stack. He would buy a bushel of fresh-dredged oysters and opened them as needed, and my mom would make the fritters.
1/2 cup flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp salt, 1/8 tsp pepper, 1 beaten egg, 1/2 cup milk, 1-1 1/2 pints fresh oysters.
In a large bowl, mix flour, baking powder, salt and pepper. In another bowl mix together egg and milk. Combine the dry ingredients with the egg mixture and stir until you have a smooth batter. Gently stir in oysters, adding additional reserved oyster liquor if needed. Pour oil in a large fry pan over medium high heat, using a large spoon drop in hot oil. Fry until golden brown, about 3 to 4 minutes on each side. Serve hot.
LIVER AND ONIONS
This is the one dish my parents didn't make me eat when they had it. I can still see the purplish brown meat laying on the cutting board waiting to be cooked. I did try it a few times but couldn't do it. Still can't.
LIVER: ⅓ cup cooking oil, 1 lb calf beef liver, 1½ cups all purpose flour, 1½ tsp salt, 1 tsp pepper, 1 tsp onion powder, ¼ tsp garlic powder, ½ tsp paprika, 1 sliced large onion. GRAVY: 2 tbsps of seasoned flour reserved from dredging the liver meat, 1½ cup water, ½ cup milk.
Preheat a large skillet over medium heat; add cooking oil and heat to 350 degrees. In a shallow dish, mix the flour, salt, pepper, onion powder, garlic powder and paprika. Dredge the liver slices in the seasoned flour, shaking off excess. If you wish to cut the liver slices in half, do so while in flour mixture as it is easier to handle without tearing the meat. Place the dredged liver slices into the skillet. Reserve a couple tablespoons of the seasoned flour for gravy and discard the rest. Sear the liver slices for 3-4 minutes per side until browned (overcooking can make liver tough). Remove from the pan and set aside on a paper-towel-lined sheet pan to remove excess grease. Next, add the onions and cook until softened or caramelized (about 5 minutes), stirring occasionally. Be sure to scrape the tasty bits from the bottom of the skillet. Next, add 2 tbsps of the reserved seasoned flour to the pan with the onions and stir to incorporate with the onions and pan drippings. Allow the mixture to cook for 2-3 minutes. Add the water and milk to the pan and stir to combine with the onion and flour mixture. The gravy will not be thick at this time. Return the liver to the skillet and reduce the heat to medium low and simmer for 20 minutes until the gravy is thickened. Taste the gravy and adjust seasonings if necessary. Serve liver, onions and hot gravy with your favorite sides. On our table was usually some sort of green veggie like green beans, string beans, collard greens with vinegar. Liver night was the night I ate bologna and cheese.
Black eyed peas on New Year's Day, Muskrat, rabbit, squirrel just about any wild game my father loved. A true lover of Eastern Shore of Maryland cuisine, most of this stuff he carried with him through the years. Growing up poor in a large family, dinner was whatever they caught, grew, trapped or shot. Ice water or a cup of coffee was the usual drink and sometimes a Coca Cola.
I hope you enjoyed these recipes and a few stories about my father.

title: 'Urban Landscapes' exhibit at AAM
author: Staff report
content:
'Urban Landscapes' exhibit at AAM

 April 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff report | Section: Entertainment 
 
 400
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Academy Art Museum is hosting a new exhibit "Richard Estes: Urban Landscapes", featuring cityscapes from Richard Estes.Estes is "one of the founding figures of photorealism," according to announcement from the Easton art museum.
The exhibit kicks off May 1 with an opening reception at AAM from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. and runs through Aug. 3.
"With twenty-five meticulously rendered paintings and prints spanning the 1980s through the early 2000s, this exhibition captures Estes' lifelong fascination with reflective surfaces, architectural symmetry, and the fleeting beauty of the everyday urban environment," AAM said in the announcement.
"Rendered with astonishing technical precision, Estes' images transport viewers into gleaming storefronts, glassy façades, and layered streetscapes—most often set in New York City—that are at once familiar and surreal. His work challenges traditional notions of landscape, offering instead a vision of place that fuses photography, memory, and hyper-observation. Though far from the Eastern Shore, Estes' worlds reflect back on our own, inviting fresh ways of seeing the places we inhabit," the announcement continues.
The exhibition is organized by the Portland Museum of Art in Maine and is supported by Art Bridges.
AAM is also hosting a number of other events including its Spring Gala on May 3. Here is rundown of the events from the Easton museum.
Spring Gala: Reflections & ConnectionsSaturday, May 3, 6 p.m.
Inspired by the sharp realism of Richard Estes: Urban Landscapes, this year's Spring Gala transforms an industrial warehouse just north of Easton into a sleek, city-loft experience. Guests will enjoy immersive projections, an original soundscape by local talent Kentavius Jones, bold cuisine by Gourmet by the Bay, and a special announcement about the Museum's upcoming Freeman Annex and Hormel Research Center. Join us for an unforgettable night where art ignites conversation, where every ticket fuels the Academy Art Museum's future, ensuring that the doors stay open, the lights stay on, and the museum remains free for all.
Reflections/Connections: Public Recording SessionsJune 28 & 29, 1–4 p.m.
Musician Kentavius Jones and his band will record original music and ambient sounds inspired by Estes' work and the streets of Easton in open studio-style sessions.
Reflections/Connections: Outdoor ConcertAugust 2, Time TBD
The exhibition culminates in an immersive outdoor concert where Kentavius Jones performs a score inspired by Estes, accompanied by projected images and community-generated art.
ArtReach Field TripsMay 1–August 1 | By request
Free K–12 field trips offer guided exhibition tours, hands-on activities, transportation, and take-home materials for local schools and youth organizations.

title: Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum celebrates 60 years
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum celebrates 60 years

 April 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 737
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST.MICHAELS — A staple of St. Michaels, the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum is celebrating 60 years.Volunteers spearheaded the creation of the museum, which opened in 1965 at Navy Point and was accredited in 1978.
"The museum really started out by a community effort," said Pete Lesher, chief historian and ambassador at large at the museum. "The collections were built with an outpouring from the community over the idea that the place is changing and we need to establish a museum to remember the way it was."
Lesher, came to the museum in 1991 as a curator. He said the museum was created in a "series of themes" to represent the Bay and people around the it.
MUSEUM HISTORY
The museum started in May 1965 with two buildings that had been on the grounds since 1850 the Higgins house and the Dodson house. The eagle house building arrived in 1870. The three buildings now serve as administrative buildings after serving as exhibit buildings for nine years in the early days.
According to Lesher, the land where the museum's lighthouse and other exhibits now sit was reclaimed from the Bay.
"This was just a shallow part of the park," Lesher said. "You would have been standing probably knee deep sinking into mud about 150 years ago.
"This area started with actually a sawmill and grist mill but moved beyond that to seafood packing houses, and by the height here in the 1930s and 1940s, there were four different seafood packing houses out on this point. Every time they wanted to expand, they simply discarded more oyster shells, which they end up on themselves, pushing them into the harbor and built more land."
William Coulbourne and Frederick Jewett were two African American business owners who owned one of the four businesses on the land.
"They were early 20th century Black entrepreneurs from Crisfield, Maryland, who moved up here," Lesher said. "They learned the business and managed to get somebody to sell them land and managed to get somebody to give them a bank loan — a remarkable success story."
The museum plans to honor Coulbourne and Jewitt by renaming its education building after the two entrepreneurs.
The lighthouse, which is featured in the museum's logo, is the first historical structure the museum collected. It was acquired in 1966 when the Coast Guard was demolishing lighthouses "left and right" because of vandalism, according to Lesher.
The museum bought the lighthouse from the demolition company and moved it 50 miles north to the museum site.
"It was so early in our history, it became our logo," Lesher said. "The lighthouse is sort of what identifies the museum."
One of the new changing exhibits at the museum is the Sailing to Freedom exhibit, which highlights the Underground Railroad on the water.
"So we think of the Underground Railroad like the Harriet Tubman story of running up the Delmarva Peninsula to get to Philadelphia and freedom," Lesher said.
"Well, a lot of people made it by boat, whether they got a ticket on a steamboat, got away that way or stowed away on a coast-wise schooner, so many of them on the Chesapeake Bay, while the Chesapeake Bay forms a natural watery highway to the north. This was a route to freedom for many of those freedom seekers," he said. "That's what we try to show with this exhibit."
HELPING THE COMMUNITY
In addition to exhibits for museum-goers, the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum uses some exhibits to help with the curriculum in Talbot County schools.
An exhibit displaying the Maryland Crab Meat Company sits where the museum holds the Chesapeake's Best Crab Cakes program, in which third and fifth graders receive math, reading and social studies credits in the curriculum.
"The Chesapeake's Best Crab Cakes program meets learning goals for for math, for reading and for social studies in the Maryland curriculum," Lesher said. "Every Talbot County third grader and fifth grader has an experience tied to their curriculum, tied to their learning goals right here in the museum."
The museum also conducts an apprenticeship program where museum staff work with an apprentice for two years, ultimately leading to a state credential.
According to Lesher, the museum has hired some of these apprentices as permanent shipyard crew.
The museum has partnered with the St. Michaels Community Center on multiple occasions.
"We're working to do more community collaborations with them because both our missions align, and we want to enrich the lives of people who live in St. Michaels," said Amy Horne, executive director of the community center.

title: From 'Sugarcane Smiles' to 'Gangsters Gone Good': Kent Poetry Festival dazzles
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
From 'Sugarcane Smiles' to 'Gangsters Gone Good': Kent Poetry Festival dazzles

 April 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 727
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Earlier this month, the Kent Cultural Alliance rang in spring with their 16th annual Kent County Poetry Festival by presenting renowned names in the poetry community: Lady Brion, the poet laureate of the state of Maryland, Guggenheim Fellow and a National Endowment for the Arts fellow, Denise Duhamel, author of "Pink Lady," "Second Story" and "Queen for a Day: Selected and New Poems," and KCA Resident Artist Austen Camille.The three-day event in Chesterdown began with some hilarity as local comedienne Lady D emceed the kickoff, a poetry jam at the Garfield Theater on Friday, presenting local and renowned talent.
Lady D warmed up the crowd of roughly 50 in the audience with her playfully abrasive storytelling. She regaled the audience with an anecdote about hot Brazilian waxing, an equally brutal administer to said "waxing" by a large woman named Hilda, culminating with a cop who Lady D flirted with as he carried her to the car.
Next, Lady Brion, at ease on any stage, asked rhetorically, "How can I follow Lady D?"
Backed up by professional musicians performing a jazz beat — Gerry Werner on keys, J.R. McKinney on drums and Vaughn Bratcher on bass — Lady Brion launched into a poem with vivid imagery and clever wordplay about her mother who died from diabetes.
"Sugarcane smile" represented her love for her mother while witnessing her demise.
Within Lady Brion's lines full of emotion are images of her mother "cooking baked mac n cheese Sundays, her body coated with infections like chocolate coated candies, with a sugar level of 501."
"This ain't no sugar pill placebo," she recites, outlining the dangers of the disease. "Diabetes will not just go away. I just can't help but fear her decay."
Her next poem was titled "Reciprocity." It compelled people to resist their light being swallowed up by the dark and remove doubts and insecurities toward their goals.
The next poet, Yvette Hynson, incorporated song within her lyrics, asking what life would look like if they were not there that very moment.
Another local poet, Sasha Bank, read from her book of poems, talking of issues like obsessive-compulsive disorder, oversharing in public conversation and addressing many insecurities.
Poet Sarah Metzger shared some of those, but it was mostly about her thoughts on her weight, and in a kind of light, self-deprecating manner coupled with lessons on body positivity.
Amber Green, founder of the Fenix Youth Project, said in a polarizing world, she chooses poetry over politics. In her poem she expressed frustration with politics, the perils of choosing a lesser evil and the importance of remembering their ancestors who fought for freedom.
After intermission, Simon Weinberg amused the audience with his off-the-cuff and spontaneous poem: "Gangster Gone Good." Weinberg talked about causing a ruckus, burning cop cars with friends, and then later finding careers and marriage partners.
That included Weinberg, who when meeting his wife, the gangster turned good.
The last poet was Sister Charnell who ministered on her spiritual journey with God. She said by praying with intention, speaking deliberately to the Father, miracles happen. In her own life, at her worst, she said somebody prayed for her, which made the difference.
The commonality between all the poets that night was vulnerability.
England's poet laureate from 1843, William Wordsworth, defined poetry as simply "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings." He never considered poetry to be unattainable by the average man. The poets on that stage showed that poetry can, and should be accessible, fun, frightening, uncomfortable and honest.
Lady D, the epitome of honesty, confessed that listening to Lady Brion's "Sugar Cane Smile" got her hankering for some mac n cheese.
Director of Kent Cultural Alliance John Schratwieser said for the first kickoff poetry jam he was thrilled. "I loved the audience and everybody who spoke."
He thanked the rest of the planning committee: Meredith Davies Hadaway, Robert Earl Price, Tess Jones, Bob Ortiz, Leslie Raimond, James Allen Hall, and Tom Martin and The Rose O'Neil Lit House at Washington College, The Bookplate, and Robert Ortiz Studios for all their hard work.
"I think this was one of our most successful festivals yet... four events over three days drew more than 150 participants and patrons to performances, readings, workshops and some great community conversation. The Poetry Festival Committee is proud of the reach this festival has gained over 16 years and looks forward to another great event in 2026 with Featured Keynote poet, Pulitzer Prize winner Jericho Brown."

title: Renovating history: Point Lookout Lighthouse reopens
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Renovating history: Point Lookout Lighthouse reopens

 April 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 691
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It helped guide ships through the hazards in the Chesapeake Bay and has a rich history in St. Mary's and mariner history.And now the public will be able to learn about some of that history themselves following a ribbon-cutting ceremony Monday that reopened the 195-year-old Point Lookout Lighthouse.
The lighthouse at the southern tip of St. Mary's County had been closed since June 2018 for renovations.
"It's incredible and once you're in there and you see, it's worth it," Maryland Department of Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz said. "I think the thing that I'm really impressed by is … having the relationship with [former lighthouse keeper families] the Yeatmans and the Gattons and just what it was really like living [back then]."
The total cost of the renovations was $5 million.
"How fantastic that folks can actually visit the lighthouse after almost a decade?" said Dawn Letts, who is the park manager of the Point Lookout State Park Complex.
The lighthouse had been closed for almost seven years.
"Historic preservations are very complex and it changed hands so many times before it came to the [Maryland Park Service] so a lot of things were added, a lot of things were taken away," said Maryland Park Service Director of Planning Jonas Williams, who previously served as assistant park manager at Point Lookout State Park. "So I think with the contractors we were able to identify a best course forward for making any modern changes to it and making sure the historic character of the building was still there."
"There was also the complexity of the project because it had to have a design for the exterior renovations," Letts said. "Then there also had to be a design component for the exhibits so there was a design build for both portions of the project."
The inside of the lighthouse features informational panels, period furniture, appliances, toys, vintage photographs and a large floor map of the Chesapeake Bay.
"It's great to see it functioning again," said Lisa Kane of Mechanicsville, who is a member of the Point Lookout Lighthouse Preservation Society.
The adjoining two sheds were also renovated and feature informational panels.
"There are two things that make this lighthouse and this site significant," Letts said.
Point Lookout is the country's oldest standing integral lighthouse, meaning that the light tower and keeper's quarters are in the same building, she said. Also, the presence of the buoy and coal sheds next to the lighthouse add a unique element to the site.
Referring to the two large sheds, which were constructed in the 1880s, Letts said, "A lot of times when the lights were automated there was no use for those buildings, however the Navy having them and utilizing them for storage space actually kept them intact and used, and that just makes the site unbelievable."
The ceremony was held in conjunction with Maryland State Parks Week, which also featured the reopening of the park's fishing pier on April 19 following a 6-month closure, as well as a stop to view Newtowne Neck State Park.
The Point Lookout Lighthouse, which was illuminated from 1830 until it was decommissioned in 1966, had over two dozen lighthouse keepers and assistants over the years, according to the U.S. Lighthouse Society.
The lighthouse will officially open several days per week to the public beginning later in May.
"I think it's also just incredibly exciting to have this to get people down here and you can just learn so much," Kurtz said. "We have a lot of things ongoing here at the park but I think all [of them] just continue to make this a focal point for the whole state."
Park to open camping in the fall
Point Lookout State Park is planning to reopen some of its camping sites in the fall.
Camping at the popular waterfront park has not been available for the past two years due to water and sewer line projects encompassing the entire park, as well as renovations of all of the pump stations.
Letts said the delay was caused by various factors, including supply chain issues and site conditions.
She said the park is hoping to reopen a couple camping loops in October for about a month and then fully reopen the campground next spring.

title: Country Cooking: The other side of the barnyard
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: The other side of the barnyard

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1187
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Driving down the country road to the farm, I realized that you always see one side of the barnyard as you turn into the driveway.This is the side where the water trough sits, and the feed containers are placed on metal tracks. The cows and hogs hang out here waiting to be fed. The corn cribs and the smokehouse are nearby.
On the other side of the barn is the area where the pony and goats hang out. At one time, we had a small lamb that we cared for while its owner was away. The goats would constantly get out and wander down to neighboring farms — eating everything in sight. They soon found new homes.
The Easter holiday is over, but I have some ham and lamb recipes I want to share with you. What was on your table for Easter dinner last week? For most, ham rates number one, with lamb, beef, seafood, turkey and chicken as other choices.
I know many families opt for lamb, but even though I know it is a very healthy choice, I just can't cook or eat lamb. Lamb meat comes from the young lambs and is a very rich source of iron, high quality of protein, zinc and vitamin B12.
I will include a lamb recipe today for those who like lamb. My mom always prepared the tastiest hams but only once or twice ever cooked lamb — probably because the children refused to eat it.
This past week I purchased a small ham — on sale — and decided to cook it instead of freezing it. It was delicious.
Ham and lamb can be eaten at any time of the year.
BONE IN BAKED HAM
This ham recipe comes from my kitchen. I have used it for many years. I purchase one whole bone-in ham, about 15 pounds and trim off any excess fat.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a mixing bowl combine one-pound brown sugar and 1/2 cup yellow mustard, mixing until you have a thick paste. Line a baking pan with foil, making sure the foil is long enough to fold over covering ham completely. Spray foil with cooking spray just in case the brown sugar mixture escapes from the foil. Place the ham on the foil and spread with sugar-mustard paste on top. Fold and seal foil. Keep ham sealed until cooking is complete — Bake for 4 hours. Check for doneness and let sit, covered, for another hour. Carve and serve.
NOTE: the ham bone will be great after Easter for seasoning in a pot of bean soup or ham and cabbage.
PINEAPPLE HAM
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Use a 8 to 10-pound ham and score the top in a diamond-shape, making the cuts half an inch deep. Place ham in a roasting pan. Mix together 3 cups brown sugar with 3 tablespoons yellow mustard, mixing until smooth and spooning onto top of ham. Mix together the juice from an 8-ounce can of pineapple rings and 1 cup honey. Drizzle this mixture over the ham and brown sugar paste. Place the pineapple rings on top of the ham and secure with wooden toothpicks. Cover and place in the preheated oven. After 15 minutes, remove the cover (foil or a lid) and baste with pan drippings, doing this several times until the scouring marks have opened, letting the juices seep into the meat. Continue baking until ham is well done according to size of ham (see package directions).
LEG OF LAMB
4 to 5-pound leg of lamb (bone-in, fat trimmed), salt and pepper, extra virgin olive oil, 5 garlic cloves (peeled and sliced), 2 cups water, 8 gold potatoes (peeled and cut into wedges), 1 yellow onion (peeled and cut into wedges), 1 teaspoon paprika,1 teaspoon all-natural garlic powder, fresh parsley for garnish (optional). For the rub: 15 garlic cloves (peeled), 2 tablespoons dried oregano, 2 tablespoons dried mint flakes, 1 tablespoon paprika, 1/2 tablespoons nutmeg, 1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil, juice of 2 lemons.
Take the leg of lamb out of the refrigerator and leave in room temperature for about 1 hour. In the meantime, prepare the remaining ingredients and make the lamb rub. Prepare the seasoning.
To make the rub or seasoning, in a food processor, combine the rub ingredients. Blend until smooth. Set aside (or in the fridge, if preparing in advance). Salt the meat. When ready, pat the lamb dry and make a few slits on both sides. Season with salt and pepper. Sear the Lamb. Turn the oven on broil. Place the leg of lamb on a wire rack and put it directly on the top rack so that it's only a few inches away from the broiler element. Broil for 5 to 7 minutes on each side or until the leg of lamb is nicely seared. Remove from the oven, then adjust the oven temperature to 325 degrees. Apply the seasoning or rub. When the lamb is cool enough to handle, insert the garlic slices in the slits you made earlier. Now cover the leg of lamb on all sides with the wet rub and place it in the middle of a roasting pan with an inside rack. Add two cups of water to the bottom of the roasting pan. Season the potato and onion wedges with paprika, garlic powder and a little salt, then add them to the pan on either side of the lamb. Cover and roast. Tent a large piece of foil over the roasting pan (make sure it does not touch the lamb) then place the pan on the middle rack of the 325-degree oven. Roasted for about 1 hour. Remove the foil and return the roasting pan to the oven for another 15 to 20 minutes or until the lamb temperature registers 125 degrees. Let rest. Remove the pan from the oven and let the leg of lamb rest for about 15 to 20 minutes before serving (the lamb will continue to cook, and its internal temperature will continue to rise to around 130 degrees).Place the roast lamb and potatoes in a large serving platter over a bed of rice, you like. Garnish with parsley. Or you may carve the lamb first, then arrange the sliced lamb with the potatoes over the rice.
BAKED PINEAPPLE
Multiple generations love this side dish. My son John will eat this even as a dessert or breakfast dish. It goes perfect with any of these recipes today.
One 20-ounce can of crushed pineapple including juice, ¾ cup granulated sugar, 2 large eggs, 2 tablespoons cornstarch, 2 teaspoons vanilla extract, 1 ½ tablespoons butter (divided into small pats), 1 teaspoon ground cinnamon.
Preheat your oven to 350 degrees. Lightly grease a 9-by-9-inch baking pan to prevent sticking. In a mixing bowl, add the crushed pineapple (with its juice), granulated sugar, eggs, cornstarch and vanilla extract. Stir until the mixture is smooth. Transfer the pineapple mixture into a greased baking pan. Evenly distribute the small pats of butter across the surface of the mixture, then sprinkle with ground cinnamon to enhance flavor. Bake for 45 minutes, or until the mixture begins to exhibit a golden hue perfectly caramelized. Let cool and serve.

title: Mentors, kids, go above and beneath with art project
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Mentors, kids, go above and beneath with art project

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 241
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The wraps came off a unique art project last Friday at Calvert Marine Museum in Solomons.The effort by 13 young people was supervised by young adults and aided by experts. A modest national grant helped with funding. The results were priceless.
"Beneath the Bay," a mural depicting the many inhabitants of the Chesapeake and its tributaries, was a work of art accomplished through the Calvert County Youth Mentor Program, which was championed and supervised by county government's department of parks and recreation.
"We all need mentors," Nate Smith, recreation division chief, said April 25 before the modular mural was unveiled to a roomful of young project participants, parents and volunteers. County Commissioner Catherine M. Grasso (R) and Commissioner Todd Ireland (R) also attended and spoke at the unveiling ceremony.
"It's been a wonderful journey," Brenda DiCarlo, the youth mentor program coordinator, added.
According to information provided by parks and recreation, during the summer of 2023 the department "was one of 29 agencies nationwide to receive a $70,000 grant from the National Recreation and Park Association to establish a youth mentor program."
The program is designed to enrich the lives of children ages 10 to 14 in the community through fellowship, education and activities that include life skills, good citizenship, health and wellness, and more in fun and interactive programs.
Last fall, Calvert's parks and recreation department debuted its first youth mentor program with 10-week sessions offered at Northeast Community Center in Chesapeake Beach and Southern Community.

title: Rain doesn't stop Oxford Day
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Rain doesn't stop Oxford Day

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 398
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Although the forecast caused many to bring rain jackets and umbrellas, the light rain didn't squash the excitement for this year's Oxford Day parade.As tiny raindrops fell, the crowd cheered on floats, marching bands, vintage cars and fire trucks making their way down the Strand and Morris Street Saturday. From the Easton Middle School Marching Band playing "Feel It Still" to the Maryland Rough Riders strolling down Morris Street atop their horses, there was something for everyone.
Jordan Daniels, an out-of-towner with parents-in-law who live in Oxford, said Oxford Day is always a fun time.
"Same as always," he said, as he celebrated his third Oxford Day.
But the parade wasn't the only thing that brought droves of visitors to Oxford Saturday. With a packed schedule of events, from pickleball tournaments and Talbot Humane's blessing of the animals to barbecues and fish fries, there were plenty of ways for people to celebrate.
Richard Bank, who spends his weekends in Oxford, said he's celebrated Oxford Day every year for the past 23 years. He said Oxford is a "community-minded" place.
"The whole community is like this," he said as people walked around Oxford Town Park, chatting with neighbors and visitors alike. "It's a great place."
Siblings John and Barbara Litschert came from North Carolina to celebrate Oxford Day with their family this year. Although the Litschert family doesn't live in Maryland, their roots in Oxford go back seven generations. The family still owns the home their ancestors built on South Street, and they visit Oxford annually.
John Litschert said he tries to come up to Oxford Day every year. He said he likes seeing his grandchildren enjoy the town that he grew up visiting every summer.
Barbara Litschert said when it comes to Oxford Day, it's all about the food, the parade, the people and seeing friends.
Before the parade began, Oxford resident Probal Gupta and his 9-year-old daughter Maya waited along the parade route. Maya said she was most excited to see the floats in the parade.
Gupta said he was excited to catch up with neighbors.
"It's a good way to see what's happening in our community," he said about the festivities.
Barbara Hartshorn, who has lived in Oxford for more than three decades, called Oxford Day a "big holiday" for the town. She said everyone does a wonderful job of putting the events of the day together.
"It's the best town in the world," she said.

title: Queen Anne's Museum of Eastern Shore Life open May 3
author: Staff Writer
content:
Queen Anne's Museum of Eastern Shore Life open May 3

 April 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 208
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Queen Anne's Museum of Eastern Shore Life will be open for visitors on Saturday, May 3, from 1 to 4 p.m. to begin its 2025 visitors season.The museum staff is in the process of modifying the floor plan and assembling new exhibits for display.
The museum is seeking additional items for display and requests that people donate household or farm items from the 1800s to the 1960s.
One very popular exhibit area for museum visitors is the family room, living room and kitchen displays, which include a television from about 1950, household furniture and appliances such as an antique oven,
an old piano and an Electrolux vacuum cleaner from about 1949.
Two popular items on display include a Ford Model T car from about 1915 and a Ford Model A car from about 1929. There are collections of antique typewriters, dolls, children's toys, and many other household items.
The museum has a massive display of old photos of people, places and things from all around Queen Anne's County and neighboring areas from the late 1800s through most of the 20th century.
Admission to the museum is free, but voluntary donations are accepted.
The museum is located at the QAC 4-H Park on State Route 18 at Dulin Clark Road between Centreville and Queenstown.

title: Meet the maker: Charm Tree Jewelry Studio welcomes steel metalsmith and author
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Meet the maker: Charm Tree Jewelry Studio welcomes steel metalsmith and author

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 375
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — As part of its regular Meet the Maker series bringing in experts highlighting their craft, metalsmith school Charm Tree Studios recently welcomed celebrated steelsmith and new author Bette Barnett, of California.Renowned for her work combining steel, gold and silver in her unique jewelry-making process, Barnett taught several studio classes about various aspects of metal working, including etching steel plates and powdered metals. Barnett also demonstrated Keum Boo, an ancient Korean art form of applying gold to metal through heat and pressure, on steel that she has perfected over the years.
Following her corporate career retirement in 2013, Barnett was drawn to crafting and beading workshops, and after learning how to solder necklace clasps, she fell in love with steelwork in particular.
"And I never looked back," she said.
Taking every class and workshop she could get her soldering mitts on and receiving fantastic mentorship, Barnett continued to experiment with different styles.
Steel is a cost effective material with a high melting point, she said, and she soon found it offered itself to mixing and playing well with other materials.
To pass on her late instructor's techniques, Barnett began teaching and writing a research paper that eventually morphed into her book.
Barnett's new book "Creating Steel Jewelry: Etching, Fusing, Keum Boo, Enameling, Stainless and More" delves into the fundamentals of metalsmithing while also exploring her own techniques and explorations into the world of smithing.
Charm Tree Jewelry studio owner and metalsmith instructor Melissa Kay-Steves is always eager to ever expand the repertoire. Since opening its doors more than five years ago, the goal of the studio has been to bring skilled and unique experts to teach and showcase new styles.
Learning the basics, "will take you anywhere you want to go," she said.
Within the metalsmith school's state-of-the-art studio and workshops, Kay-Steves lays fundamental ground work and it is often visiting masters who showcase how to perfect and hone skills, leading students through a gateway of possibilities, she said.
Charm Tree Jewelry Studio regularly hosts Meet the Maker events open to all curious jewelry lovers and craftspeople.
"There's nothing else like it in the area," Kay-Steves said.
More information about Barnett's studio can be found at studiomigoto.com. More information about Charm Tree Jewelry including year round classes and guest instructors, can be found at charmtreejewelry.com.

title: Country Cooking: Mom's recipes
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Mom's recipes

 May 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We are celebrating Mother's Day on Sunday, and this year I decided to gather favorite recipes from many moms around the countryside. I am constantly sharing my mom's cooking, and I appreciate the many wonderful comments I receive, but let's share your favorite mom recipes.As I made my calls, emails and text messages to my readers, it was amazing to find how alike our mom's recipes were.
Remember how moms dumped in, sprinkled, spread, eye measured and judged the size by holding the product? They held recipes by "memory instead of measurement."
Years ago, I asked my mom to write down some recipes and she replied, "I'll try."
When I speak of and recall Mother's Day, there are many definitions of a mom or mother. This person can be our birth mother, adopted mother, step mother, sister who replaced a mother, aunt, grandmother, close family friend who stepped in to help, father who served as both parents — it does not matter who they are.
But what does matter is they were, or still are, there to fill those shoes of a loving adult guiding your life forward.
My mom was a blessing, and her love and guidance will forever be treasured by all who knew her as Mom, Grandmother, Great Grandmother or Miss Laurie.
MRS. HOLLAND'S GREEN LIMA BEAN SOUP
Mrs. Holland is now in her late 80s and remembers her mother making this soup any time of the year to help feed the family. They grew lima beans on the farm, and this soup fed many family members and farm hands cheaply.
In a large soup pot add 6 cups of water, 1 number 10 can whole tomatoes or 1 quart jar of home canned tomatoes, 1 piece of salt pork or ham, 3-4 cups green lima beans (fresh or frozen), 1 can yellow or white corn, 3-4 white potatoes (peeled and cubed), and 1 tbsp sugar. Cover and simmer until all ingredients are tender. During the first 30 minutes of cooking, taste soup for seasonings. Serve hot with fresh baked biscuits.
COLLINS FAMILY BISCUITS
My elementary school friend Fay makes some great homemade biscuits to go with the bean soup. Fay grew up in the country and had a large family also.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees. Cut one cup shortening or lard into 6 cups flour, 1 tbsp salt and 3 tbsps baking powder. Then add 2 cups of milk. Mix well and knead at least eight times. Form biscuits by rolling the desired amounts of dough with your hands and place them on a floured baking sheet. Bake for about 10-12 minutes. Serve warm.
PECAN PIE
My friend Joy's mom, the late Mrs. Eva Dixon of Greensboro, was well known by family and friends for her delicious pecan pie. This fresh baked pie appeared at all family functions.
Prepare or purchase an eight-inch pie shell, unbaked. Preheat the oven to 400 degrees. Beat 3 eggs until frothy and add 1 cup white or brown sugar, 1/2 cup light corn syrup, a dash of salt, 1 tsp vanilla and 1 cup chopped pecans. Mix well and pour into the pie shell. Place some halved pecans on top for decorative purposes. Bake for 10 minutes, then lower the temperature to 350 degrees and bake another 30 minutes. Cool before serving.
PEPPER RELISH
My niece, Jamie, often talks about her relative who makes pepper relish throughout the year and about how delicious it is. After convincing her to share this recipe for my special column today, let's make this relish.
Prepare 12 green sweet peppers and 12 sweet red peppers (remove the seeds and chop up fine). Clean and chop 12 onions, mix peppers and onions together and pour boiling water over this mixture and let it stand for 5 minutes. Drain well. In a small pot, add 3 cups vinegar, 1 tbsp salt, 2 cups sugar, 2 tbsps celery seed and 2 tbsps mustard seeds. Let stand for five minutes. Cook gently for 10 minutes. When mixture comes to boiling point, remove from heat and pack in pint jars. Makes 6 pints. Instead of hand chopping, you can use a blender to chop peppers and onions.
FRESH CATFISH
Let's go fishing together with Donna and her husband for some fresh catfish. Most weekends, weather permitting, this couple fish and share in the cleaning and cooking.
Combine 2/3 cup yellow cornmeal with 1/4 cup all-purpose flour, 2 tsps salt and 1/2 tsp paprika. Dry the fresh fillets thoroughly and coat each side with cornmeal mixture. Fry in 1/2 cup vegetable oil for about 4 minutes on each side. Drain well on paper towels. This coating mixture can be used on any type of fish.
FRIED GREEN TOMATOES
These were submitted to me by three different ladies in honor of their mothers. So, since their recipes were almost identical, let's call this Rose, Marilyn and Edna's fried green tomatoes.
Use 3 large tomatoes (about 2 1/2 pounds), sliced crosswise about 1/3 inch thick. Arrange the tomatoes on paper towels and sprinkle with 1 tsp salt. Set aside for 30 minutes to draw out the moisture. In the meantime, make a dredging mixture consisting of 2 cups of yellow cornmeal and 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper. When tomatoes are ready to fry — place 1/4 cup solid vegetable oil in a fry pan. When the oil is hot, place a single layer of tomato slices in the pan and fry until golden on each side, turning once. Remove to paper towels for draining. serve immediately.
One note to be added — you can use green tomatoes, red tomatoes or pink tomatoes (partially green but not ripe yet). The green tomato may need a sprinkle of sugar on top at serving time.
SOUTHERN CORNBREAD
How about some Southern cornbread from a true Southern lady and mother — Ms. Bea? She's been living down in Tennessee for the past 15 years.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees. Sift together 1 cup white or yellow cornmeal with 1/2 tsp baking soda and 1/2 tsp salt. In another bowl, mix one beaten egg with 1 cup buttermilk and 1 tbsp melted shortening. Add wet and dry ingredients together, mix well and pour into a shallow greased pan. Bake for 18 minutes.
BISHOPVILLE BANANA PUDDING
Let's close with a few deserts for that special day, because one thing I know… Moms love desert.
This was always a favorite no matter what time of year in our house. Gather ⅓ cup all-purpose flour, a dash of salt, 2 ½ cups 1% low-fat milk, 1 (14-oz.) can fat-free sweetened condensed milk, 2 egg yolks (lightly beaten), 2 tsps vanilla extract, 3 cups sliced ripe bananas, 48 vanilla wafers, 4 egg whites and ¼ cup sugar. Preheat the oven to 325 degrees. Combine flour and salt in a medium saucepan. Gradually stir in 1% milk, sweetened condensed milk and yolks, and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, for 8 to 10 minutes or until thickened. Remove from heat, stir in vanilla. Layer 3 banana slices, 3½ tbsp. pudding and 3 vanilla wafers in each of 8 (1-cup) ramekins or ovenproof glass dishes. Top each with 6 banana slices, 3½ tbsp. pudding, and 3 vanilla wafers. Beat egg whites at high speed with an electric mixer until foamy. Add sugar, 1 tbsp. at a time, beating until stiff peaks form and sugar dissolves (2 to 4 minutes). Spread about ½ cup meringue over each pudding. Bake for 15 to 20 minutes or until golden. Let cool for 30 minutes.
EASY PINEAPPLE UPSIDE DOWN CAKE
Gather 3 tbsps butter melted, 1/3 cup packed brown sugar, 9 canned unsweetened pineapple slices, 9 Maraschino cherry halves, 2/3 cup sugar, 2/3 cup fat-free milk and 3 tbsps canola oil. Pour butter into a nine-inch square baking pan; sprinkle with brown sugar. Arrange pineapple slices in a single layer in the pan; place cherry halves in the center of pineapple slices; set aside. In a large bowl, beat the sugar, milk, oil, egg and extracts until well blended. Combine the flour, baking powder and salt; gradually beat into sugar mixture until blended. Pour into the prepared pan. Bake at 350 degrees for 35-40 minutes or until a toothpick comes out clean. Immediately invert onto a serving plate. Serve warm.

title: Academy Art Museum Bugatti exhibit excells
author: DAVID R. BACK
content:
Academy Art Museum Bugatti exhibit excells

 May 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID R. BACK | Section: Arts 
 
 499
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Academy Art Museum's recent display of Bugatti Family Art, deemed Bugatti: Reaching for Perfection, was an amazing success.With its four-month exhibition spanning from December through April, Director Charlotte Potter Kasic noted that this superb display resulted in attendance being up 50% from other events of years past, stating "The Bugatti exhibition has significantly expanded our reach, driving a substantial increase in attendance. We have been averaging 1,750-2,000 people per month."
"This surge demonstrates increased public engagement, fueled by the exhibition's unique appeal and broader marketing efforts," she said.
A review of the display on MotorWeek, a televised automotive magazine, also contributed to the turnout, as one patron mentioned they travelled 800 miles to attend.
Upon entering the museum, patrons were greeted by the museum's friendly staff and treated to a hallway lined with an artistic display of Rembrandt Bugatti's incredible bronze sculptures. Further down the hallway, a stunning display from the Bugatti family patriarch, Carlo Bugatti featured his paintings and sensational furniture constructed from a masterful combination of materials that included ebonized wood inlaid with copper, brass, ivory, mother-of-pearl and vellum, tastefully adorned with leather tassels, geometric marquetry and painted designs.
To either side were two rooms adorned with more Bugatti art, memorabilia and a pair of rare Bugatti automobiles designed and crafted by Ettore Bugatti and his son Jean. To the left were two Bugatti grand prix machines, one of which was converted to street use with the addition of fenders and lights.
The aluminum body work of this Type 39A Grand Prix machine gleamed as the traditional French Blue paint had been removed and the aluminum polished to accent its stunning metal work. This is a similar Bugatti to the Type 39B that William Grover-Williams raced to win the first Monte Carlo Grand Prix in 1929. To its side sat a French blue Type 45 16-cylinder Grand Prix Bugatti with a remarkable power output, making it capable of navigating the rough terrain of hillclimbs as demonstrated by Louis Chiron's victory in the 1929 Klausenrennen event.
The room to the right presented two luxurious Bugatti's, another display of Bugatti artwork, a Bugatti photograph timeline, a traditional Bugatti horseshoe radiator and two phenomenal Bugatti Coupe's designed by Jean Bugatti, a Type 57 SC Atlantic, and a Type 57 Atalante.
The two sumptuous black automobiles are both powerful and pleasantly comfortable. Both have an elegant, spectacular wooden dashboard that exudes organized excellence with gauge and control placements. As the Type 57 SC Atlantic was designed to be constructed with magnesium. Its body panels feature center seams that are riveted together, as magnesium is challenging to weld.
It was decided not to use magnesium for several concerns. Aluminum was chosen, but the riveted construction was retained.
This world class display is the result of hours of networking, coordination, hard work and dedication from the museum staff, supporters and behind-the-scenes individuals whose generosity prevailed in a splendid attraction of unequalled proportion. The next display will be Richard Estes, Urban Landscapes, which runs now through Aug 3.
For additional information, visit academyartmuseum.org.

title: Star Democrat's newest reporter wants to tell untold stories
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Star Democrat's newest reporter wants to tell untold stories

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Dorchester 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Lily Tierney, a Louisville, Kentucky native recently hired as a reporter at the Star Democrat, is looking forward to telling many different stories on the Eastern Shore.Tierney will be covering Dorchester County and is excited to learn more about Dorchester's ins and outs.
She attended Eckerd College in St. Petersburg, Florida for a few years, then decided to transfer to American University in Washington, D.C., where she graduated in 2024.
Tierney credits getting over her childhood dyslexia as her path to finding journalism.
"I am very dyslexic, and so it took me a while to read," Tierney said. "I finally did learn how to read. I was like, 'Oh, this is sick, this is a cool world,' and being able to just kind of escape into fiction I always loved.
"Then when I went into high school, I started writing poetry, loved poetry. For one of my first gifts when I was 14, I got a typewriter, and I was like, 'Alright, I'm going to be a writer. That's what I'm going to do. I'm going to be a writer.'"
Tragedy in 2020 gave Tierney her drive to tell people's stories.
"2020 hit, and that's when Breonna Taylor was shot and killed in her house. For me that was a really pivotal moment because it was insane to be from Louisville then, and it felt like I was getting a lot of that coverage just because I was from Louisville, but it took a long time for her story to get told," Tierney said. "I wanted to be someone who could tell people's stories who couldn't tell their own anymore."
While at American University, Tierney covered immigration, which she enjoyed because it gave her a chance to tell stories that might have otherwise gone untold.
Tierney wants community members to know she is very friendly and excited to get to know her community.
"I'm just excited to be here," Tierney said. "I'm excited to cover locally because, I mean, as they say in comedy, local jokes get local laughs, but I think it's the same thing in news — local reporting gets local attention, and I think that's really exciting."

Spring concert passes the baton onward

 395

 On May 7, the Brigade of Blue, Kent County High School's band, consisting of the Marching Band, Concert Band, Jazz Band, Show Choir, and Color Guard, held their Spring Concert in the auditorium.The choir performed songs such as "Ain't No Mountain High Enough," "End of the Road," "I'm Coming Out," and "ABC." The jazz band played selections from Duke Ellington and Gordon Goodwin before concluding with a group performance of "Smooth Operator" by Sade Adu and Ray St. John, arranged by Mark Fabio.
After a brief intermission, the concert band showcased their talent with "Earthdance" by Michael Sweeney and their favorite, "Rites of Tamburo" by Robert W. Smith.
Following the performance, band director Jodi Bortz and Mirelle Kraus, Color Guard and Choreography, recognized departing seniors, presenting them with yellow roses for their future endeavors and highlighting their special contributions to the band.
Departing seniors include: Ava Bower, Ja'Ciah Cooper, Audrey Copeland Spivey, Joseph Donaldson, Megan Duke, Amber Long, Henry Martinez, Teo O'Brien, Phoebe Preston, Mu Shan Rau, Sophia Santos, and Layana Wilson.
Bortz and Kraus also recognized individual student achievements and introduced returning band students to new leadership roles.
A new tradition this year was the "passing of the baton" ceremony, which featured former band majors: Donald Green (1989-1991), Jodi Bortz (1991-1992), Rondell Bryant (2000-2001), Monica Rosanova (2017-2018), Joseph Donaldson (2024-2025), and the rising Drum Major, Alden Swanson (2025-2026).
Bortz took the opportunity, with family and friends in the audience, to commend her students for their achievements during the annual band trip. This year's trip was to Dollywood and Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. The trip was both enjoyable and successful, as every group placed in their competition categories. The Concert Band placed second, while the Jazz Band, Show Choir, and Marching Band all earned top honors in their respective groups.
Bortz also thanked the Kent County High School Music Boosters, who supported the band throughout the year by organizing fundraisers. She expressed gratitude to the school board, Principal Kris Hemstetter, staff, the Kent Cultural Alliance for helping provide new instruments over the last two years, and The Hedgelawn Foundation for supporting the annual competition trips, including this year's trip to Dollywood. She also thanked the families of the students.
"Your constant support and encouragement make this all possible!" Bortz said.
With the concert now concluded, the band will shift focus to the Tea Party Parade on May 24, followed by graduation on May 30.

title: Country Cooking: The kitchen catch-all drawer
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: The kitchen catch-all drawer

 May 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Life 
 
 1212
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Before I begin my weekly column, I need to recognize a holiday that is dear to me — Memorial Day will be May 26. Fly those American flags in honor of our fallen heroes. Attend the many services held at your local VFW or American Legion.Many other organizations hold events to honor our fellow Americans. One of the many breathtaking sights here on the Eastern Shore is the Veterans Cemetery at the Buelah location outside Hurlock. Each grave is marked with a small individual American flag, astonishing to see in the breeze.
I just automatically place my right hand over my heart and remember the words of our 35th President, the late John Fitzgerald Kennedy — "My fellow Americans, ask not what your country can do for you but what can you do for your country."
Now for this week's column.
Every kitchen has one, but maybe they different names for it — the catch-all drawer, the what you call it drawer, the thing-a-bob drawer or gadget drawer. But once you struggle to get it open, oh my.
It is loaded with a little bit of everything and even though it is in the kitchen it has "stuff" for everything and everywhere. Let me pull my drawer open and see what I find. It is a wooden spring type clothespin I use to close bags with when I can't find the little plastic closure. Here is the old, handheld can opener along with the opener that punches in the top or you can "stab" a hole in a can. Now this is cool — the old handheld potato masher next to the beaters that fit on my electric beater. I have at least five paring knives in here next to the hand peeler and the core remover.
I must add this one — I just saw my modern iced tea maker, but folks, nothing tastes like the ice tea made with tea bags in the saucepan cooking over the flame, removing from heat, squeezing out bags and pouring in the big glass pitcher, adding sugar and squeezing lemon juice and serving in a real glass with ice cubes.
I will finish this inventory another day — let's use modern utensils that have replaced the above and explore the recipes.
A few weeks ago, I visited a store in Salisbury that had a whole wall of tools and modern gadgets. A few things I stopped and looked at, thinking to myself, "Wow, if only I would've had one of these 50 years ago."
In El Paso, Texas back in the '60s, when I was exposed to some many new foods, I remember the Jalapeno pepper being one I was told to stay away from. Those West Texans would eat jalapenos the way we eat apples.
I came across a jalapeno corer in this store and instantly remembered the stories of those older ladies cutting jalapenos until their fingers were numb from the oil of those peppers.
JALAPENO CORN SALAD
1 medium onion (quartered), 2 jalapeno peppers, 1 cup sour cream, 1 cup mayonnaise, 2 ounces cream cheese (softened), 2 tsps ground cumin, 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tsp chili powder, 1 tsp smoked paprika, 1/4 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp pepper, 4 cups fresh corn (about 8 ears) (cooked and cooled), 1 cup shredded sharp cheddar cheese, 1 cup shredded pepper jack cheese, 1/2 cup crumbled cooked bacon.
Grill onion and jalapenos, covered, over medium-high heat or broil 4 inches from heat for 3-5 minutes on each side or until lightly charred. Cool completely; chop into 1/2-inch pieces. Combine the next nine ingredients. Stir in corn, cheese, half the bacon and the grilled vegetables. Top with remaining bacon to serve.
QUICK DUMPLINGS
Two staples in our kitchen growing up were Flour and a rolling pin. I feel like 90% of our meals used both. Whether it was biscuits for breakfast, dumplings at every meal, or those amazing pies and many, many others. A good rolling pin is almost like your right hand when it comes to the kitchen.
While in this store, I saw one of the best inventions ever — rolling pin that had a hollow core to store flour in. As you are rolling out your dough, it can get dry. Instead of making a mess with moist dough, dry flour and getting it all over the counter, you can just shake a little out of the end of the pin as you roll.
2 cups all-purpose flour, 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 1/3 cup shortening (cold), 3/4 to 1 cup buttermilk.
Heat a large Dutch oven over medium high heat. Mix flour, baking powder and salt in a mixing bowl. Cut in the cold shortening using a pastry cutter or food processor. Gradually pour in the buttermilk, stirring until the dough comes together. Turn the dough out on a floured surface and work it just until everything is combined. The dough should not be sticky. Roll the dough out about 1/4-inch thick with your rolling pin to keep it from getting too dry. Cut into 1-inch strips. Cut each of those strips into pieces that are approximately 2 inches in length. Add the milk to the Dutch oven and bring to a simmer. Drop dumplings strips into soup and simmer for 15-20 minutes until cooked through.
That was the "quick" dumpling recipe. Soon I'll post the recipe that I have cooked probably over 10,000 times in the last 50 plus years.
SPICY SAUSAGE PASTA
This next gadget is one that my daughter-in-law Shannon uses at least three or four times a week — a garlic press. Garlic in their household is like salt and pepper in most others. It's always being used in dishes to add flavor.
I don't think my son makes anything that doesn't have fresh chopped or minced garlic in it. If you use minced, chopped or crushed garlic, you can save time by not having to peel or dice with a garlic press. Shannon also told me she uses it to crush nuts for other recipes.
8 ounces uncooked penne, 10.6 ounces hot Italian sausages (sliced and crumbled), 3 cloves garlic (minced), 1/2 cup chicken broth, 1/2 tbsp flour, 1 (14 fluid ounce) can diced tomatoes with juices, 1/2 cup heavy whipping cream, salt and pepper to taste, 6 large leaves basil (sliced/torn into small pieces), freshly grated parmesan cheese to taste.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Cook pasta al dente according to package directions. Take the sausage meat out of the casings and crumble it into a deep skillet. Cook it for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, over medium-high heat until browned. Once the sausage is browned, take it out of the pan and set it aside. Drain the fat. Add the garlic, followed by the chicken broth to the skillet. Sprinkle the flour in. Whisk it until the flour has dissolved and scrape any browned bits from the bottom of the pan. Cook this mixture until it's significantly reduced (should only take a minute or two in total).Add in the tomatoes, cream, and the sausage meat. Cook the sauce for a few more minutes until it's thickened to your liking. Season with salt & pepper as needed. Just prior to serving, add in the torn basil leaves and then toss with the drained pasta. Serve with freshly grated parmesan cheese.
