title: Cambridge veteran, photographer is behind new journal looking back at Vietnam War
author: Konner Metz
content:
Cambridge veteran, photographer is behind new journal looking back at Vietnam War

 May 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Lon Holmberg was in Charlottesville, Virginia, seeing college friends in 1969 after he received his draft notice, when novelist and University of Virginia professor George Garrett gave him some advice."Make lemonade out of lemons," Holmberg recalls Garrett telling him, encouraging him to write a book on his soon-to-be life-changing experience in Vietnam.
More than 50 years later, Holmberg did just that.
Holmberg, a U.S. Army photographer during the war, brought thousands of negatives back from Vietnam. Now 80 and residing in Cambridge, Holmberg is the author of a new journal, "Crossing the Pass of Clouds." It includes written vignettes and black-and-white photos depicting what life was like in Vietnam.
"It's really hard to take in," Holmberg said of how it feels to have the book published after decades of trying. "Like all that time put into it. It's wonderful to be able to do it. I'm very proud of it."
The journal includes photos of U.S. Secretary of Defense Melvin Laird, then-national security advisor (and later Secretary of State) Henry Kissinger and then-South Vietnamese President Nguyen Van Thieu.
But for Holmberg, the book's purpose extends far beyond the historical figures. It captures soldiers working and enjoying downtime. It captures the culture and landscape of South Vietnam itself — especially the city of Saigon.
"It really was some sense of what it was like to be in Vietnam, to see the life of the indigenous people and farming communities," Holmberg said.
He compares it to a hologram. Like a 3D image, his memoir showcases a full perspective of Vietnam through the lens of one person.
"This is not just a collection of Vietnam pictures," Holmberg said. "These are a collection from one person, from one point of view."
"You kind of have a way of looking through the book into getting a feel of what Vietnam really was like in 1971," he said.
HALF-CENTURY LATER
The book's journey didn't come without hardships; Holmberg said he was rejected 31 times. It was never an option to give up.
"After you've been doing this for years and years, you're not just going to stop," Holmberg said.
By considering a university press and learning to write concise proposals, Holmberg found his publisher, The University Press of Mississippi, a few years ago.
His journal published in March, just days before the 50th anniversary of the Vietnam War's end on March 29.
Sandy Stillwell, Holmberg's wife, said he's been "steady" and has carried himself with a sense of humor during the arduous process of finding a publisher.
"While the process itself was challenging and the rejections disheartening, Lon is an optimist at heart," Stillwell wrote in an email.
The couple has settled on the Eastern Shore, and Holmberg credits his wife with being his rock as he completed the memoir.
Holmberg, a documentary photographer and longtime English professor, says he's working on two other projects, including one from his time exploring the prison system in New Mexico as a documentary producer.
'HUMANE'
The book's 196 pages are stocked full of written reflections about life before, during and after the war. Holmberg writes on return visits to Vietnam in 1996, a quarter-century after his time in the Army, and in 2010, as the teacher of a one-month English course for Hue University students.
Photos capture moments ranging from early anti-war protests in Washington, D.C. to soldiers working on the largest U.S. military base in Vietnam, Long Binh.
The book doesn't depict brutal images of war, but that doesn't make it any less realistic or meaningful, Holmberg and others say.
"Holmberg does not show the human wreckage of war. Instead, he gives us humane, sympathetic, respectful images of civilians and soldiers, generals and government officials," reads a review on the memoir's back cover written by University of Virginia English professor Stephen Cushman.
Holmberg says he didn't have an agenda with the book. Rather, he hopes Vietnam veterans and families can reconnect with Vietnam in a candid way without it being traumatic.
"I've gotten just overwhelming feedback," he said. "People really, really love it. It brought Vietnam back."
"Crossing the Pass of Clouds" is available for purchase at Flying Cloud Booksellers in Easton, Maryland, and on the Barnes & Noble website.

 Words

 I loved the article in the Star Dem about the Academy Art Museum's Bugatti show. The show itself was really great — my son and his family came down from Philadelphia for the weekend specifically to see it, and all of us thought it was terrific.Though I liked the article and adored the show, I was perplexed/shocked/horrified that the actual curator — the person who made the Bugatti show happen — was not named. Her name is Lee Glazer. She was previously a curator at the Smithsonian's Museum of Asian Art, which also has a world-class collection of work by several American artists, including Whistler. Lee Glazer oversaw that collection — a major achievement in the competitive world of international museum administration.
Though the Academy's magazine still lists Ms. Glazer as curator-at-large, several people who were at the Bugatti show that day told me she had left. She had done at least one other show for the Academy, focused on an interesting West Virginia printmaker of the mid-1950-60s. Ms. Glazer's talent was evident: the exhibit was accompanied by a brief film that really put the artist's work in context.
It's troubling that Ms. Glazer's time in Talbot County was so short, and I hope the board will look into her reasons for leaving. I never met her, but we just can't afford to lose someone of that caliber.
JOAN WETMORE
Neavitt

title: Country Cooking: Recipe cards, boxes and books
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Recipe cards, boxes and books

 May 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country cooking | Section: News 
 
 1244
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Recently, I was doing some delayed cleaning of those "stashed away" boxes and baskets and found so many bits and pieces of notebook paper and cards with recipes I had written down.My intention "way back then" was to re-write them on official recipe cards, but it never happened. I am going to share some with you all today as I officially type and store them on the computer.
I have a large wooden recipe box that is full of recipes, and I love reading these recipes over and over. This box only lacks one recipe that I need. My friend Joy of Greensboro needs to complete my collection by giving me her locally famous lasagna recipe. Maybe soon I will be able to share it. If any of my readers have recipe requests or want to share a recipe, please email me at mmsavage21145@gmail.com
EASY FRESH STRAWBERRY PIE
Prepare one 9-inch pie shell. Bake and set aside. Wash, cap and slice enough berries to equal 3 cups. Set aside one cup of the berries. Mash the other 2 cups, adding 1 cup sugar and 4 tbsps of cornstarch. Cook together with one tbsp lemon juice and 1/4 tsp almond flavor. The mixture will become clear and thick. Mix in the remaining 1 cup berries. Pour into the cooked pie shell. Chill and serve with whipped topping. Recipe given to me by Laura from Greenwood Mennonite Church.
MARYLAND CRAB CAKES
This recipe came from a lady down in West Ocean City whose husband was a waterman. The recipe card that Joan gave me with this recipe was decorated with crab drawings from her grandchildren.
Mix well: 1 egg, 1 tsp dry or yellow mustard, 2 tbsps mayonnaise, 1 tsp seafood seasoning, 1/2 tsp salt, a generous sprinkling of black pepper and a pinch of Tabasco sauce (optional). Add one pound lump or backfin crabmeat and 1/2 cup bread or cracker crumbs. Toss lightly but well. Shape into cakes. Will make 6 to 8 cakes according to your desired size. Fry in hot oil until lightly brown on both sides.
STACY'S SOUP
I have a small clipboard on the side of my refrigerator that is filled with clippings and note cards that hold some recipes I make often. One of my favorite recipes came from Stacy Neal of Caroline County. Stacy told me years ago that if I loved peppers, I would love this soup. Stacy you were correct — quick and easy to make and delicious.
In a crock pot or soup pot, add one pound of uncooked hamburger, 1 large can of tomato soup, 1 can beef broth, 1 can diced tomatoes, 1 large green pepper (cleaned and diced), 1 large cleaned and diced onion and 2 tbsps brown sugar. Cook on low for 6 to 7 hours. The last hour before soup is done, add one bag of boil-in-bag Rice and continue cooking on low. This soup smells like stuffed peppers and tastes like stuffed peppers and is delicious year round.
GRAHAM CRACKER CRUST
This pre-baked crust is great for those unbaked pie fillings that we use quite often. Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. This recipe makes one crust.
In a large bowl, place 1 1/4 cups of graham cracker crumbs, 1/4 cup sugar and 1/3 cup melted butter or margarine. Combine well and press into a 9 inch pie plate — bake for 6 to 8 minutes. Cool and fill.
FRIED BAKED BEANS
One of my Bishopville friends gave me this recipe years ago and wanted a copy of it, so here you are, Betty.
Fry 3 slices bacon, set aside, then put one 1 pound can of baked beans and place in the skillet with the bacon grease. Fry this for about 2 to 3 minutes. Then add 1/2 chopped onion, 1 tsp mustard, 2 tsps ketchup, and 1/2 cup brown sugar. Fry all of this mixture over medium heat for 5 — 7 minutes. Keep stirring and then put on low heat to keep warm until ready to serve. Serve with pancake syrup.
SQUASH CASSEROLE
Betty Rayne from my hometown of Bishopville cooks a lot with the group at Bishopville Volunteer Fire Department.
Combine 4 large cooked squash that have been drained with 2 slices of crumbled bread, a pinch of salt and black pepper, 1 1/2 teaspoons of sugar, 1 cup milk, 2 beaten eggs, 1 cup grated cheese, and 3 tbsps grated fresh onion. Mix well and bake in a greased casserole dish for 45 minutes or until firm.
RICE PUDDING
My mom made some of the best Rice Pudding ever. Mom did it the old-fashioned way — the only way she ever knew how. Mom did not take shortcuts with her cooking no matter what she cooked. Her famous Sunday morning "breakfast" was evident by all the cars in the yard and driveway. Family, friends and whomever knew "Ms. Laura" had breakfast cooking — bacon, scrapple, sausage, fresh eggs and those melt in the mouth homemade biscuits coming out of the oven to be smeared with fresh made butter and jelly. Ask anyone in the Selbyville — Bishopville area and they will tell you the same story. Many stories were told at that breakfast table and mom loved making this meal for everyone and listening to the chatter.
Mom made the "old fashioned" rice pudding, which required using the old fashioned long grain rice.
Wash 3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp rice in cold water to remove starch and drain well. In a large heavy saucepan, scald 7 cups of milk, lower the heat and then add the drained rice, 3/4 cup sugar, and 1/4 tsp salt. Bring to a simmer and cook for about 30 to 35 minutes, stirring often with a wooden spoon to prevent rice from sticking. When rice is tender, remove from heat. In a mixing bowl, beat 5 eggs until frothy. Add 1 cup heavy cream and continue to beat while slowly adding some of the hot rice mixture, about 2 cups. Add this mixture to the remaining rice mixture and cook over medium heat for about 5 minutes or until mixture coats spoon. If you desire raisins then add 2/3 cup at this time. Remove from heat and stir in 2 tsps vanilla. Pour mixture into a large shallow dish and sprinkle cinnamon on top. Bake in a preheated 350 degree oven for 20 minutes.
BREAD PUDDING
When mom had stale bread in the bread box, she made delicious bread pudding with it. This was a different kind of pudding and very tasty. Most of our bread was homemade so she would also use biscuits for the pudding — just broke it up in smaller pieces. We would come in the house and a pan would be sitting on the countertop cooling and it smelled so good. Mom would cut the pudding in squares, and we could simply pick one up and be on our way. I have said many times that there was very little waste on the farm, and it included 'stale bread'.
Soak one loaf of stale bread in about a cup of water, breaking the bread into pieces. Let soak, in a large bowl, for 30 minutes and then squeeze all the water out and place back in the bowl. Add 2 sticks melted margarine, 1 cup self-rising flour, 1/2 cup brown sugar, 1/2 cup crushed saltines, 1/2 cup golden raisins, 1 tablespoon allspice, 1 tablespoon nutmeg, 1 tbsp cinnamon and 2 beaten eggs, mix well and pour into a lightly greased baking pan. Bake at 375 degrees for one hour.

title: Historical society aims to highlight the overlooked history of Delaware town and its founder
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Historical society aims to highlight the overlooked history of Delaware town and its founder

 May 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 839
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Few people would recognize the name Matthew Aiken, save for a few local history buffs.But a new effort by the Pencader Heritage Area Association aims to raise awareness of Aiken and the history of the village he founded, Aiken Town, or as it's known today, Glasgow.
On May 17, Pencader hosted the first Matthew Aiken Day, inviting visitors to its museum near the intersection of Old Baltimore Pike and Del. 72 for music, demonstrations, vendors and more. The organization hopes to grow the event into an annual festival.
Pencader president Keith Jackson said his goal is to highlight the history of Glasgow, which tends to get less attention than the history of incorporated towns like Newark.
"I have a fascination with Glasgow. It's the Charlie Brown of towns," Jackson said. "To me, the fascination in the story is the fact that there is no story. But within that no story, there actually is a story. You just have to find it."
Aiken's Tavern dates back to colonial times and was located at a crossroads approximately 1,200 feet north of the present intersection of Del. 896 and U.S. 40. During the Revolutionary War, British troops were quartered there prior to the Battle of Cooch's Bridge.
After the war, Matthew Aiken bought the tavern from his brother John and laid out plans to create a town surrounding the tavern. However, the construction of what is now U.S. Route 40 realigned the road and established a new crossroads, diminishing the tavern's prominence.
The area was later renamed Glasgow by Scottish settlers in the area.
Though Aiken Town never came to fruition as its namesake envisioned, the Glasgow area obviously continued to grow and is now one of the fastest growing areas of New Castle County, Jackson said.
Worried that the few remaining historic buildings in Glasgow will be lost, Pencader is working on an ambitious plan to restore two historic houses and create an event space that will host educational programming and events, like an expanded Matthew Aiken Day festival.
The proposal revolves around a 48-acre property, known both as La Grange and the Barczewski Farm, that is located at the corner of Glasgow Avenue and U.S. 40. It is one of the last remaining undeveloped properties in the area, which is dominated by Peoples Plaza, other shopping centers and housing developments.
There have been several attempts to develop the La Grange property, and the latest comes from developer Steve Nichols. He is proposing to use part of the property to build 98 homes and an assisted living facility.
Nichols would use some of the profits of the development to restore the historic La Grange house as well as purchase and restore the Brooks house on an adjacent property.
Those houses, and the surrounding 10 or 11 acres, would be donated to Pencader, which would use them for historical and educational programming and also turn part of the property into an event venue.
The La Grange house, which is on the National Register of Historic Places, was built in 1815.
It was given its name by Marquis de Lafayette, the French military officer who helped the colonists win the Revolutionary War. Lafayette visited the house during his 1824 tour of the United States and remarked that it reminded him of his home in France, which was called La Grange. The name stuck, Jackson said.
In the early 1800s, the house was owned by prominent Glasgow citizen Dr. Samuel Black, who lived there and also had his doctor's office in the back of the building. Black was an early promoter of vaccines, researched soil depletion to develop more responsible farming practices and served in public office and as a trustee of what became the University of Delaware.
Black was renowned for having one of the finest libraries in the state and for his writing and lectures on both agricultural and medical subjects, according to Jackson.
The property was purchased by the Barczewski family in the 1940s and continued to function as a farm and dairy for many years. The house has been vacant for two decades.
The Brooks house, meanwhile, is located on 1.3 acres directly next to the Barczewski farm and fronts onto Glasgow Avenue.
Jackson said less is known about the Brooks house, though it was built in 1787 and was once owned by relatives of Samuel Black.
The development plan is working its way through New Castle County's development approval process. Jackson has argued that developing part of the property is the only way to save the two historic structures.
The idea got a major boost when, at Jackson's urging, the county added the La Grange site to the list of properties being considered for the new Glasgow Library. Jackson said building the library on the part of the property that is being preserved would complement Pencader's plans for the site and make it an even more important resource for the community.
"The cherry on top is one of the things Dr. Black was known for was he had the finest library in the entire state," Jackson said. "How amazing would it be to put the Glasgow Library on his property?"

title: Middle-schooler is youngest to ever publish a fantasy novel
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Middle-schooler is youngest to ever publish a fantasy novel

 June 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 362
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Monday afternoon, 12-year-old Evelyn Klotz finished her middle school finals. The previous day, Klotz spoke to a sold-out audience at the Flying Cloud Bookstore about her newly published fantasy novel "Hero of Draconis."Klotz, a Trappe resident, set the book store's record as the first person to sell every copy of her book and sell out an event. But that wasn't the only record she broke that day.
Klotz also became the youngest person ever to write and publish a fantasy novel, according to TCK Publishing.
She began working on "Hero of Draconis" at 10-years-old. After writing on her own for some time, her father Eric connected her with a manuscript headhunter who gave her guidance on the writing and publishing process.
Klotz took a college-level writing course and edited her novel with the headhunter line by line.
"It really helped to improve my understanding of plot and characters because let's just say some of the characters were not the best before I went through it and fixed them," she said.
Klotz found inspiration in her backyard, her younger brother (who she based the character Meep on), and other fantasy novels like the "Eragon" series by Christopher Paolini. "The author of that series was only 18 when he published his first book, and I wanted to be better than that," Klotz said.
Eric Klotz said it feels like one of those proud dad moments. "I'm also a little annoyed because I feel like she's out-accomplished me already," he said with a chuckle. "But no, she's fantastic, and I'm super happy and proud of her."
Evelyn Klotz described the book as "a 340-page novel that follows the quest of four characters journeying across the fantasy planet to save the known world from total obliteration."
She said her main motivation for writing the novel was to create a world that hadn't been tainted by machines or technology while highlighting her love of nature.
Without offering spoilers, Evelyn Klotz said the novel ends with a massive cliffhanger.
"It's a big cliffhanger, an annoying cliffhanger" Eric Klotz said. He will have to wait along with the rest of her readers for answers in the second installment of her series, which is already underway.

title: 15-year-old Javion Jones a new minister at Union Baptist Church
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
15-year-old Javion Jones a new minister at Union Baptist Church

 June 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 333
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Javion Jones, 15, is now officially a minister at Union Baptist Church after he passed his minister's training class in May.After multiple tests, Jones took his final test, his trial sermon in front of the church.
On May 18, Jones conducted his trial sermon, where he preached on Luke 18:35-43. The scripture highlights Jesus coming near Jericho encountering a blind man. Jesus then preformed a miracle granting the blind man his sight.
"I picked that because as a young boy, people would say you're called, and I could just say thank you not knowing what was going on because I was blind to my calling because I was just young, and other people who were unblind spiritually could see it," Jones said.
After a church council vote, Jones was voted in as a minster at Union Baptist Church.
"I'm just a minister right now," Jones said. "I do know that shortly, my pastor will be placing me over the prayer department."
Jones' mother, Taryn Bell, is excited for what God has in store for Jones' future.
"I was just extremely proud as any parent would be," Bell said. "When I look at him, I know that being a licensed minister comes with a big responsibility, but I also know that Javion has a heart for serving. I'm someone who believes that if God called you, it's no limit to your age. But as his parent, I do try to make sure that he stays a kid and not feel the pressure that he has to have it all together. I'm just excited to see how God will continue to use him, and how he'll grow, and his ministry and the word."
Jones' long-term goal is to be elevated to the office of a reverend. Then, a couple years after, he plans to apply at a church and become a pastor. Jones also plans to study mortuary science in Catonsville after he graduates in 2028.
Those interested in contacting Jones about his trial sermon can reach him at @Javionjonesministry@gmail.com.

title: Chamber Music Festival connects community to 'world-class' talent
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Chamber Music Festival connects community to 'world-class' talent

 June 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 635
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Chesapeake Music's 40th annual Chamber Music Festival opening extravaganza connected Easton residents with world-class talent Friday evening.When the festival began 40 years ago, it consisted of one concert held in St. Michaels. Friday's concert kicked off a two-week event showcasing a variety of musical arrangements.
"We invite between 15 and 20 musicians from around the country to come and work together, sometimes for the first time, and they put on six concerts over two weeks," Chesapeake Music Executive Director David Faleris said.
Chesapeake Music is a nonprofit based in Easton that strives to bring music and music education of the highest level to Talbot County and the Eastern Shore, according to Faleris. The Chamber Music Festival is one way to achieve this goal.
The opening extravaganza featured four different pieces, ranging from the late 18th to the early 20th centuries, and a variety of chamber ensembles. The musicians included cellist Marcy Rosen, pianist Robert McDonald and oboist Peggy Pearson, along with several others.
Among the performers Friday was Catherine Cho, a violinist and one of the festival's two artistic directors. Cho has been coming to the festival since the late 1990s after being invited by Marcy Rosen, who is now her co-artistic director.
"I learned so much from playing with older, seasoned artists, and now we're trying to continue that with hiring people like Albert and Sterling and Zhanbo to kind of continue the tradition of mixing intergenerational groups together," Cho said.
As a professor at Juilliard, Cho has worked with young cellist Sterling Elliott and pianist Albert Cano Smit, both of whom took the stage at Friday's Opening Extravaganza. Elliot also performed at last year's festival, but this is Cano Smit's first time at the event.
"There's a little bit of a mentorship-mentee aspect to it, but what we end up developing is a really vibrant energy on stage with the musicians," Faleris said.
Maria Montanez said that watching the young artists was some a highlight of the show because of the energy the musicians brought to the stage. Montanez attended the festival for the first time after recently moving to Easton.
"The performers really put their heart into it and make it just so much more beautiful," she said.
Montanez was introduced to the festival by her friend from Easton, Donna Woolf, who first attended the festival last year. A former Washington, D.C., resident, Woolf appreciated having access to such high-class performances in a small town like Easton.
While some guests were only recently introduced to the festival, others, like Gale Shehan, who has served as an usher at the festival for around 10 years, were aware they will be getting elite performances.
"The musicians are world-class, and I don't think as many people realize that," Shehan said. "Us die-hards that come, we know. But the people who don't necessarily come very often don't realize the level of player that's here."
Montanez noted that she loved the show because of the unique level of intimacy between the audience and the performers, which she said she felt even from the balcony.
A reception was held after the show, where audience members had the opportunity to engage with the performers one-on-one. Cho said this is what is so special about the Chamber Music Festival — it establishes a sense of connection to the community.
"As you can feel, it's very personal," Cho said. "Everyone is connected to each other through a shared experience, usually the love of music. So I think that makes it very special here to have that feeling of closeness, not only on stage, but between the audience and the performers."
After a successful opening night, there are still performances left to experience. The festival will host the Juilliard String Quartet as well as several other musicians in its second and final week of performances running Thursday through Saturday.
Ticket information can be found at chesapeakemusic.org.

title: Pride Festival coming to Mid-Shore this weekend
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Pride Festival coming to Mid-Shore this weekend

 June 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 490
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The fourth annual Delmarva Pride Festival, taking place this weekend, is about more than festivities, organizers said."It's about creating an environment and a space that's safe for everyone," co-founder of the Delmarva Pride Center, Tina Jones, said. Jones helped create the Pride Center in 2020, along with treasurer and co-founder Kyle O'Donnell, after noticing a lack of LGBTQ+ support groups on the Eastern Shore.
According to O'Donnell, the Delmarva Pride Center organizes the Pride Festival each June, along with year-round programming, to provide fun activities and support services to help people of all ages in the LGBTQ+ community.
The money raised during the Pride Festival goes to the Pride Center and helps the center run year-round, O'Donnell said. However, the center tries to keep the events as accessible and affordable as possible.
"We do try to have as many of these events free or as low-cost as we can," O'Donnell said. "Nothing's outrageously priced."
To launch the weekend of events, "A Night In New Orleans" will showcase live jazz music by Ryan Aspirion with special guest Jackie Moreland at the Garfield Center for the Arts on Thursday. There will be a silent auction to raise money for the Delmarva Pride Center. A VIP hour will be held at 6 p.m., an hour before the event begins at 7 p.m. Tickets start at $25.
Jones is excited for this event since it is a new addition to the festival lineup and will be Delmarva Pride's first event in Chestertown.
Friday events will begin with free Candy Bingo from noon to 3 p.m. at the Academy Art Museum in Easton. Unlike some others, this event is targeted towards all ages, according to O'Donnell.
"That's just a fun, free event where we play bingo, and let down your hair and have a good time," O'Donnell said.
Later Friday evening, the Pride Drag Show will be held from 7 to 9 p.m. at Easton's Avalon Theatre. Hosted by Drag Queen Miranda Bryant, the show will feature four up-and-coming drag queens. This event frequently sells out and is restricted to ages 21 and older. Tickets start at $27.
The main event of the weekend is the Delmarva Pride Street Festival. The festival starts at 11 a.m. and runs until 4 p.m. in downtown Easton on Saturday. There will be 90 vendors at the festival.
"We expect several thousand people to come out," O'Donnell said. "We have live music, nonprofit groups that are tabling, as well as vendor artisans and people that have little small businesses and food trucks."
Not long after the festival, patrons can go to the Pride Dance Saturday evening from 7 to 11:30 p.m. Hosted by Hummingbird Inn in Easton, the free dance party with a live DJ will be open to the public.
The weekend will conclude with a Pride Brunch at 447 Venue in Cambridge. The brunch will be from noon to 3 p.m. with tickets on sale for $30.
Information about the festival and event tickets can be found at delmarvapridecenter.com/festival.

title: Talbot Treasures will showcase county artifacts, memories this Saturday
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot Treasures will showcase county artifacts, memories this Saturday

 June 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 504
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Inside the Waterfowl Festival building sit some relics of Talbot County history, such as a penny from 1794, a baton from a beloved St. Michaels High School band director, and a rare whiskey decanter decorated to celebrate America's bicentennial.They are some of the early entries into Talbot Treasures, a joint effort between Talbot250 Commission, Talbot Historical Society and Waterfowl Festival leaders to assemble a display of artifacts.
The Talbot Treasures collection will be open for the public to view on Saturday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Waterfowl Festival building on South Harrison Street. Talbot County communications coordinator Sarah Kilmon beamed with excitement Thursday as she perused through some of the items.
"We'd like to tell as many stories of Talbot County as we can," Kilmon said.
Kilmon, who leads Talbot250 and its efforts to celebrate America's upcoming semiquincentennial in 2026, contributed to the collection herself, adding photos of and items belonging to her grandfather, Louis Scott Kilmon.
He was the St. Michaels High School band director for over 30 years before retiring in 2001. His baton — the same one he's using in old photos of him conducting — and trombone will be shown off Saturday.
"He retired in 2001, but his legacy still echoes in the halls of the school and in the lives of those he inspired," Kilmon wrote on her item description.
A few items down from the trombone and baton is a special edition whiskey decanter, which dates to the nation's bicentennial in 1976. It was found in the basement of the Waterfowl Building by sheer luck and is now cleaned up for show.
Waterfowl Festival Executive Director Deena Kilmon, Sarah's mother, said the building itself — which is nearing its 100th anniversary in a couple years — is jam-packed with history. The number of groups, organizations and people that have used or borrowed the building lends itself to some neat stories, she said, such as when it was an old shooting range or when former President John F. Kennedy made a campaign stop there in 1960.
"The hundreds, and hundreds and hundreds of people that have been in here is mind-blowing," Deena Kilmon said.
On Saturday, even more history will be captured in the building formerly known as the Easton Armory.
Many other items have been brought in already or are expected. Some of the oldest include a 1794 penny from the Talbot County Women's Club and a silver spoon submitted by Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher that dates back to 1810 and the Royal Navy.
During the exhibit Saturday, attendees can vote for the item with the best story and the most unique artifact. Talbot Historical Society board members will host a panel on antique valuation and auctioning.
"Many of these stories still resonate today," said Talbot Historical Society Executive Director Peggy Morey in a press release. "We hope visitors will not only learn from these items and their histories but will also find meaningful connections to our community and the challenges we face now."
To learn more about Talbot Treasures, visit talbot250.org/events/talbot-treasures.

title: Atwood's 'A 3 Month Journey' on display at the Foundry
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Atwood's 'A 3 Month Journey' on display at the Foundry

 June 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 320
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Mary Elizabeth Atwood, a Caroline County native, presented "A 3 Month Journey" at the Foundry in Denton on Friday. The show exhibited art that Atwood worked on during a three-month period in the upstairs art room of the Foundry.During that period, Atwood created more than 40 pieces of art. She said when she begins creating, she can't stop.
"Three months of working, and once I start creating, I don't know how to stop," Atwood said. "... I meditate every day. So more like contemplation, so I don't listen to something that's just being still and I think that helps clear my mind and sometimes that's how I paint also… I will look at the canvas, and then I'll just go and pick out the paints, put them on beside the canvas, and then pretty much I know what I'm going to do."
Along with presenting her art pieces, Atwood performed another form of art, presenting multiple poems. Atwood says her writing process is the same as her painting process, except for one major part.
"It's almost the same thing except I can't sit down and just write," Atwood said. "I have to have a pen and paper beside me and pencil and paper, even when we're traveling, because if something hits me, I have to write it down. Just a line."
Atwood finished the paintings within the first month and a half in the art studio of the Foundry, but before that she also starting creating archetype figures to be presented as well. According to Atwood, those figures represent a season in life everyone man or woman may experience.
George Karos II, executive director of the Foundry, says artist like Atwood, who participate in the artist in residence program, bring exposure to the Foundry.
"In terms of visibility, branding, it opens up opportunities for us to not only be known as a little green building with the guitar player out front," Karos said.

title: Parade, performances and history mark Juneteenth at Kennard
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Parade, performances and history mark Juneteenth at Kennard

 June 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 208
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — A celebration of freedom, unity and heritage brought the community together June 14 as the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center hosted its seventh annual Juneteenth festivities.The all-day event featured an expanded parade, live music, dancing, readings by prominent Black authors, a visit from the Mobile Library, a breakfast buffet, free haircuts, basketball clinics, vendors, food trucks and exhibits inviting the public to explore Kennard's museum and resource library.
Welcoming the crowd was newly appointed Executive Director Tara Coursey of the Kennard Alumni Association, who expressed appreciation for the participants and supporters.
Carole Boston Weatherford, author of this year's One Maryland, One Book selection Kin: Rooted in Hope, participated in the event with book signings and conversation. Weatherford, who has strong ties to the Eastern Shore, is also known for writing Juneteenth Jamboree in 1995 — the first children's book to highlight the Texas-rooted holiday.
"It is a great day to celebrate with the community," Weatherford said.
What began nearly 20 years ago as a grassroots initiative to revive and restore the historic Kennard High School has become a reality. The center now serves as a hub for African American history programs and events and is home to the Kennard African American History Museum.
More information is available at kennardheritage.com.

title: 'Dorchester Dreams' becomes county song
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'Dorchester Dreams' becomes county song

 June 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 429
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Singer-songwriter Jayla Elise performed her song "Dorchester Dreams" in front of the Dorchester County Council and attending residents at Tuesday's council meeting after it being adopted as the first ever official county song.Elise's song showcases the pride, unity, hope and resilience that resonates across generations in Dorchester County. In "Dorchester Dreams," Elise honors the legacy of those who have contributed to the county, including Harriet Tubman and current families.
"To everyone who has been a part of Dorchester County or grew up here, I want to thank you for actually being the inspiration for every lyric that I wrote down," Elise said before performing her song. Elise said although she isn't originally from Dorchester County, she wanted to capture the feeling of what it means to call a place home even if you're not from there.
Elise is an independent artist who grew up in Prince George's County, where she found her voice in state choirs and formal performing arts training, according to her website.
"Being an independent artist, there's a sense of liberation behind that," Elise said. She said being independent allows her full creative control over her image, sound and process. Elise is managed by the Barzini Family Music Group, which aims to establish the Eastern Shore as an up and coming music scene.
"It's no doubt in their minds, and mine too, that this is going to be where entertainment is going to find its home very soon," Elise said. The Barzini family and Elise believe this because of Cambridge's famous former resident, Harriet Tubman.
"For the culture, there's the big three: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X and Harriet Tubman," Elise said. King was from Georgia, which has a thriving entertainment scene, Malcolm X was from Brooklynn, the birthplace of hip-hop, and now they believe it's Cambridge's time.
The lyrics to "Dorchester Dreams" were inspired by community and hopes to bridge the generational gap by highlighting shared memories among people who can be vastly different yet share the place they call home.
Elise's aspirations do not stop at the county level. She is currently working on a song for Maryland 250, an organization dedicated to preserving Maryland's history ahead of the 250th anniversary of the nation next year.
According to Council Vice President Mike Detmer, Elise's song will be performed at official events, civic ceremonies and educational programs throughout Dorchester County.
Elise wants to use her platform to build community and empower others to shoot for the stars. "Everybody has a gift. How are you going to use it in this world?" she said.
Elise's music can be found at jaylaelise.com.

title: Old Trinity Church celebrates its 350th anniversary
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Old Trinity Church celebrates its 350th anniversary

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH CREEK — The appropriately named Old Trinity Church is celebrating its 350th anniversary this year. It is the oldest church in the nation still used for regular Sunday service.The Colonial-era church was built sometime between 1675 and 1690 on over four acres and has undergone significant renovations since, but it has not lost its original charm. The Rev. Dan Dunlap said that in the 1850s, the church was remodeled in the Victorian style.
"100 years later, under the oversight of Col. Edgar Garbisch, and his wife Bernice Chrysler Garbisch and the Chrysler family, they restored the church again, but this time they went back to the colonial style," Dunlap said.
Dunlap said the church is roughly 38 feet long and 20 feet wide and was built to hold "100 souls." However these days, he said on an average Sunday worship, the same familiar 25 to 30 faces sit in the pews.
Dunlap has been the rector of Old Trinity for 11 years and was a former professor of historical theology and worship at Houston Graduate School of Theology. He has organized multiple historic services and events to commemorate the 350th anniversary of the Old Trinity Church.
In February, the church held battleground reenactments like one for the "Battle of the Ice Mound," which took place 210 years ago off the nearby James and Taylors islands as one of the final battles of the War of 1812.
The next day, during regular church service, they used the 1662 Book of Common Prayer of the Church of England, which Dunlap said would have been the prayer book early settlers used.
Old Trinity Church hosted its second of three special historical services for the 350th anniversary on June 15 using the 1789 Book of Common Prayer, the first prayer book used by the Episcopalian Church in the United States. Dunlap said the service was very well attended.
"We're having a lot of fun with this," he said. According to Dunlap, the church is planning to have a third historical service sometime this year and will be hosting an event open to the public in September.
The church's graveyard is the final resting place for six veterans of the American Revolution, four from the War of 1812, and several veterans from both sides of the Civil War. Dunlap said they are still selling plots in the graveyard.
Dunlap said the church is open to the public and wants to encourage people to come and check it out regardless of religious affiliation.
Along with the four acres of church property, which houses the cemetery, Old Trinity also owns an additional 85 acres of property right on Church Creek. "It's just a very peaceful slice of Heaven, and it's situated right on the creek," Dunlap said. "It's very scenic."
"A big slice of this area we maintain, and we do so by letting a local farmer, the same family that operates Emily's down the road, farms the property," Dunlap said. He said their recent corn crop has started growing tall.
"There seems to be an intersection between the sacredness of the place as a place of worship, but also a place where nature and faith come together," he said. "It's like an intersection of the two."

title: Juneteenth celebration honors powerful stories
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Juneteenth celebration honors powerful stories

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Juneteenth Celebration hosted by the Academy Art Museum on Saturday focused on the power of storytelling and using it to honor African American history, culture and resilience, according to Jennifer Chrzanowski, the deputy director at the museum.Chrzanowski said she and the other Juneteenth committee members selected performers who were storytellers to stay on the theme of "Our Freedom! Our Story!" Among them was Jeffrey Boston Weatherford, a children's illustrator and performance poet from High Point, North Carolina.
"Connecting the culture is imperative," Weatherford said. "They call the United States the Melting Pot, but sometimes we act like it's water and oil and not melting together, so it's necessary."
When he wasn't presenting on stage, Weatherford was manning a booth displaying his books alongside his mom, writer Carole Boston Weatherford, and his wife. Later in the event, he stepped into the museum, where his exhibition was on display.
The exhibition featured words and images from Carole and Jeffrey Boston Weatherford's book titled "Kin: Rooted in Hope," which reconstructed the history of the Weatherford family. The exhibition will be on display at the museum until June 29.
Outside of the museum, visitors could visit the vendor booths or enjoy a performance by several musical acts on stage.
St. Michaels High School student Ruby Fisher took to the stage to perform two songs and read two poems. She said her favorite part was seeing everyone's faces and getting to share her voice.
Her third time at the festival, Fisher said she returns each year because of its importance.
"It helps to bring the community together, and it helps support history and how it needs to be remembered," Fisher said.
The Academy Art Museum partnered with Building African American Minds and the Frederick Douglass Honor Society to organize the celebration. Dina Daly, the Executive Director of BAAM, said the Juneteenth event is important because it teaches students to understand and appreciate the day's history.
"I think for many years, only the Black community really knew about Juneteenth, or even some young kids didn't really understand the meaning of Juneteenth," Daly said.
Juneteenth, which became a federal holiday in 2021, marks the emancipation of enslaved African Americans.
To spread awareness of the history of Juneteenth, the Academy Art Museum holds an essay contest for middle and high school students. Leading up to the celebration, students had the opportunity to submit an essay about what Juneteenth means to the youth today, with the opportunity to win a cash prize.
"It gives them the opportunity to research it, to actually understand, and to put their thoughts into words that they can express themselves and then maybe they get an award," Daly said.
This year marked the Academy Art Museum's 14th annual Juneteenth Celebration, and Chrzanowski and Daly both agreed that the event was necessary, serving as an opportunity for locals to gather together and honor their history through a troublesome time.
"There are a lot of places that are now on these budget cuts, and they're cutting Juneteenth as a celebration," Chrzanowski said. "But we continue to go strong."

title: ‘Colorful Visions’ opens First Friday at The Artists’ Gallery
author: Staff Writer
content:
‘Colorful Visions’ opens First Friday at The Artists’ Gallery

 June 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 425
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The Artists' Gallery will feature the work of one of its exhibiting artists, Carol McClees, on First Friday, July 4, in a body of work titled Colorful Visions. McClees' goal is to create a vibrant painting that conveys a sense of life, vibrancy and movement — in her words, "ALIVE WITH COLOR!"A contemporary artist and award-winning painter, McClees' self-directed education has included studying with some of the best national and regional artists. While she has worked in a variety of mediums, she favors painting in oil.
McClees has exhibited her paintings in many juried shows throughout the United States, including but not limited to Coos Art Museum (Oregon), American Society of Marine Artists East Regional Show hosted by Biggs Museum of American Art (Delaware), Washington County Museum of Fine Arts (Maryland), and Buffalo Naval Park Museum (New York), as well as Working Artists Forum's Local Color and the Waterfowl Festival (Easton). Her work is part of many private collections throughout the Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, West Coast and New England. McClees is an active member of many art organizations, including the American Society of Marine Artists, Working Artists' Forum and Mid-Atlantic Plein Air Painters Association. Her degrees include an RN and an MBA in marketing.
Born and raised in New England, McClees is married to a native Marylander and lives in Baltimore. She enjoys sailing on the Chesapeake Bay aboard her 36-foot Skean Dhu, tennis, Nantucket basket weaving, embroidery and reading.
McClees' artistic inspiration comes from a maritime landscape, a beloved animal or an architectural delight, whether painting in plein air or in her home studio. "Striving to achieve a painterly realism one brush stroke at a time, using abundant color, and supporting textural tools is my artistic goal. I love to find and capture the unique moment in time when the subject matter comes to life — that fleeting moment when the magical effects of the sun cause dramatic play between lights and darks. When accomplished, I believe that artistic tension is at its best, revealing a painting Alive with Color, which evokes thoughtful emotion and allows the viewer to complete the story."
The public is invited to attend the Artists' Gallery's opening reception for McClees on First Friday, July 4, from 5 to 7:30 p.m. Her paintings will be featured in the gallery throughout the month of July. The Artists' Gallery is located at 239 High St. in Chestertown, and is open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sundays from 12:30 to 4:30 p.m. For more information, visit www.theartistsgalleryctown.com or call 410-778-2425.

title: Repairs to damaged Delaware church reveal historical treasures
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Repairs to damaged Delaware church reveal historical treasures

 June 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 727
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When construction workers began tearing away a damaged portion of St. John AM Church in Newark on June 23, they unearthed historical artifacts that had been hidden for decades."We were jumping for joy in here because it's part of our history. This is the oldest Black church in this city," Pastor Blaine Hackett said. "It was a very significant part of this community for a long time, and we still are."
The workers found an old wooden sign from the Delaware church's early days that was installed above the original entrance to the building, which was constructed in 1867. The sign was covered up with bricks when the church was renovated in 1960.
Also discovered was a time capsule that was hidden behind a cornerstone during the 1960 renovation. Inside was an old bible, a Book of Discipline dating back to 1907, minutes from a 1960 church trustees meeting and other old documents.
Church leaders plan to display the items inside the church and are planning to include a new time capsule in the renovated portion of the church.
The church, located at the corner of New London Road and Cleveland Avenue, sustained significant damage when it was struck by speeding vehicles twice in a six-month period, once in August and again in January.
After the church spent several months negotiating with the insurance company, hiring a construction company and obtaining city permits, work finally began this week.
"The people in the congregation are really excited about it happening because they've been asking every Sunday for months and months when it's going to start," said Bob Anderson, president of the St. John AM Church trustees.
Since the first crash, the church has been holding services in its fellowship hall, which is in an undamaged portion of the building. Hackett said he hopes the repairs to the sanctuary are complete by September.
"All I can say is, praise God, from whom all blessings flow," he said. "We're finally getting there. We've still got a ways to go, but we're just elated right now to get started."
The renovations will restore the front portion of the church, which sustained heavy damage. The stained glass windows, one of which is being professionally repaired after being damaged, will be reinstalled.
Workers will also slightly expand the footprint of the church in the front.
Currently, the brick church has a small entry vestibule that juts out from the front of the building. That vestibule was heavily damaged in the two crashes.
When it is rebuilt, the vestibule will extend across the entire length of the front of the church.
The left side, the area most likely to be hit by a vehicle, will be used as a cloakroom. The cloakroom will provide a buffer in case the building is struck again. Instead of hitting the sanctuary wall and the last row of pews, a vehicle would hit the cloakroom instead.
On the left side, the church will build a handicapped accessible bathroom.
Currently, the church's only bathrooms are located in the newer portion of the building, behind the sanctuary. If congregants need to use the bathroom during a service, they either have to walk behind the pastor to access the other part of the building, or go outside and enter through a back door. Disabled congregants have no choice but to use a wheelchair ramp outside.
The church also plans to strengthen the bollards in the front yard that are intended to protect the building from vehicles. The two vehicles that hit the building were going so fast, they pulled the bollards out of the ground.
The new bollards will be reinforced, deeper and connected underground for additional strength.
Hackett said the renovations are expected to cost upward of $300,000. Much of the cost will be paid through insurance money and donations the church has received, but Hackett said additional donations are needed, especially for items not covered by insurance, such as new carpet and repairs to pews.
Donations can be made online at paypal.com/fundraiser/charity/1500432. Checks and money orders can be mailed to or dropped off at St. John AM Church, 77 New London Road, Newark DE, 19711.
"We appreciate all the people that helped us thus far. We still have a journey to go, but we trust in God to restore us and make us whole," Hackett said. "It's unfortunate we've had these incidents, but we're here to stay. We've here to still serve this community and share the Gospel."

‘Colorful Visions’ opens First Friday at The Artists’ Gallery

 June 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 290
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Artists' Gallery in Chestertown will feature the work of one of its exhibiting artists, Carol McClees, on First Friday, July 4, in a body of work titled "Colorful Visions."A contemporary artist and award-winning painter, McClees' has worked in a variety of mediums, she favors painting in oil.
McClees has exhibited her paintings in many juried. U.S. shows, including at the Coos Art Museum (Oregon), American Society of Marine Artists East Regional Show hosted by Biggs Museum of American Art (Delaware), Washington County Museum of Fine Arts (Maryland), and Buffalo Naval Park Museum (New York), as well as locally at Working Artists Forum's Local Color and the Waterfowl Festival in Easton.
McClees is an active member of the American Society of Marine Artists, Working Artists' Forum and Mid-Atlantic Plein Air Painters Association.
"Striving to achieve a painterly realism one brush stroke at a time, using abundant color, and supporting textural tools is my artistic goal. I love to find and capture the unique moment in time when the subject matter comes to life — that fleeting moment when the magical effects of the sun cause dramatic play between lights and darks. When accomplished, I believe that artistic tension is at its best, revealing a painting Alive with Color, which evokes thoughtful emotion and allows the viewer to complete the story," she said.
The Artists' Gallery is hosting an opening reception for McClees on First Friday, July 4, from 5 to 7:30 p.m. Her paintings will be featured in the gallery throughout the month of July. The Artists' Gallery is located at 239 High St. in Chestertown, and is open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sundays from 12:30 to 4:30 p.m. For more information, visit www.theartistsgalleryctown.com or call 410-778-2425.

title: Fourth of July picnics
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Fourth of July picnics

 July 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: News 
 
 1563
 Words 

 Read News Document

 My memories of celebrating the Fourth of July holiday go back to my early childhood, since my mom was born on July 4, 1911, in the small town of Selbyville, Delaware. Mom would be celebrating her 112th birthday this year — she left us at age 86 almost 27 years ago.In my early memories, the family packed picnic foods and traveled to visit various sites such as the Philadelphia Zoo, Virginia resort areas, state parks and sites of historic events. We visited historic military sites nearby. Eventually as my parents grew older, the celebrations came back home where we gathered at local swimming areas, campgrounds, parks and, finally, at the site of our small schoolhouse, now a small park, in our town of Bishopville.
One of my favorite memories of those Fourth of July trips would be going to visit my late Aunt Irene and Uncle Fred in Chester, Pennsylvania. Early that morning, my mom got up and started making fried chicken, biscuits, potato salad, cucumbers and onions, corn-on-the-cob, sliced tomatoes, fresh beets, and fresh baked cupcakes. Finally, she made two big jugs of homemade iced tea and a large jug of fresh water.
Daddy backed the big four-door Oldsmobile 98 to the back door and start loading the food. In go the boxes of food, coolers of iced tea and water, coolers of side food and the big roaster pan of fried chicken, finally the picnic tablecloths, wet and dry hand cloths, and plastic ware with plastic cups. The kids load up, and off we go to Pennsylvania.
The ride was wonderful, especially along the C & O Canal and Delaware & Pa. Canal areas. Eventually everyone is hungry, and my father pulls off at a rest area campground. How amazingly beautiful — railroad with a train passing, ships in the ocean, tugs in the canal and a plane overhead.
Mom would also include some of the large dill pickles that we could snack on while riding in the car. I remember the big thick glass gallon jars that were filled with the whole dill, sour or sweet pickles you bought at the store. The lid was a wide-mouth metal lid. The jar was to be saved, washed really well, used to make jugs of tea, lemonade and water. I remember packing one of these pickles, wrapped in saran wrap or foil, in my lunch box, something my grandkids still do.
You know how it is loading kids up in a vehicle to travel. Just before you leave, you line them up to "go to the bathroom" one last time. Well, 20 miles down the road somebody has to go and then all the others start with "I'm thirsty," or "I'm hungry" or "are we there yet?" To stop this, Mom made us all get out, walk around the car, and handed us some pretzels to munch on — Mom thought of it all.
We usually ate before we got to my relatives' house because they enjoyed making a freezer of homemade ice cream and a fresh banana cake or strawberry cake. My favorite part of the trip was just "being in a small city with sidewalks" and "city talking folks." The last thing mom would say as we pulled up in front of the house was "act like you got some raising" and "behave." Remember those words my friends because we were told this wherever we went.
Our last family gathering with our mother was held in Bishopville at the site of our local elementary school park on July 4, 1997 — the day mom turned 86 years old. Mom died four months later. Our father had died 23 years earlier.
Gatherings changed through the years, but those memories have not.
Celebrate the Fourth anywhere or however you want, but have plenty of delicious food, much laughter and fun and games — the day will arrive that you have those memories to cling to.
Happy birthday, America.
COUNTRY FRIED CHICKEN
2 cups buttermilk, 1 tbsp Dijon mustard, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp ground black pepper, 1 tsp cayenne pepper, 1 whole chicken (cut into pieces), 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1 tbsp garlic powder, 1 tbsp onion powder, 5 cups vegetable oil for frying.
Whisk together buttermilk, mustard, salt, pepper and cayenne in a bowl. Pour buttermilk marinade into a resealable plastic bag. Add chicken pieces, coat with marinade, squeeze out excess air, and seal the bag. Marinate in the refrigerator for two to eight hours. Combine flour, baking powder, garlic powder and onion powder in another resealable plastic bag; shake to mix thoroughly. Working with one piece at a time, transfer marinated chicken to the dry ingredient bag, seal the bag, and shake well to coat. After all chicken pieces are coated, repeat the process by dipping them in buttermilk marinade and shaking in the dry coating again. Then heat oil in a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Place chicken in the pan. Fry chicken in batches in hot oil, turning chicken occasionally, until golden brown and juices run clear. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the meat should read at least 165 degrees.
OIL AND VINEGAR POTATO SALAD
1 1/2 lbs. potatoes (red-skinned or Yukon gold), 1/2 medium red onion (chopped), 2 tbsp chopped fresh parsley, 1/2 tsp granulated sugar, 2 tbsp Dijon mustard, 1/4 cup cooking vinegar, 1/3 cup extra virgin olive oil, 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper.
Place potatoes in a large pot and fill with water. Place the lid on the pot and bring to a boil over high heat. Continue to cook until potatoes are tender, about 10 minutes. Remove from heat, drain and rinse with cold water until they are cool enough to handle. Chop into 1-inch chunks and place them in a large mixing bowl. Add onion, herbs, sugar, mustard, vinegar and oil, and toss until well coated. Stir to mash the potatoes slightly until they reach your desired texture. Add salt and pepper, and stir to combine. Season with additional salt and pepper to taste, if desired. The ingredients in this recipe don't require refrigeration and make for a perfect road trip side dish.
NO MAYO COLESLAW
1 head of green cabbage (finely shredded), 1 large carrot (grated), 1/2 yellow or red onion (finely sliced), 1/3 cup apple cider vinegar, 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 tbsp honey, 1/2 tbsp Dijon mustard, 1 tsp celery seed, 1/4 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp black pepper.
Add the shredded green cabbage, carrot and onion to a large bowl. In a smaller bowl, whisk together the apple cider vinegar, Dijon mustard, honey, olive oil, celery seed, salt and pepper to create the dressing. Taste the dressing and decide if you'd like to add more honey. Add about half of the dressing to the cabbage, onions and carrots and gently toss. Slowly add more dressing until you've reached your desired consistency.
PUFF PASTRY STAR COOKIES
All-purpose flour for work surface, 2 sheets puff pastry (thawed), 1 large egg beaten, 1/4 cup jam, sanding sugar for sprinkling.
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper. On a lightly floured work surface, roll each sheet of puff pastry into a 10- by 12-inch rectangle. Using a 3 1/2-inch star-shaped cookie cutter, cut out 12 stars from each sheet. Transfer to prepared baking sheets. Brush the points of half the stars with egg; carefully spoon jam (about 1 teaspoon) onto the center of each star. Using a 1 3/4-inch star-shaped cookie cutter, cut out smaller star shapes from the centers of the remaining 12 larger stars. Place stars with the holes over the jam, doing your best to line up the points. Press edges gently to seal. Brush the tops with egg and sprinkle with sugar. Bake, rotating halfway through, until golden brown, 10 to 12 minutes. Cool slightly before serving. Cookies can be made 2 days ahead. Store, tightly covered, at room temperature.
NO MAYO DEVILED EGGS
6 large or extra-large eggs (hard-boiled, peeled and chilled), 1/4 cup sour cream, 1/2 tsp yellow mustard, 2 tsp sweet pickle relish, 1/4 tsp salt, 2 tsp chopped fresh chives or dill plus more for garnish.
Slice each egg in half lengthwise. Remove the yolks and place in a separate bowl. Set the egg halves aside. Add the sour cream, yellow mustard, pickle relish, salt and herbs to the bowl with the yolks. Using a fork, mash everything together until all the ingredients are combined and the mixture is smooth. Using a spoon or a piping bag fitted with a star tip, fill the empty egg whites with the mixture. Garnish with a dash of paprika and more chopped herbs. Serve cold. Use extra paprika for garnish.
STATE FAIR LEMONADE
6 lemons, 1 ¼ cups white sugar, 5 cups cold water.
Wash lemons and peel off all the zest using a vegetable peeler; set peeled lemons aside. Add lemon zest to a bowl and cover with sugar; toss to combine. Cover and let sit for a minimum of 2 hours, or up to overnight. Bring water to a boil in a pot over high heat; turn off heat and pour in lemon-sugar mixture. Stir and let sit until sugar is completely dissolved, about 5 minutes. Pour through a mesh strainer back into the same bowl and discard the zest. Let cool to room temperature, 20 to 30 minutes. Cut lemons in half and squeeze juice into the bowl. Pour lemonade into a serving pitcher and use when needed.

title: A marriage of inconvenience at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
A marriage of inconvenience at the library

 July 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 995
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Not too long ago, I was trying to decide what to give my nephew's fiancée for her birthday.A professional singer-songwriter, Sophia is brilliant, beautiful and, for one so young, uncommonly comfortable in her bones. She once seriously considered becoming a Buddhist nun.
What do you give a woman who doesn't seem to need anything at all?
Sometimes my brain reminds me of those magic 8 balls we played with as children. You would ask the thing a question, shake it, and à la the oracle at Delphi, a tiny black placard with an enigmatic answer on it would float up into a small window on the 8 ball's surface.
À la the 8 ball, a tiny black placard now floated up into my mind with the phrase "Black Dogs" inscribed on it.
I first read Ian McEwan's novel "Black Dogs" when it came out in 1992. In those days I was rather protective of Mr. McEwan. I'd discovered him a few years earlier when his 1987 novel "The Child in Time" came out, and though the literati were doubtless already celebrating him, no one I knew was as yet reading the man. I thought of him as my discovery.
And, so far as I was concerned, "Black Dogs" confirmed my prescience.
So I bought a copy of the thing, wrapped it in gift wrapping as best I could (picture a spider's untidily bundled prey), and shipped it off to Sophia. And, of course, as soon as I pulled out of the post office parking lot, I began to fear I'd screwed up.
It had been 30 years since I read "Black Dogs." What if the book wasn't as good as I recalled?
Depending on how you define "library," Melissa and I have three. There are the formal shelves in our living room, full of first editions, art books and field guides; there is the library in my study — poetry, languages, a set of Britannica and Melissa's history texts; and there's the paperback library in the attic — fiction, more textbooks and a bookcase devoted to histories of early monasticism and Anglo-Saxon England.
I found my old copy of "Black Dogs" in the attic, picked it up, and soon discovered that, once again, I couldn't put it down.
McEwan's novel is presented as a memoir of a couple's on-again, off-again marriage. Bernard and June meet while working for British Intelligence during World War II, marry at the conclusion of that conflict, and, for their honeymoon, go on a long walking tour through northern Italy and the south of France.
As was fairly common among intellectuals in the '30s and '40s, the two of them have seen the rise of Hitler's fascism as the natural enemy of mankind and, consequently, become attracted to what seems fascism's equally natural opposite, communism. Before setting out for war-torn Europe, the young idealists have taken what they think of as both a daring and exciting leap into the future: they have officially joined the Party.
But in Languedoc, toward the end of their walking tour, June has an encounter with a pair of feral hounds that utterly upends her faith in communism, to say nothing of any other –ism. It is an event that, for the rest of their lives, will haunt, trouble and blight their marriage.
Curiously, "Black Dogs" is told from the point of view of the couple's son-in-law who, orphaned at an early age, comes to think of his wife's parents as his own. The book recounts the role he plays in trying to reconcile them to each other and to each other's divergent views of reality: Bernard's materialistic and socialist, June's entirely metaphysical.
As it happens, the son-in-law proves to be the perfect foil for both. While in Bernard's company, he finds himself drawn to the man's optimism, his belief that the world's problems are caused by perfectly rational forces and, therefore, are susceptible to perfectly rational solutions. While in June's, he is equally affected by her spirituality, the notion that he is in the presence of someone who has achieved an uncommon and otherworldly wisdom.
But he also finds their ironclad certainties maddening, the fact that neither will admit the other might not be entirely wrong.
Again and again, though, we come back to the dogs. Bernard sees the animals as representing a minor episode in his life, one that, due to his wife's improbable obsession with the things, has driven her from him and the life they had once hoped to share. June sees them as the proof of Hamlet's declaration that "There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy…" — though she would substitute Bernard's name for Horatio's.
Better than I have here, McEwan piques his readers' interest by referring repeatedly in the book to June's encounter with the dogs without ever actually explaining what that encounter entailed. It is only in the last 40 pages of the novel that he returns us to that arid plateau in Languedoc in the spring of 1946 to witness the event itself in a rush of writing that is as fine and evocative as any I have ever read.
It has been one of the great privileges of my life to hike in the south of France — cicadas droning in the heat, air scented with rosemary and thyme — to round a promontory and find myself looking out over a vast gorge, a gap in the mountains opposite revealing a sparkling sliver of Mediterranean Sea.
If that sounds like something you'd like to do, I recommend you take a walking tour through Ian McEwan's "Black Dogs." You'll find it in the fiction section of the Talbot County Free Library under the call letters MCEW. Later, at the end of your day, as you sit in the shade in front of the local auberge, a glass of rosé resting on the table before you, I'd ask that you send a little book lover's request heavenward that Sophia will enjoy the experience as much as you have.

title: Two new shows opening at Easton's Zebra Gallery
author: Staff Writer
content:
Two new shows opening at Easton's Zebra Gallery

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Arts 
 
 423
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Friday, July 18, from 5 to 7 p.m., the Zebra Gallery will open two new shows featuring artists Gabriel Lehman and Evan Fitzgerald.Gabriel Lehman's show, "A Bird's Eye View," will feature his fanciful, dreamlike landscapes with a particular emphasis on clouds, imbuing a sense of joy and wonder into his art. Lehman is a self-taught artist who started painting in 2009 after a career in construction with a focus on flooring for 14 years. Despite not having any formal training, Lehman's unique perspective and whimsical style quickly gained him a following.
Lehman is also offering painting classes from July 14 to 19 to learn his secrets to gorgeous clouds and fantastic creatures. Classes offered include "Three-Color Clouds," where students will learn the secrets of capturing the softness, depth and movement of clouds while transforming three simple colors into breathtaking skyscapes.
The "Sunset Skies" class offers students an enchanting journey through the colors of dusk as they learn to paint breathtaking sunsets on 16-by-20-inch canvases. In this immersive class, students learn how to capture the delicate gradients, vibrant hues and ethereal beauty of the sky at its most magical moments.
The "Rays of Light" class guides students through techniques to achieve the perfect balance of light and shadow, subtle color blending and atmospheric perspective, making the clouds look like they could float right off the canvas. This class invites participants to explore the endless possibilities of acrylic paint while creating stunning skyscapes that will brighten any space. All skill levels are welcome to all of these classes.
Evan Fitzgerald's current work explores the ideas of persona. The word persona is rooted in the Latin word for a theatrical mask. Carl Jung described persona as a social mask that we all put on — something to embody, a different mask for a different setting. By obscuring the subject's face, their headdresses are the focal point. The individual is merely a pedestal for displaying these objects.
"Both of these artists bring such creative and whimsical works to the gallery. I hope visitors will be mesmerized by the details these painters bring to their paintings. We are thrilled to have them exhibiting here," said Susan Schauer John, owner of the Zebra Gallery.
For more information or to sign up for Gabriel Lehman's class, call 410-253-9131 or email thezebragallery@gmail.com. The Zebra Gallery is located at 5 North Harrison Street in Easton (across the street from the Historic Tidewater Inn). The gallery hours are Thursday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. or by appointment. For further information, visit sfsfiber.art or thezebragallery.com.

title: Ann Lord credits 'doing your own thing' as key to her 100 years
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Ann Lord credits 'doing your own thing' as key to her 100 years

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 458
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Born on June 16, 1925, Ann Lord celebrated her 100 birthday with a party on June 22, at The Residence at Eden Green in Denton where she lives.Lord enjoys animal watching at Eden Green. She has a bird feeder on her back porch where she can watch all different kinds of birds fly in.
Born in Hobbs, Maryland, Lord is the youngest of 11 children. She can recall when her family moved from Baltimore to Hobbs.
"My mother and father lived in Baltimore, and they came down before the new bridge was built; they had a ferry that came across," Lord said. "... My great-grandfather enlisted my dad in the Spanish-American War. So while he was in the war fighting, he came home on a weekend and married my mother who lived in Baltimore, and they both lived with my great-grandfather.
"My great-grandfather saw an advertisement in the paper, and it was advertising Hobbs, Maryland; they had a position open for a worker. Well, right away my great grandfather thought, 'Well, that's a good job for his son.' So they applied, and he got the job, that's how they got down here to Hobbs. They supplied a home for them to live in, and he took care of them."
Lord graduated from high school in 1943. She met her husband, Malcolm Lord, through her older brother. Malcolm graduated two years before Lord did, and she wrote letters to Malcolm during the time he was in World War II. When Malcolm came back, he married Lord in 1948.
Lord and her husband had four kids, five grandkids, seven great-grand kids and lived in Denton their whole life.
Right after high school, Lord began working at a bank in town for about three weeks, then after a conversation with the owner, she began working at Townsends.
After working at Townsends for seven years, Lord opened her own florist shop that was attached to her home in Denton.
After closing her florist shop, Lord worked for Caroline County Board of Education until she retired in 1986.
Lord's advice to a husband and wife having kids is to "think first."
"Think first about how your life is going to change completely," Lord said. "You just have to grow either with it or forget it. Most of them are forgetting it and getting divorces."
Although her age comes with a lot of wisdom, Lord regrets how forgetful she is at her age.
"The worst is is your forgetfulness," Lord said. "You really regret that you can't remember a lot of the things that were so important to you two years ago that now you forget about them."
Lord's advice to anybody going through life is to "do your own thing and decide what you want to do with your life and pursue it."
