title: Fourth free gospel concert in Denton marks the halfway point for series
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Fourth free gospel concert in Denton marks the halfway point for series

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 311
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The fourth free gospel concert of the eight-concert series is set to take place at Calvary Baptist Church in Denton on Friday, July 11, at 6:30 p.m. Russ Yates, vice president of Holiday Park, hopes the series can reach people and teach them about Jesus."Well, hopefully it reaches a lot of people that need to know about Jesus," Yates said. It certainly gives the Christian community an outlet to do something, that's basically free."
The free concert will feature groups Port City Quartet, from North Carolina, and The Hyssongs from Rockport, Maine.
Holiday Park campground hosted concerts and events before COVID-19, after COVID, Yates closed the park, but recently with the direction from God, he was led to continue events but at a different venue.
"We did 30 years from 1989 to 2019 here at the campground. And then when COVID hit we had to shut down everything," Yates said. "Then we lost all of our people that volunteered to help because we needed about 50 people to put on the concerts. I really thought that was the end of it. Then last year during the winter, I started getting the feeling the Lord wanted us to start this up again, and I called the church and asked them what about us doing it there.
"Pastor Don Reynold said 'Russ, I've been praying you would start this up again,' and I was like, 'Well, looks like that's what we're going to try to do.' So the church was all behind it and have been real supportive."
Yates said events like this are good for the community because it's free, and it gives believers fun activities to enjoy.
"We just hope the outreach reaches a number of people that need it," Yates said. "I hear all the time from Christian people there's nothing for Christians to do. We certainly are trying to do our best."

title: QACHS art students partner with Haven Ministries to share 'hope for homes'
author: SUBMITTED NEWS
content:
QACHS art students partner with Haven Ministries to share 'hope for homes'

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SUBMITTED NEWS | Section: Arts 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The Queen Anne's County High School Chapter of the National Art Honor Society continues to shine a light in the community through their ongoing partnership with Haven Ministries and their Art for Your Home project. In 2025, students donated 13 framed original soft block prints to support individuals and families in transition — offering not just artwork, but a sense of hope and dignity for those facing financial hardship or transitioning into permanent housing.The Hope for the Home extension of the project was established in 2018 through a collaborative effort between Queen Anne's County Public Schools Visual Arts Supervisor Michael Bell, Haven Ministries, the Hope Warehouse, and Rick Strittmater, executive director for the Queen Anne's County Centre for the Arts. It has since become a valued tradition in the school's arts programming, one that allows student artists to earn Service-Learning credit while making a meaningful contribution to their community.
"It's been incredible to see this meaningful project grow year after year," said Bell. "I'm proud to see our students still partnering with Haven Ministries, and using their talents to bring light and beauty into the homes of those who need it most."
This year, students learned soft block printing techniques to produce unique, framed works of art for the Haven Ministries Art for Your Home program. These pieces are displayed on the walls of the Hope Warehouse, where clients can select one to take home — free of charge.
"One of my core beliefs as an artist and a teacher is that we can each use our talents and efforts to lift people up and give back to the communities we live in," said Stephanie Zeiler, Queen Anne's County High Art Department Chair and district Lead Visual Arts Teacher. "It is my hope to instill community stewardship in my students and show them they can make a positive difference in this world, even at their young age."
Sophomore artist Lilly Askew shared, "I feel very fortunate to have had the opportunity to create art for someone that may not have access to it because of whatever barriers they face. I hope our art makes their space feel a little more like home and helps brighten their walls."
Peter Grim, executive director of Haven Ministries, praised the initiative: "This personalization of space helps to create a feeling of home and develop a sense of worth and value. Without you and so many other wonderful supporters, this important opportunity would not exist."
Through compassion and creativity, Queen Anne's students continue to leave a lasting impact — one artwork at a time.

title: World-renowned husband-wife duo present concert in Oxford
author: Staff Writer
content:
World-renowned husband-wife duo present concert in Oxford

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Local News 
 
 215
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Leon Fleisher Academy brings a superb concerts to Oxford this week. The concert features Yury Shadrin and Tian Lu who will present an all Chopin recital on Thursday evening, July 10, at 7 p.m. in the Parish Hall of The Church of the Holy Trinity, 502 S. Morris St. in Oxford. This husband-wife team is widely known throughout South America, Asia and the United States as concert pianists, orchestra soloists, teachers and clinicians.Their superb technique, musical intuitiveness, energy, musicianship and exuberant personality brings out the music's poetry and charm. It will be exciting to hear how the lyricism, drama and incredibly beautiful melodies of Frederic Chopin, a 19th century Polish Romantic era composer, will be brought to life. Please join us for a wonderful experience of the timeless elegance of Chopin's masterpieces.
The Church of the Holy Trinity is privileged to present these world-class pianists in an intimate setting. When Yury and Tian have performed previously in the hall, people have been amazed how these exceptional musicians bring music to life with our special piano, filling the room with small, intimate to large, full sounds touching everyone's soul.
There are no tickets for this concert. Donations will be accepted to help with artists' expenses. For further information, contact the church office at 410-226-5134 or office@holytrinityoxfordmd.org.

title: James Beard Finalists: Cultural collaboration of cuisine, character
author: Lily Tierney
content:
James Beard Finalists: Cultural collaboration of cuisine, character

 July 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 781
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Fusions of flavor, cuisine and culture came together Wednesday evening at Easton's Bas Rouge for a five-course inaugural "cultural collaboration dinner" series.The event showcases Bas Rouge and 2024 James Beard award winning Chef Harley Peet's commitment to honor fellow James Beard finalists through dynamic culinary partnerships that highlight the rich diversity shaping Mid-Atlantic food culture.
Peet and Bas Rouge welcomed five-time semi-finalist and 2024 Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic Finalist Kevin Tien alongside 2024/2025 James Beard Finalist, Pastry Chef Susan Bae of Washington, D.C.'s Moon Rabbit to Easton to kick off the dinner series.
Although the five-course meal did not have a theme per se, every dish honored the Mid-Atlantic seasonal produce through Peet and Tien's unique and distinct cooking styles. For each chef, seasonal cooking and sustainable sourcing are baseline practices at their restaurants.
Peet and Tien met at the James Beard Awards in Chicago and hit it off from the jump. After a little over two decades in the industry, Peet said he now has an eye for picking out chefs who have something special.
"There's Michelin Stars handed out all the time, but there's special ones," Peet said. "And Kevin and his team and his concept and everything he's doing, it just struck a chord in Chicago. We struck a chord."
Peet describes his culinary style as "all over the board" meshing Japanese, classic French, "redneck s--- from Tilghman Island," and Americanized dishes with Italian twists. Tien described his style as "Cajun Asian."
Tien's Vietnamese background and Louisiana upbringing have shaped his approach to cooking. However, he said he didn't truly embrace Vietnamese cuisine until the pandemic when he had a pivotal mindset shift. He said he stayed away from Vietnamese food because it was seldom regarded in fine dining, but when he changed his mindset and opened Moon Rabbit, the possibilities were endless.
"People come to our restaurant and they expect traditional Vietnamese food, and there's none of that on the menu. So either they, like, really love what we're doing or they hate what we're doing," Tien said. "And I'll be honest, the people that hate what we're doing are actually our own people, which can be a little frustrating."
Tien said these days, he tries not to take it too personally and is focused on his and his team's happiness and the ability to continue to foster relationships with other chefs and restaurants outside of D.C.
Peet and Tien said that historically, chefs were siloed and collaboration efforts like this were not a common occurrence, but this is beginning to change in the industry.
"I think the humanitarian side is super important as well, the chef has been brought out of the kitchen, and the customer's been brought into the kitchen," Peet said.
With the rising popularity of shows like "The Bear," a movie-like version of chef's berating their servers, yelling at kitchen staff and being all around hateful has become the picture of back-of-house life, but Peet said it's not like that anymore.
"I've been in some kitchens with some old-school guys and, you know, it's just not fun," he said. Tien said he thinks this is partially because chefs have less ego and are respecting each other's work more.
Tien and Peet certainly respect each other's work, and it showed through each plate that was delivered to the table.
The Menu
The meal began with canapés by Bas Rouge which included an incredibly refreshing avocado agua fresca in a shot glass and local blue crab Causa, a cold, savory Peruvian-style potato dish.
This was followed by canapés by Moon Rabbit, a blend between French and Vietnamese flavors, which included Ga Ran Pâté, Vietnamese fried chicken, chicken presse and pâté, and Bo Luc Lac, a classic Vietnamese dish with marinated cubed beef and black pepper beef served in a crunchy tartlet.
Then guests were presented with fluffy taro milk bread served with an earthy culantro garlic butter followed by scallop crudo in a light yet acidic coconut sauce. The next plate was a beautiful display of octopus and Viet Cajun blood sausage with crunchy golden raisins and mostarda. Servers then presented guests with a gorgeous crab cake Wellington with a vegetable demi-glace in the middle.
For dessert, pastry chef Susan Bae made a Vietnamese coffee mousse that was almost too beautiful to eat. The stunning dessert tasted as good as it looked bursting with flavors of coffee, chocolate and citrus in every bite.
"It keeps things exciting too," Tien said about the collaboration. "Sometimes I get really lost in the day-to-day grind of our restaurant, and I forget to take the blinders off, so this is also a good way for me to get away, even if it's just for a day or two and reset mentally and go back really inspired."

title: Maryland church is 'officially' historic
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
Maryland church is 'officially' historic

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: News 
 
 387
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Mountains of paperwork and research later, the congregation of West Nottingham Presbyterian Church in Colora celebrated the official designation of their building as part of the National Register of Historic Places.A plaque noting the designation was unveiled Sunday, July 6 after morning worship services. The Maryland church is located in Colora near Rising Sun in the northeast part of the state.
Credit for completing that application went to Emily Kilby and Cindi Lamb-Wiley.
"We worked for over a year," Lamb-Wiley said of the process. "Emily was a better writer. I'm a better form filler."
Kilby said the church building on Firetower Road in Colora was already on the National Register but the information was inaccurate.
"The person who wrote it, their information reads the chapel was built in 1880 but it was built in 1804," Kilby, a noted local historian, said of the decades-old submission.
Kilby and Lamb-Wiley discovered that, what in the past had been a two page, hand-written file, would now be 50 pages of documentation to include a description of the historic attributes of the stone building.
"My brother Rick helped a lot," Kilby said. "He got up in the rafters and took pictures of the chestnut beams."
Rick Kilby said ship-building techniques were used in the construction.
"These beams weigh 3,000 pounds each," he said of the massive support beams in the rafters. Equipment that would have been used to raise the mast of large ships of that era were brought to the site.
"Can you imagine in 1800 trying to raise these heavy beams?" Emily Kilby said.
West Nottingham Presbyterian Church originally was in Rising Sun; the location of which is still not determined, Kilby said. The Colora church replaced that building.
The ladies had to write, re-write and re-submit information, challenged by the online technology of today.
"You have to fill it out just so and the photos have to be the right size," Kilby said.
Her research — which included issues of the Cecil Whig that covered the construction — gave her new insight about West Nottingham Presbyterian Church. Her research included the cemetery.
"The woman who invented the eye chart is buried here. So is the man who was the vice president of US Steel," Kilby said. "It's amazing, the richness of the history here."
"We don't want to have that history forgotten," she added. "This really is an amazing piece of history."

title: Eastern Shore singers perform at D-Day ceremonies in France
author: SUBMITTED NEWS
content:
Eastern Shore singers perform at D-Day ceremonies in France

 July 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SUBMITTED NEWS | Section: Local News 
 
 462
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NORMANDY, FRANCE — Each year on the sixth of June, visitors from all over the world gather in Normandy, France to honor the sacrifices made during the D-Day invasion on that day in 1944 and this year included Queen Anne's Chorale.Many special events and wreath laying ceremonies take place to commemorate D-Day and the landing of Allied Forces on its shores during World War ll.
Each year the premier All-American D-Day Band and Community Chorus is assembled to perform at some of these commemorative events. The band and chorus are comprised of instrumentalists and singers from across the United States. With their music, they are the American musical ambassadors to France.
An invitation to sing in the All-American Community Chorus was sent to a local group, the Queen Anne's Chorale in Centreville. In addition to this honor, their Artistic Director, Robert Huntington, was chosen to conduct the chorus. Fourteen singers, along with family and friends, participated in this memorable trip.
Before leaving, however, they met several times to practice so they were ready to rehearse with the other singers upon arrival in Paris. The concert repertoire with an "Americana" theme included "Down to the River to Pray," "The Yellow Rose of Texas," "Swinging on a Star" and "Let There Be Peace on Earth."
Their itinerary for the nine-day trip began with a special guided tour, stopping at several significant areas dedicated to the D-Day battles of Normandy Campaign. Both the Chorus and Band joined forces for a Wreath Laying Ceremony at the Utah Beach Memorial. The Choir traveled to the American Cemetery at Omaha Beach and were able to tour the solemn place of honor. The Chorus presented concerts in the town square and in the Church in Sainte-Mere-Eglise as part of the Musical Salute to Liberation. They also participated in the annual D-Day Memorial Parade held there.
Before returning home, the Chorus also had an opportunity to explore Paris and perform an afternoon concert at La Madeleine Cathedral.
As Chorale singers began planning their trip to France, they found that their town of Centreville had yet another connection to D-Day, 1944. Sadly, one of its young men, U.S Army Private First-Class William H. Quillen, fought with the 29th Infantry Division and lost his life on the sixteenth of June 1944 during an ensuing battle. He received the Purple Heart and is buried in the Normandy American Cemetery.
Upon learning about Private Quillen, the Chorale, with the assistance of the Queen Anne's County Library in Stevensville, researched and identified his grave site coordinates. On June 5, Chorale members placed a flag on his grave in Normandy honoring his courage and sacrifice for the United States and the Allied Forces. A picture was taken with Chorale singers holding flags from both Queen Anne's County and the town of Centreville.

title: Historic Christ Church bell to be restored
author: REBECCA PLACEK Special to The Star Democrat
content:
Historic Christ Church bell to be restored

 July 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: REBECCA PLACEK Special to The Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 287
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — The Historic Christ Church Bell Tower in Stevensville will be restored with proceeds from the May 3 Maryland House and Garden Tour of Queen Anne's County.On July 7, board members from the Queen Anne's County Historical Society presented a check for $9,010 to Nancy Cook of Friends of Historic Christ Church.
Cook gave a talk on the 1631 founding of Kent Fort on Kent Island, the third-oldest permanent English settlement established by William Claiborne.
He and settlers built the first Christ Church on the south tip of Kent Island. In 1680, a new town and Christ Church were moved to the new town of Broad Creek, where Bay City is now. Then, in 1880, Christ Church was moved to the new town of Stevensville.
The new Christ Church was built in 1880 in Queen Anne style. The bell tower is in the "lancet" chimney style. Wooden pegs and bricks were reused from the earlier Christ Churches. Historic Christ Church recently was designated as the Arts & Cultural Center of Historic Stevensville.
Mike Thomas has researched the church bell. The bell was made in 1880 by the McShane Bell Foundry of Baltimore, America's oldest bell company, established in 1856. The bell is bronze, rings in C sharp, and weighs 400 pounds including the mountings. In 1880, the bell was shipped to the Rev. Thompson, Christ Church, Stevensville. Church bells are rung for religious and ceremonial purposes such as Christmas and for significant events such as weddings.
Donations also are needed for Christ Church upkeep. Checks may be sent to: Nancy M. Cook, 124 Bryce Road, Queenstown, MD 21658. Historic Christ Church is nonprofit organization registered with the state of Maryland. Donations are tax-deductible to the fullest extent of the law.

title: Country Cooking: Fresh fish for supper
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Fresh fish for supper

 July 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1276
 Words 

 Read News Document

 An Eastern Shore tradition is certainly fresh caught fish from the local waters being served tonight in the local restaurants or Mom's kitchen. I have great memories of a fish for supper on West Line Road — near the Bay, the river and the ocean.My family were recreational fishermen and only fished on weekends or vacation days. Down the road from our farm, the late Mr. Frankie Savage spent his retirement years fishing locally and was known as "the fish man" by all in our area.
Mr. Frankie came in the yard in his old "fish pickup" with the back full of tubs of ice covering fresh caught fish — it was always in the afternoon, as his mornings were spent fishing. Mom would come with her "fish basin" ready to get her desired amount.
I will never forget Mr. Frankie's routine — pull up, uncover the iced fish, hang the scale on the sturdy pole and tell the kinds of fish he had caught. Mom would get "her desired amount of fish," better known in the country as "a mess of fish."
After weighing them, the fish were poured into Mom's basin, and she brought out her change purse to pay. Before Mom turned to return to the outside kitchen to clean them, Mr. Frankie would throw in some more fish and say, "Ms. Laurie, the wife and I loved that cornbread you sent down."
Mom would smile and say, "I'll be making more" as she walked over to the fish she was about to scale, clean and slice for pan-fried fish supper.
In the summertime, Mom always had freshly cooked collard or turnip greens, fresh garden picked homemade stewed tomatoes and a pan of cornbread. Did I mention the gallon jug of iced tea and/or lemonade?
I never heard Mom complain about these delicious meals that required a lot of work or about how it was too hot to cook. Mom always said her joy came from her family coming in the door saying, "Supper smells good, Mom" or "Hurry and wash up 'cause I'm hungry."
SHAD FISH ROE AND EGGS
2 eggs, 1 tsp milk, 1 sac of shad roe, 1 tsp butter, salt and pepper, green onions (chopped) — optional.
Scrape shad roe into the bowl. Mix eggs, salt, pepper and milk in a different bowl. Add roe and mix again. Melt butter in a medium size skillet. Cook the mixture just like you would be cooking scrambled eggs.
BAKED CATFISH
1 lb blue catfish fillets, 1/4 cup flour, 1/2 cup milk, Canola oil for frying, 1 cup ground yellow cornmeal, 2 eggs, 2-3 tsps Old Bay or J.O. Crab Seasoning (or to taste), salt.
Whip the eggs and milk together and add Old Bay or J.O. Crab Seasoning. Mix the cornmeal and flour together and place on a plate. Dip fillets in the seasoned egg mixture and place on the cornmeal/flour mixture, sprinkling the top of the filet with the dry mixture and pressing it in with your hand. Place prepared fillets on a baking sheet and let stand for 15 minutes. Preheat oil to 350 degrees on medium heat in a heavy cast iron skillet and carefully place fillets in oil when it is hot (to avoid crowding you may have to cook fish in batches). Fry until golden brown and crispy, about 2-3 minutes per side. Fish is done when it can be easily flaked with a fork. Place cooked fish on a plate lined with a paper towel and season with salt.
OVEN BAKED FISH
2 lbs fish (cleaned and filleted), 1 tbsp salt, 1 cup milk, 1 cup dried bread crumbs.
Cut fish into serving size portions. Add salt to milk. Dip fillets in milk and roll into dried bread crumbs. Place in a well greased baking pan. Sprinkle each piece of fish with minced or chopped butter pieces. Bake in a preheated 500-degree oven for 10 to 12 minutes or until fish flakes easily when touched with a fork. Serve with fresh vegetables and macaroni and cheese.
SALMON CAKES
1 lb. fresh salmon meat, 2 beaten eggs, 4 tbsps bread crumbs, 3-4 tbsps milk.
Combine salmon meat with eggs, bread crumbs and milk. Add one tablespoon of milk at a time to determine consistency. Mix and form into cakes. Fry in hot oil until golden brown on both sides.
BAKED FISH WITH TOMATOES
1 1/2 lbs fresh fish fillets, 2 tsps mustard, 3/4 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp Old Bay, 1/4 tsp black pepper, 2 fresh tomatoes, 1 cup grated parmesan cheese, 1/4 cup butter or margarine.
Cut fish fillets into serving sizes and single layer fish in a well greased two quart casserole dish. Spread mustard over the fish. Sprinkle salt, Old Bay seasoning and black pepper on top of mustard. Peel and slice tomatoes over top of mustard mixture. Mix together Parmesan cheese with butter or margarine and spread over the fish mixture. Cover and bake in a preheated 325-degree oven for 30 minutes.
GRILLED MARYLAND BLUEFISH
2 lbs Maryland bluefish fillets, 2 cups Italian salad dressing, 2 lemons (cut in wedges).
Place bluefish fillets in a baking dish. Pour dressing over fillets, cover and refrigerate for 2 hours. Place fillets on a hot, oiled grill. Baste fillets frequently with dressing and cook for about 10 minutes. Turn and baste again. Fillets are done when they just begin to flake when tested with a fork. Serve with lemon wedges. For convenient cooking on charcoal grill, cover grill with foil and poke holes in foil to circulate heat.
MARYLAND BAKED PERCH
3 lbs perch (dressed), 1 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp pepper, 3 medium sliced mushrooms, 1/2 cup sliced onion, 1/4 cup chopped green pepper, 1 cup orange juice, 3 tbsps 1 tsp grated lemon rind, 1 tbsp flour.
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees. Season fish with salt and pepper. Place fish in a baking dish. In a bowl, combine mushrooms, onions and green pepper. Spread vegetable mixture over fish. Combine remaining ingredients in a saucepan. Cook over moderate heat, stirring frequently until mixture thickens. Pour sauce over fish and vegetables. Bake for 6 to 8 minutes or until the fish flakes easily with a fork.
SIMPLE FRIED BLUEFISH
4 bluefish fillets, 1 bowl of milk, 2 eggs (beaten), 2 cups flour, 1/2 inch olive oil in a large skillet, 3 tbsps parsley (chopped), 1 tsp paprika, 1 tsp lemon pepper, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 lemon (cut into wedges).
Place all of the fillets in a bowl of milk and let soak for several minutes. Dip fillet in a bowl of well beaten eggs. Season flour with parsley, paprika, lemon pepper and salt. Roll each fillet in flour. Heat oil to medium-high. Place fillets in hot oil. Fry to a golden brown, turning once. Remove fillet from pan and layer over paper towels. Serve hot or cold with wedges of lemon.
GRILLED MARLIN STEAKS
2 large marlin steaks (about 3/4-inch thick), 1/3 cup pineapple juice, 2 tbsps grapeseed oil, 2 tbsps sesame oil, 1/2 tbsp low-sodium soy sauce, 1 large clove garlic (minced), 1/2 tsp fresh ginger (minced), freshly ground black pepper to taste.
In a small bowl, combine pineapple juice, grapeseed oil, sesame oil, soy sauce, garlic, ginger and black pepper. Whisk all the ingredients until well blended. Put marlin steaks in a large resealable bag and pour the marinade over. Close the bag and massage/flip it until the steaks are well coated. Transfer to the refrigerator for 1 to 1 ½ hours, turning and massaging steaks once or twice. Preheat barbecue to 500-550 degrees. Place the marlin steaks on a plate and discard the marinade. Transfer the steaks on the hot grill, close the lid and grill for 3 minutes on one side. Flip them and cook for another 2 minutes with the lid closed.

title: Plein Air Easton artists take on Tilghman Island in paint-out competition
author: Konner Metz
content:
Plein Air Easton artists take on Tilghman Island in paint-out competition

 July 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 501
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TILGHMAN ISLAND — Artists took to Tilghman Island on Monday to paint some of the island's most iconic spots and views for Plein Air Easton's annual Paint Tilghman competition.Many of the 58 juried artists put their talents on display in Tilghman Island as part of Plein Air Easton's 21st annual weeklong outdoor painting competition.
By Monday evening, around 50 paintings hung in the Tilghman Island Inn, many for sale. Some depicted Monday morning's sunrise, while others showed views of Knapps Narrows Bridge. One artist painted the renowned Tilghman Island Country Store.
The artists chose their spots Monday morning and had until 4 p.m. to complete their works before heading to the inn for submissions.
Coakley Brown, of Richmond, Virginia, said she loves the environment around the Chesapeake Bay. The chance to paint around Tilghman wasn't as much competitive as it was fun, she said.
"This is play time," Brown said.
It was Harsh Agrawal's first time at Plein Air Easton. He came all the way from London and gained a deep appreciation for how unique Talbot County's different towns and islands are.
"All the towns, they have a different character," Agrawal said.
Agrawal completed two paintings, both of which were sold Monday. Driving around the island during the day, he happened upon the perfect view: a unique, battered barn house with dark clouds looming over it on an otherwise sunny day. During the hot and humid afternoon full of mosquitoes, Agrawal painted the barn.
He typically does two plein air events in the United States each year. He said the competitions are a great chance to explore new places.
Port Republic artist Freeman Dodsworth has been on the plein air circuit for three years, but 2025 is his first time in Easton. He sat in front of a radar tower in Tilghman Island on Monday overlooking the waters, about seven miles from his house on the western shore.
"The best way for me to meet other plein air painters is to paint outside," Dodsworth said.
Jess Bellis, the Avalon Foundation's chief financial and operating officer, said there's a "higher concentration of new artists" this year than Plein Air Easton has seen in a long time. It gives a "freshness" to the entire week, she said.
Many pieces sold during Monday's exhibit. One piece of note, a 20-by-16-inch canvas of boats and a large cloud passing over, hadn't sold as of around 6:30 p.m.
But that soon changed when the artists' choice award was announced. Baltimore County artist Palden Hamilton and his oil painting, "Passing Giant," was named Paint Tilghman's most outstanding work by the judging artists.
Following the announcement, it was only a matter of minutes before Avalon Foundation volunteers placed a "sold" slip of paper next to the artwork.
"Thank you so much. It means so much to me to be awarded by my peers," Hamilton said, accepting his award. It was his second consecutive year winning an artists' choice award.
While competition-based, many of the artists said the Plein Air Easton event is a week of creativity and camaraderie.
"It's always good energy," Agrawal said.

title: Paint-by-numbers project brings Easton community together
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Paint-by-numbers project brings Easton community together

 July 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 525
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Downtown Easton visitors paused Friday to help paint a community backdrop at Plein Air Easton.Outside the Tidewater Inn and the Avalon Theatre, a large paint-by-number canvas united community members to participate in Easton's Plein Air event. This is the first time Plein Air Easton has had a community paint event.
The artist behind the creation and organizer of the event is Maggii Sarfarty. A Plein Air Easton alumnus and art director of the Factory Arts Project, Sarfarty partnered with the Avalon Foundation to bring community members together to paint, regardless of skill level.
"Plein Air Easton has just always been about coming and seeing competition artists and other art in our community, but I think the Avalon really wanted to reach out and find something that everybody could participate in," Sarfaty said.
The painting for the project was "Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose" by American artist John Singer Sargent. Sarfaty said the original Plein Air piece was painted in a garden in Worcestershire, England, in 1885.
The painting was divided into three panels that would later combine to form a single backdrop. Participants grabbed paint cups labeled with numbers and followed the design.
The project was created in collaboration with the Factory, a nonprofit performing arts organization in Easton. The finished product served as the backdrop for the Factory's radio show, which began about 30 minutes after the community paint project was finished.
The paint-by-numbers design allowed people of all skill levels and ages to contribute. Both young children and older adults picked up brushes and brought the painting to life.
Sue McWilliams, of Easton, spent the event with her young niece, Sutton Martin, who was visiting. McWilliams said the event was a great opportunity for kids, and Sutton agreed. It was Sutton's first time painting with a large group.
"Everybody helps, and you get to talk a lot, and it's just harmony," Sutton said.
A two-hour event, people came and went, and most of the painting was completed by the end of the first hour. Sarfarty estimated about 70 community members stopped by to paint.
"I love getting creative, but I never like to start things from scratch," Sarah Kilmon, of Easton, said. "So, having a project that is made to help people get creative together is so much fun."
Kilmon, who has modeled and acted in prior years at Plein Air Easton, decided to have a more relaxing experience this year. She said painting alongside the community was peaceful, and the radio show backdrop "is totally the Factory's vibe."
Jessica Bellis, director of finance and operations at the Avalon, led an applause for Sarfarty at the end of the event.
"This is a totally wild and weird idea that we just executed on," Bellis told the crowd. "This paint-by-numbers masterpiece that Maggii made is awe-inspiring."
The finished painting hung behind the performers during the radio show. Instead of seeing it close up, split into sections and flat on a table, the three boards came together on stage to reveal the intricate piece the community had helped create.
With the first-ever community paint event over, there are still plenty of opportunities for community members to participate in the Plein Air Easton festivities. The annual event ends Sunday.

title: Adkins Arboretum plans to add Woodhenge
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Adkins Arboretum plans to add Woodhenge

 July 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 493
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGLEY — Vicco Von Voss is working with Adkins Arboretum to erect "Woodhedge."A local woodworker and artist, Voss said the idea of a Woodhenge, an art installation modeled after Scotland's famous Stonehenge, came from the emotions of his work.
"I'm a woodworker, and part of what we do is we salvage local trees that have been diseased or fallen," Voss said. "We have a mill here, and we cut these trees open. I've noticed that when my sawyer, he's cutting a tree, and the tree is really beautiful, everybody feels really good. Then when we get to a tree where the tree is kind of diseased and rotten, the mood kind of changes.
"I said to my sawyer, I said, 'Isn't that interesting when you have a tree that is all good and healthy and beautiful, your energy is good and positive. When you get a tree that's all diseased and rotten inside, you might be blaming it on something.' Isn't it interesting that you're exposing the energy of the tree and you're really receiving what is happening within the tree."
Voss hopes Woodhenge will make visitors think and feel emotions and energy from the tree.
According to Abby Lorenz, director of public engagement for Adkins Arboretum, conversations with Voss went on a for long time, but the energy shifted on the project after receiving a grant in July.
"More recently the energy and movement around this project is through a Public Arts Planning Grant with Maryland State Arts Council," Lorenz said. "He received a grant funding to focus on the planning of the installation, so right now we have created a survey for people to give feedback on what they think on the project. So I think that's a big part of what we're looking for because this is not just art for artists, it's public art."
The next step for Woodhenge is applying for a second grant for $30,000 in the fall to begin construction, but according to Voss, they will need to do some fundraising to complete the $75,000 project.
Lorenz said the focus right now is informing the community about the project and getting their thoughts and ideas.
"We just recently had a community meeting where we invited people that had knowledge of Stonehenge and cultural landscapes to come together and give their feedback and ideas, and Vico shared his plan and intention of really opening one tree so that you feel like you're inside of one tree," Lorenz said.
At the feedback meeting, residents shared on how they felt visiting Stonehenge and how that same feeling and cultural significance can be conveyed in a tree landscape.
"I think there's excitement, there's intrigue and in a way that people are interested in really what does it mean," Lorenz said.
While there is no set timeline for the project, Lorenz and Voss believe Woodhenge will be built and open to the public in 2026 or 2027.
Woodhenge would sit on Nancy's Meadow on the north side of the Adkins Arboretum property.

title: Listen to the rhythm at the Chestertown Farmers Market
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Listen to the rhythm at the Chestertown Farmers Market

 July 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 461
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTEROWN — Each Saturday morning at the Chestertown Farmers Market on High Street, customers can find a refreshing variety of items from produce to baked goodies and handwoven crafts.Last weekend, among quilters, painters and wood carvers, author Marianne Laino Sade was selling her children's books, "TAPUM" and her latest "TA DA".
"TA DA" is especially welcome as baby's first book, recommended for ages 0-4 and their caregivers. "Children need their parents, grandparents, caregivers and guardians to read to them. It is so important for fundamental growth," Sade said.
So the books need to be interesting to the babies and those reading to them. And they certainly are.
Sade's offerings Saturday were each signed by the author. The artwork in her book is created in a collage style, using cut outs and concepts gleaned from her experiences as an English major and librarian across Maryland, New York and Pennsylvania.
Her first book published in 2022, "TAPUM" features a colorful drum on the cover and each element within the drum: the sun, the sea, a lion, are all pages in the book.
Done in that unique collage style, using patterns and dark and light contrasts, there is great attention to detail on each page.
You can hear the song playing along as you read.
"TAPUM!" is the sound of the drum in the world all around. Can you hear its rhythm? "TaPUM, Tapum, TaPUM!"," the back panel reads.
Sade said "TAPUM" came to her while awaiting a bus in New York in the 80's and just hearing that sound repeated. She was again inspired from attending a drum event featuring many world drummers including Babatunde Olatunji, hailed as the father of African drumming in the United States.
"TA DA" came about a little differently. Sade combined animals and music, visualizing frogs, dogs, birds and other colorful critters wanting to be a music band. With a nod to the Chester River Packet, the animal band perform at the end of High Street by the water.
The book talks about the universal appeal of music: "TA DA" celebrates the joy of making music together" and is a companion book to "TAPUM" following a musical theme.
Both books have thick, durable board pages and were appealing to families passing through the market such as Joseph and Amanda Carchi and their baby daughter Marie and son Owen. Little Marie smiled widely pointing at the pictures while Joseph read to her.
"These are very cool," Amanda noted.
So far, "TA DA" is doing well in sales too, selling at least 100 out of the 500 they ordered, Sade's husband Chris pointed out.
And perhaps as many authors tend to do, she is toying with a trilogy.
Sade said she has been reflecting about her childhood but would say nothing further, not wanting to spoil the big surprise.
Check out her books at msadeart.com.

title: Plein Air Easton inducts 2nd Hall of Fame class
author: Konner Metz
content:
Plein Air Easton inducts 2nd Hall of Fame class

 July 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 593
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As Plein Air Easton wraps up its 21st year, the largest juried outdoor painting competition in the country is adding to its Hall of Fame roster.This year, Plein Air Easton inducted eight new members to its Hall of Fame, which began in 2024 with 11 inductees. This year's class is made up of Mary and Hall Kellogg, Hali and Scott Asplundh, David Grafton, Diane Dubois Mullaly, the Troika Gallery and the Working Artists Forum.
All inductees were nominated and then selected by a five-person committee.
Some are artists, while others are dedicated supporters of the plein air event over the years. But all of them have been integral to the competition's growth, said Avalon Foundation Executive Director Al Bond.
On Monday, Tilghman Island residents Mary and Hall Kellogg were recognized at the Paint Tilghman exhibit, a venture they helped begin over a decade ago.
Bond told the crowd that the Kelloggs — also the founders of the Tilghman Watermen's Museum — are to thank for the Paint Tilghman tradition.
"They saw the potential for plein air painting to tell those stories to new audiences," Bond said. "Thanks to them, an entire island has become a part of Plein Air Easton's history."
"Their generosity, their warmth, their belief in the value of preservation have left a lasting legacy for Plein Air Easton," he added.
Bond discussed the impacts of the other Hall of Famers in an interview Friday.
The Alspundhs, regular patrons of the festival's art every year, were some of the first people to make Plein Air Easton a fun, family tradition, Bond said. Thanks to Hali and Scott, he said, families and groups of friends began to see Plein Air Easton as a social outing for those that love art.
"The Asplundhs sort of showed the way," Bond said.
Grafton and Mullaly were two artists inducted into the Hall of Fame this year. Both have been involved since the jump, Bond noted.
Grafton died before the pandemic, but his impact on the festival has been lasting.
"David was a very well-known artist, so I think that his early involvement, it lent some legitimacy to what was a brand new thing at the time," Bond said.
Meanwhile, the executive director said that Mullaly was one of the original organizers of quick draw, a painting competition open to the public every year during the festival. Bond called Mullaly a "very accomplished artist."
Located on South Harrison Street, the Troika Gallery has been around for nearly three decades. Leaders at the art gallery helped get Plein Air Easton off its feet 21 years ago.
"They've been there the whole time in a very roll-up-your-sleeves and solve-the-problem kind of way," Bond said.
Bond credits the involvement of local artwork to the Working Artists Forum, an Easton-based nonprofit group of artists. The forum hosts a Local Color exhibit during Plein Air Easton, showcasing and selling art from Delmarva-based artists.
On Monday in Tilghman Island, Mary Kellogg thanked the Avalon Foundation and Bond for the recognition, but was quick to point out the volunteers that have made Plein Air Easton's 21 years possible.
"This has been a huge, huge honor. It's not just us," she said. "It's all those people out there, many of them wearing green aprons. The volunteers at the museum who are tireless workers on weekends and throughout the year."
Kellogg shouted out the Avalon Foundation's leadership, including Bond, chief financial and operating officer Jess Bellis, art director Suzy Moore and Plein Air Easton coordinator Marie Nuthall.
"They should have their own Hall of Fame," Kellogg said.
Plein Air Easton continues through Sunday. For a schedule of events and more information, visit pleinaireaston.com.

title: Kent County finds music that moves them at fair
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Kent County finds music that moves them at fair

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Headlines 
 
 504
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TOLCHESTER — Wednesday night, at the Kent County Fair, beneath the stars, local line dancing instructor Minnie Maloney guided folks on how to shift their weight, stepping to the beat to country, rock and hip-hop songs.After a sweltering afternoon judging chickens, canines and hogs, from 7 to 9 p.m., at the main pavilion, 4-H'ers let their hair down to line dance, something Maloney has been doing for over 20 years.
Everyone had something to dance to from music like "Barsong" by Shaboozey, "I was on a Boat" by Old Dominion, "Boots on the Ground" by 803Fresh, and "Jacked Up" by Colt Ford.
"It was an honor to bring some line dancing joy to the Kent County Fair," she said. "Even through the heat and sweat there were smiles and comments about how much fun it was."
At age 40, with fiery red hair and cowboy boots, she ain't stopping any time soon.
"I'm back dancing, it feels great," she said, recently recovering from plantar fasciitis, an inflammation along the bottom of the foot resulting in heel pain.
Yoga and proper stretching is getting her back to full strength, teaching Monterrey turns, (like 180 dance turns) rock steps and rock forwards.
Whether at the 4-H fair, teaching at the local VFW, or conducting classes in private parties, she loves seeing people having fun, memorizing the routines and producing all the positive results from line dancing.
For Maloney it is more than a hobby, it is a life choice that affects her on many levels and shares that joy she found early in life.
At age 12, she fondly remembers dancing with her father at the VFW in Fairlee learning her first line dance: "Baby Likes to Rock It" by the Tractors. The steps just made sense to her, clicking, connecting to her skill when dancing with her friends making up their own routines.
Past her teen years and 20s, dancing was not only fun but therapy for her. Maloney struggles with anxiety and depression, she acknowledges, and there is no better healing than scooting and scuttling past that.
"Dancing forces you to stay in the moment. You forget everything going on in your life."
While bartending for extra money at the American Legion in 2015, there was a push to draw more people. Maloney told them about her line dancing, and they gave her a shot instructing once a week, bringing joy to patrons.
Then she participated as a line dance instructor in the Wild Wild West fundraiser event for St. Martin's Ministry to help generate funds for those battling poverty.
Since then she has been teaching Mondays at the YMCA in Centreville under "Dancingontheshore," at the VFW, as well as private lessons, going off what she has seen from other instructors.
"It's a community builder. We're right beside you helping you. There is no race, age, no discrimination. We're here together."
She watches her students gain self esteem and confidence, relaxing and having fun.
"Some people come in having never danced in their life. They can be real self conscious at first, but I get them to lighten up."

title: Country Cooking: Shrimp, an Eastern Shore tradition
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Shrimp, an Eastern Shore tradition

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1529
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Growing up on the farm, surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean and Chesapeake Bay as well as the many rivers, we ate many types of seafood, but shrimp was not my favorite dish.Shrimp has a long history in the Delmarva region, particularly in the Chesapeake Bay and its estuaries. While not typically fished with a large-scale commercial harvest due to gear restrictions like the beam trawl ban, shrimp populations have been present and studied for decades. Recent observations suggest increasing shrimp populations in the area, possibly due to factors like warming waters.
Shrimp have always been found around the Chesapeake Bay, which is replete with the marshy, muddy habitat they love. Shrimp like to bury in sediment and can be found in both the Bay and its river estuaries, from shallow to deep water. Around the last week of October each year, a sudden drop in temperature drives the shrimp to funnel out of the Bay and into the southern Atlantic, where the water is a little warmer.
The shrimping industry is most popular in the Gulf states of Louisiana, Alabama, Florida and Texas. In the last five years, shrimp sales volume increased from 275 million pounds to 415 million. The percentage of households buying fish has also increased from 44.2% to 48.6%. This growth is seen in all areas of the country.
Shrimp is an excellent, affordable meal option for families. Shrimp can be enjoyed as an appetizer, snack, main course or side dish. Shrimp is a great addition to many popular favorites as it's easy to toss some shrimp into a creamy pasta or grill up some prawns to top your preferred cut of steak.
In later years, I discovered shrimp and became a "shrimp lover." My parents really didn't care for shrimp, so therefore when I became a cook in my own kitchen, I ventured into exploring many different foods. The same happens generation after generation, introductions to different foods.
JUMBO STEAMED SHRIMP
1/2 cup vinegar, 1 tbsp Old Bay seasoning, 3/4 cup water, 1 tsp salt, 1 1/2 lbs jumbo shrimp.
In a medium sized saucepan combine vinegar, Old Bay, water and salt. Bring these ingredients to a boil. Add shrimp. Stir gently to coat the shrimp in the liquid. Cover and steam for 5 to 6 minutes or until tender. Drain and serve.
SHRIMP AND RICE
1/4 cup butter, 1/4 cup chopped onion, 1/4 cup chopped green pepper, 3 tbsps flour, small can tomato sauce, 1 cup water, 1/2 tsp hot sauce, 1 1.2 lbs pre-cooked shrimp, rice.
Melt butter, add onion and green pepper, mix well with the butter. Mix in flour, stirring until bubbly. Add tomato sauce, water and hot sauce. Cook slowly for about 10 minutes. Add shrimp and cook slowly for another 10-15 minutes. Serve over cooked rice.
SHRIMP SCAMPI
1 1/2 cups olive oil, 1/4 cup lemon juice, 4 crushed garlic cloves, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp black pepper, 4 lbs raw shrimp (shelled and deveined).
In a large skillet, place olive oil, lemon juice, garlic cloves, salt, and pepper. Heat thoroughly and add shrimp. Stir well and cook until the shrimp are pink. Serve with rice.
SHRIMP STIR FRY
2 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, 1 lb shrimp (peeled and deveined), Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 1 tbsp sesame oil, 1 small head of broccoli (cut into small florets), 1 red bell pepper (seeds and ribs removed, thinly sliced), 8 oz sugar snap peas, 3 garlic cloves (minced), 1 tbsp finely chopped peeled ginger, 1/2 cup reduced-sodium soy sauce, juice of 1 lime, 2 tbsps light brown sugar, 1 tbsp cornstarch, pinch of crushed red pepper flakes.
In a large wok or skillet over medium heat, heat olive oil. Add shrimp; season with salt and black pepper. Cook, turning halfway through, until pink, 2 to 3 minutes. Transfer shrimp to a plate. In the same skillet over medium heat, heat sesame oil. Add broccoli, bell pepper, and peas and cook, stirring and adding a splash of water if browning too quickly, until softened, about 7 minutes. Add garlic and ginger and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute more.In a small bowl, whisk soy sauce, lime juice, brown sugar, cornstarch, and red pepper flakes. Add to the skillet and toss to coat. Add shrimp and cook, tossing frequently, until heated through, about 2 minutes.
OLD BAY SHRIMP BURRITOS
For Old Bay aioli: 1/3 cup mayonnaise, 1 1/2 tsp Sriracha, 3/4 tsp fresh lime juice, 1/2 tsp Old Bay seasoning (plus more for serving), Kosher salt. For shrimp filling: 1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, 1/2 yellow onion (finely chopped), 1 small green bell pepper (diced), 2 cloves garlic (thinly sliced), 1 lb small shrimp (peeled and deveined, tails removed), 1/4 tsp ground cumin, 1/4 tsp paprika, Kosher salt, freshly ground pepper. For assembling burrito: 4 large flour tortillas (warmed), 1 cup cooked long-grain white rice, 1 cup cooked black beans (rinsed and drained), 3/4 cup shredded Mexican cheese, 1 cup shredded lettuce, 1 cup pico de gallo (drained), 1 avocado (thinly sliced), 2 tbsps chopped chives (plus more for serving).
Make aioli: Whisk together mayo, Sriracha, lime juice, Old Bay, and 1 teaspoon water. Season with salt, if desired. Make shrimp filling: In a large skillet over medium-high heat, add oil, onion, bell pepper, and garlic. Cook, stirring occasionally, until lightly golden, about 2 minutes. Stir in shrimp, cumin, and paprika. Season with salt and pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally, until opaque and just cooked through, about 4 minutes. Assemble burritos: Lay a tortilla on a serving plate. Add 1/4 cup each of the rice and beans. Top with ¼ each of the shrimp filling, cheese, lettuce, pico de gallo, and avocado slices. Sprinkle with chives and drizzle with aioli. Roll the burrito tightly and repeat with remaining tortillas and ingredients. Slice each burrito in half and serve with more aioli, Old Bay and chives.
SWEET CORN, SHRIMP & RICE SKILLET
1/2 cup basmati rice, 1 bunch scallions (divided), 1 medium red bell pepper (chopped), 6 garlic cloves (5 roughly chopped, 1 minced), 4 tbsps white miso, 1-inch piece ginger (thinly sliced), 1 1/4 tsp turmeric powder (divided), 1 tsp Kosher salt (plus more for seasoning), 1 tsp granulated sugar (optional), 1/4 tsp ground cayenne pepper (optional), 4 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil (divided), 1/2 lb medium shrimp (peeled and cleaned), freshly ground black pepper, 3/4 cup water, 1 cup frozen corn (rinsed in warm water and drained), lime wedges for serving.
Rinse rice well, until water runs clear, then transfer to a medium bowl and cover with water. Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Cook 5 roughly chopped garlic cloves and ginger in a pan for around 1 minute. Remove roots and ends from 4 green onions and roughly chop into pieces. Add chopped scallions to blender or food processor, along with the bell pepper, garlic cloves, miso, ginger, 1 teaspoon turmeric, salt, and sugar and cayenne if using. Blend until all ingredients are finely chopped and thoroughly mixed, then slowly drizzle in 3 tablespoons olive oil while running the food processor or blender. Blend until mixture is smooth. Pat shrimp dry and transfer to a medium bowl. Add remaining turmeric and minced garlic clove, and season with salt and pepper. Heat remaining tablespoon of oil in a 12-inch oven safe skillet over medium heat. Add shrimp and cook until opaque, 2 to 3 minutes per side. Remove cooked shrimp into a bowl just big enough to fit and cover with a plate to keep warm. Return the skillet to heat and add prepared puree. Cook on medium-high heat, stirring frequently, until the liquid has cooked out and paste has darkened, 8 to 10 minutes. (You'll know it's done when the oil starts to separate from the paste! Reduce heat to medium and whisk in water until smooth. Strain rice, and add rice and corn. Drain any cooking juices from the shrimp into the skillet, using the plate to keep the shrimp from falling in. (Be sure to keep shrimp covered. Stir to incorporate everything, then bring mixture up to a simmer. Place in a preheated oven and cover tightly with a lid or sheet pan. Bake until all liquid is absorbed and rice is tender, about 23 to 25 minutes. Meanwhile, thinly slice remaining green onions for garnish. Fluff rice with a fork, then scoop into serving dishes. Top with cooked shrimp and green onions and serve with lime wedges on the side.
SHEET PAN SHRIMP
1 lb. baby red potatoes (quartered), 1 1/2 lb raw medium shrimp (peeled and deveined), 2 ears of corn (cut crosswise into 4 pieces each), 2 links smoked andouille sausage (thinly sliced), 2 lemons (sliced), 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tbsp Old Bay seasoning, 2 tbsps melted butter, 2 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 2 tbsps freshly chopped parsley for garnish.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. In a large pot of salted boiling water, cook potatoes until just tender, about 10 minutes. Drain. In a large bowl, combine cooked potatoes, shrimp, corn, sausage, lemons, garlic powder, Old Bay, melted butter, and oil and season with salt and pepper. Toss until combined, then divide between two large baking sheets. Bake until shrimp is cooked through and corn is tender, 13 to 15 minutes.

title: Temple B'nai Israel welcomes new permanent rabbi
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Temple B'nai Israel welcomes new permanent rabbi

 July 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Nearly nine months after the previous rabbi retired, a new permanent rabbi has stepped into the role at Temple B'nai Israel.Rabbi Jordan Goldson assumed the position on July 1, following the retirement of Rabbi Peter Hyman in October.
In the search for a new permanent rabbi, the temple's Board of Trustees created a list of potential candidates for interviews after establishing priorities, according to Barbara Spector, the board president during the selection process. Spector said the board was looking for a Reform rabbi with more experience to fit Temple B'nai Israel's established congregation.
Before coming to Easton, Goldson had extensive experience leading congregations. After being ordained at Hebrew Union College in 1987, Goldson became a full-time Reform rabbi at Temple B'nai Tikvah in Calgary, Alberta, Canada, where he served for 12 years. Upon leaving the temple, Goldson lived in Israel for some time before moving back to the U.S. to lead several congregations around the country. Most recently, Goldson served as the rabbi at Har Sinai Temple in Pennington, New Jersey.
"He has a very calm demeanor and a wonderful background with his experience in being part of an inclusive congregation," David Holtz said. Holtz took over the position of temple executive director after Goldson was selected.
Holtz described him as "one of those very nice people that you're grateful that you've been able to encounter, particularly in a role that will mean so much to the community and to the congregation."
Hyman described Goldson as very bright, engaging, warm, creative and people-focused.
As the former rabbi at the temple, Hyman said maintaining a presence in the community was always his first priority, and he has great confidence in Goldson building on that foundation.
"He's really terrific," Hyman said. "He's going to continue to grow the congregation, and I know he'll be successful."
Hyman's years of dedication and congregation building have not gone unnoticed. Goldson recognized Hyman for his "spectacular job" in expanding the congregation and said he will build on what Hyman has done to increase the temple's reach.
Focused on inclusivity, Goldson said his plans to grow the congregation, creating an environment where "people feel that they matter."
Temple B'nai Israel is the hub for Jewish life on the Eastern Shore and represents a vast community. Goldson said he will reach out to the community and welcome people who may not know about the congregation.
"We'll be doing a lot of different things that I think are going to attract people to the temple," Goldson said.
The temple offers a religious school for students in kindergarten through 12th grade. Spector said she expects Goldson will help attract more young families to the temple and expand the religious school.
"We're just hoping he can help us get ready for the next decade by helping us educate young Jewish children," Spector said.
To support this effort, Goldson plans to expand the temple's programs, including youth, community service and religious education initiatives.
As he becomes more comfortable in his new role, Goldson has enjoyed the positive energy and dynamics of the community, and he recognizes that it will take more than just him to grow the congregation's impact.
"I can see that this is a community that embraces each other," Goldson said. "It's a very tight-knit, religious community and I'm really looking forward to working with the larger community here to see what we can do to make Easton and the surrounding areas the most wonderful place it can be."

title: Country Cooking: Memories of crabbing and clamming
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Memories of crabbing and clamming

 July 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: News 
 
 1366
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Pulling away from the local seafood store yesterday with a basket of fresh caught and fresh steamed crabs surely brings back memories of the 1950s and 1960s.Mom would set aside the designated weekday for crabbing. The other chores would be done. Mom would back the pickup out, and we would load the supplies, which included the baskets with inner tubes attached to help the baskets to float, the chicken necks for bait, the heavy string to tie the hook and sinker to, crab nets, towels, a picnic basket with sandwiches and a big jug of water with chunks of ice inside.
We loaded up and rode in the back of the truck so we could hoot and holler at our friends as we rode through town. Our friends would holler, "Take me" as we passed because they knew the fun we would have along with the work involved.
Our destination would be one of two country landings with docks for crabbing and areas for swimming. The first one was Mumford's Landing off St. Martin's Neck Road (now a development off the Route 90 bridge outside of Ocean City) and the second one was a little dock called Little Georgetown, just down the road from our farm on the Delaware side.
Upon arriving at the landing, Mom picked a spot to tie our strings on the dock poles. We took the lines and hung the nuts, bolts and sinkers on the bottom so the weight held the line down. Then we tied on the bait.
You had a choice — go swimming now or later, but you had to move down a good distance to stay away from the baited lines. Mom would get two baskets ready, grab a crab net and walk along the shoreline and crab. Someone stayed back with another net and basket to gradually pull up the lines, placing the net under the line to catch the falling crabs. Sitting on the dock would be one- or two-bushel baskets with lids to place the freshly caught crabs in.
If it was a slow catching day, the bushel basket would be set at the shoreline to partially filled with water to keep the crabs alive. Meanwhile, back on the farm, whoever stayed behind was pulling out one of the largest iron pots, used for winter hog killing and summer beet cooking. They placed stick-seasoned pieces of wood to start the fire to steam the crabs.
Upon arriving at home, the still kicking crabs were unloaded, the fire started and the Old Bay seasoning was put in. Once the crabs were bright orange/red in color, the fire was pulled away and the crabs pulled and placed on the picnic tables to be picked.
Of course, we ate the delicious meat until we were full, and then we put it in containers to be carried to the kitchen to be made into dishes such as crab cakes, crab soup and much more.
So let's explore what to make with our crabmeat.
CRAB CAKES
1 large egg, 1/4 cup mayonnaise, 1 tbsp chopped fresh parsley (or 2 tsps dried), 2 tsps Dijon mustard, 2 tsps Worcestershire sauce, 1 tsp Old Bay or J.O seasoning, 1 tsp fresh lemon juice (plus more for serving), 1/8 tsp salt, 1 lb fresh lump crab meat, 2/3 cup saltine cracker crumbs (about 17 two-inch crackers).
Whisk the egg, mayonnaise, parsley, Dijon mustard, Worcestershire sauce, Old Bay, lemon juice and salt together in a large bowl. Place the crab meat on top, followed by the cracker crumbs. With a silicone spatula or large spoon, very gently and carefully fold together. You don't want to break up that crab meat. Cover tightly and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 1 day. Preheat oven to 450 degrees. Generously grease a rimmed baking sheet with butter or nonstick spray, or line with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat. Using a 1/2 cup measuring cup, portion the crab cake mixture into 6 mounds on the baking sheet. Don't flatten. Use your hands or a spoon to compact each individual mound so there aren't any lumps sticking out or falling apart. Bake for 12–14 minutes or until lightly browned around the edges and on top. Drizzle each with fresh lemon juice and serve warm. Cover leftover crab cakes tightly and refrigerate for up to 5 days or freeze for up to 3 months.
MARYLAND CRAB SOUP
1 28-oz can whole tomatoes (cut into small pieces), 3 cups water, 2 cups beef broth, 1 cup frozen lima beans, 1 cup frozen baby carrots, 1 cup frozen yellow sweet corn, 2 tbsps chopped onions, 1 tbsp Old Bay or JO seasoning, 1 lb lump crabmeat.
Place all ingredients, except crabmeat, in 4-quart saucepan, Bring to boil on medium heat. Reduce heat to low; cover and simmer for 5 minutes. Stir in crabmeat; cover and simmer for 10 minutes.
CLAMS WITH GARLIC SAUCE
Clamming was also something we enjoyed doing. This meant a trip out into the water knee to waist deep with the clam rakes and innertubes. While we were there crabbing at the Isle of Wight Bay, my brothers would walk the edge of the marsh back towards Ocean City and clam near the rocks. It had to be low tide to get the best clams. Otherwise we'd buy them from the waterman who'd clam near Assateague.
3 dozen clams (scrubbed), ½ cup cornmeal, 1 tbsp salt, ¼ cup olive oil, 1 small onion (minced), 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 small dried red chili, 2 bay leaves, ¼ tsp hot paprika, pepper.
In bowl, cover the clams and cornmeal with water; add the salt and soak 45 minutes; drain and rinse. Heat the oil in a large non-reactive skillet. Add the onion; cook until soft. Add the clams, lemon juice, chili, bay leaves, paprika and pepper. Cover and cook over high heat, stirring constantly, removing the clams as they open. Garlic Sauce:4 garlic cloves minced,¼ cup parsley minced,½ cup fish stock or ¼ cup bottled clam juice diluted with ¼ cup water, In blender, puree garlic with 5 tbsps of the parsley, add the fish stock and garlic mixture to a skillet; cook until sauce is slightly thickened. Divide the clams among four soup plates. Spoon the garlic sauce on top and garnish with remaining parsley.
CLAMS LINGUINE
Kosher salt, 1 lb linguine, 6 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, ½ cup finely chopped shallots, 6 cloves garlic (coarsely chopped), ½ tsp red pepper flakes, 2 lbs Littleneck clams (scrubbed), ¼ cup plus 2 tbsps fresh flat-leaf parsley (finely chopped), 3 tbsps unsalted butter, 1 tsp lemon zest, 1 tbsp lemon juice.
In large pot over high heat, bring 4 quarts of water and 2 tbspss of kosher salt to a boil. Add the linguine and cook according to the package directions until just shy of al dente (the pasta should still be firm to the bite since it will cook another minute or two in the sauce). Drain in a colander (do not rinse), reserving ½ cup of the cooking water for the sauce. Meanwhile, in a very large sauté pan over medium-high heat, heat the olive oil until hot but not smoking. Add the shallots and garlic and sauté until just golden, about 30 seconds. Add the wine, red pepper flakes, ¾ tsp kosher salt, clams, and ¼ cup of the parsley; bring to a simmer and cook, covered, until the clams open, 6 to 8 minutes. Discard any unopened clams. Add the pasta to the sauté pan with the clams. (If you don't have room for everything in one pan, transfer the clams to a plate and cover to keep warm. When ready to serve, add them back to the pasta on a serving platter). Increase the heat to medium and cook the linguini with the clams, tossing occasionally, until the pasta absorbs most of the sauce and is just tender, 1 to 2 minutes. If necessary, add some of reserved cooking water to keep moist. Remove the pan from the heat. Add the butter, lemon zest, lemon juice, and the remaining 2 tbsps of parsley; toss to coat. Taste and adjust the seasoning with more salt, lemon zest and/or lemon juice, if necessary. Transfer to a serving dish or bowls and serve.

title: 'Dorchester Dreams' provides fresh role models
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'Dorchester Dreams' provides fresh role models

 July 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 383
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County Council members giggled and pointed at the cartoon depictions of themselves as they passed around the first iteration of the "Dorchester Dreams" children's book.The children's book depicts comic-like versions of residents and tells the story of the Barzini Family Music Group coming to Dorchester and joining the community.
The Barzini Family Music Group was created in 2023 and moved to the Eastern Shore from the DMV area last year. Founder and CEO, Derrick "AB" Taylor said the group has plans to create a book series along with their music projects to provide children in the community with contemporary, relatable role models.
"I've always been a big advocate of education. And, like I said, everybody in the Barzini Family are all under 32," Taylor said.
Though the members of the music group are young, they are determined to make a lasting impact on the Eastern Shore. Taylor, originally from Philadelphia, said he sees the Shore as the next premier music destination and the children are paving the way.
"The children kind of dictate the market in a way," said Taylor.
For Taylor, seeing the music industry as a well rounded machine rather than a single engine is critical. He puts an emphasis on alternative career paths within the industry, highlighting that success can be achieved through education in fields such as finance, writing, and business rather than solely through traditional routes.
The book gets its name from a song written by one of the music group's young members. Jayla Elise wrote "Dorchester Dreams," which became the official song of Dorchester County in June.
In the team's book series, they also plan to have one on "The Heart of Maryland," which ties into the team's efforts to accomplish a state song.
Elise will be performing "The Heart of Maryland" at minor league baseball games across the state beginning on August 8, 22 and 28.
The Barzini Family team is planning to read their children's books at the Girls and Boys Club in Cambridge. They have even purchased a blue crab and muskrat costume for the occasion.
"It's kind of like the Batman effect. We don't really have superpowers, but our power is that we keep going," said Taylor. "I wanted them to see themselves as like, 'I probably don't think I can do it, but at least I can try.'"

title: Find your personal landmarks at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Find your personal landmarks at the library

 August 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 1027
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Do they still teach "the classics" these days? They certainly did in my time. And they were presented as faits accomplis, no questions asked."These are the classics, you will read and remember them: 'Tess of the D'Urbervilles,' 'Moby Dick,' 'A Tale of Two Cities,' 'Huckleberry Finn,' 'Wuthering Heights,' 'The Scarlet Letter.'" — the titles apparently handed down from on high.
Occasionally a teacher would pitch "1984" or "The Grapes of Wrath" into the mix, as if to prove he or she had indeed survived into the 20th century, but for the most part, classical literature seemed to have thrived in the 19th century and promptly expired at its conclusion.
But nothing is permanent in life, not even "the classics," and from what little I know of current pedagogical fashion, most of the titles listed above probably figure in few syllabi these days (though I pray "The Grapes of Wrath" and "1984" still make the cut). Which is probably for the best.
I'm sure the advent of "World Literature" has introduced any number of worthy novels to the canon that my little mid-20th century Kentucky school would never have heard of.
I will probably miss out on most of these new discoveries. I just don't have the time or the inclination anymore to keep up with literature's latest wunderkind. Which is not to say I don't have my own personal list of classics, works that have opened my eyes not just to new ways of seeing, but, just as important, to the way life is actually lived.
Graham Swift won the Man Booker Prize in 1996 for "Last Orders," but to my way of thinking, "Wish You Were Here" and "Waterland," are his best books. These past few weeks, my wife recovering from surgery, I've found myself rereading "Wish You Were Here." It is, in my opinion, a powerful, disquieting "classic."
The story is told in the third-person singular, primarily from the point of view of its main character, Jack Luxton.
The book opens with Jack sitting upstairs in his bedroom, awaiting the return of his wife Ellie. It is raining hard, a scattershot drumbeat on roof and windows. As Jack waits, he recalls important passages from his life. From time to time, he glances at the shotgun lying on the bed beside him.
Jack was raised in southwest England, on a farm that generations of Luxtons had called home. It was all he knew. There were his father and mother, his little brother Tom, and the dairy cows they milked twice daily. Life was simple, local. Everything had its time and place. Life had always been like this. Life, so far as he was concerned, would always be like this.
But then Jack's mother died, and Jack had to become a sort of mother to his little brother, whom he loved — though love was a word no longer spoken in that now motherless house.
But Jack, a large man, unsure of himself, a bit of a fumbler, still felt love, and some of it he felt for the little girl growing up on the farm next door, Ellie. And Ellie returned that love. In their teens, they began to meet secretly whenever Ellie's father was away.
I have to admit, I have only a vague memory of the mad cow disease that struck England's beef and dairy industries in 1996. I read about the outbreak in the papers, felt, I'm sure, a passing sympathy for the farmers affected, and then moved on. We learn of catastrophes every day now; spending too much time on each would leave us paralyzed.
But when the catastrophe strikes you … Well, that's another story altogether. And that's what happens to Jack.
Jack, his father and his little brother must watch as their livelihood, the cows they have known and cared for all their lives, cows that to all outward appearances remain perfectly healthy, are rounded up by government edict and "culled," their carcasses set alight.
First his mother dies — his mother who held the family together, his mother who was the keeper of the family history and traditions — and then the cows that gave that history, those traditions, their meaning, are destroyed in a single seemingly senseless act of butchery. Well, it would take something out of you.
And, as it turns out, those deaths are just the first in a series of deaths Jack must face and try to bear. We all have our tragedies to contend with, no one escapes life unscarred, but for most of us, if we're lucky, providence punctuates the bad times with long spells of the good. But that is not true for everyone.
And as we learn of the multiple sorrows and paltry joys of Jack Luxton's life, that shotgun remains on the bed beside him.
Reading back over this column, reading the previous line, I find myself wondering why anyone would want to read this book. Why do I want to read, and reread, this book?
Would it help if I told you Swift's writing is masterful? Would it help if I told you Jack and Ellie's relationship — with all its human flaws and human tenderness — is as true to life as any I have ever read?
What do we want from classics? What makes a classic a classic? Do we want fairy tales, pie in the sky, or do we want life as it is actually lived, life as we have lived it?
I don't know. I'm not sure. Certainly there are times when I want escape, when I want Jack Reacher to step into a scene and save the day; but when it comes down to real life, I find Jack Luxton's clumsiness and uncertainty, his feelings of incompetence, closer to my own experience of life as it must be suffered — and as it must be enjoyed — every day.
So let's leave it at that, like Jack Luxton, I'm uncertain why Swift's novel moves me so. All I know for sure is that reading "Wish You Were Here" always gives me, oddly enough, a sense of strength, the feeling that, if I have fears and loves in common with a man as basically good as Jack Luxton, then maybe there's hope for me yet.
