title: Unmasking Chessie: Historian discusses sea monster's cultural consequenses
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Unmasking Chessie: Historian discusses sea monster's cultural consequenses

 August 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 770
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PRESTON — Eric Cheezum is an Eastern Shore native. He worked the fields with his family, grew up spending time on the Bay, and, like many on the Shore, was raised with the lore of Chessie, the Chesapeake Bay monster.Cheezum remembers obsessing with his older brother over the Loch Ness Monster, Bigfoot and the TV show "Unsolved Mysteries." Little did he know, he would spend his career becoming the expert on a related mystery, but not for the reason one would think.
Cheezum spent his undergraduate years at Salisbury University pivoting from one major to another until he found his true passion: history.
Initially, he wanted to do historical research on Woodrow Wilson and the Progressive Era, and later move into studying Herbert Hoover.
"I gradually started to discover that writing presidential and foreign policy history was sort of old hat and not very trendy at the time, this was 25 years ago," Cheezum said. "And what we used to call social history was really in the ascendancy then."
Cheezum loves pop culture but at the time, had a disdain for social history. He described social history as "studying history through the lens of race, class and gender." He said he's always been more inclined to seeing history through an economic and diplomatic lens.
Cheezum sat in a history course for his doctorate degree at the University of South Carolina, where Professor Paul Johnson introduced him to his book "Sam Patch, The Famous Jumper." The novel is a historical analysis of how public natural spaces, such as areas around waterfalls, were transformed into exclusive, middle-class domains over 150 years ago.
Newly established middle-class Americans began to develop near the waterfalls, building gardens to exclude public access. Sam Patch began jumping into the waterfalls, which drew large crowds.
His dare-devil jumps evolved into popular carnival-like events, which re-opened these spaces to the public, even if it was temporary.
Chessie's story is similar, Cheezum said.
He said when he first started to investigate Chessie, he wanted it to be something fun. But the more he researched, the more he found it wasn't that. There were consequences to Chessie.
The consequences of Chessie
"The people who see Chessie are almost invariably people who are either tourists or people who have moved into suburban developments that were just being built there in that same time period," Cheezum said.
"When you start looking at the actual sighting reports, you see an awful lot of conflict going on under the surface between that group of people who are doing the seeing and the people who are natives, who clearly regard this phenomenon as yet another imposition upon them," he said.
Sightings of Chessie began in 1980, simultaneuously with regional development and the rise of water tourism.
Cheezum said the tension between those who have seen Chessie and the natives who reject the sightings exists for many reasons.
A waterman has never reported seeing Chessie. "When you're out on the water, you really don't have time to be looking for sea monsters, right? And you know what's in the water because of generationally passed down knowledge about the water," Cheezum said.
A majority of Chessie sightings have been by transplants or tourists who spend a good portion of their time on the shore watching the water. When transplants and tourists claim Chessie sightings, Cheezum said they are inadvertently questioning the waterman's knowledge.
"What the outsiders are starting to do is question the knowledge base of the people who are living here and saying, well, 'You don't really know what you're looking at because you're not educated enough to know.'"
Cheezum doesn't think they do this purposefully, but he said that's how it can come off.
Kent Island, particularly Love Point Avenue, has become Chessie central. In 1980, public beach access was ubiquitous according to residents. Now, it's difficult to find an access point. For Cheezum, this is the second consequence of Chessie, similar to the newfound middle class building gardens around the waterfalls.
The final consequence of Chessie is what Cheezum calls Chesapeakeiana, which is an objectification of the Eastern Shore.
"People are encouraged to come down and buy oyster tongs that they'll only use once and they name their condominium Oyster Cove Estates and attach the word 'Chesapeake' to it, and it's a real winner every time. That's the cynicism that is kind of built into Chesapeakeiana," Cheezum said.
Though tourism and gentrification were well underway before the first Chessie sightings, Cheezum said Chessie was an outcome of changing times.
"That wasn't because of Chessie, but Chessie is a symptom of that in the way, Chessie is the intellectual justification because anybody can have a slice of the Chesapeake. You can have your own sea monster," Cheezum said.

title: 'Made with love': Delaware film festival will feature 58 short films
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
'Made with love': Delaware film festival will feature 58 short films

 August 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Newark Independent Film Festival is returning for its second year next week.The Delaware event is set for Aug. 14, 15 and 16 at Chapel Street Players on Creek View Road.
"We're offering audiences something completely different, something that was made with love," organizer Kazy Tauginas said. "Regardless of genre, the filmmakers that made these films, they put their souls into them, and you can feel it on the screen. I think that people will be very pleasantly surprised at the quality of the films that they're going to be watching."
The festival will feature 58 short films spanning many genres, including horror, drama, comedy, documentaries and art-house films. Filmmakers are coming from all over the United States and from as far away as Germany.
"Just hearing the stories and what people went through just to tell something that they felt was really important to them at that time, that separates us from what studio films are all made for," Tauginas said. "They're all profit-driven. Indies are a lot of times just driven by the heart."
There are also a number of films that were shot right here in Delaware, including "Return to Hockessin No. 107C," which is about the history of the Hockessin Colored School, and "Unseen American Dream," a documentary about a blind couple from Wilmington raising sighted children.
"Delaware locals have their own category at my festival," Tauginas said. "And then, of course, we have filmmakers from Los Angeles and New York and everywhere in between."
Tauginas is an actor, director and writer who has written and starred in more than 20 independent films. His acting career also has included guest spots in major television shows, and he has appeared in several movies, including "The Equalizer 2," starring Denzel Washington.
He lives in Newark and also works as a real estate agent and serves on the Newark Planning Commission.
The film festival will include the premier of the feature film "Mirror Life," which Tauginas wrote, directed and starred in. The movie is about a woman who's searching for her cousin who disappeared after entering an illegal human clinical trial.
Tauginas said that major film studios are moving more and more of their productions overseas, leading to fewer opportunities for actors here. That's part of what inspired him to start the film festival, to provide an opportunity to showcase more independent films.
"Filmmakers are going to be able to see their film on screen, in front of an audience, on the big screen with a dynamic sound system in a proper venue, so that it can get the attention that it deserves," he said. "I think it's a really important thing, especially for independent artists."
He added that he hopes the festival is an economic boost for Newark as the filmmakers from out of town arrive in Newark, stay at the Hyatt Place hotel on Main Street and patronize local restaurants and shops.
Tauginas, who used to own the Korner Diner on Main Street, said he knows that the summer is a slow time for Newark businesses. With a location right off Interstate 95 and a walkable downtown, Newark is a great place for the festival, he said.
"I can't think of a better place that you would want a film festival," he said.
The Newark Independent Film Festival will show 58 films in seven blocks spread over three days. Tickets for each block are $15. For more information and to buy tickets, visit newarkindependentfilmfestival.com.

title: A 'one of a kind' exhibit in Cambridge shows Tubmans strength, softness, humanity
author: Lily Tierney
content:
A 'one of a kind' exhibit in Cambridge shows Tubmans strength, softness, humanity

 August 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 494
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The walls of the Harriet Tubman Freedom Center look a bit different these days.Currently, they are covered by a "one of a kind" art exhibit depicting Tubman in various artistic mediums through the lens of 40 artists from all over the globe.
"Harriet: A Taste of Freedom" was curated by Maryland-based artist Larry Poncho Brown and will be featured at the center through Sept. 30. The exhibit is free and open to the public.
"It gives a different twist here in Dorchester County with Harriet Tubman and people to engage in a modern view in some type of atmosphere with art expression," Harriet Tubman Freedom Center President Alex Green said. "It's a really cool exhibit."
The walls emphasize Tubman's strength through her serious and intentional facial expressions, show her softness through depictions of her as a child, and allow her humanity by representing her in such a multifaceted way.
For Green, inspiring people to learn and understand history, particularly Tubman's character of unselfishness and community support, and adopt community-minded values can help prevent communities from repeating past wrongs. It is particularly important for the younger generations, which is why the center provides youth programming, Green said.
"We want to understand how history pretty much played out, with information, not partisanship. We just want to understand," Green said.
Green said the exhibit is a great opportunity to inspire youth to learn the history of Tubman and Dorchester County.
"The younger generation can carry the torch further with understanding. The lack of it is going to cause us to repeat the things that have happened," Green said. "So I think it's very important that children get a chance to engage. Get Harriet introduced, let them make a decision on how they want to process it," he said.
There is an emphasis that everyone is welcome at the freedom center, as long as they believe freedom is the ultimate goal. That is why the door says, "Turn into freedom," Green said.
"In here, we want you to feel free with your opinions as long as it's in the context of freedom," Green said.
The different styles of the gorgeous depictions of Tubman are true representations of freedom. Green said it was difficult for some of the artists to give them away because they've grown so attached.
The Harriet Tubman Freedom Center is located at 3030 Center Drive in Cambridge, and "Harriet: A Taste of Freedom" is open from Tuesday to Friday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Saturday from 9 a.m to 3 p.m. It will run until Sept. 30, with the potential of the exhibit being extended through Dec.
"That way we give people more of a chance to be engaged with it, because you come out, look, walk around, you can leave a donation, or you don't have to. You can sign your name, or you don't have to. It's not a requirement. It's not like $5 at the door. But you just can come and take in this amazing exhibit," Green said.

title: 'Brings back memories': Local artists take stab at famous art
author: Konner Metz
content:
'Brings back memories': Local artists take stab at famous art

 August 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 558
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Inside the Troika Gallery, an exhibit gives local artists the chance to display their own takes on some of the most well-renowned pieces of art.Twenty-two works make up the "Fabulous Forgeries," an annual tradition where artists choose a historic work to model on their own canvases.
The artists of the original works must be dead for at least 100 years, and the recreations have to be two inches smaller or larger to avoid copyright issues, said Troika Gallery owner Laura Era.
"It brings back memories because most of them are beloved pieces," Era said.
Era and gallery manager Peg Fitzgerald say Fabulous Forgeries is Troika's most popular exhibit. Fitzgerald notes that it's educational for adults and kids interested in art history. Plus, it's an artist favorite.
"The artists that do it, love it," Fitzgerald said. "They're probably even thinking right now for next year."
Some like John Eiseman have a personal connection to their works.
As a kid, one of Eiseman's favorite paintings was an 1872 work by French painter Claude Monet titled "Argenteuil." It is kept in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.
Eiseman, 66, spent his childhood years between St. Michaels and the nation's capital. Monet's depiction of a town and river near Paris reminded Eiseman of the Miles River.
"It reminded me of a placid day somewhere on the Miles," Eiseman said.
But something was always missing. More than 40 years after falling in love with the painting, Eiseman got to add that missing piece: his granddaughter's late American retriever. He placed the dog on a long, empty road that leads toward a castle in the background of the painting.
Era herself has four works in the forgeries collection.
Her favorite is a recreation of an 1873 self-portrait by German painter Anselm Feuerbach. She saw it online and couldn't miss the opportunity to recreate it.
"I just kept coming back to it because he was doggone handsome," Era said.
Era says Fabulous Forgeries is all about studying the history of art. Modern artists can learn from the technique, brushwork and color combinations used by the original painters, she said.
"It's a nice exercise, and it's certainly a learning exercise for any artist," Era said. "And many times, if you go to museums nowadays, you'll see people, there'll be artists that will be copying the old masters with their easel."
The exhibit was judged by Dan Weiss, former president and CEO of The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Palden Hamilton was awarded judge's choice award for his work, "Roses," after Abbott Handerson Thayer.
Other awards and honorable mentions were handed out to Era, Eiseman, John Davis Held, Christine Drewyer and Lynne Lockhart. The exhibit is open through Aug. 30. Voting for the people's choice award remains open.
Some of the works model the originals as closely as possible. Others add their own twists.
Drewyer drew inspiration from an 1888 flower pot painting by Vincent van Gogh. She added a cat, which tore up some of the flowers, and titled it, "Vincent's Bad, Bad Kitty."
The unique flair of each artist has cemented Fabulous Forgeries as a fan favorite each year, Fitzgerald said.
"They just love it," she said of gallery's viewers. "They just love to see how it's interpreted, how the artist decides to do their painting."
The Troika Gallery, located at 9 S. Harrison St., is open on Mondays and Thursdays to Saturdays from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.

title: Free walking tours capture downtown Easton’s rich history
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Free walking tours capture downtown Easton’s rich history

 August 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot Historical Society strives to keep the 360-year history of Easton alive with free historic walking tours held on the third Saturday of each month. Two tours are offered, one at 11 a.m. and another at noon, each providing a unique perspective on the town's history.The 11 a.m. tour takes participants on a walk through central Easton, highlighting important buildings and sharing stories about the town's rich history. The noon tour focuses on the architecture of the six buildings that make up the historical society's campus.
The historical society began offering these tours around 10 years ago. Archivist Patti Rockwell joined the society around that time and is now one of several tour guides.
"The people that live here are just blown away by the history," Rockwell said. "They said 'I had no idea.'"
The tours attract both tourists and locals, who often bring their visiting guests. They are free and open to the public, but registration is required.
The tours start at 25 South Washington St., in front of the historical society, and continue through downtown Easton, looping back to the starting point. The main tour features about 15 stops.
"I think what's really important is finding out how we've evolved to where we are today," Rockwell said.
The tours focus on the impact of the Revolutionary War and the Civil War on the town, as well as fires that brought destruction to several areas. One surprising fact, Rockwell said, is that the town of Easton took an early stand against British control — something many visitors are unaware of.
"You always hear about Boston, but this community took a stand at one time prior to the war starting too," Rockwell said.
Each tour is unique since tour guides create their own scripts. Rockwell said her favorite story to tell involves a hidden armory that stored weapons during the Revolutionary War. That site is now a parking lot partially used by the Easton Farmers Market.
Along with their information cards, tour guides carry a collection of photographs showing what Easton's buildings looked like a century ago. Some include drawings of Easton from before photography existed.
Rockwell said she hopes participants leave with greater awareness of the town's past.
"This town has done a remarkable job of preserving the past, keeping the same buildings here, if we can, without tearing them down so that people can see what it was like at least 100 years ago," Rockwell said.
"These buildings are still downtown, waiting for people to find out a little clue as to what was going on."
More information can be found at talbothistory.org.

title: Watermen’s Appreciation Day attracts almost 3,000 attendees
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Watermen’s Appreciation Day attracts almost 3,000 attendees

 August 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 327
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — On Sunday, almost 3,000 Eastern Shore residents came out to the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum to celebrate Watermen's Appreciation Day.This was the 14th year of the event, during which he museum partners with the Talbot Watermen Association to show appreciation to watermen.
"It feels great to have so many people supporting the watermen," said Jeff Harrison, president of Talbot Watermen Association. "The Bay is something that we cherish, all watermen cherish. We understand our responsibility as far as keeping it clean and keeping it productive. Watermen's Appreciation Day really is about us showing our appreciation to our customers, people that buy our seafood."
The association had 92 bushels of crabs donated by local waterman to sell at Appreciation Day. The crabs were sold for $40 per dozen, and hundreds of people enjoyed.
In addition to the crab donation, the association brought in 115 volunteers to make sure the event ran smoothly.
Shannon Mitchell, vice president of engagement for the museum, credits the association's many volunteers for the event's success.
"It feels great that we have such a strong partnership with the Talbot Watermen Association," Mitchell said. "They play a huge part in making this event a success. They oversee the boat docking competition, the crab feast and so many other things to happen. They have core volunteers, probably like hundreds. It's just, it's impressive to see all the families that are involved to help make this event possible."
All the proceeds from the Crab Feast and from the event's silent auction go to the Talbot Watermen Association. Mitchell said Appreciation Day as a whole plays a big part in accomplishing the museum's community mission.
The biggest crowd-drawer every year is the Boat Docking Competition. The competition saw 11 boats compete with 12 contestants this year.
Derrick Hoy, owner of boat The Crusher, won the shootout competition with a time of 21.8 seconds. While she didn't win, 11-year-old Peyton Reiss received many cheers from the crowd with her impressive boat docking skills.

title: Artsway Banners back in Denton
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Artsway Banners back in Denton

 August 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 223
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Artsway Banners are back in Denton for the third year in a row.In partnership with 12 artist, the Caroline County Council of the Arts placed the banners around town, with this years theme highlighting "Everyday Magic."
According to the Council of Arts website, the theme represents "the magic you experience on a everyday basis in Denton, showcasing the beauty, unity, and positivity that define our community."
The program is important for showcasing the county's arts scene, organizers said.
"It facilitates the presence of art in the community," said George K. Karos, executive director of Caroline County Council of Arts. "There's a wonderful opportunity for Caroline County artists countywide to take the banner and create what they want...
"It's this wonderful collaboration with the artist and the community, and the government, and really, I think it does create, kind of positive aesthetic, offering and visibility that certainly is captured by the warm weather in the sun."
The banners well be hung up for a couple of months and will be auctioned off after they are taken down.
The arts council credited local businesses as sponsors for the project, including Pizza Empire, Craft Bakery & Café, Night Kitchen, Market Street Public House, Mary Elizabeth & Tom Atwood, Caroline Review, Shore Strategies LLC, Caroline County Public Library, Red Light Liquors, Purple Peak, Paperwork Pros & Burke and Herbert Bank.

title: Country Cooking: Peach picking on the Eastern Shore
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Peach picking on the Eastern Shore

 August 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1406
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Some prefer to pick their own peaches, and others simply get them from the local stores or local produce stands. No matter where or how you get them — enjoy this delicious fruit.Growing up in a family that harvested, froze or canned whatever was in season, I always enjoyed the peach canning time because I knew the "season" was finally coming to an end and the canning and freezing equipment could be "retired" to the storage space until apple picking time.
Mom always waited until late July and into August to begin the "peach adventure." The day of peach picking always seemed to be very hot. We would leave early in the morning and get home by lunchtime due to the heat and crowded orchards.
Mom always carried plenty of water and light snacks. We loaded the pickup with plenty of containers to store the peaches — we never stacked the baskets or wooden crates higher than 14 inches per container to avoid bruising the peaches.
Upon arriving home, we laid down newspapers to separate the peaches individually. The bruised or mushy fruit was washed, peeled and eaten immediately or made into pies, ice cream. The firm fruit was used within a couple of days for canning and freezing.
This involved a lot of work being shared by all who would enjoy the peach jelly, jams, canned peaches, frozen peach slices or whatever else Mom decided to make. Let's get cooking.
COUNTRY PEACH PIE
For the crust: 3 cups all-purpose flour (plus more for dusting), 2 tbsps sugar, 3/4 tsp salt, 2 sticks cold unsalted butter cut into small pieces. For the filling: 4 lbs peaches (peeled and cut into wedges), 3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp sugar, 1/4 cup all-purpose flour, 1 tbsp fresh lemon juice, 1/4 tsp ground cardamom, 1/4 tsp ground cinnamon, 1/8 tsp ground allspice, 2 tbsps unsalted butter cut into small pieces, 1 large egg.
Make the crust: Pulse the flour, sugar and salt in a food processor. Add the butter and pulse until the mixture looks like a coarse meal with pea-size bits of butter. Add 1/2 cup ice water and pulse until the dough just starts to come together. Divide the dough between two pieces of plastic wrap and form each into a disk; wrap tightly and refrigerate until firm, at least one hour.
Make the filling: Toss the peaches in a bowl with 3/4 cup sugar, the flour, lemon juice and spices. Lightly dust a large piece of parchment paper with flour. Roll out one piece of the dough into a 12-inch round on the parchment. Ease the dough into a nine-inch pie plate. Add the filling, mounding it slightly in the center; dot with the butter and refrigerate. Roll out the second piece of dough into a 12-inch round and cut it into 1/2-inch-wide strips. Lay half of the strips on the pie in one direction, leaving about one inch of space between each strip. Lay the remaining strips on top, crossing them diagonally to make a lattice pattern (no need to weave); trim the edges of the strips, leaving a small overhang. Fold the overhanging dough under itself and crimp the edge of the crust with your fingers. Beat the egg with 1 tbsp water and brush on the crust edge and lattice top. Sprinkle with the remaining 1 tbsp sugar and refrigerate until firm, about 30 minutes. Position a rack in the lower third of the oven. Put a baking sheet on the rack and preheat to 425 degrees. Put the pie on the hot baking sheet and bake for 20 minutes. Reduce the oven temperature to 375 degrees and continue baking until the pie is golden and the filling is bubbly, 50 minutes to 1 hour. Cover loosely with foil if the top is browning too quickly. Transfer to a rack to cool completely before slicing.
SOUTHERN PEACH COBBLER
8 fresh peaches (peeled, pitted and sliced into thin wedges), 1/2 cup white sugar plus 3 tbsps, 1/2 cup brown sugar, 1 ¼ tsp ground cinnamon, ⅛ tsp ground nutmeg, 1 tsp fresh lemon juice, 2 tsps cornstarch, 1 cup all-purpose flour, ¼ cup white sugar, ¼ cup brown sugar, 1 tsp baking powder, ½ tsp salt, 6 tbsps unsalted butter (chilled and cut into small pieces), ¼ cup boiling water.
Mix together 3 tbsps white sugar and 1 tsp ground cinnamon. Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. In a large bowl, combine peaches, 1/4 cup white sugar, 1/4 cup brown sugar, 1/4 tsp cinnamon, nutmeg, lemon juice and cornstarch. Toss to coat evenly and pour into a two-quart baking dish. Bake in a preheated oven for 10 minutes. Meanwhile, in a large bowl, combine flour, 1/4 cup white sugar, 1/4 cup brown sugar, baking powder, and salt. Blend in butter with your fingertips, or a pastry blender, until mixture resembles coarse meal. Stir in water until just combined. Remove peaches from the oven and drop spoonfuls of topping over them. Sprinkle the entire cobbler with the sugar and cinnamon mixture. Bake until the topping is golden, about 30 minutes.
PEACH PANCAKES
1 cup white flour, 1 ½ tsp baking powder, ¾ tsp ground cinnamon,¼ tsp salt, 1 tsp butter (melted), 2 tsps vanilla extract, ½ cup plain nonfat Greek yogurt, ¾ cup milk, ½ cup finely diced peaches.
Whisk together the flour, baking powder, cinnamon and salt in a medium bowl. In a separate bowl, stir together the butter and vanilla. Mix in the Greek yogurt, stirring until no large lumps remain. If the butter is still lumpy, briefly microwave the mixture for 10-15 seconds. Alternate between adding the flour mixture and the milk, beginning, and ending with the flour, stirring just until incorporated. Gently fold in the peaches. Lightly coat a large nonstick pan or griddle with nonstick cooking spray and preheat over low heat. Using 2 tbsps of batter for each pancake, dollop the batter onto the hot pan, and spread into a circular shape if desired. Let the pancakes cook for 2-3 minutes, or until a slight skin starts to form around the edges and the bottom is light golden brown. Slide a spatula underneath, and flip. Continue to cook for another 1-2 minutes or until light golden brown on both sides. Remember to re-coat the pan with nonstick cooking spray before cooking the next round of pancake batter. Top the pancakes with pure maple syrup, if desired.
PEACH JAM
3 1/2 pounds peaches (peeled, pitted, and cut into chunks), 2 1/2 cups sugar (you can start with less sugar and add more if needed, but don't add too little or your jam won't gel), juice from one lemon.
Add peaches and lemon juice to a medium saucepan. Bring to boil over medium-high heat, using a spatula or masher to crush peaches to desired consistency. Reduce heat to medium. Add sugar. Bring peaches back to a boil, stirring frequently. Continue to boil and stir, until peaches reduce and reach desired consistency, anywhere from 15 to 25 minutes. Jam should stick to spoon when lifted and turned sideways. Let the peach preserves cool. Sterilize the jars and lids. Add the Peach jam to the jar, leaving 1/4 inch headspace. Use a skinny spatula to help remove air pockets. Wipe down jar rims and add the lids. Seal to fingertip tightness. Process for 5 minutes in the boiling water. Turn off the heat and let the jars sit in the water for another 5 minutes. Remove jars and let cool for 12 to 24 hours.
PEACH SODA SELTZER
1 cup sugar, 2 tbsps minced fresh ginger, 2 very ripe peaches ( halved, pitted and thinly sliced), 2 liters seltzer (chilled), 16 fresh mint leaves for garnish.
In a medium saucepan over medium-low heat, bring 1 cup water, sugar and ginger to a gentle simmer, stirring to dissolve sugar. Remove simple syrup from heat, cover and steep for about 30 minutes. Over a medium bowl, pour syrup through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing minced ginger against the sieve with the back of a spoon to extract flavor. Discard ginger. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and refrigerate until well chilled. Evenly distribute peach slices among 8 tall glasses. For each glass, lightly press peaches with the back of a wooden spoon to release their juice. Pour about 2 tbsps of chilled syrup over peaches. (Store remaining syrup in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks.) Add ice cubes; then top with seltzer. Stir to distribute syrup, peach juice, and seltzer evenly. Garnish with 2 mint leaves.

title: Country Cooking: Canning day on the farm
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Canning day on the farm

 August 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1454
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The fresh vegetables were picked, washed and ready to be processed for "canning day" on the farm.Canning day was decided by the ripeness of the vegetables. Let me tell you right now, canning involves a lot of work.
Outside in the storage building, there were baskets full of empty jars. The jars were made by Mason or Ball, and those jars, if handled correctly, could be used year after year.
Two washing tubs were set up outside, one with hot soapy water and the other with clear water for rinsing. The bushel baskets holding the canning jars from the previous year's canning day were carefully carried to the house and placed on the long counter tops in the old-fashioned country kitchen. On top of the kitchen stove would be two heavy duty kitchen pots filled with vegetables, and as soon as they were blanched, the veggies were placed in the canning jars, leaving about 1 inch space from the top. The jar lids were put on lightly and the jars placed in the canning pots — usually the big blue agate pots with inserts inside to hold the jars in place.
The canning pots started rolling on the fire, thus cooking the vegetables. Mom just seemed to know when it was time to turn off the heat, remove pots from the stove and wait for the heat to cool enough to remove the jars, tighten the lids and begin again. This scene lasted all day, or until the veggies were all used.
Let's do it the modern way.
CANNED PEACHES
4 lbs peaches, 1 1/2 cups granulated sugar, 8 cups water.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Fill a large bowl with ice water. Using a paring knife, cut a shallow "x" into the bottom of each peach. Add peaches to boiling water and let boil for 3 minutes. Remove peaches and place directly in a bowl of ice water. When peaches are cool enough to handle, peel peaches. Slice peaches and discard the pit. Divide peaches between four sterilized canning jars, being sure to leave about 1 inch of space from the top of the jar. Make simple syrup: In a medium pot over medium heat, add sugar and water and bring to a simmer. Stir until sugar is dissolved. Pour simple syrup over peaches, leaving about 1/4 inch of space from the top of the jar. Gently tap jars on the counter to settle peaches and syrup. Add more syrup as necessary to each jar. Tightly seal jars with lids. To seal, fill a large stock pot about halfway with water and bring to a boil over medium heat. Once water is close to a simmer, use tongs to carefully lower jars into hot water. Let water come to a gentle boil and boil for 25 minutes. Carefully remove jars from the stock pot and let sit at room temperature until completely cool. Press down on the lid of the jars to test if they are properly sealed. If the lid bounces back or pops the jar is not sealed. Repeat the sealing process or refrigerate and eat within a week. Once jars are properly sealed and cooled, store in a dry, dark space until ready to eat.
PICKLED BEETS
4-5 lbs small beets, 2 tsps pickling salt, 1 1/2 cups white sugar, 3 cups white vinegar, 2 tbsps mixed pickling spice tied in cheesecloth bag, 1 cup water.
Wash the beets and remove most of the tops, leaving about 1/2 inch of beet top remaining. In a large boiling pot of water, cook the beets until barely tender. Remove from the stove. Submerge the beets in a large bowl of ice water, I find this helps the skins come off with more ease. Cut off the tops and the roots completely, then remove the skin. Peel and slice beets into preferred size, I like larger chunks and not slices. Combine the vinegar, sugar, water, salt and pickling spice in a nonreactive pot and bring mixture to a boil; reduce the heat and simmer for 10 minutes. Add the beets to the pickling liquid and return to a boil. Remove the spice bag. Carefully ladle the beets and pickling liquid into hot sterilized pint jars, leaving 1/2 inch headspace. Remove any air bubbles with a non-metal utensil. Add additional pickling liquid, if needed, to keep the proper headspace. Wipe the jar rims thoroughly with a clean damp cloth. Seal the jars and process for 35 minutes in a boiling water bath.
PICKLE RELISH
2 1/2 lbs cucumbers (peeled, seeded and finely diced), 1 large yellow onion (finely diced), 1 small red bell pepper (finely diced), 1 small green bell pepper (finely diced), 3 cloves garlic (finely minced), ¼ cup kosher or pickling salt, 3 cups white vinegar, 1/2 cup sugar, 2 tsps dill seeds, 1 tbsp yellow mustard seeds, 2 tsps celery seeds, 1/2 tsp turmeric, 2 bay leaves.
Place the diced cucumbers, onion, bell pepper and garlic in a large mixing bowl. Combine with the salt and pour water over the mixture until covered. Let sit for at least six hours or overnight. Drain the cucumber mixture in a colander, rinse thoroughly with water, and drain again. In a large stock pot, add the sugar, vinegar, and spices and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer for five minutes. Add the drained cucumber mixture and return to a boil. Reduce the heat to medium-low and simmer, uncovered, for 10 minutes. Discard the bay leaves. Ladle the hot relish into hot sterile jars, leaving ¼ inch of headspace. Wipe the rims of the jars clean and seal tightly with the lids. Process the jars in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes. Sealed jars will store in a cool, dark place for a year. If the seal is broken, the relish will keep in the fridge for at least a month. Makes four pints (you can use pint-sized or half pint jars). Best eaten at least a week later after the flavors have had time to meld and the vinegar mellows out a bit.
STRAWBERRY JAM
5 cups crushed fresh strawberries, 4 16-oz containers, 7 cups granulated sugar, 1 packet original Sure-Jell Premium Fruit Pectin powder, 2 tbsp lemon juice, 1/2 tsp butter.
Wash jars, lids and bands in hot soapy water, dry completely and set bands aside. Simmer lids in warm water in a saucepan until ready to place them on jars. Keep jars warm by simmering in hot water until ready to use. Do not boil. Fill a 20 quart stock pot or water bath canner with hot water, and place on the stove over medium-high heat. You'll need enough water to later cover your jars with at least 1 inch of water, crush strawberries in a large mixing bowl or shallow glass baking dish using hand masher until nice, smooth consistency. Small chunks are okay. Transfer crushed strawberries to 8-quart stock pot. Add pectin, lemon juice and butter to the pot, and stir constantly with a wooden spoon over high heat, while bringing to a rolling boil. Once boiling, add sugar, return to rolling boil, then boil for 1 minute while stirring constantly. After 1 minute, remove foam from top of jam by skimming it off with a metal spoon. One by one, remove a jar from hot water, transfer to a cookie sheet, place regular mouth canning funnel on jar, and ladle in strawberry jam mixture leaving 1/4 inch empty head space at top of the jar. Then wipe off the rim of the lid and threads of the jar with damp cloth. Continue until all jars have been filled. Remove warm lids from the saucepan and place one lid on each jar. Then screw one band on each jar just until snug but not overly tight. Place filled jars on a rack in a 20 quart stock pot or water bath canner, then lower down into hot water. Make sure there is enough water in the pot that there is at least 1 inch of water above the jars. Place the lid on your pot, and bring to a gentle boil. Once water is boiling, set your timer for processing and boil for 10 minutes, once jars have finished boiling, turn off heat, remove the lid from the pot and let jars sit for 5 minutes before removing. After 5 minutes, lift up the rack to an elevated resting position, then carefully remove jars one by one using a jar lifter, and transfer to a folded towel to cool. The lids on the jars will begin to 'pop' into the sealed position, signifying the jam has been preserved. Jars can be stored in your pantry, or a cool, dry cupboard for up to 1 year.

author: Post staff report
content:
‘By the Book’ exhibit in Delaware showcases art inspired by novels

 August 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Post staff report | Section: News 
 
 302
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A new exhibit at the Newark Arts Alliance showcases artwork based on novels."By the Book: Art Inspired by Novels" runs through Sept. 19. A free reception is set for 6 to 8 p.m. Sept. 12. Light refreshments will be served.
The exhibit features 40 pieces of original 2D and 3D art by 26 local artists. Displayed alongside the artwork is description of what within the novel inspired the artwork and how the artist created the piece, making this gallery a unique visual and literary experience.
The juror for this exhibit was Bill Buck, a longtime member of the Newark Arts Alliance. A scenic and lighting designer, scene painter and props artisan, Buck has designed more than 250 theater, dance and opera productions.
He's taught at James Madison University, the University of South Carolina and Mount Holyoke College and is a graduate of Rowan University and the Yale School of Drama. His artwork has shown recently at the Delaware Foundation for the Visual Arts, the Newark Arts Alliance, The Delaware Contemporary, Oxford Arts Alliance, The Community Arts Center in Wallingford, and the Havre de Grace Maritime Museum.
Buck has divided his career between theatrical design and the art studio where he works with a variety of mixed media. His design background is often informed by a textural, sculptural and three-dimensional approach.
"I've never known if I wanted to be a painter or a sculptor," Buck said. "In museums, I am tempted to cross the security barrier to touch the canvas. Not a good idea! But I encourage the viewer to step forward and touch my work, within reason."
The Newark Arts Alliance gallery is located in the Shoppes at Louviers on Paper Mill Road and is open to the public from noon to 4 p.m. on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays and noon to 8 p.m. on Fridays.

title: Lost sign finds its way back to Dorchester's Old Trinity Church
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Lost sign finds its way back to Dorchester's Old Trinity Church

 August 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 503
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH CREEK — Members of the small congregation of Old Trinity Church, Maryland's oldest active church, were surprised to see one of Old Trinity's former signs being sold at auction this month.After the sign sold to the highest bidder, the congregation thought it was gone for good.
But the following Sunday, The Rev. Dan Dunlap walked into the vesting room of John's Chapel, the other church he serves, where he was greeted by the sign. A close friend of Dunlap's heard about the auction, tracked the sign down, and bought it for Dunlap.
"I said, 'I'm just overwhelmed, I'm humbled.' I mean, it was such a gift," Dunlap said.
Gage Thomas, a collector of Dorchester County artifacts who sold the sign to Dunlap's friend at the Aug. 23 Foxwell Auction, said he was happy the sign had been returned to Old Trinity. "It's a historical location in Dorchester County. I'm happy that the sign has made its way back to there," Thomas said.
Old Trinity Church predates its relationship with the Anglican Church and the creation of the Episcopal Diocese. It was built through private funds roughly a decade before the establishment of the Episcopal Church, Dunlap said.
The church has undergone multiple iterations and bore several names, initially being called The Church of Dorchester Parish. In 1853, it was renamed Trinity. Community members referred to it as "the old church," and over time, the name "Old Trinity" stuck.
The small, red-brick church building was built around 1670 and was restored to its original colonial style in the 1950s. The restoration was made possible by legacy funds bequeathed to the church, which are now held in accounts to accrue interest.
"I've served at a number of churches, but I've never really been part of a church quite like this that felt that its roots were in this community," Dunlap said.
The sign was not the church's original sign. It came along sometime in the centuries after, though Dunlap did not know exactly when.
Dunlap said it was a strange feeling when he saw how much the sign was sold for. He figured the old piece of painted wood that was likely thrown in the trash would sell for maybe $100.
Thomas said he bought the sign about 15 years ago for $200. This time around, the sign was sold for $400.
"My first thought was, 'I didn't realize we were that important,'" Dunlap said.
After that initial thought passed, a weird feeling sank in. "But not all bad. I mean, I wasn't troubled by it, I was just confused by it," Dunlap said. "And then just to see it the next Sunday, waiting for me at the vesting area of the other church, I was just I, I shed a tear. I just couldn't believe it."
For Dunlap, the sign being sold at auction has highlighted the church's importance to the community.
"The church is here for people to come and to enjoy it, to add their story to our story. That's why you can't say who owns Old Trinity," Dunlap said. "It's the community's church."

title: Country Cooking: Memories and recipes from grandparents
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Memories and recipes from grandparents

 September 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1276
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Grandparents Day is Sept. 7 this year. In 1978, the late Jimmy Carter, who was the president, designated the first Sunday after Labor Day each year to honor grandparents.What a wonderful day to honor those important people in our lives. My grandparents died many years ago, but the memories live on. Generations have changed; grandparents are younger (it seems), lifestyles are somewhat different, but we still have Mom-Mom and Pop-Pop.
My mother and I would sit and talk about days I spent with my paternal grandparents. They too had a large farm, and my older siblings and I would help with farm work.
I recall thinking that the grandparents' farm duties were out-of-date compared to the "modern" equipment my dad used. Then my older brother's fourth generation farm down on the river was ultra-modern.
My grandparents were an important part of my life. My maternal grandmother died at age 18 when my mom was 2 years old, so I never had the pleasure of knowing this person who gave me the best mother ever. My paternal grandparents were dear to me as they were all I had.
I have lots of stories to share with you all in the coming months. Stories of mischief and fun growing up with large families on large farms.
Food seemed to be a very popular activity for grandparents when the grandchildren came. I have many great memories of special dishes such as fresh made biscuits, pies, dumplings, soups, stews, beans and fried chicken.
Cooking is a tradition that still happens today with my own grandsons.
A few times a month, one of my grandchildren has spent the day with me. A few years ago, when we ran out of things to do, we started baking. This has been so much fun.
Not only have we developed math skills, reading skills, and the ability to follow directions, but we have also developed an awesome relationship between generations.
Our first bread to be made was banana bread.
BANANA BREAD
1/2 cup shortening, 2 eggs, 1 cup sugar, 2 cups flour, 1 tbsp sour milk, 1 tsp baking soda, 2 ripe crushed bananas, 1/2 cup crushed nuts (optional).
Cream shortening with eggs and sugar. Add flour, sour milk, baking soda, crushed bananas and nuts. Mix well and bake in a preheated 350-degree oven for one hour. For best results, use a medium size baking pan.
PUMPKIN BREAD
2 2/3 cups sugar, 2/3 cup shortening, 4 beaten eggs, 2/3 cup water, 1 can pumpkin puree (1 lb), 3 1/3 cups flour, 1/2 tsp baking powder, 2 tsps baking soda, 1 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1/2 tsp ground cloves, 2/3 cup chopped walnuts, 2/3 cup chopped dates.
Cream together sugar and shortening. Stir in eggs, water and pumpkin. Sift together flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, cinnamon and cloves. Mix well with the wet ingredients. Add walnuts and dates. Pour into two greased 9-by-5-inch pans. Bake at 350 degrees for one hour and 15 minutes.
GRANDMA'S ROSEMARY DINNER ROLLS
1 package (1/4 ounce) active dry yeast, 1/4 cup warm water (110° to 115°), 3 cups bread flour, 2 tbsps sugar, 1 tbsp minced fresh rosemary, 3/4 tsp salt, 2/3 cup warm 2% milk (110° to 115°), 1 large egg (room temperature), 1/4 to 1/3 cup canola oil, 1 large egg yolk, 2 tbsps 2% milk.
In a small bowl, dissolve yeast in warm water. Place the flour, sugar, rosemary and salt in a food processor: pulse until blended. Add the warm milk, egg and yeast mixture; cover and pulse 10 times or until almost blended. While processing, gradually add oil just until dough pulls away from sides and begins to form a ball. Process 2 minutes longer to knead dough (dough will be very soft). Transfer dough to a greased bowl, turning once to grease the top. Cover and let rise in a warm place until doubled, about 1 hour. Punch down dough. Turn onto a lightly floured surface; divide and shape into 12 balls. Roll each into a 15-inch rope. Starting at one end, loosely wrap dough around itself to form a coil. Tuck end under; pinch to seal. Place 2 inches apart on greased baking sheets. Cover and let rise until doubled, about 30 minutes. For egg wash, in a small bowl, whisk egg yolk and milk; brush over rolls. Sprinkle it with remaining rosemary. Bake at 350 degrees until golden brown, 18-22 minutes. Remove from pans to wire racks; serve warm.
EASTERN SHORE SWEET POTATO BISCUITS
2 cups mashed sweet potatoes, 3/4 cup sugar, 2 1/4 cups flour, 1 1/4 tsp salt, 2 tsps baking powder, 5 tbsps shortening.
Mix sweet potatoes with sugar, flour, salt and baking powder. Add 5 tablespoons shortening last and mix dough. Roll dough and cut with biscuit cutter or roll into small balls 3/4 inch thick. Bake at 450 degrees for 20 to 25 minutes.
FRIED CHICKEN
1 frying chicken, salt, 1 1/2 cups flour, pepper, paprika, 1 1/2 cups shortening.
Wash chicken in cold water and cut into pieces. Soak in cold water for a few minutes with 1 tsp of salt. Drain chicken. Season flour with salt, pepper and paprika to taste. Heat shortening in a fry pan. Dredge the chicken in the flour mixture and place in the oil. Cook until golden brown on both sides, about 20 minutes on each side. Drain on paper towels. I usually mix my flour mixture in a brown paper bag and shake to coat. I also save the flour mixture to make a gravy in the grease when chicken is cooked.
GRANDMOTHER'S SOUTHERN COLLARD GREENS
2 tbsps lard or shortening (divided), 1 large onion (chopped), 6 garlic cloves (minced), 1 1/2 pounds smoked ham hocks, 6 cups water, wine, 2 tsps seasoned salt, 1 to 3 tsps crushed red pepper flakes, 1/4 tsp sugar, 1 large bunch collard greens (coarsely chopped).
In a six-quart stockpot, heat 1 tbsp lard over medium heat. Add onion and garlic; cook and stir until tender. Add ham hocks, water, seasoned salt, pepper flakes and sugar. Bring to a boil. Reduce heat; simmer, uncovered, until meat is tender, 55 to 60 minutes. Add collard greens, wine, and remaining 1 tbsp lard. Return to a boil. Reduce heat; simmer, uncovered, until greens are very tender, 55 to 60 minutes. Remove meat from bones; finely chop and return to pan. Discard bones. Serve with a slotted spoon.
GRANDMOTHERS CORN PUDDING
4 large eggs, 1 cup whole milk, 1 can (15 ounces) cream-style corn, 1/2 cup sugar, 5 slices day-old bread (crusts removed), 1 tbsp softened butter. In a bowl, beat eggs and milk. Add corn and sugar; mix well. Cut bread into half-inch cubes and place in a greased 9-inch square baking dish. Pour egg mixture over bread. Dot with butter. Bake, uncovered, at 350 degrees until a knife inserted in the center comes out clean, 50 to 60 minutes.
GRANDMOTHER'S TANDY CAKE
4 large eggs (room temperature), 2 cups sugar, 1 cup 2% milk, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp salt, 1 3/4 cups creamy peanut butter, 5 milk or dark chocolate candy bars (1.55 ounces each) chopped, 2 tbsps butter.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a large bowl, beat eggs and sugar until thick and lemon colored. Beat in milk and vanilla. In another bowl, combine flour, baking powder and salt; gradually add to egg mixture and mix well. Spread into a greased 15-by-10-inch baking pan. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes or until lightly browned. Cool for 15 minutes on a wire rack. Spread peanut butter over top; cool completely. In a double boiler or metal bowl over simmering water, melt chocolate and butter; stir until smooth. Gently spread over peanut butter. Refrigerate for 30 minutes or until firm.

title: Art exhibit in Easton uses small items to explore larger themes such as war, homelessness
author: Konner Metz
content:
Art exhibit in Easton uses small items to explore larger themes such as war, homelessness

 September 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 416
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A new art exhibit in Easton uses small-scale items like twigs to tell large-scale stories involving war, poverty and conflict.Inside the Academy Art Museum, "To the Edge of Your World" by Dutch-Irish artist Anita Groener welcomes viewers into a peaceful setting of grid-like drawings and bird-chirping sounds.
Two main displays — Cradle and Shrapnel — are sculpture works by Groener. They include materials like twigs gathered from walks with her dog that she started collecting more than 10 years ago.
Groener hopes the sculptures help people understand some of "their own baggage" and history.
"Everything's very small, which creates a psychological distance," said Groener, who lives in Dublin, while inside the Easton exhibit space last month. "And that's important because we witness all these world events."
For her, the exhibit is largely motivated by time she spent in the southern United States visiting civil rights monuments, as well as Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Its meaning continues to evolve today, Groener said.
"Like we in Ireland watch what's going on in America," she said. "But it's such a distance, and I'm not taking part in that. Yet it affects us all. Everything that happens in the world, in our lives, affects us and is connected."
The Ireland-based artist doesn't want people to walk in thinking the art will yield certain takeaways. Rather, Groener hopes her art is open to interpretation.
"I like ambiguous readings, because as an artist, you can't be prescriptive," she said.
Groener's exhibit is the Academy Art Museum's first ever international exhibit. Charlotte Potter Kasic, the museum's executive director, said it took "many hoops to jump through" to make happen, but she's happy it panned out.
The opening weekend for the exhibit and a sister documentary film last month drew more than 250 people, Kasic said. They watched "Shelter," a 30-minute short film addressing homelessness on the Mid-Shore. Groener, the Talbot Interfaith Shelter and filmmaker Matt Kresling collaborated on the project.
At the front of Groener's exhibit is the main shelter structure, which is shown at the end of the film. She took around 10,000 pictures of the structure to make the stop-motion scene possible.
Groener said the scene is a "coming together of people" and all about community. Kasic said the audience on opening weekend was captivated by the film.
"No one moved," Kasic said. "They were all very engaged."
The film is slated to show at the Chesapeake Film Festival on Oct. 10 at the Ebenezer Theater in Easton. Groener's exhibit is open at the Academy Art Museum through Oct. 27.

title: Talbot County celebrates its most famous native son
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Talbot County celebrates its most famous native son

 September 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 857
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Over the years, Edinburgh University's Professor Celeste-Marie Bernier has taught me a great deal about Frederick Douglass, though her most important contribution to the study of the man may be, curiously, the research she has done not on Douglass but on Douglass' wife and children.Bernier's work has revealed just how important his family's support was to the Great Orator's success.
All of which has gotten me thinking about the other people that must have made the road Douglass trod a tad easier. Probably the most important of these would also be the least known: the people that helped him escape slavery.
We know that his wife Anna put the money together and sewed the clothing that would make her husband's flight possible, but we also know there would have been others, perhaps many others, involved as well: conductors on the Underground Railroad, people who took him in for the night along the way, and who knows, perhaps a boat owner or two, or even someone with a wagonload of hay.
We know that these people — however nameless now — existed because they are in Douglass' autobiography, though he alluded to them obscurely. Douglass always carefully avoided providing their names or any particulars that might aid those intent upon derailing their clandestine work. "The peculiar institution" was thriving when Douglass first penned his autobiography, and the last thing he wanted to do was reveal routes, methods and personnel still being used to funnel enslaved African Americans to freedom.
But there would have been others too, perhaps not as dramatic in their assistance, but important to Douglass's eventual success nonetheless.
Some of these are well known: Polly and Nathan Johnson, who sheltered Douglass and Anna in their home when the couple first arrived in New Bedford; William Lloyd Garrison, who brought Douglass to the attention of the abolitionist movement; and Abraham Lincoln, who befriended Douglass and wrote the pass that would allow him to travel unimpeded during the Civil War.
But what about the other people who must have made contributions, perhaps only small contributions, to Douglass's journey from property to prophet? We all depend upon people like this, the childhood friend who stuck up for us when we were bullied, the person who helped us with some difficult task, the passing stranger who gave us a smile when we were feeling down. Life is often obstructed, but then something gives, and, for a moment, there is an intoxicating sense of forward motion. How many now anonymous souls helped remove an obstacle from Douglass' path? Helped send him sailing toward us?
Perhaps more important still, how many would-be, could-be, Douglasses do we unknowingly lend a hand to today?
On Saturday, Sept. 27, the people of Talbot County will come together once again to honor the legacy of Frederick Douglass, their most famous native son. The parade this year will feature, among others, the Easton High School Junior ROTC Color Guard, the Easton Middle School and White Marsh Elementary School marching bands, Randy Welch on bagpipes, the Hispanic Dance Group, and, for the first time, engines from both the Easton and Oxford Volunteer Fire Companies.
At the Welcome Ceremony on the courthouse lawn, 15-year-old Javion Jones, a minister at Union Baptist Church, will give the opening invocation, county and city officials will offer their thoughts, Washington College fellow Darius Johnson will read a portion of a famous Douglass speech, the MidShore Community Band will play two pieces and Dana Bowser will sing a capella.
Afterward, at the Children's Village set up in front of the library, there will be story time with St. Michaels library branch manager Shauna Beulah, face-painting, the ever-popular portrait booth with Frederick Douglass, Frederick Douglass coloring books with sticker insert, a prize wheel with toy giveaways, and the opportunity for youngsters to sign up for the Frederick Douglass Reading Challenge (featuring six $50 Target gift certificates as prizes).
Within the library itself, the National Park Service will have an exhibit of Frederick Douglass artifacts on display, and, at 1 p.m., Nicholas Buccola — the Dr. Jules L. Whitehill Professor of Humanism and Ethics at Claremont-McKenna College — will lecture on his book, "The Essential Frederick Douglass," copies of which will be available for purchase and signing.
From noon to 3 p.m., the festival's entertainment stage will feature performances by the Bay Country Chorus, Sofia Fernandez, the New St. Johns Male Chorus, the St. Michaels Middle School Choir, Friends in Faith, Ruby Fisher, the Allegro Academy, Ayla Dennis and the Asbury United Methodist Church choir, as well as line dancing and block party music provided by Allan Butler.
Oh, and of course, once again, there will be food vendors on hand with delicious food to satisfy the most demanding hunger.
All in all, it's shaping up to be a fun day for people of all ages and interests. Moreover, it's a day where your attendance, your enthusiasm, could end up encouraging some youngster (think the BAAM kids who will be in attendance, or the recipient of one of the Frederick Douglass Honor Society's scholarships) to set his or her eyes on the prize.
Like so many before you, you could be clearing the path for America's next great freedom fighter.

title: Black watermen’s monument proposed for Wells Cove
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Black watermen’s monument proposed for Wells Cove

 September 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 653
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The Queen Anne's County Commissioners approved Wells Cove as the site for a proposed Black watermen's monument Aug. 26, further representing the history and legacy of the county's iconic industry.Tilghman Hemsley, a Queenstown artist and director of American Patriotic Monuments Inc., who created the original Kent Narrows watermen's monument 20 years ago, said he had been approached about the lack of Black representation in that project.
Seeking commissioner approval to establish the new monument on county property at Wells Cove, Hemsley presented mock-ups of the detailed sculptures.
Symbolizing the rich heritage of Black watermen, the monument will depict life-size bronze sculptures featuring a conversation between a head boat captain and an oyster boat worker, according to Hemsley. The piece will also feature other important aspects of the industry, including a man working with clams, a woman picking crabs, another cleaning fish, as well as a young boy with a fishing pole along for the experience.
"It's a sculpture that leans into the whole industry," Hemsley said.
"The piece is designed for the public to be able to come through and be part of the sculpture," he said.
With the history of the Black watermen engraved into the side of the pieces, "it's all about education," he said.
The monument is slated for a location between Bridges Restaurant and the Jetty restaurant. Hemsley emphasized the interactive nature of the work, allowing visitors the opportunity to pass between the pieces and engage with the sculptures as they visit the local area.
The watermen will be life-size bronze sculptures while the boat pieces will be stainless steel and powder-coated, he said.
Hemsley said the design of the pieces should make the monument low maintenance.
The project has already received approval from the Queen Anne's County Parks and Recreation Department and a letter of recommendation from the Kent Narrows Foundation, he said.
The commissioners unanimously approved Wells Cove as the site for the proposed monument. Commissioner Jim Moran noted he would have preferred a competition among artists to design a tribute to Black watermen but supported the plan.
Hemsley noted time is of the essence if the statue is to be ready by July 4, 2026, in celebration of the country's 250th anniversary.
Serving as director of the project, Hemsley said various other artists will be involved in the sculpture work. The proposed monument has an advisory committee that includes watermen, he said.
With commissioner approval, the next steps include seeking funding grants, according to Hemsley.
Although highly appreciated, just like the original watermen's monument, the project would not be solely dependent on county support, he said.
The total cost for the project is estimated at about $475,000. The previous watermen's monument cost about $300,000, he said.
Statues typically take about three years to complete, but Hemsley was confident as long as funding came through.
"It's aggressive, but we can do it," he said.
A fundraising event with auctions, games and music will be held at the Kent Island American Legion Nov. 8 starting at 7 p.m., he said.
Hemsley is also working with the Centreville Veterans Information Committee to create a life-size statue honoring the more than 400 Black soldiers of Queen Anne's County who fought for the Union during the Civil War.
Working with Chesapeake Charities, the veteran statue committee has been hard at work establishing itself as a nonprofit, according to John Wright, statue committee chair.
Wright credited the enthusiasm of the committee in working to establish a historic monument.
"I'm glad I am in a position to help," he said.
With the sculpture to be completed in stages, the committee foresees about a year and a half before a statue stands in front of the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center.
Donations can be sent to United States Colored Troops Memorial Fund, P.O. Box 42, Centreville, MD 21617.
As a Maryland nonprofit, American Patriotic Monuments Inc. seeks to lead public arts projects and monuments that celebrate American legacies.
More information, including sponsorship opportunities, can be found at apmiart.org.
Information about Hemsley's work can be found at tilghmanhemsleyfinearts.com.

title: Family Bible finds its way home to Dorchester County family
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Family Bible finds its way home to Dorchester County family

 September 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NECK DISTRICT — Bernie Dryden perused an auction in late August, viewing every item. An old tattered Bible that sat on the very last table caught his eye. Dryden purchased it for $12.50 as the very last item sold at the auction.He figured he would give the Bible to his grandson, who is currently studying theology, but upon thumbing through the pages, he found extensive records from a singular family dating back to the Civil War Era. While analyzing the text, he realized one of the final names listed in the birth records was his friend, Alan Wright.
"This is a family Bible, and I recognized the surname as being prominent down in the Neck District, where I live. So I kept looking, and there was an entry there documenting a birth, and I knew the guy," Dryden said.
Dryden's grandson didn't accept the gift, saying it was more Christian to return it to the original family.
Wright was unaware the family Bible even existed before its return.
"When I got to look at it after Bernie gave it to me, my sister's name was in there, my brother's name was in there, and my father's," Wright said. This is the fourth family Bible in the Wright lineage.
Wright said his sister Ellen Paul is the family's historian, having compiled a detailed family tree and collected all the obituaries she can find.
Paul has spent the past 10 years compiling family records and has found the Historical Society and the Maryland room at the library particularly helpful. She has been able to trace the lineage of her family back to the early 1800s.
For Paul, the Bible was the missing piece of multiple family documents, helping verify important family dates and lineage. It even contained a marriage certificate from six generations back, providing a marriage date previously unknown.
A majority of the surnames in the Bible are Marshall until Paul and Wright's great grandmother, Lydia Marshall, married a Wright. "It's a Marshall Bible. Most of it is Marshalls, but it does have him (their father) and us three kids in there," Paul said.
The return of the Bible comes at an interesting time when another religious relic in Dorchester County that was purchased at the same auction was also returned to its original home.
A decades-old decommissioned sign from Old Trinity Church in Church Creek was sold at the same auction for $400. Members of the congregation were upset that someone was profiting off the church's name and expressed these feelings online.
The following Sunday, the sign showed up in the vesting room of St. John's Chapel, where The Rev. Dan Dunlap, rector of Old Trinity, serves as Vicar. A friend of Dunlap's purchased the sign back and gave it to Dunlap as a personal gift. He said it brought a tear to his eye, and he was deeply touched and humbled.
This time, a religious family relic has found its way home in an extremely similar nature — same auction, same seller, and also returned by a friend.
Wright said it felt fantastic to get the Bible, which was auctioned by Gage Thomas, a relative of Wright and Paul's, and to have it returned by a friend.
The religious relics finding their way back home are seen as somewhat of a parable to the Old Trinity Church congregation and to Wright and Paul.
"I mean, it's come full circle, right back to us, you know?" Paul said.

title: Southern gothic author Wiley Cash named WC Patrick Henry History Fellow
author: Staff Writer
content:
Southern gothic author Wiley Cash named WC Patrick Henry History Fellow

 September 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 442
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Washington College's Starr Center for the Study of the American Experience announces the 2025-2026 Patrick Henry History Fellow — Wiley Cash, a best-selling author versed in southern history, mystery and family drama.Cash will be joining the Washington College community for the academic year and teaching an English class while also working on his sixth novel — in his words, "a retelling of the Lost Colony [of Roanoke Island, NC] that braids three storylines while interrogating the tendrils of white supremacy that sprouted from the American colonial experiment."
The Patrick Henry History Fellowship supports outstanding writing on American history and culture by scholars and authors; it offers a $45,000 stipend for the academic year and an opportunity to work with and teach Washington College students and faculty, as well as a book allowance and a nine-month residency in a historic 18th century house in Chestertown. Past fellowship topics have ranged as broadly as the early history of the slave trade, American religious minorities, and the LGBTQ rights movement. Past Patrick Henry fellows have included National Book Prize winner Edward Ball and Scribe Book Award recipient Wil Haygood.
Cash is an award-winning and New York Times bestselling author of four novels. He often uses a multi-character perspective in his works, deploying a range of character voices to tell a richer, more nuanced story.
His work has won numerous awards, including the Southern Book Prize three times, and the Crime Writers' Association's CWA New Blood Dagger and Gold Dagger. He has published extensively on a range of issues, from the environment to music, and is the host of the Our State Book Club podcast and the founder of "This is Working," an online creative community.
"Wiley's work perfectly embodies the Starr Center's approach to history," said Starr Center Director Adam Goodheart. "He's an elegant writer and accomplished storyteller who reaches broad audiences, while also engaging in complex ways with some of the problems and paradoxes at the root of American identity. We're delighted to have him here with us and excited that our students will have the opportunity to learn from this nationally eminent fiction writer."
In the spring, Cash will teach "Signifying on the South" for the College's English department, exploring popular literary portrayals of the American South.
"I'm thrilled to serve as the 2025-2026 Patrick Henry Fellow," Cash said. "My family and I spent a week in Chestertown this summer, and we can't wait to return to such a historic, kind, welcoming community."
On Tuesday, Sept. 23, at 6 p.m. at the Rose O'Neill Literary House at Washington College, Cash will read from his novel, "The Last Ballad." The event is free and open to the public.

title: Nause-Waiwash Band's festival showcases Indigenous heritage in Dorchester County
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
Nause-Waiwash Band's festival showcases Indigenous heritage in Dorchester County

 September 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Dorchester 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA — The Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians' annual Native American Festival has had many locations in its 33-year history.It began on Elliott Island, then moved to Andrews, then Cambridge before settling at its current location on the baseball fields in Vienna 21 years ago.
"We've been all over the county," Chief Donna Abbott said. "But the entire county is our ancestral homelands, so it's worked out well for us."
That history was at the forefront of the event Saturday, Abbott said. As she surveyed the field shortly before the Grand Entry, she reflected on how the festival has helped support one of the Nause-Waiwash's most important goals — education.
The festival was designed to celebrate Nause-Waiwash history, culture and traditions and share these with the public.
"And definitely, after 33 years, it has become a tradition," Abbott said.
Since its beginnings, the festival has evolved, incorporating more Indigenous heritages.
At the event Saturday, Abbott highlighted performers from throughout the Americas, including Aztec fire dancers from near Mexico City and hula dancers from Hawaii.
"We also celebrate other nations," Abbott said. "We celebrate the South Americans, we celebrate the Mexicans, the Canadians, the Alaskans. We're all about all Native Americans."
The festival features vendors, demonstrations, food and dancing that aim to educate attendees.
In a shady spot near the back of the baseball field, Leigh Hunteman and her pack of dogs provided information about dog sledding, which finds its origins in Indigenous communities from what is now Canada and Alaska, according to an encyclopedia of Indigenous culture and history produced by the University of Saskatchewan.
Hunteman, a longtime Eastern Shore resident, said she has been coming to the festival since it was located in Cambridge and has been bringing her dogs to Vienna for several years.
The event is a good opportunity for Hunteman to teach people about competitive dog sled racing, which isn't commonly practiced in Maryland, she said. And the dogs are always excited to meet new people, she added.
Abbott said that longtime vendors like Hunteman, along with newer sponsors and vendors, have helped shape the festival into an evolving event that showcases more aspects of Indigenous cultures with each year.
Growing the event is important, she said, because of a shared goal between the festival's participants.
"We're all striving for the same thing," Abbott said. "We're all striving for the same goal, and that is to keep our history alive. There's so much of it that's been lost, and not just ours, but all the Indigenous history."
Abbott said preparations are already underway for next year's festival, which will be held Sept. 19 in Vienna.

title: Denton redesignated as Arts and Entertainment District by state
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Denton redesignated as Arts and Entertainment District by state

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News

 DENTON — Denton has received a redesignation from the state as an Arts and Entertainment District.The redesignation is followed a 10-year process that must be completed to continue to be named as one of these districts. It allows the town to keep tax incentives that encourage economic development through arts and tourism.
For the tax incentives, Denton is still working on a program or credit that will be given to businesses within the district for promoting arts and entertainment within the town.
The art and entertainment distract program was created in 2001 by the MSAC to provide local governments interested in encouraging arts activity with tools to incentivize artists to live, create and sell work in their towns.
According to a press release from the Maryland State Art Council, in fiscal year 2024, visitor spending in Denton and the 28 other designated districts generated $136 million.
"Small business development in our rural towns and cities is vital to winning the decade," said Gov. Wes Moore in the press release. "The A&E Districts program has a proven track record, showing that state and local investments in the arts not only improve the quality of life for Marylanders, but also lay a foundation for entrepreneurship to thrive."
To earn redesignation, the town of Denton has to apply every decade, demonstrating progress toward economic development goals and continued commitment to attracting and retaining arts activity.
"Essentially, it's a wonderful opportunity to work with our local leaders and create tax incentives for businesses, expand economic opportunities, but also to add to our already established arts and entertainment district designation," said George Karos, executive director for Caroline County Council of Arts.
Karos and town administrator's aide Lisa Orendorf and town council members helped throughout the redesignation application process.
"It's one more amenity, and it's a diverse amenity which is nice for our town," Town Administrator Scott Getchell said. "Just like we have business districts at our shopping centers and so forth, that's an amenity for people to come to… So this is one more thing that makes our town special that we have this Arts and Entertainment District that is managed by the Caroline County Arts."
