title: Local artists celebrate 20 years of creativity together in Cambridge
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Local artists celebrate 20 years of creativity together in Cambridge

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 383
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Every Wednesday, a group of local artists from a diverse set of mediums and backgrounds comes together to share their latest creations. This segment of their meetings is called "brings and brags."Twenty years ago, the group began meeting at the Dorchester Center for the Arts when it was still in the historic home on High Street. They then relocated to a deli inside of a strip mall, which didn't survive the pandemic. The loyal members began meeting at a park until finding their spot at Peach Blossom Place.
"It's a beautiful building," the group's leader Susan Lester said. "We've had a wonderful experience being here."
The Wednesday Morning Artists are an eclectic group, who bring their unique skillsets together in mixed-media collaborative pieces, one of a kind oil paintings and an array of other media. On the fourth Wednesday of the month, there is a live art demonstration that often includes hands-on participation.
The group is led Lester with support from Robert Gladney and Nancy Hoffman. The members also showcase their work outside of "brings and brags" at the Hyatt Regency on Saturdays during the summer, at community events like Taste of Cambridge and at pop-up art events around town.
Lester said her favorite part about the Wednesday Morning Artists is learning and collaborating with the members. "The fact that we're so diverse, we have such a range of artists, I never even heard of some of the stuff they do," she said.
The wide range of art forms include weaving, pine needle coiling, jewelry designing, photography, sculpting, music, woodcarving and the more traditional forms of art like oil painting and pottery.
"We have pine needle weavers, who knew? I never heard of that," Lester said. "You know, when you think of art, you think of acrylics or oils or watercolors, and it's way beyond that."
The group has also created fellowship outside of Wednesday morning, enjoying monthly dinners and an annual fall picnic at Gerry Boyle Park.
Lester said they are always accepting new members. "And trust me, we don't judge based on level of experience," she said. "Pros, beginners, we want you all, and we'll help you learn how to do it or you can help us learn."
For more information on the artists, future events, and how to join, visit the Wednesday Morning Artists Facebook page.

title: Colonial remains reburied during ceremony at Historic St. Mary's City
author: Madison Bateman Special to Southern Maryland News
content:
Colonial remains reburied during ceremony at Historic St. Mary's City

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Madison Bateman Special to Southern Maryland News | Section: News 
 
 758
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In a powerful moment of remembrance and reconciliation, Historic St. Mary's City hosted a Ceremony of Return on Sept. 20, reuniting the remains of some of Maryland's earliest settlers, including colonial leader Philip Calvert, with the sacred ground where they were first laid to rest nearly four centuries ago.In 1990, archaeologists at Historic St. Mary's City were preparing to reconstruct the 1667 Brick Chapel on its original foundation. In the process, they uncovered three lead coffins buried beneath the chancel of the building. Lead coffin burials were rare in colonial America and typically reserved for individuals of high status.
The remains in the chapel coffins were identified as members of Maryland's founding Calvert family, including Philip Calvert (chancellor, fifth governor of Maryland and son of George Calvert, the first Lord Baltimore), Anne Wosley Calvert and the infant son of Philip.
Archaeologists also dug up the remains of 56 other individuals buried in and around the Brick Chapel. Not much is known about them beyond that they were laid to rest sometime between 1634 and 1730.
Over the past 30 years, a team of archaeologists, historians and scientists from the Smithsonian Institution studied the coffins and their contents to gain insight into early Maryland life, health, diet and funerary practices.
Over the weekend, Historic St. Mary's City hosted a reinterment ceremony, marking the final step in this long-term research effort and returning the individuals to their original resting place in the reconstructed Brick Chapel.
"The Ceremony of Return marks a moment of great significance to Historic St. Mary's City and to our shared understanding of Maryland's past," Travis Parno, the museum's acting executive director and director of research and collections, said. "For the past three decades, nearly 60 of Maryland's founders have shared their stories with us and now they have returned to rest. Their contributions to the establishment of Maryland and the United States cannot be overstated."
About 275 guests gathered to take part in the solemn and symbolic ceremony honoring Maryland's early settlers.
The event began with the thunder of cannon fire from the Maryland Dove, the museum's reconstructed 17th-century tall ship that recently returned from Washington, D.C. The ship, which represents one of the original vessels that brought settlers to Maryland in 1634, also carried back a Maryland flag used during the event.
Next, a formal procession led by a horse-drawn hearse moved from the reconstructed State House to the Brick Chapel.
Among the participants were descendants of the Calvert family, members of the Ark and Dove Society, the St. Maries Cittie Militia, and historical interpreters dressed in authentic 17th-century attire. They were joined by museum visitors and invited guests, all walking together in tribute to the lives, struggles and enduring legacies of Maryland's founding colonists.
At the Brick Chapel, guests heard remarks by historians, archaeologists and other key figures, including Douglas Owsley, curator of biological anthropology at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History. Following the speakers, a rite of reinterment honored the individuals being laid to rest.
In the Town Center area, costumed museum staff distributed bundles of rosemary, all grown on-site, as a symbolic gesture of remembrance. In the 17th century, rosemary was commonly used in funeral rituals, a tradition closely tied to Anne Wosley Calvert, one of the individuals recently reinterred.
When her lead coffin was excavated in the early 1990s, archaeologists found her remains carefully wrapped in a burial shroud with silk ribbons at her wrists and traces of rosemary scattered across her remains, according to the Maryland State Archive.
"These people have been completely forgotten but this investigation is changing that," Henry Miller, senior research fellow and an archaeologist who worked on the project, said during the ceremony. "They built the foundation on which we stand … they deserve to no longer be forgotten."
DeAnna Poling and her sister, Debora Hanson, recently discovered they were descendants of early Marylanders when they found a document in their grandmother's desk which implied a relation to Gov. Thomas Greene and his wife Anne Cox. The pair were on the initial voyage of the Ark and the Dove that sailed from England to Maryland in 1634.
"I am honored to be here and serve as a pallbearer at this event," Poling said. "I am especially excited we are not just descended from one person but two from the ship. They had the first Christian marriage in provincial Maryland."
"We are finally able to bring these individuals home," Kelsey Bush, descendant of Eleanor Butler, said. "It took over 30 years to get to this point. … Who would have thought we would be standing here today with the reconstructed chapel."

title: Maryland map hooks artists together
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
Maryland map hooks artists together

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There's an interesting piece of art on the wall of the Cecil County Arts Council in Elkton that pays homage to each county in Maryland; made by fiber artists from other states.Colleen Tiefenthal connected with artists in Washington, Florida, Connecticut and New Jersey and each turned out a piece that represents one of the 23 counties for the projected entitled "The Maryland Counties Rug Hooking Project."
"It was a really fun project," Tiefenthal said. "It was my concept and design. Then I reached out to my fellow rug hookers."
The North East woman — an Ohio transplant — hasn't met any rug hookers in Cecil County yet so she's the only local connection to the project. Tiefenthal knew all but two of the 16 rug hookers who had a hand in the map.
"I thought, 'how cool would it be ... that we could do one thing together,'" she said.
She got a grant from the Maryland State Arts Council to fund the project. That $4,000 covered the cost of materials and postage. Tiefenthal said the project taught her how to use a new computer program: Canva.
Work began with her cutting all the pieces of linen for the backing and much of the wool that was used to create each county.
"I sent them kits. They did their parts and sent it back," she said. "One person, it was their first attempt at rug hooking but she's a fabric artist." Most received more than one county to complete. They held several virtual meetings before the rug hooking began.
A board Tiefenthal painted to mimic the Maryland flag in grey tones is the base and each piece is wired onto the board. Accompanying the map is a legend with numbers corresponding to each county. Tiefenthal also created a booklet about the project and added a rug hooked segment of the Maryland flag. Each county is represented by something central to its heritage. For Cecil County, it's the Turkey Point Lighthouse.
Admitting she was nervous waiting for the pieces to return, Tiefenthal said the fear dissolved as she opened each package.
"When the first five to six pieces came back and were wonderful, it gave me confidence," she said. She knew the pieces were going to fit together.
Tiefenthal said it was her husband, Jim, who suggested a separate panel on the bottom of the display.
"It was Jim's idea for the "Touch This" panel," she said. This way the curious can feel the texture of the work but not touch the map itself.
The map visited Salisbury, Md. last weekend and has already made a stop at the North East Library. It's on display at the Arts Council, 135 East Main St. in Elkton until Oct. 7 then it moves to the Elkton branch library Oct. 7 through Oct. 28.
In 2027, it travels to a fiber art show in Newport, R.I. held by the International Guild of Handhooking Rugmakers and to Sauder Village for a similar show in Archibald, Ohio.

title: Local author delivers sing-along Christmas magic aboard 18-wheeler
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Local author delivers sing-along Christmas magic aboard 18-wheeler

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Grab your trucker hats and road maps — and save room for milk and cookies — as local author and musician J. Brandon Boron of Queenstown is bringing Christmas magic with Santa Claus behind the wheel of an 18-wheeler in a new sing-along illustrated children's book this holiday season.When Santa's reindeer come down sick one Christmas, Santa Claus must take the wheel of a magical flying 18-wheeler to deliver presents on time. Readers are invited to climb aboard and join Saint Nick and his pals as they make the most important delivery of the year — all while performing jaunty trucker tunes.
Fun for the whole family, Santa's 18-Wheel Chrome-and-Steel Sleigh is a sing-along storybook highlighting the holiday spirit and how any challenge can be overcome with resilience, humor and friends by your side.
A lifelong musician, Boron has always loved country music, particularly the fun and upbeat tunes of the truck driver genre. The story of Santa driving an 18-wheeler started as a truck song Boron created that practically wrote itself, he said.
With the song's quick rhymes, upbeat tunes and big imagery, Boron soon discovered it could engage children with fun illustrations. He set to work with others to develop a story for the whole family.
Bringing Santa's "wheely" important mission to life has been a fun experience, especially collaborating with illustrator Shaun Ivie to build on each other's ideas and bring colorful imagery to the pages, according to Boron.
Showcasing cheer and the feel of the holiday season, everyday characters are illustrated throughout the story lending a hand to assist Santa, including police officers safely holding traffic.
Boron said he grew up understanding the important role of truck drivers. His father hauled military missiles and his uncle also drove trucks.
Boron has always loved Christmas and is eager to share that love and inspire others.
Santa's 18-Wheel Chrome-and-Steel Sleigh includes a QR code so families can sing and dance along with Santa's "tireless," one-of-a-kind magic journey.
The end of the book features a discussion guide for readers as well as a template for them to pen their own letters to Santa.
Boron was born in Great Falls, Montana, but has spent most of his life traversing the United States and beyond.
After studying art, music and biology at Colorado State University, the University of Massachusetts and the University of Nevada Las Vegas, Boron currently serves as a musician with the U.S. Army, where he has spent the last two decades performing across Europe, the Middle East and the United States.
Living on the Eastern Shore since about 2018, Boron and his wife, Thordis, fell in love with the area. The two regularly perform as local musicians throughout the community.
A release party is scheduled for Oct. 21 at Uno Mas in Centreville, featuring live music by Brandon and Thordis.
Santa's 18-Wheel Chrome-and-Steel Sleigh goes on sale Oct. 21 from Mascot Kids.
For more information and to hear the original song, visit santas18wheelchromeandsteelsleigh.com
.

title: National Music Festival alumni to perform at benefit concert for Emmanuel Episcopal Church
author: Staff Writer
content:
National Music Festival alumni to perform at benefit concert for Emmanuel Episcopal Church

 September 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 437
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The National Music Festival, a community-driven event in Chestertown that supports young professional musicians through mentorship, lodging, meals and scholarships, will hold a special fundraising concert Sunday, Oct. 5, at 4 p.m.The concert, hosted by Emmanuel Episcopal Church, will celebrate the church's contributions to the Festival each June. Two acclaimed Festival alumni — cellist David Agia and pianist Leili Asanbekova — will return to perform at Emmanuel Episcopal Church, 101 N. Cross St. Tickets will be available at the door for $20, with proceeds supporting the free lunches the church provides to Festival musicians.
Emmanuel Church's role
Emmanuel Episcopal Church plays a pivotal role in the annual Festival, offering spaces for rehearsals and performances and providing weekday lunches to musicians, mentors and staff.
Festival Executive Director Caitlin Patton praised the support, saying: "It's the generosity of the Chestertown community — particularly our host families and Emmanuel Church — that makes our Festival possible and our community special. This fundraising concert will recognize, at least in a small way, all the essential volunteer effort and generous support that Emmanuel Church provides."
Featured musicians
Cellist David Agia has performed as a chamber musician, recitalist and orchestral player at venues including Carnegie Hall, Alte Oper Frankfurt, Palacio de Festivales, Symphony Space in New York and Historische Stadthalle Wuppertal. He has appeared in numerous festivals and master classes. Agia is an adjunct professor of cello at Rowan University.
Pianist Leili Asanbekova began studying music at age 6. She has performed at concerts, government events and festivals, and won several local and international competitions. She has collaborated with conductors including Marek Moś, Vladimir Spivakov and Yuri Simonov. She is pursuing her Doctor of Music degree at the University of Maryland.
Concert program
The concert will feature three works for cello and piano by Italian and Spanish composers.
Alfredo Casella and Mario Castelnuovo-Tedesco were members of Italy's "Generazione dell'80," tasked with creating a "new Italian sound." Both had complicated relationships with the fascist Italian government. Castelnuovo-Tedesco, who was Jewish, emigrated to the United States in 1939, finishing his career in Hollywood.
Early 20th-century Spanish composer and cellist Gaspar Cassadò's music reflects his Catalan roots. A student of Pablo Casals, he dedicated his cello and piano piece Requiebros to his teacher.
About the Festival
The National Music Festival brings together world-class mentors and young professional apprentices for two weeks each June. The 14th season will run May 31–June 13, 2026.
Apprentices receive full scholarships and housing, mostly with local host families. They rehearse and perform alongside mentors in orchestral, chamber and solo recitals, presenting more than 30 concerts and dozens of open rehearsals.
More information on the Festival, tickets and donations is available at https://nationalmusic.us

title: 'Friendship set to music': Club aims to keep square dancing alive on the Eastern Shore
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'Friendship set to music': Club aims to keep square dancing alive on the Eastern Shore

 October 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 469
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Dorchester Square Dance Club is a lively bunch who enjoy each other's company just as much as they enjoy dancing.Some members joined a few months ago. Others have been a part of the club for over 15 years.
According to longtime member Roger Parks, there used to be around 17 square dancing clubs on the Eastern Shore.
Now, there are only two.
To keep the Dorchester Square Dance Club alive, Parks went to caller school and called for free to sustain the club through pandemic-era challenges. The caller plays a critical role in square dancing, directing dancers through the steps.
The group's current caller, Dennis O'Neale, began calling in 2006.
"Calling is a matter of me telling people what to do. We split it up into two parts, what we call the patter part, which I move people around and get them used to whatever calls I tend to work with," O'Neale said.
The second part is a singing call, during which O'Neale gives the instructions taught during the patter part through song. He changes the words of the songs to fit the calls, which is melodic and smooth.
"Square dancing is one of the most unique things because you can go all around the world and its the same. There's square dancing in Japan, Germany, China, Russia, and every caller in those countries calls in English," O'Neale said.
According to the club's head Bill Mocarsky, this is because all of the training for calling is done in English.
O'Neale described square dancing as "friendship set to music," emphasizing community and family over competition. While watching the members dance, their smiles were noticeable and if someone missed a call or messed up, everyone giggled and kept it moving.
The club is not only fun, but O'Neale and Parks are grateful that it offers mental and physical engagement while still being affordable at $10 a night. The members sometimes mix it up by doing round dances, easy line dances and other family-friendly dances like the Virginia Reel and Bingo Waltz.
Square Dancing is generally correlated with country music, but the club dances to a diverse range of genres and artists. Bob Dylan, Joni Mitchell and Fleetwood Mac were among the artists O'Neale called to on Tuesday night. He said Patti LaBelle's "New Attitude" is his favorite song to call to.
"We're having a good time socializing. We don't smoke in our dance area, we don't drink in our dance area and we could be a church group or not, but the key is, we're making a family," O'Neale said. "Anywhere you go, if you're a square dancer, or you go to a square dance club, you instantly have a new family."
The Dorchester Square Dance Club is always accepting new members of all ages and backgrounds. They meet every Tuesday at Maple Elementary School in Cambridge at 5:30 p.m.

title: Museum of the Rockies to open immersive multimedia exhibit on the legacy of Jane Goodall
author: MSU News Service
content:
Museum of the Rockies to open immersive multimedia exhibit on the legacy of Jane Goodall

 October 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MSU News Service | Section: News 
 
 429
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Jane Goodall, founder of the Jane Goodall Institute and a United Nations Messenger of Peace, created an indelible legacy in the fields of science and conservation.That legacy is celebrated in "Becoming Jane: The Evolution of Dr. Jane Goodall," a new exhibit opening at Montana State University's Museum of the Rockies on Friday.
The museum will host a member-only opening at 5:30 p.m. It will feature a video that Goodall recorded exclusively for museum members. The evening will include family activities, a ribbon cutting and a discussion with primatologist Isabel Behncke.
Produced in partnership with the National Geographic Society and the Jane Goodall Institute, the exhibit explores Goodall's life, from her early years as a young woman with a dream to learn about animals in Africa and years establishing herself as a renowned scientist in Gombe, Tanzania, to her role as an activist, mentor and advocate for creating a better world. "Becoming Jane" will remain open through Jan. 18, 2026.
Goodall died Wednesday at age 91.
"We join the world in mourning the loss of a legend: a champion for conservation and the natural world," said Christopher Dobbs, the museum's executive director. "Her passing makes it all the more important to carry on her message. By hosting this traveling exhibit, we honor the remarkable legacy and memory of Dr. Jane Goodall, celebrating her life's work and the inspiration she continues to share with the world."
Highlights from the exhibit include:
A multiscreen experience where visitors are introduced to Goodall's work, alongside surprising encounters with virtually rendered chimpanzees.
A replica of Goodall's research tent where, in a hands-on experience, visitors can envision themselves as scientists.
A hologram-like projection of Goodall, who shares her memories in Gombe and recalls her thoughts, feelings, impressions and lessons learned while living among chimpanzees.
An immersive projection of Tanzania's Gombe Stream National Park.
Interactive augmented reality activities, including one in which visitors can test their skills at matching the pant-hoot vocalization of a chimpanzee.
Updates on the current state of Gombe Stream National Park and the chimpanzee range in Africa, along with the work of the scientists and conservationists who are following in Goodall's footsteps.
A call to action to visitors from Goodall to join the Jane Goodall Institute and National Geographic to ensure a more sustainable future.
A pledge station where visitors can share what actions they will take to help advance Goodall's mission and legacy.
Museum of the Rockies is open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the "Becoming Jane" exhibit is included with admission. Learn more at museumoftherockies.org.

 OXFORD — The Oxford Community Center hosted its first ever scarecrow building event on Wednesday. The scarecrows will be placed around town, and one fear-inducing, straw-filled figure will take home the grand prize.The town-wide scarecrow contest is a newly added element that aims to encourage residents and visitors to explore Oxford. The scarecrows will be placed on front porches, business and perhaps even on the beach.
"It'll just be really fun. And we wanted to create a space where when you're visiting Oxford, you can sit next to the scarecrow and take your selfies and be like, 'hashtag Oxford scarecrows,' and just make it a whole reason to come and explore during the holidays," said Oxford Community Center Executive Director Liza Ledford.
The idea to have the scarecrow building contest came about through a collaborative committee including members of the Oxford Fire Company Auxiliary, Oxford Community Center, Parks and Recreation, and Oxford Business Association.
Ledford said by combining forces, the group is able to reach a broader audience within the town.
The contest echoes a past town scavenger hunt that encouraged residents and visitors to find picket fences placed around in town.
"We used to do a thing where there were picket fences all over Oxford, and people would go and look and try to find them," Ledford said. "So we're like, well, if people put a scarecrow on their front porch, people will wander through town, they'll enjoy Oxford."
Ledford hopes the scarecrows are a particular hit on Oxford's upcoming Community Day on Oct. 18. The event kicks off at 9 a.m. with a 5k walk/run and beer truck to really tie in the Oktoberfest vibes.
From then until 2 p.m., there will be bouncy houses, food and a live band.
Community Day originally featured around 17 tables for nonprofits and Oxford associations, but Ledford said foot traffic was limited, which prompted the shift to an Oktoberfest/fall fun theme.
"So it just rolled all together where there would be great foot traffic, a beer truck, Bratwurst and community," Ledford said. "And then a whole month where you can check out Oxford and see the scarecrows all over town."

title: Country Cooking: Fall for these apple recipes
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Fall for these apple recipes

 October 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1473
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We all love the fall season and the farm products that are freshly grown and available — turnips, pumpkins, apples, late cabbage, and more.My friend Joy said they had picked two baskets of lima beans from their garden recently.
One of my favorite fall delicacies happens to be the apple. Before it was a multibillion-dollar communications or computer company, it was just a plain old fruit with many uses.
This week, we are doing the annual apple recipes — from simply washing the apples and eating them to making fresh pies, apple dumplings, apple crisp and more.
We never had apple trees on the farm growing up, but there were many local apple orchards nearby. Check your local newspaper or roadside stands for locations near you.
Once the two storage sheds were filled with potatoes, sweet potatoes, turnips and other fall vegetables, there would be a small spot set aside for storing some apples.
Different varieties of apples found on the Eastern Shore include Gala, Fuji, Honey Crisp, Golden Delicious, Red Delicious, McIntosh and Stayman. Everybody has their favorite.
With my favorite cook's (Mom's) influence, I use the following guide for cooking with apples:
The best apples for apple pies and apple crisp are Honeycrisp apples. They are known for their sweetness and crisp snap.Fuji apples are known for their largeness, crispness and sweetness and are popular for eating raw — perfect for lunch boxes or a snack any time of the day.Granny Smith is my favorite to use in apple dumplings due to their firmness.
Remember growing up with our parents saying, "An apple a day keeps the doctor away." It isn't true, folks.
We ate lots of apples but still had to go to town and get those "torpedo size needles." But there are health benefits.
Apples contain pectin, which help lower cholesterol and reduce the risk of heart disease. And the fruit is rich in antioxidants.
Before we begin exploring this week's apple recipes, I need to remind you of the upcoming Apple-Scrapple Festival being held in Bridgeville, Delaware. This year is the 33rd year Bridgeville has held this Festival. The celebration begins Friday evening, Oct. 10, at 4 p.m. with the opening ceremony and on Saturday, Oct. 11, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.
There is something for all ages to enjoy — including those delicious scrapple sandwiches, apple pies, apple dumplings, candy apples and more.
Now, let's cook with apples.
APPLE CRUMB PIE
7 1/2 cups apples (peeled, cored and sliced), 1 1/2 cups sugar, 2 tsps cinnamon, nutmeg to tase, unbaked pie shell, butter, 3/4 cup flour, 1/2 cup margarine.
Toss apples with 1 cup sugar, cinnamon and nutmeg . Put this mixture in an unbaked pie shell and dot it with butter. Make a topping consisting of 1/2 cup sugar, flour and margarine. Mix well and top the apples in a pie shell with this mixture. Bake at 350 degrees for one hour or until the apples are tender.
APPLE PIE COOKIES
3 tbsps salted butter, 2 apples (peeled and diced), 1/2 cup packed light brown sugar, juice of 1/2 lemon, 2 tbsps apple juice or cider, 1 tbsp cornstarch, 1 (14-oz) package refrigerated pie dough (2 crusts), 1/2 cup powdered sugar, 2 to 3 tsps heavy cream.
In a medium saucepan, melt the butter over medium-high heat. Add the apples and cook until they start to soften, 3 to 4 minutes. Stir in the brown sugar and lemon juice, bring to a simmer and cook until the apples are soft and the liquid is starting to reduce, 3 to 4 more minutes. In a small bowl, whisk together the apple juice and cornstarch and add it to the pan. Cook, stirring, until the mixture thickens, about 1 more minute. Remove from the heat and let cool. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper. Roll out one piece of pie dough into a 12-inch round. Using a 3-inch cutter, cut out 12 small rounds and arrange on the baking sheet. Re-roll the scraps and cut out two more rounds. Roll the other piece of dough into a 12-inch round. Cut into 1/2-inch-wide strips. Cut the strips into shorter 3 1/2- to 4-inch pieces (you should have about 56 pieces). Arrange the dough rounds on the baking sheet. Place 1 tbsp of the apple mixture in the center of each. Lay 2 parallel strips of dough on top, then lay 2 more strips perpendicular to the first to look like a lattice. (Alternatively, weave the strips into a lattice.) Trim the edges of the strips, then press around the edges with a fork to seal. Bake until golden, 18 to 20 minutes. Remove to a rack to cool. For the glaze: In a small bowl, whisk together the powdered sugar, heavy cream, and cardamom. Drizzle over the cookies. If you are a diabetic like myself, instead of 2 tbsps of apple juice you can use water.
SOUR CREAM APPLE PIE
2 beaten eggs, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 cup sour cream, 1/3 cup + 2 tbsps flour, 1 tsp vanilla, apple pie spice, pinch of salt, 2 apples (peeled, cored and sliced), 1/3 cup brown sugar, 1/4 cup butter.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Combine eggs, sugar, sour cream, 2 tbsps flour, vanilla, 1 tsp apple pie spice, pinch of salt and apples. Mix well and place in a baking dish. In another bowl mix brown sugar, 1/3 cup flour, 1 tsp apple pie spice and butter. Mix until crumbly and place on top of the apple mixture. Bake for 30 to 40 minutes.
APPLESAUCE
Here is one you can make with your kids.
4 sweet apples, 1/2 cup water, 1/2 tsp cinnamon.
Wash apples, cut into quarter pieces and place in a saucepan. Add water and cinnamon on top. Simmer with a cover on top until just tender — about 20 minutes. Let the children mash the cooked apples with a handheld potato masher.
HOMEMADE APPLE BUTTER
2 quarts apple cider, 4 quarts apples (thinly sliced), 2 cups sugar, 2 cups dark corn syrup, 1 tsp cinnamon.
Boil apple cider until reduced to only one quart. Put the apples into the cider and cook slowly, stirring frequently, until it begins to thicken. Add sugar, corn syrup and cinnamon and continue to cook until thick enough to spread when cool. Seal in sterilized jars. Makes 5 to 6 pints.
COUNTRY APPLE DUMPLINGS
2 large Granny Smith apples, 2 10-oz. cans refrigerated crescent rolls, 1 cup butter, 1 1/2 cups sugar, 1 tsp cinnamon, 12-oz can Mountain Dew or Diet Mountain Dew.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Grease a 9-by-13-inch baking dish. Cut apples into eight triangles and set aside. Unroll crescent rolls into eight triangles. Roll each apple wedge in the, starting at the smallest end. Pinch to seal so the dough is fully closed around the apple wedge and place in the baking dish. Melt butter in a small pan and stir in sugar and cinnamon. Pour this mixture over the apple dumplings. Next pour Mountain Dew or Diet Mountain Dew, if you are a diabetic like myself, over the apple dumplings. Bake for 35 to 45 minutes until golden brown.
SOUTHERN FRIED APPLES
½ cup butter, ½ cup white sugar, 2 tbsps ground cinnamon (or to taste), 4 Granny Smith apples (peeled, cored and sliced).
Melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add sugar and cinnamon; stir until sugar dissolves. Add apples and cook until softened, 5 to 8 minutes. At this point you can let them cool a little or dig right in.
DEEP FRIED APPLE RINGS
The best options are Granny Smith or Pink Lady for this recipe.
½ cup all-purpose flour, 3 tbsps milk, 1 tsp rum, 1 large egg, 1 tbsp granulated sugar or vanilla flavored sugar, 2 apples (large), 1 1/4 cups vegetable, ¼ cup granulated sugar or powdered sugar, 1 tsp ground cinnamon.
In a small bowl, mix flour, milk, rum, egg and 1 tbsp of sugar until you get a nice smooth batter. Wash and peel the apples. Slice them into thin slices (you should get 5-6 slices out of each apple). Remove the core using a small round cookie cutter. Or use apple corer, if you have one. Heat up the oil in a frying pan/skillet or deep fryer. Dip each ring in the batter and fry until both sides are golden brown. Place each apple ring onto a paper kitchen towel to get rid of the excess oil. While it is still warm, coat them in cinnamon sugar (mix sugar and cinnamon together).
Wait a minute. No Apple Pie recipe, Marie?
Not this time. I'll save that for my yearly pie column around Thanksgiving.
Also, as I put in the diabetic substitutes for some of the recipes. I'm working on a few columns for certain diets such as diabetic, fatty liver, heart healthy etc. If you have a certain diet, you'd like me to throw it in here, I'd be glad to do it. Reach me at mmsavage21145@gmail.com.

title: Portraits preserve Indigenous leaders' legacy
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespubcom
content:
Portraits preserve Indigenous leaders' legacy

 October 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespubcom | Section: News 
 
 580
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — "Astonishing Portraits, Untold Stories: The World of Thomas L. McKenney" opened Oct. 4 at Wright's Chance, weaving together national and local history through portrait recreations of Native American leaders commissioned by 19th-century Marylander Thomas L. McKenney.At a time when policies of removal and displacement threatened Indigenous communities, Thomas Loraine McKenney (1785-1859) sought to preserve and immortalize the history of Indigenous leaders and their families through portraiture, Queen Anne's County Historical Society volunteer Barb Pivec said.
McKenney was born in 1785 in Somerset County to a Quaker family and attended Washington College in Chestertown.
In 1816 McKenney was appointed superintendent of Indian trade under the War Department by President James Madison, and in 1824, McKenney served as the first head of the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
McKenney traveled the country and published accounts of Indigenous nations, negotiations and the traditions.
"The councils and landscapes I witnessed revealed both the dignity of the Native nations and the urgency of their uncertain future," McKenney wrote in "Sketches of a Tour to the Lakes," recounting his 1826 journey to the Great Lakes.
In the early 19th century, Indigenous delegations traveled to Washington, D.C., to meet with government officials as sovereign nations and negotiate treaties to shape the future of land and people.
McKenney initiated the Indian Gallery to commission dignified portraits of visiting leaders as a "national project of preservation," between 1821 and 1830, Pivec said.
McKenney ensured each portrait was paired with a biography, recording personal histories, orations and family lineage.
Housed at the Smithsonian, nearly all of the original painted-from-life oil portraits of the Indian Gallery were lost in an 1865 fire.
Fortunately, Pivec said, McKenney's foresight in ensuring historic preservation continued with his insistence on lithograph reproductions published in the book "History of the Indian Tribes of North America (1836-1844)."
With these lithograph reproductions, dedicated contributing artists, historians and writers were able to recreate the portraits. Surviving against odds, the image copies on display at Wright's Chance stand as powerful reminders of resilience, diplomacy and cultural identity, Pivec said.
"Without him, we would not have these images. We would have none of this understanding of these people from this era if McKenney hadn't had the foresight to have portraits painted," she said.
Enhancing visitor immersion, the exhibit features the society's first guided audio tour, led by McKenney's "voice."
"The intent is to engage people with discussion," Pivec said.
The inspiration for the exhibit collection at Wright's Chance came about as Pivec became incredibly engaged reading "The McKenney-Hall Portrait Gallery of American Indians" by James D. Horan, and sought to share the important history, particularly with its local relevance.
McKenney's Eastern Shore roots also run deep, with family ties connected directly to Centreville and the Wright family of Wright's Chance, she said. The McKenney family were prominent business leaders in town, at one point owning close to 100 farms, she said.
A smaller exhibit also featured local heritage artifacts and materials discovered from around Queen Anne's County.
Weaving national history with local legacies, the Society aims to showcase how the work of one man connects the history of Native American policy in Washington with the heritage of Queen Anne's County.
"These genealogical links remind us that national history and local history are inseparable," Pivec said.
Artifacts and portraits were provided by the Queen Anne's Museum of Eastern Shore Life and the private collections of Stephen K. Wilson and James H. Barton III.
The exhibit was made possible through the Wright family of Queen Anne's County and an Inclusive History Grant from the Maryland 250 Commission.
The exhibit runs through mid-January.

 October 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 217

 If you've walked downtown recently, it's hard to miss the giant crab staring right at you.In a remarkable display of sculpture work, a Maryland crab made out of pumpkins decorates the corner of South Washington and Dover streets in Easton.
With carvings scattered throughout town after this weekend's Fall Kickoff festivities, the pumpkin crab takes the cake in terms of size. It was done by sculptors at the Ice Lab, a professional sculpting and carving company with offices in Glen Burnie and Cambridge.
Holly DeKarske, director of the Easton Economic Development Corporation, said it took the sculptors eight to nine hours to create the display. It was "nerve-wracking" to watch them carry the masterpiece on a pallet out of a truck, she said, but it stood solid and hasn't lost its crab form one bit.
Just like the pumpkin crab, Easton's two-day Fall Kickoff was a success. Pleasant weather brought lots of people downtown, said DeKarske, who added that this year's opening October weekend was one of the best in recent memory.
To read more about the town's leap into the Halloween season, make sure to pick up a copy of Wednesday's Star Democrat or visit our website. Below, you can learn about some upcoming events and catch up on other news from over the weekend.

title: Easton's Fall Kickoff adorns downtown with pumpkins
author: Konner Metz
content:
Easton's Fall Kickoff adorns downtown with pumpkins

 October 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 252
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Downtown Easton is beginning to look a lot more festive.As warm summer-like weather persists, the town continued its tradition of hosting a two-day Fall Kickoff event during the opening weekend of October. Families walked downtown streets for live music, pumpkin painting and more on Friday and Saturday.
Easton Economic Development Corporation Executive Director Holly DeKarske said the event went well, especially compared to past iterations.
"This is probably one of the best years that we had it," DeKarske said.
On streets like Harrison and Washington, many businesses placed carved pumpkins outside their doors, making a decorative walk for residents and visitors. A contest for the best decorations is being held, with voting open on the Discover Easton Facebook page until Oct. 13.
A giant crab made out of pumpkins was placed in front of Thompson Park on the corner of Washington and Dover streets — a display that took professionals about eight or nine hours to create, DeKarske said.
Live music and performances entertained residents and passersby at Thompson Park, while many stopped in the Waterfowl Festival building for a Breast Cancer Awareness month fundraiser by the Working Artists Forum.
The Academy Art Museum hosted a pumpkin-painting event for kids. DeKarske said around 150 children participated, maybe twice as many as last year.
DeKarske noted she saw families walking around even after storefronts closed to enjoy the decorated downtown.
"We want people to hopefully dine and stop into the stores," DeKarske said. "But at the same time, getting people out and offering something that's free and family-friendly."

title: Artoberfest draws crowds to historic Stevensville
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Artoberfest draws crowds to historic Stevensville

 October 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 538
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Queen Anne's County came alive with outdoor events featuring arts, music and dancing in support of local creators and performers throughout the community over the weekend.The streets of the Arts and Entertainment District of Historic Stevensville transformed into a bustling hub of activity Oct. 4 with the annual artistic extravaganza Artoberfest, bringing together a day of creativity, entertainment and community for all ages.
Hosted by Queen Anne's County Parks and Recreation in partnership with the Stevensville Arts & Entertainment District, the free, vibrant community celebration of arts and culture was complete with artisans and crafters, live music and DJ, food and plenty of entertainment.
Giving dancers the opportunity to groove beyond the studio and showcase their talents, performances took to the street.
Considering it "exercise in disguise," complete with fitness as well as cognitive and social fellowship elements, dancing incorporates everything needed to live your best life, DMW Soul Fitness owner and instructor Diane Moorman-White said.
Celebrating DMW Soul Fitness' second year of business, Moorman-White has been dancing for more than 10 years. Moorman-White teaches classes throughout the area including through the county Parks and Recreation department, at 55 and older communities, and in Annapolis.
A retired veterinarian, Moorman-White said she has always been drawn to helping people and animals.
Soul line dancing is beginner friendly and incorporates all styles of music, she said.
Performing with her students, Moorman-White also invited audience participation to groove and learn some moves.
"We are happy to be part of a festival that feels so good about the arts," Moorman-White said.
Nancy Ceccorulli, of Arnold, has been dancing with DMW for about a year and a half and was excited for the opportunity to come to Artoberfest and showcase what she's learned.
As an instructor, Moorman-White breaks down steps in simple ways beginners can understand well, said Ceccorulli, and dancers are always encouraging of each other.
Moorman-White welcomed potential dancers held back by a perceived lack of rhythm or claim two left feet to give a dance class a chance.
"I love a challenge," she said. "Everyone can dance and move their body in a way that feels good to them," she said.
Performances also featured dancers from Parallel and Paradigm Performance Company of family dance studio Step 1 Dance 2 Academy in Chester.
With the local area such a strong supporter of the arts, "Getting out in the community is one of the reasons why we do what we do," said owner and instructor Jessica Gallew, of Chestertown.
Following in his mother's dance footsteps for years in performance, Gavin Gallew, 15, said dancing felt "ethereal" and it was more than just movement. "It's about expression."
Addison Redmond, 15, of Queen Anne's County High School has been dancing since she was two and loving every moment of it. "Getting to have fun and perform is amazing," she said.
The Historic Stevensville Arts and Entertainment District was home to all manner of artistry, including craft and artisan vendors, and a kids zone nurtured creative spirits with a plethora of activities, balloon animals, pumpkin decorating and face painting.
Visitors were also beckoned to explore the Kent Island Federation of Arts and tour historic sites.
For more information about Queen Anne's County Parks and Recreation, visit qac.org/parks-recreation.
More information about the Historic Stevensville Arts and Entertainment District can be found at stevensvilleartsandentertainment.org.

title: Chesapeake film fest explores Bay, global stories
author: Konner Metz
content:
Chesapeake film fest explores Bay, global stories

 October 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 459
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Chesapeake Film Festival has a packed slate of short films, documentaries and animations on tap this weekend in Easton.The 18th iteration of the three-day event kicked off Friday afternoon with a showing of "Loving Vincent," an oil-painted animation made up of 65,000 frames by more than 100 artists worldwide. The Oscar-nominated film drew a packed crowd to the Ebenezer Theater. Patrons stayed afterward for a short panel discussion about the film and its intersection with art.
There's much more to check out on Saturday and Sunday, with films alternating between the Ebenezer Theater, Academy Art Museum and Talbot County Free Library all weekend.
During Friday's premiere, Chesapeake Film Festival Board President Irene Magafan encouraged viewers to take it all in.
"Over the next three days, I challenge you to experience these films with a completely open mind," Magafan said. "Absorb the characters, the messages, the visuals, the soundscapes. Let them wash over you. I promise, you're going to walk away having learned something."
Cid Collins Walker, the festival's executive director, said the weekend is a time of not just celebrating the wonderful films, but also of building community and creativity in a "shared space."
"Theater today becomes more than just a venue," Collins Walker said. "It becomes a gathering place, for stories, ideas and the vibrant spirit of independent filmmaking."
This year's theme is "Our Bay, Our World, Our Festival," featuring a number of environmental films. Friday evening is Environmental Night at the festival. Collins Walker pointed out "The Grand Salmon" as a must-see feature film — it follows a group of women paddling 1,000 miles, mimicking the path of wild salmon in the Pacific Ocean.
On Saturday, a live podcast will be hosted at the Talbot County Free Library from 10:30 to 11:45 a.m. The podcast will feature John O'Hurley, the award-winning Seinfeld star and former Family Feud host.
Later that day, environmental blocks of films will be hosted at both the Ebenezer Theater and the library.
Over at the Academy Art Museum, seven short films will be shown during a block from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Then beginning at 1 p.m., the museum will show 13 different student shorts, ranging from three to 18 minutes in length.
To cap the festival, the 2025 documentary film "Holding Liat" will give viewers a deep dive into how an Israeli-American family grapples with a family member being held hostage during the Israel-Hamas war.
Collins Walker said the film — which won a documentary film award at the Berlin International Film Festival earlier this year — is "thought-provoking" and takes a "really interesting perspective."
Tickets are available for purchase at chesapeakefilmfest.ticketspice.com/chesapeake-film-festival-2025. VIP passes for the entire weekend of films are $150, while single tickets for most of the program blocks and feature films run from $20 to $25.

title: Ayreheart opens National Music Festival’s resonance season in Chestertown
author: Staff Writer
content:
Ayreheart opens National Music Festival’s resonance season in Chestertown

 October 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 371
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The National Music Festival will open its 2025-26 Resonance concert series with a performance by Ayreheart, a Renaissance and folk music ensemble, at 3 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 26, in the Parish Hall at St. Paul's, Kent.Founded by Grammy-nominated lutenist and composer Ronn McFarlane, Ayreheart performs Renaissance music from the time of Shakespeare, along with traditional folk and original pieces. The ensemble's instrumentation includes lute, vocals, colascione (a bass lute), violin, guitar and percussion.
"Ayreheart was an audience favorite when they performed here in 2019," said National Music Festival Artistic Director Richard Rosenberg. "We're thrilled that they're returning to Chestertown to open our concert season."
The program will feature works by Renaissance composers John Dowland and William Byrd, as well as traditional ballads and folk songs from England, Scotland and Wales. McFarlane said his goal is to connect audiences to the enduring vitality of the lute.
"I want 21st-century listeners to hear the lute as a vibrant, modern musical instrument, able to reach their hearts and their feet, too," he said.
McFarlane, who founded Ayreheart in 2010, will be joined by vocalist and guitarist Heather Aubrey Lloyd, bass, violin and colascione player Willard Morris, and percussionist Mattias Rucht.
The Resonance concert series brings five intimate performances to Chestertown each year, from October through April. Concerts are held Sundays at 3 p.m. in St. Paul's Parish Hall, where a fireplace adds to the cozy atmosphere in colder months.
Upcoming Resonance concerts:
Oct. 26, 2025: Ayreheart
Nov. 16, 2025: Francesca Anderegg, violin, and Joy Cline Phinney, piano
Feb. 22, 2026: Matchstick Percussion
March 15, 2026: Jennifer Parker-Harley, flute, and Camilo Carrara, guitar
April 12, 2026: Manuel Barrueco, guitar
Tickets for Ayreheart's concert are $25 for adults and $5 for students with ID and children ages 5 to 14. Tickets may be purchased online or at the door beginning one hour before the concert.
Season and combo passes for the 2025-26 Resonance and National Music Festival performances are now available. Combo passes include admission to all Resonance concerts and ticketed events during the 2026 National Music Festival, May 31–June 13.
The National Music Festival is supported in part by the Maryland State Arts Council, Kent Cultural Alliance, Mid-Shore Community Foundation, The Peoples Bank, and donations from music lovers. For more information, email info@nationalmusic.us or call 443-480-0221.

title: Country Cooking: Fresh baked bread on a cool fall day
author: MARIE SAVAGE
content:
Country Cooking: Fresh baked bread on a cool fall day

 October 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE | Section: Life 
 
 1772
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The temperatures are dropping slowly. What a great time to begin making fresh bread.The family will love the warm kitchen with great smell of fresh baked bread. Have plenty of whipped butter on hand with jam, jelly or honey to smear on top.
In the winter, I will feature my favorite biscuit recipes. Contact me to feature your family favorites to share.
Here are six tips to consider when baking your breads.
Place a small ovenproof dish with water in the oven when baking to help prevent the crust from getting too hard or brown.Use margarine or oil shortening to grease the pans as margarine and oil absorb more readily into the dough or batter.To make self-rising flour, mix 4 cups flour, 2 teaspoons salt, and 2 tbsps baking powder.Hot water kills yeast. One way to tell the correct temperature is to pour the water over your forearm. If you do not feel hot or cold, then it's just perfect.When making nut bread, they are better stored 24 hours after baking and before serving.Use an empty and clean salt shaker to store flour to be used for shaking when recipes call for it.
BASIC WHITE BREAD
When I began making bread, this was the recipe I used until I felt more confident. Give this a try if this is your first attempt.
2 envelopes yeast, 4 cups water (90-100 degrees), 2 cups sugar, 2 tbsps shortening, 2 tbsps vinegar, 2 tsps salt, 12 cups flour.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Place all ingredients except the flour into the liquid in a large mixing bowl. Stir slightly until dissolved. Add 6 cups of the flour and beat. slowly stir in the remaining 6 cups of flour and let rest for 10 minutes. Place on a lightly floured board and knead for 2 minutes. Let rise until doubled in size. Punch down and let rise again. Shape into four loaves, place into loaf pans and bake in a preheated oven for 40 to 45 minutes. Enjoy.
SOURDOUGH BREAD
4 ¾ cups bread flour (or more as needed), 3 tbsps white sugar, 2 ½ tsps salt, 1 package active dry yeast, 1 cup warm milk, 2 tbsps margarine (softened), 1 ½ cups sourdough starter, 1 extra large egg, 1 tbsp water, ¼ cup chopped onion.
Combine 1 cup flour, sugar, salt and yeast in a large bowl. Add warm milk and margarine. Add in the starter mix. Mix in the remaining 3 3/4 cups of flour gradually; you may need to add more flour depending on the climate. Turn dough out onto a floured surface and knead for 8 to 10 minutes. Place dough into a greased bowl, turn once to the oil surface, and cover. Allow to rise until doubled in volume, about 1 hour. Punch down dough; cover and rest for 15 minutes. Divide dough in half and shape into two loaves. Place loaves on a greased baking pan. Allow to rise until doubled in volume, about 1 hour. Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Stir together egg and water in a small bowl until well combined. Brush over the tops of loaves, then sprinkle with onion. Bake in the preheated oven until the loaves are golden brown and cooked through, about 30 minutes. An instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of a loaf should read 190 degrees.
HOMEMADE ARTISAN BREAD
3 1/4 cups bread flour (plus more for hands and pan), 2 tsps instant yeast, 2 tsps coarse salt, 1 1/2 cups water (close to room temperature at about 70 degrees).
In a large, ungreased mixing bowl, whisk the flour, yeast and salt together. Pour in the water and gently mix with a silicone spatula or wooden spoon. The dough will seem dry and shaggy, but keep working until all the flour is moistened. If needed, use your hands to work the dough ingredients together. The dough will be sticky. Shape into a ball in the bowl as best you can. Keeping the dough in the bowl, cover the dough tightly with plastic wrap or aluminum foil and set on the counter at room temperature. Allow to rise for 2-3 hours. The dough will just double in size, stick to the sides of the bowl, and have a lot of air bubbles. You can continue with step 4 immediately, but for the absolute best flavor and texture, I strongly recommend letting this risen dough rest in the refrigerator for at least 12 hours and up to 3 days. Place covered dough in the refrigerator for 12 hours — 3 days. I usually let it rest in the refrigerator for about 18 hours. The dough will puff up during this time but may begin to deflate after 2 days. That's fine and normal, nothing to worry about. Lightly dust a large nonstick baking sheet with flour and/or cornmeal. Turn the cold dough out onto a floured work surface. Using a sharp knife or bench scraper, cut dough in half. Some air bubbles will deflate as you work with it. Place dough halves on prepared baking sheet. Using floured hands, shape into 2 long loaves about 9-by-3 inches each about 3 inches apart. Loosely cover and allow to rest for 45 minutes. You will bake the dough on this prepared baking sheet. During these 45 minutes, preheat the oven to 475 degrees. When ready to bake, using a very sharp knife score the bread loaves with 3 slashes, about 1/2 inch deep. If the shaped loaves flattened out during the 45 minutes, use floured hands to narrow them out along the sides again. Place the shaped and scored dough on the flour dusted pan in the preheated oven on the center rack. Bake for 20-25 minutes or until the crust is golden brown. Gently tap the loaves—if they sound hollow, the bread is done. For a more accurate test of doneness, the bread is done when an instant read thermometer inserted in the center reads 195 degrees. Remove the bread from the oven and allow it to cool for at least 20 minutes before slicing and serving. Store leftovers loosely covered at room temperature for up to 5 days or in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.
HONEY SPICE BREAD
2/3 cup packed brown sugar, 1/3 cup 2% milk, 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 1/2 tsps baking powder, 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon, 1/2 tsp ground nutmeg, 1/8 tsp ground cloves, 2 large eggs (room temperature), 1/2 cup honey, 1/3 cup canola oil. GLAZE: 1/3 cup confectioners' sugar, 2 tesps 2% milk.
Preheat the oven to 325 degrees. In a small saucepan, combine brown sugar and milk. Cook and stir over low heat until sugar is dissolved. Remove from heat. In a large bowl, whisk flour, baking powder, cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves. In another bowl, whisk eggs, honey, oil and brown sugar mixture until blended. Add to flour mixture; stir just until moistened. Transfer the batter to a greased 8-by-4-inch loaf pan. Bake for 50-60 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean (cover top loosely with foil if needed to prevent over-browning). Cool in pan for 10 minutes before removing to a wire rack to cool completely. In a small bowl, stir glaze ingredients until smooth, drizzle over bread.
AMISH WHITE BREAD
2 cups of warm water (110 degrees), ⅔ cup white sugar, 1 ½ tbsps active dry yeast, ¼ cup vegetable oil,1 ½ tsps salt, 6 cups bread flour.
Dissolve sugar in warm water in a large bowl and then stir in yeast. Allow to proof until the yeast resembles a creamy foam, 5 to 10 minutes. Mix oil and salt into the yeast. Mix in flour one cup at a time. Knead dough on a lightly floured surface until it is smooth. Place it in a well-oiled bowl and turn dough to coat. Cover with a damp cloth. Allow to rise until doubled in bulk, about 1 hour. Punch dough down. Knead for a few minutes and divide in half. Shape into loaves and place into two well-oiled 9-by-5-inch loaf pans. Allow it to rise until dough has topped the pans by one inch, about 30 minutes. Meanwhile, preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Bake the risen loaves in the preheated oven until golden brown for 30 minutes.
COUNTY WHOLE WHEAT BREAD
2 1/2 cup warm buttermilk (body temperature is good), 2 tbsps honey, 1 tbsp dry active yeast, 5 1/2 cups fine grind whole wheat flour, 1 cup unbleached bread flour (plus more as needed), 1 tbsp kosher salt, 1 egg, 3 tbsps unsalted butter (soft), 2 tbsps poppy seeds, 1 egg white mixed with a tablespoon of water.
Warm the buttermilk to body temperature. In other words when you stick a finger into it you shouldn't feel it. Place the buttermilk in a large bowl. Add a tablespoon of yeast and honey to it. Let the yeast dissolve either by whisking it or letting it bloom. Add the whole wheat flour, 1 cup of bread flour, egg and salt. Using a thick handled wooden spoon mix the dough in a circular fashion adding the softened butter once the dough has started to form. Once the dough has formed remove it from the bowl to a clean countertop and knead the dough until it is smooth, elastic and the gluten has formed. Consider this your workout for the day. Roll the dough into a tight ball. Place the dough back into the bowl, cover it with a damp warm towel and set it in a warm place. Set a timer for 1 hour. At the end of the hour punch down the dough and set the timer for another hour. At the end of this hour the dough should be doubled in size. Punch down the dough and divide it in half. Roll it into a ball and either divide it into thirds so you can roll it into logs and braid it or roll it into two big logs. Place the loaves into prepared pans. I always oil and then shake flour into my pans. The thin coating of flour lets the baked bread easily release from the pan. Cover with a warm damp towel and let the dough rise for 40 minutes to an hour. Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Once the loaves have doubled, brush them with the egg wash and sprinkle with poppy seeds or sesame seeds. You can also dust the tops with flour but if you do this don't use the egg wash. Bake the loaves in the oven for 45 to 50 minutes, rotating them halfway through baking. Remove the loaves from the oven and remove them from the bread pans to a rack and let them cool.

title: A new tour explores Maryland’s witch trials
author: Aline Behar Kado Capital News Service
content:
A new tour explores Maryland’s witch trials

 October 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Aline Behar Kado Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 1049
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Rebecca Fowler was an indentured servant here in the late 1600s, working the land for years until she and her husband were finally lucky enough to own a plot of land.But her luck ran out after he died and she took full title. She was soon charged with a deadly crime for a woman of the period: witchcraft.
A long trial led to her sad end as the only person executed for witchcraft in Maryland history, but the story didn't die there. It's getting told anew on nighttime tours around this historic city.
"The gallows would have been there," said Melissa Huston as she stood on a cobblestone street in the old part of Annapolis on Wednesday night, gesturing to the town's execution site.
The story sent chills up the spines of the tour group, never mind the fact that Fowler was executed in her hometown of St. Mary's City. This self-made woman from centuries ago still figures prominently in the story of the Maryland witch trials.
Huston debuted her tour this week, featuring the history and legends of Maryland and connecting each one to a landmark in Annapolis, the capital city and the center of the state's witchy history.
"I am a history storyteller," said Huston, creator and tour guide of the Annapolis Witches & Legends Walking Tour. "We don't do gimmicks. We do pure, authentic storytelling."
It's not a coincidence that her attention has turned to the Maryland witch hunts this particular fall. She defines a witch trial as an irrational accusation or case based in fear.
"Even today, everything is called a witch trial," said Huston. "Which is what we are doing today to trans communities, immigrant communities and other minority communities. It translates across lives."
"It is such a small percentage of this population just trying to live their honest, true lives, and they're being vilified and demonized by people in power and being blamed for things that are way out of their control and have no business being blamed for," said Huston. "That's a modern witch hunt."
Back in the colonial period, there were around 25 cases of alleged witchcraft in Maryland. Most cases were treated as slander, leading to just two convictions and one execution. Three of these cases happened in Annapolis.
Massachusetts had about 200 cases during the more famous Salem witch trials. But Maryland's religious tolerance allowed for a more measured approach, according to Huston.
Huston's interest in witches started years ago when she learned two of her ancestors died during the Salem trials.
She has been researching witches and witch trials in Maryland for the past year and decided to pitch doing a witch tour around Annapolis.
She's not the only one who's haunting the antique streets. Mike Carter, CEO and founder of Annapolis Ghost Tours and Crawls was excited to introduce something new.
"I feel like a lot of people think, 'Oh, well, Annapolis is old, there must be lots and lots of witches,'" said Carter. "The tour we do is to cover all the cool stuff that we do know about the history of witches in Maryland."
Huston and Carter believe that there could be medical or scientific explanations for the so-called witchcraft women in that time were accused of. Most of these "witches" tended to be, after all, single, older women and widows.
"The tour also tries to highlight and celebrate the power and the resilience of women," said Huston. "I think a lot of us, especially because the Gen X women are starting to hit their 50s. I'm hitting my witch era."
"You get to an age where you're more comfortable in your skin, and you're more comfortable speaking your mind, and filters start to come off," she said. "And I think that's also why a lot of women of a certain age are the ones that are accused of witchcraft."
Huston says she is glad to be doing something different from the ghost stories she's used to.
"I have been looking forward to telling these stories," said Huston, who works as a tour guide for the Annapolis Ghost Tours and Crawls's Hidden History Pub Crawl.
People in the crowd shared Huston's interest.
"Women have been vilified throughout history," said Celeste Dean, an Annapolis resident who participated in the tour. "I think that was just one of the ways that that took form."
They weren't there for ghost stories. The participants, mostly women, came to learn about other women of generations past.
"I believe in spirits," said Deb Leonard, another tour participant. "The definition of a witch is the problem."
The tour group gathered one recent night, next to a giant pumpkin near the harbor. Flags fluttered on sailboats. The sun crept behind clouds and a nearly full moon rose behind the nearby State House.
Huston dressed in a flowing black skirt, a patterned top and a wide-brimmed, velvety hat. Around her wrist, she wore several glow stick bracelets.
She led the tour through the cobblestone streets, reaching stops like the Governor Calvert House and the State House. After an hour of walking and listening to history come alive, the tour reached the St. Anne's Parish cemetery.
Almost 30 people crowded around the grave of a man named William Bladen. Huston told the story of Virtue Violl, the last person charged with the felony of witchcraft in Maryland.
It was 1712. Violl had gotten into a dispute with another unmarried, older neighbor.
The story goes that she must have made some comment about the other woman's tongue. Witnesses claimed the victim was spelled speechless. To them it was obviously witchcraft.
Bladen, then the attorney general and vestryman at St. Anne's, brought the case to trial. But the jury was made up of "more sophisticated" men, according to Huston. Maybe the victim had a terrible allergic reaction that made her tongue swell, Huston mused. Or perhaps Violl said something so shocking that the other woman was unable to respond.
In any case, the jurors most likely believed this was just a dispute, as Huston recounts it, and found Violl not guilty. The parties went their separate ways, and prosecutor Bladen lived four more years before coming to rest, here, in the St. Anne's cemetery.
Huston didn't condemn Bladen, but she did choose to stand on his grave to close her tour. As she did, the bells of St. Anne's tolled to mark the 8 o'clock hour.
"Perfect timing," one participant said, sending scattered giggles through the crowd.

title: One Book One Maryland presents “Kin: Rooted in Hope” author talk at Chesapeake College
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
One Book One Maryland presents “Kin: Rooted in Hope” author talk at Chesapeake College

 October 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 840
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WYE MILLS — Exploring family and freedom, 2025 One Maryland One Book author Carole Boston Weatherford and illustrator Jeffery Boston Weatherford presented a discussion on "Kin: Rooted in Hope" as part of the state's largest annual reading and discussion program at Chesapeake College on Oct. 7.Originally published in 2023, "Kin: Rooted in Hope" is an illustrated verse novel that serves as a work of art, history and personal genealogy through the authors' search into their family tree.
Conjuring ancestors and tracing historical roots from the Maryland plantation where Frederick Douglass was also enslaved to Civil War battlefields and to the founding of a black, Reconstruction-era village, "Kin" interweaves rhythmic poetic imagery verse and stunning visuals to give voices through multiple perspectives.
Author of 80 children's books, Carole considered poetry her "first literary language," which lends itself to a different flow of words to convey emotions for her than traditional prose.
Carole is no stranger to addressing tough topics for young people in verse, including her 2021 picture book "Unspeakable: The Tulsa Race Massacre."
Carole said it is important not to shy away from telling children the truth and to ensure critical thinking and socially responsible civic contribution.
A pin drop could be heard in the Todd Performing Arts Center auditorium as Carole recounted tracing her ancestor's lineage back to the Wye House plantation in Easton.
Visiting the Wye House for research, Carole noted moving moments and powerful connections, including holding the enormous iron antique key to the home, something her ancestor must have held as well.
Carole recounted visiting the plantation's burial ground, now hallowed with a plaque marking where the enslaved people of the house were laid to rest.
"I knelt down and cried and it was almost as if my ancestors had said, 'We have been waiting for you,'" Carole said.
Carole learned of an ancestor, Isaac Copper, mentioned in Frederick Douglass' autobiography, who was enslaved at the Wye House at the same time.
The Weatherfords' ancestors went on to fight for the Union in the American Civil War and helped found the historically black communities of Unionville and Copperville.
In creating the book, the Weatherfords came to discover, "Knowing your history is generational wealth," Carole said.
The mother-son duo were proud to collaborate, and Carole said it was a dream come true to experience it all with her son.
In reconnecting with ancestral roots, the two's travels included the Door of No Return at Gorée Island, noted as the last thing Africans of the area saw before they were enslaved and shipped away from their home.
Jeffery utilized a scratchboard medium to "bring people out of darkness into the light" and often used his own family as character models.
Jeffery said working on the book gave him a greater appreciation and understanding for the work his mother has been doing since he was a child.
One of the biggest challenges faced while working on the book was connecting the dots, Carole said.
Comprehensive research brought Carole's nose into captain ship ledgers and the meticulous records kept by the Lloyd family, owners of the Wye House plantation.
Carole noted the emotions in seeing the names of ancestors inscribed in estate inventory alongside bought and sold goods.
Some information remained out of reach, like the exact ship names that brought her enslaved ancestors over, she said. Along with the tremendous amount of research that went into every page also came a certain amount of artistic license to create stories, she said.
For those piecing together their own family tree, Carole gave permission for imagination as long as it fit the narrative historically.
"Informed by facts, it is up to you to fill in the gaps," she said.
Carole encouraged everyone to know their own history and seek out their own family stories regardless of ethnicity to inspire future generations.
Amateur genealogy hunting doesn't have to break the bank, she said, with public libraries a wealth of information and often having access to ancestry data resources.
"When you are the only one who knows, you tell somebody," she said.
Stories are essential to know exactly what ancestors went through. "Without stories, a family tree is just a map," Carole said.
"All of our histories are intertwined," Jeffery said, and by connecting with history, warts and all, we will find we have more in common than different.
"Names, dates and places are the branches of a family tree," according to Carole. "But stories are the leaves that bring the family's past to life."
"Kin: Rooted in Hope" is the winner of a Coretta Scott King Honor, the Claudia Lewis Award from Bank Street College of Education and the Boston Globe/Horn Book Award.
The Weatherfords have toured across Maryland to discuss the book as part of the One Maryland One Book program to encourage a love of reading and develop a deeper sense of community through connecting events.
The event at Chesapeake College was made possible in partnership with Eastern Shore Regional Library, Washington College, Caroline County Public Library, Kent County Public Library, Dorchester County Public Library, Queen Anne's County Public Library, ShoreLit, Talbot County Public Schools and The Needle's Eye Academy.
More information about the Weatherfords can be found at cbweatherford.com.

 EASTON — The 42nd annual Easton Prayer Breakfast was held Oct. 16 at the Easton Volunteer Fire Department with Talbot County Sheriff Joe Gamble presiding as the master of ceremonies.The breakfast included full programming with prayers and speeches from Easton residents. Prayers covered government, those who protect and serve, educators, churches, families, businesses and Thanksgiving.

Daron Miller was the keynote speaker of the event. Miller discovered the gospel during his 13 years as a Navy SEAL. He said he successfully completed the basic underwater Navy SEAL training with "supernatural assistance" rather than with natural aptitude, even if he didn't know it at the time.
Upon moving to Easton, Miller discipled at Talbot Bible Church and followed successive steps to biblical studies, seminary and chaplaincy.
Sts. Peter and Paul High School sophomore Chase Olavsrud presented his essay "More Than a Fisherman, The Making of a Saint." The work detailed Saint Peter's journey, emphasizing faith, failure, repentance, leadership and sacrifice as the path to holiness.
Deputy John Coleman belted the hymn "How Great Thou Art" from Psalms 150 before Gamble closed the breakfast with a final prayer.

title: Grave marking ceremony held for Revolutionary War patriot
author: Riley Dauber rdauber@somdnews.com
content:
Grave marking ceremony held for Revolutionary War patriot

 October 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Riley Dauber rdauber@somdnews.com | Section: State News 
 
 474
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It was an act of bravery nearly two and a half centuries ago, but it has not been forgotten.The Thomas Stone Chapter of the Sons of the American Revolution, which includes members from Calvert, Charles and St. Mary's counties, dedicated a patriot grave marking to Hatch Dent, who fought in the 1776 Battle of Brooklyn, this past Saturday.
The ceremony took place behind the Dent Memorial Chapel at the Charlotte Hall Veterans Home, where Dent and his family are buried. The new patriot grave marking was installed in the center of the grass, right in front of Dent's grave, to remember his sacrifice on the battlefield.
According to Mike Morthland, president of the Thomas Stone Chapter, the idea for the grave marking came from the late George Owings, who spoke at Morthland's induction ceremony in 2022.
Owings was a member of the Thomas Stone Chapter and a former state delegate and secretary of Maryland Veterans Affair. He died in 2023 before the grave marking could be installed, so Saturday's ceremony honored both Dent's sacrifice and Owings' wish.
Members from other local organizations, including the Sons and Daughters of the American Revolution, greeted the crowd following Morthland's introduction.
"Events such as this remind us that our freedom was hard won, and it is our responsibility to keep alive the memory of those who made it," Stacey Park, regent of the Major William Thomas Chapter of the DAR, said.
Sandy Sterrett, Dent's fourth great-grandson and a member of the Society of the Cincinnati, read Dent's biography and introduced the crowd to Dent's other fourth great-grandchildren.
Dent was born in Charles County in 1751. At the age of 24, he joined the First Maryland Regiment as a third lieutenant before being promoted to second lieutenant.
He was one of the only survivors of the Battle of Brooklyn, which took place on Aug. 27, 1776. About 65% of the Maryland army died in battle, and their sacrifice earned them the name "Maryland 400."
During the battle, Dent was captured and held until April 1778. He later resigned in 1779 and gave back to his community through his roles as a reader and rector at Trinity Church and principal and professor of languages at the Charlotte Hall School.
"Our organization … is dedicated to keeping the history of this wonderful county alive and perpetuated so that others in the future can understand both why we're here in such a unique place and the people that made this county what it is," Peter LaPorte, the executive director of the St. Mary's County Historical Society, said.
After the marker was unveiled and the organization leaders delivered their wreath presentations, the Maryland Society SAR color guard performed a musket salute. U.S. Navy Veteran David Osborne played "Taps" while the crowd sang memorable renditions of "America the Beautiful" and "God Bless America" to remember Dent and his role in the Battle of Brooklyn.
