 WYE MILLS — As the hunt for legendary cryptids comes to the cornfields of Chesapeake College, join the Community Theater's Peake Players as they return with their annual Harvest Horror, an immersive outdoor Halloween experience on Oct. 24, 25, 26, 30 and 31.Just be sure you find the beast before the beast finds you.
More than your typical haunted house or sitting and watching a play unfold, Harvest Horror is a different type of interactive experience that invites audiences to feel part of the story right alongside the theatrical players as they delve through the area, according to Todd Performing Arts Center Technical Director Savannah Verrette.
"You get out of the experience what you put into it," she said.
With monster sightings reported in the area, this year's story welcomes audiences as new recruits to the world-renowned Ostridea Paranormal Society seeking out the elusive shadow beast before it finds them.
A fun, spook-tacular event for actors and audiences alike, Harvest Horror is a big hit that toes the line between comedy and horror, she said.
"People really love how different it is, you don't see anything like this," she said.
With the main plot written by Verrette and Theater Director Rob Thompson, the event allows actors to dive into creating their own unique characters, she said.
"It is a truly original community experience creating it and then when people come they get to play along with it," Verrette said.
This year marks the fourth annual Harvest Horror, and with a new theme each year and monthslong details put into every performance, work occurs year-round, Verrette said.
Harvest Horror is supported by the Maryland State Arts Council and will include a special appearance by The Mid Shore Dance Academy.
The event is located behind the Eastern Shore Higher Education Building, and guests should enter the college at the main entrance from Route 213.
Splitting into groups of 12, each show lasts about an hour.

Light concessions will be available on-site by cash or by purchase in advance online.

 In 2025, led by its founding director, Virginia "Cookie" Brohawn, the all-volunteer Chorus of Dorchester is marking the 50th anniversary since its inception in 1975.Earlier this year, the chorus assembled its 70 members to develop and perform two concerts. title: Celebrate Octoberfest with these delicious recipes
author: MARIE SAVAGE
content:
Celebrate Octoberfest with these delicious recipes

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE | Section: Food 
 
 975
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Oktoberfest celebrations were first held in Munich, Germany, in 1810 to celebrate the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria and Princess Therese Charlotte Luise Friederike Amalie of Saxe-Hildburghausen Germany. The celebration lasted for several days. Eventually Oktoberfest was held as an annual event and was held outside of town in a large meadow and lasted for weeks. The celebration exploded with costumes, gun salutes, beverages and a tremendous supply of food.This festival grew to include horse races, thousands of kegs of beer, games, amusement rides and dancing in the streets. Many cities in the U.S. participate due to the thousands of Germans living here. The festivities are enjoyed by young and old alike and all nationalities. Let's try some tasty foods that appear at the festivals!
Let's get started today with German chocolate cake. This cake has long been a favorite of my family. German chocolate is a very sweet chocolate invented by a man named Sam German in 1852 for the Bakers Chocolate Company. The name stuck and this sweet chocolate has always been known as German chocolate — having nothing to do with Germany. When preparing this recipe if you can't find it in the store you can substitute it with milk chocolate or semisweet chocolate.
GERMAN CHOCOLATE CAKE
4 ounces German sweet chocolate chopped
1/2 cup water
1 cup butter, softened
2 cups sugar
4 large eggs, separated, room temperature
1 teaspoon vanilla extract
2½ cups cake flour
1 teaspoon baking soda
1/2 teaspoon salt
1 cup buttermilk
FROSTING:
1½ cups sugar
1½ cups evaporated milk
3/4 cup butter
5 large egg yolks, room temperature, beaten
2 cups sweetened shredded coconut
1½ cups chopped pecans
1½ teaspoons vanilla extract
ICING:
2 ounces semisweet chocolate
1 teaspoon shortening.
Line three greased 9-inch round baking pans with waxed paper. Grease waxed paper and set aside. In a small saucepan, melt chocolate with water over low heat; cool. Preheat the oven to 350°.
In a large bowl, add cream butter and sugar until light and fluffy, 5-7 minutes. Beat in 4 egg yolks, one at a time, beating well after each addition. Blend in melted chocolate and vanilla. Combine flour, baking soda and salt; add to the creamed mixture alternately with buttermilk, beating well after each addition.
In a small bowl and with clean beaters, beat the 4 egg whites until stiff peaks form. Fold a fourth of the egg whites into the creamed mixture, fold in remaining whites.
Pour batter into prepared pans. Bake 24-28 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean. Cool for 10 minutes before removing from pans to wire racks to cool completely.
For the icing, in a small saucepan, heat sugar, milk, butter and egg yolks over medium-low heat until mixture is thickened and golden brown, stirring constantly. Remove from heat. Stir in coconut, pecans and vanilla. Cool until thick enough to spread. Spread a third of the frosting over each cake layer and stack the layers. In a microwave, melt chocolate and shortening; stir until smooth. Drizzle over cake. This is not a cake that requires refrigeration, since the flavors will be best at room temperature.
GERMAN POTATO SALAD
10 medium peeled potatoes
6 slices of bacon
3/4 cup sliced onion
2 tablespoons flour
2 tablespoons salt
2 tablespoons sugar
Dash of pepper and a tablespoon celery seed
3/4 cup water
1/3 cup vinegar
Cook potatoes until just done. When cool, cut into slices. Fry bacon, remove from pan and drain.
Meanwhile, in the bacon grease, fry the onions and add the flour, sugar, salt, pepper and celery seed. Cook until bubbly. Add the water and vinegar and stir nil slightly thickened.
Pour this mixture over the potatoes. Crumble the bacon over the top or mix in and serve warm. Do not refrigerate.
This next one you might want to get a head start on for next year or for next time as it is better the later you use it after you make it.
HOMEMADE SAUERKRAUT
1 medium green or red cabbage 2.5 lbs. You can also add a mix of chopped veggies to the cabbage such as carrots, turnips, beets, Brussels sprouts, and even apples. 4 tsp salt. Discard outer limp cabbage leaves and core cabbage. Slice the cabbage into desired size. Try to make it uniform but you can do anything from a round chop to a fine shred. If you have larger, thicker rib slices you may want to discard those for use in another recipe.
When you have cut cabbage in the bowl, sprinkle the salt over top and begin massaging the cabbage. Keep rubbing until the cabbage is quite soft and pliable and there's at least 1 cup brine in the bottom of the bowl. Depending on the water content of the cabbage this could take 5-20 minutes. At this point you can add in flavor options such as caraway seeds, celery seed, grated ginger, fresh dill if you like.
Pack the cabbage tightly into a jar or crock and pour the brine over all. Press the cabbage down so that it is submerged under the brine. If you absolutely do not have enough brine, do not panic. Add a 2.5% salt and water brine (1/2 tsp salt/1 cup water). Allow to ferment at least one week and up to 3 weeks. Refrigerate.
CROCKPOT BRATS AND SAUERKRAUT
2-3 pounds brats or sausage cut into coin-sized pieces
1 sweet onion chopped
2 cloves garlic minced
32 ounces sauerkraut store bought of your own from the recipe above
1 honey crisp apple or other sweet apple peeled and chopped
1 tablespoon caraway seeds
1 cup of water
2-4 tablespoons brown sugar.
Heat oil on the stove and cook onions and garlic on the stove until soft. Add the sauerkraut, apple, onion and garlic mixture, and caraway seeds to the slow cooker crock. Stir.
Cut brats or sausage into ½-inch pieces. Add to the crockpot. Mix water and brown sugar together in a separate bowl. Pour over the sauerkraut mixture. Stir ingredients together.
Cook on high for 3-4 hours or low for 4-6 hours.

title: Museum creates immersive Harriet Tubman experience
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Museum creates immersive Harriet Tubman experience

 October 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 476
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — The Harriet Tubman Museum and Educational Center closed in May due to water damage. Since then, the museum has secured a grant that has allowed them to renovate the facility.Tuesday there was an open house for residents to see the progress and vision for the museum's reopening. Director of Programming and Events Linda Harris said the museum will be an immersive and interactive experience that follows Tubman's journey from slavery in Maryland to freedom in Pennsylvania.
The museum walls will depict different scenes of Tubman's life, integrated with lighting, sound, music and narrated walkthroughs to attract a young audience and evoke spirituality and community.
"I think it's something divine. Being connected to this story, marvelous things happen," Harris said. "We had a flood in May. Lots of water damage, and it took us until about three weeks ago to get the insurance company to pony up."
Though they received a check from the insurance company, it wasn't enough to cover the renovations. But as Harris said they received a large anonymous donation that made this dream come true.
Harris' daughter-in-law Erica Carson-Harris is an interior architect and is leading the museum's renovations. Artist Michael Rosato, who painted the "Walk With Me" mural — which can be found on the wall outside of the museum — is doing the paintings on the walls and floors.
"We're painting a path on the floor and certain areas lead to a certain part of the wall, that's gonna tell her story. So there will be a story of her standing out in the marsh, looking at the shooting stars having revelations, to a story about where she was enslaved, the cabin and the fields outside of that, to meeting Frederick Douglass, to leading the troops at the Combahee River, and then through the end in Philadelphia," Rosato said.
For Carson-Harris, she hopes the museum will create an emotional connection that provides knowledge about Tubman. Both Carson-Harris and Rosato want to encourage the public to come and visit during the renovations to see the work they're doing and if they feel called, to leave a donation.
"With Linda opening it up for people to see this, I encourage people to come and visit, as we're in the midst of this transition. You know, definitely just come out and look at the transition. Be a part of the journey as well," Carson-Harris said.
Harris plans to create the exhibit as a virtual reality experience where those who don't have the opportunity to see it in person, can experience it firsthand online.
There is still no projected date for the re-opening, but Carson-Harris is hopeful it could happen within six months. She encourages residents to donate to the museum that runs solely on donations.
"My mantra is find the Harriet in you," Harris said. "To all of us love, community, passion, resilience, courage. Embrace those things, and we got this."

title: Easton artists fair offers handmade treasures
author: SUBMITTED
content:
Easton artists fair offers handmade treasures

 October 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SUBMITTED | Section: Life 
 
 281
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The annual Autumn Artists & Crafters Fair, offering an impressive display of original creations, will take place Saturday, Nov. 1, from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. in the community center of Easton Club East at 29600 Lyons Drive in Easton.Visitors are invited to start their holiday shopping early while exploring handmade work in a diverse range of categories — jewelry, embroidery, greeting cards, crochet clothing, sea glass art, original photography and more. This show offers something for everyone — whether it's a thoughtful gift, unusual home accent or useful kitchen accessory.
"We promote crafting and artistic expression in our community," said Kathy Chroniger, the show organizer and lifestyle director at Easton Club East. "We hope shoppers will enjoy these handmade treasures as much as our artists enjoyed making them."
New exhibitors this year include Richard Roney-Dougal, a designer goldsmith who retired to Easton two years ago after working in art and jewelry on multiple continents and many U.S. states. He has exhibited in many of America's most elite shows, including the Philadelphia Museum of Art Contemporary Craft Show and American Craft Council's prestigious American Craft Made Show in Baltimore.
On Nov. 1, Roney-Dougal will be showing a series of small repoussé plaques made with copper and gold leaf. He calls them "fragments," with the "of what" left to the imagination of viewers.
Other exhibitors include pastel artist Donna Finley, jeweler Norma Lynch, crochet designer Reba Kushner, nature photographer Cal Jackson, embroidery artist Nancy Mocarsky and others.
Easton Club East is a large subdivision located off Dutchman's Lane in Easton. It hosts the annual show in its community center next to the subdivision entrance. In addition to free admission, the show offers plenty of free parking.

title: Historic Wye Church hosts 60th annual bazaar
author: Staff Writer
content:
Historic Wye Church hosts 60th annual bazaar

 October 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 242
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Wye Parish Bazaar will mark its 60th anniversary on Saturday, Nov. 1, from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Parish Hall and on the grounds of Old Wye Church on Route 662 in Wye Mills.The Christmas Shoppe will feature decorations, many handmade by the church ladies. Winter blooming plants including amaryllis, Christmas cactus and paper whites will be available. Trinkets and Treasures will offer jewelry and other items, while Handmades will include mittens.
The Sweet and Savory Shoppe will sell homemade cakes, cookies and pies, as well as brandied cranberries, fruitcake, jams and jellies, bread-and-butter pickles, basil paste and herbed olive oil.
New this year is the Emporium, located under a tent by the church, offering bargain-priced items. The Christmas Book Cottage in the Vestry House will sell books at 80 percent off, including adult and children's titles, holiday-themed books, cookbooks, puzzles and stocking-stuffers.
The Bazaar Cafe will serve vegetable crab soup, sausage and potato soup, Italian wedding soup, country ham biscuits and Smith Island cake.
At 11 a.m., the Wye Parish town crier will announce a performance by the Queen Anne's Chorale of Christmas music in Old Wye Church. Church tours will be offered throughout the morning. The church has been restored to its original 1721 condition.
The bazaar is a fundraising activity of the Episcopal Church Women of Wye Parish. Proceeds will be donated to Haven Ministries, Compass Regional Hospice and Tides of Grace.
For more information, call the church office at 410-827-8484.
